You'll be hard pressed to find a game as detailed and nuanced as GTA V. I've played since June 2017, so I can't attest to how the game has changed over the years. However, from the time I've spent, I can say that GTA V is most definitely a worthwhile purchase whether it's on sale or not. I've spent the vast majority of time in Online, so that's what this review will be focussed on.
All in all, GTA V does have it's flaws but there are ways to minimise said flaws. Besides, in my opinion, all the things that make the game great still outweigh the problems that plague it. Pick it up on a sale if you're still unsure. If GTA Online doesn't suit you, the singleplayer is still worth getting the game for.

Based on the original Snake game, where eating fruit grows your length. This is a deceptively simply looking puzzle game on the surface but is actually extremely challenging and therefore rewarding when you succeed.

You should not be fooled by the cute-sy wute-sy looks of this game, as it is incredibly difficult and serves up a hearty challenge to anyone who dares enter the world of the Snakebirds.
With an interesting spin on the "Snake" game, you control small creatures called "snakebirds" around in a world of small islands and underwater worlds, where your job is to collect fruits, grow bigger and reach the exit without getting killed by spikes, the water, or your own dimwittedness.
As I mentioned before, it is unbelievably difficult, much more so than a game with this visual aesthetic should be allowed to have. You WILL rip your hair out and you WILL be tempted to go look up a guide, but trust me, when you finish each level on your own without any help from the outside, it is one of the most satisfying feelings you will ever have. You will pump your fist and go "F*** yeah! I am god! I am invincible!"
Just be aware that the further you get in the game, the harder it gets.

tl;dr: Don't buy this game unless it's on sale. If you do buy it here, try not to waste your CD key on the Steam version (if it's possible to activate on Origin). This game is a solid argument for why NFS Underground 2 and older NFS games would be great on Steam.
When this game came out, the reviews were mixed, but the forum members absolutely slammed this game for being of a lower caliber than EA's usual fare. It was on sale for $2 during the Winter Sale in 2014, and I purchased it to satisfy my curiosity (or possibly vindicate the game for myself), only to find that - while the game isn't awful - it's also not anything incredibly special compared to older NFS series titles.
The game, overall, is a distilled sample of the worst problems plaguing the NFS series in the Underground (2003) through Prostreet (2007) era. The AI has a severe 'rubber band' effect that makes some early races easy, but others, like the "Outrun" races, virtually impossible (and dependent on luck and blocking rather than skill). The car customization, like Prostreet, uses "Autosculpt" for everything, making it difficult to create a good-looking car unless one sticks to stock parts. The "Action Driving Engine" makes the cars eagerly jump into caricatured silver-screen maneuvers and dramatic donuts every time you take a turn a little too hard.
Visually, the game is actually impressive, especially for the time. The city map looks incredibly well made. However, between the overwrought bloom and motion blur, and the fact that the game defaulted to the lowest graphical settings through the otherwise fairly nice introduction scene (and I couldn't go into the options until the scene was over), the overall effect of the graphics is largely underwhelming. I later disabled the motion blur and realized that it was a graphical prop to hide the fact that the cars handle in an absurd manner.
The inability to access the menu up front on game start is one of many things that points to the PC game being a hasty console port. In addition, every time I quit the game, the game lost my control settings and I had to set them up again. The menus are also incredibly clunky and unresponsive. Moreover, the online mode works WORSE on Steam - EA has purposely broken intercompatibility between the Steam version and other versions. If you buy it here, activate your key on Origin.
The only positive part of the game, one I wished was present to the same extent in other NFS games, was the fairly impressive story and cutscene sequences. These were present to some extent in Underground through Carbon, but this game and The Run (2011) apparently dissuaded EA from using the same cinematics in later games until NFS 2015.
My recommendation is that you get Most Wanted (2005) instead, if you can find a copy, or else Hot Pursuit (2010). This game's reputation among the NFS community is deserved. At least, for $2, my curiosity was satisfied, and I was pretty sure I made the right call the first time around by skipping it.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: I never really was all that great at the Stealth genre, given my very guns-a-blazing kind of playstyle. Nevertheless, I usually have a lot of fun with the games. Mark of the Ninja is one of the most fun stealth games that I've played in a long time, as well as being one of the most immersive. The reason why is because of the stage design. Stages are absolute monsters that sometimes feel like a Super Metroid level than anything else. This game has a lot of exploration capabilities as well as plenty of non-linear apporaches you can take to meet objectives. There's even plenty of items to suit your playstyle. Do you wanna have fun scaring the pants off of enemies? String up bodies on grapple points. Are you a fan of the "out of sight, out of mind" mentality of guard AI? There's a suit that allows you to have full motion silence with the tradeoff of not being able to bring a sword with you. I'm more of a fan of going undetected and (preferably) not killing anyone, as I feel that stays truest to the stealth genre as a whole. However, if combat becomes a necessity, you could always hack your way out of a scenario.
While I hardly did any fighting myself, the enemies seem to have pretty good AI whenever they've caught a glance at you, often backing up for reinforcements then pushing hard. There's also enough enemy variety to keep things interesting, but most of the time the thing that makes the game interesting are the stages themselves. Usually I get a bit annoyed whenever a game doesn't have any boss fights, but I wasn't that annoyed with it in this game, as an actual boss would've felt counter-intuitive to the design of the game. As far as the challenge of this game, I could see this being pretty easy for the stealth savant, but for the average person, I think the difficulty is just about right, if a bit too easy at the beginning. I think that the game could've done with a few less checkpoints per area so that you really have to slow down and not make things a trial and error fest, but I could also see the reasoning for the checkpoints. Checkpoints can screw you over at times, although this only happened to me once (a checkpoint put me in front of an enemy, ruining my chances for a no detect for that level), so be sure to take it easy for a couple of seconds once you see the checkpoint symbol.
Apart from that, there really isn't too much more to talk about. It's a stealth game with a ton of great design sensibilities, it allows you to take things however you want to, and it's overall just a really fun game that's definitely worth your time. 10/10.
Story: Everything up to the ending: pretty not bad, but not anything terribly memorable. The ending: should not be as good as it was. No seriously, dat ending. Actually, in retrospect, one of the main purposes of the plot up until the ending seems to be setting seeds for the final areas. As for the characters, they're kind of prototypical Japanese ninja movie characters, but oh well. Dat ending. 8/10.
Graphics: I don't need to tell you that this game is absolutely phenomenal looking. You've got eyes. As for the technical aspects, the game fullscreened to my native resolution of 1080p without any hassle. Also, if you do happen to skip cutscenes, you may find that areas lag for a bit but then sort themselves out afterward. It's only a minor annoyance, since once you get past those spots, the game runs at a perfect 60FPS. 5/5.
Sound: The soundtrack is pretty dang good, and once again, the ending is the thing that really takes the cake. Most of it is pretty ambient stuff, but it does a very good job at setting the mood. Fortunately, there weren't any sound glitches I experienced. As for the voice acting, it works fine. It's good enough. No award winning material, but hey, we can't expect that from everything. Disappointingly, it doesn't seem like the Special Edition comes with the soundtrack, but oh well; that's what Youtube is for. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 10/8/5/5; cumulative score of 9.3/10. I noticed that this review ended up being a lot shorter than a lot of my others. Honestly, I think that's because I don't really have anything else to say other than, "It's good. You should go get it."

(The first thing that comes to mind about this game is its great potential. However, if you do not already have the game don't buy it. At least not yet. After the last update the shadow class has been very OP and I have lost track of the matches that turned into who can get luckiest with their sword swing timing and/or lag. The Developers do not seem to pay attention to real gameplay issues i.e. lag, class balance, cheating, team balancing for matches etc instead they focus their work on graphical updates and other things that will make the game pop visually. Overkill desperately needs more players but I don't see many new players and the ones that are new are easily convinced to quit because of the unbalanced nature of the game right now. Also Aquarius has taken the vote to kick system out of the game because they claim that it has been abused too much in the past when this was f2p, imo this has crippled the community from self policing unacceptable behavior and no substitute has been offered.
Bottom line this game should be a 20/10 right now best I can say is 4/10. If you played this game when it was in f2p its probably worth 7 USD it won't be any more frustrating than it was when players were flying around or throwing infinite grenades. If you are new save your money for something else now and come back later to see if some of these issues have been fixed. The game needs a large player base and hopefully it will earn it soon. Review thumbs down)
*****EDIT******
Shortly after writing this review I was contacted by Jesus Fabre one of the Developers for this game and we started a great relationship and began addressing many of my initial concerns. Since that time several of the issues have been addressed. Shadows are now easier to kill and they can be annoying still but no more so than any other class in the hands of a good player. As to new players after the most recent update(s) many more have joined in to play this great game. I am still concerned by some of the persistant issues such as team balance and lag but not everything can be fixed right away. Also the vote to kick system has not come back but now there are ways to have hackers banned from the dedicated servers after review of the cheating by the Devs. While still not a finished product I think that this game has taken a turn for the better over all. The customer service and interactions I have had with Jesus Fabre and others on the Discord channel have been fantiastic and they are willing to listen to carefully given constructive feedback even of a negitive type. All in all the customer service was the reason I am changing this review. Come join the great community in this game and I think as I said above this game will be 20 out of 10 as it should be one day soon!
****** EDIT TWO********
I have put almost 700 hours into this game at the time of writing this edit (not counting the hours I spent playing Ballistic when it was f2p. Simply put after all that time I find myself very frustrated every single time I play this game anymore bar none. Let me give some specifics. 1) LAG: The servers for this game have horrible issues. I do not know why but it is almost impossible to get a match that does not have server lag issues. One time I was testing in a private server with one player and was able to shoot through a wall and kill my friend and both of us saw the shot as through the wall. Even with players that have good computers and good internet lag can show up randomly. This game was the childhood of most 20-something year-olds who played video games. And, really, what's not to love? Traveler's Tales had a well-built and finely constructed vision of a galaxy far, far away entirely made of LEGO bricks (well, not
). What's there to say that hasn't already been said?
Now that we're all adults, it turns out, there's quite a bit more to discuss about this.
The episodes focusing on the Prequel Trilogy have had slight adjustments to account for the improvements made in Lego Star Wars II: The Original Trilogy. Minikits are now playable in some sections, and powerups drop, enabling increased stud pickup radius, invicibility, and increased stud value. I personally prefer the Prequel Trilogy sections of the game, but the entire experience is phenomenal in a familiar way.
The game is definitely rough, visually, but seeing famous Star Wars characters and locations in LEGO form is still a treat. Music from the series is used to great effect, and the sound effects are spot-on. Canned character animations can get old, but you'll hardly care since you're controlling DARTH MAUL IN LEGO FORM. Most relevant sections from the movies have been included in some form, and the silent, physical humor is still hilarious.
Having to complete each level in one sitting is a little bit of a pain, but the levels are short enough that this usually isn't an issue. In Free Play, unlimited access to characters removes this problem as you create shortcuts or decimate enemies in ways the level never intended.
Red Bricks, which grant bonuses at the cost of studs, are gradually unlocked. Some are amusing, some are useful (magnetically drawing in studs is a godsend), and some break the game (the higher levels of the stud combo multipliers, invicibility, perfect deflection), but all are welcome.
The character roster is huge, and while a few too many spots are devoted to joke characters or clones (no pun intended), it's still a welcome sight to see the number of available characters increase. The manner in which certain areas are locked off to certain characters is never frustrating due to how they steadily allow you to unlock the characters you need to revisit previous levels and get everything that can be found.
The episodes are all consistently good, though some of the vehicle sections and camera angles don't quite hold up when it comes to quality.
Gold Bricks can be used to unlcok several bonus levels, and while some are entertaining, most you'll only complete to get the Gold Brick needed to get closer to 100% and then never look back. Lego city and its counterpart are particularly frustrating.
The only other unwelcome aspect is the Super Story: while fun in theory (speedrunning through each movie using only the characters accesible when you first played the level), the fact that its needed to acquire 100% is a bit of a tough pill to swallow considering that Super Story adds nothing new. I have ~99% completion, but the thought of replaying levels I've already finished without being able to swap characters turned me off from that final completion point.
Overall, though, this game is as fantastic as you remember. If you haven't played it, there's a huge amount of content here, most of it excellent. If you have, give it another go. You won't regret it.

Batman: Arkham Asylum might very well be the first great Batman game. Although there's been plenty of Batman games in the past, I think this one perfectly captures the essence of the Dark Knight. Set in Gotham's famous asylum, you'll find yourself fighting against Batman's greatest rival: the Joker himself, as he attempts to pull out one of his greatest plans.
The fact that this takes place in the asylum, means that the Joker will not be the only member of Batman's rogues gallery you'll be encountering. Harley Quinn, Killer Croc, Poison Ivy, to name a few. Not to mention that the asylum is filled not only with Joker's henchment, but you'll also run into a few of the crazier inmates as well. Finally, the place itself really makes you feel that you're in Arkham, and it adds a sense of isolation.
As far as gameplay goes, you're the Dark Knight. You'll spend a lot of time either beating up several thugs at once, or scaring the heck out of them as you take them out one by one in the predator rooms without being noticed. All of this can be accomplished with the help of Batman's arsenal of gadgets, from the classic Batarangs, to explosive gel. Then there's also Detective Mode, which allows you to scout the area to detect enemies and possible ways to take them down.
It's a really good game; I recommend it.

I refrained from playing DE:MD until September 2017 due to the critical reception by the community and critics.  I recently completed my first mostly-stealthy and fully pacifist playthrough over the course of five or so engaging nights of play and I wish I'd gotten to it sooner.
This review concerns only the base experience, as I haven't gotten into any of the DLCs.  It also does not comment on the microtransaction model, which I understand has caused some uproar.
It may be the separation of years between playing HR and MD, but I think MD is equal to its predecessor in terms of story engagement.  I did all but one of the side quests and each one of them was well-written and impactful, with the possible exception of the one concerning the underground news ring.  Each step in the story felt like a big deal - I didn't feel like the game was wasting my time, and the world is absolutely chock full of interesting background information if you're the literary type.  I didn't use the Universe app, and I understand there's more there.
Pro/Con lists seem to be popular so here's mine.  The pros:
-Meaningful progression - Praxis points make you way better at whatever it is you're trying to do.
-Rewarding exploration - especially in the hub city, which is just full of neat stuff.
-Good level design that supports the stealthy approach without making it too easy to bypass everything.
-Interesting side quests.
-Fantastic world-building and environmental storytelling.  Seriously, hats off to the devs for all the attention to detail in environmental design.
-Interesting "conversation boss-battles" in the form of debates with significant characters.  CASIE might make these too easy, but they were fun anyway.
The cons:
-Actually atrocious voice acting for people who aren't named Adam Jensen.
-Groan-inducing bad-guy tropes such as (MINOR SPOILER ALERT) "I could shoot you, but instead will poison you and dump you somewhere under the assumption that you are dead."
-Story threads that end abruptly or were not wrapped up properly.
-Fairly lengthy load times when moving between the northern and southern regions of Prague.  Probably better on an SSD.
-A couple of bugs, notably one with a telescope that traps you there until you reload your game.
All in all, I really enjoyed it and would recommend it as a worthy successor to HR.
For anyone worried about the ability to buy Praxis kits and how it might affect the accrual of kits without microtransactions, I finished with more Praxis points than I knew what to do with.  Six more, in fact.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is dense with an atmosphere that really captures the essence of brooding Gotham City and the Batman franchise. Though linear most of the time, the game still offers you to roam Arkham island and discover its many secrets, never letting you feel bored. In its first hour the game introduces you to its mechanics, so bear with the hand-holding and the game will eventually let you loose on your own.
Its finest moments are definitely when you successully bring down a small army of thugs without even one of them catching a glimpse of you. Even so, the moments where you find yourself in an all out brawl is wonderfully exectued, letting you feel in control of Batman and his moves. Button-mashing will lead you nowhere but timing and inventiveness will.
At times the game may feel a little too linear but it always delivers a thrilling experience, whether you are a die-hard Batman fan or not. Recommended!

After many games before it where you merely play 'as' Batman, Batman: Arkham Asylum allows you to 'be' Batman. From being able to take on multiple foes to actually wielding the great detective's Holmes like observation of a crime scene, this game really makes you feel like you're the Dark Knight.
The controls are fairly simple to get a grip on. The main challenges are can you take on so many enemies and are you really paying attention? The last part can be somewhat frustration as the Arkham Institute is so detailed you might find yourself, as I did, overlooking that one simple air vent because there is so much stuff!
The Riddler's, collect as you go, side quests are actually quite enjoyable. Some of them are clever enough to actually make you smile once you figure it out.
I really only have two criticisms of the game:
1) At times some of the Boss Battles don't give you even an inkling of what you're suppose to do to break them down until after they've beaten you.
2) Some of the Riddler's quests require equipment that you don't get until much later in the game to access. This at time  led me to waste time futily trying to get to something just because I thought I wasn't being artful in my employment of the abilities I did have. Also once you do get that equipment you have to do a lot of back tracking.
All in all, a very fun game where you actually get to be a top hero in the DC Universe.

is a story driven narrative exploration game that strolls around quite loaded terms like choice, goals, drives, relationships, priorities and compromise. The concept that the game revolves around - influencing social dynamics to observe the result of interrelated choices and their consequences - is an interesting and hard to accomplish one. Sadly its presentation within the game both in definition and execution, is definitely flawed.
Here, we take a quick glance at the Kaplans - a family of three going through a though time. Dan is an author who's stressed out to complete the novel that he's been working on, Linda has some worries about her marriage and family ties - also struggles on going back to being a painter. Tommy, their only son is having some adaptation and learning difficulties who needs his parents' attention and support full time. At the beginning of one summer, the Kaplans decide to pass their vacation in a rental villa by the seaside to have some quality time and possibly work through their problems, a villa that YOU reside in... In this detached little game, you are a ghostly entity - who's presence within the house will never be explained properly. You have the ability to stalk, observe and influence the Kaplans, thus deciding the story of this specific family in the end.
The game has two distinct modes: Stealth or Story. In Stealth Mode, you have to avoid being seen by the Kaplans if you'd like to explore everything. If you are seen, they get nervous and focus on their annoyance rather than their actual problems. You are capable of travelling through possessing light sources within the house while you hide from their perception. This mode quickly gets annoying and breaks the immersion of the storyline that you are trying to reveal quite fast. In Story Mode, you are free to roam as you wish without worrying for them to see you, but even excluding that limitation, everything becomes boring and repetitive. You are stuck within the same house with the same tense mood and you basically memorize the possible locations a note may spawn after the second chapter. They never change or surprise you. It is not possible to miss something. You roam around, read notes, watch some memories, whisper what you decided to Dan while he is sleeping and you are done. Another chapter conquered. You only decide whose need is a priority and see the accumulated conclusions in the end.
In each episode - there are 9 in total - you are presented with a couple of conflicting desires of family members. Everyone got different priorities and you must choose one specific desire to influence and accomplish, and maybe another one to half way accomplish through "compromising" which leaves you with one desire completely ignored. This is where things get a bit ridiculous. These 9 encounters oddly end up defining the whole being and interdynamics of a whole family! The definition of compromise in the dictionary is "a settlement of differences by mutual concessions; an agreement reached by adjustment of conflicting or opposing claims, principles, etc., by reciprocal modification of demands". Here, there is no middle ground between parties, no given opportunity to work on different needs, there is basically no settlement. Even real life doesn't work like this! We surely either act selfish or make sacrifices on things little or grand, but a human being is capable of undertaking more than one deed, feeling or accomplishment in a timely manner.
A human being comes with dimensions - which is another huge flaw in this game. The Kaplans are obscenely selfish - without much appreciation for sacrifices or understanding of shortcoming. Their personal desires never seem to even coincide with the desires of others. It is not possible to sympathize with any one of them. Heck, they even do not talk within the same house hold! You are a ghost, stuck within their household for his/her all being and never see them talk more than a couple of automated remarks and some memories. They seem to communicate through written notes scattered around the house. I mean, what kind of family does that?
I surely do understand the limitation of the developer team, thus I won't mumble much about the scenes, the environment and chapters being dull, stolid or repetitive; but I cannot accept the term "compromise" being misused for "forced priority and selfish desire". No remotely eligible father of a small boy would be so consumed with his ongoing artistic pursuit that he'd end up not putting together a toy car that would take 3 hours to assemble for 3 months! This really is ridiculous! So, I personally think this game comes with a possibly good concept executed without much sentimental or even practical depth. Don't get me wrong, I'm all for narrative exploration. I actually love games like

they are capable of presenting the echo of an emotion, an idea or at least a state of being. In its current state and price,
surely doesn't deliver. Wait for a huge sale to satisfy your curiosity if you wish.

[---]This game caught me by suprise. When first hearing about Mark of the Ninja and looking at it , I was reminded of some old school ninja games.The game plays like a 2d platforming assissination/stealh game with puzzle naturally thrown  in.You play the role of a ninja who is tasked with taking care of some major tasks the head of your clan chose. The game touts native controllers and mouse & keyboard controls and strangely enough, the game play wonderfully on both styles.No button lag at all,you can even play using both if you want.
The game can be anywhere from 10hrs + long depending on if you seek to engage every enemy, and look for each item.
[---]Combat in this game is very fluid and responsive.You have a choice of going stealth,offense, or both.Going the stealth route you can sneak through vents,crawl walls/ceilings,grapple across trees,poles,freak out guards,distract enemies,and other struckers or use helpful items. The offensive route  you get to assassin people in various ways.There are many kill animations ,which change depend on your killing options you picked.Weapon wise you use a katana for killing and some traps but thats all.This does not make the game limited in any way and actually makes the game more entertaining.
[---]Mobs for the most part can find you via hearing or sight (sorta like Metal Gear Solid). So you need to watch how you approach an area.There are items through the maps that allows you to do things like: hit a gong to draw attenton,destroy lights to get more cover,using items to aide you,etc.The assissination takes place when you are withing range to be able to initiate the animation. This animation is presented in a "quick time" style so if you mess up you will not get a silent kill which the death cries could alert nearby hostiles.
[---]There are no boss fights, but there are some mini boss type targets you have to deal with or avoid.The mobs themselves vary in behavior and ways you need to take  them down.
[---]Skills are pretty straight forward in the game.Many designed for hand to hand combat to take down enemies or stun them so you can finish them off.Others are for doing platforming maneuvers like dangling down from a gabble location. In order to unlock these skills and itms you have to earn it. This is done by playing the game, stuff like silent killing,no killing,hiding bodies,etc.Just generally playing the game will determine how many points you earn for spending on skills/items.
[---]Graphically this game is fantanstic.The background,forgrounds,levels,effects,etc all ar esplendily done and do not destract you while playing at all. There are some areas you might just want to stop moving and take a moment to look.Truely a visual love fest that might remind some people of great looking tv animated cartoons like Avatar. Thumbs up to Klei with deciding on this visual style for Mark of the Ninja,it works for the games style.
The game is great,don't let the fact its an action/puzzle game fool you it is a gem that you will love to replay.Completionists out there will love it and those looking for enjoy a assassination game might find their bloodlusts quinched with this. Playing this game its sure makes being a ninja tops.
Get the game, on sale,full price,in a bundle,w/e get the game its worth playing and the puzzle are not brain busters so you should be fine if puzzles are not really your thing. I spent 17 hours playing it trying to do parts with 100% accuracy and it never got dull.

From now on, every time you see "Klei entertainment" seal on a game, the game is going to be good. I don't know if any of you guys ever played Splinter Cell mobile games on a cell phone, but imagine a 2D scroller with stealth mechanics + some ninja mythology- it's a blast. Klei really outdid themselves with this beautiful indie hit.
Story of the game is interesting with a few twists which add to the game, it not a fall-off-your-chair story but it's a gripping one. You play a nameless ninja who wants to uncover the man who attacked his master and ninja brotherhood in their own home. Pure gem is that it's the modern times so you have lasers, gun turrets, guards with guns and other equipment, and you have the traditional ninja weapons: sword, grapple chain, bamboo darts, and many other.
The gameplay is a pure 10. You have multiple ways to enter a building, multiple ways to approach the enemies (kill them or avoid them), but the major thing here is that you can choose your way of engaging the enemy: you can simply kill and hide the bodies, you can mindscrew the enemy by throwing the body in front of him, really many possibilities. In every mission you have 3 optional tasks which represent the stealth approach, predator approach and aforementioned mindscrew approach plus you have 3 collectible haiku scrolls and sometimes a puzzle room is required to be beaten in order to get the haiku scroll, and you have artifacts which only boosts your score.
Graphics are well done in my opinion: 2D sprites, smooth animation of executions and movement, "Shank" style drawn cutscenes and actual gameplay graphics, in one word, really beautiful, in spite of stealth genre and many dark places involved, you're going to see the beauty of every hand drawn rock on the playfield.
The only bad side I felt was the controls. In my case, I only use mouse when I need to control the camera (3D games!), why would I need a mouse in a side scroller? Maybe it's just me, I don't know, but I configured the controls to be more bearable in my case, so I play the game, ah I have to throw the dart there, let me enter focus, grab my mouse, aim and throw, put my hand back on the keyboard, it's a little time consuming, but I completely understand that there was nothing they could do.
Well, all in all, the game is awesome, the only thing I gave minus is something that is my preference, so it might not affect your play style. Game is definetly a must buy, really good and revolutionary gameplay, nice 5-6 hours long story, with new game+ so you can get all the abilities and scrolls, buy it, you won't regret it.

Above all else, The Novelist succeeds at its stated purpose: to examine the continuous struggle of balancing conflicting needs. Through the lives and thoughts of the three Kaplans, this constant give and take becomes apparent, as does the internal back and forth between their own personal needs. The player is then put into the position of deciding both whose desire will win out and also what individual needs are going to have to go unfulfilled that week. Then they must stand back helplessly while their choices play themselves out. Due to the stress involved, it's likely that more game time will be spent deliberating than exploring or interacting with the Kaplans, which is a good thing as the actual act of playing gets rather repetitive and dull. There is only a single cabin with a handful of rooms to search and an explicitly limited number of things to uncover per chapter. The experience of playing as a whole quickly changes from pleasantly defined to restrictive and joyless.
In addition to guiding the Kaplans, the player is also given the opportunity to learn more about the previous inhabitants of the haunted cabin. Those vignettes, however, end up falling equally flat as they seem to avoid any real answers to the mysterious nature of the player's ghostly presence. But those shortcomings are easy to forgive, and forget, due to the slow-forming, but genuine emotional bond with the Kaplans and how their tangled lives turn out. That is the focus after all, and unless you were taking notes, that's likely all you'll remember about this flawed but brilliant game.

ASM is a game made in RPGmaker, which already earns it negative points because RPGmaker is an awful engine, that is all about your choices, expect not really. You're allowed to pick your character from a handful of characters in a room, and then you can pick your LI from a handful of characters in another room. Yes, you can choose to be a gay man, or a lesbian, because this game wants you to think its ~progressive~ when the entire game is written to be pretenious. The game has you going from town to town and sometimes experiencing flashbacks, trying to earn money and fix the "main problem" in each town so you can get to your LI and try to stop her wedding. Of course, you also get dialogue choices that allow you to say "Nah, I'm over her", but they don't matter and I'll tell you why soon. The game has four "towns" for you to deal with, with the first town having the most content. It's an awful place that lets you see first hand how choices don't matter at all. You did Option A? Ending A happens. Did Option B? Ending A still happens, but with a teensy-tiny variation. The only time where the game isn't sniffing its own ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is in the second town when it decides to correctly say Republicans and Democrats are both terrible people who are in corporate pockets.
There are also flashbacks, as mentioned, about your college life and the life you had with your LI. These flashbacks, for me, only confirmed that my old college friend and my LI were both huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who I would refuse to deal with if I had the choice, which I don't, because this game provides as much "freedom of choice" as a Fable game, but at least Fable can provide variations in the endings for each choice. Anyway, when you meet your LI, it turns out they didn't want you at the wedding, but your friend, who is marrying LI, invited you. The same friend that your LI told you to screw over and the same friend that your LI called a creepy little stalker. Turns out your friend managed to get a publishing deal even after you screwed him (guess your LI only wants to go with whomever is gonna get the deal), and the LI's father decides to confront you on your choices in the game, even through it doesn't matter, because all you can say is "I regret it" and "I don't regret it". You are also asked for the reason you're around, and I reconfirmed that I was around only to say goodbye to my LI. You're forced to go to Vegas and gamble because you probably only got $1000 to your name and you need $15000 if you want to buy a tuxedo and get the best "ending" for you and your friend (otherwise he dies or you lose your book deal).
Wedding happens, I let the girl go so she can get married, and yet despite me saying repeatedly that I did not want to get back with my LI, I turn out to become a bum because she was my TRUE LUV and without her, despite the fact that I could easily get a job and find someone else, I'm just a useless sack of♥♥♥♥♥♥
So I replayed it, this time going for the girl, slightly changing my choices, mostly taking the bad ones, dealing with that AWFUL boxing minigame in the third town, telling the parent I regret all my choices and I want the girl back, and then I win her back. Woo. Now my friend is the bum because she was his TRUE LUV even though he had his own book deal he could finish, and he was doing pretty god damn fine before he got with the girl.
This game doesn't respect your choices. It doesn't even care about them. It's a game about you being in true love with a huge ♥♥♥♥♥ (or huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if its a guy), your friend being a prick, and everyone you know being useless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, except for the cowboy guy in Town 3, who was the only person in the game worthy of any respect. I was tempted to play a 3rd time and make all the worst choices, because I suspect so long as you say "I regret", you want the LI back, you make sure your book deal is safe and that your "friend" lives, you can get the "best end", which is you getting back with an awful person.
I regret the money I paid for for this game on GoG and regret the dollar I gave to Humble Bundle, since it included this piece of crap. 3/10, and that's only because I'm feeling generous. I wish Steam would increase the character count for reviews so I can really get into how awful this game is. Now to remove this piece of crap from my computer again.

(Thematic spoilers, especially concerning the ending.)
By the end of this game, I felt bitter.
A few hours later, remorseful.
"Do the ends justify the means?" is a question that keeps playing in my head. For me, the theme of this game is passion and lost dreams; how blinding passion can be and what extremes we'd go to to recapture those dreams. Actions, of seemingly little consequence within the game, remained in my mind long after finishing. I'd done desperate things to reach an ultimately bitter, and cold conclusion. Can my actions be blamed on circumstance, or is it how I reacted to circumstance that levels the blame back at me? I'd only questioned my actions once the ends didn't match my expectations. Could I be this cold in real life?
Always Sometimes Monsters is a dissection of storytelling and progression in video games. It plays like an interactive novel/combat-free RPG, with the main resource being money. You require it to buy food, but also to progress and reach new towns. Each one is filled with 'story' events, though there are also plenty of others that play into the morality aspect of the game. These events build your character's personal arc, and ultimately your expectations for the ending.
Though mini-games for gaining money can become tedious, the story shines and will keep you pushing on; it may not be the most original, but it's well told, and has a brilliantly cruel, nihilistic ending that will probably hurt your soul. Also, the soundtrack is a retro, pulsing, electronic fuzz of awesome.
The only thing that disappointed me was the engine choice. RPG Maker is really starting to show its cracks, and I would have loved to experience this in something less... vanilla. It's a game well deserving of that.

Having played Dwarf Fortress a long time ago, I was interested in this title, as it clearly wear it's influence on it's sleeve. This game is literally trying to recreated DF but with actual graphics and UI (and vaguely replaces dwarves by gnomes, but that really easy to miss). Sounds great on paper! ...however, it fails in execution and content.
- While it's trying to emulate DF, it keeps very little of the charm of the original, and only covers about 2% of it's content. The only feature that seems to be unique to Gnomoria is the tinkering mechanic, which I haven't been able to really use as it takes literally hours to produce anything.
- The isometric view, while prettier than looking into DF's matrix, makes it pretty damn hard to see and target constructions correctly. Half the time, you realize you just ordered to build a floating staircase. A lot of the UI could also be improved, it's serviceable but not very good.
- The game might be promising if it was still being updated, but the developer disappeared about 2 years ago. Currently, it's bare-bones, and there's a serious lack of diversity in the content.
- Balance also seems pretty poor. It could just be bad luck, but a single goblin naked wielding a door (that he broke down), killed 2 of my fully armored and armed soldiers that had been training for 1 year straight.
- Bugs, lots of them. "Oh what's this odd thing on the ground? I never built this" No clue as the game crashes everytime I click on it...
I know the learning curve of Dwarf Fortress is basically a cliff, that has been oiled up... and is on fire, during an earthquake... BUT trust me, it's way more worth it than this poor imitation, and it's also free (with optional donations). The DF wiki has lots of info for beginners (meanwhile the official Gnomoria wiki has it's domain expired...).
If nothing else, encourage devs that care about their games instead of devs that runs away with the sale money without saying a word.

In it's current state the game is playable and fairly entertaining.  However, there is still a lot of work to do before calling this rock crawling "simulator' a finished product.
The first true annoyance is the vehicle audio.  It's awful, simply awful.  It's super loud, sounds like the recording mic was directly in the engine bay of a semi-truck.  It sounds nothing like what you'd expect from whatever vehicle you're using in game.
The very next, second, annoyance you'll find is with the camera.  I swear the camera in "orbit" mode is literally trying to get you killed.  It's actually worse than the obit cam from BeamNG, which is saying a lot.
Physics model seems ok.  However, the suspension set up, amount of grip, and power are completely out of wack.  The suspension is way too stiff.  Vehicles bounce all over the place because of this.  Tire grip is greatly exaggerated, so much so that you can actually flip the vehicle back on it's wheels in some roll-over situations.  Lastly, now I don't think I've ever said this before, but the power these vehicles put to the wheels is just way too much.  290hp, sure, but the vehicles all feel like they're pushing well over 1000 ft lbs of tourqe,  Wheelies are cool on a strip of pavement, but not when you're precariously positioned on a rock.
Game crashes occasionally.
The game has tons of potential, though, don't get me wrong.  It's fun, too.  But I just can't recommend the game in it's current state for $11 cdn.

Do not be fooled by Snakebird's adorable, mobile-esque presentation. This is an original and extremely challenging puzzle game. Every level is carefully designed to make you THINK you know the solution, only for it to blow up in your face, and make you update your understanding of the limits of the puzzles to derive the in-retrospect obvious and brilliant answer to that level's question. If you thought Dark Souls, DotA2 or whatever was hard, try Snakebird and eat your words.

A wonderful game!
I saw this a few days ago on Youtube, and had bought it before the video was even 5 minutes in. The presentation oozes charm, and the core mechanic of combining the classic Snake with a variation on traditional Klotski puzzles intrigued me no end.
I was not disappinted! This may very well be the most enjoyable puzzle game I've ever played. You're eased in gently for the first few levels, but the difficulty increases very quickly. Mercifully the game does let up now and then, giving you a couple of easier levels after introducing a new mechanic, such as moveable blocks and portals. Also, while the stages are numbered sequentially, you are not forced to play them as such, so if one particular puzzle is giving you a headache you can move on and come back to it at another time.
The later levels pose a formidable challenge, and a few took me close to an hour each to figure out. It never feels cheap however - while difficult, the puzzles are fair and after each mistake, I usually felt one step closer to finding the solution. With puzzles such as the aformentioned Klotski, I find my interest wanes and I eventually turn to a guide, but Snakebird engaged me in such a way that I was compelled to persevere, and the feeling of satisifaction at finally cracking some of the trickier stages was palpable.
Snakebird is a prime example of how to do Indie games well. By focussing on one relatively simple core mechanic, Noumenon have been able to craft a finely honed gameplay experience, with far more complexity than you might expect. The delightful presentation and adorable characters only serve to enhance the experience even further.
Highly recommended!

This game is unlike all the others in the Total War series, so calling it the best would be like saying an apple is better than an orange. But by the same coin, I don't think there is another game that I can say is better than it.
What the original MTW does really well is the campaign. I don't care much for the battles, as later Total War games have greatly improved on them (particularly the first Rome), so I personally never do battles manually in MTW. But the beauty of the game is that it is a lot of fun without doing the battles at all. I am sure that there are many who love the battles, which is fine, but this review is from the perspective of a pure campaigner.
One reason you can skip battles is that the autocomplete is very fair - if you have the superior army, you will win, and casualties will be reasonable. If you have similar armies, it is a dice toss. This is different from later Total War games, where even a battle between 1000 men against 100 men needs to be resolved manually, because higher difficulty settings will attribute unreasonable losses against the human player, even though the battle would be trivial and boring to do manually.
Because of the fair autocomplete, you do not need to do dozens of repetive unbalanced battles, which seem to bog down each successive Total War Game more than the last. MTW is much more fast-paced, and if you do want to manually complete battles, you can focus just on the interesting ones. If you don't want to autocomplete battles, then the game becomes one of pure campaign strategy, which is fast-paced due to the lack of interruptions from manual battles.
Adding to the fast pace of the game is the fact that you are moving armies from province to province in the same way that you would move around pieces in checkers. It is not as realistic as in later Total War Games, but it makes things a lot faster - no slow 20-turn marches across the Russian Steppes to take a minor settlement, as in newer TW games. And you are less likely to return to a save file if you get defeated, because you don't need to go through the same tedium again.
Another aspect that makes the game fast is that you can move an army from a province with a port to any province in the world that you have an uncontested line of naval control too. This greatly speeds up the endgame, and gives you the most tangible reward for naval power in any TW game. There are some kinks in the mechanic (I'll talk about them later), but it is a fun and interesting mechanic if nothing else.
Ok, so what I have gotten to so far is that the game is designed to be fast-paced, and playable just on the campaign map. The map itself has a very clean and attractive aesthetic for what it is, and I never bore of staring at it while I play. The music is excellent. There is a well-developed building tree, and a very good economic structure. It is balanced enough so that a good player playing at the appropriate difficulty setting for his skill will be neither too broke nor unreasonably wealthy.
There is a large variety of units that are available, though you will probably focus on recruiting a particular type of mid-range infantry if you are concentrating on auto-battles. This is a possible weakness of the game, because you are essentially building basic armies in the same way you do in Risk, since the auto-complete give little consideration for spear-beats-horse type combinations. But this doesn't matter much if you are not doing manual battles, and it is fun experimenting with the building trees of different factions to determine the most cost-effective and technically feasible main battle infantry to try to build recruiting buildings for.
What is perhaps best about the game is that the weighting of the difficulty settings is done very well. An amatuer player on medium can probably complete the campaign in just a bit more time than an experienced player can complete expert difficulty. In many other games, increasing difficulty means slapping more health bars onto the AI, or removing your resources, or do any one of many things that just makes the game more annoying. I think (correct me if I'm wrong) that MTW simply gives more resources to the enemies, so that they can expand more aggressively. They feel more and more human, so it is more satisfying to overcome them.
There are some things about the game that will really put some people off at first. In particular, it is notorious for having a number of mechanisms that can put your whole empire into rebellion with little notice, especially near the end of the game. You will have everything in hand, then you will realize that half your empire wants to rebel (you hold shift for a summary of public order, and half the map has gone from green to red!). You try to settle things down, but a number of provinces rebel. But many of the rebels are not ordinary rebels - they are factions you have defeated reemerging, usually with 4 massive armies that are going to need a concerted effort to defeat. In an instant, all is lost, and it is frustrating because it seems random.
It isn't random though. An expert player knows all the tricks. The main culprit is usually your king's influence. The closer the line of communication between your king and a province, the higher the public order. Influence can take a shortcut across oceans if you have a pure line of naval communication. So if you control all the seas and your king is at a province with a port, there will be a big public order boost almost everywhere. But if that influence is broken for a second, everything can fall apart. If your king dies, the heir will pop up in your most important city, which may no longer be your capital. So if you capture Constantinople and it has no port, then your king dies, your heir will probably appear there, and you will have a public order crisis until you can get him somewhere better. Another possibility is that you start a war with a small nation that has a navy. Even if your navy is vastly superior, if there are any contested waters breaking your line of communication, expect rebellions. So if Spain has one ship in the straights of Gibralter and you have a dozen when war breaks out, you are still going to have rebellions at least until the next turn when you sink that ship. And since they might be building another ship that will appear next turn, or maybe the ship they have is fast and they intend to move it to the next province before you can hit it, it might not be so simple to solve this problem. You can also have the same naval problems if a storm sinks one of your ships, so it's always good to have at least 2 in every sea. A final problem too is that some factions have a tendency to split in two when an heir rebels, even if your empire is healthy, so you may want to keep your heirs in the same army as your king, just to be safe.
The above issues are frustrating, but there are always ways around them. Some of them are a little cheap (I shamelessly go back to a saved game when I lose too many naval battles, because they are more luck-based, and I don't want it to affect the main game), but most of them are just being careful (keep your king in a good position, don't overextend your navy, aggresively take down nations with strong navies, etc), and there is a certain degree of pride when you can overcome all these challenges.
At the end of the day, this is an excellent game. It's challenging and fair, and it's one that I never tire of. I start playing this game again at least once per year, every year, and I am glad that it is finally here on Steam!

This game is one of my favourite games, having played it as a kid for hundreds of hours, so i might not be completely unbiased, but man, this game. It takes you through all the original 6 star wars movies in a very unique lego-y way, with each episode/film split into six parts; every part is one level, taking approximately 20+ mins to complete. The main storyline takes about 20 hours or so to complete, and is fairly simple (apart from some details you might miss about what you have to do). But the game does not just hand everything to you. To get really OP, you need to replay levels and discover every little detail and corner you could not explore with the story mode team, basically just completionism. This is completely optional though, so don't freak out.
There's just so much to this game. From the amazing music with the original soundtracks, to the small little details like lando kissing leia's hand when pressing the action button, to the cheesy lego humor, to the big variety of characters to unlock, to the overall star wars-feeling overall; this game is simply a joy to play. (I found airship levels to be particularly enjoyable, with an amazing feeling to them) Admitted, combat is kind of lame, and the graphics aren't fantastic due to the fact that it is a 10 years old lego game, but the game is still enjoyable. The last complaint I have about it is that money is annoying to pick up sometimes. That's it. For a ten year old game, that's not that bad i would say, so go buy it.
Tl;dr version:
+game has loads of unlockables and secrets
+great music
+airship levels are great
+option to play hard or even extremely hard levels, but easily playable normal levels
+a sh** ton of small details that make the game so much better
+easy playability; even a brick could handle this game
-Graphics are not always the best
-combat is fairly easy
-money is annoying to collect
Straight 8.5/10

This is actually one of the worst games I have ever played. The map and graphics are the only things the game has going for it. The rest is either mediocre or just plain bad. It baffles me how people say that this is better than GTA IV or even San Andreas.
Let's start off with the story. The story sucks. It can be boiled down to "Rob bank, get money", since that's really the only goal that these "characters" have. You'd think with 3 playable characters that there would be the most amount of missions in the franchise? Nope. There are only 69 main missions and 4 of them are optional, which is less than GTA 4 and San Andreas might I add, and only about half of them are good. The heists are really the only highlight I have for this game. They're great, but aren't good enough to excuse the other bad apples that this game has.
The characters are awful. AWFUL. Franklin's likeable but as deep as a puddle, Michael is just the generic rich, drunken father with family issues and Trevor is just a psychopath. Not a badass, an unlikeable psychopath. I get that he's supposed to be like that but I'm controlling this guy for a good portion of the game. The side characters are boring, too. Lamar's just a generic gangbanger, Ron is just... there and Wade's only purpose is for comic relief. Compare these characters to Niko,  Sweet, Big Smoke, or even Roman if you can put the memes aside.
The weapon arsenal is okay. There are simply too many guns and they all feel the same as eachother other than minor stat differences. You will be hard-pressed to find the difference between the Assault Rifle and Carbine Rifle other than looks. They aren't punchy, either. They feel like plastic guns because of the lack of recoil/accuracy hinderance after shooting for a long time, and the gunshots are extremely quiet. Agian, compare that to GTA IV when the gunshots nearly drown out the noise of everything else around you and how the weapons actually got less accurate the longer you shot them for?
This game has a lot of content but said side content is just not fun. Want to do a 30 MINUTE triathlon? Want to play Tennis, a "mini-game"
that is only fun the first time you do it? Want to play Golf which, like Tennis, gets boring after the first time you play it? Want to collect 50 letter scraps which makes you go on an hour long wild goose chase around the map? Want to collect 50 spaceship parts that, like the letter scraps, sends you on a wild goose chase around the map? Want to do the Strangers and Freaks missions, that are okay but extremely forgettable? Go right ahead, this game is so
in-depth!
The Online Mode is a P2W-fest. Worse than some MMORPGs I have played. Want to grind for hours, days even WEEKS to afford something, or do you want to spend $20 to get said something immediately? It's a grind-fest, but the bad kind. The kind that gets repetitive not even an hour in. Rockstar have clearly put all their heart and money
into making as many fans happy
from this Online Mode.

Early-ACCESS Review
WOW...wow what a GEM of a FPS Game.
This is a pure and simple FPS Game that goes back to it's roots of the FPS Genre.
Casule players can easly pick up and play without having a learning curve to adjust too
The pace of the game is fast, not as fast as with the Quake's and Unreal games, but diffidently alot faster than the C.O.D and Battlefields series.
This is a very good Arcade Lone-Wolf Close Quarter Combat in your face style_ground pounder action game. PVP skill vs PVP skill
If your a tactical fps player-it is not for you. (Insurgency, AA: proving grounds, ARMA)
If your a realistic gameplay fps player-it is not for you. (BF: series, C.O.D series)
If your a teamwork fps player- it is optional for you
If your a arena / arcader fps player- then this game is for you
Pro: Early-ACCESS
1. Very lightweight game around 2 GB so far.
2. There is a FREE Dedicated Server to host your matches online or maybe host a LAN Party
3. Hardware requirements are low enough for aging systems to play on.
4. Spawn area protection from spawn campers, this is a nice touch which gives the teams a small barrier for them to regroup and plan out the next move.
5. The Color pallet for this game is awesome, they are bright, shinny, and they just pop on the screen
6. The graphics, textures, model scaling are done well. No need to have high graphics to have fun.
7. The maps are mirror design which is fine, but what is important is that they are not a cheap blocky level design
8. The game is no pay-to-win
9. Hit register is very good on servers that are close to your area.
Cons: Early-ACCESS
1. Sound in general needs a little work, example: the players footsteps could be soften when walking. As it stands, it sounds like another player is in the area.
2. A time limit to be in safe area, "afk" example: a player could kill only once and then hide in the safe area until the timer runs out. Automatic win
3. No in-game voting or kicking undesirable players out of the room: example to have_
A. Players who starts a server / or create a match should be able to have the option to kick players out of the room instantly.
B. Players who join a game that didn't start nor create a match have the option of vote kicking and the player that started the server or created the match is immune to their kick.
4. No in-game auto balancing, "Match Team KDR" to balance the matches
5. No in-game control menu while in active game match
6. No in-game reporting of hackers
7. No support of submitting evidence of hackers, glitchers or exploiters.
The game still has alot of work to be done and I hope they stick with it.

This review is inspired by the Steam Awards - nomination for "the CHOICES MATTER" award.
It is a sad day in gaming when you wake up and hear the news that a company who has the brilliant imagination and fortitude to create a masterpiece such as Torchlight II ... is shut down?  A company that has former Blizzard North co-founders who were closely tied to the Diablo franchise ... is shut down?  and for the reason to focus on games as an online service?
Choices do matter.   And one day, Perfect World (the Chinese company who bought a majority stake into Runic in 2010 and this past month shut down Runic games) is likely to wake up and realize they made a huge mistake.
This game is marvel to behold, and the fact that a company who puts out a product this polished and so well embraced can be dismantled overnight... is mind blowing.
Runic, I hope there can be a rebound someday, any company will benefit from the talent and imagination of your employees.
If you haven't played this game, you need to. Support creativity and the companies trying to put out good releases.  I fear the changing landscape of gaming could ruin the production of some good franchises... just look what's happening with the Mass Effect saga.
Choices do matter.

Life is hard. Working is hard. Having a family is hard.
The Novelist tells the story of The Kaplan family during their summer break. To which through playing the game you can heavily influence the events of that summer.

You are some sort of ghost that when not inside a light bulb you are probably slightly more opaque or corporeal than what the traditional notion of a ghost is. You can either play the game having the Kaplans react and cause you to fail upon discovery or just throw it into story mode and become invisible and focus on the objectives. The ladder is what I did.
The game revolves Dan, his wife Linda and their son Tommy. You explore the home WASD'ing around and teleporting between lights. You must find notes, pictures, documents and items laying about the house; additionally being supernatural (I guess) you can delve into the memories of the characters as well and see what they are thinking at any given moment. Each chapter you'll find clues of what each characters desires are and how they want to go about moving forward. You will choose which (by this I mean whose) outcome you want each chapter and possibly working out a compromise with one other character. My only complaint is that this really, more or less, is just a walking simulator; It might have been served better as a text adventure to be honest.
Yeah, its one of those sticky indie art games that you've already made a decision if you like or not. However, this is one of the better ones yet its still not stellar. Its interesting.

In The Novelist, you play a meddling ghost that seemingly cares about the family renting your summer home, but actually doesn't give a darn what they want, leaving you to invade their minds and choose their life paths for them.
Skulking around from room to room, you discover clues to what Dan (a struggling author), Linda (an once and possibly future painter), and Tommy (lonely child) want to do that week. You then can choose whose desire is most important and go that route. Afterward, still images show the fallout of your 'wisdom.'
At nighttime, you can seek clues granting additional insight to the house and your role, and you can creepily hover over the sleeping family and listen to their dream thoughts.
This game offers two modes, but I don't know what the developer was thinking. This isn't Splinter Cell -- skip the stealth mode, and focus on the story. After all, what's the fun in ruining-- I mean, guiding lives if your ghostly powers can be stripped from you by being spotted?
-----
Time to put on my serious pants. I think the premise of The Novelist is brilliant, and there are some powerful moments, but the choices often ring artificial. There were a handful of times that all three members could have compromised, but -- as per the game's rules -- only two of three could be chosen. Also, there were moments where it seemed like there would be positive gains for one or more family members, only for negative ramifications to be thrown in your face because the game's writer didn't think things through.
Finally, the endings -- especially Tommy's -- seemed at odds with his own personality, let alone some of the story paths.
And that whole stealth mode nonsense...
Basically, The Novelist is interesting and worth a playthrough, but I can't really call it good. Nonetheless, I'd at least recommend it if you can nab it for a deep discount. On September 8, 2015, it was $2.24 and I think adventure and narrative fans would absolutely get their money's worth.

I have not tried it but that sounded really annoying so I stayed in purely story mode when you're totally invisible to the humans around.
This game can be haunting, especially if you're an adult with kids. Playing at work during lunch I needed a couple of minutes to get my thought process out of the Kaplan's life back into my own.
Pricing might be a bit high, but this is steam.. just wait..

A man takes his wife & young son to a secluded vacation home so that he can focus on writing his next great novel; little do they know that the house is also home to an unknown supernatural force that can worm its way into the father's mind. No, it's not The Shining, it's The Novelist. In it you play a spirit (or something?? it's not actually specified) haunting a house on a cliff. Your goal is to influence the choices of the father/husband character, Dan, by learning as much as you can about him & his family through written & drawn clues scattered around the house as well as by entering each character's memories. Each chapter presents a situation to which there are three solutions: one that most benefits the dad, one the mom, & one the kid. You can also make a secondary "compromise" choice that will at least partially satisfy one of the other characters if not totally please them.
If "Stealth" mode is enabled you have the potential of being spotted by the family while you gather clues during the day, which causes you to lose certain opportunities. You can become invisible & move from one place to the next without being seen by possessing the home's light fixtures, but you can't gather clues when you're in a lamp, so you also have the ability to make a light flicker to distract the family away from where you want to go. There is an alternate "Story" mode where you are invisible no matter where you are. In both modes there are some situations where characters will close doors on you (usually if they're mad about being neglected); you can't open or pass through the doors but the family usually opens them again soon enough. There's a subplot that involves gathering clues about the house's past, but that is not mutable based on the player's choices so it feels more like filler material.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward, if a little tedious at times. Think "Gone Home" in a scaled-down form. The graphics are quite lovely, especially the vistas visible through the windows. Several people have singled out the voice acting as exceptional but I didn't find anything remarkable about it. The plot is... okay. I didn't care much for any of the characters, but I still wanted to make good choices for them. There are multiple happy endings & sad endings possible, although not very many, & none too exciting (certainly nothing close to The Shining in that respect!).
Overall though this was a nice game to spend a bit of time on; it's pretty relaxing & there's definitely not anything high stress about it. I enjoyed playing through making choices "organically" the first time & then running through it quicker in subsequent replays to get different outcomes. I would definitely recommend doing "Stealth" mode for your first playthrough to get the most out of the experience; enable "Story" for replays so you can move from choice to choice & clue to clue much quicker & don't have to deal with spending time on repeated material. It goes quickly enough when you do that.
Even though it would seem there's a lot of responsibility on your shoulders, spending time in this game's world really is soothing, & having different options & routes to take is fun. I like that it's an indie game too. I am happy with my purchase -- but, after all, I bought it on sale, which I would recommend.

Batman: Arkham Asylum
Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first game in the Arkham franchise that released in march of 2010 and was the reason for the cancellation of The Dark Knight video game and in place this was developed by Rocksteady studios and published by Warner Bros this is the best superhero game ever created.
Story
The Dark Knight captures The Clown Prince of Crime but too easily, The Joker has set a trap and Batman falls right into it Joker and Harley Quinn take over the mad house and plan a much more destructive and chaotic masterplan, to amass an army, as the inmates run free upon the island you must face 7 of Batman's greatest villains Scarecrow, Killler Croc, Poison Ivy, Bane, Zzasz, Harley Quinn and The Joker.
Gameplay
The combat is the core of the game and the main reason why people play the Arkham series it is a punch and counter combat system, this is the first of it's kind and many games have attempted to copy it's design like The Amazing Spiderman and more sucessfully Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor it is the combat system that I would choose as the best over all other action games. The other side of Gameplay is the predator system which brings stealh to the Arkham franchise which really makes you feel like Batman striking above and from the shadows. One other feature that is never featured in the other Arkham games are the Scarecrow platformer parts where you must hide from a huge Scarecrow and reach a bat signal light to escape and resist the fear from Scarecrow.
Graphics
Considering the year this was released Batman: Arkham Asylum is a very nice looking game that contrasts the darkness and grittiness of Batman's world while making it look as bright as possible in a Batman game without removing the darkness that Batman strikes from.
Final Verdict
As this is my favourite game series and always will be I am slightly biased to this game however I will give it a fair review The story is good, the Combat is perfect, the Graphics are great considering the year it was developed in.
(and because this is my favourite series I am biased to it over other titles)

Personally, one of the best games I've played. Where do I begin?
The artwork is stellar. Rendered in beautiful cartoony graphics reminiscent of cartoons like Samurai Jack. The animations beautifully rendered. Every bit of movement a love letter to that little kid inside of us that always wanted to become a bad♥♥♥♥♥ninja.
The soundtrack is like riding out a storm whilst perfectly content and in zen with yourself. It's exhilarating without being exhausting.

From the way sound travels, to the dynamic lighting & many more factors that come into play later in the game. I really wanted to like Gnomoria, but the learning curve is huge, and it just doesn't look like there is going to be any payoff.
Basically once you manage to wrap your head around how to make the gnomes do the stuff you want done, and you can look at the map and say "we need to do that," and then you send them out to make it? That will be pretty cool.
But "pretty cool" is like all it will ever be. I don't see any particular promise that the game will ever be FUN.
Meanwhile, I don't understand what like eighty percent of this stuff does. It's like I have to jump through eighty hoops to make a little minor thing like a sawmill and then I jump up and yell "YATTA!" because I can make planks.
Which means now I have to set up a brand new little production line of cutting down trees and bringing them to a stockpile close to the sawmill where they can be picked up and brought to the sawmill and made into planks which now must be moved to a NEW stockpile which... should... be somewhere close to whatever I am doing with the planks. What was I doing with the planks again?
Oh yeah, nothing. I have no idea what I need planks to do. I have some vague notion that I can do something with them, but I don't really know what and I'm not even sure I need to do it in the first place. But, hey, there are planks. There's got to be a reason, right? So I should have some. Just in case.
I appreciate the idea here, which is kind of like someone said "what would happen if we combined Minecraft with Dwarf Fortress and the Sims?" but it looks to me like the answer is "we would do it wrong and it would suck, so we would lose interest and abandon the project."
Gnomoria basically fails to be a good building and crafting game because it doesn't give you any real agency and control. Then it fails to be a good tower defense game because getting to the tower defense parts requires ploughing through the tedious and difficult crafting game. And then it isn't a good sandbox game because it makes you build very specific things in and around the sandbox before you get to play in it.
So essentially, it's three tolerable alpha releases - there are way too many bugs, although nothing I ran into was really game-breaking - wrapped up into a package where none of them make the others any better and have arguably made them worse.
It's a decent case study of where good intentions lead, though. It's clear that throughout this project, the developer WANTED it to be a good game, and tried really hard to make it one. It isn't really even his fault that it's not. But it's, you know. Not.

Ive clocked in about 74 hours and over 1000 battles in Brawlhalla. I think im ready to review
As a free to play Smash clone, i was a bit skeptical at first. Im used to traditional fighting games like Street Fighter, Killer Instinct, Mortal Kombat, and Skullgirls. I played a bit of the smash series, but it didnt really hold.
Then Brawlhalla came and changed my opinion
Lets get the cons out of the way
This game is built around competitive play. Its clearly evident with the lack of a 1v1 casual mode. If i wanna just kick some casual butt without risking ELO, i gotta play in experimental, yet there are some things in experimental i may not like!
The lack of variety. Lets be real, how every character has the same unarmed play and every weapon plays the same with light attacks sucks. the ONLY variety is within 6 moves out of a 33 move pool. that kinda sucks. In games like smash bros, where anime sword fighters infest the game, only a few play alike. and even with those, they still have their differences.
The community. Most people around my elo, which i assume is popular due to the fact it is mid tier elo, is pretty toxic. If i use the same move twice in a match, im suddenly a no skill spammer. remember, i have 33 moves to work with, and i can only use about 11 of those at any given moment.
Now the pros:
Games are quick. You can easily get in 10 games in about 45 minutes. Thats great game design. If im having a bad game, i can just shake it off and go into the next one in like 3 minutes. Games built around competiton, especially MOBAs, dont really appreciate this.
Clans. Its really fun to create a clan and have a bunch of friends in thie clan. There is so much potential with these, be it finding a doubles partner for ranked, grinding out gold to get that hero you want, or just having a good time playing with 8 Vraxx's in a timed deathmatch with 300% dmg on. Its a great way to meet people to play with.
Character diversity. I know i mentioned the lack of variating attacks, but the character diversity is insane. You have an inventor from the 16th century, a cowgirl from the Wild West, a 1950's mobster who uses demons, LITERAL MAD MAX, and a half bear person. Thats some amazing charcter design, Blue Mammoth
Skin Matchups. This one is just personal for me, but some of the matchups with certain skins can get pretty funny. You havent lived until youve done an 8 player deathmatch with Alien Elvis, Jason Vorhees, Wonder Woman, Obama, the Bride from Kill Bill, Sun Wukong, Krampus, and Shark Tale. Brilliant
Microtransactions. Mictrotransactions are usually a turn off. For example, i dropped 2 bucks on a game i already spent 10 for just to find a character I like. In Brawlhalla, they are purely cosmetic, even occasionally donating the funds from a certian weapon. Blue Mammoth also keeps a steady supply of cosmetics rolling in for us to use, and even gives us cosmetics to reward high ranking or mastery with a certain character or weapon
All in all, Brawlhalla isnt the perfect fighting game, but its a good one
