Medieval Total War: The original and best.
Why?
It's simple. Before a time when the series became so bloated and feature saturated, we had a game where every fundamental Total War mechanic was present and made sense. Battle map speed, AI and morale. Campaign map immersion, music, elegance and clarity.
You can assign titles to generals and develop them as characters. You can manage an entire empire by dragging and dropping chess-like strategy pieces with maximum overview. Want to invade a region? Just pick up your armies and put them on the enemy's territory. And with an extremely satisfying "BOOM" sound effect too!
The AI works better in this game due to not having to manage pathfinding on a vast map like in Rome Total War and onward. If the enemy has troops in a province or attacks you, those are the armies you have to fight - every time. No micro stacks wandering about aimlessly. MTW allows massive battles to take place thanks to its very structure.
Battle mode looks outdated and clunky, but has several things going for it that other Total War titles often lack. Proper collision between troops means that a heavy and formidable unit can push back and scatter an inferior peasant militia. Arrows have a proper physics system that's based on elevation, line of sight and unit depth - archers should be placed in 2-3 ranks and given a clear line of sight to their target.
This is on top of the atmosphere that gives the game an ominous medieval feel that fits perfectly, and that perhaps only Total War: Attila comes close to out of all the games in the franchise.
There's even mods!
10/10 a true classic.

Warning, this game does not work with ultrawide resolutions!
This game is forced to fullscreen and can't be set to windowed mode. The game's 'ingame resolution' scales so badly, that on ultrawide screens half the game will be cut off to the top and bottom of the screen.

Also the controls require you to drag the spider into one direction to shoot it to another -- on ultrawide resolutions it is impossible to shoot the spider in certain directions because the screen blocks your ability to drag the spider properly.
So, if you have an ultrawide monitor, you will not be able to play this game -- so do not buy it.

You'll meet a spider sitting on a slingshot, which would like to eat some flies. This is likely
, our protagonist. You'll have to shoot him towards flies using the slingshot. On that way, the spider will stick to availible slingshots and require you to change the direction. It seems like the controls consist of mouse movement and the left mouse button only. There are no instructions availible and the player is required to figure this out all alone. You can guess that this game does not support controllers, because the gameplay requires you to drag and drop
, which is too hard to be done using a controller. Still not impossible, but it would loose a lot of precision.
Keyboard controls would be an option but they are missing.
Riaaf The Spider is a game designed for mobile devices with touchscreens. The menu buttons are just a few, but round and big. Animations and transitions are smooth and look familiar.
The store description includes very obvious grammar mistakes, and these even got translated into other languages...let's get back to the game. After playing just two levels, you will already have 56 unlocked achievements. Every time a level is completed, a bunch of achievements appears. Funnily the 28 achievements coming from the first level were all named as 'A', the ones from the second level are titled as 'B' and so on. After 15 levels, there are enough achievements unlocked for each letter of the alphabet, making a total of nearly 400 achievements.
In case you did not care about achievements before, you'll care now, as this heavily affects the gameplay for the next 30-60 seconds until all notifications finished showing up (there is no way to speed this up). They will be in your view, so that you cannot even see some flies before all achievements finished showing up. The images for the achievements have different colors, so you'll at least get the option to showcase them on our profile in many different colors.
For $0.99 it looks like a bargain, but you will need to consider the fact that the invested effort in this game seems to be very low. According to the credits screen, the programmer was also the designer. While the game art seems to be unique, the game was actually just thrown together by taking the game "Fergus The Fly" and replacing its name and (only) some graphics in the user interface. The original game name can still be found when browsing the game's install directory. It is also an excellent demonstration of how Steam's achievements can be used as a handicap in games.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a superior game but does that make Mankind Divided bad? Not by any means.
I really don't understand the hate this game got, it's a truly stunning experience full of everything you loved from Human Revolution. It has the same freedom of choice combat where you can go in guns blazing, go in quiet or just not engage in combat at all. The new augmentations are truly great and cater to any play style and unlike the HR you won't be left scratching your head because you chose one playstyle and a certain boss requires another. (I manage to make it from start to finish without using lethal force including bosses)
Graphically it's pretty damn good, an improvement over HR for sure and the soundtrack is on par if not better. The world is pretty cool in design, it's not as big as the world from HR but there's still plenty to explore whether on mission or not. The characters aren't as forgettable as others have made out, I actually quite enjoyed interacting with most of them and the dialogue options and player choice seems a lot better.
The story isn't as good as HR but that doesn't mean the story in MD is bad, it just lacks a certain magic that HR managed to capture.
Performance issues seem non-existant. Playing with everything maxed out on DX12 and I haven't encountered a single frame drop, bug or stutter and for a title like this that's pretty damn amazing.
As for the apparent abrupt ending that caused people to slam the game I honestly have no idea what they are talking about. The ending was just fine to me and it left things open for a sequel which I really do hope comes around at some point.
Microtransactions are here and I have a firm standpoint that I do not believe that sort of things should ever be in a single player game so that is a HUGE negative for me BUT they don't shove these down your throat, there is a shop menu in the pause menu that you can go to and buy things but if you never look in that menu you wouldn't even know these microtransactions were here. The game doesn't constantly tell you or tell you at all for that matter "Hey buy this stuff"
It's a great experience and on this playthrough I just finished I got 22 hours out of it which is me doing every side mission and main mission, it might end up shorter if you go in guns blazing though (I took the stealth approach)

You play as the Marked One, a ninja with a tattoo that is supposed to make him stronger, faster, and all that good stuff... but you don't know really notice it until the tattoo is completed and you get this crazy OP ability that is basically a teleport.
Stealth is the emphasis here and it does it well. Things get pretty tense as you try to slip around unnoticed or stay just out of view of approaching guards. Some enemies, you can get away with grabbing them from a hiding spot or dropping down from the ceiling, but as the game progresses, you encounter a couple new types of guards that it's in your best interest to stay out of their way completely.
As the story progresses, you'll unlock new abilities, side weapons, and distraction tools that can help you out depending on your style of play. To use those upgrades though, you'll need to spend points on them that you acquire from finding scrolls, I believe. There are some rad upgrades too, like throwing flesh eating bugs at an enemy, or the ability to terrorize other guards by hanging the corpse of one of your victims up for them to see. Good times.
All in all, it is one of the best stealth games I've played, and it was definitely the most fun. After finishing the game, I went back and ran through a couple levels I really enjoyed. It appears there's several different costumes with their own advantages/disadvantages as well, which helps the replayability factor.

A 2D stealth game which encourages solving a given situation in different ways. The game does not favor one playstyle over the other (lethal or nonlethal) except for scoring purposes or optional secondary objectives that help unlock more toys that modify the multiple solution experience. And you'll want to unlock them--you can get a cardboard box, hide in it, and shiv anybody who passes by. This game is worth playing through at least twice to see how creatively you can get through a given mission. I swear some of the ways you can dispatch guards almost makes you feel more like Rube Goldberg than a ninja.
However, I would advise against getting the "Special Edition" DLC before completing the game as the unlockables from that pack make things way too easy--you can one-shot elite guards with one dose of fungal spores and an additonal two from the resulting infected body, scaring any sap unfortunate enough to see the death you just dealt while their only solution to cope with such horrors is to recklessly shoot any friend who wants to help. You know what? Let's count this as a recommendation for the DLC too.

The gameplay goes something like this: sneak around in the shadows, if a guard walks by without niticing you, you get points. If you do something to distract the guard, points. Kill the guard from behind, points. Hide the guard's corpse, points. Kill a guard indirectly, more points. Use the guard's corpse to scare another guard, points. If a guard spots you or finds a dead body, you lose points. Besides that, you have to work your way through "puzzles" to get to your destination. Overall, the gameplay is solid. In every level the game introduces new gameplay elements to try to prevent things from becoming too repetitive.
Some mercenaries kill a lot of your ninja clan members. That's not as much of a story as an excuse to go and kill a bunch of people. The comments from the creators throughout the game make it very clear that they built the game for the gameplay and didn't actually have a story to go with it. Not only does the main character not have a background story, but he doesn't even have a name (His name is not Mark). This causes the game to feel somewhat dry and a chore at times. Instead of going from point A to point B to advance the story/character's development, you do it to flip a switch/pull a lever/destroy something...
Very cartoony, the short cutscenes look very poorly drawn. The backgrounds are interesting looking, but not something that will hold your attention for more than a few seconds. Again, this game is about the gameplay.

Minimal ambient music, somewhat Asian sounding. The ending theme is the only real music that the game has.
I recommend this game for the stealth gameplay.

-The addition of after grenade kill points

All in all, the game is more enjoyable and i plan on playing it often from now on.

This game combines both the LEGO Star Wars prequels and original trilogy in one epic Star Wars game. Although it's 2 games in 1, the prequels content is about half the size of the original trilogy. Those 2 LEGO games were the first to use a license, and The Complete Saga is still one of the best LEGO videogames. The gameplay is similar to the other titles, with a mix of platforming, puzzle solving and some combat. It's a LEGO videogame at it's core. What distinguishes it from the others is the awesome use of the Star Wars license. The atmosphere of the movies is always present, with their soundtrack always playing in the background. Compared to the others (before the open-world ones), there's also way more content here. Like the others, there's story and free play mode. Here, you also have challenge mode, in which you have to collect 10 additional minikits under 20 minutes, and super story, which is essentially a speedrun through the 6 chapters of an episode. They add a lot more playtime, but they feel a bit rushed in, and that's why they were removed later. I enjoyed the super stories though. Lastly, there are plenty of bonus stages, and most of them are fun. To 100% the game, it'll take you somewhere between 40-60 hours. The game shows some age, but if you love Star Wars and like the LEGO videogames, i recommend it. It's one of the best.

I decided to replay this game and make a review out of it. You know, for science and stuff. As usual, I will talk about the bad stuff first:
First and foremost; Uplay. I shouldn't have to say anything else about that, but some people might not know much about it, so let's go into it. Uplay is a Steam-wannabe created by Ubisoft. It's laggy. It's crap. And if it wasn't bad enough, Ubisoft forces everyone to use it on their games. The thing is, you start the game and while other Steam games would likely start right away, with Ubisoft games you have to wait until this thing starts as well, and then the game starts. With singleplayer games ain't that bad, but if you have it on a new one, DEAR BUDDHA HAVE MERCY ON YOUR PATIENCE, as it will constantly ask for updates and crap like that. Uplay is even worse than Origin, and that's a big f#cking statement. And somehow, it still exists. Thankfully there are ways to disable it, and I seriously recommend you do it.
The other problem the game has is this lenght. For 15€ you would expect at least 6-8 hours of content, however on my new playthrough I barely got 4 out of it, clearing everything at 100%. The main story itself barely has arround 5 missions, the rest are side-quests to unlock upgrades to your weapons; stuff you will surely want to get your cyber-arms on. What's sad about this is that this game is quite original and fun, and I feel like Ubisoft got lazy when they could've turned this little standalone mod into a game of it's own. It also doesn't help that, while the island is decently sized, the character runs and swims so fast that even vehicles are pointless when traveling, and you even have Fast-travel.
That being said, is it good? Yeah. It's good. Have you seen any generic action movie from the 70's to the 90's? This game is pretty much a parody of all of them combined, throwing some game references along the way. The plot is so cheesy and idiotic that feels completely right.
The gameplay is, obviously, quite similar to Far Cry 3. The only important stuff that has changed are things like upgrading your weapons to insane levels, and the main character throwing one liners non-stop.
There's not much variety on enemies, and the NPC's indeed seem to be f#cking r#tarded, but they offer a decent challenge (until you upgrade your weapons, a fully upgraded shotgun pretty much kills anything on your screen in one or two shots).
The soundtrack is what stands out the most in the game, always delivering this special 80's style. The item descriptions and graphics also show what dumb humans from the past though earth would look in the future, which was actually quite hilarious.
There are also collectibles on the game, which you will need to get some of the collectibles, however you can buy maps that will show to you their exact location. With the speed you have, you can get them all in an hour.
Granted, it's a fun experience. But a short one. And after clearing it 100%, I can't bring myself to recommend it at full price AT ALL. You should totally experience this, however wait for a sale. 7,50€ is good, but 5€ or bellow is perfect for this game. I just hope a sequel actually comes out someday, and it's longer and more 80's.
TL;DR: The game's cool, but not worth the 15€ pricetag. Wait at least for a 50% sale.

Pretty good game.  I enjoyed it a lot.
I especially liked how clear the stealth elements were.  You always know exactly how much noise you'll make and who will hear it, and you also always have a strong idea of how well and where the enemy can see.  Good times.
The stages are long, however, and if you intend to kill all the dudes/do all the things expect to take about 30-50 minutes per level.  I had difficulty playing more than one stage at a time and I very often got kind of bored about halfway into a stage.  As fun as the game is, it gets very monotonous: there really isn't a whole lot of variety going on here.
The music and sounds are pretty solid but the voice acting is lacking (much like it was in Shank, whatcha gon' do).  The story, while basic, is good and I liked it.
There's an upgrade system but there might as well not be for how much it comes into play.  You'll grab the super useful things, like the ability to kill dudes from behind doors or in cover, almost right away and then just not really want anything else.  Nothing is bad, necessarily, but a lot of the abilities just aren't really useful.  Additionally, by completing x number of different objective types (terror, stealth, kill things and maybe a few others) you unlock different suits.  The different suits change the basic gameplay somewhat, such as allowing you to carry two attack items instead of an attack and distraction item.  The different skillsets are neat but I never really found myself wanting to use anything aside from the basic set because it's so balanced.
The first playthrough isn't so difficult but when you do make mistakes you usually won't have to repeat large chunks of the stage.
I got about 8-10 hours of play out of this, which was about double the time I spent on Shank, so that's good.  Additionally I wasn't so big on gathering all the hidden stuff or acing all of the stages, and I also didn't do NG+, so there's a lot of potential for this game to eat up a lot of time (assuming that's what you're into).
Overall I considered this a very positive and enlightening experience.  If nothing else, it had me thinking about platformers and general stealth elements differently than I had in the past, and that's great (from a design perspective, at least).  It's a good game and it should definitely be in your library.

Arkham Asylum is, for the most part, great.
Starting from the beginning, it has a simple plot in the typical Batman settings. There's not much unique to that. If you like Batman, you're likely to enjoy the game in that regard, if you don't like Batman, well, it's not bad either way. For one reason or another you're trappen in the Arkham Asylum, the one place in Gotham City where every crazy demented criminal goes to waste. The Joker has taken control over the place, and as Mario jumps till he reaches Bowser, you fight thugs and sneak around to get to the Joker.
The good part about the Arkham settings is that it makes the perfect excuse to introduce a lot of known Batman's villains, because, well, they were all jailed in there. This makes the game a whole lot less monotone that it coudl've been if the whole plot was centered around one villain, as it's the case with Batman movies and comic issues.
Regarding the gameplay, let me start with saying it is wonderful. There's mostly two sides to it, The sneaky parts and the action parts, those often come in tandem, sometimes it's your choice which one will reflect a specific section of the game, and sometimes you're forced to walk either path. This actually helps the flow of the whole storytelling a lot, since the tension of the Sneaky Sections contrast nicely with the, well, action of the Action Parts.
The sneakaround parts come with a ton of gadgets that characterize the Batman, most of them giving you that extra mobility to navigate a given level in a varied array of directions. These sections of the game truly give you freedom to approach them however you want with easy to understand mechanics and a ton of possibilities. It reminded me of one of my favourite games ever in that regard, Metal Gear Solid 3.
The Action bits, though, are completely different from MGS3. It's a whole lot more like an spectacle fighter than anything else I can think of. In all honesty, I dont have enough experience with that kind of games to be able to gauge it against a titan of the genre. That said, the combat flows wonderfully, you get a great sense of motion and control when you start getting a big combo against several enemies.
The melee combat is pretty simple, you mash the hit button till a visual indicator tells you it's time to counter, and you do that aiming to the direction of the upcoming treat and hitting the counter button at the right time.
That said, there's a bunch of things you can do mid combat depending of the gadgets you have acquired and the types of enemies you're facing.
But more than the blunt melee combat itself, what I enjoyed the most where the handful of levels that allowed me to set up the arena before engaging into inevitable combat. You can plant explosives, bait enemies, make surprise aerial kicks from afar, knock 'em down silently, distract them with noises, hanging them upside down from a gargoyle in the roof, and a bunch of other stuff as well.
There are some levels that allow you to bring down every single enemy without them detecting you, Dark Knight Style. The enemy AI is decent enough, and its quite satisfying hearing them talk to each other and ramble in fear because The Bat Is Here.
The Content - Ive beaten the game in about 15 hrs. playing on normal difficulty.
There's enough extra content to pump it maybe to 20 hrs if you're a completionist.
I bought the game on a steam sale, paying 4.99 USD for it and it was totally worth it.
Of all the side missions and extra content I'd say the most noteworthy for me where the Riddler's Challenge. I spent a few extra minutes on each level that had one trying to figure them out, and you get to feel pretty clever when you find one of the hardest ones out.
Regarding the game visuals, It has a pretty visceral, almost gross look to it, and I think that fits pretty well with the grittiness of Gotham, and even more with Arkham. Not a fan of the Joker's design on this one, but that's about it.
Going back to the gameplay part a little, the boss fights strike a weird place in the whole concept. It's almost as if they were done by a different team. They're usually good, don't get me wrong, but they lack the freedom and thinkering every other level has that makes you feel like you're the Bat.
Each boss is usually beaten one way and one way only, It's pretty intensive and some of the encounters are pretty hard until you figure out how the enemy actually works and what you're supposed to be doing. You also get to see the Genius Detective at work in these ones, but it usually happens in a cinematic and it's usually the part where the boss gets beaten.
There's a lot of extra lore to learn and listen from the secrets you find in each level, though I wish they'd just done whats has been proven to work in games like Bioshock and let you listen to those "interview tapes" while you keep playing - having to stop in a menu to listen to them sometimes really screws the pacing over and while you *can* play the tape and exit the menu to listen to it while you play, any enemy dialog that accidentally comes to play will stop the tape, making you sometimes have to replay the tape completely just to hear the 2 last words you missed. Pretty annoying.
TL;DR? - It's a good game, if it's in a sale, definetly worth it. If it's not on sale and you can afford it, make sure it's your type of game, then sure. It has my recommendation.

Imagine if you took "Super Meat Boy" and "Dishonored": Mutated them together into one game and gave it the art style of the TV show "Teenage mutant Ninja Turtles". If you like anything that I just listed, you will like this game. The 14 hours I spent playing the game were extremely enjoyable. The game has about 12 level which are huge and allow for multiple paths and solutions to problems (Just like any good stealth game should be). The stealth mechanics are rock solid and very satisfying. If the 14 hours of gameplay I encountered maybe 3 bugs where the player character couldn't decide what it was I was trying to do. Probably the worst part about the game is the story. It's not bad, it's just it could have been executed a lot better. The opening and middle are very weak, but the final level and conclusion is by far the best bit (it actually made me stop and think for a second). I warn you about this because halfway through the game I was thinking to myself:
"Yeah this game is fun, but I hardly know these characters and I hardly care about them"
At that point the game did feel like a bit of a drag, like it was just padding itself out. While the end of the game is fantastic in terms of story, just know that you have to fight your way to get there. I think the game could have either gone for a simpler story with a shorter run time, of could have gone with a more comprehensive one. The end result is a half-way house which isn't very satisfying, mostly due to the lack of characterisation and direction. If you are curious, I could very easily liken the story to that of Spec Ops the Line. There are a lot of similarities between the two from a story perspective, it's just that Spec Ops told its story a lot better than this one did.

It's not really a game, but not an interactive movie either. On one hand, it does have a bit of gameplay. On the other, it doesn't really have cut scenes and whatnot. What it really feels like is reading a book where you can influence a story to some degree (doesn't look like too much, though).

Subjective: ★★★★★
Objective: ★★★★★ — Graphics: ★★★ — Content: ★★★ — Handling: ★★★

The Novelist is a story-based game that sees the player take on the role of a ghostly character, assisting the Kaplans, Dan, his wife and his son, in their decisions over the course of a summer break. Gameplay-wise this means finding letters and memories to find out what each family member wants and then finding a specific item in order to fulfil that want. However, you can only please one person each time, compromising with one other which results in there always being a third that doesn’t get their wish. Unfortunately, in terms of gameplay, this becomes very repetitive, quickly turning into a hidden object style game. Where the game hooks you though is from the responses of your actions from each character. Each action’s consequence can be felt emotionally from them and a connection between them and the player is formed. As this is seemingly a rather rare occurrence within the medium, this was a delightful thing to happen. Hopefully future videogames can draw on this and help to create more connections between their players and the characters in their game.
The small scale of the story and the before-mentioned repetitive gameplay will put many off, but for those that can look past those points then there is something worth experiencing here.

In The Novelist, the player has control over some spirit or being which resides in the house this family came to spend the summer in, and you're supposed to influence their lives for the better by making decisions for them. The family consists of a father who is a novelist and came to this remote location to get past his writer's block and reconnect with his family, a mother who loves painting but hasn't been able to focus on it after becoming a mother, and finally a son who gets bullied at school and doesn't have very many friends. The father has become quite neglectful of his family because he is way behind schedule on finishing his novel, and through the course of this game you see him struggling to manage the progress of and ultimately finish his novel as well as keep his family happy.
The gameplay consists of stealthing around the house by possessing light sources in order to find and read diary entries or letters written by or to the family members, as well as read their thoughts and explore their memories. After having found enough of these for a character, you can see what they want and choose that as the resolution for this chapter, disappointing the other two characters. But if you managed to also find out a desire of at least one other character and haven't spooked them by getting detected by them, you can choose their desire as a compromise for the chapter, making two characters happy. To finish a chapter, you whisper your decisions to the father in his sleep, which makes him execute the choices you made. Well, in most cases at least.
There were plenty of things which bothered me about this game, such as having choices I made conflict with others when they really didn't have to, characters just not doing what I chose for them to do or all characters' desires to be small and trivial enough to all do in one night but still being forced to only make up to two happen, and so on. Yet in the end every character's outcome was just as I had hoped, even though it felt pretty awful being forced to disappoint at least one character over and over again, and because of conflicts and such I didn't always get the outcome for a chapter that I had hoped for. I can't tell how much my choices even mattered in the end, if at all, but I like to think they did because the outcome I got in the end was what I was trying to achieve. I can definitely see one of the final choices allowing for drastically different outcomes, but since you can't start from specific chapters I won't play through it all again to see if it actually does, especially since I'm very content with how it turned out.
This game isn't the best when it comes to its narrative, and especially not when it comes to its gameplay, which gets very repetitive. But when it comes to teaching players a valuable life lesson and delivering an important message, this game is probably one of the best out there. For example, having to decide on whether the father should continue writing his novel which is already way behind schedule, write an ad for his wife's art exhibition so she has a bigger chance to break through and achieve her dream or spend a good few hours every day tutoring his son who is behind on a school subject really captures the fact that life is all about making sacrifices and that no one will consistently get what they want. Another messages that this game delivers really well is that you should never take your family for granted, and  that having a nice and functional family requires effort from everyone involved. Other than that it also emphasizes how stressful it is to try and contribute something that lasts to the world and make your existence matter, and that you should never give up on your dreams.
It was quite a reality check for me, making me think about some things I usually don't or haven't before, as well as an inspiring experience overall.

I admit defeat. Don't get me wrong, the game is exceptionally well done. It looks beautiful and the game mechanics are extremely smart and intuitive.
But it is unbelievably hard. I have played Braid, The Talos Principle or The Swapper before and never really got stuck. Those games teach you basic principles and then present you with bigger problems where you can use your new knowledge. Not so Snakebird. Every level is a random puzzle without any connection to the one before. There is no communication happening between the developers and the player. Unfortunately, when this silent communication happens it is when I love puzzle games the most.
I mean, anyone can come up with exceptionally hard puzzles. I could present you with a random chess board and ask you to show me the least number of moves in order to get to that same chess board configuration. There, you have a hard puzzle game. Unfortunately, the only way to solve it is to know the movement rules of each figure and then think it backwards, keeping infinitely complex decision trees in mind.
A Rubik's Cube is the same and I think this is the best analogy. This game feels (and looks) very much like a Rubik's Cube.
I made it to level 15 without cheating. After that, I had to look up the solutions for most maps on Youtube. At level 25 I gave up.
The thing is, I don't even know how to improve the game. It is a quite perfect game. It just doesn't invoke any fun for me.

The Snakebirds are hungry and want their fruit! By combining everybody’s favourite Nokia game and one of the weirdest looking necks on an animal, Noumenon Games released an unexpectedly thoughtful 2D puzzler that’s receiving criminally low attention. While not everyone might want to trade their scales for feathers, it’s worth finding out why this indie title is even greater than the old cell phone sensation.
On a first glance Snakebird is deceptively simple, with soft bright colours and shapes giving the game its child-like innocence. Your perception is corrected quickly however, with puzzle designs that are extraordinarily tight and meticulous, and often only have one way to be solved. The mechanics are simple; there’s no real tutorial because the pick-up and play style and the game’s method of subtle teaching doesn’t need it. The objective in each stage is to collect every piece of fruit before successfully reaching the goal portal. Just as in the classic game of Snake each fruit you eat adds an extra unit of length, a mechanic that makes some levels an experiment in discovering which fruit should be eaten first. Players can move in a forward direction with only immediate turns available to them, turning what seems to be a stage that can be easily traversed into an abstract thought exercise. You’ll quickly run into a problem where you can’t back out, it starts to sink in that there’s a lot more to this title. Levels are precisely crafted, there’s no wasted space and everything presented has been a contemplated part of the puzzle. Stages begin with a single Snakebird, but soon players are asked to manage 2 or three at a time, quickly adding layers to the challenge. Later on moveable blocks become staples to puzzles as well, and being able to handle using these objects to interact together effectively is what’s key to success.
For the amount it stumps you the game hardly induces a serious level of frustration, and when it does it’s often just enough to motivate you to attempt a different tactic. Answers often require out of the box approaches; there’s almost a paradoxical feel to many of the game’s solutions. You’ll discover what needs to be accomplished and spend 10 minutes exploring every way why that’s impossible, only to eventually arrive at a moment where the entire puzzle makes sense. It’s about discovery in little ways, and learning how to test every theory your mind can toss at a problem and then some. Despite the sometimes impossible-feeling difficulty progression never really feels too far away. Upon death you’re replaced where you were just before your last move, and the always available quick reverse option to undo any mistakes you’ve made is a great design choice to make the player want to experiment as much as possible without feeling punished.
The classic world map layout is a great way to present non-linear stage progression; more skilled players can attempt harder levels after only completing a handful, but most will likely stick to the beaten path and enjoy the gradual rise in difficulty through the well thought-out introductions to new concepts. You’ll start to learn optimal movement patterns and ways to contort your birds just through design and ramping complexity. It’s refreshing how much credit the game gives to the player’s intelligence; puzzles are created in a way as to tempt you into all sorts of traps, but it has enough sense to let you work out what exactly needs to be done about a situation. There’s absolutely no fat to weigh anything down either. A great deal of care has been taken in presenting what’s vital in each stage without distraction, allowing each player to absorb every idea at their own pace. With such simplicity, it manages to teach complex ideas without uttering a word.
There’s a stark contrast between the feelings brought out by gameplay and what’s experienced through the game’s visual tone. The simple but elegant aesthetic relaxes you even on long sittings of little progress. The fine attention to detail is there too; there are adorable facial expressions on the birds to show their excitement or fear, and various clickable objects to randomly interact with. The multiple control setups allows for great ease of access. Players can engage through keyboard, controller, or even use the mouse to drag Snakebirds around. This control scheme leads us to believe that it wouldn’t be much of a stretch to see this game on the mobile market, and it would be a magnificent addition.
On the surface it might even look like a game for children, but Snakebird is far from it. With its excruciating difficulty and great feeling of reward upon completion, it deserves to be regarded among more well-known complex indie puzzlers. If you’re ever up for some serious low cost brain-bending just try to feed the Snakebirds.

Excellent purchase. Zero problems with the game. I just put the resolution up in the graphics menu and that was that. The AI is one of the best in the Total War games, especially with the introduction of the Vikings in Viking Invasion. The atmosphere is brooding and the contours of the land are very nice on the eye. The enemy AI is very reactive - unlike in Rome/Medieval 2 whereby troops will just sit and take archer fire, in this game you will get charged off the field more often than not as the enemy tries to counter you quite forceably. Very good fun and every battle can be significant and is often decided in one moment..
PS The other great thing about the game is how you can fight two different armies on the battlefield like the Vikings and the rebels. Trying to position yourself in the right way while taking on two different enemies is really exciting. You often don't have a clue how the battles are going to turn out.

So, I just beat Batman Arkham Asylum..and it was incredible! The best superhero game I have played to date. The story was well-paced, the gameplay was fun, tense, and action-packed. The graphics were great for a game that came out in 2009, and the voice-acting was absolutely stellar. Here is a breakdown on Batman Arkham Asylum.
Story: 8.3 out of 10
Batman has just captured the Joker without much of a fight and transports him to Arkham Asylum, home to all of Gotham's greatest criminals: Bane, Killer Croc, Poison Ivy. Suddenly, the Joker comes alive in the asylum and you find out that it was all just a trap set by the Joker. As the Batman, you must put a stop to this and take back control at the asylum. I am not going to say anything else, but the story is excellent, well-thought out, and well-paced that you never feel bored of the story. The cast is absolutely amazing, and the voice acting is some of the best I have ever heard in a video game. Just like the Batman Animated Series back in the 90s, this game made me feel like a kid again!
Gameplay: 9.0 out of 10
The gameplay of Arkham Asylum is broken into two sections: stealth, and all out action. The stealth in this game is intense. The amount of ways you can approach each scenario is great, and singling out one inmate at a time is absolutely thrilling. The fist fights in this game are also very satisfy and take a bit of skill to get good at. Instead of button mashing, you need to counter enemy attacks, dodge gunfire, and use a handful of gagdets at your disposal. Overall, I found every aspect of the gameplay to be immensily satisfying, especially the 240 Riddler challenges thrown in the game. This really made me want to explore all of the nooks and crannies of Arkham Asylum, and was another great addition to a fantanic game.
Sound: 10 out of 10
I do not do this often, but Batman Arkham Asylum truly deserves top marks for its sound quality. The voice acting is absolutely some of the best I have ever heard, Mark Hamill steals the show as the Joker. I always looked forward to what the Joker had to say, and the script did not disappoint. Regardless, all of the gagdets sounded cool and how they should have sounded. The fist fights were meaty, and felt like they had impact. The sound in this game was just amazing.
Graphics: 9.5 out of 10
For its time, Batman Arkham Asylum was stunning and rightfully so. The lightning is great, the textures are crisp, and the atmosphere is almost on par with Bioshock. It is just one good looking game, and absolutely immerses you inside of the gritty, twisted Arkham Asylum.
Conclusion:
Overall, Batman Arkham Asylum had some pretty big shoes to fill, and I think the game completely surpassed anyone's expectations (in a good way). The game truly is a masterpiece, and is a must buy especially being so cheap now. If you have not played this game, there has never been a better time to get into the series (especially with Arkham Knight coming out in June 2015). Every aspect of this game comes together to create something truly amazing.  If you remotely like the Batman or even if you don't, you owe it to yourself to play this game!
Batman Arkham Asylum: 9.2 out of 10
Off to play the next game in the series, the highly anticipated Batman: Arkham City!!!

Mark of the Ninja puts you in the role of a nameless ninja of the Hismou ninja clan. After your clan is attacked by armed forces of an evil business man, you must sneak your way through elaborate puzzles and areas to kill the men responsible for the attack.
MotN incorporates core elements from traditional steath games (Splinter Cell, Thief, MGS) with puzzle solving and platforming into a well-designed 2D enviornment. The controls, for the most part, are quite responsive though it seems to suffer from what I call "Sonic Adventure 2 Syndrome" in that many actions are mapped to the same button which can cause frustration while playing (The button to hide behind cover and pick up a body, for example, are on the same button. If there is a body next to a hiding spot, which can happen alot, this could cause frustration if you want to pick up a body but hide instead)
One thing to note is that you are NOT playing as Ryu Hayabusa or Joe Musashi. Your ninja is very weak, a few hits from the guards will be more than enough to take you down. So, much like Splinter Cell, you MUST avoid getting into fights with the guards; They will gun you down and bullets hurt. This doesn't mean that you CAN'T kill enemies. You just need to excersise CAUTION and COMMON SENSE before going in for the kill. In fact, the great part about this game is that each level is designed in such a way that you can take a lethal or non-lethal approach whenever you please (Though, you get more points for staying out of sight and leaving gurads alive). At first, it's quite difficult to do either because of the limitations of the character. As you progress, you will gain access to new weapons and costumes (or "paths" as the game calls them) to fit whatever gameplay style you want. I stuck with the Path of Silence, which is perfect for non-lethal runs and adds a significant challenge to the game (as you can't directly kill enemies and must stay within the shadows. JUST LIKE A REAL NINJA! WOW!)
There isn't much to say about the overall "graphics" in the game. The artstyle is very much similar to Klei's Shank which was also 2D and animated in Flash (in fact, it even runs on the same engine as Shank 2). The environment direction is top notch and really gets you in the mood for sum good 'ol stealthin'. Lots of dark areas engulfed with deep hues of dark purple and green. Even the brightest area still maintain the dangerous and ominous tones that the darker levels had. The music is also quite mellow during the normal sequences and you just might not even notice it. If you do pick up on it, don't expect anything heavily melodic though. Still fitting though
Overall excelent game. Not exactly a ton of replay value, though but it's still worth buying.

Mark Of The Ninja is, without any doubt, a solid candidate for the best stealth game in recent years which rivals classics such as Thief 2: The Metal Age and Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, considering that it is essentially a 2D side-scroller.
While the story and soundtrack are interesting enough to notice them, the gameplay is where it steals your attention due to its execution being so meticulous and flawless. From the typical stealthy backstabs to avoiding loud noise near guards, it has everything a stealth fanatic would imagine in a wet dream and more. The stealth mechanics are simply fluent and responsive, making them user-friendly. While not all are available from the start, which is somewhat understandable, more can be unlocked based on the player's performance. The various in-game puzzles are also well implemented even if they are generally very easy to figure out.
Surprisingly, the trial-and-error approach here is not as blunt as in other stealth games thanks to the indicator mechanic which shows the player any interactive hotspots within range and the exact throwing distance. This is a helpful mechanic which does not take away from suspense nor ease the difficulty. In fact, it makes the game more accessible while still being challenging. The player can now take their time, plan their moves and then execute them the way they want without the fear of messing up and being immediately punished. There are plenty of opportunities where death can be easily avoided even after a miscalculated move. If this helpful mechanic is not your cup of tea, then there is a Plus Mode which can be unlocked once the main story is completed which removes these indicators, thus ultimately increasing the difficulty drastically for stealth elitists.
While not all portions of the map are required to be explored to advance to the next stage, it is satisfying to acknowledge that there are different routes which the player can take which can also lead to potential hidden items through hidden paths. Want to infiltrate the building from the rooftop? Go ahead. Want to crawl through the sewers instead? Go ahead. However, while the game does offer route options, as a whole, it is more or less linear in the sense that these different routes are not always in the same area or, in some occasions, not available at all. There will be moments where a particular underground corridor is the only way to get across to the other side of the map.
The art direction in the style of Samurai Jack and Xiolin Showdown is fantastic and blends perfectly for a side-scrolling game. The backgrounds are captivating and set the atmosphere fittingly. The lighting effects are also used appropriately and are in fact part of the gameplay mechanic, so it is wise to take down all the lights down a corridor or hide yourself from lightning from the stormy weather in the latter levels.
Mark Of The Ninja is one of those games which does what it was designed for so well that its near-perfection is its downfall, weirdly enough. The game is so satisfying and engrossing that by the time you finish it, you want more; a lot more! Also, while the ending has a psychological twist to it and the special cutscene leading up to it is amazing, the overall story does lack depth for someone expecting a deeper story. This is something which keeps the game away from being perfect all-around. Nonetheless, the narrative is solid but nothing special.
Conclusively, it is challenging to call Mark Of The Ninja the best stealth game ever created (yet) since it is not perfect as a whole game, but as a stealth game in terms of gameplay it definitely rivals the best classic stealth games out there. Highly recommended!

I'd have to say, if you're interested in this, do not buy it, at least not now.
Bought it a while ago for my son and I to play, after he was watching a let's play of it. Seemed like a goofy game to mess around with.
It is, actually.
For maybe a round or two.
When we first got it, it had issues, but hey, it's early access, right? Well, as each update came out, it seemed like there were more and more issues. Weird lag, objects not working, getting stuck, random people joining our password protected custom game, etc.
Then, out of nowhere, it's 'released'. I'm sorry, but this game is NOT ready for release.
Not sure where to begin.
How about performance? Pretty abysmal. Can be running smooth, but then the framerate just plummets, mouse movement is all jerky, and it just feels rough.
Graphics-Quite poor. I'm not one to judge a game by it's graphics by any means, but overall, the game just looks bad. Looks like the devs just slapped it together and called it good. Character models are atrocious (hats and glasses are humorous though), textures are all over the place. Some look fine, but others don't make any sense. Go outside and look at the achievement room. The room is flat, but the 'bricks' taper off. Good example of it being slapped together.
Controls-Serviceable I suppose, although picking up items and using them is a major chore.
Balance-absolutely ridiculous. It's not a matter of who is going to win? The baby or the daddy? It's a matter of if the baby dies in one minute or two. The daddy has only a couple things he can do to stave off the baby's death, but there are sooo many options for the baby to off itself, it quickly turns into a race to see just how fast the baby can kill itself, especially with warping through vents.
Idea/concept-brilliant. Actually a really good idea for a game, but there are so many issues right now, I'd stay away. We'll probably keep playing it off and on for a while to see if things improve, but it's quickly becoming tiresome.
One thing I forgot about, and just remembered. The soundtrack. One of the most annoying and grating soundtracks I've ever heard.

- Mark of the Ninja is an excellent stealth based 2D platformer.
The story is "OK", but not much more. It has it's twists and turns as you'd expect from any story, and is enjoyable to follow.
I found the artstyle tastefull. You can probably see if you like it or not by looking at the pictures in the store page.
The mechanics of the game itself is where the real fun comes out in my opinion.
There are several ways to complete a map, be that as an oblivious-to-pain-sword-swinging-maniac, sneaky stealth kills or even non-lethal takedowns.
The maps could have been a bit more "explorable", but that's just the sandbox enthusiast in me grasping for straws, trying to squeeze the most out of every corner of the map.
The puzzles are on the easy side of the scale, but then again, they are not the main focus of the game and are mostly used as a gateway to "secret" areas or point-loot.
The controls as snappy and feel nice.
There were occasions where I grapple-hooked the wrong ledge, but that is down to my own incompetence rather than the games controls.
On my "non-lethal" playthrough certain areas felt a bit too unforgiving, but I guess that is a part of the "non-lethal" challenge. You are an elite ninja killer after all.
Upon completion of the game I wanted more, and that says something since the game actually is decently long.

GAMEPLAY: The game's core unique asset, brings something way different from any other PC fps, in fact, if you're looking for a Multiplayer only time splitters sequel, you're gonna get an early 2000's breeze of awe in result, movement, jumping and aiming are well timed, shooting and zooming as well.
DESIGN: The only drawback, while it's presentation looks kinda sporty and barely original from any "near future realistic bullet game", it adds plenty of unnecesary space on the UI, it doesn't bother anyone in the short game, but it starts to annoy you how little it shows for a gameplay and concept that it represents, specially;
Main screen: Remove, that annoying berserk's shotgun reload sound, remove the character's stats and add enviremonent appreciation, add a Social and General Stats tab, that black ribbon up top looks lonely.

The Short Version: widespread technical issues and incessant crashes render the game unplayable for many PC users.
The Long Version: I jumped into the stormy, explosive waters of Far Cry right with its third installment, tasting the salt and bullet baffet for the first time with Far Cry 3.
Blood Dragon's parent game was an interesting adventure and for the most part a fun ride, but both Far Cry 3 and this wacky incarnation of it seem to fail the most basic requirement of a PC game:
...You have to be able to play it.
For that lofty goal to be achieved, it simply needs to be a thing that can run on the PC.
Unfortunately, this is not the case for a great many PC users, myself included.
When I first purchased Far Cry 3 (and later Blood Dragon), my computer met every single one of the minimum requirements to run it, but I haven't been able to get the game running. Technical support was of no help at all, and even after upgrading my computer (which I shouldn't have had to do, since I already met all the requirements), finally getting the game to work was an ordeal when I discovered that the game would crash on me almost every five minutes of play. Worse, it would often give me the Blue Screen of Death, forcing me to reboot. Even after trying everything I could from every advice, tip and tutorial I found online written for (and by) the many users who have gove through the exact same issues, the game would still crash.
Since the game doesn't let you decide when you save your progress, most of my original run of Far Cry 3 was devoted to trying to get through the mandatory tutorial (that felt like it was 20-minutes long) in the beginning of the game, hoping it would not-crash long enough for me to get to a checkpoint and not have to start all over again when the game inevitably freezes my computer, forcing both a reboot on my part as well as a long wail of frustration, curled fingers reaching for the uncaring dark skies above.
Blood Dragon, I was hoping, would be an improvement and the issues with its parent game (which were reported not only by yours truly, but a great many users who practically flooded not only the official game forums but a big chunk of other threads and discussion boards) - unfortunately, the game crashed right in the middle of the (again, mandatory) tutorial in the beginning, shortly after the opening scene and before I could get two minutes into the thing.
I wish I had more to say about both games, but this abyssal experience has not allowed me much of an opportunity to actually play the game itself, and since it shouldn't be on me, the customer, to spend months of my life sifting through forums and struggling against the current, trying to get the game I paid money for to actually PLAY, I simply deleted both games from my computer and consoled myself only with the fact that I bought this one on sale.
Still, it doesn't wash away the bad taste of the promise of a little video gamey fun being ruined by the video game not actually running.

Lego Star Wars is a game I consider a classic from my childhood and the Star Wars VII hype got me to pick up this game in the Winter sale (Damn you marketing tactics!). This doesn't mean I think it's one of the best games I ever played as a kid but it's one I have very fond memories of and pretty much anyone I talk to about it has played it at some point. It's that perfect blend of co-op, collectathon, movie tie-in that's just great to play when I'm not feeling something very intense and just want to relax.
The game is most certainly flawed, the artificial difficulty and lack of any complex combat is the one of the big complaints; I never felt challenged playing this game but I also died a lot because the game throws enemies at you non stop and while they only take one hit to kill avoiding all the blaster bolts can prove annoying if you aren't a character with auto dodge. This really slows down the game and while I don't expect the most from the combat every lightsaber battle was jump attack, jump attack, jump attack ect. It's impossible to hit someone while they're blocking with anything other than the air attacks which are undodgeable by the AI if you're in range. I know this is a kids game and not meant to be challenging but after a while even kids would find this tedious at best.
The lack of online co-op is my biggest grind with this game. At first I thought it was an issue with it being such an old game that relies on single screen co-op but after checking other Lego games I realized that it was nothing more than a trend of laziness. I did manage to take my laptop to a friend's and play it with them and it was great fun except that save files are harder than needs be to locate and impossible to get working on a separate machine to the one it came from meaning we had to start a fresh with none of the cool characters I'd unlocked. Besides some of the vehicle levels being a bit lackluster and Superstory being total BS and a lazy way to recycle content these are my only real complaints with the game so from here on out it's all positive.
The Lego formula has practically been perfected now but that doesn't mean it wasn't always great. Star Wars has so much charm in its cutscenes and is very humoresque due to it's recognizable and lovable characters acting out the Star Wars story in a silly and joking way. There is so much to do in this game and so much to find. While some levels practically hand you the collectibles some can prove a real challenge to find, but if your smart you can aim to collect the stud multipliers and minikit/red brick detector red bricks giving you a hint on in which direction there is a collectible. There's also some extra game modes in the complete saga that add that make 100%ing this game a real journey as you try collect all the gold bricks.
One of the best things about Lego Star Wars is that it's well, Star Wars. Playing all your favourite Jedi battle it out on all those great planets from the Star Wars universe is immensely entertaining and even more fun in Lego. I would enjoy this game even if it wasn't Star Wars but the real heart and charm of the game comes from seeing your favorite scenes re-acted in Lego form.
There were dull moments while playing this game but I thoroughly enjoyed it and I felt both a sense of fulfillment and emptiness once I reached 100% which shows just how great this game is. May the force be with you all.

"LEGO® Star Wars™ - The Complete Saga" is basically as the name implies, it's a Lego game that contains the saga of Star Wars, well until Episode VII just released haha.
This game features a hub world where you first start and includes all 6 Episodes and within each Episode there are six Missions and one/two Bonus missions. Only Episode 1 is unlocked in the beginning, but if you complete the first mission you'll unlock all the other Episodes. So if you don't like the prequels just do the first mission and then skip the rest and jump straight into Episode 4. There is also a "Gold" bonus area that has extra content to do if you get all Gold blocks in the game.
You're not going to find voice acting in this game unless it's the droid sounds, so there is little to none of the political scenes from the movies(at least so far in Episode 1). If you're looking for pretty much an all action version of Star Wars this is the game to get that experience. However there are some missing scenes from the movie that I would have liked to see in this game like the underwater ship in Episode 1 is skipped when that could have been part of a mission for more collectibles/blocks. There is also no space scene with Anakin when he's in the N-1 which I thought could have been a cool addition. The pod racing is included however. So very mixed so far in Episode 1 of what scenes you'd expect to see. Probably more missing scenes like this in the later Episodes.
As for performance I'm getting 60fps 100% of the time in-game at 1920x1080, but when there's cutscenes I've noticed there are framedrops occuring but they come back to 60fps. So a bit stuttering when in cutscenes. Not sure what the cause is, but it isn't that big of a deal to me since I'm just watching and not playing.
Controller support does feel perfect in the game, I don't have the time currently to find a local co-op partner and test two controllers plugged in, but I'm assuming it works fine. If it doesn't I'll update my review and make note of it.
So far I'm very happy with the game. I used to play Lego games a long time ago on my original Xbox back when it was split into two parts and this Complete Saga on PC plays exactly how I remember it years ago. I'd say it's worth $19.99 if you know you're going to be playing this and wanting to collect everything and it's 100% a for sure purchase at $5.99 on sale even if you're just going to casually run through it.

TL;DR: A great nostalgia trip for Lego and/or Star Wars fans, but rough around the edges and it shows.
I had the original two Lego Star wars games for Gamecube way back in the day. I played and enjoyed the hell out of both of them. So you can imagine my excitement when I realized that I could play both, in one game, on PC. I picked this title up in the winter sale and I've been playing it off and on since then.
It's just as fun as I remember it. The absence of their cringeworthy dialogue and forced love story make the prequels much more enjoyable, though it might be hard to understand if you don't already know the plot. The slapstick and Lego dismemberment gags never get old. There's easter eggs hidden everywhere, encouraging exploration, and the game's puzzles are challenging and rewarding enough to solve for players of any age without getting frustrating (most of the time).
You can play as all your favorite characters, along with many others whose names you never knew and never really cared about, like Grand Moff Tarkin or Ki-Adi-Mundi. Most of the main characters have unique and sometimes hilarious melee animations, like Princess Leia who ♥♥♥♥♥slaps everyone, or Chewbacca who will leap on stormtroopers and rip their arms off (it's all bloodless Lego gore so it's okay for kids, obviously).
However, no game is without sin and this one commits quite a few of them.
A lot of the optional characters, especially the blaster-wielding ones, have little differentiation between them besides their general appearance, so you'll probably just end up using Luke Skywalker (Jedi), Boba Fett (grown-up), and Darth Vader most of the game.
The most glaring flaws are perhaps the myriad of bugs littered throughout the game, from texture, shadow, and Z-ordering glitches (where background meshes pop through foreground ones) to areas where the Lego studs you're supposed to collect (as currency) simply clip through the floor or walls or other decorations and disappear. Since this game was released in 2009, I very much doubt that these issues will ever be resolved.
Some puzzles are far more tedious than challenging; oftentimes the solution is obvious but requires a lot of work simply to make it seem more difficult than it actually is. This is a trap that many otherwise very good puzzle games (like Portal and The Talos Principle) fall into to pad out their runtimes, and I wish it would stop. Some of the optional puzzles have such obscure and nonsensical "solutions" that you're basically just trying to guess what the game designer was thinking.
There is no brightness slider, so some scenes can become very overblown, especially with the excessively strong bloom shader included in the game. Disabling bloom helps but makes other scenes look much more drab so it's a lose-lose either way. Also, and this is more of a nitpick than anything, but the screen-space reflections on windows and polished floors are inconsistent in resolution, so some are crystal clear while others are horribly pixellated.
Otherwise, the game's graphics have aged about as well as they could have, considering they're rendering a world which is supposed to look like it's made of plastic. I'll have to look at other more recent Lego games and see how they've improved the engine.
However, I really, really, really, really hate the third-person camera. This is one of those games that tries a little too hard to imitate cinema: the camera is often either in a fixed position and pans to show the characters, or pans while following a dolly path through the level. There's also the seemingly intentionally added tracking latency, where it takes a second to catch up to movement of your characters. In addition, some of the levels with mandatory platforming sections have preset camera positions which give very poor depth cues, so sometimes you have no idea if you're going to hit the platform you want or if you're going to fall to your death. Put that all together, you end up with a distracting, oftentimes misleading, and sometimes downright sickening visual ride.
You might be wondering why I'm still recommending this game, even with all these complaints. It's Lego freaking Star Wars, man. This♥♥♥♥♥♥sells itself.

Snakebird is one of the best puzzle games I played ever.
It made me realize that the way I played puzzle games before was mostly by trial and error - try every possible action until it works. And that's not the way you play Snakebird.
Puzzles in this game force you to clearly state a problem that you face ("How can I reach this fruit?", "How can I push this block without making the snakebird fall?"), solve it in your mind, and try to execute your solution in game. This sounds like any puzzle game, but Snakebird just won't let you solve a puzzle by chance.

Shortly after gaining this understanding and getting more familiar with the positioning and physics of snakebirds, the game became so easy that I easily breezed through all the levels I had trouble with and all the final levels, in which the last one was disappointingly easy.

I recommend this game to most puzzle players.

I know it says I have little time played but I have plalyed it for a long time on the PS3(Not Anymore) But I figured I'd leave a review for the hell of it...
In the end I vote the game 8/10.
The story is cheesy and feels like almost no work is put into it, you see scenes with cops, handling stuff... Chase Linh shooting a guy... and some gangsters, but in the game play itself all you have is driving, most of what the player does doesn't feel connected to the scenes/story line.
My goal each time I have played was to complete the lame story ASAP to unlock the map, tracks, cars, etc..
Those are the best aspects of the game. You get all the good vinyl cusomiztions from older games like NFS Carbon.
You get an extensive car list, featuring EU, Japan, and American models.
The track and world is the largest map(I have seen in a NFS Title) - and I've played every NFS since HP II on PS2.
You have your standard freeroam, and cop chases like the  old Carbon and Most Wanted did.
There is a huge selection of tracks and game modes, like High Way Battle where you struggle to gain 1000 feet ahead of the other car, while avoiding HUGE levels of traffic(comparing traffic to other NFS games).
My personal favorite track is "East I-85" its the best track for me because it's an all interstate course, and you can really test the handling and top speed of cars.
Next I will discuss the handling and driving, it is not bad, it is different from other NFS games.
You can do more realistic moves with your cars than in other games, but some times the handling is overkill, put max parts on a high end car, you can catch yourself turning, then snapping into an object as if the object were attracting you.
It's easier to drive if you don't hold it left or right for too long, or use nos while turning.
Next I will discuss the glitches, there is lots of them. I've plalyed online matches where players could, on some tracks, exploit the driving engine and launch over clear barriers(and basically access a online-like freeroam)
There is also this god-awful(but halarious) falling glitch, where you begin a race and upon starting you fall in the ground, stuck at 460mph(rounded that up), and the car doesn't reset. This glitch happens randomly and you basically have to wait to loe or quit :P
There is other glitches... I turned too hard eon time using the Audi R8?(Le Mans?, forgot) and hit an object, bounced several hundred meters in the air doing almost endless flips.
You can also reset your car during freeroam and quickly drive inside a civilian car before your car becomes solid, then pause, swap cars, and you can twitch, flip, and do odd stunts involving yourself and your little civilian :D
I made a semi truck literally bounce away doing that one.
The glitches are fun, helps make up for the bad textures and story.
Yeah the sky textures, and ground textures aren't great. The ground almost seems yellow, yellow concrete... ew.
The car details are great, and that's probably the best part.
Then we have the music. It's what you expect from any EA game, you get a random list of songs(that were popular when what ever game was released). Rock, Rap, and some Techno stuff, similar to MW 05 song list and Burnout 3.
8/10 game, would launch the semi again.

Easy game to recommend.
Fans of the character need not think twice about buying this game as the game is teeming with Batman lore.  The gameplay itself is very entertaining and makes good use of Batman's arsenal.  The story although, simple and linear, serves as a proper thread to join all the different elements of the game together.  There are some parts where you are required to clear the area of goons that may frustrate you due to the trial an error nature of it, but pacing is good for the most part.  There is a wealth of optional items to find in this game as well as weapon upgrades.  Another fun aspect of the game is gliding, a mechanic which feels very natural and begs to be used.
Technically, the game runs very well and at a rock-solid 60fps on my R9 280.  The graphics will not blow you away as a more modern game like Tomb Raider would but the art design is top notch.  The only annoyance I encountered were shadows that tended to shift and flicker a bit, especially on Batman's body.  Also, the launcher does not have a command line argument to go straight into the game but there are work-around's for this  (symbolic links or renaming the game's executable to BmLauncher.exe).
In terms of shortcomings, there aren't many except perhaps that the Asylum setting feels somewhat limited in terms of environment variety.  Also, the fighting can feel repetitive on a few occasions but you can mix it up by attempting a more stealthy approach to taking down the enemy.  Stealth is actually required in a few parts.
In all, this is a terrific game and unless you are not fond of 3rd person adventure games, or you are the Joker himself, you are likely to enjoy it.

suffers a bit because of it - though the story doesn't seem to be special by any means - then you might should give this a go.
The User Reviews are Mostly Positive. I don't believe I've ever seen a game with 5+ reviews rated as either strictly Positive or Negative; thus, The Novelist is... just above average, as it were.
I agree with that assessment. That second sentence seems to contradict itself, but I find the game as a whole to be sum-how greater than it's parts (teehee).
The story is one of a family on the verge.
From the game's tutorial, it seems the father is the priority.
You are some sort of entity; it is implied at the end of the first night that
. Your purpose is to play implicit life-coach for the residents.
The father is a struggling author what wanted to get away from it all and make things simple so as to better concentrate on his work.
The mother is a fretful wife who makes better use of the solitude of the rented vacation home by painting, all the while yearning to bridge the rift that's formed between her and her partner.
The child is a son wondering about this thing called "life," wanting to be a kid, to spend time with Dad, to be just like Mom.
You do not wish to let the family know of your presence. You can possess light fixtures to move about the house and can walk freely when the coast is clear. There are notes, letters and images to read and view strewn throughout the house. From these - and from the thoughts of the people themselves' - you can gain insight into their relationships and into their pertinent desires.
If they are between you and one of the papers, you can cause the light fixture you're currently possessing to flicker, so as to distract. If they catch a glimpse of you, they apparently become wary (to say the least) and are less susceptible to your methods.
There are two difficulties to choose from: Stealth and Story. The former necessitates the use of traveling from light fixture to fixture, the latter renders the game a walking simulator. Having picked Stealth, I have been in plain view, albeit a bit to the side, of the people and (as far as I can tell) not been detected. Maybe their cones of vision are something like... 37°. This is to call into question the integrity of The Novelist as a
.
After having learned as much as there is to presently, you can go into each individual's memories and glean a bit more from a few snippets. Upon exiting their mind, you can read their thoughts once more and discover what their wish (end-goal for the chapter) is, what item you must collect for it.

If you find all of the notes and memories of either or both of the other two - once you make your primary decision -- once everybody goes to bed --- you can, both, scour the house for notes that reveal the history of the house
and find the item for a secondary objective; you whisper your decisions into the man's ear and get a cutscene explaining the consequences of that compromise. There will always be at least one family member that doesn't get what they want/(")need(").
This is a game about the balancing of relationships, of choices, of stealth... and of being creepy.
I have spent minutes just staring at people sleeping and hanging out in bathrooms... just waiting...
Ha. And again. ha.
Seriously: If any of that sounds interesting - and I don't know how it can't, at least in theory - I recommend you at least try the game.
I will say that some will NOT find the product to be executed as well as the premise suggests, when considering that it's a video game; either find the gameplay to be lacking, or the story (which is the focus) to be too mundane.
Indeed, the one YouTube personality I follow - Jim Sterling - holds the opinion that, too often, walking simulators commit the crime of telling rather than showing; of having the game focus on, i.e., the aftermath of a much more interesting event than the one you, as the player, are involved in, i.e. learning of the event afterwards. Though this specific critique couldn't be laid on this game, I feel the core complaint is the very essence of The Novelist. Though you influence the outcomes, you are not directly involved in the story at all, and are thus a glorified camera-person.
EDIT: Practically, $15 is far too substantial an asking price. Not to suggest that the work put into the game isn't worth that, but it is to say that, as a gamer, I can tell my fellows that there are more competitive titles in the Market, though I will concede that many of those have even less traditional gameplay (i.e. mechanics that make them more'n walking simulators / visual novels (not that there's anything inherently wrong with either, but to say that there's a difference between story-driven games and games built to tell a story... yeah, so the latter might be written as "(")games(")"))... I'd wait for
a 25% off sale.

There are some genres that I have a love/hate relationship with. There are your sports games, your racers, your zombie games (that’s more on the hate side) and then we get to stealth. Some things I love about them: Tactical thinking, the challenge of never being seen while I clear a room, the different weapons. Some things I hate about them: the constant waiting, the fact that in some cases if you get caught that’s the end of the level and you have to restart (and then some other times you are halfway through, get caught, and it reloads you in a place where you can't avoid the mistake you made before...arg), the repetitive rooms to clear.
Mark of the Ninja is one of those stealth games that avoids the constant pitfalls others make. The art is wonderful to look at, the storyline is light, but engaging enough, the action is awesome, and the powers you can choose from are all pretty fun. Where Shank (another Klei property) is a shootem up 80s action movie, this is a classic martial arts revenge flick. Your ninja clan has been wronged and you are given the power to regain your honor, but the tattoos that give you your strength also are poison and will eventually kill you. The theme of honor, revenge, and what that means comes up throughout the game and comes to a head towards the end.
The game plays our over maybe 8-10 hours, depending on how fast your clear each level, but I've played it a few times and had fun after every run through. It’s one of those games that you can install and play idly to kill some time, but then realize you've been playing for so long that you’re an hour late to the movie.
Or something.
I mean so I’ve heard.
All in all I love this game. The music, art, and gameplay work well together and draw you into the world Klei has created; a place where you can meld with the shadows, sneak past armed guards, slit an unsuspecting gaijin’s neck, dragging the body into an air vent without tripping any alarms, then escaping into the night while lightning strikes behind you.
Or something. I mean so I’ve heard.
