This is an extended review on Batman: Arkham Asylum.
Content: 9/10
A 10+ hours campaign story along with a great challenge mode, which also has DLC challenges included, that can extend the length of the game up to 30 hours or even more in some cases. Unlockable character bios which include character interviews that you can listen to and character trophies, all of which are rewarded to you for your play time or geekness for searching and finding the Riddler's trophies. Very nice. Worth mentioning is that the game features a "Game +" which can extend the game's play value and play time by a lot more. (for those who are daring enough to endure the harder combat and lots of deaths that will follow)
Graphics: 9/10
Except from the eventual low res textures, which are hidden very well that in some cases are not even noticeable, the game looks amazing even to this day when maxed out. And this is a console port, which shows that the developers gave the time and effort to make it look as good as it could on a powerful enough machine.
Aesthetics: 10/10
This game catches the nitty gritty and dark enviroment, in which the Dark Knight fights villains for the good of Gotham. The Arkham Asylum really feels like a psychiatric prison that went wrong!  Not much more can be said.
Sound: 9/10
- Sound Quality: It is excelent, crisp and clean as it should be in any game.
- Soundtrack: Be it on scenes, menus, combat or non-combat it fits the spirit of the game and that's what matters. It is great, it feel like soundtrack for a Batman licenced product.
- Lip synching: While it is really good it feels like it could be better. One of the better lip synching i have seen in a game though.
PC Port: 9/10
- Display Settings: From Anti-Aliasing, Dynamic Shadows and Distortion to Harmonic Lighting, Ambient Occlusion and PhysX, this game has a lot of settings that will satisfy the PC enthusiants just fine. (Although the FOV slider is missing. I know, its not a FPS game but still, its not there. you can mess with the files though and set it to your liking)
- Controls: This game supports controllers and rebindable keys which is a god send! Only 2 problems, 1 minor, 1 big. 1) You cannot rebind your keys while in-game, you have to do it before you launch the game via the game launcher and, 2) As many console to PC ported games tend to do, there are actions, many of them in fact, that are binded to a single key and that can cause some problems and a lot of frustration. Be aware.
- Optimization: This game has been tested and completed using an Nvidia GeForce GTX 570 Sonic Edition. With Motion blur being turned off (cause my eyes hate it) and Bloom being turned off (cause apparently my card hates it), this game was being maxed out on 1080p 60 fps (with V-Sync turned on). Greatly optimized in my opinion.
Story: 10/10
You are Batman, escorting the Joker, an unpredictable and very dangerous villain to a psychiatric high security hospital-prison called the "Arkham Asylum", where he escapes, and its up to you to stop him, the prison break he just caused and the other "super-villains" that are lurking free in the asylum.
Gameplay: 9/10
While simplistic in its design, Batman: Arkham Asylum's gameplay is so good and successful that it already has spawned a mechanical clone (namely the Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor game) and probably many more will follow.
- Combat: The combat in theory is an action beat-them-up with counter moves and special moves that can be executed when you have reached a big enough combo on the press of a button, but it is so much more in praticality, making the game the opposite of a chore. Satisfaction is the word that can describe it. And of course you can make Batman learn new moves and combos while leveling up, making the combat even better while you progress through the game.
- Non-Combat: When there are no enemies to fight, the game includes a lot of puzzles to solve (the Riddler's trophies) but most of them are no big deal (key word being "most" of them). Use the batclaw to traverse through the island or just use your feet!
- Present in both combat and non-combat is the dedective mode, which helps you solve riddles or progress the storyline in some cases in non-combat and helps you indentify the weakness of special enemies or super-villain encounters/bosses in combat. Also, the Bat-gadgets, like for example the iconic Batarang or the Batclaw, these tools are there to help you battle enemies, traverse through the island or solve Riddler's puzzles. You unlock new gadgets while progressing through the game.
Although i will mention that combat has its hic-ups. There are times that Batman wont counter when you press the button or wont target the correct enemy or even wont hit an enemy because he isnt close enough when that isnt the case. There is room for improvement here.
To conclude, Batman: Arkham Asylum is a shining example of how a Batman game or generally a superhero game is ought to be. Full of great content, amazing story and satisfying gameplay, this is a game that you are doing yourself a disservice if you actually havent purchased and played it yet. Full price or on a Steam Sale this game is worth your buck.

Arkham Asylum is the original "Batman Simulator." You are Batman, bringing the Joker into Arkham Asylum (again). All of a sudden, things go wrong, and you are tasked with fixing the problem. As you try to fix the problem, more problems arise. And thus, you are taken through this amazing adventure as Batman, where an implausible amount of action and heroics happen in just one night.
This game is a stealth game, first and foremost. It is incredibly gratifying to come into a room filled with cocky gun-toting henchmen, only to see (and hear) them become more and more terrified as you pick off their comrades one-by-one. Between your utility belt filled with gadgets, and the environment itself, you have so many options at your disposal to remove your enemies.
This game also breaks up the stealth with some great beat-em-up mechanics that has you taking on tons of enemies. You feel like you hit the enemies hard, and it adds variety to the game.
The atmosphere in this game is also incredibly well designed. The environments on Arkham island are varied and beautiful (in their grungy sort of way), and it's amazing how much "stuff" is just strewn about for you to discover. Luckily, you have "Detective Mode." The Detective Mode is a very good way to get the "game mechanics" to fit into the game without breaking immersion. However, this leads to my only gripe about the game (and it's a small one): Because the Detective Mode is so useful, I feel I spend too much time in that alternate view, and it takes away from all the details and color that went into making this amazing world. Not a bad problem to have.

The
fanbase is a tumultuous one. At the time of
’ release, the franchise consisted of a fantastic trilogy, an awful trilogy and a mess of other content of varying quality. There are various groups of
fans with different opinions—some defend the prequel trilogy wholeheartedly while others are more down-to-earth, insisting that there hasn’t been a good
film in over 30 years.
One of the biggest strengths of
is that it doesn’t seem reminiscent of either trilogy, instead bringing forth its own style of simple, family-friendly humour and simplifying down the plots of all six
film into a cartoony mashup of the popular sci-fi series and the equally popular line of children’s toys.
In theory, it’s a bizarre concept, but in practice it works rather well. The Lego adaptations of the various sets and characters from the films look fantastic, providing a wacky, cartoony art direction complemented by the game’s child-oriented sense of humour. It consists mostly of slapstick comedy by way of over-the-top animation. In fact, the graphics overall are actually very good. While the ‘photorealistic-in-2005’ textures on some of the non-Lego environmental objects are a little ugly, everything that’s made of the titular plastic bits looks great. It’s quite amusing to see well-known icons of the franchise like the famous
rendered as an excessively detailed Lego model.
There is, however, a bit of a disparity in overall visual fidelity between the episodes taken from the original 2005
game and the 2006 sequel. The original trilogy characters taken from
each have unique animations and each has an exotic look about him. Han Solo winks knowingly at the camera as he twirls his laser pistol on his finger before he holsters it, Darth Vader simply taps his foot in front of security cameras rather than give the wave of acknowledgement an average Stormtrooper would. My favourite is the animation that plays when you try to punch Princess Leia as Lando Calrissian—rather than attack her, he plants a gentle kiss on her hand and bows. It’s the little details like this that make
such a joy to look at.
Characters from the prequel trilogy, however, all share the same set of generic animations. I didn’t notice any of the detailed animations with them, and there was even one character I noticed who kept the ‘generic Lego smile with soulless black eyes’ expression regardless of the situation he was in. It was unnerving and honestly just felt like a bit of a cop-out. I understand that these characters were from an older game, but I think if the developer is going to re-release both of these games in a package like
, the least that could be done is an update to bring these parts of the game up to the quality level of the original trilogy.
Surprisingly, the quality gap doesn’t stop at the animations. Allow me to give an example. Characters from the original trilogy who use laser pistols have access to a ‘dodge’ move, allow them to quickly step out of harm’s way in combat. This feature wasn’t implemented in the original game, so the characters from it cannot use this ability. This is baffling laziness on the developer’s part, and it actually makes about a quarter of the game’s characters obsolete by comparison. It’s especially embarrassing when you consider how much effort it would take—all the characters are almost exactly the same model, and all the animations are already in the game. In fact, the entire amalgamation is rife with this kind of laziness. All that’s really been done to the original game's content is a slight graphical tweak. Don’t get me wrong, everything that’s here is fantastic, even the older stuff, but I just don’t quite understand why a developer wouldn’t take the time to even out the quality so that even the content from the 2005 game feels like less of a re-tread and more like a remake.
The gameplay itself is essentially a 3D platformer with an emphasis on combat, puzzles and collectible items. The levels are beautifully rendered as Lego models, though there are a lot of models and textures designed to look like real-world objects. It’s a little disappointing that not everything’s made of Lego, but it still a treat to look at.
The controls are sufficient. I did find that far too many actions are bound to the B button, and the vehicle-based levels are an absolute nightmare in general, but the ground-based levels control well enough. The combat is extremely simple—it’s not really viable to use more than two buttons—but I still found it engaging, perhaps because of the (mostly) superb animations.
uses sounds taken almost exclusively from the films, and it works fantastically. John Williams' score speaks for itself, but it’s not even just that—every sound effect is authentic to the point where just listening to the game’s audio could leave you thinking you were actually watching one of the films. The way the characters collide with a soft click is so charming, and fits with the game’s overall style perfectly.
has a whole lot of content. There are 37 levels total, 20 side missions (given out by the illustrious Jabba the Hutt), 160 characters and a variety of vehicles. I do have a problem with the character roster, however. Out of the huge selection, there are maybe 8 that aren’t just remodels of other characters. To make matters worse, a lot of characters are just another character minus one ability. Every Jedi is identical, and every Sith is just a Jedi with an extra ability, thereby invalidating the need to ever play as a Jedi outside of story mode. There are a ton of other comparisons that can be drawn up, which I’d bet would invalidate over half the roster. I get that they want to include everyone from the films, but it feels like they could have buffed up a lot of the weaker guys. Sure, that may end up with most characters being reskins of others, but that’s still a better alternative to what happens now.
On the topic of content, a lot of
’s replayability feels pretty contrived. For instance, within each and every level there are 10 ‘minikit canisters’ that will give the player a new vehicle once collected. The problem is, most of these canisters can only be acquired using abilities that the player does not have in story mode, thereby mandating a second playthrough of the level in ‘free play’ mode to reach 100% completion. ‘Free play’ mode is the same as story mode, but it removes the cutscenes and allows the player to choose one of their unlocked characters to play as throughout the level. They may then swap between a select group of characters on the fly. This party of characters is selected based on their abilities, ensuring that you will always have access to every ability in the game as long as you’re in free play mode. It’s good fun to go back through early levels searching for collectibles as Darth Vader (obviously the best character), but I just wish it didn’t feel so much like the game was trying to force multiple playthroughs. It’s a minor criticism, however. I still had a great time in free play mode.
Overall,
does feel like a bit of a lazy compilation of two fantastic games, but I’m still going to recommend it based purely on the outstanding quality and unique style of those original games.

Few games manage to tell such a breathtaking story with such admirable minimalism as Always Sometimes Monsters does. What’s even greater is you are in control of the story, and how the game will pan out. For me, calling this a game is an understatement of what it really is. Always Sometimes Monsters is a declaration about life, about how our choices are all we really have, and about how those choices, no matter how small, can reorient our life in ways that we can never predict. In life there is regrets, happiness, anger, wishfulness and countless other human feelings. Always Sometimes Monsters shows that while experiencing these feelings is inevitable, you will never be able to travel back and reshape your life with different choices, so you have to make the best of what you have and never sink into regret with the decisions you’ve made in life, or you will never be able to move forward in the unique journey that is your life. 10/10

is a pure grid-based puzzle game. Every key press responds to one action. You can undo any number of steps.
You control one snake at a time. You can move it like in the popular game
, and eat fruit as well. But what is this? The game takes action in a side view, so the snakes fall like in
! The "snake" remains rigid, never rotates, and falls down only if there is nothing below it. The "bird" part, I suppose, refers to the fact that the creatures can slightly lift off the ground, only to fall afterwards.
And there is not much more to explain. This concept gives birth to a vast amount of combinations and gameplay possibilities, especially if there are multiple snakes! Of course, some additional gameplay concepts are present, all very natural and intuitive. Spikes, movable blocks, portals and whatnot. Even the level exit portal acts as a gameplay element, because losing a snake often renders the level unsolvable for the other snakes.
The graphics are immaculate. Don't be fooled by the cuteness, though. The game is very, very difficult. Not much to do here for (most) kids.
The soundtrack never gets boring.
It may be "a little" early, but I would dare call this the puzzle game of the year.

Do you think this is kinds of cute and casual puzzle game?
No! The puzzle in Snakebird is brutal!

This game's core mechanic - moving around snakes - is amazingly intuitive. It is a very solid puzzle game - and it's a good puzzle game, not just a good game. I know I wanted a puzzle game that wasn't deceptive towards the player and this game does just that - that's why it's a good puzzle game, and not simply a good game.
Snakebird is a difficult puzzle game. Use the Steam achievements to check out the completion rate of this game - that was an instant-buy for me. The art style happens to work wonders to keep players from the verge of frustration. Despite it looking like a children's puzzle game from the outset, it quickly ramps up and its audience changes drastically.
The game itself has incredibly varied graphics and mechanics, which helps for keeping your mindset changing throughout levels. Despite being abstract, it still manages to be immersive with a pleasant art style and great sound design to go with it. The level progression allows you to visit several individual levels at one point in the game, so a spike in difficulty in one level will not prevent you from playing the rest of the game.
The only flaws I could recall in the game are that your level progress does not get individually saved (however, if you quit the game during a level, it will save that, but only that). Another "flaw" could be the lack of a hint system, but such a feature would be a detraction from the main selling point of the game's challenge. The sound and music also lack sliders to change their percentage.
One word of note: your snake can stand on the fruits, just like any other block. I did not realize this at first because I thought the background scenery was the limit of the snake's movement path.
EDIT: The undo mouse bind being on the fourth button is now on middle mouse, so I've changed my review to reflect this.

I've not experienced a title as interesting as this within Need for Speed for a long time. Where do I even begin? The endless flaws and general glitchy gameplay? The hidden charm?
Let's start with the positives first:
+ The smoke seems as good a place to start as any. It is gorgeous! In ProStreet, EA BlackBox (the developer) gave the tire smoke a new look and it was stunning as it wrapped around the tires in a drag race. It is the same here, with the smoke seemingly blurring your car amidst it. It even changes to brown if you're driving on dirt!
+ Car selection is slightly more positive than negative I'd say. 54 cars in total with a great variety of muscle, exotic and tuner. There are no SUVs but I will never care again if they forget about SUVs entirely. They were terrible in Underground 2 lol. Each car can be upgraded (albeit with not a lot to choose from) both performance and aesthetic wise.
+ Core mechanics. What I mean is the underlying gameplay, where you find the genuine fun of NFS Undercover. If you look at Undercover at the surface, you'll find something drasticly wrong with it. But scratch underneath that and you can see EA Black Box tried something a little different. The cars handle differently to any previous NFS before it, giving them an incredibly unrealistic but extremely fun feel! This is due to the "Heroic Driving Engine". It certainly gives the cars a slidy feel, but it's not to the point of feeling like you're driving on ice. You can do doughnuts easily, and then suddenly pull away. You can be driving at over 150 MPH and then suddenly veer off round a corner going nearly the same speed. You can pull off J-turns like nothing at all. It offers the chance to drive easily but with some flair.
+ Graphical tuning. Undercover actually offers a pretty nice list of graphical fine-tuning for you to choose from. From anti-aliasing to texture filtering, adjusting the car detail to world detail, it provides some good things for you to match the game to what your computer is capable of.
+ Photo Mode. I love taking photos of my cars! I've taken advantage of "Photo Mode" in every racing game, not just NFS however. So an inclusion in this title is no different! The graphics are... average... but they provide enough for some sweet photos.
OK, I have to admit this is where the positives end.... erm... yeah, so on to the negatives I suppose.
- The AI is the most FRUSTRATING, BROKEN, IDIOTIC and UNDECISIVE piece of CRAP. I have never felt so angered than I have playing Undercover. Let's start with the traffic: what traffic?! If you're driving along on your own, or in a race, it doesn't matter because the world is dead apparently. Every so often it will breathe life into a race with a car or two, but that's it. The ONLY time you'll find a busy stretch of road is during a Highway Battle. That's it. When you're in a Circuit Race, the civilian cars will randomly drive THROUGH the barriers and suddenly smash into you as they come out, or they'll drive into the barrier and get in your damn way as they turn off! When they're changing lanes, I kid you not, they LOVE to do it when you're about to pass them! They'll suddenly veer off to be in front of you, and completely screw you up! I have even found them to turn a corner and actually come off of the road... for NO viable reason. They just swerve suddenly and come off the road. It's so broken it's hilarious. And they randomly crash too! I drive over hills or around a corner, and I find a small pile up of cars, or cars that have somehow crashed into the wall... As for the bloody racers? They're just as bad. RUBBER BANDING. Why the HELL is EA still allowing this kind of crap? You had rubber banding in UNDERGROUND 1! And that is 11 years old! I could be scraping the rear end of an opponent, I make them hit a wall, I then use some Nitrous to get away, and the opponent is somehow matching my speed. I mean, how is that possible? I know NFS is not realistic in any sense of the word, but rubber banding takes the biscuit. I detest it.
- Unbalanced difficulty. I guess this just relates to the AI again, but I feel this needs its own category. In a Sprint Race for e.g. I would be so far ahead of the competition that I could not even see them on the map. I didn't need to even think about them at all. And for the most part it would be like that in most races. As soon as I crash because of the poorly designed AI traffic, or my car decides to skid off the track, within seconds the opponents are closing in extremely fast! And because of the rubber banding, they can suddenly keep up with me. It's a joke. In other races, I've been struggling to even keep up with the racers in 1st or 2nd. I had a Mazda RX-7 with "Street" level tuning, and I struggled to keep up with a Nissan 240SX. It was endlessly overtaking then falling back again. Eventually I would win, but not without difficulty. And what about the cops? Man oh man are they strange. As soon as I slow down they go nuts! They smash into me like there is no tomorrow. But when I speed up they trail off, leaving me to wreck the joint. One more thing: when I'm literally cruising along the street in my car, and I cruise past the Police, they suddenly go after me, claiming I'm speeding or whatever. It's useless and this just proves how messed up the AI is.
- Useless display of points. I'm not sure if I'm missing something, but when you perform tricks etc. you seem to rack up "points" for lack  of a better word. They add up, but they add up to nothing. And I can't seem to figure out why there are points in the first place. There is no tactical advantage, no bonus, no unlocks for gaining a certain amount of points. It's the same when you smash a fence or hit a car and you see some money pop up for the damage. I understand you causing the "State" money during a pursuit, but whilst cruising in free roam? What's the point in even having either come up?
- Unbalanced tuning. Let me put it this way: My Mazda RX-7 with "Street" level tuning could OUTRUN a LAMBORGHINI. Lamborghini, do you even tune brah?
- Most pointless story I have ever come across! Again, let me put it this way: You're a typical nameless nobody with no voice or face. You are an undercover police officer trying to worm your way in to a drug-smuggling ring of "thugs" (EA's terminlogy, not mine). It literally takes ONE race respectively to impress the top guys and you're suddely their new favourite pet lmao. And before you know it, within a couple of missions, you're already taking them all down by smashing their car's into a thousand pieces. Story writing at its utter worst.
- Also the shortest story ever. You'll complete it I'd say in 5 - 6 hours at best. If you put in maximum effort, I'd say possibly under 5 hours. What a joke.
Look, I could go on and on and on and on with this review, but the truth is, there are SO MANY NEGATIVES and things wrong with this title that I would never be able to recommend it.
After everything however, I can honestly say it has heart. This is a game aimed at the most casual audience possible. This would be enjoyed by young teenagers and children. But I'm 23 years old (today lol it's my birthday!) and I want a game waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay more polished and fleshed out than this. There is some fun to be had with the driving thanks to the "H.D.E." and it will offer something to do for a few hours, but this will quickly dissolve into boredom. EA's more recent efforts with Hot Pursuit 2010, Most Wanted 2012 (despite what people say, it's a great game) and even Rivals (amazing first effort from Ghost Games!) is enough to keep you coming back. I'm not surprised EA Black Box was wiped away as even EA stated that they were being overworked. Here's to 2015, and hoping that two years worth of development time can give us the Need for Speed we've all been waiting for.

I once said, in another review, that I used to play Lego Indiana Jones with my little brother a lot when I was a kid, but it was difficult because of our lack of skill and faulty hardware at every level. Well, there's a secret backstory for that review, because I'm fairly sure that Lego Star Wars was the first game I ever played, and the conditions and brother were even MORE trying then. The disc and laptop were worse, we were younger and thus worse at games, the shared keyboard was even more compact, and we only ever got to play it on long car rides, where every bump on the road knocked the disc around in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ holder and spawned another game-breaking glitch. Truly a crucible of early gaming.
Well, it wasn't the entire thing. The version we had was just Lego Star Wars 2, which was Episodes 4-6 (which happen to be the ones I just completed the story mode for). We didn't get the full package until a couple of years later, when it was one of the two games we got along with our new Wii for Christmas. To justify its existence as 2 games stapled together, it added a few new features, like new bonus levels, a 1v1 mode, and powerups scattered throughout the levels, all of which are fairly pointless. As to the levels themselves, episodes 4-6 are far stronger than episodes 1-3, for what I think are a few reasons: 1, more interesting things happen in the originals; 2, it came out a year later, when all the developers had finally earned their game design degrees; 3 (and this is complete speculation), the devs probably had more love for the originals than for the new ones; and 4, I have more nostalgia for the parts I played first and therefore those parts are better. Shut up, it's true.
And as for the game itself? Well, it's not nearly as polished as Lego Indiana Jones (the devs clearly learned more the more games they made, which is a trend I support), but for what it is, it's fantastic. Coming back, not only was I realizing how much fun I was having in just the first level, but I was also experiencing almost crying levels of nostalgia for things that had all come rushing back from almost a decade ago. I remembered that puzzle with the crane! I remembered wanting to be R2-D2 or Captain Antilles! Oh my God! Rebel Friend! I remembered Rebel Friend!
Anyway, nostalgic tangents aside, the same rules apply for this as they do for Lego Indiana Jones; everything's either good game design, funny and/or goofy, or probably broken (or John Williams's score). Tell you what, if I ever make a game, I'm going to hire all the animators from Traveler's Tales, because those guys know how to do an incredible amount with very little. Look up the intro cutscene for Episode 6, Stage 5. See how they convey all (or at least most of) the conflict and emotion of the scene in the movie, in the space of about 30 seconds, using absolutely no dialogue, with F*CKING LEGO FIGURES? These people are masters!
Also, they managed to nail the vital Stormtrooper balance of adorably bad but taken completely seriously. You should buy the game for just that.
P.S. If you think it's just a game for kids, go to the Zero Punctuation for Lego Indiana Jones and listen to what he has to say about kid-oriented vs. family-oriented. This one's family-oriented.
P.P.S. Like the Indiana Jones review, I haven't played the whole thing through here but I did when I was younger, and I remember all of it.

DLC Quest is a video game that makes fun of microtransactions.
Like this review?  Buy the full version to access the reviewer's commentary, fully revealing his thoughts on the game!  $59.99.
That joke aside, DLC Quest truly is a game which satirizes the practice of games using downloadable content to rake in the Benjamins, so to speak.  Now, if you're wondering, no, this game does not actually use downloadable content in it that requires you to actually pay real life, "earned from your job" money.  That would be redundant.
No, rather, DLC Quest has you collect in-game coins to purchase DLC that is required to progress in the game.  Some of the "DLC" you collect is the ability to walk in a certain direction, and another one goes as far as to require you to buy it if you want to double-jump.  Along your journey to buy them all, you'll encounter several video game references as you stride across this land of imaginary paywalls.  It is a hilarious satire game, but as it stands, if you do not get or like the humor, it is pretty much not worth your money if a satire based on the practices of downloadable content are not up to your liking.
But if you are intrigued, great!  It is not anything too revolutionary gameplay wise, but hopefully it will give you quite the chuckle then and there, and I highly recommend it to anyone who is invested in the video game community or industry.

Love-hate relationship with this game. There are so many ways to play. Even after several playthroughs there are unexplored paths left; just when I think I've seen every option, something new happens. You can play plenty of times without getting bored and the player's adventure always gets me thinking- the main character has a pretty common backstory: they're a struggling artist. That could've just been it, and in real life that's pretty much as far as it goes, but instead they end up on an adventure. It feels realistic in the sense that anybody playing COULD do something like that, but they won't, but as they play they can't help but wonder "What if I did, though?"
The gameplay itself is great; equal parts lighthearted and serious, compelling, many ways to play, and overall good enough to overlook what I'm about to say, but I'm still saying it: The story doesn't make sense. The devs put so much time into character development early on and then just throw it away for the sake of moving things along towards the end. The characters do things that go totally against their development for the sake of setting up a twist ending. The thing about twist endings is that it's supposed to be shocking at first, but then the player thinks about it and has a eureka moment where they realize all of the subtle little hints and nagging things throughout the game that now make sense. It's supposed to ultimately make sense once it sinks in, and this one doesn't.
Despite that, it's an enjoyable game and I'm happy to own it.

I'm not sure how to really start reviewing this game...
It's riddled with mini-games, some better than others (I really hated the boxing, I'll just say that) but overall, this is not what this game is about.
Always Sometimes Monsters is a decision-simulator; you screwed up your life, your ex invites you to his/her wedding, and you try and get there.
You make decisions. Some good, some bad. You never know. Not until your first playthrough.
Because this is a game that requires multiple playthroughs to really "grasp" it, and see all of its endings.
But I guess that's kind of the point. You can play as a character with which you recognize yourself, that you can play as yourself really. It's part relationship simulator, so you can have straight/gay relationships no problem, part eNovel.
And the game can be emotionally hard. Myself, I took a decision at the end which resonated with my own personal history and decisions in the past. And I did have a tightening of my heart. Because I recalled that moment and it made me actually tear up a bit.
But then, the elation that comes with knowing that, right now, I'm good.
The more I think about it, the more I feel it's an introspection simulator. You get from the game what you put into it. You can be good or you can be bad. The choice is definitely yours. Just like in real life.
And as you play, especially on the first playthrough, you'll take decisions... which later on, you might regret taking. Or you may not, especially if you want to know what happens in the storyline if you take a decision instead of another.
Bottom line is, I am not sure how to review this game.
I can definitely recomment this game, that's a given.
But I'm not sure how to describe it or how to review it.
Other than "it's worth the money", I don't know what else to say...

This is, at its core, the story of a family struggling to keep one another's priorities straight. "Video game" is not really the right word for it; I consider this more of an interactive short story. The gameplay is not part what shines here; it's the characters, the choices, and the consequences. The well written and engaging storyline is directly affected by your decisions from beginning to end.
I love that this game forces you to make difficult choices that adults can relate to, without leaning on cheap tropes like many other games that attempt to do the same thing. The family is not fighting for their survival; for once, we have a game where everyday life is enough of a challenge.
Overall I highly recommend this to anybody who appreciates games that really make you feel.

Mark of the Ninja takes a number of risks and does a damn good job in their execution. And speaking of execution, this is the game you want to play if you're looking for more slicey-dicey and killing in your stealth games.
The biggest for starters is the way sight works in this game, basically if they aren't in your line of sight, you can only hear them which is marked by footprints. Different levels of exposure mark how you see your opponents. New Game Plus adds more by further limiting what you can and cannot see. It's hard to explain so I recommend watching a gameplay video to get a better understanding. It all works well and adds an interesting atmospheric effect that really helps the setting.
Even more commendable, each stage is incredibly open ended despite a linear progression. You can really approach a problem from multiple angles which, again, is commendable seeing as the game is a 2D adventure-platformer. It's also entirely possible to go the pacifist route through the levels, it'll certainly help to get used to it as eventually you'll be fighting some nasty foes you can't easily dispose of. Getting to really know your little gadgets and abilities will make your life easier. I also loved how every item had a clear use with only a couple being really situational. Nothing will get you further than learning to outsmart enemies with your darts however, so practice up.
Mark of the Ninja is a good looking, good sounding, smart 2D platforming stealth game that should be worth your attention.

I've now bought this total war 4 times over the course of 12 years. (CDs got scratched up, lost or borrowed and never returned) That alone is a good enough idea of how good this is. Invested at least a few thousand hours over the years, and I can't say that for any other total war. It's no where near as stylish as the new ones graphically, but, that's to be expected.
The gameplay on the strategic map is the best. Possibly one of the best ai that they've made. They will send a lot of assassins after your agents, sneak spies around and try to take away a general teetering on the edge of rebellion and make some surprising attacks. The pope is kind of , to put it mildly, the brown eye in everybody's rear. He'll excommunicate you in a heartbeat. The early game consists of mass stacks of peasants and archers, eventually leading to pretty diversified armies later in the game. The ai is prone to making "specialized" armies on occasion, however, in those situations they're usually attack with 3+ armies. The viking invasion expansion is a smaller campaign that's just as good as the early, high, late period campaigns with some different mechanics/building trees and some different standard of units.
Battle controls come off as aged compared to this day and age, but you won't be losing many battles due to clunky controls. You may run into path finding issues, which has always been a problem with the series for the most part. Seiges get epic later on in the game with you having to breach several layers of walls under archer/early musket fire. Artillery is really only effective during sieges until about mid way through the game when you start to get the more impressive pieces of machinery. Armies are generally well balanced, however, an army of gothic knights with crossbows/archers can just wreck face left and right if used properly. It can still be countered, just with a more specialized army.
On the modern systems, this will run quite well. I have windows 7, never had a problem with the disks and I don't expect any problems on here. I will say, 1920x1080 resolution makes the interface incredibly small and a bit laggy. Best off played at 1280x800 or so just to have the interface and text be able to be read without having to get right up to the monitor. If you played it back when it came out, you won't notice a difference in much of a performance from then compared to now. If anything, battles are more stable when there's 4k units battling it out compared to how it was way back.
For 10 bucks, you honestly can't go wrong for a great classic strategy game. If you still have the disks, buy it anyways just so you won't have to worry about it being gone forever.

*Too long? Scroll down for Pros & Cons.*
Batman: Arkham Asylum. It's the game that re-instilled faith in super hero games. It's the game that inspired the play style of Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor. It's the story of how movie/book characters CAN translate into videogame format and succeed.
So, why do I not recommend this title when it has a sea of positive recommendations? Well...first you have to understand super hero games have been floundering for years. We've had the insanely difficult Silver Surfer on NES and the infamous Superman 64. In the years since then, comic book fans have endured those outsourced, tight budget movie tie-ins with unforgiving gameplay and numerous glitches. It's only been in the last several years that Marvel and DC have taken gaming seriously. Batman: Arkham Asylum is...or was the first step in the right direction. This felt like a fresh start. From its professional voice cast to cinematic gameplay, we knew the glitchy games of yesteryear were gone.
Unfortunately, for everything it does right, it falters at the home stretch. For starters, combat is repetitive and does not become any better with upgrades. You'll be punching with one button and countering attacks with another. There's also little diversity in the opposition. You'll either be fighting venomous plants or humans with guns/fists. The most disappointing part for me was fully upgrading all four kinds of batarangs and not having a single type KO mobs (the sonic batarang can be upgraded to KO a *specific* kind of enemy, but it is only usable once per room). Each one will only daze opponents for a few seconds. Fist fighting is really the only way to take care of threats permanently. In addition to these disadvantages, baddies are super aware of every batarang you throw at them. They'll alert their friends and make life miserable for Bruce should they be carrying guns. Add up all these traits and the Caped Crusader becomes the disaster of stealth, rather than the master of it. Oddly enough, the game doesn't seem to have a mini map. I assume this is to give it a cinematic feel, but in doing so it limits my sense of location to the pause menu map. I've spent a good portion of the game just looking for my objectives and secrets through that menu. I've hardly played an open world in recent years that forewent the mini map. Games like Just Cause 2, Red Dead Redemption, and L.A. Noire wouldn't be as easy to play or for that matter, entertaining without one.
In closing, I guess DC overall just isn't for me. I bought this for only $5, hoping I could finally say I'm a Batman fan, but alas it isn't so. The gameplay is a mixed bag, the story doesn't draw me, and Bat's "don't kill the villain" ideology has never felt more tedious to achieve (now that I'm in his shoes).
Batman: Arkham Asylum is the Batman game longtime fans deserved, but not the one I needed. For all the faults and failings it corrects from the stained past of super hero games, it still lacks sufficient bat weapons, bat gameplay, and bat story.
I give Batman: Arkham Asylum a 6.5 out of 10
Pros:
+ Wonderful voice performances for Batman and all major villains
+ Grappling hook action
+ Remote Control Batarang (that you can catch!)
+ Batman's suit takes a beating over the course of the game
+ Blowing up walls with explosive gel
Cons:
- Voice actors Tom Kane (Warden Quincy Sharp/Amadeus Arkham) and Wally Wingert (Riddler/various voices) each voice more than one character... resulting in a loss of unique identities
- No ingame mini map
- Four different types of batarangs with very little chance of subduing the opposition
- Enemies with guns will shoot you down easily even in fully upgraded armor
- Mobs blend in too well with the normal environment, making Detective mode preferable
- Difficulty ranges drastically from room to room
- A forgettable story with a weak pay off

Despite stunning visuals and an enormous budget, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a convoluted, inconsequential, frustrating, tedious and badly concluded addition to the franchise.
The full review:
Prague is the game's overworld, and it is impressively rendered. While there isn't much sense of the city being alive (cars are eternally parked, there's no day/night cycle etc), it is beautifully designed.
Much of the voice over talent is perfectly decent and obviously well-funded. However, the uninspiring script detracts from the performances.
Although there's little innovation of the Praxis levelling system itself, the game introduces a lot of fascinating new abilities for Adam Jensen, and several are quite inspired.
The game's combat and stealth remain reasonable and engaging, and the choices of play styles (combat vs stealth) meaningfully affect how levels progress.
The writing is long-winded and uncompelling: the story lacks the expansive, exotic and atmosphere-building elements of the original and best Deus Ex game. Instead we receive what boils down to a narrowly-focused office drama. No amount of graphical glitz can conceal this mediocrity, and for Deus Ex (a game for whom plot is essential) it is unforgivable.
Mankind Divided's characters are forgettable. Amid the sheer volume of expository dialogue, which I soon found myself skipping, the people I was working for, investigating, or otherwise became a blur of tedium. They were uninteresting, without any mystery or passion behind them, and I could not be moved to care about any of them.
The game's attempts to shed linearity fail, and badly. The second mission, where you head to a sort of prison area for augmented people, is designed in many layers. Progression however is over-complex obstacle course of ascending/descending these layers. The repetitive voice over clips of the inhabitants and the guards make the entire experience unpleasant to navigate. Also, a couple of pistols and plenty of ammo sits around in the residential areas, destroying any sense that this is a credible jail.
With the plot so dull, and the action/graphical elements the stronger points, I had the sense of playing a high budget but banal action game, not a Deus Ex title.
--
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided has little sense of mysterious discovery or adventure, no rabbit hole of revelation, let alone a sense of danger or pursual by malevolence. In short, everything that made Deus Ex unique and memorable is replaced by middling narrative and tedium.
The gamer must go through the motions and wade through lots of reference-stuffed babble padded out with espionage tropes and caricatures. The game's abrupt ending, perhaps the most acutely awful and disjointed portion, is a final, clumsy coup de grace from what is a monumental fumbling of the franchise. I can't recommend this title, other than as an example of how not to do Deus Ex.

I once said, in another review, that I used to play Lego Indiana Jones with my little brother a lot when I was a kid, but it was difficult because of our lack of skill and faulty hardware at every level. Well, there's a secret backstory for that review, because I'm fairly sure that Lego Star Wars was the first game I ever played, and the conditions and brother were even MORE trying then. The disc and laptop were worse, we were younger and thus worse at games, the shared keyboard was even more compact, and we only ever got to play it on long car rides, where every bump on the road knocked the disc around in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ holder and spawned another game-breaking glitch. Truly a crucible of early gaming.
Well, it wasn't the entire thing. The version we had was just Lego Star Wars 2, which was Episodes 4-6 (which happen to be the ones I just completed the story mode for). We didn't get the full package until a couple of years later, when it was one of the two games we got along with our new Wii for Christmas. To justify its existence as 2 games stapled together, it added a few new features, like new bonus levels, a 1v1 mode, and powerups scattered throughout the levels, all of which are fairly pointless. As to the levels themselves, episodes 4-6 are far stronger than episodes 1-3, for what I think are a few reasons: 1, more interesting things happen in the originals; 2, it came out a year later, when all the developers had finally earned their game design degrees; 3 (and this is complete speculation), the devs probably had more love for the originals than for the new ones; and 4, I have more nostalgia for the parts I played first and therefore those parts are better. Shut up, it's true.
And as for the game itself? Well, it's not nearly as polished as Lego Indiana Jones (the devs clearly learned more the more games they made, which is a trend I support), but for what it is, it's fantastic. Coming back, not only was I realizing how much fun I was having in just the first level, but I was also experiencing almost crying levels of nostalgia for things that had all come rushing back from almost a decade ago. I remembered that puzzle with the crane! I remembered wanting to be R2-D2 or Captain Antilles! Oh my God! Rebel Friend! I remembered Rebel Friend!
Anyway, nostalgic tangents aside, the same rules apply for this as they do for Lego Indiana Jones; everything's either good game design, funny and/or goofy, or probably broken (or John Williams's score). Tell you what, if I ever make a game, I'm going to hire all the animators from Traveler's Tales, because those guys know how to do an incredible amount with very little. Look up the intro cutscene for Episode 6, Stage 5. See how they convey all (or at least most of) the conflict and emotion of the scene in the movie, in the space of about 30 seconds, using absolutely no dialogue, with F*CKING LEGO FIGURES? These people are masters!
Also, they managed to nail the vital Stormtrooper balance of adorably bad but taken completely seriously. You should buy the game for just that.
P.S. If you think it's just a game for kids, go to the Zero Punctuation for Lego Indiana Jones and listen to what he has to say about kid-oriented vs. family-oriented. This one's family-oriented.
P.P.S. Like the Indiana Jones review, I haven't played the whole thing through here but I did when I was younger, and I remember all of it.

I took a trip back to my childhood with this game and I gotta say: playing through both LEGO Star Wars games in one collection is pretty neat. I still remember the novelty of battling across the stars with my friends as we discovered the secrets of Free Play mode in every level. Tt Games really nailed replayability in these games, encouraging players to return to previously inaccessible areas of a level by using unlockable heroes with their special abilities.
One thing has to be said about the original LEGO Star Wars, though: it hasn't held up especially well. I found the sequel to be the much more enjoyable and memorable of the two thanks to its clever level design and quirky humor. The first game is noticably slower paced and lacks the visually gags that add so much to its sequel. Regardless, it was nice to take a trip down memory lane and remind myself what all successive LEGO franchise games built themselves upon.
It's really hard to say no to a package that packs in so much content. Hundreds of iconic Star Wars characters and tons of replayability keep me coming back for more from the galaxy far, far, away.

This is a very easy game to review. If you like Diablo-like games, Torchlight II is right up your alley. I played the first Torchlight for quite a while, but never finished it because it felt incomplete. Torchlight II addresses and fixes many of the issues I had with the first Torchlight.
It's not up to the gold standard that Diablo 2 was (despite that game's archaic mechanics and graphics), which I would still recommend over any other loot-based ARPG. But, Torchlight II scratches Diablo itch better than any other Diablo-like game I've ever played. No always-online requirement, no micro-transactions or P2W, you don't even need a 3rd party account. What you get is a fully featured Diablo-inspired game.
The only negatives I can come up with is that it's often hard to see massive improvements in weapons and skills when you upgrade them because of how incremental it can be. But, that's not much different than Borderlands. Secondly, I've no idea what the story is in this game. Something about an alchemist bad guy that you're supposed to stop and magic batteries and something. I don't care. The story interaction is minimal in this game and can be complete ignored if you want (like what I'm doing). That might be a turn-off for some, but I like that I can just pick up this game and do crazy AoE attacks on bad guys for a half-hour at a time and not need to worry about story arcs.
If you've any interest in ARPGs, this for $4 is an amazing deal, especially with the mods.

I usually don't take the time to write reviews, but this one deserves it. Gnomoria is a fantastic game that I have been playing on-and-off for quite a while now, since it was in early access. I haven't played a lot of similar games, like the one most compare it to: Dwarf Fortress, but I was hooked on this one pretty fast.
The main reason I want to write this review though is to counter the recent reviews the game has received for being 'abandoned by the developers'. First of all, if you're going to say something like that, do your research. This game was made by one guy. A single person. Not a development TEAM. One person, who had a dream. He put in massive amounts of work on this game, even worked with the modding community to help them integrate everything before he was even finished. I think that, taking that into consideration, this is a pretty amazing piece of work. Then he had a kid, so his life got a little hectic, but he still did what he needed to do, because this game was a big deal to him.
All that being said, is the game perfect? No. Very rarely do I ever see a 'perfect' game. If that's what you're looking for, go to sleep and have some dreams. Maybe you'll find one there. But for what it is, this game is fantastic, and I love it dearly. Even in early access when it was super buggy, it was worth the cost. I'll keep coming back to this one every so often, simply because it's fun and addicting.

Prior to Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon, I had only played the original Far Cry on PC. I did play Instincts, but found it so profoundly mediocre I actually returned it without finishing it first. My memories of the original are faint, and limited to an alternately boring and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hard jungle game with completely nonfunctional stealth mechanics. While it's only marginally easier to stealth in this game, that really doesn't matter worth a♥♥♥♥♥♥
Why? Because in Blood Dragon, you are US Army Sergeant Rex Power Colt, Mark IV Cyber-Commando. Half man, half machine, and 100% one-liner-spewing, cyborg heart-crunching, gun-toting, tanto-swinging, Michael Biehn-voiced ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Your mission: infiltrate a tropical island that has been taken over by rogue Colonel Sloan and his motorcycle helmet-wearing cyborg flunkies, the Omega Force.
Blood Dragon is a love letter to the cinematic excesses of the '80s. The cutscenes are rendered in low resolution a la Ninja Gaiden, the vulgarity is plentiful, creative and childish, everything down to your guns is plastered with neon lights, visible scanlines cross your screen, the collectibles consist largely of VHS tapes and old TV sets, the bad guys look like Rollerball players, the music is all synths by Powerglove, almost everything is prefixed by cyber- or robo-, and it is absolutely crammed with stock tropes, lampshade hanging, tongue-in-cheek one-liners and references from start to finish, starting with Rex's pistol: no less then Robocop's burst-fire Beretta, replete with its enormous vented compensator. The sniper rifle (with optional explosive rounds) also looks much like the Cobra cannon from the same movie. And, amusingly enough, the shotgun is the lever-action Winchester made famous by Terminator 2- and it is among the nastiest shotguns in gaming, able to be upgraded to a whopping four barrels, with incendiary ammo. You also have access to a bland-but-effective assault rifle modeled on the Calico M950, like the plasma rifles of Terminator, that can be upgraded to fire lasers, a bow for silent ranged kills, a flamethrower, and a minigun. Get close enough to enemies and you can also perform instant-kill animations, which can be chained if enemies are close together, and into finishers such as throwing a shuriken at a nearby enemy, which is as satisfying as it is lucrative, rewarding a large experience bonus.
I don't have any experience with the more recent Far Crys aside from this one, but if the combat is at all similar I'd probably enjoy those, too. However, I have the sense that Rex is deliberately overpowered in comparison to Whitey Mc-Shootsbrownpeople of Far Crys 1, 2 and 3, or the not white-but-still-raised-in-the-US dude in Far Cry 4. From the get go, you can sprint at great speed, breathe underwater and survive any fall without damage. You also enjoy 2000s-era FPS-style sectional health regeneration, with the ability to carry up to three instant, full-health restoring injectors. Rex gains experience from dispatching enemies, completing objectives and stealing their all their crap, and upon leveling gains either an additional health section or a new passive ability. You can carry four of the game's seven guns at any one time, as well as a stack of grenades, remote charges and mines, ensuring you are well-equipped for any encounter. There are handful of vehicles scattered about, including off-road trucks, motorboats, jetskis and gliders, though your high sprint speed combined with free fast travel between liberated garrisons renders them somewhat superfluous. The trucks and boats do have mounted miniguns though.
There are a handful of story missions that comprise lengthy, entertaining battles. Outside of that there is some freeroam play in the form of a handful of garrisons to liberate, which in turn unlock sidequests that consist of freeing a hostage or hunting down a specific target enemy. These sidequests unlock new attachments for your weapons, which can be purchased at vending machines at any liberated garrison. Collecting certain numbers of the aforementioned VHS tapes and TVs, as well as text logs from a certain evil scientist, also unlock weapon parts. I clocked in about six hours total to do everything I wanted to do, which is honestly a respectable length for a game of this type. I have grown sightly weary of sandbox action games, mostly in their plodding length, but Blood Dragon is mercifully brief for the kind of game it is, and never wears itself out in that time.
I received Blood Dragon as a birthday present from a friend, but I would have gladly purchased it myself and I encourage you to do the same. If you like old-school, action-heavy FPS, 80s media, cheesy one-liners and a story that doesn't jump the shark so much as punch it in its stupid sandpapery face, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a game for you.

I'm writing this review because recently I made the decision to quit playing this game. I peaked at 19th in EU and 59th globally. When I started playing, this game was great to play with my friends, we used to have alot of fun and I enjoyed learning the mechanics of the game and getting better. But as I became more competitive, and started winning more games, problems with the game started  to reveal itself. There was an increasing amount of passive play, and although this does the job of winning, it's not awfully fun to watch or play against. The developers tried their best to change this by adding chain dodges, a feature which allows you to move faster and encourages the use of strings. But this was really a small fix for the much larger problem at hand- The game encourages passive play. It's very hard to approach someone that's camping on a wall or chaindodging backwards without being punished and eventually losing the game. If you have no clue about what i'm talking about and you just want to play for fun or casually with your friends then that's really what this game is for. It's definitely the most fun casual game i've ever played, but if you play these games competitively it's probably not good and I wouldn't recommend it.

There have been many superhero games throughout the years.  Most of them have been sidescrolling "beat 'em ups" in the  vein of the Final Fight series.  Others were horrible adaptations like the Superman game for the N64.  Arkham Asylum has been, with few minor exceptions, one of the most on-point adaptations of a superhero property into a game that I have ever played.
First, the format, a 3-D "metroidvania/Legend of Zelda" type deal where new tools open new areas and items to get, plays nicely into the feel of the game.   That same format also helps with the "lone hero" feeling that is in many ways the essence of Batman.  You feel like yes, you are alone, but you aren't out of your depth.  Also, the classic animated series voices help set the tone of the game; dark with just a bit of humor here and there.
The game world is lush and well rendered, created in that gritty style also befiting a game about The Bat.  Ruined sewers, secret tunnels, and crawling through airways and up walls all give this sense of being secretive, careful, and thought out.  The world you have been given to play in is tailor made to adhere to the common action/stealth tropes that exist in other Batman works.
The combat and movement can be . . . halting at times.  In particular the "hold button to run" command, something that I thought I had seen the end of when analog sticks came to prominent use, feels forced and unintuitive.  When the combat flows, slighlty pauses on a big hit, and Batman is leaping to and fro kicking, punching and generally kicking♥♥♥♥♥ it looks good, and it feels good to be doing it, but there aren't any ways to "do" the one move you like, really.  And the combat system is at its best when you have maxed out all your available attack options.
The fightable enemies are simple and never waver from the basic human stock of "Joker goon fight"; they are either unarmed, armed with a melee weapon, armed with a firearm, a stun baton, or they are giant mutant freaks.  This includes the "boss fights", making the gameplay and world far more engaging than the actual combat.  That said, most of the combat is short and simple.  I think the longest normal skirmish took maybe a minute.  And the best parts of combat aren't specifically the combat so much as the setpieces where you have high perches to disappear to.  You can swoop down, take out a goon, and then grapple up into the shadows, listening and watching as the other goons start to freak out as you take them down one by one.
And finally the story, which at least matches the quality of the old animated Batman series movies for plots.  Joker has a crazy plan, and Batman has to stop him.  The winding way Bruce has to do this is what makes up the bulk of the game.  Some of the story points feel contrived, but overall, the story flows from point to point in a logical way.  What helps in this is that Batman himself often tells the player (and Oracle over his headset) the next step.  And when Batman tells you something in this game, a combination of the voicework and the writing just seems to make the next plotpoint make sense.
With solid voicework, a lonely, beautifully crafted world, and a combat and stealth system that is only sometimes marred by its own trappings, this is a solid, wonderfully made title that anyone who counts themselves as a superhero fan in general or a Batman fan in particular should own.

The Novelist unfortunately represents the main issue that afflicts choices-driven games. If it is possible with just a little common sense (i.e. not actively trying to fail) to obtain the best possible scenario che makes all the member of the Novelist's family happy, I really think this game wasn't able to get its point across. What is the purpouse of going through hard and heartbreaking choices, putting someone's interests above the other's if in the end everybody will be able to fullfill themselves?
In the end, while the idea of observing a family from an "outside" point of view could be interesting, the choices you make bare so little value it makes the whole experience extremely bland.

If you like a story that is all about narrative, you will like the Novelist. If you are looking for a game where the choices can make a large difference, or it provides anything beyond narrative, you’ll be vastly disappointed.
The Novelist is a lightweight choose-your-adventure story about a family of artists: a novelist father who is struggling with his new book; a painter mother who tries to get back to work and save her marriage; and a son with great artistic potential, but serious learning difficulties.
All nine chapters follow the same pattern: each family member has a problem where the solution just happens to contradict the others’ needs. You play as a “ghost” reading aptly placed notes and peeking into their memories, then you must choose one of them who gets their wish fulfilled, one that gets a half-solution, and leave one of them hanging.
So, in essential, all family members have a good, a neutral, and a bad outcome. This is true for the entire game: no matter what you did in the individual chapters, the final “score” determines their individual fate, which makes the core mechanic of the game largely pointless.
The narrative itself is great and the chapters randomise at each play through, yet the replay value is still quite low. So, if you don’t mind paying this much money for what is essentially a 2-hour story about a Hallmark-card family and their completely storybook problems, you won’t regret playing it. But otherwise it’s nothing but a nice artistic experiment.

The Novelist is mostly in the "explore the house and find out what happened" mold of games like Gone Home, with two major differences. One is that your choices do explicitly change the story -- so much so that the game makes it explicitly clear what will happen if you make your choice. And it's not just CYOA; there are nine chapters, and a choice to be made concerning each of three characters at the end, plus the ability to add in a compromise between two characters if you've done enough exploring.
The other difference is that you have the option to play in story mode, in which you're free to run around however you like. You are a ghost, and you can inhabit any light source, so it becomes quite easy to zip around the house instead of having to walk everywhere. The other mode is stealth, in which you cannot let any of the family see you, or there are consequences. In this mode, you have to use the lights most of the time, although the level of difficulty added is minimal.
This is a fun game for anyone who likes this kind of storytelling, but especially for people who aren't gamers. The controls couldn't be simpler, and there are permanent prompts as to which key to push. The info screen tells you precisely what you've done and what you still need to do at all times, including optional choices. A less charitable way of putting it is that the game holds your hand, but experienced gamers won't even notice after a while.
Other reviewers have noted that as well done as the game is, and as much as it feels like real people in their real lives, it is all a little depressing. There's an optional part of the game where you find clues, mostly letters, from things that happened in the past, and while there's hints of your existence being sensed by others, the horror aspect mainly ends there and it's all just rather sad, though the whole game is splendidly written enough that it doesn't bore. I was just hoping for a little more to do with the supernatural aspects that are teased, but never deliver.
I'm going to replay it at least once with a completely different approach. Instead of trying to basically appease everyone with my choices, I'm deliberately going to ruin one of their lives. It's giving nothing away to say that the title character has taken his family to a very secluded, possibly haunted place so he can deal with his writer's block, so you can probably guess which movie I'm going to try to enact.

Somewhat quick and pretty heartwrenching, The Novelist is a game all about choices and juggling way too many things.
You don't play as Dan, the Novelist in question, but as a benevolent spirit possessing the house whispering things to its patrons. Most of the gameplay is just going from lamp to lamp, going around the house without being spotted, though there's also an option to turn it off and just play for the story. Either works fine though you might want to have it off as while the stealth mechanic is immersive, it's mostly a way of keeping it more interactive which is weak enough already. It lives in an interesting fashion in this way.
The story itself is much stronger as you have to make small decisions which will help Dan with his writing career, keep his marriage together, and put some time aside for their son as well. If you spend time learning about the whole story you can make some good decisions, though more often than not you'll have to make painful compromises leaving few happy though proper planning and reaction can bring a happy ending for all three members of the family. I didn't, but I got close. All the while rather sad atmospheric piano music plays in the background making everything a lot harder than it needs to be. Oh, and every playthrough randomizes the different events that occur in the household which livens things up a bit.
So overall it's a good interesting engrossing yet short game. If you feel on the ropes about it you should probably wait for a sale. Otherwise it's definately worth a play/read.

Story (9/10):
Batman: Arkham Asylum is one of the best games I have ever played.  You play, as the title suggests, as *dramatic pause* Batman!  Armed with many iconic gadgets like the batarang, grapple, smoke bombs, and many more, it is your mission to put a stop to the Joker's plans within the Asylum.
The story is exciting, and unique.  As you progress, you must adapt and master new skills as objectives become more difficult to complete.  Iconic characters will make appearances as you progress.  Most will try to kill you, some will try to pull a fast one and try to backstab you, still one in particular will even try to eat you.  You will be in danger from start to finish, captivated by the eerie environment and developing story.
Visuals (10/10):
Arkham Asylum is a bit dated now, so the graphics are not considered as stunning as they once were.  However, maxed out, it still looks very good.  The asylum is true to its comic book origins, meaning it is dark, depressing, and gives off the feeling that something more sinister is lurking behind the walls than just the criminally insane.
Gameplay (10/10):
The world of Arkham Asylum is free exploration, but to stay interested and invested in the game, you can't really deviate from the story because the story is linear and without side missions to distract you.  Personally, I am not bothered by this because there is quite a bit of problem solving and each area you enter presents a new challenge that require different approaches, so you aren't doing the same thing over and over.
The main story is fairly long probably about 15 to 20 hours depending on the difficulty.  On top of that, you have a couple of miscellaneous “missions” like doing all of the Riddler Challenges and examing the artifacts found in the Asylum.  While many find these boring, I personally enjoyed going back and doing these because they offered sereral easter eggs by referencing events and characters from the comics that I enjoyed.  If this isn't your kind of thing, it is easily skipped.
This game is in third person, so it relies on a very effective free-flow combat system based on combos.  It mixes classic fighting with silent takedowns and special combo moves that create the classic Batman that can take anyone in a fight.  Included in the fighting system are the gadgets.  The gadgets create a whole new host of ways to creatively finish off opponets in both direct and indirect combat.
Many complain about the fact that the Batmobile and Batwing are not present in the game except for short stints, and are not even player operated.  While this is unfortunate, the nature of the game taking place inside a small, finite area really defeats the use of either one.
Sound (8/10):
In terms of music and sound effects, Arkham Ayslum employs them to great effect.  While the soundtrack isn’t really memorable, the small things like dripping water, metal clanking against metal, and other small things add to the immersion.  The environmental and combat sounds are actually quite good.  Unfortunately the dialogs are hit or miss, which sometimes hurts the characters.
Replay value (9/10):
While the plot is linear and there aren't any choices which would change the story in any way, the game provides countless hours of fun as probably the best batman simulator on the market.  If the story mode gets boring, there are always the numerous challenge missions that are not part of the story that are fun to play.
Conclusion (9.2/10):
Batman: Arkham Asylum is a very good game, with an unforgettable setting, an engaging plot, and a loose ends that set up future games.  Overall, it is definitely one of those games which you have to play at least once and I highly recommend it.

Cons -
The interface has not aged well, it's usable but hardly intuitive, hotkeys are lacking and WASD navigation of the campaign map isn't possible.

I highly recommend this game!
The long awaited sequel of the award winning Deus Ex: Human Revolution!
Was it worth the wait? I would say yes. With a tiny but….
I has anxious and hopeful of the time when Adam Jensen would once again grace my computer screen, and when he finally did I nearly cried with happiness.
Having recently upgraded to a, worthy of the name, ‘gaming computer’ I was able to appreciate the full beauty that is Deus Ex: MD. However, as the saying goes, looks aren’t everything; but they help! :D
I finished the game with a slight taste of: “Oh… that’s it?” But boy what a ride!
Please play this game, if you are a fan, if you love stealth games that give you the option to Never kill! and if you yearn to be in a world where every detail makes you feel that you are part of it and that your actions have meaning. Adam Jensen kicks butt literally or not, to your heart’s content, and if you are patient, Deus Ex will wow you again in 3 years or so! *hint*hint* :D
What did I like?
+ The characters
+ The story
+ The gorgeous graphics
+ The voice acting
+ The world
+ The music
+ The path choices
What did I dislike?
- The short length
- The somewhat linear story
- The A.I. of the enemies
- The cliffhanger
*the rest of this review may contain spoilers*
If you are not familiar with Adam Jensen, the phrase ‘tall, dark and handsome’ might be of help, to describe him, if like me, you are a woman ;)  otherwise I would say, a serious, quiet, intelligent, tough as nails, secret agent, who is 10 million times cooler than 007 (sorry Sean).
A short and albeit simplistic description, but I’d rather leave you to find out more for yourselves.
If you know Jensen from the previous Deux Ex then introductions are unecessary. If you are playing this game I would hope that it’s as much thanks to the main character as to the game itself.
Rest assured that, the cast is not reduced to Jensen, the number of interesting people who our character interacts with have, thankfully, increased in this game. Between the ‘Hacktivist’ the ‘Director’ the ‘Brother in arms’ the 'Augments Doc' the ‘Pilot’ the ‘Martyr’ and the ‘Bad guy’ the stories they bring into the plot keep you, not just curious but more importantly, hooked. Mind you, this isn’t just the second game but rather chapter 1. More on that later.
Choices matter! Now more than ever, there will be more than one occasion where you won’t be sure what to chose or who to help. And you may lose access to certain areas or rewards for it! This however, simply means that you must replay the game. :)  Or, my advice? Multiples saves at certain moments of the game. You will be able to redo a specific mission or chapter without restarting the game from scratch! Nothing new but practicality ‘oblige’.
But enough about the RPG aspect, let’s be serious, that’s not what this game is about. :)
It’s all about the gadgets the tech, and my doesn’t it look shiny! All the main options from the first game are there, but you can add a few neat tricks to them.
Whether you prefer stealth or action, both will have their share of goodies fear not.
I’m a stealth player myself, no connection with the achievements, lol.
Going invisible, being silent, immunity to electricity, hacking from the distance; very cool.
For those of you who like a more confrontational style, you won’t be disappointed either, plenty of fire and explosions will be available, the ‘shield’ and the ‘cannon’ are very interesting appliances. You may run short of bullets but, grab all fallen weapons and sell them! ;)
Be warned however, the game has at least one mission which will require either the perfect stealth agent or the toughest as nails tank. Best of luck either way!
Running out of inventory space? You may remember Jensen's appartement, you have a safe there, or if you can't be bothered, drop your stuff on the floor. :D
I know I placed I.A. as a negative aspect, mostly because, often times, it makes the game either irritating or too easy. Neither good you’ll agree.
The story itself. Yes I’m back to that, sorry it’s my favorite part. XD It IS somewhat linear in the sense that all roads lead to Rome, you’ll never be in doubt as to where you’re going next, or even how to get here. However in between mission’s you’re free to explore Prague as you like, and in it you will find hundreds of bits of story in the form of emails. Read them carefully, they will tell you everything, or almost. There I felt was an amazing idea! And it's an integral part of the game.
More areas (within the city itself) become available throughout the game, but the world could be considered as small.
Finally, the biggest fault with Deus Ex: MD is for me, it’s short length. Mind you, I explored and re-explored and replayed this game quite considerably, so that accounts for my 107 hours of game time. But, it is possible to finish it, the main story at least, in 15 hours, for a non-hardcore gamer like myself. Half that for a pro!
Worse still, is the Single Boss Fight. Yes you read that correctly I’m afraid.
I did not use the word ‘cliffhanger’ by chance earlier, the game does not end here. The real 'bad guy' is still out there, so Jensen's job, and ours, is not finished yet.
It is my hope therefore, that, however relative the success may be for this game, Eidos and Square Enix do not make us wait too long for the sequel.
The story has promise, but you can’t help but feel that the best is still to come, in another game. But until then, this Deus Ex gives us a glimpse of what the future will bring, and boy is it worth the wait!
Finally please note that all opinions written here are personal and I mean no offense to anyone.
Kind regards,
Keiyan

If brutally hard, well-made puzzle games are your thing, as they are mine, this is a must-get.
...But:
Just going to set one thing clear, from my initial playthrough of this game (about 10 levels beaten so far): If you see reviews like "GAME SO HARD ugggggh" and "HAHA PUZZLE GAME DARK SOULS" and buy this because HA HA you beat the first boss of Dark Souls eventually, you're going to get dunked on by this game within the first 5 minutes. Seriously, the cutesy graphics and oddly calming music and sound effects may remind you of a casual/mobile game, but this is definitely NOT a casual puzzler.
This game doesn't have a difficulty curve, but a difficulty cliff. For Dark Souls type games, this is fine. It's a challenge. In the puzzle genre, this idea works VERY differently. "Getting used to the mechanics" in a puzzle game is a lot different than in a real-time combat game. If the puzzle genre isn't your bag, you will not get any bang for your buck on this one, as 15 minutes in, the literal 4th puzzle in the game will prove extremely difficult.
...As for me, I love the puzzle genre, and feel starved for hard yet well-made games in it. And this one has both the difficulty and the polish. Huge thumbs up for puzzle game fans.
...and a probably-will-be-ignored  but definite "no" for the RAAAAAAGE SO HARD ARRRRRRRGH crowd.
