So this is Lego Star Wars - The Complete Saga, it's the sequel to Lego Star Wars II, which was in turn a Sequel to Lego Star Wars. If you've played this as a kid on the Ps2 like I have, you know what you're getting into, but regardless here's a review.
The Complete Saga features the 6 pre-force awakens episodes - the prequel era episodes through the original trilogy - and levels are based on scenes and events in the movies.
So the game starts you off in the first level of Episode 1, the Phantom Menace, in the Trade Federation blockade ship Episode 1 largely started in. You play as Qui-Gon and Obi-Wan and try to escape from the ship, the first level serving as a tutorial on how the functions of the game work, such as the force, building, studs, minikits, deflecting blaster shots, and access panels only characters can access.
After you finish that level, you're free to go to any of the other episodes of the Prequels/OT. Which is rather nice and actually really well thought out, while you can continue with the plot of TPM, you're allowed to jump to any of the other episodes and start off at level 1. You don't have to complete all the levels of TPM to move on to AOTC, for example. The game is really open and free, and as such comes off as a really good title.
The gameplay is just what you would expect from a Lego game, it's fun, interactive, and runs great. Most props are composed of Legos in the game, with the exception of environments (Which still look good) and it gives the game and levels a great atmosphere that you expect from a Lego game.
As you go through the game, you can unlock more things with money, be it custom characters, cheats, or hints from the store. And can use the characters when replaying missions.
Meanwhile, the explanation of the story in the game is arguably better than how it's explained in some of the films. This being an early Lego game,(since modern Lego games seem to have dialogue) there is no dialogue and thus the cutscenes explaining the story have to rely on only visuals to get the plot across, and it's honestly genius how they explain some of the Episode Plots. The cutscenes for the Phantom Menace Episode, for example, are not only more funny than the actual film it's based on, but the game's explanations of the story in the episode in the cutscenes more easily explain the plot of the film, and you're able to get a gist of what's going on. Which, in the case of TPM, where the conflict is based on a trade blockade dispute,(and honestly one of the most difficult plots to explain due to how messy it is for a Star Wars film) is very important for game cutscenes to be short and to the point, and this game is great at explaining stuff by way of 15 second cutscenes.
The game runs fantastically and I've yet to find a PC of mine that cannot run it, it's greatly optimized and allows for great customization of settings, including the controls. Though the mouse cannot be bound as a key, which confused me until I realized that the setup of the game is for it to be entirely played without a mouse, which is cool, but if you have a controller I suggest you use it for this.
If you're looking for online Multiplayer though, you won't find it here, the multiplayer service is local (i.e two people would have to share the PC screen) but I don't blame the game for this as the original game on the consoles was also local and without online multiplayer connection. Though if you want to set up Steam Big Picture and grab some remotes, it's probably possible to mimic a console.

LEGO Star Wars - The Complete Saga, takes the Original Trilogy of; A New Hope, The Empire Strikes Back, and Return of the Jedi, and combines it with; The Phantom Menace, The Clone Wars, and Revenge of the Sith. It was released in 2007.
As is custom with LEGO games, you collect Gold Bricks to unlock additional content, collect coins to purchase things, and complete missions to further the story. A difference between the Complete Saga and the original  LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game, are two previously deleted levels, The Bounty Hunter's Pursuit, and Anakin's Flight. These are unlockable by obtaining Gold Bricks.
As with many of the other LEGO games, Single Player Mode as well as Co-operative Two-Player mode is available locally. Having played this particular game on both the PS3, as well as PC, I can say I haven't seen any difference. If you enjoy the LEGO series, this is a must have for the collection. If you are new to LEGO games, LEGO Star Wars - The Complete Saga is a great place to start.

The biggest accomplishment of this game is how it opens a window into the hell of struggling game design, self-aware in its obsession to deliver complex game structure and say something meaningful. The developers are present as background characters poking themselves for constantly failing at this, usually with a good dose of humour.
Everything in this game is built around choice and consequences, and gosh dang can it bring you down. It's probably best not to go into the story if you're interested in playing at all--just surprise yourself and and look up no discussions...until maybe you hit the requisite twist ending unprepared.
Most of the design faults pop up near the end. So many decisions and their impacts snowball together; it ends up falling apart fairly sadly, reminiscent of Mass Effect's closure(--in reasoning, not in disappointment). The structure also moves more and more away from being purely dedicated to itself, to petering out in game-y design with minigames or cartoon scenarios that don't fit the game's atmosphere, a side-effect of cramming in too much ambition.
But maybe that design is the point, and is part of the story. The protagonist is writing it every night--or at least imagining it--after all. Maybe it's supposed to cross borders into blatant fiction by the desperate author(s).
A unique recommendation goes out to fans of the original Deus Ex. This game shares a number of thematic and quest similarities, as well as taking clear inspiration in its color palette.

I really want to be able to recommend this game....but I can't. Always Sometimes Monsters has a lot of potential but is just lacking overall. The pace is juuuuust slow enough to be considered a hindrance, and while it is definitely a game that makes you think about the morality of your choices, there's a final step it isn't taking. In the end nothing really ends up having consequence. I got it half off so it's not like I'm upset about buying it, and honestly I think I would have been okay paying $10 even because it does have a lot of good qualities. But overall it sits pretty neutral with me so if I had to say yes or no, I'd say no- the bottom line is you're not missing a life changing experience by NOT playing this.
I'm not completely done and I do plan to finish and maybe play again to see if much changes depending on your choices, but I'm far enough along where I'm pretty sure my feelings won't change by the end. Again, the game isn't awful by any means, but I can't exactly justify raving over it.
One thing that did really frustrate me though: the game quits when you try to take a screenshot! Another review had stated this but stupid me tried to do it anyway, and of course I was right in the middle of something...waaaay annoying. I wonder if this is something with games made in RPG Maker? because To The Moon does the same thing...except instead of quitting the game pauses, which I think is a thing Always Sometimes Monsters could use to incorporate to save some frustration.

Brawlhalla is one of the most underrated games on Steam. It's really fun and addicting, and it's even better with friends.
It's gameplay isn't about spamming a few keys, there's a lot to learn such as combos, dodge mechanics and advanced movement. There are currently 6 ranks, but climbing them isn't that easy and takes a lot of practice, and as of August 12th of 2017, there are 34 characters, each one of them with different stats, weapon combinations, and signature attacks.
You can play 4 FFA, 1v1 & 2v2 Ranked, and many more game modes in custom game lobbies or during the Brawl of the Week.
It's design is chibi-like and cartoonish. Each legend has a few skins, and each skin has different colours to choose from, there are also exclusive cosmetics that are only available for purchase during special events.
The game is frequently updated adding new cosmetics, fixing bugs, and more. Also, if there's lag in game, leave the match, then rejoin it, worked every time for me.
Overall, it's a great game that everyone should try. Many hours of fun ahead.

This game happens to be one of the best story games I have played in a long time. It contained the perfect balance of free roaming and linear storytelling. While you always knew what to do next in the story you had the liberty to cavort around to solve Joker's riddles or brawl thugs.
On the technical aspect it looked incredible and combined with Nvidia PhysX it made a beautifully intrigueing game. I did not notice a single problem with the game and my refresh rate remained at a solid 60 frames. The game appeared fluid with Batman perfectly transiting from running to gliding to fighting. You could almost feel the coming devistation of the following strike. If I could change anything I'd have the cutscenes not be limited to 30 frames.
The game also features the ability to pick what and when to upgrade certain abilities tuneing Batman to your play style. The story was surprisingly long even just focusing on the goal. I am not one for games of this type, but this one sold me well enough to continue on to Batman: Arkham City.
I highly recommend this title.

This game turned out more fun then I anticipated and it was quite accidentally that I gave it a chance.
In short this is a 3D side platform race runner. Your aim is to get from start to finish in the shortest time available. To do that you've got to navigate the course and use various slides, jumps, boosts and a grappling hook to your advantage. Gameplay wise it reminds a sonic game. It's fast, it's not easy but really rewarding.
The environments are pretty detailed and colourful. At times I found them a bit too distracting but it's not a game breaking problem. The controls are tight, very responsive and make sense for the most part. Some slope jumps are not intuitive but you can learn them by watching the AI ghost runs. Sound design seems appropriate with the game's theme - bold, loud and cartoony.
The race length is long enough too enjoy and short enough to quickly restart when you fail. Getting a gold medal on the run at certain races is really challenging. Global score sheets are really nice addition as well.
This seems like a perfect fit for multiplayer although I've not tried it.
Overall enjoyed the game very much. And was happy to go trough all of the tracts. Can easily recommend to any sonic fans or people liking runners with tight controls.

Let me tell you about Jenut Farmer.
In the early days of her gnome colony, Jenut was assigned to militia duty when goblin raiders came a-calling. The colony only had armour for one gnome, and it wasn't Jenut, so she fought bare-handed. With one lucky blow from a goblin's weapon, Jenut lost her right arm.
But if anyone had ideas about withdrawing Jenut from the militia, they quickly changed their minds. Her comrades reported that losing an arm barely slowed her down. On the ground after being knocked down, Jenut had throat-kicked the goblin attacking her and killed it in one blow. She survived her injuries, and even with one arm, her combat skills were rated the best in the colony.
So Jenut remained with the militia. With every goblin incursion and wild animal hunt, she racked up more and more kills. Still bare-handed, still unarmoured, Jenut punched, kicked, and bit to death anything that crossed her. By the second year of the colony, she had killed over a dozen goblins. Ogres started coming on goblin raids; Jenut called them "oversized kickboxing bags" and smashed their ribs into their lungs.
Oh, and she was also a good farmer. She baked the legendary loaf of wheat bread, "The Bakersmasher". I like to think she made that one into a goblin sandwich and ate it herself.
"Was"? Well, Jenut's still alive, but the colony has a real military now, with proper weapons and all. So she doesn't see as much action as she used to. But she's still on militia duty, and she's still got the most kills of anyone on the roster, if you don't count the crossbowgnomes and their nice, safe runs in the beetle-killing gallery. She's a legend in the colony, too. They say she can see a goblin-skull helmet and show you exactly how her fist or foot fits the odd dents in its side. They say that when she plants saplings, she punches them into the ground, not because it's efficient, but because it freaks out the gnomads. And they say that when she finally does die, she'll kick Death, hitting the upper body, splintering the ribs, puncturing the heart and piercing through the heart... and take his job.

Gnomoria is a fun and potentially addictive micro-simulation game.  It's greatest strengths lie in playing it as a sandbox and building and designing your own structures out of the various building blocks, or challenging yourself to build some functioning machines using the mechanical elements that can be researched (switches, windmills, hatches, pumps).
The 'game' part of the game, where you build up your population and wealth while trying not to get killed off by raiding monsters, lacks polish.  It feels like the development was never truly completed.  It needs some sort of campaign with more meaningful interaction with a surrounding world to be a strategy game.  It's still a lot of fun to play, though, if you don't take it too seriously.  Options allow you to configure it to exclude some or all of the monsters and adjust the size and frequency of raids, including a mode where things get increasingly tough with time (by default raids depend only on your wealth not on time passed).
There is also a modding framework that allows changes and additions to crafting items and building materials and creatures.

I don't have thousands of hours in this game or have much experience playing fighting games at all, in fact, I hate fighting games. I hate the community more than any first person shooter game out there, Brawlhalla doesn't make it better. I really tried to get into the genre but this game failed me.
I'll start with the good first; the game is fun casually, with friends especially. If you want a game that ressembles Super Smash Bros, try it. If you need the itch to play a fighting game but have a low grade PC, try it. The game takes very little memory and seconds to download. The controls on an Xbox controller are easy but you can learn with a keyboard too, I prefer playing on a controller where I can sit back and relax and try to have a fun fighting experience to get myself into the genre.
The characters are interesting as far as design goes, I like a few of the map arenas but they aren't that detailed and remind me more of a browser fighting game than anything else. As far as the rest of the graphics go, there's not much and it's simple, fairly smooth overall for the quality.
The bad now; pretty much everything except for the things I mentioned above. Starting with controls, while the game is easy, simple, and takes not much to learn. There's not many moves to learn, each character only has two weapon types and even then, none of the weapons are specific to one character. If you use a sword on one character, it's pretty much the same on another character whom has a sword as well. The basic attacks are pretty much copy paste, heavy attacks are the same except different sound effects or visual effects but it really did fool me thinking the game was more divers between characters.
Since the game is primairly online, it relies on a good internet connection, DO NOT play with anyone outside your region unless you're paying loads of money for the best internet because this game DOES NOT handle lag in a good way at all. I played the game with multiple friends whom all live in different places across the USA, I live in the west and a friend in the mid west wants to play. Yeah, right. I don't have the best internet and neither do they, well the experience with my friend basically went "My character just teleported off the stage" or "What? How did I die? I hit you perfectly when you weren't moving" or "I just hit you, how did you not take damage?" or "I don't know what I'm doing, my character won't stop teleporting. Wait, did you just kill me?" I wouldn't complain but this was a constant thing between all of my friends. The game can handle lag way more better.
I muted the music, it's loud and obnoxious.
Casual without friends is alright, it's a mixed bag and kind of fun when you find people with your skill level, a 4v4 free for all is meh. It's frustrating when you're the one being taken out all the time with barely a chance when everyone ignores eachother for no reason but that's my own experience, I didn't play with them before so I don't know what happened.
Competitive, I hate this part of the game. I'm not a skilled person when it comes to fighting games, after about 10 hours of playing I thought I might be able to do something. The first few matches were alright, I felt like I was being faced against people who had maybe a few minutes in the game. Then, a few hours of a winning streak later, I start getting matched with people whom feel like put hundreds of hours in this game.
I started getting spammed by players who know how to use the move sets correctly and in perfect timing to where you can't move unless they pause to reset their stamina or whatever the game uses to keep doing specials or doging. Then continue to land hits on you until you die.
The sportsmanship is non-existant in this game, if the demographic was kids, that sounds about right. You don't spawn with a weapon, the weapons drop from the air and you have to pick them up, well, in competitive, good luck. I tend to be a friendly player, I give people a chance, obviously in the fighting community, you're stupid for doing that. But I let people pick up weapons after they respawn, but they kill me, then start picking up weapons and throwing them away so I don't get any, then start to defend weapon drops and never allowing me to pick up a weapon. Even after I let them pick up their weapon.
I tried to give competitive a chance, I just can't do it. While the two things I mentioned don't sound like much, just try the competitive yourself, it's a frustrating expereience.
The options are meh for the game being simple as it is. You also have to buy characters, while you can buy them all without spending a dime and buying the legends pack or whatever it is, you can't buy any cosmetics. The only real cosmetics that you can earn are colour changes for your character. I don't have any positive to say about that, yay, my character is yellow instead of the original blue. You can't buy cosmetics using in-game currency which I think sucks, at least you can buy in-game icons, wooh? I understand it helps fund the devs but I think some cosmetics could be free or at least one choice when you purchase a character with in-game money.
There's a hot key you can press after every round to say "GG"
The devs can remove this.
Overall, if you're looking for a fighting game and are desperate to play one, play it. If you're looking for a game to play with friends, you can do better but only if you really want a fighting game to mimic Super Smash Bros, sure. I just can't see any positives this game brings to the fighting genre for a new player other than it's free.
Literally if you're new to fighting games and are interested in playing this, the real reason you have is because it's free. It's not that fun after a while. Once you play one round, you've experienced the game to its fullest potential on a regular basis.
If you play a custom game there's a few things you can tweak but it doesn't change the mechanics of the game. So there's no true benifit.

This is a very okay "rouge-lite" game, however enemies are boring and so are the items and powerups you find. I've only unlocked about half the items (which is quite a lot) after beating the game (and about 8 hours of play) but most of the ones available are stuff like "get more mana" or "health potions heal a bit more". The rooms you enter are also just bland - some of them look a bit different, but they are essentially all just box like spaces to fight enemies with very little variation. Bosses are giant versions of regular enemies that usually summon smaller enemies and have an extra attack. The weapons you find are generally more powerful than your base wand however even they don't offer that much variety.
My point overall being, the game is boring both as an FPS and as a Rougelike. Tower of Guns, also on steam, does this concept much better, and even Paranautical Activity succeeds more than this one. The game isn't outright "bad", but it offers neither the randomness and suspense of a run through a great rougelike, nor satisfying shooting mechanics or varied enemies.

If you like rouge-likes and RNG dungeon crawlers, then get this game on a big sale. It’s fun, but has a lot of problems. Most rooms are huge and empty, nothing besides enemy kills and damage inflicted is carried over between runs, the perks awarded upon level up seem random (and some are rather stupid). If you’ve played the dungeon once or twice, then you’ve pretty much seen all the interior design has to offer. Plus, a small gripe of mine is that you can’t move the map screen around; want to see the top of the map? Well run to a room higher up then open the map again…
This game is an absolute grind-fest, and most of the characters are not very good. There’s very little that a new character offers besides a different weapon attribute (poison) or increased speed. There are room conditions called “Scavenge” on Fl 2 and up where you must collect crystals strewn about while being pelted by enemy attacks, and even though your character can jump, you can’t actually jump over ground-based attacks, like the Imp’s fire.
I wouldn’t keep playing this game if I didn’t enjoy reaching the goals for character acquisition, like deal 35,000 alchemic damage, or defeat 200 Kobolds. All in all, a fun enough game in short bursts, but many games out there get the genre right far better.

One POSITIVE reviewer below said, "You won't get much out of Ziggurat the first few times you play; starting gear and perks put you at a disadvantage. "
Uh, yeah. That's a POSITIVE review. LOL!
And that's a radical understatement! You are FAR worse off than "at a disadvantage!" And you get FAR less out of the game than "not much."
I find the game-play simply not worth how stupid-hard it is (on "normal"), and it's just not worth the "progression" to deal with the levels that might become better-balanced later. It's a game-design MISTAKE to make it so ridiculously hard (on "normal") to even get started!
Your initial weapons and health are SO weak that you're basically just dodging around, strafing and trying to kill a few of the hordes of enemies who can far too quickly kill you.
If you survive (with drained health) one or two of those encounters, then you're forced into initial boss-fights that are an absolute absurdity of difficulty. I ran into a boss within 2 minutes on the first level that fires this stream of burning skulls. They almost immediately blast through what cover there is, and they TRACK you, so there's no dodging. And you have this little wand that by my calculations would take you 200 hits to finally kill him. Meanwhile, in just seconds, he drains your health with these tracking skulls. Have I mentioned STREAMS of these things? Absolutely absurd!
Strafing? No good. Dodging? No good. Jumping? No good. Hiding behind cover? No good. Basically, it's IMPOSSIBLE to damage the boss even CLOSE to how quickly he damages you, and this boss-fight is really nothing more than a timed-damage game that you cannot win with your little wand. You're not at a "disadvantage!" You simply cannot kill him as fast as he can kill you, and HE can dodge your shots, while his track you.
Really? This is "fun"? Well, not for me.
I can't speak to how the game plays if you ever reach the mythical point where your weapons/health/enemies feel somewhat balanced, because the START of the game is so unbalanced that it's just not worth it to progress.
If you have nothing better to do with your life than persevere through the pain, have "fun" with this. Not for me!

The Novelist brings the player a handful of difficult decision between life, family, and work. This occurs at the end of each chapter and it is impossible to satisfy all of the characters wants and needs which ultimately makes your decisions hard to make. The effect of each decision is designed to draw you emotionally into the characters. For example, if your decision leads to making a character unhappy, if you feel empathetic and sorry for that character then you will try and make sure in the next chapter that your decision will make that character happy.
The gameplay element is interesting at first as you get to discover the memories and needs of different characters by wandering around the house and finding clues. For example, finding a drawing or walking up to a character and viewing their memory. However, at later stages of the game this mechanic of gameplay becomes repetitive and all you feel like doing is rushing and finding out what the character wants and progress with the story. To make the game less boring in this sense, you can activate a mode in which you have to be stealthy and not be seen.
Although the gameplay aspect is somewhat lacking, it certainly makes up for it in the story telling department. With the many different possible endings as a result of your decisions, this is an incentive to go through multiple playthroughs to find out what can possibly happen to the different characters. For the full price of this game i would say that it probably isnt worth it if you aren't into story driven games, however if you pick up this game on sale or in a bundle i would certainly recommend playing it, even for one playthrough as it is a relaxing experience :)

A playthrough of this indie pet project reminds us of the tried and true Parker/Stone adage: "When you have plot outlines and you can put the words "and then" in between each one, you're f***ked".
plot barely qualifies it for a listing at The Daytime Emmy Awards. Typical Hallmark-esque tribulations of a fading marriage, childhood innocence, and a writer-protagonist so stereotypical that leaves the player wondering how boring the actual writer of this narrative actually is files this sappy indie title under "do something else with your morning".
What's more,
serves as an example of why game mechanics simply cannot be bolted onto a story and the final build be thus christened a Game. It's odd that the designer opted for a "spectral" approach to experiencing the narrative. In other words, why is the player banished to look on the game's character as a non-character herself? The premise of this game is great and I couldn't wait to try it out. It succeeds in the sense that I found the conceit interesting (you're essentially a spirit, possessing objects and rifling through the family's things for clues about their goals in life), and it was fun to play through in a single sitting. I enjoyed the compromise system because it added a little weight to the game that otherwise would have been too simple.
That said the constrains of the gameplay system made it difficult for me to relate to the Kaplan family. Unfortunately it ended up making them all a bit unsympathetic. For example, I would think in a real family when the mother's relative passes away unexpectedly, your child wouldn't respond to a change in plans with a screaming and crying fit, especially not at ten years old. Also I didn't understand why Mom and Child couldn't leave Dad alone until his novel was done. The deadline is set and it will be a finite project, so stop asking him to play and all that until he's done! Or when you have the option of taking the kid to a fair, the mom on a trail hike, or dad to a campfire. The mom goes on the hike if you don't compromise with her, but she twists her ankle and isn't able to complete it. This makes her angry. It just felt way too codependent to me then, like go on the hike by yourself and enjoy it! Lastly, Dan giving up on writing after that just makes me feel like he wasn't serious enough about it in the first place.
Still a fun and interesting adventure remeniscient of the Stanley Parable but played much straighter.

Basically the illegitimate lovechild of Call of Duty and Team Fortress 2.
Jokes aside, it really is somewhere in the middle between the toon artstyle and diverse classes and loadouts of TF2, and Call of Duty's fast-paced, more realistic style.
Regarding the game's history as a F2P browser shooter, it's come a long way. The devs have moved away from the F2P model to the traditional model of buying the game once and unlocking everything. This allows the game to be much more balanced, and doesn't encourage paywalls and Pay-to-Win balancing like a F2P model often tends to do.
Overall, if you're looking for something new to try in the class-based shooter genre, Ballistic Overkill is well worth the $6.99 price tag. The balance isn't perfect yet and the community is small, but this game has loads of potential if the FPS community at large is willing to give it a chance.

In a day and age when a great deal of triple A titles end at the 40 hour mark (and often alot sooner) I am really suprised to see so many negative reviews complaining about the hub play area, the story and microtransactions.
In brief:
Yes you are mostly confined to one hub, this is as opposed to Human Revolution where you played in Detroit, China and a final area. However, Prague is hugely more detailed, varied and interesting than most of HR's settings which were very uniform and mostly empty other than a few repeating props. MD encourages exploration a little more than HR did, and to be honest it's alot more rewarding too. Think back to Heng Sha Island in the original game, did any store front stand out too you more than the others? It was row after row of near identical shop counters, usually either a chef or an electronics store (is that a spoiler?) and generic back rooms. Sorry, but this complaint doesn't hold water for me. Quantity doesn't outweigh quality.
Not much to say about the story. Im gripped by it, even the side quests are gripping and I am genuinly interested in them. They're fleshed out and there is a great deal to be learned from data mining and interacting with the environment. I don't know whether people who have issues with the story don't like that aspect of the game and want something more direct, but Deus Ex has never really been that way has it?
The microtransactions. Never been prompted once to purchase anything. In my entire playthough I did not see a single option to purchase anything, perhaps its been removed or made less obvious in later patches? I don't know, but if you were to ask me how to make a microtransaction I genuinly wouldnt know. So again, quite unfair.
In Summary:
Human Revolution was a great game but not as expansive and free roaming as people are making out, unless you count fairly bland copy and paste scenery which was typical of a game of its time - so comparing that to this - which is a beautifully detailed game that in my opinion has been sculpted with a great deal of thought, is unfair. You will find that, generally, the more unique detail a game has the less content there is. Again, quantity doesn't outweigh quality.
Mankind Divided is not perfect of course but I can't see what everyone is getting so annoyed about. Is it just me or are people jumping on the bandwagon because of some nerd rage directed towards the company that owns it?
The game isn't as bad as everyone makes it out to be. I would at least want you to try out the games demo, and see how you like it, but I don't want to waste your valuable time.

Never having played a game like this before, I found it rather interesting (though I know I'm not its target audience).
In short, you try and take any number of girls from enemies to lovers by buying them things, taking them on dates, and talking to them. Wash, rinse, and repeat. You increase your wealth by taking more lucrative jobs, or staying in one for a sufficient amount of time for a promotion. Likewise, you increase your hobbies (motivation, funniness, suaveness, etc) over time, both of which unlock other girls, jobs, or hobbies. You can increase the rate at which this happens by resetting your game - essentially wiping out your progress with the girls in exchange for a multiplier which will accelerate things the next time around. Do this enough times and you can finish the game this decade.
I recommend this game because it is a nice diversion and the writing and skill trees are interesting. The art is nice, though if you're looking for the adult version of the game you'll need to go elsewhere - the Steam version is strictly PG-13. I'll likely stop playing this at about the 50% point as it seems to beat the game in a timely fashion you'd need to spend some real-world money and I'm not one to grind. The one nice thing to note is game time
elapse even if you're not actively playing it. Check in once a week and reap your earnings.

is not for the faint of heart. Don't expect any remorse on the game's part: it has the potential to be far more bitter and unforgiving than it appears. In it, you play a struggling young author on a journey to pick yourself up from the gutter, but there's a catch: you only have 30 days to turn your life around. As I feel that the game is best enjoyed with little to no prior knowledge of its plot, I'll try to keep this review as nonspecific as possible.
The concept is standard decision-based RPG fare: the choices you make will determine your future. I've always been a big fan of decision-based games, especially those that test your morals - and
is brutal in this respect. A Paragon through-and-through, I'm always trying my hardest to take the moral high road in video games: tell the truth, abide by the law, and be the hero. Similarly to Lucas Pope's
, the decisions you make in
are far too morally ambiguous for this to ever be an option. Due to the complex and difficult nature of these decisions, it's not so much a fun game as it is a captivating one - there's no good or evil, and you'll find yourself making a lot of difficult choices that reflect those we make in reality. In its complete rejection of black-and-white morality, events chain together and intersect in a myriad of different and surprising ways. You'll often have to choose between your own welfare and that of others: the game forces you, an individual struggling to stay alive, to choose between money and morals, but there's more often than not a third option that might help you unintentionally...or hinder you just the same.
Ultimately, I found the events of the game to be dissatisfying and irritating - but that's not necessarily a bad thing, as these feelings were born more from a desire for in-universe justice than anything else (how dare they treat my Marcus like that)! I've got a lot of respect for any work that can evoke this sort of reaction. I was not angry with the game itself, rather, the cruel nature of the world within it, and the way it had treated me.
As the player, you're forced to take what is handed to you, and often feel as if your hard work has no purpose. I felt myself constantly frustrated, unable to have my character's life turn out how I felt it should, regardless of the effort I put in. I was equally upset when characters berated me for choices I made that I had originally judged to be morally sound. You're always presented with easy ways to make cash or advance further in the game, but they're never without their lasting consequences. I found the range of emotions this game stirred up in me to be surprising, as they were very much unexpected during my first hour or so of playtime. I did, however, find the required menial tasks quite frustrating - whilst I understand this is likely the intention of the developers, much like the aforementioned
, this kind of gameplay was severely limited by the RPGMaker engine, whereas the former tackled it in a very unique way.
Despite the serious themes the game explores, there's still a good helping of well-written humour. One thing I found particularly amusing was the fact that there are self-inserts of the developers in the game, and interacting with them produces a host of self-referential (and occasionally self-deprecating) jokes. I found this to be very clever, and it was a great way to break up the tension in the game, along with the occasional mini-game (
, though clearly a Vagabond Dog inside joke, was quite amusing).
Unfortunately, the game lacks the defined visual style found in conceptually similar games such as
and
. The character designs were not very memorable, although I did find the overworld sprites to be more aesthetically appealing than the character portraits (which, sadly, most characters only had one of, making intense scenes with smiling characters somewhat offputting, though I can understand this given the sheer number of designs). I honestly felt this to be to be my only major complaint with it, as the substandard quality of the artwork was made up for by an excellent plot and soundtrack. The music ranges from melancholy and atmospheric to gritty and unsettling, comprised of thumping 80's synths that wouldn't sound out of place on the
soundtrack. Sadly, however, I did find myself picking up a host of grammatical errors in the dialogue that could have been fixed very easily.
Finally, I think it's important to note two things about this game, though I'll try to be as ambiguous as possible so as not to spoil anything: the all-important LGBTQ+ representation, racial diversity, and the replay value this ultimately results in. The character selection process can yield a huge range of different combinations for the player and their partner - much like life itself - and I'm yet to replay the game in order to explore the possible combinations of genders, races, and their influences on the game, let alone those of my choices. Characters will suffer racism, sexism, and/or homophobia, an unfortunate reflection of reality.
I certainly recommend this game to anybody who's looking for something that deals with human nature at its very core. Though it does lack polish in some areas, it's an outstanding game, and it's definitely worth a play. If you're anything like me, just try to have tissues handy. And maybe a stress ball.

After some 10 hours I beat
. It was definitely one of the more interesting games I've played but, ultimately, I felt its own gaminess was its downfall.
The story pushes you thru a number of challenges, like getting evicted or needing to get to another city. I tried to play it realistically, putting myself in the shoes of the characters, but the suspension of disbelief was quickly broken by ridiculous video game quest trope. Cue having to win 4 boxing matches to get new tires for a car or casually hacking into a government computer to rig elections. The occasional horrible minigames are more of an annoying hindrance than a fitting part of the story.
For a game that focuses on choice, it gives you none as far as the main goal goes. You spend 30 days trying to get to a wedding of an ex-girlfriend because... plot? It's never really explained until the end and the few flashbacks don't do much to make you want to win your old love back. It's even more awkward when several times the NPCs ask you why you are going through all this trouble to get there. Frankly... I had no idea. Because that's what the game tells me to do?
I was also a bit disappointed with how the game evaluates all your choices. Towards the end, a character calls you out on all your "evil deeds" which kinda made me scratch my head. So I am a horrible person because I didnt smash a doctor's car to help a junkie "friend" I only met through a few skimpy lines of dialogue? Really? And the very final flash-forward scene literally depicted me as homeless and asking to be killed because I've become a monster... wtf? I've never harmed anyone, never stole, even helped a few people along the way. I can see this ending working for some choices, but it clearly backfired with my playthrough.
Would i recommend it? If you are into these kind of narrative games, it is an interesting experience and good food for design thought. If not, well, you probably shouldn't be looking in this genre in the first place.

If given four words to describe the contents of Always Sometimes Monsters, they would all happen to begin with the letter 'C':
Coincidence, circumstance, choice, and consequence.
Unfortunately, if I were to give a letter grade to the overall game and my experience, I would have to be quite forgiving to remain using the letter 'C'.
A "life simulator" if you will, this is a game that plants you into a world where your hopes and dreams haven't proceeded as planned.  In a time where it has become a struggle to earn enough money to pay for food or keep a roof over your head, you find yourself invited to a wedding in a distant city.  You are tasked to find your way there within a month's time, and along the road many scenarios and options are presented to tailor your experience in exactly how you will (or will not) achieve your goal.
The freedom of choice is apparent upon starting the game and persists throughout to an extent.  Sacrifice to help a friend or be selfish?  Take sides with party X or organization Y?  Take the high road or the low?  Many situations might give you pause to stop and consider your choices before committing.  Do you want to retain moral character or will the means justify the ends?  All of it is left to you as the player and will ultimately decide your fate.
In the end, however, I was left rather unsatistfied with the game as a whole.  I felt as though my personal choices led to the same general path I might have ended up at had I gone the opposite direction.  Sure, one or two characters would have had different opinions of who I was in the end, maybe they'd be there in the final scene or maybe not.  But what impact did I have on the world?  ...Very little, it seems.
I chose to go with more of an upstanding citizen and aide (though not in EVERY scenario, hence the appropriate title), and as a result the choices seemed rote.  As a game that asks you to make difficult decisions, there was never a moment where I felt like I NEEDED to break out of the role I had chosen.  It felt no different to a Mass Effect game: if you play a paragon character, you make paragon choices in just about every situation.  Therefore, for a game all about choices and consequences, Always Sometimes Monsters rarely presented anything that felt meaningful.
As for the "game" part of the game, it's pretty messy and rarely flows well.  Conversations are held up and constantly prolonged with bubbles floating above characters' heads displaying elipses or hearts or exclamation points, none of which can be hurried with button presses or disabled in the options.  Just as disrupting is a big clock that pops up and remains on screen for at least a full five seconds whenever each "stage" of the day transitions from one to the next.
And the mini-games.  OH, the mini-games.  Some exist to reward you in the form of money or key items.  Some are there just to spice up the world and give you something else to do off the beaten path.  However, ALL of them are rather monotonous, if not downright frustrating from time to time.  Need to puzzle out a mini-game over five or ten minutes for some cash once, that's okay.  Need to repeat that same puzzle a dozen times with hardly any variables changing, each lasting the same five to ten minutes?  It's boring and tedious.  I spent twelve hours in the game, and I would have been much more satisfied with the experience if it were cut in half.  ...At a bare minimum.  And when a mini-game causes you to savescum a few dozen times, there's something wrong.  This is a piece of work that asks you to consider your choices and their consequences, so its aim has gone awry when you're in a postion where you find yourself quitting and reloading to go back to previous saves.
Due to the nature of how this game plays with its choices, I know that I missed a lot of content by making the decisions I did.  There's a lot left to see and experience.  Normally I'd be gung ho to get right back into it to see everything I could.  ...But not with Always Sometimes Monsters.  I didn't finish it excitedly to see what ending might unfold; I finished it over a few play sessions, each start more and more begrudgingly, only to get it done and out of the way.  I was not invested in my character or the world or the emotions it tried (and failed) to stir within me.  I was only pushing buttons to see what the game had to offer, and in the end I wasn't all that interested, surprised, or all that enthralled.
For a "cerebral" game that wanted me to think or care, it failed with me.   It doesn't stand up to similar "head space" games.  Gone Home made me curious and sympathetic.  To The Moon gave me wonder, tugged at my heart, and literally brought me to tears of joy and sadness simultaneously.  ...Always Sometimes Monsters far too often made me slump in my chair, toss back my head and roll my eyes, and caused me to breathe out grunts of annoyance and exasperation. Thus, I can't recommend it.
Sorry, Vagabond Dogs.  I wanted to like it.  It just didn't do it for me.

Playing the game was a really nice experience, and I absolutely see myself playing through this again to de-stress.

MY REVIEW
Quick Summary: Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon is better than Far Cry 3
Why?
My taste in games is much different than the "norm". To put this game in perspective, Uplay combined the game and used:
- Far Cry 3 game mechanics with some tweaks to simplify the looting/leveling system.
- Borderlands 2 Humor.
- Tron in-game lighting.
- 1980's art, music, cut-scenes, and story themes.
Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon has that wonderfully facetious mockery of 80's movies and video games I love. As a person who experienced the pop-garbage of the 80's, the game pulled out all of the best cliches and one-liners and mashed them together into an absurd blend of story and gameplay. The deliberate plot holes and the cheesy phrases were a perfect reflection of the history and mindset of American and Hollywood thinking in that era.
I admit, starting the game was difficult. There was lots of hand-holding and extensive cut-scenes, but once you get past the first hour, then the game becomes open-world like Far Cry 3.
I fully played the game inside-out by taking over all the outposts, doing all the kill missions, and collecting all the crappy items (which unlocked powerful gun attachments) to prepare for the end-game big boss fight with Sloan. Well, I was surprised and entertained at the ending, as silly and destructive as it was. The game was much shorter than Far Cry 3, but amused me more only because I love mockery entertainment.
As a side note, the blood dragon dinosaurs were a nice challenging touch to the game. I can see myself purchasing Far Cry Primal for this type of hunting.
Since I purchased this DLC for less than the cost of a Starbucks coffee, I once again received a huge beneficial cost/entertainment ratio.
Rediculous 80s cheesy sci-fi fun, better and cheaper than Far Cry 3.

I don't have thousands of hours in this game or have much experience playing fighting games at all, in fact, I hate fighting games. I hate the community more than any first person shooter game out there, Brawlhalla doesn't make it better. I really tried to get into the genre but this game failed me.
I'll start with the good first; the game is fun casually, with friends especially. If you want a game that ressembles Super Smash Bros, try it. If you need the itch to play a fighting game but have a low grade PC, try it. The game takes very little memory and seconds to download. The controls on an Xbox controller are easy but you can learn with a keyboard too, I prefer playing on a controller where I can sit back and relax and try to have a fun fighting experience to get myself into the genre.
The characters are interesting as far as design goes, I like a few of the map arenas but they aren't that detailed and remind me more of a browser fighting game than anything else. As far as the rest of the graphics go, there's not much and it's simple, fairly smooth overall for the quality.
The bad now; pretty much everything except for the things I mentioned above. Starting with controls, while the game is easy, simple, and takes not much to learn. There's not many moves to learn, each character only has two weapon types and even then, none of the weapons are specific to one character. If you use a sword on one character, it's pretty much the same on another character whom has a sword as well. The basic attacks are pretty much copy paste, heavy attacks are the same except different sound effects or visual effects but it really did fool me thinking the game was more divers between characters.
Since the game is primairly online, it relies on a good internet connection, DO NOT play with anyone outside your region unless you're paying loads of money for the best internet because this game DOES NOT handle lag in a good way at all. I played the game with multiple friends whom all live in different places across the USA, I live in the west and a friend in the mid west wants to play. Yeah, right. I don't have the best internet and neither do they, well the experience with my friend basically went "My character just teleported off the stage" or "What? How did I die? I hit you perfectly when you weren't moving" or "I just hit you, how did you not take damage?" or "I don't know what I'm doing, my character won't stop teleporting. Wait, did you just kill me?" I wouldn't complain but this was a constant thing between all of my friends. The game can handle lag way more better.
I muted the music, it's loud and obnoxious.
Casual without friends is alright, it's a mixed bag and kind of fun when you find people with your skill level, a 4v4 free for all is meh. It's frustrating when you're the one being taken out all the time with barely a chance when everyone ignores eachother for no reason but that's my own experience, I didn't play with them before so I don't know what happened.
Competitive, I hate this part of the game. I'm not a skilled person when it comes to fighting games, after about 10 hours of playing I thought I might be able to do something. The first few matches were alright, I felt like I was being faced against people who had maybe a few minutes in the game. Then, a few hours of a winning streak later, I start getting matched with people whom feel like put hundreds of hours in this game.
I started getting spammed by players who know how to use the move sets correctly and in perfect timing to where you can't move unless they pause to reset their stamina or whatever the game uses to keep doing specials or doging. Then continue to land hits on you until you die.
The sportsmanship is non-existant in this game, if the demographic was kids, that sounds about right. You don't spawn with a weapon, the weapons drop from the air and you have to pick them up, well, in competitive, good luck. I tend to be a friendly player, I give people a chance, obviously in the fighting community, you're stupid for doing that. But I let people pick up weapons after they respawn, but they kill me, then start picking up weapons and throwing them away so I don't get any, then start to defend weapon drops and never allowing me to pick up a weapon. Even after I let them pick up their weapon.
I tried to give competitive a chance, I just can't do it. While the two things I mentioned don't sound like much, just try the competitive yourself, it's a frustrating expereience.
The options are meh for the game being simple as it is. You also have to buy characters, while you can buy them all without spending a dime and buying the legends pack or whatever it is, you can't buy any cosmetics. The only real cosmetics that you can earn are colour changes for your character. I don't have any positive to say about that, yay, my character is yellow instead of the original blue. You can't buy cosmetics using in-game currency which I think sucks, at least you can buy in-game icons, wooh? I understand it helps fund the devs but I think some cosmetics could be free or at least one choice when you purchase a character with in-game money.
There's a hot key you can press after every round to say "GG"
The devs can remove this.
Overall, if you're looking for a fighting game and are desperate to play one, play it. If you're looking for a game to play with friends, you can do better but only if you really want a fighting game to mimic Super Smash Bros, sure. I just can't see any positives this game brings to the fighting genre for a new player other than it's free.
Literally if you're new to fighting games and are interested in playing this, the real reason you have is because it's free. It's not that fun after a while. Once you play one round, you've experienced the game to its fullest potential on a regular basis.

Review Disclaimer — 
1) Old-school shooter
Mechanically Ziggurat plays like a good old-school shooter. Here is a detailed examination of what this means:
2) Theme - Fantasy
Ziggurat is a fantasy shooter in the vein of Hexen and Heretic. This feels unique and you ought to yourself to experience at least one such shooter
3) Roguelite
Ziggurat is roguelite but the difficulty is so well done that it does not have the negatives associated with the genre. Similar to other roguelites, level layouts are somewhat randomized and as you play life after life, you will unlock new characters, weapons, skills, enemies. All of those feel brilliant.
4) Mutators
The game has multiple mutators. Sometimes when you enter a new room, a random mutator (special rule) will be applied - darkness, slippery ground, enemies that spawn from dead enemies, maybe you can shoot only when in the air, quad damage for everyone, etc. This feels just as awesome as it sounds. Battles are always fresh
5) Push forward combat
The Doom from 2016 implemented something its game designers called “push forward combat”. Basically when you are near death and you execute a finishing more on an enemy, you are rewarded with health. This rewarded aggressive play style. Ziggurat does something similar. Enemies drop health and ammo. Those pickups disappear over time. During combat you need to move towards the enemies in order to pick up resources from the dead before the resources disappear. The system is not as good as Doom, but it still works

Ziggurat is an FPS, rogue-lite with mediocre level and enemy designs, but an addicitive and rewarding progression system.  You won't get much out of Ziggurat the first few times you play; starting gear and perks put you at a disadvantage.  Ziggurat rewards repeated attempts through a constant power creep that feels like you are truly mastering the arcane.  When you die, you are given several perks depending on how far you made it.  This game truly shines once you start unlocking the progression through perks, weapons, characters, and skill.  After a half dozen runs you should start to see the potential... and either the game will hook you or leave you wanting more.
The hook is power.  As you go deeper into the dungeon and/or die to it, you will unlock new perks and weapons which provide you with new abilities or expand on what you already have.  These unlocks are then available for future runs.
Perks mostly affect your health, movement, resource pools, and defensive ability; a few of them later on can drastically alter how you play, requiring a tactical shift to play effectively.  As you delve into the dungeon and level up, you select from a random draw of available perks (2-3 per level).  Given certain perks at certain times, you will become stronger.  Sometimes the perks aren't useful and given enough bad RNG, the enemeis can begin to overpower you.
Weapons are interesting, with each one having a slight variation on it's base function.  They are granted at the beginning of each level, and sometimes from chests or shrines.  Wands are the base weapon, typically varying only oin power and firing pattern, and will recharge over time.  Spellbooks tend to be the heavy hitters but at the cost of casting speed.  Staves can affect multiple enemies quickly but often are weaker or provide damage over time.  Artifacts are some of the strongest weapons, but consume the most resource.  Amulets have a variety of useful functions, and may be used intermittently, recharging as you kill more enemies.  I found the weapons pleasing and fun, for the most part.  Unlocking particular weapons can greatly enhance your power and allow further/faster progression.
A good deal of variety comes from the game's playable characters, game modes, and characters.
The 16 characters are unlocked as you comnplete certain milestones (e.g. spend x mana on use of staves).  Each has inherent perks from the start, strengths/weaknesses, and a unique wand.  The mix includes Sorcerer, Witch, Templar, Harlequin, Bard, Vampire, and Seer just to name a few.
Game modes include the standard Ziggurat of 5 levels, an arena-style Gauntlet of spawning waves of enemies until you become overwhelmed, and an Endless mode where the dungeon gets progressively harder and doesn't end until you do.
On top of all of these selections, difficulty makes a big impact.  Starting players should start on easy for 4-5 runs until they can complete the Ziggurat.  Normal provides the standard challenege, and Hard will truly test your mettle.  DIfficulty seems to affect the number of enemies, the composition of enemies, AI behavior, room modifications (special conditions that affect rooms both good and bad), and drops.
So should you play Ziggurat?  Consider all the positive aspects mentioned, but temper it with the reality of the game:  the mechanics and gameplay are smooth but not overly complex.  It's a simple shooter at it's core.  The rooms and enemies don't have enough variety to warrant extensive play, just enough to tease you onward with the rewards.  If you enjoy the often relaxing flow of combat and exploration, and you casually carry forward, you may get 12 hours out of this game.  If you want to master hard difficulty and see almost everything to unlock, I'd wager about 20 hours at most.
I didn't like ZIggurat for the first hour or two.  It felt bland.  The progression saved the game, and is it's shining feature.  If Ziggurat ever gets a sequel, I will be on board.  If this solid concept is expanded with more rooms, abilities, items, characters, enemies, and a few new gameplay mechanics for spice... it could be somethingh really great.  Ziggurat is a charming and interesting game that just needs a little more under it's belt to be considered a fully matured title.  It can entertain you for sure, but don't expect to form a lifelong bond.

First of all, I've played way more than Steam shows, I'd say about 8 hours at the moment of writing.
HumanKind has been adapted to Digital and it's... well... Let's just say it needs a couple more weeks in the oven.
If you've never heard it, basically it's four factions of superhumans called Deviants fighting over key areas for the control of the world, each with their own vision of what to do with it. They were rebooted in this version but they're still interesting and range from "guiding humans to achieve a superior life", "don't intervene with them and let them have their own freedom, at any cost ", "controlling them in order to achieve ultimate order and structure" and, of course, "destroying them all as an inferior lifeform".
Most things you read are true, UI is still somewhat clunky, no friendlist/directly challenge a friend yet, and various things missing or needing improvement. Sound design ranges from bland to annoying. Storylines, a huge factor from the original TCG, are still there but a little left aside or hidden, thankfully they're making good improvements about it with the recent addition of thematic leagues and tournaments as well as faction reputation.
Why do I still recommend it then? First; It gets updates and fixes pretty regularly, the game inside it is as solid as always, and the artist(s) clearly knew how to adapt the theme of the factions into a new age; art design might not be as unique as the TCG but it works far better for a digital version and is still great. Factions work uniquely enough and according to their own concepts. More cards are needed, but the ones already in-game will entertain you for enough time. There's been many more serious issues but they have been fixed, I'll take that as a good sign; altough you won't find lack of small technical problems.
Jump in if you're interested, but with a pinch of salt. It's still a very unfinished product, but one worth trying out anyways for how unique it is.

Buggy, slow, and poor english translation. A ton of keywords that make no sense, and frankly just all around worse than other options.
Let me give a specific example of all of the above: A creature card that says "tap this card, target enemy can't block". Except it really says "exhaust this card, choose an enemy, that enemy gains demoralize". Because demoralize is the keyword that says "can't block", for some reason. Now, you click on the card, it gives you a prompt saying "tap this card or cancel". If you tap it, then you get another prompt that tells you to select this card and click ok. Now you do that, and it gives you another prompt to click the enemy card and then click ok. Then it gives the enemy 10 seconds to respond. Then you get a confirmation window of your own action after their response.
And now you've spent ~60 seconds to perform an action as simple as "tap this card to make a creature unable to block" and you can see why turns can take 5 minutes.

The text on both the UI and the cards themselves is in shambles. Much of the localization from Spanish to English hasn't been finished (you will get your registration email in Spanish from the English client). Cards that reference themselves have different names in their title and card text. The symbols for used for Volition and Sancuary are missing from card text and have been replaced with a letter instead (a uniform symbology is vital for any card game, the lack of one here is pretty amatuerish). When an effect changes the values on a card it is shown as a text modifier outside the card, rather than changing the values on the card themselves (why be a DIGITAL tcg if you aren't going to utilize the benefits).
This is less finished than many early-access titles.

The game is uninspired and once again you play as Jensen. The man with zero personality who does a Timothy Olyphant impersonation.
The gameplay is one of those games that offers you choices on how to approach a situation but rewards you more for being non lethal and non confrontational (run and gun). FPS/RPG lite elements. You advance the story through dialogue and the game does give you choices in dialogue...sadly none of those choices really affects much.
In fact you only have 2? 3? Maybe 4 or 5 choices that have any kind of impact. These choices are handled with a heavy hand usually with a pop up telling you to pick one or the other. Left or right. Save a person or do what's the greatest good!
The atmosphere is ok. More a less shiny Minority Report vibe than what you think of when you hear Cyberpunk.
The NPC's offer you only a little better than in castlevania 2: Simon's Quest and in a way are less interesting as they don't say random crap. Supporting cast is an area that was also uninspired, cliche and offers little advantage or insight other than random remarks.
Weapons are ok but due to weapons able to use different kinds of ammunition you'll find that you use only a couple depending upon your approach (stealth or combat). The same goes for upgrades that Jensen can get. A good thing about the upgrades is you won't feel ineffective if you don't invest everything into stealth or combat. You can mix and match as you please and still do well.
They more or less enhance your already capable skills. The bad thing with that is outside of 1 or 2 the rest of them aren't actually needed (unless you plan on hacking every little thing for example).
The AI isn't tough and can be easily led into making a stupid move and the enemy types aren't quite varied. The story is a run of the mill penny store paperback novel that is more pushed along than carried by its cast. You don't really feel engaged, it does a terrible job building suspense, wonder or have you questioning.
The graphics are ok. I've heard of some people having issues so make sure you remember the return policy for Steam incase you're one of those peeps.
In short. Even on sale I recommend you pass. For the purpose of this review I'll downvote it but I don't think it's a bad game. Just one we have played through before many times and other games on the market provide much better in 1 or more areas that this game misses the mark on.

A wonderfully cute puzzle game that takes no prisoners and doesn't hesitate to throw you into a nest of snakebirds.

Snakebird is a deceptively hard puzzle game that leads to frustrating but very enjoyable play.
The simple child like graphics would initially have you believe the game to be a kids game. However hidden behind this charming visual style is a game so difficult that it could possibly put dark souls to shame.
The concept of the game is present in the name of the game. You control a "snakebird" which is simply a mixture between a bird and a snake obviously. The game has a control method very similar to snake. You travel with your snakebird in a grid based pattern. Although you are allowed to touch yourself, unlike in snake, you do often find yourself getting your head trapped between the wall and your body making it impossible to escape. This concept carries through the entirety of the game and makes for very interesting gameplay.
Now this concept may seem to simple to you to be considered a difficult game. Although the trick comes with the implementation of gravity. Your snakebird has to be touching the ground to be able to travel across the air. If not you can end up finding yourself falling. This can put you in some very tricky situations when trying to manouvere across the games obstacles such as water and spikes.
I won't have you believe that I am good at this game though. I am not. So far, over 1 hour in, I have completed 7 of the games 53 levels. These probably took me way longer than they should have done. But although I absolutely love puzzle games, I do completely suck at actually playing them. So maybe my judgement of the exceedingly hard difficulty is clouded  by this factor.
However there is one interesting little trick the game uses to help people like me along the way. When completely a level you are not only given one level to continue on with, but a selection of a few of them to try. This means if you get stumped on a level, then you can try out other ones at the same time that you may find easier to figure out. At the current stage of the game that I am at I have access to 5 different levels to try. Not that this helps me at all though because I have managed to get completely stumped on all of them. But that's just me, because remember I suck!
This game does have a delightfully charming art style to it that made the game very satisfying to play. The art style represents a very simplistic manor with very few shades of colour present. This would usually lead me to dislike the graphics style but in this case it does not. The slow swaying animations of almost every item in the game including trees, snowmen and clouds lead to an impressive visual style that expertly represents the cartoon-like graphics style I believe they were going for.
A beautifully calming soundtrack complements this unique graphics style very well. The soundtrack is equally as simple as the visuals but works perfectly well with it. The calming nature of it manages to keep you sane while attempting the ludicrously hard puzzles. I do have one minor flaw with this soundtrack however. The songs on levels run on a continuous loop. It can get boring after a while and can even get a slight bit annoying to put up with. Couple this with the fact that you sometimes spend a large amount of time on a single level and it can end up getting to be a rather annoying soundtrack.
I also feel since this is a PC game it is customary to mention PC specific parts of the game. There are some key options that are missing in the options menu for the hardcore PC gamer. The current options menu shows a large range of resolution options, fullscreen toggle and sound and music toggles. It also includes a grid option that is specific to the game which is a nice addition. I don't believe the options menu needs to have any kind of graphics options due to the very simplistic nature of the graphics. But it is missing a key option. It needs to have present seperate in game sliders for sound and music. I personally believe this option should be instantly present in every game and it is a flaw to not have it.
Overall I absolutely adored my experience of playing snakebird. Even if it was rather frustrating at times. It was largely satisfying when you finally managed to figure out how to complete a level you have been stuck on for so long. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of hard puzzle games. The game is an absolute steal at the current price of £4.99. Although don't buy it if you get easily frustrated by hard games. This game is not for people wanting a simple experience.
Disclaimer: I was provided with a early review key by the developer of the game.

Novelist in a very interesting game, and one that I enjoyed more than I expected, actually!
When I started, it felt very much like Gone Home, only with more characters than objects to help you piece the story together. Also, there is a ghostly mystery surrounding the whole thing. Too similar, I thought.
However, by the end, this succeeded for me, as a result of the choices you make throughout the game.
In fact, if you can identify with some parts of the characters, this game can really make you question a lot, not just about the game. Each choice felt significant, with trying to balance each character's goals with their problems, and I often had to "put myself in their situations", which worked surprisingly well!
I've played the game once and I'm satisfied with that. Replaying it would probably destroy some of its charm. There are tiny things the change as the game advances, and the whole thing comes off very coherently.
Also, very nice music! And it's done in a unique way: as I understood it, the music is procedurally played, meaning, the game has a pool of little musical phrases/scales, and they play at random. A bit like Thomas Was Alone.
As a result, the music is not memorable at all, but rather textural. It sets the ambience very well. I thought it totally fit the experience, being very calm and serene, with some moments of dissonance. I'll be listening to the OST.
If you want some narrative experiment, give this one a go. It has non-trivial interaction, for once!
Solid recommendation, on this one.

Rocksteady Studios have taken a beloved character and given him the treatment he deserves, what we have is one the greatest games made today and one of the best superhero game out at the moment.
The story is that The Joker held the mayor of Gotham City hostage, Batman swooped in, rescued him and caught The Joker and is bringing him back to Arkham Asylum. Batman doesn’t like how easy it was to capture The Joker so he walks him through the Asylum, which shows how great the game looks and sounds. Of course The Joker gets free and it is up to Batman to stop him and end the madness that The Joker has unleashed at the asylum.
Game play in Arkham Asylum is broken into three types. “Freeflow Combat” which is very fluid, responsive and just fun to experience. Point at an enemy and press X and Batman will attack that enemy and he can launch himself a good distance so no need to worry about range most of the time, counters are easy to pull off with the Y button when an enemy is about to hit you, you can stun enemies by using Batman‘s cape with the B button, jump over enemies and dodge them with the A button and use gadgets in battle as well to mix it up. With higher combo chains counters look better and more brutal and with upgrades you get in the game you can get a throw move and a really nasty takedown. At the end with combat it is exhilarating and really fun to do.
The second type of game play is stealth, in this mode it is usually the safer option as most of the instances of stealth in the game play involves taking down The Joker’s thugs who have guns. A few bursts from a machine gun will kill Batman very easily, so the gargoyles, vents and walkways make taking out enemies easier. There are many different options to take out the goons in your way. From exploding weak walls with Exploding Gel, pulling enemies off walkways with The Batclaw, Sonic Batarangs, Inverted Takedowns and many others.
The third type of game play is exploration, in this way discovering all the hidden riddles, Joker Teeth and collectibles to find that have been left by The Riddler to test Batman’s mental strength. For finding these collectibles you will be rewarded with interview tapes of some of the inmates at Arkham, character bios a whopping forty-two in all, 3D renders of characters, an intriguing mystery of the asylum and challenge rooms to unlock. You can find a map left by The Riddler for each area to find the collectibles easier.
To give Batman the edge against all the enemies in the game he has a vision mode called “Detective Mode” which gives him limited x-ray vision, highlights which enemies have guns, helps track down specific people and highlights objects that you can interact with. Classic Batman gadgets such as the grapple gun and his cape also help with navigating the massive environment.
Every enemy you defeat, objective completed and Riddler Trophy found will give you experience, once the experience circle is complete you can choose one of the many upgrades to obtain. From health boosts, new combat moves and more options for Batman’s gadgets.
There is so much more to say about this excellent game but that would be spoiling the surprises to come. The game looks incredible, it is really fun to play, is challenging, immersive and so much more. So give it a go, you won’t be disappointed by one of the best games made about Batman and one of my all time favourite games.
