This game delivers on a Batman experience every fan has been waiting for: gritty, dark, and unique as Batman has to dwell into the madness that is Arkham Asylum.
Right away the atmosphere is noticeable. It's dark and tense, especially in the Predator stealth missions. The villians you meet have unique and demented personalities; unlocking biographies further allow you to sink into the Batman mythos, and in fact, many of the Riddler challenges require you to know Batman lore in order to solve most puzzles.
The gameplay is simplistic at first: press M1 to strike and M2 to counter and create combos. They do add more for you to play with, like throws, quickfire Batarangs, and other gadgets.
The best part of the game for me was the Predator stealth missions. You have to grapple up to the gargoyles or crawl into a vent and hide as you use Detective Mode to find out how many enemies there are, where they are, and if they're armed or not, as well as other nifty places to hide or use or objects that can be used to take out enemies.
The voice acting is well done, especially with Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker.
The only gripe I have with this game is that in some parts later on in the game, it can continue on for a while. The bosses, unfortunately are atrocious and simple.
Apart from that however, the content that you get from GOTY is great. Put all of what I said in a package and you get this game. I highly recommend it.

I'm sorry. I WANT to recommend this game. The story is actually fairly good, if a little cliche and predictable at times. The combat system is actually really well fleshed out. The fact that Batman is the world's greatest detective is made clear, unlike most other Batman media I've seen (NO live-action Batman movie points out this fact). This game has spawned at least three games in the same vein, meaning that it has to have done well financially to even warrant ONE sequel. It's just... the two primary flaws I found in this game end up overwhelming all of the good. Oddly enough, BOTH of my main complaints stem from the same exact point - IT MAKES THINGS TOO REPETITIVE.
Also, spoiler alert. Just in case.
Let's start with the series you do things in. You go through an area, beat up a bunch of mooks, save a couple of people, and then go into detective mode to follow a trail to your next objective. Sometimes, you fight a "boss" (more on that later). Then... you do it again. And again. And again. In fact, it's been a while (nine months since I last opened the game when writing this review), but I'm pretty sure you end up following a trail in detective mode a total of SIX TIMES throughout the game. Now, while detective mode is a cool idea, and the ability to follow a trail that is normally invisible makes Batman even more awesome, making the player do it SIX TIMES just makes it feel stale and uninteresting. What makes things worse is that a couple of these sequences are pretty long, making the player feel a sense of "when is this going to end?". And believe me when I say that feeling like that is NOT a good thing for game design. Another problem I have with the detective mode sequences is that the trails are WAY too easy to follow, for the most part. There is seriously a trail where there are points to follow literally FEET from each other (well, from Batman's perspective). It's not a major search for where you need to go next, it's "follow this line to go where you need to in order to advance the plot". And it happens SIX TIMES. This, however, isn't the biggest problem I have with this game. If this was the only flaw, I would still recommend this game. No, the second flaw is FAR worse.
The second flaw is that there is only one fight in the entire game that I would call a boss battle, and no, it's not the final battle of the game. The only actual boss fight in the game is against Poison Ivy. Every other boss fight in the entire game is the exact same enemy you've fought several times already (with the exception of the final Joker fight, which is only MOSTLY unchanged compared to the other Titan enemies), or just a larger-than-average number of generic mooks. The repetitive fights are all based on Bane's fight, and seriously, once you figure out how to beat Bane, you know how to beat ALL OF THE SO-CALLED BOSS FIGHTS AFTER IT. ALL of the "Titans" you fight, INCLUDING THE TITAN JOKER BATTLE, are as simple as "hit him in the face with a Batarang when he goes to charge at you, making him vulnerable, then punch him a few times while he is stunned". AND YOU FIGHT THEM NO LESS THAN EIGHT TIMES, which really don't make them seem like bosses and make them seem more like stronger-than-average mooks. Titan Joker changes it up SLIGHTLY by leaving the fighting arena (and sending MORE mooks after you), making you end up having to get your classic ADHD enemy to pay attention to you again. When you have the boss fight against the Scarecrow, another classic villain, it is seriously as easy as "kill enough skeletons for the fight to advance to stage two". You don't even have to do anything, IIRC - the damage is dealt in a cutscene that you don't even have to initiate, followed by Scarecrow summoning more mooks for you to fight. Really, the only difference in several "mook fights" is the arena, only ONE of which actually makes a different. Harley Quinn's "boss fight" is another mook rush, but the floor is electric and can hurt you. Really, that's not a boss fight. That's a normal mook fight with environmental hazards. You beat Quinn in a cutscene that you have no control over. AT ALL. There's an optional fight near the end of the game that you trigger by punching any one of twenty-ish mooks in a room, and they all rush you as a result. I had to retry that fight more times than ANYTHING else in the game. It took me eight tries to do that one fight, as opposed to the two for Bane, the three for Poison Ivy, and the ONE for every other "boss" in the entire game! Even the Scarecrow sections, which I will admit that I only failed a few times because I tend to suck at platforming games, took me at most three tries to beat. A generic mook rush that I'm put up against twenty-ish enemies at once, though? EIGHT TRIES. THE JOKER TOOK ME ONE BECAUSE IT WAS SO SIMILAR TO THE OTHER TITAN ENEMIES.
Look, I'm not saying the game is bad. It's iconic, and it had one of the most intricate, fluid combat systems of any game I've ever played. There have been times I have been tempted to start the game up again, and play through it. Each time, though, the sheer lack of boss battles (or at least boss battles that weren't utterly disappointing) and the repetitive-but-still-overly-long detective sequences remind me why I didn't really like it. Arkham City didn't have EITHER disappointing factor, and as such is a far better game. Yes, it's not fair to compare a game to its sequel (well, unless the sequel is inferior.... Looking at you, Final Fantasy X-2...), but really, can you blame me? I enjoyed this game until I got about 2/3 of the way into it, at which point I was just looking forward to an actual boss fight and tired of the detective sequences.
tl;dr version - I would love this game if not for the very repetitive and boring detective sequences and the lack of boss battles.

If someone were to ask me what was my favorite Superhero game. Arkham Asylum would pop into my head first. It's as close to being Batman(aside from it's sequels) as it gets.
Game starts out with Batman having captured the Joker yet again and brought him back to the asylum. Shortly after bringing him in, Joker escapes custody and it comes apparent that he had planned this all along and Harley Quinn had taken control of the Arkham's security systems. So Batman sets out on the hunt for the Joker to stop him from whatever he is planning.
The visuals are stunning and still hold up and they convey Gotham's dark Gothic scenery perfectly. The audio work is equally as good with solid voice acting from everyone especially Mark Hamill's Joker.
The combat in the game utilizes a fluid simple to use but difficult to master system allowing you make to make combos from one enemy to the next. Batman also carries a wide variety of tools and gadget to allowing him to fight crime such as his trademark batarang for knocking out enemies and his grappling hook for reaching ledges from a distance as well pulling on enemies or opening new ways to go and  in his cowl he has system that allows him to detect pretty much everything around, like evidence, location of enemies and more. He acquires more as you play through the game.
Aside from the main objective there are also a ton of extra things to uncover like riddles and prizes that the Riddler has hidden all over Arkham Island. There are also tapes with treatment sessions with some of Batman's greatest adversaries and markings left by a mysterious unknown called the Spirit of Arkham.
Main storyline is great and involves many of Batman's greatest enemies and will leave you satisfied at the end when you beat it and when you do you'll have a ton of riddles and secrets to keep you busy for awhile longer.

If you haven't picked up Batman: Arkham Asylum, you're a crazy person. The game came out about a year ago and I declared that it was the best comic book game of all time. What's your deal? Get it. However, if you ignored me, Batman: Arkham Asylum (Game of the Year Edition) has come along and it's a worthy addition to your videogame collection.
Batman GOTY is the original game I loved along with four additional challenge maps and the newfound ability to play in 3D. Basically, it's more bang for your buck.
Now, before visions of Avatar-like 3D go running through your head, it's important to point out that the 3D in Batman GOTY is super-basic. You turn on the 3D filter from the main menu, pop on a pair of paper glasses with pink and green lenses, and play. It works – the HUD is at the forefront and there's definitely a depth of field effect – but it's not amazing and the glasses wash the color out of the game. That sucks seeing as how the environments and action look so good in Arkham Asylum.
The challenge maps are cool. Crime Alley is a fist-fighting challenge where you need to beat four waves of the Joker's men, and it's set in the very alley where Bruce Wayne's parents were killed. Nocturnal Hunter is a silent challenge where you need to take out a bunch of guards and complete some objectives. Meanwhile, Totally Insane and Scarecrow Nightmare throw enemies at you until you fall. All are fun and welcome additions to the regular game's challenges.
If you haven't picked up this game, you should have no qualms about grabbing Batman: Arkham Asylum (Game of the Year). If you already own Batman, the 3D and challenge maps (a few of which you can just download) really don't warrant you plunking down your pocket change to buy this one again.
Batman: Arkham Asylum is a third-person action game casting you as -- you guessed it, chum -- the Dark Knight himself. The title opens with Batman racing back to Arkham, Gotham's home for the criminally insane, with the Joker in tow. Seems the Clown Prince of Crime broke out a few weeks ago, but Batman was able to track him down and re-apprehend the baddie. However, things are never what they seem with the Joker, so after getting the wiry maniac back into the building -- a building stocked with hundreds of the Joker's goons after a "mysterious" fire at their prison -- Mr. J breaks free with the help of Harley Quinn, takes control of the penitentiary, and releases all the inmates.
Holy plot twist, Batman!
From there, you're off on an adventure that ranks right below The Dark Knight movie in terms of awesome Batman experiences. The actual Arkham campus is a loony bin spread across multiple buildings on one massive rock. With the Joker in charge you're going to have to swing over rooms filled with gas, save doctors, rip vent covers off the walls so you can make a path around locked doors, and move as fast as Batman can to stop the Joker from releasing an army of monsters on the people of Gotham City.
Now, that might sound like your typical Batman story -- and it kind of is -- but it's important to point out that this is a fairly adult title. Yeah, some of the folks from Batman: The Animated Series are back to reprise their roles (Mark Hamill is the Joker, Kevin Conroy is Batman, and Arleen Sorkin is Harley Quinn), but this isn't the cartoon. Harley's wearing a fairly skimpy outfit that shows off her lady parts, Poison Ivy's in some painted-on panties, colorful language like &quot♥♥♥♥♥quot; and "♥♥♥♥♥" is peppered in, and there are people getting murdered left and right. Arkham itself is a dark and dingy place that just had every psychopath housed there run through the halls tearing the building apart. Dead guards are laid out on the floor, papers are strewn about, and the facilities have seen better days.
These adult themes tied in with a very, very Batman-looking world really drive home your connection to the story. I don't think I'm ever going to forget Mr. Zsasz holding a knife to a female doctor, her screaming for me to save her, the Joker screaming at Zsasz to kill her, and Zsasz screaming at me to stay back. After years of the Riddler being goofy, I realized Arkham's version of the character was on a different level when he told a Riddle that ended in dismembering a baby. Plus, the segments where you're under the Scarecrow's influence and Batman's worst fears are realized are some of the coolest, most cerebral parts of the game. These are the moments that wrapped me up in the experience and made me feel like Batman on the longest night of his life.
Gameplay in this dark, creepy world breaks down into three main portions -- fist fighting, attacking from the shadows, and exploration. As you move from room to room chasing Harley or Commissioner Gordon's kidnapper, you're going to run into bad guys. Lots of times, you'll find a crew milling about or the Joker will spring a trap with handfuls of guys who are ready to kill you. This is when you'll make use of your straight hand-to-hand moves.
Fist fighting in Arkham Asylum is pretty much the definition of an easy to learn/hard to master combat system. The game allows Batman to move faster than his enemies (He's a trained ninja, people!) and engage them in 360 degrees. You just point your left stick towards whatever enemy you want to attack and Batman follows suit. It's hard to find any flaws in Arkham Asylum.  It's a solid action/adventure game that is very successful in making the player feel like they are Batman.  This is something just about every Batman game released before Arkham Asylum failed to do.  It manages to achieve this through a perfect combat system that allows you to utilise gadgets while throwing enemies around.  I couldn't find any faults in the control system or combat mechanics.
The game offers fantastic voice acting, great graphics, enjoyable story, an upgrade system that flows well with the story, the combination of puzzle and stealth elements.  Then when you are finished with the story, you can spend time collecting trophies within the game.  Collecting these trophies never even felt like a chore.  You can then test your combat skills in the challenge section, as well as your stealth instincts in the predator challenge section.
You have plenty to discover in the game, with many villains making appearances, full bios, hidden recordings, riddler trophies and many hidden areas within the map.  If you combine everything I have mentioned, you have an unforgettable experience and a game that is quite possible (at the time of writing) the best comic game ever made.

Since this is the first game in the franchise, I will review it as if the sequels did not exist.
Batman Arkham Asylum is an action-adventure game and the first title on the critically acclaimed Arkham franchise. The game was released in 2009, developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Brothers Interactive Entertainment. Arkham Asylum currently (as of the writing of this review 2014), holds the Guinness World Record for “Most critically acclaimed superhero videogame” as well as several Game of the Year awards. The Story was written by Paul Dini who's notable work include Batman: Animated Series and Batman Beyond.
In this game Batman, after just having apprehended the Joker,  takes him to the now infamous Arkham Asylum. Unfortunately, Batman soon realizes that it was all part of Joker's plan in an elaborate scheme to stage a major prison riot and take over the Asylum. Now trapped, Batman has to stop the Joker and at the same time, discover whatever sinister plot the Joker has started which seems to involve a new drug called Titan.
+ Graphically beautiful with amazing locations, well textured characters and environment
+ Excellent Voice acting from the cast, specially on Kevin Conroy (Batman) and Mark Hamill (Joker)
+ Combat Mechanic (Free Flow Combat) that goes well with...
+ Fluid Animation quality where Batman can chain attacks with absolute grace
+ Lots of cool gadgets and upgrades that can aid you in several situations
+ Perfect blend of Action and Stealth without sacrificing either one
+ Scarecrow Segments and Riddler Challenges
+ Great use of the Batman Lore with cameo appearances or references to other characters and locations in the Batman Universe
+ Excellent Story that really draws you in
+ Re-playability due to unlockable Challenges and a New Game Plus
+ Easy to learn controls and game mechanic
+ Relatively medium sized map that rewards exploration
+ Excessive amount of bone breaking physical violence
- Detective mode can be abused by perpetually leaving it active since it has no real drawback
- Underwhelming Mini bosses who can be defeated in more or less the same manner
- VERY disappointing Boss (Super Villain) battles which is perhaps the game's greatest flaw
- Combat mechanic can potentially become repetitive
-
- Game does not include a Shark Repellent
GREAT GAME and a GOOD BUY. Arkham Asylum provides you with tons of enjoyable hours playing as the Dark Knight because of its excellent story and game mechanics.
Highly recommended to Batman, Martial arts or Stealth fans out there. At $20 for its full price this game is worth every penny and it should be a no-brainer when you see it on a sale.
The game is a great comicbook / cartoon to video game adaptation of Batman. Easy to learn and use of the freeflow combat mechanic coupled with a well implemented stealth system makes the gameplay fun. The story is true to the formula that made most Batman cartoons and animated movies great with some added violence and mature content. Engaging and lovely atmosphere that is amplified by the excellent voice acting quality from the cast. Although the bosses in this game does not live up to the build up of the story, it still nonetheless wraps up each story arc pretty neatly.

Fun, definitely. You can follow the (admittedly somewhat cheesy) storyline or just drive for fun. The cars handle well, you have to adapt to each one's unique characteristics, and there's a real satisfaction in getting away from a large pack chasing you across the large region.

The game itself isn't bad. The graphics on everything are nice and the freeroam is great because of the miami/LA-esque scenery. The story, while it does get a bit monotonous and requires you to grind for levels to advance, still offers you a challenge. The cops are relatively competent and will give you a run for your money on later levels. Cars handle well, feels great to drive around at 200 km/h, and has plenty of variety. Even with the lacking customization options; you can still personalize your car to a very good degree.
Why won't I recommend this? It's using an incredibly frustrating version of rubberband AI for racers. It is not noticable during the first few hours of the game since the AI's still tame, but as you progress higher and higher, you'll soon see how the AI has an unfair advantage over you.
For starters, unless you're racing against lower-tier enemies, regardless of how far you leave the competition behind, they -will somehow catch up to you- (Example? I left my opponents with a 10-15 second advantage for the entirety of the race, but when I was at the 80%ish completion mark, they somehow managed to catch up and close the gap to 3 seconds and got to 2 seconds by 90%. That's not possible in any way and mind you, I didn't crash or slow down either.). They won't nessesarily beat you by default, you can still win, but it still pretty much makes your whatever careful driving you do redundant. Additionally, the AI has this amazing ability to clear chicanes, even those full of traffic, without noticibly slowing down like it's none of his business.
Additionally, the AI -really- hates you. They aren't programmed as racers competing against eachother, they're programmed as a pack of wolves who will do everything to make sure you lose. They will gang up on you, rough you up, and attempt to spin you out at the cost of their progress on every turn and the director will sometimes spawn traffic at the most inconvenient of times just to throw you off.
All in all, unless you really love to get angry, I'd recommend you pass this.

Always Sometimes Monsters is definitely not a game that has disappointing moral choices, as it most certainly lives up to every expectation I leveled at it, and performs more than admirably in it's execution. And what a treat it is that the moral choices in Always Sometimes Monsters are so complex, because this gem which can be seen as inaccessible at times and obtuse at others, tells a story that is a standout title in video games as a whole, one that confronts the player with mature subject manner that is almost never discussed in games, the exact stuff that anyone who loves video games has been begging to see for years.
Always Sometimes Monsters is complex, potentially one of the most layered and intricate games I've ever played. It was even explained in an interview with the devs I was privy to that the average player will see less than 50% of the game. Rarely is a game so ambitious to try to explore such a complex story in a complex way that is actually meaningful, and you would be a fool to not see how uniquely Always Sometimes Monsters accomplishes this goal.

My girl left me, my publisher fired me, I'm broke, AND THE PROM IS TOMORROW!
On a more serious note, this is a great game that got me geniunely involved with the characters. Most games make you abundently clear that the characters are just that- characters. But in Always Sometimes monsters, I really felt like they were real people, with real consequences for my actions. This isn't a game for everyone, but for someone who likes adventures, a smidge of romance, and grey-and-grey moral choices that could end in disaster or in triumph, this is a shining example of what an RPG should look like. My only qualm was that it wasn't long enough.

While playing this game, a few people asked me about the title. It isn't really that difficult to figure out. It is talking about the nature of people. We are *always* sometimes "monsters." It means that no one is ever completely innocent in life. That's the game's overall theme. While it's admirable to try to be a good person in life, you can't always help everyone. Sometimes, you have to consider self-preservation. A lot of the games major choices are centered around just that: do what's considered "good" or self-preservation? A lot of times in life, you can't have both. The game causes the player to consider some serious topics. I found it very enjoyable to play.

There was once a browser game called Ballistic, and it was absolutely phenomenal for a browser game. I know it doesn't sound impressive to be the best browser game around, but it was
good. Probably better than many of the games currently on Steam, but that isn't exactly an achievement either. I logged many hours in that game (I know, what a casual scrub) until Aquiris, the developer, took down the browser game and put a more polished version on Steam.
This game brings back so many memories and nostalgia,  yet the game feels somewhat different. It's like Aquiris kept all the parts of Ballistic that I liked, but removed the bad parts. It keeps most of the game mechanics, so on the most basic gameplay level, it feels the same. I was always a fan of how while anyone can pick up this game and have a good time, the skill ceiling is also very high, and it's possible to become very good at this game. There are classes, and each has unique weapons and skills. Players can gain an edge by playing to the advantages and disadvantages of a certain class. It is easy to pick up a class, but it is much harder to truly master it, just like in the old game. Even the best players can always improve, making for a game that can be very competitive if that is your thing. This competitive nature is further reinforced by the fact that all weapons and skills are available immediately for all players, and that Aquiris has removed the microtransactions and pay-to-win aspect that haunted the original game. Immediately, new players are presented with a level playing field, and do not have to deal with more experienced enemies toting massively overpowered weapons.
This game isn't 100% perfect, and there are some balance issues. Just like the original game, spawn camping is a major issue, and it is sometimes impossible to get out of spawn without being killed by the entire enemy team waiting to kill you. Thankfully, a small area of spawn is protected, but Aquiris should really do more about it. In addition, some weapons are ridiculously unbalanced, such as the grenade launcher. It doesn't really take skill to get kills: just spam grenades in the general direction of the enemy and profit. It should really be nerfed so that it rewards practice and skill.
Despite a few issues, Ballistic Overkill is a very enjoyable but difficult game. Unfortunately, not many people play this game. There are usually a few populated servers with some very dedicated players. Sadly, this game is far too overlooked. It deserves more players.

As a big fan of what Ballistic originally was, it pains me to give this game a negative review.
When the game was on Kongregate just as Ballistic, it was so much better. A F2P FPS with pretty good graphics for a browser game, lockboxes (crates for weapons), multiple events for special lockboxes, a ton of classes to level up, so many weapons! It was amazing! I played the game for a long time, levelling up my classes, opening lockboxes, participating in the various events, unboxing those lockboxes. There was a little bit of character customization too, just some little hats or miscs that you could put on from Holiday Events. The game was so ALIVE! I would get in a party with my friend and find a match instantly no matter what time of the day it was. Ballistic was more than I ever expected when it came to a Browser-Based, Free2Play FPS game.
Unfortunately, Ballistic Overkill is NOT Ballistic. Before I get into why, let's start with the Pros. Ballistic Overkill still has the good graphics that were in Ballistic, possibly even better. The game has all the classes from the original Ballistic and you can still level them up. They've also kept old maps from the original game. Gameplay feels like it used to. It hasn't changed a bit. The way you play the game now is the way the game was played before it came to Steam.
Now, let's go to the Cons. Lockboxes are gone. There is no way to play the game and earn any type of lockbox. Special lockboxes, mostly event ones, would give you the same gun you can buy in the store but with boots and/or camos to the guns. Not to mention, you didn't even have to buy the lockboxes if you didn't want to. You could just play the game and over time you'd earn enough points for them to unlock for you right after the game. The game eliminated the idea of being F2P, but did they really have to get rid of the idea of lockboxes for boosts or skins or anything like that? I mean, it'd still be cool to have a way to personalize your gun through them. Rather than lockboxes, all the guns are already given to you. Seriously? There's no feeling of a grind to unlock a gun you want? There's no sense of achievement after doing so? (Not to mention that not all of the guns from Ballistic are in Ballistic Overkill!) Everything is already given to you. It's like you've already beaten the game just by buying it and pressing play. It gets so boring after a while because once you use all the weapons, there's nothing more to the game. That's it. Also, where the heck are the servers? This game was always so alive when it was on Kongregate. Now I open the game and I see about 3-4 servers. If I'm lucky, 5. Most of these servers don't even have good connection. After seeing multiple red 1 bar connections on almost all the servers, there's that 1 server that either has a 3 bar or the lucky, green 4 bar connection. Even if the connection is good, sometimes it still won't join. I click cancel and try again, but no luck. After a bit of time I click cancel again, and then the cancel button doesn't work. Cancel. Cancel. CANCEL! It doesn't cancel. Then I have to restart the game. That's just annoying.
Ballistic Overkill is far from the original Ballistic. Sure, the gameplay is the same, it has the same maps, it has same classes, it has SOME of the same weapons, but does it add anything new? Is the game better in any way? No. Not at all. In fact, it takes away things that made the old game so much fun. Lockboxes, weapons, events, especially players and servers. It just makes the game worse. It's so boring to play. The original Ballistic was so much fun! I loved it! I don't hate this game, but I definitley don't like it. I don't want to hate this game! This game either needs to go back to its old self, or it at least needs to add back everything that made Ballistic what it was. This game is really nothing special or unique now. It's just anothe average shooter that you could easily find on a browser.
The cons easily overweigh the pros, I do not recommend this game to anyone.

What can I say about Arkham Asylum? It's one of the greatest starts to a franchise I've ever had the pleasure of playing and although it's not as good a game as it's follow up Arkham City it still has a ton of appeal even 5 years after it came out.
Many games have come since Arkham Asylum yet none have had controls that are as responsive and well put together (except other games in the Arkham franchise).
The control system uses a unique take on the classic beat-em-up style by incorporating what you need.
Every button has a purpose whether it's for grappling, throwing, fighting or gliding.
Games can still be fun with little to no story but it's a mistake too many companies make. When I play a game I want to become engrossed in the world I've invested hard earned money into.
Arkham Asylum is one of the greatest original Batman stories in a long time. It doesn't get carried away and go over the top but instead manages to include nearly ever iconic villain you've ever seen or heard of in Batman lore. It even manages to do all that without making it seemed crowded, that's no mean-feet.
The gameplay is generally broken up into different sections which are fighting, stealth and roaming.
Fighting is fantastic and feels completely natural. It becomes harder when you try some of the more advanced moves but nothing a load of practice won't help with.
Stealth, or more aptly names predator encounters, are environments where you can swing from gargoyle statues, hide under vents or creep up behind enemies in the hope of getting a take-down.
Roaming isn't as important in this game as it is in Arkham City but it's still fun gliding around the courtyards or venturing around the asylum looking for clues to find and puzzles to solves.
The game is fantastic and does an excellent job of really making you feel like Batman. No other games have ever come close to that feeling which is why Arkham Asylum is a true classic.

Ziggurat is fun. Pure and simple.
A lot of the time games (especially roguelikes) have fun mechanics and then water them down with frustrating difficulty, slow movement, stilted combat, and other things that feel more like limiters to your fun than anything else.
Ziggurat is not afraid to remove all of these boundaries.
You sprint along at the speed of sound, bunnyhopping is effortless and fun, combat is fast and controls are responsive, arenas are varied and interesting. The graphics have an almost surrealist theme, with things looking cartoony and innocent from a distance and turning into these nightmarish creatures upon closer inspection. The weapons all feel fun to use, although AoE could use a bit of a buff. The big part is that it hardly ever feels unfair. Similar to binding of isaac or enter the gungeon, when you enter a room it will have a predetermined design that the devs made, and certain enemies will spawn, meaning there's no random unbeatable clumps of enemies that make levels unpassable. the difficulty and variety come in the form of modifiers, which are randomly assigned to rooms, and make combat insane. From the intense "All damage 4x" modifier which brings back haunting memories of quake, to the wit testing "Enemies invisible" modifier, where enemies are only partially visible when they are attacking, to the ball-bustingly difficult "scavenge" rooms (good luck)
This game offers a fun, arcad-y first person shooter experience, something much needed among all the skin-a-box shooter games that companies♥♥♥♥♥♥out so very often.
I would absolutely recommend.

Having stayed far away from Batman games since they've never been up to my expectations, I avoided Arkham Asylum. Little-known studio at that time, Rocksteady, created what we can call the perfect superhero game. And I've played the early 2000 videogames of Spider-Man, X-Men: Wolverine's Revenge & The Last Stand and Marvel Ultimate Alliance, to come down to this conclusion.
If Asylum was a blueprint for what a truly excellent gaming experience is, City most certainly raised the bar for open-world superhero games (currently finishing the original game's side missions). Having beat all achievements in Asylum in under 20 hours, I tell you, this is one of the best games I've ever bought and played. And the difficulty is just right, even on hard mode.

Ziggurat is a first-person roguelike which throws you into a mystical temple and hands you the towering task of finding your own way out. You’ll fight your way through rooms upon rooms brimming with enemies, some typical fantasy foes, some taking a rather silly twist, all with the capacity to put you in an early grave if you aren’t mindful of the fighting. You’ll face these foes with all sorts of wands, explosives, staves, and even a gun or two if you’re lucky. Upon starting the game you’ll pick one of three starting characters, with more that can be unlocked from certain achievements throughout the game. Like with many rogue-likes, there is really little to no story to speak of here in Ziggurat, but the little I gathered involved you being part of a cult and getting sent into the Ziggurat as part of an initiation rite, nothing really of note. Ziggurat really doesn’t bring any revolutionary new features to the table, though plenty of the mechanics do feel unique in their own ways, but the game itself handles just about everything extremely well.
One of the most significant factors for a first-person rogue-like like Ziggurat is the combat: especially important in Ziggurat as it’s something you’re going to be doing in just about every room. The combat never ceases to be extremely thrilling, even though much of it stays the same from room to room. Your enemies will change, the weapons you obliterate them with will change, but the satisfaction you gain from the combat will not. There’s three main schools of weaponry: spells, alchemy, and staves, each one with unique themes and weapons to unleash. The first type, spells, are probably the flashiest of the three, seeing as they’re all magical abilities. The spells in Ziggurat are really fun to use, though in my experience they’re somewhat limited in their variety, since a lot of the spells bear striking similarities both in how they look when held and how they look when casted. Then there’s the alchemical contraptions found throughout the Ziggurat, which are memorable and more steampunk-esque in both in their use and design. These include arms such as cluster and firebombs, as well as even an explosive-firing handgun, and are definitely the most unique and fun to use out of the bunch. Finally come your staves, which all tend to look either the same or remarkably similar, which is certainly disappointing, though their effects are what makes them stand out. Each staff has a unique effect, such as being able to fire a vicious shotgun spread of magic bolts or even calling forth lightning in one case, but these effects are considerably weaker when it comes to visuals and are more focused towards functionality, which is fine, but it does start to make you not want to use them as often. Now each of these weapons has a limited amount of ammo that you’ll need to ensure stays well supplied, though you won’t be using the special weapons often enough to actually run out that often. What you will be using is the wand: your main weapon with an unlimited pool of ammunition, though once you run out it will have to recharge, and two main fire modes. This mystical wand is your bread and butter throughout the ziggurat and thankfully it’s incredibly fun to wield, sending sharp violet daggers across the battlefield and straight into the skulls of your foes. All these weapons may seem overwhelming but the rate at which you acquire new ones very often, only really at the start of each new floor, is spread just far enough to keep you hungry for something new, a desire Ziggurat is eager to satisfy.
Ziggurat also has a rather mysterious ambience, which only increases as you clear the floors and edge ever closer to its peak, which is where I feel a bit let down. This mysterious ambience is fantastic but is let down by the environments of the Ziggurat itself, each floor feeling more and more similar the closer you get to the top. Don’t get me wrong, I think that the environments can be quite beautiful and at times you really feel like you’re inside of a theme park but I still end up feeling like I’ve been through it all before after just one or two playthroughs as there simply isn’t enough of them. The environments on each floor remain the same every playthrough which is disappointing, as it isn’t nearly as enchanting seeing the same massive lava dungeon on the 20th playthrough as it was on the first or second. The room layout leaves a lot to be desired as well, most of the time you have no incentive to explore as most of the rooms end up as an abomination-filled monster mash rather than having something to reward your exploration. You can argue that your reward is the experience you get from those enemies, leading to more skill points that are unlockable, yet even still I think Ziggurat would benefit from some other kind of explorative reward as well. Speaking of skills and experience, this is another key part of the Ziggurat: leveling up. Every new level you pick a new skill, all of which have cute little artworks to go with them, which is a pleasing sight in the middle of a monstrous dungeon. These skills are what keep the gameplay and experience as a whole from getting stale, allowing you to make your own build and shape how you go about each run. Coupling this with the strong monster and boss variety, and that makes the dungeon-crawling feel even just a little bit different every time.
You’ll willingly toss yourself into the Ziggurat, but after experiencing the frantic combat and seeing the gaudy weapon effects, you just may not want to leave.

This is a game that I am going to give a very soft recommendation for, because while this game has plenty of faults, I still enjoyed playing through it and I think others would too.
At it's core, The Novelist is a game about interpersonal conflict and the moral and ethical struggles that comes with trying to balance the wants and needs of individuals in a family. Each chapter in the game presents the player with three desires, one for each member of the family, and you are asked to make a decision based on these desires. I personally enjoyed exploring the house to find all the clues to each family member and I also enjoyed going through their memories to learn more about the situation as well.
However there are several problems I have with The Novelist, the chief one being that the story in and of itself isn't that interesting. It's a typical story, Dad wants to work on his novel, Mom wants to save the marriage and get back into a profession she had to give up when the kid arrived, and the kid wants to play with Dad and is struggling in school and is bullied. We've all seen stories that use these elements elsewhere, and they used them a lot better there. Another issue I had was that the individual chapters didn't seem to be all that connected. Each chapter felt more like variations of the same 3 or 4 issues and the decisions made in the previous chapter seemed to have little influence in other chapters.

The Novelist was such a superb game; just what you'd want from an indie title. The game is basically a story about a family struggling to balance priorities. Your role is to help nudge the decision making along the way. You play as some kind of paranormal entity that moves around the house unseen and silently influences the choices that the characters make.
The actual gameplay is very limited but the story here is excellent. It's a lovely story, brilliantly voice acted, and the whole thing just has a unique style to it that's hard to explain but really works.
It has replayability too because in each chapter you cannot please everybody; you have to make compromises and so by the end of the game you wonder how it might have turned out if you'd made different choices.
The game is fairly short and I wouldn't pay full price for it (I obtained it through trading) but if you see it on sale then snap it up!

The Novelist is, not surprisingly, a story telling game.
You’re a being, a spectre or ghost. It is never explained. There’s a family of three and the entire game takes place in a small cabin in the woods. The goal? Make decisions for the family.
Gameplay is.. lacking. All you do is move about the house while trying to avoid being seen. Each chapter you need to find a certain amount of items, over and over. Once you’ve found all the items, you can enter the memories of the family members to find three memory snippets, again and again. The items aren’t very well hidden, nor are the snippets which can easily be tracked by listening. This cycle repeats itself for the 9 chapters it counts. It’s mind numbingly repetitive.
The story is tailored towards the choices you make, a promise made in lots of games these days. This game does deliver. For the purpose of this review I’ve ran through the game twice, making different choices each time. I’m avoiding spoilers, but you can choose to truly neglect a family member, with devastating results. While this is pretty interesting, the final outcome is given in a typewriter animation, which fails to make you care about the results.
The Novelist has potential, but it doesn’t utilize a lot of it. It’s not a fun game and it doesn’t have a great story either. While the character are relatable they never really come to life inside the game – only in the diary segments which got narrated. That only leaves you with a tale with an interesting dynamic outcome, but sadly that isn’t enough to make this a recommendable title.
+ Your choices truly matter
+ Decent cell-shaded graphics
+ Fairly original
± Solid voice acting, but not everything is narrated
- Boring, repetitive gameplay
- Too easy
- Small scale
- Lacking conclusion
4+ / 10

I do not have anywhere near the hours that many giving reviews have, but I believe I've earned what it takes to give input.
This game is very grindy, but it's not completely unforgiving or P2W has many have complained about. My steam shows close to 600 hours with an average of 50 per week recently, that is highly inaccurate. In game I've roughly 330 hours on the ground across the past 5 months.
In this time I've ground out every weapon for infantry, paratrooper, and recon... along with most tanks and planes. I personally disagree with the arguments that grinding takes too long, especially those who say it takes months for a weapon or two. I finished off a new german paratrooper buying and modding FG42 in the most expensive way in two days. This game's grinding isn't nearly as bad as many games, for example Warframe.
This game is not P2W by any means, everything you can get in this game can be bought by putting time and effort in or by paying cash. Every game needs this since developers can NOT support such MMO games without money, you honestly think someone would run a game they're losing money on...? No. Game developers have to make a living too, that doesn't make this pay to win. Game of war is pay to win, you pay or you leave there.
Many argue veteran is P2W but if you're a serious player than 1.7M credits in 3 months is nothing. Every time I blink I have 200k credits sitting with nothing new unlocked to spend it on.
One issue I would bring up with this game is that you jump from bronze to gold matchmaking too quickly, and that can be a serious kick in the face to newer players. Even sitting in silver a little longer would be nice. Also, a huge warning to new players against war would be nice, considering it makes gold look like bronze.
For those looking for a WWII game, you should move on. This game is so flooded by inaccurate info that WWII buffs generally have heart attacks every time they see it. If you're looking for a fun FPS to burn time on, come grind with us. I personally find it fun and will recommend it, but it's not for everyone.
Most players will have varied inputs on this game based on how long they've been here, not how many hours but merely how long they've been here. In it's glory days, of which I was not part of, this game was amazing. Many of them will highly dislike the newer changes and you honestly cant blame them. I however see it as another fun game. Again, note my hours. It's inaccurate on steam considering it states 100 hours in the past two weeks while I (might) have only played maybe 60 in that time. Yeah yeah, no life.
In the end, to each their own. If you like FPS games, and are looking for something free to try... It's a small download, no matter what anyone says it's fun with friends. Try it, can't hurt just to try. Ignore the butthurt buffs and vets complaining bout horrid changes, you never know... you might not mind it. Have fun, good luck, and don't die too much ;)

Heroes n Generals isn’t a bad game to say it has problems I’ll go through a few later on but first I will warn you this reviews going to be long
now for me I must admit I am a war monger I love war and all that comes with it and so I have sought after games that fit a timeline of war from early days such as Rome 2 to the cold war era and I have found some games that fit the puzzle well this game fits the puzzle for WWII ground warfare very well I have seen many games similar however none this accurate not even the new call of duty WWII would fit as close the reviews I have seen coupled by the videos makes it a mockery to WWII.
Now having said that this game does have many of draw backs for instance there is only three factions Russian, Germany, and the United States during the war there were other factions depending on the location.
With these three factions there come major imbalances such as the Russians having weapons with the highest rate of fire, accuracy, and damage as many would state that this has not changed since the games beta. The Germans are second in line as their weapons are more balanced however still high on damage there rate of fire is also high as well however during the war German firearms were designed that way. And so that leaves the last faction on the list the United States there weapons are weak mostly slow and poor accuracy while there machine guns have good rate of fire the damage is drastically reduced which makes it hard to fight.
In this game there are also troop classes and ribbons that you unlock through experience which unlock new weapons but that will come after right now the classes, there are several classes of troops ranging from simple infantry, paratroopers, recon, tank driver, pilot, and general in that order now when you start you start with the simple infantry each has a simple semi-automatic rifle and as you fight on you gain silver which is the main currency of the game however the other troop classes are far too expensive in my opinion as it limits the game as I have had matches where on the enemy team you have people sniping everyone from half the map away with bolt action rifles that’s always a one shot kill to matches with pilots that spam the air and bomb players with far too good of accuracy. Now as to the ribbons these ribbons unlock new items but you half to buy them after unlocking them such as for the United States simple infantry to anyone who has played WWII infantry games they know of the weapons used for the United States and the very end of the ribbon for semi-auto and bolt action weapons is the M1 Carbine an iconic firearm of the war however in my time when I had but one soldier class it took me a month to get to ribbon level nine on that so I could unlock the M1A1 Thompson sub machine gun and the M1 is at ribbon number twelve so there is shows a rather hard grind and then there’s another aspect of the game is the prises to get these items there not cheap the M1A1 was as expensive as a tank driver which isn’t cheap as it goes the cheapest class is the infantry, paratrooper, tank driver pilot, recon, and then General in that order the wiki for the game can show you the costs as I will not get into the numbers.
There is also game play as the game lacks in both networking as well as balance such as when I first started I could only play one map a simple king of the hill map take the point and hold it but there was a large issue and that was in many of cases I was forced to spend from one to four hours waiting for a match and that didn’t change when I unlocked other maps to play on it got worse there’s also the issue of too few maps as there is only nine maps in total to issues on balanced teams I have been in matches many of times where my team was out numbered the max the team can be is twenty players vs twenty payers and in a number of cases I had found myself along with five others against twenty players not very fun and that’s not including map problems or enemy team compositions on some maps it allows the enemy team to spawn camp your spawn points to enemy’s hiding in bushes and moving from bush to bush killing everyone that crosses their sights while going an entire game with few deaths as it is almost impossible to find them or as I mentioned allow them to be expert snipers now there is another problem that adds to this and that’s cheat programs they do exist for this game and people have been caught using them however the development team doesn’t care and lets them get away with it. I have looked up some of these programs and what they can do is impressive from allowing you to see where everyone is be it friendly or enemy to aim bots to even damage reduction the programs very.
Another issue is balance among other classes such as the tank driver certain tanks of the other classes are very difficult to destroy as with the Russians being over powered in all aspects it for the tank driver the German variety is the most powerful even in the lowest of tanks the Pz2 in the game is a light tank however it has the firepower of a medium tank as it has a cannon where the other two factions first starter tanks have heavy machine guns that can deal with light armour however as for the Pz2 if you were to go one on one with it starter to starter the Pz2 would win due to the fire power.
Now in some instances the game for me has been fun however I would not recommend this game as it is way too unbalanced and is in need of work and perhaps a new development team one dedicated to fixing the issues. If I were to start fixing the problems one thing which is apparent is the cheat programs you can’t fully prevent them on PC so I would integrate aspects of one into the game such as the finder to allow you to see everyone’s positions most weapons as well would need work as the ones for the United States need a damage increase the German bolt action needs a reduction and the Russians need to be either removed or reduced to make them fair as one out of every ten battles against the Russians are a defeat from there more maps are needed as there are too few maps, prices on everything is too high and make it a grind that takes months to achieve anything however I believe the development team doesn’t care and would rather make a publicity stunt like there latest in a contest for the prize of a visit to their studio and to meet the developers and see their latest work a rather cheap prize especially when you see the winners as one is a notorious cheater who apparently was banned and came back so that there speaks for itself.

Deus Ex: Game Divided was supposed to be a really nice sequel with interesting story and stuff like that, but it managed to fail horribly in most aspects.
Core gameplay hasn't changed - you are given freedom to achieve tasks in any way you like. This is one of the good aspects of the game. Unfortunately, quests with these tasks lead nowhere. Their outcome is supposed to influence the rest of the game, but the game ends before any quest characters can do something (aside from forgery girl, I think). Almost every NPS was made with 'I'll help you later' in mind, but they never help, because game was divided into parts.
Friendly characters have nice stories and it is almost impossible to say if they are 100% on your side. But since game is cut, there is not enough time to tell their backstories through some personal quests, which makes them dull, unlike characters from HR.
Graphics are nice, but the price you need to pay for ultra settings is too high. Levels are littered with garbage - bottles, cans, books, whatever. Every room is filled with stuff, that is supposed to show the player that real people live there. Because of that, some levels look too busy (such as Golem city); the reason is understandable, but I'd take a couple of semi-empty locations with more plot instead of detailed surroundings.
Music is good as usual, McCann hasn't lost his touch.
The game looks good in general, but abrupt ending kills all the joy. Were developers thinking that players will say 'thank you for leaving Adam in such a weird position, I will gladly wait three more years for 12 missions and 2 dlcs'? Whoever chose to split the game in parts should be fired.

Well well well, Always Sometimes Monsters. When I read this title on the internet, I don't need to tell you that it catched my attention, I didn't know what was the game but the title was almost enough to convince me. I read the description, I said "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ (I'm not the polite type of person) that's what I was searching for" : a story, not an another indie game that looks exactly like the others. I thought of To The Moon right away, the graphics, the story over the gameplay, over everything. And it made me buy it.
So, if you don't want to read more, yes, I recommend this game. I highly recommend it. If you liked To The Moon, you'll love it because it's longer, it's a "real" game, you're free to do whatever you want.
+ First of all, you chose the hero, you chose who you are. That is the first important choice you have to make, and, I think that in a game like that, you have to be able to chose you character, for the immersion. You can identify yourself tohim/her, even if you've got nothing in common.
+ Let's talk about the choices because, well, you obviously play for that. You'll have a lot of choices to make, sometimes they seem useless (and they sometimes are), sometimes, they are lifechangers. You really feel the importance of the importan choices you've made.
+ About the freedom of choice and action, I think that, even if you'd like to be able to interact with some things that you can't interact with, you'll never feel like a prisoner of the game, you have an objective that you can reach or not, and you can reach it by any means necessary. You want to be a good person ? So, be a good person. But, the "bad" way seems easier ? Nobody will stop you. You write your fate. You choose how to find what you're looking for. Or to give up. Great game based on one of the greatest superheroes of all time--Batman. The combat is immersive; if you ever played Spiderman, the combat mimicks that of Spidey and counter measuring your enemies is very satisfying. Nothing beats dodging and throwing Mike Tyson punches and spin kicks to thugs. Majority of buildings and structures are mountable with your Batlaw to scout areas for enemies or to strategize how to pick them off one-by-one. The latter will apply to situations when there are enemies with machine guns as bullets take a good chunk of Batman's health. Yet this is where it gets fun; you as The Dark Knight can use the Batclaw to mount on a gargoyle and press Y button to hang an unsuspecting thug onto the gargoyle while he screams "Let me down!" Others nearby will hear their comrade and rush to him. What do you do? Grapple to the next gargoyle and repeat. You can also take them out silently by sneaking behind them or using certain gadgets. For enemies with only fists and melee weapons, you can just zerg in and counter when necessary.
Graphics are amazing as are the movie-like cutscenes. The voice acting is superb. I recommend playing with Physics on. I played with the GTX 295 with Physics set to High and it was outstanding. The game is very fun. Only part what I viewed as tedious was Croc and his lair. Scarecrow was literally creepy and disturbing. Poison Ivy was, well, hot! Just finished this game and I admit it made me understand why the "Arkham" series of Batman games is so popular. The game has very nice and well-balanced mix of combat, puzzle solving and platforming. Lots of effort was put into all mechanics and as a result the player never gets bored with one part or another due to constant variation.  Mechanically the game is very solid and it does give you a variety of things to learn in order to be able to progress without getting too overwhelming. All new tricks are introduced at a reasonable pace and most are explained well enough (also thanks to the fact that you are immediately forced to use the new unlocked gadgets in order to progress forward). The game is not entirely open-world and gives you a number of "hubs" or areas to explore and act in while unlocking them one after another. This makes the experience a bit more linear than some might like. Although, once again, the level design is really good and it will make your exploration enjoyable throughout the whole title.
The voice-acting is very well done and so are the cutscenes. The lore obviously adds a lot of charm to the game with lots of nice little details like interviews (voiced dialogues telling about the characters' past) and biographies to unlock and collect. The in-game graphics still look pretty good although some textures and objects do look at little bit outdated (i.e. low-resolution). Some tweaking with the usage of Steam forums might also be required in order to make the not-entirely-optimal port run at maximum resolution and with maximized visual effects even on reasonably modern systems.
The story is reasonably entertaining and holds the game together well to make it interesting for the player. The main questions the game asks (as its name states) are those of sanity and madness and how one can slide from the former into the latter while also asking the player whether the criminals can be considered as "ill" and/or "uncurable". Obviously, the aesthetics of the game is somewhat grim although not without some jokes inbetween (if you like the gags Joker produces).
One (non-crucial) problem consists in the fact that one can not access all in-game secrets that one detects immediately (special gadgets that unlock later are required for this). Thus I have spent some time in vain wondering whether I could not find the right approach to the secret before I gave in and Internet told me those secrets can only be accessed later on in the game.
The DLCs barely add anything to the main game as they do the same thing as other in-game stealth and arena combat pieces only in new locations. So if you are dying to do more combat/stealth, they can serve as some additional fun, but otherwise they are nothing really interesting. Same goes for the challenges, which basically repeat the in-game locations for arena combat and stealth missions with slight variations (enemy composition and/or additional environmental restrictions). While all of them can serve to improve your in-game stealth and combat skills, the main game learning cruve is so nicely adjusted that it is quite enough to just play the "Normal" difficulty mode continuously to gradually learn and use everything that might be necessary to beat the game.
Overall, if you want to start off with the first Batman game that made the whole series so famous, you will not be disappointed and enjoy your time. I heartily recommend this title.

In the Novelist you play as a vauge, intangible, but somehow visible, entity that can somehow influence the decisions of people living in a secluded house. You must sneak around teh house examining letters, journals, and even combing through the memories of the inhabitants, then make a choice for one of them that will necesarily mean sacrificing the happiness of the others. It's an interesting idea that's realized well in purely mechanical terms. I'd slike to try a game using the same engine that tells a more interesting story. Unfortunately, the actual game is terrible due to being the poorly told story of a horrible clan of boring idiots.
The people in the house arbitrarily fixate on doing particular things, and then cannot be happy unless everyone else is forced to do that and only that. They'll decide to go camping, for example, and then they will talk of nothing else until ti's been decided. You can literally peer into their very soul and all you will find is them saying they want to go camping. To be sure, there's existential terror to that idscovery, but not the kind the creator intended.
If you really want to see a good idea squandered, maybe pick this up in a steep sale. Otherwise save your money.

Or, Life is Tough Simulator. The Kaplans are a family of three, each one living through their own struggles; the writing is very effective in letting their dilemmas resonate with the player: if you've ever had to make a difficult decision, prioritizing one aspect of your life to the detriment of another, there's a good chance the Kaplans will click with you.
If you've liked The Walking Dead, you'll probably like this game too, even though the tone is a lot more domestic and down to earth, more slow burning than the life or death choices or gut-wrenching moments TWD has. It's also an excellent game for introducing new players to first person games, for a variety of reasons, some of which are explained below.
Playing in Stealth mode is very easy, but adds a little tension I appreciated, and I'd recommend keeping it on for a first playthrough, while Story mode (which will let you explore unhindered) is probably more suited to replays, should you be interested in finding out how your decisions could have shaped the story differently.
The interactive sections will have you looking for 'clues' in order to advance the story, are not challenging at all and work well to break up the game in different sections that support pacing and the sense of time passing. However, there is a degree of repetition in them, and your enjoyment of the game will likely be greater if you don't try to finish it in one sitting (two worked well for me).
The music is minimalistic and fits the game very well, complementing and lending extra power to the writing, the voice work is also well done. The visuals are a little sketchy, and the environment limited, Gone Home this isn't, but it's obvious the budget and the size of the team were very different (The Novelist is a one man project), overall the artstyle works well for this game IMO, and there's just enough detail to support the interactive sections.
Two thumbs up from me.

"It's like if Painkiller and Magic: The Gathering had a baby, and that child was then orphaned but it was raised by Hard Reset and then, when it got older, it became really good friends with Heretic and Hexen, but then it fell in love with a roguelike and then they got married and lived happily ever after." - my original full review for this game.
Ziggurat is a room-based arena first-person shooter, much like Painkiller. Unlike Painkiller there are a multitide of different characters, most of them unlockable, all of whom are JUST different enough to justify their existence but not so different that they require completely different playstyles.
You have 4 weapon slots: A Wand (unlimited ammo, but doesn't do much damage), a Spell (varies, but usually for short range attacks), a Staff (varies, but usually for long range attacks), and Alchemy (explosives).
The game itself is about 5 maps long, and can be finished in approx. 45 mins to 1 hour.
But every playthrough is different because of the roguelike aspect: weapons (inc. types), maps, shrine bonuses, even the bosses at the end of the levels etc. are aways random, level-up perks give you a choice between two or more random perks, and so on.
So, it's hard to actually *build* a character. And that's where the fun is - you might not get ANY SINGLE item you wanted for any given playthrough.
The only negative experience I had with this game was with one of the possible 2nd map bosses, Lady Audrey. Because I am a stupid old man, I didn't realise that you have to shoot her tentacles to make her vulnerable.
Oh stop looking at me like that, she's a giant flytrap plant and it's not creepy at all.
But I would happily have paid approx $20 AUD for this game, based on my experience and playtime so far.

Ziggurat is a dungeon crawling fps, with a focus on the magic arts.  There are four attacks: wand, spell, staff, and alchemy.  As you advance through the Ziggurat, you have a chance of getting new weapons and abilities that make life a lot easier during your adventure.  Ziggurat is a roguelike fps in that dying starts you from the beginning, but you unlock abilities that are shared among all characters.  The variety in characters makes replayability high, as does the random maps, random weapons, and random abilities.  A thorough playthrough runs about 50-60 minutes for me, but there are multiple difficulties and game modes to extend replay value further.

Heroes n Generals isn’t a bad game to say it has problems I’ll go through a few later on but first I will warn you this reviews going to be long
now for me I must admit I am a war monger I love war and all that comes with it and so I have sought after games that fit a timeline of war from early days such as Rome 2 to the cold war era and I have found some games that fit the puzzle well this game fits the puzzle for WWII ground warfare very well I have seen many games similar however none this accurate not even the new call of duty WWII would fit as close the reviews I have seen coupled by the videos makes it a mockery to WWII.
Now having said that this game does have many of draw backs for instance there is only three factions Russian, Germany, and the United States during the war there were other factions depending on the location.
With these three factions there come major imbalances such as the Russians having weapons with the highest rate of fire, accuracy, and damage as many would state that this has not changed since the games beta. The Germans are second in line as their weapons are more balanced however still high on damage there rate of fire is also high as well however during the war German firearms were designed that way. And so that leaves the last faction on the list the United States there weapons are weak mostly slow and poor accuracy while there machine guns have good rate of fire the damage is drastically reduced which makes it hard to fight.
In this game there are also troop classes and ribbons that you unlock through experience which unlock new weapons but that will come after right now the classes, there are several classes of troops ranging from simple infantry, paratroopers, recon, tank driver, pilot, and general in that order now when you start you start with the simple infantry each has a simple semi-automatic rifle and as you fight on you gain silver which is the main currency of the game however the other troop classes are far too expensive in my opinion as it limits the game as I have had matches where on the enemy team you have people sniping everyone from half the map away with bolt action rifles that’s always a one shot kill to matches with pilots that spam the air and bomb players with far too good of accuracy. Now as to the ribbons these ribbons unlock new items but you half to buy them after unlocking them such as for the United States simple infantry to anyone who has played WWII infantry games they know of the weapons used for the United States and the very end of the ribbon for semi-auto and bolt action weapons is the M1 Carbine an iconic firearm of the war however in my time when I had but one soldier class it took me a month to get to ribbon level nine on that so I could unlock the M1A1 Thompson sub machine gun and the M1 is at ribbon number twelve so there is shows a rather hard grind and then there’s another aspect of the game is the prises to get these items there not cheap the M1A1 was as expensive as a tank driver which isn’t cheap as it goes the cheapest class is the infantry, paratrooper, tank driver pilot, recon, and then General in that order the wiki for the game can show you the costs as I will not get into the numbers.
There is also game play as the game lacks in both networking as well as balance such as when I first started I could only play one map a simple king of the hill map take the point and hold it but there was a large issue and that was in many of cases I was forced to spend from one to four hours waiting for a match and that didn’t change when I unlocked other maps to play on it got worse there’s also the issue of too few maps as there is only nine maps in total to issues on balanced teams I have been in matches many of times where my team was out numbered the max the team can be is twenty players vs twenty payers and in a number of cases I had found myself along with five others against twenty players not very fun and that’s not including map problems or enemy team compositions on some maps it allows the enemy team to spawn camp your spawn points to enemy’s hiding in bushes and moving from bush to bush killing everyone that crosses their sights while going an entire game with few deaths as it is almost impossible to find them or as I mentioned allow them to be expert snipers now there is another problem that adds to this and that’s cheat programs they do exist for this game and people have been caught using them however the development team doesn’t care and lets them get away with it. I have looked up some of these programs and what they can do is impressive from allowing you to see where everyone is be it friendly or enemy to aim bots to even damage reduction the programs very.
Another issue is balance among other classes such as the tank driver certain tanks of the other classes are very difficult to destroy as with the Russians being over powered in all aspects it for the tank driver the German variety is the most powerful even in the lowest of tanks the Pz2 in the game is a light tank however it has the firepower of a medium tank as it has a cannon where the other two factions first starter tanks have heavy machine guns that can deal with light armour however as for the Pz2 if you were to go one on one with it starter to starter the Pz2 would win due to the fire power.
Now in some instances the game for me has been fun however I would not recommend this game as it is way too unbalanced and is in need of work and perhaps a new development team one dedicated to fixing the issues. If I were to start fixing the problems one thing which is apparent is the cheat programs you can’t fully prevent them on PC so I would integrate aspects of one into the game such as the finder to allow you to see everyone’s positions most weapons as well would need work as the ones for the United States need a damage increase the German bolt action needs a reduction and the Russians need to be either removed or reduced to make them fair as one out of every ten battles against the Russians are a defeat from there more maps are needed as there are too few maps, prices on everything is too high and make it a grind that takes months to achieve anything however I believe the development team doesn’t care and would rather make a publicity stunt like there latest in a contest for the prize of a visit to their studio and to meet the developers and see their latest work a rather cheap prize especially when you see the winners as one is a notorious cheater who apparently was banned and came back so that there speaks for itself.

Mandagon takes less than 30 minutes to finish, which is good because it really doesn't offer much.  The game's strongest feature is the pixel graphic world you explore.  The gameplay revolves around nothing more than walking through the world to pick up 6 tablets, then walking through the world again to place the tablets.  I found that once I had seen the world once, I really did not want to have to walk through it again, so half the game was wasted on me.  Thankfully there is a fast travel system that allows you to skip most the the redundant walking.  There's also some sort of story told while you play, but it is missable if you don't find all of the totems hidden throughout the world, and even if you do find them, it's not much of a story.

Brawlhalla is a mediocre platform fighter with enough glaring problems to make your time better spent elsewhere.
1. Monotonous Movesets
There are eight weapons and several dozen characters. Each character gets two of the eight weapons (only one can be used at a time). When multiple characters use the same weapon, they have the same exact moveset aside from three signature moves (heavy attacks). In my opinion, having eight out of eleven attacks per character is extremely boring, and I may even go as far to say that it makes every character a semi-clone of one another. In terms of playable characters, this game definetly puts quantity over quality.
1.5. Lackluster Combo System
In addition to the small amount of movesets that players have access to, the combos that you can perform with said movesets are far too simple. Other games in the genre allow you to pull off different combos or "freestyle" a combo in real time depending on how far your opponent was knocked back from each hit depending on their accumulated damage. This game has various "set up" attacks that have virtually no knockback, allowing the same combos to be pulled off regaurdless of the damage your opponent has taken prior. For example, when using a bow, using a "forward light" attack into a "down light" attack into a "neutral light" attack will combo flawlessly every single time, save for user error. It may just be personal preference, but I very much perfer a game with various combos that can be made up on the fly instead of  this boring "dial-a-combo" system.
2. The Community
At the time of this review, I have fourty-four hours on record, and it is safe to say that I have spent half of the time in a private game with friends, and the other half in ranked 2v2 matches. That being said, I have never seen any positive comment come from the enemy team, aside from the rare usage of the "GG" quick command. About half of my games, If not more, ends with people accusing me of spam when they lose, or them saying "trash" "ez" or "git gud" when they win. It also feels like the developers support toxicity when they include several victory poses such as the "so salty" "calculated" and "the reads" poses. I have played fighting games where characters say taunts akin to "come get some!", but I never seen a game with a poses that portray, "wow, you really suck at this game, LOL, get rekt kid. learn how to play. Salty, loser?"
As a sidenote in response to various reviews and players complaining about spam. There are only eleven moves available to a character at any one time (including air attacks). That is a pretty small number compared to most platform fighters, and in practice, that leaves two or three different attacks for each direction.  When someone hits you with the same move three times after you approach from the same direction three times, that is
spam. That is just players being limited by their small movesets and using common sense to swing in the right direction.
Thanks for reading!

I can recommend you watch youtube videos, there are some excellent let's plays that will teach you the basics. You're also able to turn off enemies if you want to go through the learning steps a few times.
Some cons though: Now let's be fair, this doesn't have the complexity of Dwarf Fortress, I don't know if that's possible for any game right just because of what I know about DF. But it doesn't say that it's trying to be a DF clone so that's OK. One other thing is I hope the developer continues to develop the game and add new features, such as more workshops, more armors, more weapons, more traps, etc...right now the game has JUST enough material to justify $15, but I can only say that because I've played it. If I did not play it maybe I could not be convinced to pay that amount, I don't know.
All in all I DO recommend this game, if for nothing else but a step towards Dwarf Fortress.
