This is honestly one of the most amazing games I have ever played.
GAMEPLAY:
It's a perfect example of how the principle "easy to learn, hard to master" should be implemented into a game. It only has a very limited amount of controls, only run, jump, reset (to start or checkpoint) and, in some levels, hook. That means you don't have to remember much. Finishing the track at all isn't hard at all (excluding the very last set of levels). But getting a time good enough to beat the gold medal (for beginners) or the rainbow medal (for more advanced players) gets very hard very soon. And even IF you manage to beat all normal tracks with the rainbow medal, defeat all your opponents in challenges and collect all the coins of the bonus levels in time, that doesn't mean that the game doesn't offer anything anymore. There is still an online multiplayer to play with friends or meet new ones. You can build your own tracks or play some of other members of the community. You can try to further improve your time on tracks to reduce your combined time of all tracks to get a better rank on the global leaderboard, or to get a top 10 time on a track, or maybe even a world record. Once you master all the little mechanics that might be hard to pull off, but save you alot of momentum and time when done correctly, you can spend countless hours grinding levels to get a better time. And when you think you got everything done, then someone finds a new mechanic, a new route or a skip, and it starts all over again.
COMMUNITY:
The members of the community are all awesome people. Never have I found people that are more friendly than the Action Henk community in any game. Once you reach a certain level of play, and you get in touch with some of the higher ranked members, you get tips and tricks on how to get better times pretty much daily.
On top of that, the developers are extremly supportive in every possible way and really try to give everyone the best possible experience. I've never seen devs so nice anywhere (thanks for the awesome time at Gamescom while I'm at it <3)!
WHAT IS BAD?
Sadly, multiplayer is pretty empty most of the time, but that's not the game's fault. Also, if you are not into grinding, doing stuff over and over again until it's perfect than the game doesn't offer much to you after a while.
SHOULD I BUY IT?
If you are impatient, get upset easily and can't stand doing stuff over and over again, then it's questionable. Getting the rainbow medal everywhere is certainly not easy and will take quite a long time, so if you only want to go for completion, this game offers you probably between 30 and 60 hours of gameplay, depending on how good you are. If you like getting stuff as perfect as possible and if you are a competitive person, then this game offers you at least 200 hours of gameplay, but probably more, as more routes and strats are getting found weekly. For the little price of this game you get more gameplay than in alot of AAA titles that cost 4 times as much, so I would definatly say: Buy it!

Action Henk is a video game where you jump, slide, combine the two then slide and jump to get more speed on your next run. I very much like the concept of this game and it has phenomenal graphics. If you are in a position where 17 dollars is not very much to you (or however much it is in your country), then by all means this is a great buy.
However... this review is very borderline positive as I was rethinking my opinions on this game. I love all of its content, but the combination of it in a game like this makes it seem less than it is after you've played it enough. Let me explain.
Jumping, Sliding, Hooking, Landing Properly. That's all this game consists of. Because of this, getting a world record time in this game is next to impossible, because all you do is literally practice this combination. In a game like trials, mechanics are its #1 priority before graphics and sound design. In this game, however, its architectural design and all of the major appealing features seem to be the key. In terms of feature diversity, it takes but 10 minutes for you to gain and lose a world record. I would like to emphasize, however that this paragraph is not intended to be directed towards cheating players, as that is an entirely different topic. This game is deceptively difficult.
Oh yeah. Multiplayer works, but nobody ever really goes on it... so there's that.
But where I stand about its flaws, I think anybody can agree that not only is the sound design near flawless... So is the graphics, mechanics design and momentum rules. That alone merits a +1 from me. It's very easy to tell that years of work went into a game like this and the level editor makes it a lot more enjoyable to a first time player. If you are the type of person who is just looking through steam to see which games are worth buying, please don't let my negative views on some of the content discourage you from buying it. If you aren't competing for world records or looking for some interesting game content to impress you, it's worth every penny.
Would I recommend it to my friends? Not at its current state. The ending of the game is not beginner friendly and it gets needlessly complicated near the last levels. If the authors of this game could pad the game a lot more between these levels, I would consider recommending it. The game makes an absurd difficulty spike at the end. If you don't have the patience for it, the spike is worse than trials'.
Just thought I would voice my opinion about it. Thanks for reading!

If you're fan of the Batman: The Animated Series (or Tim Burton movies), from early '90s, you'll love this game.
If you're not, you will probably love this game too.
Batman: Arkham Asylum is a breakthrough for Batman games (or maybe even for all the Comic Book-based characters - at least from action point of view) ever!
When the game came out, I didn't pay any attention to it, because all the games based on Comics, up to that moment, were... let's say; not really good. But then I played a demo of Batman:AA and boy, was I surprised.
This game had so many pros, that it took me few hours to actually start looking for the cons.
So, let's start with...
The Pros:
- amazing environmental setting of the game in the Batman universe. Unlike in the modern Batman movies, showing Gotham and surroundings in a present day. More like in original Batman movies, where the surroundings looked like depressing part of '30s - '50s... it's dark and gothic... and it's in an Asylum!
- innovative and challenging (free-flow n' gadgets) fighting system, which from some point of view may look lame and easy to handle, but it mostly isn't (if you haven't play this game a LOT!).
- voice acting is done more than professionally (and done by professionals, who voice-acted characters in the animated series). The announcements via PA in the game will make you smile, and at some point even laugh or giggle.
- this game has movie-like soundtrack. It actually fits the game so good, that you'll probably never find it annoying or repetitive. Don't get me wrong, there are numerous variations of tracks and compositions in the game, which are fitting every situation or environment you're in.
- a plot, which is really entertaining ...and I won't say anything else, so I won't spoil a thing to those who didn't yet play the game.

The Cons:
- biggest of all; the detective mode. It will eventually become a huge part of your gameplay, because it's easier to find everything in the environment... but it's... ugly. You will sometimes switch to normal mode, just because you would like to see the beauty of the game, but mostly you will find yourself playing with Ugly mode on
- the soundtrack is definitely missing the Danny Elfman's Batman Title Score
- some minor engine glitches, which are not happening often and may not happen at all - if they do, they are not affecting the gameplay.
- map can be a little confusing, mostly when going between different floors or when looking for Riddler's challenges.
- game is much-much-much better playable with a X360 controller (in-game supported), rather than with mouse and keyboard.
- keys for keyboard aren't (re)mappable, which is understandable, in order to make it more challenging for players to perform some 'special' moves (therefore I recommend a gamepad controller, where you have all the keys on the reach of your hand/fingers)
Nevertheless, if you like action, 3D platformers, good story, challenging fights... and you're fan of Batman (in any form), this game is for you - even though I don't believe there is anyone out there, who still haven't played it.

EDGE is a great little platform/puzzle game where you roll a cube around an isometric world formed out of blocks. Your task is to find and pick up a number of little 'prisms' scattered around the level, before making your way to the exit. This would be easy, if each level were not so precisely and fiendishly designed to hinder you in your mission.
EDGE originated on the iPhone where it had an innovative finger-slide control system. Luckily, it has not suffered from the conversion to desktop formats, and I found it easy to play with a joypad or keyboard.
The level design is the reason I am writing this review - it is masterful, with only a few mis-steps. The way the game establishes a language of cubes, switches and sliding blocks and then makes humour out of them needs to be experienced by any student of game design.
This is one of the few retro styled games that actually captures the spirit of 8-bit gaming as well as the appearance. It has the same kind of feeling as Nebulus or Marble Madness, and seems like the kind of game Ultimate: Play the Game would release if you sent a modern PC back in time to 1984.
I must mention the incredible soundtrack, which while completely modern, constantly recalls the sounds of 8-bit gaming, both Western and Japanese. Highly recommended.

Why do I not recomend this game?
Is it because it's too "hardcore" and I'm a "filthy casual?"
No, not really. While it does have a low amount of ammo and a unforgiving restart from the beginning of the level when you die mechanic with no ability to save if you want to stop playing, I didn't really mind that and thought it actually added to the  game. In fact the only other part of the game I did enjoy was the climbing, for some reason. I thought it was well implemented with the stanima meter and pitons, and enjoyed it way more than I probably should have.
The combat in this game is god awful. It's super basic and mostly just unenjoyable. Not to mention alot of it is based on pressing a button when close to someone to kill them, which sometimes doesn't even work (I died several times trying to kick a guy off a ledge because I couldn't get the prompt to come up and was to close to him so he started stabbing me). Most of the depth in the combat just comes from not wanting to die and restart the level.
It's mostly a linear affair, with only a few side quests and minimal exploration coming into play as you progress. This wouldn't be a negative at all if the story wasn't so average. There is nothing new, unique or impressive here, and most of the characters, and largely the story, are mostly forgettable.
The game also has a very small options menu, which is compounded with the fact that the user settings file is encrypted. The only way to remove things like motion blur and film grain is to install a third party patch (I recommend finding Peixoto's patch), the only way to make the game look good if you don't like those. [insert argument for developer asthetic choice].
Not to mention the only way I could comfortably play it is with an XBox controller, as the game only supports Xinput controllers. This is a sub-optimal way to play a shooter. The game has a bug, which there is no fix for that I could find, where when the game is loading world data, all mouse movement has no effect in game.
So, in my opinion, this is an average game that has a few issues and bugs perventing me from recommending it.

I'm a little late to review this game - but it must be done.
I Am Alive is a game based around a fallout type scenario - You start off instantly on the outskirts of what seems to be a larger city, and it puts you instantly into action. In order to reach the city you must climb over a decaying bridge which feels like it could fall at any moment, and the major mechanic of the game is introduced - Stamina. While climbing buildings and other objects or running your stamina bar will lower slowly as you continue, jumping higher will use more stamina as well and jumping to farther object horizontally. Once the first bar of stamina runs out you will be forced to sacrifice the capacity of stamina in order to keep climbing. In my opinion a very cool concept and makes you think twice about going for that last little inch of climbing. Might I also add the graphics at this point are stunning and give a great first impression.
Once across the bridge, you will enter the sewers in search of your family. Where you came from is unknown at this point and you are praying that your family stayed inside the city and barricaded themselves into the home. The city is overrun with bandits and scavangers trying to survive off the scraps left laying around. Stumble around for a bit and you will come across a bandit who seems to have supplies and other amentities - And he draws his gun and points it directly at you. This leaves you with an option - If you listen to the guy speaking and do as he says you will walk back fearing that he has ammo in his weapon and simply just move onto the next part of the story. If you stay for a little his story starts to seems a little fishy, and it starts to seem like he is bluffing, maybe he doesn't have any ammo in his gun? The combat is based around this idea. If you point an empty gun at one enemy, they will fear that you might actually kill them and they will submit to you and put weapons down. Now if you are faced against 3 enemies, they might start calling that same bluff they introduced you to. Ammo is very hard to find so you need to conserve it as much as you can, if you only have 1 bullet left you won't win against 3 guys. Soon they will slowly start moving towards you and if you aren't pointing your gun at them they will keep getting closer, finally they call your bluff and attack.
In the end this game has the climbing aspects of Assassin's Creed - The astmosphere of fallout - and a very eerie story hiding behind all this climbing. If you are looking for a fun single player survival experience, this is where you will find it.

Flywrench is a sublime experience. Everything about it feels
and completely natural. The wrench (let's call it that) has among the most fun physics I've experienced in a game, moving gracefully but with the precision you need.
The game has a perfectly crafted difficulty curve, introducing you to mechanics and letting you figure out techniques without telling you explicitly, eventually culminating in some pretty hard levels that take a while to get down. We're not talking Super Meat Boy level hard, but I had significantly more fun playing Flywrench and never got frustrated, even when I was bashing my head against a wall.
The aesthetic of Flywrench is also superb, with a distinctive and appealing art style that still conveys gameplay easily. Even as a colourblind person I could distinguish the yellow walls and green barriers easily. The white and cyan ones were a little trickier but still distinguishable based on context.
Flywrench's soundtrack is phenomenal and is basically just "What does Orbi like? Put that in there" with a compilation of tracks that all work both thematically and to keep you excited. There's an OST available on

Since it's on sale I figured I would write a review. It's been a long time coming anyways.
In a way, Flywrench is similar to precision platformers such as Super Meat Boy (it was even an unlockable character in meatboy). However, in many other ways it is not. For one, the game isn't a platformer, it's hard to even label the game under a specific genre. Flywrench is its own very unique thing, and plays like no other game I've played. The game has a fantastic sense if flow to it making moving through the game a really enjoyable experience. This sense of flow has contributed to me spending 60+ hours doing time trials and speedruns in this game, as moving through the game quickly is one of the most satisfying experiences I have had with a game.
I do personally have a lot of problems with the game though. Firstly, I personally feel that the levels are way to short. This gets fixed later in the game however early levels only take 1-3 seconds to clear which makes clearing them feel really trivial and a bit silly. Some of the levels especially are more about getting the angle or bounce the game wants rather than taking any actual skill from the player. Get past the first half of the game however and it really starts to pick up with the final set of levels being one of my favourite parts of any game. Secondly, the game is very short. Don't let the hours on my account fool you, a first playthrough of the game will only take the player 2-4 hours, depending on their skill level. While there is a lot of extra content with time trials and the level editor, if that sort of thing does not interest you there's very little to keep you playing a long time. I would personally say that with how enjoyable the game is, 4 hours of gameplay is worth full price, but I understand that this differs greatly from person to person.
Overall Flywrench is a fantastic package. Despite it's issues it remains the best experience I have had in 2015 and I will likely continue to play it well into the future. Unique gameplay, interesting level design, and fantastic music and presentation make this game something special. If you interested in these sorts of games, I highly suggest you check this out.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is not only one of the best games out there but it's also one of the best versions of Batman ever. This game sets up some pretty solid game mechanics with both combat and pedator areas on the spooky Arkham Island, in which Batman has mastered. It's not the same thing over and over, even though it may seem that way. As you progress through the story you encointer more things that make both combat and predator rooms more challenging and unique. The atmosphere is actually wuite haunting. Certain areas of the game make it seem like there are spirits roaming around the Island with you. The story is great, seeming like a simple escape attempt but later revealing to be a full island takeover with more to it than meets the eye. As the world's greatest detective you must track down your allies and enemies to discover what Joker is really up to. The voice acting is supurb. Kevin Conroy (Batman), Mark Hamill (Joker) and Arleen Sorkin (Harley Quinn) all return from their roles from Batman The Animated Series making for a pretty solid cast along with some newcomers for characters like Bane, Poison Ivy, and Killer Croc. Batman: Arkham Asylum sets a great example of what Batman should be in games and other media and also sets a great example of what other superhero games should be like. This game is a must have to any gamers collection.

Vertical Drop Heroes works with a simple premise: get through 10 levels to the Holy Sanctuary. When you begin you can choose from one of three different heroes, each with their own weapons, abilities, and stats. Once you choose your hero you enter the Temple of Knowledge which is kind of like your starting point for your adventure. Take a few minutes to look around and talk to everyone. There’s a really good chance you’ll be back. Often. Once you’re ready head on into the portal to begin your adventure. Chances are that adventure will be really short lived.
Each stage is vertical (hence the title of the game) and the goal is to reach the end and defeat the boss, though the boss can be avoided altogether if you have enough keys. As you progress, each stage you’ll be tasked with defeating enemies, finding gold and gems, collecting keys to open chests and cages (the latter containing non-player characters that can help you out), and even completing the occasional side quest for gold and experience. You’ll also come across shrines that you can activate for various effects, such as generating enemies in exchange for gems, experience, or keys, or can even fire off weapons like fireballs and ice bolts.
All of that sounds simple enough, right? So why am I making a big deal about your adventure being short lived and that you’ll be going back to the temple often? Well, that’s where the main premise of the game comes into play. The first level isn’t incredibly difficult, which is fine as it eases you into the game. The next level though starts to see a bit of an increase in difficulty to the point that unless you defeated every possible enemy in level one, you stand a good chance of dying, which means you have to start all over. Almost. After you die you go back to the character select screen with three more randomly generated characters to choose from, but now you’ll notice something different. First off you’ll notice that all of your gold remains intact, minus five gold for having to reroll new characters (there has to be a penalty somewhere). Second, during each stage you might come across someone who will give you new abilities for future heroes in exchange for gold. Each character has two ability slots and these will be filled with the abilities you purchase.
You can also talk to a couple of people in the Temple of Knowledge and pay them gold to increase various stats for all new heroes. These include paying a blacksmith to increase the starting damage for all new heroes as well as visiting an apothecary to increase starting HP for all new heroes. You can also talk to someone to make XP orbs appear in a stage as long as you don’t defeat any enemies. As soon as you defeat an enemy though the orbs all disappear. All of these are a good idea to invest gold into as it helps level your heroes a bit faster.
Okay, so you’ve died several times, bought some new abilities, increased your starting damage and hit points and are ready to set out again. Now the game begins to get fun as you’ll notice that you can take out enemies a lot quicker and easier than before. With your newfound abilities and skills you can now progress further along the way to the Holy Sanctuary. However, things will keep getting tougher as you progress, but starting in level two a new shrine makes itself available: the ability to teleport directly to a level. This can be both a good thing and a bad thing. The good thing is that it allows you to skip previously cleared levels. The bad thing is that not only does it cost a lot of gold to activate (though to use it in the temple is incredibly cheap at first), you don’t retain the exact experience level you had when you activated it. For example, when I first activated the level eight teleportation shrine I was around experience level 32. When I died and decided to skip right back to level eight I actually started at experience level 22. I’m not exactly sure of how the game determines what experience level you start with, but it does put you at a disadvantage.
The graphics are nice, the music fits the atmosphere of the stages, and the progression of the game with the new abilities was really enjoyable. There are a couple small things that bothered me though, but I didn’t feel like they were enough to warrant several paragraphs explaining them. First is that once you gain a lot of abilities, the final stage (the sanctuary itself) is rather simple to finish. There’s an ability called Ice Age which pelts the area in giant ice balls and freezes everything they hit for a few moments. You get four uses of that per level, but it pretty much makes the final stage a non-issue.
The other thing that sometimes gets to me is that while you’re gaining new abilities and increasing the starting stats for new heroes each time you die, get used to the first couple of stages as you’ll be seeing them a lot.  The attacking can definitely seem a bit annoying, mainly because while you can swing your weapon you can also just walk up to them and hit them, similar to the arcade game Gauntlet. That’s actually a more reliable way to hit an enemy using melee weapons because it just felt like the weapon wouldn’t hit an enemy’s hit box when manually swinging with it. This led to me dying a lot in the first couple of stages while I got my stats up. For a while I was really getting tired of them.
In the end though, Vertical Drop Heroes is a really solid game. It’s one of those games that’s challenging at first, but as you keep dying you get opportunities to better your chances for the next try. The final area was kind of surprising and unexpected, though again it can be a little on the easy side with the right abilities. There’s also some replayability as once you clear the main game you can unlock new game+ which is an endless game where you shoot for a high score. You can also play with a friend either split screen or over a local network. It works the same way, except experience shrines (where you summon enemies and gain experience for it) only give experience to whoever activated it, and once you die you have to wait for your friend to either die or complete the level (in other words, when you die you’re done for that level). On the whole this is a pretty fun game. If you’re looking for something simple, definitely give it a go.

Survivor: The Living Dead's promied additional content is really going to be the making of it. The groundwork is solid; at the moment, it's an enjoyable zombie defense title based on Romero's seminal 1968 movie in which you repel the undead menace from a two storey house by way of various weapons and traps. You begin in the reasonable 7 minute mode before heading into bumpier territory with th 12 and 14 minute challenges, unlocking multiple bonus weapons and gameplay variables as you go.
The controls need tweaking. The mapping is fine and feels comfortable but command areas for certain item pick-ups and especially the stairs are a little too small to comfortably use in the middle of a zombie panic. Dev also needs a fullscreen fix as soon as possible as the text is a nightmare to read in the tiny windowed mode that Survivor boots in.
Easy thumbs up at this stage though. Plenty of potential.

Disclaimer: I was provided a key by the developer for a review
I just beat the 7 minute mode and this game seems promising. Basically this game consists of finding weapons/supplies or keys to unlock more weapons and supplies. Certain weapons are best suited for crowd control or single target and managing use of your resources carefully is crucial to beating the game. After beating the 7 minute mode, you unlock upgrades to your ammo capacity + small health and running meter upgrades which seem essential for surviving the longer modes. I did not like how you could get stun locked by several zombies, as when hit by one you drop your weapon and are stuck for a few seconds, and able to be immediately locked again if another zombie is nearby. Overall this game has a lot of potential and updates are still being done regularly.

Well aware of the ridiculously low amount of hours listed, but I assure anyone reading that I've actually been playing the game a fair bit ever since its original freeware release - I'd say the time I've spent is honestly closer to somewhere between 8 and 12.
Anyway! I do feel I can give the game a fair shake at this point.
Despite what you may expect from the screenshots, "Survivor: The Living Dead" honestly feels more like an action-puzzle game that'll require some exploration and quick work on your part in order to do well in. You see, you start in a position of distinct disadvantage - very few weapons are ready-to-use at the very start of the run (or in the game in general, but we'll get to that) and you need to - very quickly - start searching the area for anything that can be used as a weapon, for anything that can be put together to make weapons, or a means to create environmental hazards for later use - as the stuff you can easily reach immediately is nowhere near enough to take you to even the 7-minute run, let alone the longer game modes that come after it.
Even if you know exactly what to do in order to make every weapon in the area available and usable, you're not out of the woods, and that's when you'll need to find ways to use what you've got to the best of your ability, as you're generally going to have JUST enough weaponry in total to take you to the end of the time limit - miss a few too many shots, use a weapon that's obviously meant to eliminate a crowd of zombies on LESS than a crowd of zombies, inappropriately use your barricades to give you the few decent chances to keep crowds together FOR those crowd weapons, don't act fast enough to get the weapons outside INSIDE, or any get any number of steps of the overall puzzle wrong, and you're simply going to run out of options, and most likely quickly die.
To keep the game fresh, there's a significant number of unlocks that will simultaneously give you far more tools to play around with, and which will honestly be outright NECESSARY to complete the longer game modes as you won't have enough overall ammo to beat the game otherwise - one thing I definitely like about the game is that if you know what you're doing, you'll always have what you need - but only just! - to win, keeping the game tense no matter how much you've unlocked (or if you wanna just run roughshod all over the easier time limits, that's fun too ;3 ).
There ARE a few flaws in the game, of course. Due to how the infection mechanic works, getting bitten even once is a huge, irreversible handicap that can make a game basically unwinnable if it happens too early (though one can argue that it's just another way of making sure you never allow the zombies to get past your guard in the first place), and some weapons can be a bit inconsistent in their damage output, leading to an unexpected bite when what you thought was a sure kill, well... isn't, and typically at the worst possible time, in strict accordance to Murphy's Law. And you might want to be careful about throwing all your weapons into a big pile; it's not the most pleasant experience trying to get a single specific weapon you need out of the pile once you hear the telltale crash of a door coming down.
Additionally, I must note that the game hasn't currently changed a whole lot since its original release, and while there's a lot to do on the maps you're given and the house is very well-designed to keep you on your toes, the fact is undeniable that there are only two maps, of which one you'll only see in the Story Mode. This said, it HAS been said that there will be new levels, so this may cease to be an issue in the future. Additionally, the game was originally made in 2010 by a small team, and kick me in the nuts if it doesn't LOOK it, with dated visuals and a UI that's just ugly to look at. However, being fair to the game, everything you need to know is perfectly identifiable with the graphical style, and I've certainly seen a hell of a lot worse, so unless you're a graphics wh... graphics service provider, there shouldn't be a huge problem here.
Overall, I think there's a lot to like about the game and I've got confidence that the planned new additions will ensure it's worth the reasonable buy-in price. If you can skip the cost of a couple of burgers or something, you just might have fun with it too. =3

Ziggurat is a good game, but one with enough flaws that it never truly becomes great.
To sum it up, you're a sorcerer who's being tested. To complete your test, you must beat the Ziggurat. The Ziggurat is a procedurally generated maze of encounters and traps. You pick up different weapons along the way, and as you level up you get different perks that help you customize your character. At the end of each level there is a boss that must be defeated, but to start the encounter you must first find the key.
The visuals are timeless. The design is sufficiently cartoonish that the graphics will probably age well. Everything has a slight claymation-feel to it, and it's very pleasant to look at it. The only problem the game faces in this regard is that the bestiary isn't particularly expansive, and it won't take you very long to encounter everything once.
The gameplay is solid. It feels weighty and satisfying, but it also harkens back to oldschool shooters like Quake, as you dodge and weave your way around enemy attacks, while trying to get in a few blasts of your own. The fact that you unlock new classes to play as helps keep the experience a little more fresh, as the game would otherwise quickly become repetitive.
It does have a few issues though. A select few of the bosses are very poorly designed. It's procedurally generated nature means that you can, at times, face off against groups of enemies that are virtually impossible to beat. A lot of enemies have homing attacks, and others have excellent tracking and an uncanny ability to predict where you're going to try and run to. Champion-enemies are empowered basic enemies that are slightly larger than the others and a different color, and I still haven't quite managed to figure out what powerup does what. In fact, the game is really stingy with the information. It's hard to figure out what anything does, including different weapons. You essentially just have to try and guess on your own.
Oh, and whoever thought it was a good idea to include enemies - Especially melee-enemies - that can turn invisible, deserves to stub their toe really badly. When trying to beat the game on hard-mode, roughly 7/10 runs were ended by invisible enemies.
And that concludes my review of Ziggurat. It's a flawed gem. A great game for people who are new to first-person roguelites, but one that might get old for more experienced roguelite-players fairly quickly.

Action Henk is a Trails-like racing runner where you play as an action figure named Henk. The story really isn't important, the game shines in its gameplay. Graphically the game is pretty 'eh' with its pretty low res textures, but the backgrounds are full of references and nice enough to where its not really a big deal that the characters, up close look pretty gross.
There are over 50 different racing tracks to challenge yourself on if your looking for gold or rainbow badges. The other 2 levels, bronze and silver, are super simple and if you have any exprience with this type of game you'll have no problem beating them. The game really shines when racing against ghosts of your friends or gold-level ghosts or higher.
The momentum in the game feels really solid so I don't really have any complaints there, except with the hook. It feels very weighty to me, so its harder to get used to. It works alright, its not horrible, but its definitely not on the level of something like speedrunners when it comes to its hook mechanics, but it does have strong momentum mechanics otherwise. The different boss levels are challenging and change things up a bit from the basic levels, as do the coin collection bonus levels you unlock after beating an areas boss. There is a lot to do in this game without even mentioning its steam workshop support with several different expert levels made by the community.
Overall Action Henk is a great Runner with very well done momentum mechanics, Highly recommended. This game is super underrated In my opinion, its like it got overlooked by some of the other great titles released around its time. But if your into games like Trails or Bit Trip Runner, you need to give Action Henk a shot.

This is a real review however, this is a recipe for a delicious pie.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

As a huge fan of the series, 6 years later, I'd still contend that Human Revolution is the best Deus Ex game made so far - if not the best FPS / Stealth / RPG hybrid ever. It's seamless blend of stealth and combat, good level design and hub areas, and coherent self-contained storyline all add up to one of the best games ever made. I felt it achieved everything the original Deus Ex game was trying to do, but didn't quite manage.
Sequels are always tricky, especially in the Deus Ex universe, but I don't think this measures up in any way. And it's a shame, because it was probably avoidable - most of the decisions seem to have been deliberate, for one reason or another.
Stealth and combat still work, but on a run-and-gun playthrough I was constantly running out of ammo - certain types just aren't available in the battlefield, after all - and the meagre weapon set is even worse than the original. Most of the game's content is made up of side missions in the single hub area, requiring you to travel between two main zones via a long loading screen to pad the game out. The core storyline is extremely short and consists only of a few missions, with a very abrupt and unsatisfying ending. What's there is very good, especially how they begin to tie the story back into the original Deus Ex, but there just isn't enough of it.
Then the really bad stuff: third person take-downs are still jarring, especially when Doom managed first-person 'glory kills' so seamlessly. Breach mode is a needless addon. But the worst part is the abysmal facial animation: for all the hate Mass Effect received, I'd actually argue this is worse. Facial movement almost never lines up with what characters are saying, their mouths just wobble around seemingly at random. Maybe this was an intentional nod back to Deus Ex's awful lip sync, but I doubt it.
Overall, if you liked Human Revolution's take on the formula, you'll still enjoy this. It's a damn good experience, but when you consider the legacy of it's predecessor, it comes across as half-baked. Then again, I really liked Invisible War, so maybe I'm just wrong about the series.

Environments also look like the designers went out of there way to make sure each level was able to be beaten in different ways, hacking, climbing, breaking through walls, guns blazing. Although I did enjoy the freedom of choice, it sometimes made me feel the environments where artificial and gamey.
Overall it's a good game, a bit worse than Human Revolution but surely an enjoyable romp through a sci-fi, dystopian Prague. Recommended, especially if you can get it on a sale.

Honestly, I expected better. This is yet another console port (are there native PC games anymore?!), with the usual problems of console ports. Like what? You name it: mediocre controls, especially during fights (there is something with timing and combat flow and all that, it basically means that you have to press the exact button at the right moment the game expects you to do so; more or less equivalent to the ideas behind QTEs); ultra-linear plot (go there, do that, rinse, repeat), repetitive gameplay (you will encounter two main types of ennemies: melee fighters, and ranged fighers. And quite rarely, a stronger melee figher type) with the same strategies all along the way, and so on.
Of course there are worse games out there; but we're not searching for the worst game, are we? So to summarize, this game has an experience which goes from amusing to boring, with an average much closer to boring; can cause an impressive amount of frustration at times (especially when fighting, something which is not really interesting to begin with, given the small amount of strategy you can use; it's more of a standardized suite of buttons to press, as an answer to a visual stimuli the game shows you); it has an okay plot, and is worth playing once, provided that you stop playing as soon as you feel the frustration growing in you; and get back to it later. Not a game I would recommend to people prone to easy anger. In any case, the replay value is close to null, and to be honest (I'm writing the review as I do a second play-through, for achievements - I waited two years or so, since I did swear to myself that I would never touch it again, after the first one), I would advise anyone to avoid it at all costs. Too bad, a Batman game would have the potential to be so much better... =/
Bottom line: More or less okay game, if possible get it on a sale, and play it once, with small sessions preferably.

I got to admit, I've been playing this game since half a decade ago and got to enjoy playing most select characters after receiving it as a free gift. After beating the game three times or so while on different difficulty tiers, Torchlight 2 began to bore me with the same enemies starting with Estheria to the Broken Mines, and then on way to the Mapworks.
That all changed when I discovered the Steam Workshop for Torchlight 2. After finding the workshop, I went crazy and got my hands on a number of fan-made mods. This includes the Synergies mod, extra classes mod, extra gold mod and recently getting the storage mod. As a result, this breathe new life and interest into playing Torchlight 2 once more while sticking to play on the Veteran tier. In other words, it's a great game that maintains its original storyline even while having mods installed from the workshop at the same time. I must admit, at the time I type-down this review, my record is at 661 hours of gameplay.
Here are the following pros and cons that I encountered during my time of playing Torchlight 2.  And for those of you new to the game, don't get angry at me for divulging spoilers found in the game.
PROS:
01: Mysterious items are often good to have early in the game.
02: The storyline that talks about the Dark Alchemist's schemes to destablize the Clockwork Core took hours to complete, but seeing him defeated for the third, last time has been statisfying.
03: My favorite has always been the Engineer for his/her ability to wield heavy weapons and gain the right skills to deal increased attack speed later on, among other awesome skills.
04: Taking advantage with farming for gold and mysterious items towards the end of the storyline are beneficial to advance your character(s) in the long run.
05: Most embers of select elements (fire, ice, electric, poison, skull, chaotic, etc.) gained throughout the game can be useful for increases in armor or weapon enhancements.
06: Your choice of pet can be cute with your option of name change as long as your companion can handle the heat of battle and given the proper collar with two select tags.
07: As long as you focus on your vitality while having the right equipment for your class, along with strength, focus, or dexterity, you will do well in combat either in range or melee.
08: It's often good to take on side-quests for better equipment and gaining additional experience, along with earning more gold, such as the one at Vyrex's Tower found in Grunnheim being my personal favorite.
09: One of the best things of beating a map quest is getting to have a Vendor Boon scroll to blow your hard-earned money on plenty of mysterious items and/or a legendary item.
10: Furthermore, you are to be commended for reaching level 100 on your character(s) like I did.
CONS:

Although the graphics and controls are simple, Flywrench is a fun game.
The main mechanics in Flywrench involve avoiding obstacles while also occasionally shifting the color/form of your ship in order to pass through obstacles of the same color. While the gameplay is simple, requiring only a couple buttons, the game does a great job creating interesting levels. Most of the levels take between five to twenty seconds to complete but you will die a lot as you work out how to avoid all of the obstacles.
Games where you die constantly usually frustrate me but due to the short length of the levels it's not so bad since you lose little progress when you die. Also a majority of the game is moderately difficult. Only the last two or three worlds become really challenging.
If the idea behind the game doesn't interest you, you probably won't like the game. If the concept does interest you though I think you will should have quite a bit of fun with game.
Note: I received a free review copy of Flywrench. Other than the free review copy I received no other compensation and the free review copy had no impact of the content of this review.

I'm quite a fan of this one! A 2D pseudo-platformer action RPG roguelike game. I say pseudo-platformer because jumping badly or falling doesn't have a detrimental effect unless you run in to an enemy or spikes, as going down is the goal. Just... Hard to say platformer; I think you'll understand if you play it.
"Leveling up" is something that occurs quickly and with every playthrough you start at Level 1. The progression comes in the form of Strength and Health upgrades that you can buy in the world hub for increasing amounts of coins. Weapons unlock through various different means of unlocking achievements. Traits, a passive ability of which you can have two, will be unlocked by buying them from a wandering merchant hanging around in random places throughout your playthrough; Abilities, simply put skills or special attacks, are also acquired via the wandering merchant. All upgrades, traits, abilities, and weapons carry over from playthrough to playthrough, the latter three of course being options for characters and upgrades applying no matter the character used. So, while you do start at level one with each new playthrough, you do at least carry over your strength/health increases and the new character options. The game creates excitement and rewards for progression very well considering the format of the game!
There's also a "Pacifist" system that allows you to collect orbs that give experience and coins, and can also be leveled up to increase the amount of experience and coins you receive. Killing a monster of any kind will result in losing the "Pacifist" label for the remainder of the level, removing Pacifist orbs from the map.
Can't help but recommend this game; I found it to be incredibly charming, and a whole lot of fun!
Fun Fact: Vertical Drop Heroes HD is a remake/reboot/sequel to a browser game known simply as Vertical Drop Heroes; the game plays with a very similar style, but is also significantly different. Check it out if you liked this one!

250 hours put into this game, specifically the online mode... My experience was a mix of fun, frustration, boredom, and excitment.

Picked this up because I heard good things about it. It's another FPS roguelite that is basically a 3D Binding of Isaac with challenge rooms that are chosen and arranged randomly on each playthrough. Similar games I've played include Tower of Guns and Paranautical Activity, and Ziggurat mostly differs by the fantasy theme and maybe a stronger cross-playthrough unlock system (like Rogue Legacy but weaker).
I can't recommend this game, even compared to ToG & PA. It's just too punishing:
- Experience is gained by picking up orbs left by dead enemies, which DISAPPEAR AFTER A FEW SECONDS. This is horrible! Just give me the XP directly, or make the orbs last forever!
- Puzzle (non-combat) challenge rooms, many of which involve precise timing and/or jumping. Navigating a matrix of fireballs just doesn't work in 3D, and I hate FPS jumping puzzles with a passion. Combined with the health attrition issue, puzzle challenge rooms are overly-harsh in terms of their impact on survivability.
- Combat is mostly open-arena circle-strafing while enemies lob ranged attacks and/or themselves at you, hoping that your health doesn't get whittled down too much while you're dodging around waiting for your mana to recharge. I don't really find this fun, especially after doing it for 2-3 rooms in a row.
- Initial mana pool is small enough that you always get starved, at least early on. This makes you constantly feel weak.
- Health attrition is too severe. They try to balance this with the ability to unlock health restoration/conservation abilities on level-up, but it's just not enough.
I'm not going to bother leaving suggestions for the developers, because they've obviously stopped maintaining the game now that they have released some other game (just check the news feed - it's an advertisement for another game, full of comments from users requesting updates to this one). Instead, I'll just close by saying that you should only check this out if you REALLY like procedural challenge room dungeon FPS games.
P.S. The game's trading cards don't sell for squat.

I really liked Heretic and Hexen which seem to have served as an inspiration for this game but sadly this game is vastly inferior to those classics.
It's an okay game but with lots of problems:
* Loot disappears during combat, meaning you have to run around collecting drops while fighting mobs instead of doing it after the fighting like good games
* You are a midget / child - you often have to jump up doorsteps and generally feel like you are really small but by the lore you should be a normal sized human. I hate when games place the point of view too low.
* Rooms randomly spawn enemies which means they can easily spawn behind you. A better option would be set spawn locations or preplaced enemies
* Underwhelming perk system - None of the level-up choices really make much difference, if any, in gameplay.
* Weapons dont have oomph to them, most feel quite weak and aren't satisfying to use.
* Bland levels missing the hand crafted goodness from heretic/hexen. Some extra contrast would certainly help.
* No real music to speak of
* Enemies don't react to getting hit, at least visibly
* Attack animations are sometimes not visually clear enough
* Enemy animations seem floaty
* Wall edges have hitboxes causing me to aim at the enemy and hit the air around the wall
So game seems like it is playable for some hours but I don't feel it is worth the full price. I can already feel the repetition kicking in after some hours despite the developers trying so hard to make it non-repetetive. Guess you just can't make randomly generated worlds as interesting as hand-made ones.

Even though I've only played this game for two hours, I can honestly say it's one of the best new games I've played this year. Basically, this is a speedrunner's dream/nightmare come to life. You play as Henk, an old action figure who retired and got a bit of a pudge. The story is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ named Kentony stole a trophy of yours, and you gotta get it back. Yeah, not much story, but this game doesn't need it when you GOTTA GO FAST!!! Yes, I used a dumb meme, but that's the point of the game: GOTTA GO FAST!
As a young man who absolutely loathed time trials as a child (looking at you Crash Bandicoot: Warped), the fact that I'm racing against the clock to get medals doesn't discourage me in this game. If anything, the time trials actually encourage me to get better at the game. Yeah, you can say that about most games with a time trial mode, but the fast-paced nature of this game makes it fun to practice. And if you do rage-quit and hit Alt-F4 because you're too mad to do it normally, the game actually rewards you with both an achievement and an unlockable skin for one of the characters you can play as. Honestly, that was a nice, clever little thing RageSquid did there, and I approve of it.
In all honesty, there aren't many games like this that come in mind other than Speedrunners, and this is basically that game, except you play as a pudgy action figure instead of a YouTuber of your choice. But still, this is a fun game, and if you got a spare 15 bucks on hand, go get this game. It's fast, fun, and damn fun to play. Take it from a guy who doesn't really love time trial games; this game is good. And you get to go FAST!!! BY BUTTSLIDING!!!!

"Jesus is watching you." Freaked out, he shone his light around frantically, looking for the source of the voice. Finally, in the corner of the room, his flashlight beam came to rest on a parrot. "Did you say that?", he hissed at the parrot.
"Yep," the parrot confessed, then squawked, "I'm just trying to warn you."
The burglar relaxed. "Warn me, huh? Who in the world are you?"
"Moses," replied the bird.
"Moses?" the burglar laughed. "What kind of people would name a birdMoses?"

Action Henk is an Indy racing platform like SpeedRunners but your performance is based solely upon your ability as a player without having to worry about traps set by your opponents. It's a fun game either playing by yourself or with friends. Simple concept but with some intricate control timings that will allow you to eke out a better time.
Single player: Each level has 3 preset time medals to shoot for (bronze, silver, gold). The quicker the time, the better the medal. This will allow you to know how you are doing and where you're supposed to be. Also your time is record via record boards against all other players to also let you know how you stack up.
Multiplayer: You're given a set amount of time to complete the course as quickly as possible. Whoever finished the course as quickly as possible wins. Simple concept, yes, but when you add in trash talking and other general ribbing against your opponents it can get pretty hilarious, pretty quickly.
Overall: I'm loving this game and I see it becoming a staple game in the future for all LAN parties that I will be partaking in.

Whether you loved the Sonic games on the Genesis/Mega Drive, or Uniracer/Unirally on the SNES, or if you're a fan of Speedrunners on Steam, you will absolutely love this game too.
Speed, momentum and flow are the words of the day in this 2.5D platform game, as you race through awesome levels that twist and turn, full of obstacles and difficult maneuvers. Levels start off easy enough to complete, and steadily become more challenging as you unlock more of them, with extra features and game mechanics introduced.
This is not a game for those who get frustrated easily: You will fail, and fail, and fail again as you try to speed up and optimise your path, leaping over "lava", sliding down hills, using the hookshot to try and build momentum, and figuring out where to best jump, to run, and slide to improve your run.
The amount of love that went into this game is obvious: The game has an awesome art style, with great details put into the backgrounds of the levels, and into the individual characters: Each of which has multiple outfits you can unlock - and these aren't just reskins - each outfit has been individually modelled, with a completely different theme and voice pack, and I'm fairly certain that many of them have their own character animations, with Swan Henk (a ballerina outfit for Henk, and one of the first you unlock) doing split jumps as you leap around the levels - I've not noticed others yet, but I've not had a chance to play with all of them.
Anyone worried about the longevity of a speedrunning platform racer will be happy to know that there's a level editor available, which should allow for players to share their creations, and provide plenty of challenges even once you complete the main level pack. Multiplayer is also available, though I haven't had a chance to check it out yet.

Always Sometimes Monsters: The game about you.
Unlike most rpgs where you're immersing yourself into the shoes of another person, Always Sometimes Monsters takes a different approach and asks you the question: "What would YOU do?" and that is the game in a nutshell.
It asks you to be honest with yourself, to play through the story with the mindset that you are the pixilated sprite that's moving around the world.  Thus the game becomes more an exercise on self-discovery and seeing how high or low you would go if thrust into similar situations, when you're backed into a corner would you really do what you did in game.
In the end the game is handicapped mechanically due to the limitations of the RPG Maker engine but solid writing throughout covers those shortcomings easily.  On occasion the writing can be a bit pretentious which adds a bit of disconnect seeing as the game is willing on to poke fun of the game and the developers themselves joke about in a cameo.
With branching avenues to take with every choice you make the game lends itself to multiple playthroughs which if you decide to play through all of them which could take you 15+ hours depending on if you skip through parts you've already seen.  Considering the price of the game if length is a factor in your purchases with its current price there's little reason not to pick it up if you're interested in a game about self discovery.

I think this title is more important for the potentialities it creates and the horizons it illuminates than for its individual greatness. Overall, the game delivers the desired emotional effect but some of the weaknesses in character development make it difficult to fully engage with some aspects of the narrative. The game would have benefitted from a little more backstory. Ultimately, the game is a great vehicle for reflecting on one's own decisions and priorities as well as broader matters like family, career, and (maybe) freedom.
The game revolves around a family's three-month retreat. Dan, the main character, is an author who is negotiating the demands of family life and the challenges of creative work. Similarly, his wife, Linda, who is herself a painter, struggles to balance life as a mother and wife with her desire to develop her artistic career. Lastly, Tommy, is Linda and Dan's child. He is mostly occupied by the preoccupations of any average child: the desires to make friends, please his parents, and to explore new possibilities. The player's task is to make decisions, through Dan, that try to take into account everyone's priorities.
The Novelist is more narrative than gameplay. Yet, unlike other games in the same spirit, the Novelist does attempts to integrate gameplay into the narrative by offering the player the option of whether they will engage with the narrative on a "story" mode or a "game mode." The game mode requires that a player stealthily navigate the house while finding clues to progress the story. Exposing one's self to the family may cause story options  and decisions regarding how the family should proceed to dissappear. Alternatively, playing in story mode removes the elements of stealth and gameplay, allowing players to focus solely on developing the story and unlocking as many options for developing the story as available. The developers did a good job of integrating traditional elements of gameplay with the newly-developing narrative style.
The Novelist does a good job of capturing the impact that apparently mundane decisions can have on the present and future lives of individuals. Nevertheless, the narrative has some weaknesses particularly in the development of Tommy's character. Unlike Dan and Linda, whose career and family challenges feel more genuine from the start of the game, Tommy's concerns do not feel as important until later in the game when he is dealing with his relationship to his father, friends at school, and academic success. I think the writers could have done better by emphasizing the relationship between Tommy and Dan from the beginning and developing his psychological status in the same way that the writers did with Dan and Linda. Ultimately, Tommy's character is a weakness and not a flaw. I don't get the sense that the writters didn't try to make a complex character, only that the complexities did not emerge as successfullly as those of the other characters.
Overall, I found the game to be worthwhile. The novel approach of the game made it a useful platform for reflecting on my own priorities in life as well as broader philosophical questions. To the extent that players approach this game as a reflexive experience, I think the Novelist will find a special place in your gaming heart.

This game is an interactive story, the time played on my account (2 hours at time of writing) was enough to run through the game once on it's 'stealth' difficulty (i.e. with some 'game' elements) without missing any compromises, so if you are expecting a long game this is not it.
What this game does provide is a very interesting story about a struggling writer and his family and how the choices they make (or you make for them) as a family can have lasting effects on their lives.
People who dislike fiction or find it hard to empathise with a character will want to avoid The Novelist, but if you are willing to engage the characters emotionally then you will find yourself faced with difficult choices about who to help and who to dissapoint and I was often left feeling guilty about my decision to go with one over another, wondering if I had made the right choice as the descriptive scenes outlined the consequences of my decision.
The game appears to have a great deal of replayability in that there are multiple choices to be made along the way, but as someone who tends to go with the decision that feels 'right' I imagine my playthroughs would all end with the same outcome!
Overall this is a very good piece of interactive fiction with minimal gameplay elements (hide and seek), recommended for people who enjoy the characters in a story more than the action and seeing the consequences of decisions playing out and changing them for better and worse.

The view from the windows was lovely and changed with weather and time of day...I found myself admiring it and Imagining myself there. The characters' concerns & dilemmas rang true and the decision-making for a player was worrisome because choices involve consequences and there were some reached in the end. I WISH there were more games like this, it was creatively innovate, interesting and artistic (in my opinion). My only "con" was when I originally tried to play in Stealth mode: I was supposed to be a ghost out of view but the characters kept spotting me and shouting out in fright and this startled me in my own home and it was a jumpy/spooky game for me....so I changed to Story mode and it all worked fine with no interruptions. Kudos to the developer!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

Honestly, this game kept me entertained. It has a nice intro sequence, some fun missions and side-missions, incredible atmosphere, and it pretty much retains everything I loved about Human Revolution's gameplay.
That's the good stuff. Now the bad stuff is, unlike Human Revolution where you have plenty of unique locations for your missions, and 2 sort of open-world locations with side missions that you revisit twice each, in Mankind Divided there's only one location you revisit 3 times, fewer unique locations, and some of those locations you don't get to spend much time in. So a big chunk of the game for me was spent in this one area, doing side-missions, and I wished there was more plot in-between.
Also, like everyone else is saying, it ends out of nowhere. You're expecting more and it just sort of stops dead in its tracks. You get one neat boss fight (when Human Revolution had 4), and then it's done.
But hey, I got 28 hours out of it, so it was definitely worth it. 8/10

The game is set in a post apocalyptic world, in the city of Haventon, a year after the Event destroyed the world and reduced cities to rubble and dust. Survival of the fittest at its best, the protagonist must survive the dust, ruins and hostile people while searching for his wife and daughter, and meeting other people along the way.

The way to deal with enemies, using psychological tricks, is also a particularly cool feature, combined with the sheer lack of resources. Even a gun with no bullets is useful against another guy if he doesn't have a gun either.

All in all, really good experience.

Last Played: March 2014 (with XBOX controller)
PROS: + Who doesn’t want to be Batman? + Fighting system has its moments, though also has frustrating times. + Feels like a Batman movie/comic.
CONS: -Way shorter than expected (~15 hours first time playthrough). – D-pad inventory selection clunky at best. –Some frustrating sequences.
REVIEW: When a game this highly rated goes on sale for $5, who can resist? I had very high expectations for this game, and looked forward to “being” Batman. And if we are being honest, that is really the main point in playing a Batman game, so the fact that this one does a really good job making you feel like the “caped crusader” is commendable. Since Batman relies on non-lethal force, this game puts an understandable emphasis on hand-to-hand combat, which is for the most part fluid and rewarding (though button-mashers will probably find it hard). Players also get to sneak up on the baddies and knock them out one at a time-it is pretty gratifying to listen to the others get increasingly panicked as you nab them one by one. Also-the story, while patchy, is at least not outrageously dumb (“Injustice”, anyone?), or at least it isn’t too dumb for characters that normally exist in books with fewer than 1,000 words.
Unfortunately, I still think this game has been overrated-or maybe it was just judged against other independently developed games, I don’t really know. Firstly, unless you insist on getting all of the collectibles (this game has an absurdly large number of them) this game will not take more than 15 hours to beat on a normal difficulty, even on the first run through. The areas are re-visited with different bad guys to help make them seem different, but really the maps are kind of small, so recycling them still gets noticeable by the end. Secondly, some of Batman’s gizmos are kind of useless, but this is actually a good thing, because switching between active gadgets using a poorly integrated D-pad is actually a huge pain, so the less you have to switch, the better. Finally, this game has some frustrating sequences. Not the “man, I’m not good enough and I need to practice to beat this awesome game” kind, the “wtf how did that guy kill me now I have to do the whole 5-minute thing over again” kind. Furthermore, although the sneaking “predator” combat mode is cool at first, there simply aren’t enough options for sneaky takedowns to make the later sequences fun-you can either use the 1-2 vents in a room or the 5-6 ceiling grapples to remain unseen and late in the game one of the options is removed from this list, which makes the exercise kind of a chore.
I guess what it boils down to are a few questions you need to ask yourself: Do I want a game that will make me feel like Batman? Do I mind a small map if there are new enemies to give it variety? Is this game on sale? Depending on how you answer these, Arkham Asylum may be a good buy.

Much like Nidhogg, Messhof takes a simple game mechanic and creates a challenging game that fans of Velocibox, Superhexagon, etc. will enjoy.  In addition, fans of Nidhogg's soundtrack will also love this game as it once again features a pounding soundtrack with returning Daedelus as lead music designer, while featuring additional highly influential electronic music artists.
This game will likely take players 3-4 hours to complete, but the game offers a degree of replayability for those wanting to do time trials, or for those wanting to use the in-game level editor to make their own levels.
I believe the biggest negative for this game is the exponential increase in difficulty towards the latter part of the game.   My biggest critique of the game is, rather truly exploring and using the new obstacles to their fullest in each planet and gradually scaling difficulty, the game holds back until you get to Mercury.  On average, it took me maybe 10-15 mins to completely clear a planet. I would even often clear levels on my first try. However, upon getting to Mercury one level would take me up to 15-20 mins to complete.  Don't get me wrong, I loved Mercury because it really showcases Messhof's creativity, but at the same time why couldn't we have more of these levels?
Another minor gripe with the game is that difficulty isn't presented through use of in-game mechanics, but rather exploiting the limitations of the keyboard. Levels in Mercury often have you going diagonal, which is inherently more difficult and imprecise than using a controller. I would've like the game to be more challenging through use of spinning and fluttering than trying to awkwardly move sideways. But, as I've said this is only a minor gripe.
Overall I was very satisfied playing the game and I will be returning to it. Time for time trials!

With the Final Cut edition of the entire trilogy out soon, I am just in the nick of time to write a Van Helsing review. Despite the nitpicks of other players, this is a solid ARPG. As can be said of any ARPG, they are a treadmill, and a time waster. And this is where Van Helsing III falls short. There is a low level cap. About 30.
Secondly, your beastie shares the same level cap. Game was over before I knew it. BAM! Levelling was consistent thereout. The loot system was solid. Combat felt great! The skilltree? Underrated. Picking passives is awesome. It means your skills never lose their utility, but unlock different variables and special abilities as they go.
Powering up your abilities detracted from the whole game, as time spent waiting is time I'd rather spend killing. It seemed rather superfluous to the whole system, as well. Was it fun? Yes. Does it beat Path of Exile and the competition? It stands alongside. Proudly, in this reviewers estimation.
I'd really like to praise the devs in making old skills feel new again. As expected, this is a narrative-driven Diablo, and there are bugs. Batman Arkham Asylum is one of the most awesome videogames I have played in years.
The plot revolves around the Joker taking over Arkham Asylum, after being arrested and taken there by Batman, and you have to stop him, while playing as Batman. The story is a lot more in depth than that, but I am not going to spoil it for you. Needless to say it is one of the most exciting and enjoyable storylines I have seen in videogames (although to be fair I have only ever played platformers, which for the most part are gameplay based rather then storyline based).
The graphical quality is gorgeous. In the game you can see every wrinkle on the Joker's face. The graphic designers for the game have added lots of little touches which you need to pay close attention to notice but whihc really add to the gameplay experience. For example, as the game goes on Batman's suit gets more and more battered, and the walls of the asylum are coverd in really faint graffitti.
The physics engine is also really realistic. As pointed out by other reviewers, the enemies behave like rag dolls once they have been defeated, but I have found that both barely noticable and forgiveable, especially considering the really cool small touches they have added to the game, for example making the paper rustle and fly about as you walk through it in the library (although admittedly it doesn't work properly but you can appreciate the effort.)
The gameplay is fresh and innovative. You fight enemies by pressing x to attack and y to block,  you then move your control stick in the direction you want to attack. This freeform system of combat really captures Batman's athleticism and makes you feel like you are the Caped Crusader.
I still have more to discuss in part 2

So I always heard good things about the Batman Arkham games, but never got to play them. Last week I installed and played the copy of Batman: Arkham Asylum I had lying on my endlessly growing Steam backlog for the first time. After 30 hours of gametime, which included beating the campaign on both normal and hard difficulty, collecting all of the Riddler challenges, getting 3 stars on all the extra challenge mode games, and acquiring all of the achievements, I can confidently say that B: AA is one of the best games I ever played in a long time.
I just want to preface the upcoming gushing I'm about to lay down by saying I love metroidvanias, am not very proficient in high execution gameplay, enjoy a good collect-a-thon, and think Batman is the♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game pushed so many of the right buttons for me as a result.
The best description I can give for the gameplay is that it’s the perfect Batman experience. You can do most of the typical kind of platforming tricks you see in modern 3D action adventure games like in the Assassin Creed games but as Batman you have a variety of tools like a grappling hook that clings on almost all climbable ledges and a cape that helps you glide over larges distances. I found going around the titular asylum a very enjoyable experience, especially the occasional pure platforming and Scarecrow sections you’re encounter throughout the campaign.
The combat is probably the best part of the game. It really feels like you’re playing out a fight scene in a Batman cartoon or movie. It’s very simple to jump around the area pummeling your foes but you need proper timing and twitchy fingers to avoid getting hit and keeping your combo score up. You get a lot of tools and techniques that make the combat a breeze later on but I found myself being tested in some hard mode gauntlets and the dedicated challenge modes you unlock later in the game. Climbing on the larger titan enemies and forcing them to smack around the smaller goons is always a satisfying experience.
The predator sections where you have to stealthily take out a bunch of armed enemies in a huge room is fun. Pure fun. There are so many ways to dispatch them that they made a dedicated game mode for it. And the way the goons start getting freaked out after you pick them off is hilarious as ♥♥♥♥. Like I said, a very Batman-like experience.
While the campaign is pretty linear, there are a ton of collectables sprinkled throughout the island. In a way this game is pretty metroidvana-like in that aspect, as you can backtrack to older areas and use the new items you acquire as you progress through the game to find even more secrets.  While the trophy collecting was pretty basic, the riddles sprinkled throughout the world are brilliant. I got a kick out of finding all of the solutions. You’ll also find these little perspective puzzles that require you to find 2 parts of a question mark hidden on the architecture and align them with your camera so they look whole. It’s hard to explain but they were cool.
The game is a visual and audible treat. The game looks very good, especially for an early-to-mid last gen game. I love all the minute detail for the world, like how Batman gets more visually damaged and grows a stubble as the campaign goes on. All the classic Batman characters get a gritty look that makes them look pretty badass (even though Batman still is wearing his underwear on the outside).  Getting some of the voices from the old animated series was pretty cool. Can’t say no to Steve Blum either.
/gush
Now, I do have some gripes with the game, though. You more and less fight the same kinds of goons throughout the game. The boss fights aren’t very good either, especially the final boss fight. Spoiler:
Anyway, I love this game and I am so looking forward to playing Batman Arkham games in the future.
