Harlequin-type ichthyosis is a very rare severe genetic disease, which causes thickening of the skin. At birth, the child’s whole body is encased in an 'armour' of thick white plates of skin, separated with deep cracks. In addition, the eyes, ears,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and limbs may be abnormally contracted. Because of resultant cracked skin in locations where normal skin would fold, it is easily pregnable by bacteria and other contaminants, which can result in serious risk of fatal infection.
It is an autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, which is a group of nonsyndromic disorders of keratinization. It is associated with a mutation in the gene for the protein ABCA12. The disease can be diagnosed in the uterus by way of fetal skin biopsy or by analysis of amniotic fluid cells obtained by amniocentesis. Common features of the disease can be recognized through ultrasound, and follow up with 3D ultrasound to diagnose the condition. Ultrasound can reveal abnormal facial features with ectropion, eclabium, short foot length, incurved toes, clenched fists, poor delineation of nostrils, and polyhydramnios.
Constant care is required to moisturise and protect the skin. The overall rate of Harlequin ichthyosis is 1 in 300,000 births.The harlequin-type designation comes from the diamond shape of the scales at birth (resembling the costume of Arlecchino)
Newborns with Harlequin-type ichthyosis present with thick, fissured armor-plate hyperkeratosis. Sufferers feature severe cranial and facial deformities. The ears may be very poorly developed or absent entirely, as may the nose. The eyelids may be everted (ectropion), which leaves the eyes and the area around them very susceptible to infection. Babies with this condition often bleed during birth. The lips are pulled back by the dry skin (eclabium). Joints are sometimes lacking in movement, and may be below the normal size. Hypoplasia is sometimes found in the fingers. Polydactyly has also been found on occasion. In addition, the fish mouth appearance, mouth breathing, and xerostomia place affected individuals at extremely high risk for developing rampant dental decay.
Patients with this condition are extremely sensitive to changes in temperature due to their hard cracked skin, which prevents normal heat loss. Respiration is also restricted by the skin, which impedes the chest wall from expanding and drawing in enough air. This can lead to hypoventilation and respiratory failure. Patients are often dehydrated, as their plated skin is not well suited to retaining water.
The diagnosis of Harlequin-type Ichthyosis relies on both physical examination and certain laboratory tests. Physical assessment at birth is vital for the initial diagnosis of Harlequin ichthyosis. Physical examination reveals characteristic symptoms of the condition especially the abnormalities in the skin surface of newborns. Abnormal findings in physical assessments usually result in employing other diagnostic tests to ascertain the diagnosis. Genetic testing is the most specific diagnostic test for harlequin ichthyosis. This test reveals a loss of function mutation on the ABCA12 gene. This gene is important in the regulation of protein synthesis for the development of the skin layer. Mutations in the gene may cause impaired transport of lipids in the skin layer and may also lead to shrunken versions of the proteins responsible for skin development. Less severe mutations result in a collodion membrane and congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma-like presentation. ABCA12 is an ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter, and is a member of a large family of proteins that hydrolyze ATP to transport cargo across membranes. ABCA12 is thought to be a lipid transporter in keratinocytes necessary for lipid transport into lamellar granules during the formation of the lipid barrier. Biopsy of skin may be done to assess the histologic characteristics of the cells. Histological findings usually reveal hyperkeratotic skin cells, which leads to a thick, white and hard skin layer.
Constant care is required to moisturise and protect the skin. The hard outer layer eventually peels off, leaving the vulnerable inner layers of the dermis exposed. Early complications result from infection due to fissuring of the hyperkeratotic plates and respiratory distress due to physical restriction of chest wall expansion. Management includes supportive care and treatment of hyperkeratosis and skin barrier dysfunction. A humidified incubator is generally used. Intubation is often required until nares are patent. Nutritional support with tube feeds is essential until eclabium resolves and infants can begin nursing. Ophthalmology consultation is useful for the early management of ectropion, which is initially pronounced and resolves as scale is shed. Liberal application of petrolatum is needed multiple times a day. In addition, careful debridement of constrictive bands of hyperkeratosis should be performed to avoid digital ischemia. Cases of digital autoamputation or necrosis have been reported due to cutaneous constriction bands. Relaxation incisions have been used to prevent this morbid complication.
In the past, the disorder was nearly always fatal, whether due to dehydration, infection (sepsis), restricted breathing due to the plating, or other related causes. The most common cause of death was systemic infection and sufferers rarely survived for more than a few days. However, improved neonatal intensive care and early treatment with oral retinoids, such as the drug Isotretinoin (Isotrex), may improve survival. Early oral retinoid therapy has been shown to soften scales and encourage desquamation. After as little as two weeks of daily oral isotretinoin, fissures in the skin can heal, and plate-like scales can nearly resolve. Improvement in the eclabium and ectropion can also be seen in a matter of weeks. Children who survive the neonatal period usually evolve to a less severe phenotype, resembling a severe congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma. Patients continue to suffer from temperature dysregulation and may have heat and cold intolerance. Patients can also have generalized poor hair growth, scarring alopecia, contractures of digits, arthralgias, failure to thrive, hypothyroidism, and short stature. Some patients develop a rheumatoid factor-positive polyarthritis. Survivors can also develop fish-like scales and retention of a waxy, yellowish material in seborrheic areas, with ear adhered to the scalp.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a visually pleasing game with the atmosphere and soundtrack dripping with tension and adventure. The land and buildings are brooding and never seem repetitive. Each building is unique and I enjoyed exploring each and every one of them.
Batman’s “Detective Mode” was fun to play with but sadly, I found myself in Detective Mode more than 80% of the game in order to detect crates and destructible walls trying to collect all 240 Riddler items. While in Detective Mode you lose out on the beauty and detail of the land and interiors. Which is a shame because there is so much packed into this game. Each area has something a little unique. It could be an odd plaque on a table, Calendar Man’s cell covered in dates, Harley Quinn’s room with Joker pictures everywhere, and other random things all tied to Batman’s lore and rouges gallery.
The fighting in Batman is amazing to watch. When I first started I was button mashing. As I progressed I learned that everything must be timed. Once I realized this and started learning all of the combos and counters, fighting became a joy. Each boss fight is different and I died many times each time until I figured out how to actually beat each one.
Last, but not least, the story is engaging and showcases Joker as the “Mega-Super-Planner”. The opening scene is great comedy. By the time the game starts, you really like the Joker. I laughed often listening to Joker as he berates you as you progress through the game. The interview tapes you find scattered across Arkham Island really add to the game and story. You learn a lot about all of the different villain’s backgrounds and motivations. When all is done and the night is won, you'll be left wondering why anyone would ever live in Gotham.
This game is great fun to play and I enjoyed every minute of it. Even the frustrating ones.

It has a plot twist... I HIGHLY recommend this game.

Pros: Graphics, Sound, Controls
Cons: Gameplay, Realism
Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first Batman game to truly glimpse into the adventures of the Dark Knight.  From the gritty, dark atmosphere to the nervous, superstitious ramblings of the inmates, every detail creates a sense of not just playing Batman, but being Batman.  Simple controls allow for excellent combat sequences or tight, stealthy getaways.
Although some parts are truly innnovative, such as those with the Scarecrow, others are much more monotonous.  Finding all the Riddler trophies (not the actual, more interesting riddles) can sometimes feel like a glorified pixel hunt.  Some mechanics simply break the realism: Gotham should have spent more money on the concrete walls that are literally being pulled apart instead of the indestructible laser gates right next to them.
Still, Batman: Arkham Asylum truly captures what it feels like to be the Dark Knight.

Describing this as a game is difficult, so I'll use the developer's own description: "a story-driven experience". The graphics and gameplay, both neither good nor bad, are not the focus of the game. If ASM has your attention it's because you're looking for a story to be told, a story you can shape with the decisions you make (and the ones you don't), a story where the world is built upon the path you select. And ASM gives you precisely that. And much more.
Put in simple terms, ASM is a love story gone to hell. Your story starts at the pit of broken dreams, and everything is piling up to get much worse. As you start a journey to seek what could possibly be the last bit of hope left in your life, you'll be faced to make choices that will define who you are, who you were and more importantly, who will you become. It gives you the building pieces of your past and asks you "How did it all go wrong?", and then it makes a wonderful job at creating a story out of what you've done.
I'm not going to say ASM is something I'd recommend to anyone. Story-driven game with an unremarkable gameplay paired with the laundry list of trigger warnings the story has, it's likely most people will simply ignore this and move to something else. But for those that are still willing to try ASM, I can recommend this game for you. It is an enjoyable experience you will not want to miss.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first Batman game to truly glimpse into the adventures of the Dark Knight.  From the gritty, dark atmosphere to the nervous, superstitious ramblings of the inmates, every detail creates a sense of not just playing Batman, but being Batman.  Simple controls allow for excellent combat sequences or tight, stealthy getaways.
Although some parts are truly innnovative, such as those with the Scarecrow, others are much more monotonous.  Finding all the Riddler trophies (not the actual, more interesting riddles) can sometimes feel like a glorified pixel hunt.  Some mechanics simply break the realism: Gotham should have spent more money on the concrete walls that are literally being pulled apart instead of the indestructible laser gates right next to them.
Still, Batman: Arkham Asylum truly captures what it feels like to be the Dark Knight.

Somewhere on the edge of platformer and puzzle game sits... uhh, EDGE. It's kind of a puzzle platformer, but a lot of the puzzles are trial and error, and the lack of a jump button makes it hard to consider a platformer.
I'm really impressed at the creativity of the level design given the 5 or so distinct level design objects in this game, they really did their best to keep things fresh an interesting in that regard. Not even every level is that good, there are some pretty garbage ones, of course, but I never felt like I was playing the same thing over and over again. It's surprisingly diverse and there's some neat spectacle to be had as well.
That being said... the game isn't as fun as I wish it could be. I think this is mostly the fault of the physics engine, which seems mildly glitchy and not precise enough for some of the things you're asked to do. I've had instances of clipping through walls before, and aside from that there are many instances where holding a button for just the slightest bit too long gets you stuck on another object and prooobably pulled to your death in some way or another. It just leads to frustration. And sometimes the trial and error gets to be too much, too many things to learn between checkpoints or too much time between checkpoints. These aren't problems that every level has but a lot of them certainly do.
I also have no clue how to get good times on these stages, the S+ ranking seems strict even for what I'm used to; maybe I'm missing something or something wasn't explained to me, but there seems to be a huuuuge gap between getting A's on every level and getting S+ on every level. Oh well.
I did enjoy this game more than I disliked it, overall, but it's on the cautious side of positive, Considering that it seems to go on a pretty heavy discount during steam sales, though, I doubt you coudl do wrong picking it up for cheap.  And there's no lack of content to begin with, either. I can't think of any other game like it, as well, so it also has that going for it.

Action Henk is a fun casual game that should appeal to gamers of all ages. The premise is simple. The game is a series of "race" tracks where you're racing against the clock or against other people in the multiplayer modes. If you've ever played a game from the Joe Danger series or to a lesser extent in terms of comparison, the Trials series, you'll have an idea of what Action Henk is all about. Another game I found it easy to compare is the Bit Trip Runner series. Basically every course is based on simple physics, speed and momentum. Your goal is to finish the track in the fastest time. There is a good deal of variety throughout the courses, with your buttslide and grappling hook coming into play at various times. You'll have to learn to time your jumps and nuances of particular courses to get the fastest time.
Pros:
+ Very fun graphically. This game doesnt take itself seriously.
+ Variety of tracks.
+ Friends leaderboard.
+ Steam Workshop support. Create your own tracks!
+ Wide range of courses that unlock after a certain amount of medals in the section prior.
+ "Ghosts" and replays to see where you messed up or how to tackle a tough obstacle.
Cons:
- The music is abysmal.
All in all, Action Henk is a good entry into this genre of game. It encourages competition, but at the same time keeps it light and fun. The track creator is fairly robust and hopefully Workshop support will encourage people to make new and even better tracks.
I recommend Action Henk if you are looking for a fun game with a competitive spirit.

There is a lot of good things and a lot of bad things to say about this game. Some of the negatives may not be "deal-breaker" but it is for me.
I'll start off with some of the good stuff, the presentation of the game is excellent, the game looks fantastic, the soundtrack is great and the voice acting for Adam Jensen is superb. The biggest improvement for the game for me is the gameplay, the cover system, gunplay, hacking, takedowns and general fluidity of the gameplay is so much better than Human Revolution. And approaches to combat is much better and it's much easier to do a complete stealth or non-lethal playthrough thanks to the addition of new augmentations. Lethal combat is still fun although it's in credibly difficult on the hardest difficulty.
Moving onto the bad stuff, the weakest part of the game for me was the story and the new characters they introduced. Without spoiling it, apart from a couple of characters. None of the characters feel like they have emotions and they are usually not interesting, even the main villain is just generally boring. This is mainly down to the story writing and some of the mediocre voice acting when you compare it to Adam Jensen.
The story is also another weak part of the game, it starts off rather well but it kind of gets to full of itself and the game teases that the story will be expansive and large but in reality, it really wasn't anything close to it. The story ends when you least expect it and there are multiple plot lines that are introduced but aren't finished or even mentioned by the closing credits.
This review comes from someone who put a huge amount of time in Human Revolution and the original long ago. My opinion of the game is mostly negative, mainly because of the story and weak characters which were one of the best parts of Human Revolution. However, I can't deny that gameplay wise, the game is superb and it's a really enjoyable stealth game and it has replayability and you can complete the game without killing anyone (which is what I did in my playthrough).
If you don't mind the issues, you will enjoy this game.

Oh boy, this game is quite something...
Quite frankly I have no idea what the heck went wrong with this one. The original Deus Ex is a masterpiece despite it's rough edges at times, HR was an "alright" game, though it clearly was no where near as good. Never bothered with IW.
Let's start with the positives, gameplay has improved upon HR, navigating the environment in cover is a lot more fluid and easier now, switching to different cover is much better due to the added mechanics. Visuals are, on a technical level at least, very beautiful and downright atmospheric at times. Some of the new augmentations are kinda fun to use, though it feels a bit like they were taking a few cues from Dishonored (Icarus Dash is basically Blink), though not a huge deal. Stealth/Combat balance was improved, I found no shortage of Stun Gun or Tranq Rifle ammo compared to the other guns, this was an issue with HR (fixed in the buggy DC version) that was thankfully welcome. A few of the side quests were fun, including Neon Nights and Cult of Personality. The Prague Hub is very dense with a lot to discover and explore. Oh, and the last level was a lot of fun, felt like a true Deus Ex level compared to the rest of the game.
Another thing to mention. The side quests did offer a lot of choice in regards to their outcome. Some can be quite significant and fairly hidden unless you really play around with your options. Needless to say, it was quite impressive for some of them.
Sadly that's where my positives end. First things first, the game is simply too short. Sure, you may look at my play time and say "Oh it took you around the same amount of time to complete as HR Director's Cut", true. But that was with all the side missions, and you have to keep quick loading to account as that would have extended the gameplay time by quite a bit. The main factor is that the plot "felt" short, since it was essentially a giant first act that was dragged out over 9 hours. The game doesn't have a missing ending like some claim, but it doesn't feel satisfying and this goes against the other Deus Ex games which always ended on a rather closed and well rounded note. Basically the plot felt like an episode rather than a proper fully fledged story.
The hub is dense, but boring. During the second act of the game, the hub became rather boring and just became kinda uninteresting since most of the areas that needed exploring were already explored. So it was just basically running from objective marker to objective marker. Very disappointing and clearly should NOT have been the main focus of the game, the other Deus Ex games having multiple hubs. The music is very forgettable most of the time, a few tracks stand out but nothing amazing. The visuals are good on a TECHNICAL level, but most of the character models and animations are pretty poor. It's not ME: Andromeda bad but look very flat and dull. That's a major issue with the game, it's dull. The plot and characters are insanely uninteresting for the most part. And the characters that could have been good are underdeveloped, so you don't have people you really care about as the main focus of the game. The dialogue is badly paced too and feels really boring most of the time. Most of the side missions were pretty boring too, even if they were well structured a boring plot doesn't save it.
On a greater issue with the plot. The story seems to be using Augmented people as an analogy for minorities/oppressed groups in this game. The game is incredibly unsubtle about this, the developers referring to it as "Mechanical Apartheid". The whole game is centered around this premise, all the ebooks and characters revolve around this in some way or another, making the whole thing feel very one dimensional. It's one thing to have a game centered around a theme, but to just have all the characters be related to augmentations in some way or another got incredibly boring fast. This is unlike the original which had multiple different things going on, including conspiracies, one world governments, augmentations, plagues, helping triad leaders, nanotechnology etc.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this. Get the original Deus Ex or even Human Revolution, I wouldn't bother with this one.

If you play games for the gameplay mechanics, then you will probably like this game. Batman: Arkham Asylum is a third person action game with a focus on melee combat. There are some ranged attacks, but no gunplay. The fight system is fluid and somewhat challenging to be proficient at. Two special moves can be unlocked via skill points, and these require the player to reach 8 consecutive hits before being able to use them. This can be brought down to 5 with another skill point. There are 20 or so upgrades ranging from special moves, increased health bar and improved utility items. XP is aquired by defeating enemies and locating hidden items. I was able to attain all of the upgrades shortly before the final boss battle by defeating every enemy I came across during the story and finding all of the hidden items. Aside from the story, there is a challenge mode. At least some of these challenges were unlocked by finding hidden items during the story, but I'm not sure if there are any available from the start. I didn't try out any of these, so I can't offer any insight into them. This game could probably be classified as mix between "open world" and "metroidvania", since it takes place on a small island with 5 or 6 buildings that the player will be going back and forth between.
If you play games for the storytelling, then you might not like this game unless you are a fan of Batman. I felt that the voice acting was OK, but I often felt that the performances were off in some way. The dialog was mostly OK in my opinion, but I there are definitely some cringe-worthy moments. I felt that the story was a little silly, but that's probably because all of the villians in Batman stories are mentally insane. The whole story takes place in a mental asylum, which I found to be disconcerting at times.
I thought that the game world looks pretty good, but I was questioning a lot of the "flavor" items littering the buildings. Why are there skulls and human bones just randomly lying around in a mental facility? The character design is pretty good in my opinion as well, but I felt that the surface of every character resembled shiney plastic. That may have been my graphics settings, though. For the most part, then sound design was OK. There were a lot of sound effects that started to annoy me by the end of the game, though. I don't really recall any music other than some orchestral music in one of the rooms in the gardens.
Ultimately, I enjoyed my time with this title. The combat was enjoyable for the most part, but I did get sick of it towards the end of the story when bigger brawls started to occur. I didn't care too much for the story, and I the insane asylum setting just creeped me out. I found all of the hidden items, but that caused me to get frustrated with having to go back and forth between buildings.

This is a weak recommendation, mostly for people who want to see how the story ends, or if you want to receive the Final Cut edition for free next month.
This is the final installment of the Van Helsing series, and if you had hoped it would end on a high note you'll be disappointed. VH3 is definitely a downgrade over the previous games, the biggest regression being the skill system, it has been dumbed-down by removing many skills and changing others, this leaves you with very little choice when it comes to creating your build. The toughest decision you'll have to make is which of the skills you'll max out first, as you'll end up maxing out most of them by the end anyway. Another major issue with the game is simply the classes aren't fun to play, the skills are boring, the skill trees are bland and I honestly felt only two of the six classes were enjoyable enough to finish the game with.
If you can get past the boring classes and restrictive skill system another backtrack from previous games is the loot, much like in VH1 you will rarely find any legendary items, by the end of my play-through I only had two equipped. In VH2 this was fixed and the loot progression was great, I was regularly finding interesting, build changing legendaries and I have no idea why they went back on this in VH3.
Now if you can look past the bad, underneath it's the same old Van Helsing, so if you enjoyed the first two games you'll probably enjoy this one too, just not as much as the previous entries. The solid voice work and humor once again carries the game and makes you forgive certain downfalls, and if you want to see how the story ends I would suggest picking the game up when it's 50 - 75% off as it's not worth full price. That being said, if you own all the Van Helsing games you will be entitled to the Final Cut edition for free which is releasing next month, it's basically all three games combined and improved (although we're not sure how, but they have said they're overhauling the skill system which was absolutely necessary IMO). My advice would be to wait and play the Final Cut edition, instead of playing VH3 as a standalone game.

Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon is a stand alone expansion of Far Cry 3 set in a satirical and trope filled cyberpunk 80's.
This game is a smaller much more condensed version of Far Cry 3. The main campaign is only about 4 hours but there are plenty of collectables to extend the playtime. As well as what has become something of an expectation, outpost takeovers. Upon liberating those outposts you'll unlock a side mission or two. Consisting of a hostage rescue or hunting specific animals with a specific weapon type affairs.
Its pretty strait forward, its enjoyable. Its Far Cry. One complaint I have with the game is that it is way too red, I realize it was an aesthetic choice but its kind of over powering.
It feels as good if not better than other Far Cry games, however the main character is kind of a show off and does a lot of flipping guns and spinny junk which looks really cool but when you're looting corpses or switching weapons in the heat of battle it can get a little annoying.
It has some genuine laughs, Ubisoft poking itself for collectables “I hope I don't have to collect any feathers” The cut-scenes are also a throwback and done in a rather decent pixel art style.
One aspect I really enjoy due to the games length is everything regarding character progression is sped up. No hunting a number of animals for their skin to expand wallet size or weapon holsters. Most abilities are unlocked immediately but still leaves room for more progression. Fall damaged is removed which is nice, movement speed is also much faster to the point where I never even bothered getting into a vehicle.
Its nice to see Ubisoft do weird things like this instead of delving into the money machine with their cookie cutter prowess (Not that that's inherently a bad thing) Its also nice to see Ubisoft turn criticism into something fun; giving us, the players, a nod that they have heard you.

I respect this game for what it's trying to do: it's putting the player in a situation of desperation and asking "How far are you willing to go to escape this?"
And it does it very well. The game begins with you in the dumps, with nothing to your name and a practically unattainable goal - that is, if you were to stay on the straight and narrow. The question becomes, how flexible is your moral compass? What would you do to improve your situation? Would you lie? Steal? Kill?
How much is your happiness worth, and how many people can you hurt before you no longer deserve it? At what point do you become a monster?
The first act of the game is very strong, as is the ending. However, the two cities in the middle are significantly rougher - they seem emptier, with less to do, some noticeable bugs and insufficient testing. Interesting plots and elements will appear without being satisfyingly resolved. It feels like that part of the game was pushed out the door.
Even with its shortcomings, Always Sometimes Monsters has a very engaging story to tell, and if you have the patience to slog through the middle of it, it does reward you for your time. I wish the devs had maintained a high standard throughout the whole thing, but they are also sometimes monsters.

I tend to avoid games made in RPG Maker engine, mostly because of the annoying turn-based combat getting in the way of the actual story. I honestly do not care if the character had to kill all the chickens on the way to get to the end, especially since I had to waste so much time in random encounters with angry squirrels on the way.
Always Sometimes Monsters thankfully doesn't have any of that nonsense, which means that the developers had more time to focus on the actual story. There are few minigames here and there, but those are pretty much optional maybe except for one that player will have to go through if they chose to do the things the hard (also more honest) way. Provided they will get to that point though. But more about that later.
As I mentioned earlier, the game was apparently made in an RPG Maker engine, I think it was RPG Maker VX Ace to be precise but apart from short mention on the forums, I didn't really do too much investigation about that. What I do know though is that the control scheme is your everyday RPG Maker-ish one. You move the character with cursor keys, you take actions and pass the dialogue with space or Enter (by the way you can't skip through the dialogue) keys you can speed up your walking with left shift key, and go to the menu with ESC key. There is no options menu so you can't rebind the keys to something "more comfortable" such as standard WASD scheme I would use since it'd allow me to play the game with one hand. But then again you don't really need mouse so having that hand on the cursor keys shouldn't be a problem. It's matter of personal preference more than anything else. The graphics is your everyday RPG Maker chibi style pixel-art kind of style, whole thing runs in a window which you can't resize, although you can turn it into fullscreen with a key if you want. Again it's up to personal preference. On top of roaming around talking with random people, you can also play some minigames that have similar control scheme. There is a time limit tied to the story which I feel is kinda standard to games like that. That brings me to
This is where this game's main strength is coming from. Without spoiling too much it's about human relationships and choices one has to make on daily basis. At the beginning you get to chose your protagonist and their partner, all is good and well, everybody's happy and looking forward for what future brings. Then about a year later things got a bit bumpy - Your didn't get a dream job, you broke up with your partner, landlord is getting mad at you because you forgot to pay rent, and on top of that you get an invitation to from your ex who is getting married at the end of the month. From this point you take a long journey and it's up to you what steps you take and what choices you make along the way. Not every choice is easy to make and you'll often end up deciding between what is "moral" or what is "lesser evil" or flat out "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ move". No matter what you choose, there will always be a consequence. Kind of a "choose your own adventure" kind of story which gives the game good replay value. You have 30 in-game days to get from where you are to the place where wedding should take place, and it's a long journey. Each day is split into three parts (Morning, Afternoon, Night) and it goes on as you complete each task such as having a conversation with key character, or taking a nap etc. On top of that you need to keep your character fed, because sleeping with empty stomach isn't very good idea needless to say that food costs money and you don't really have too much to spare which adds to kind of a desperate atmosphere.
Since this game is so heavily focused on the story and since it's made in RPG Maker, there'll be a lot of text for you to read. A looot of reading so
If you are expecting more action-focused adventure, get bored with long dialogues which you can't skip through, or don't like reading at all, well you might want to give this one a pass.
If you're looking for a game where story actually matters to you at all, You might want to give Always Sometimes Monsters a shot.

Toy story meets Sonic the Hedgehog in this high-octane 3D speed-running platformer dedicated to 90s nostalgia. From a basic prototype in 2013 to a highly praised Steam Early Access game, Action Henk has now finally been released upon the world in all his glory.
The protagonist of the story is the titular Henk, he’s an out-of-shape beer-bellied action figure who’s past his prime but trying hard to hold on to the glory of days gone by. Unfortunately, a nefarious doctor has stolen his “Toy of the Year” award and so Henk must return to action to reclaim his title.
Before I delve into the in’s and out’s of the game itself I first want to make one simple statement, this game is ridiculously fun. Built on the very simple control structure of running, jumping, butt-sliding, this game is impressively immersive, interesting and adrenalin-fuelled.
The main story campaign contains more than 70 tracks, all with varying degrees of difficulty and each with their own target times. The mode plays out in a very standard way for the genre, there are three target times per level, one for bronze, one for silver, one for gold, collect medals based on your performance and these medals and then used to unlock further levels are you progress through the campaign. All in all a bulk standard approach given the type of game. Where the game excels with this genre template though is in it’s overall design, it’s clear that the game has been thought out in advance and the limitations of progression are nailed. What I mean by this is, you don’t have to gold every race in order to progress,
Where the game excels with this genre template though is in it’s overall design, it’s clear that the game has been thought out in advance and the limitations of progression are nailed. What I mean by this is, you don’t have to gold every race in order to progress, Action Henk doesn’t intentionally try and hold you back, it’s new areas open up quickly and it’s fairly easy to progress through the entire campaign in hours not weeks.
This may not sound like the highest priority with the game design, but it does compliment Action Henk considerably given that the game’s primary focus is speed. This approach also removes the need to grind and instead leaves you wanting to return to levels for fun rather than necessity.
Once you’re done with the campaign, you don’t have to return to past levels to continue enjoying the game thanks to a level creator. Why not create your own work of insane art and share it with the world through the Steam workshop? If you’re feeling less than creative or you need a bit of inspiration then you also have the option to download track which the Steam community has created.
Moving on to the gameplay itself, it’s exactly as you would expect, an interesting mix of fun and frustration. Action Henk is far from forgiving if you make even the slightest mistake and rookie players may find themselves spending hours on the first set of levels. This may be an issue for those with less than sharp reflexes, it can be incredibly painful, but master this game and you get a genuine sense of accomplishment out of it.
The level designs themselves are superb, if a little nauseating at times, the fact that this game can actually inflict motion sickness is both terrifying and impressive in equal measures. Unfortunately, this does mean that Action Henk can quickly become one of those game that you only play in small chunks. This isn’t a game to dedicate hours to in one go but one that having played short term increasingly calls you back for more once you’ve freshened up somewhat.
There is so much going on in each level and given the amount of levels on offer, two tracks rarely feel alike. That said many of the tracks are over in less than a minute and so gameplay comes thick and fast. As you progress though, you will begin to discover that a number of levels have multiple routes and so there is definitely a degree of replayability outside of simply wanting to beat your own score.
Every inch of every track has some toy reference associated, these levels are almost entirely constructed from toys. Making up the majority of the track action are the kind of orange ramps you’d expect to get with Hot Wheels sets, throw in the wooden train tracks and blocks kids use for tower construction and you’ve got a complete track filled with many obstacles, the attention to detail is impressive.
For those at the higher end of the gaming age bracket (if there is such a thing in this day and age), this game oozes nostalgia. The video game and pop culture references are abundant throughout, everything from Pokemon to Jaws gets a nod as well as a smorgasbord of the random childhood games we enjoyed in the 1990’s, there’s definitely a lot of love for the past in Action Henk, which I’m assuming also refers back to Henk’s heyday.
The characters really seal the deal with this game, they each have their own unique look, personality, issues and strengths. It’s very easy in a game of this nature to provide the user with throwaway characters, at the end of the day you don’t need an in-depth storyline and a cast of unique characters to make a speed-runner but Henk proves that when you do it adds a lot value and enjoyment to an otherwise standard setup.
The attention to detail, the nostalgia trip, the likeable characters, these all make up a brilliant package that is only fully realised by the stunning artwork this game has to offer. If you take a look at the video that developer RageSquid released on YouTube showing how the game has evolved over the last 18 months, you can see how much time and effort has gone into the look of the game.
While the majority of the early game action takes places in the bedroom (hehe), it isn’t long before our overweight action figure is butt-sliding his way through a beach resort and later on swinging through a jungle environment. There is a great deal of differences between these environments yet each is beautifully rendered, colourful and full to the brim with life.
It’s actually extremely difficult to take in everything going on in the background due to the speed at which the game play moves but every so often it’s very easy for your line of sight to wander and you will get a glimpse of something brilliant, especially on the disco levels.
Complementing the visuals is the soundtrack, it’s that perfect mixture of fun, happy, yet fast-paced music, the kind of that made Sonic such an enjoyable experience (enough with the hedgehog already). It’s very easy to zone out of what’s coming out of the speakers when playing a game of this nature but playing Action Henk, I never did, it helped motivate me.
Overall, Action Henk is one of the best speed-runners that has been released in a number of years. The gameplay is fun, exciting and rewarding, the visuals are easy on the eye and impressive and the audio complements the whole package, but you need to be a fan of this genre to fully appreciate the game
It’s one downside is the balance between fun and frustration but with a little practice this game quickly turns in favor of enjoyment. This isn’t a game to play at length over many hours in one go but one to jump in and out of in small bursts for the most enjoyable results, especially if you suffer from motion sickness. If speed-runners are your thing then you will be hard-pressed not to find a reason to invest in this title.

Action Henk is an indie racing platformer developed by RageSquid.  You play as Action Henk, a 90’s action figure who has let himself go a little bit over the years. It is your job to race against other action figures to prove that you are the best toy – I mean action figure
The first thing that pulled me into playing Action Henk is that it had a similar gameplay style to Sonic and SpeedRunners, both games that I love. Action Henk does not disappoint in this aspect, if you like Sonic and/or Speedrunners, get Action Henk right now!  In Action Hank the aim of the game is to gain as much momentum as you can to get through the track in as best of a time as you can (although you do need to beat certain times to get a bronze, silver or gold medal) You run, jump and skid through the Hot Wheels esque track to reach the finish line. In later levels you are given a grappling hook style power-up which you use to swing through some of the track. The grappling hook is the old extra power-up you can get in this game, it is a very fun tool to use, but the game feels like many other power ups could have been included to change up how you play.
There are 9 different themed zones, each with 5 levels and an extra boss level. Each theme looks vastly different from each other and it is a lovely change of environment when you have just spent the past 100 deaths on the previous level. Each theme also has it’s own music, so you will not grow tired of the same song throughout the entirety of the game. The finishing boss battles are a race against another action figure, in this mode you do not try and beat a set time for a medal, you just need to beat the opponent (but your scores are recorded on a leaderboard, so getting a great time is always a good thing to strive for)
Action Henk has ghosts. Not the haunting, poltergeist kind, the helpful kind that gives you something to race against. You;ve seen them before, they are a semi-transparent character that run through the track to give you someone to race. The great thing about these ghosts is that they are customisable- you can race against the par time for bronze, silver or gold medal, so you know that if you beat the ghost, you earned the medal for whichever ghost you were racing. You can also race against your friends ghost (their best time) or your best time. You can even switch off ghosts completely. You also have the option to view the leaderboards for the world and watch an action replay of other people, however, you cannot seem to be able to race against their ghosts – which although I will never be able to beat them, it would have been a nice addition.
I found the progression of each level to be a little strange. The game starts off quite easy and remains quite easy up until the end, and then suddenly it seems to introduce new mechanics that I didn’t know how to do. Luckily I was able to watch someone else’s replay on the leaderboards to find out how to do it.  (on the last theme there was this triple jump back-flip thing you have to do, which took me forever) I would have preferred a more stacked progression i.e. starting off easy, getting a bit hard, bit harder, hard, very hard.
Once you complete all the levels, which shouldn’t take you long (unless you go for gold on each level) then you may be bored playing this game. Actually, you won’t at all – this game has Workshop support with a built in map maker! At the time of writing this review, there are currently 207 custom user-made maps which will keep you entertained for a VERY long time. You can even try and make your own track!
Action Henk also includes a multiplayer feature, although I could never find another player to have a game with. There was 1 lobby open, but the person seemed to be away from their computer, so I easily beat them and got the achievement. It could have just been an off day, but at the time of writing there is currently 1 lobby open with 1 person  -so maybe an off week? However, if you get a group of friends to play this with, it will be a blast, great party game!
Currently on Steam for £10.99, it is a little pricey when shown next to a similar game, Speedrunners (currently £6.99) but I still think the game is worth that price. Action Henk has wonderful graphics and the environmental scenery looks great. The music is catchy and since it changes style on each zone, you will not grow tired of it. It is a very fast paced, fun game and I’m sure that if you get it, you will have a blast. You can even grab a slightly discounted double pack to play with a friend! (or they can buy it themselves, the cheap b****rds)

Crush Crush is a clicker game with one major hook - most of its major characters are seductively-drawn females (the exception being the player's own character, who appears in cut scenes).
The advancement method in the game is actually quite well thought-out.
The player has to court each female character by buying gifts, but can only buy gifts by getting money from taking on various forms of employment; the women can also be impressed by the player developing his skills, abilities, or extracurricular activities.
There are several stages to be gone through with each character, until finally you become lovers.
Each new female character is harder than the one before.
The higher up you go, the longer it takes to complete each level.
To get a skill, ability, or extracurricular activity to advance to the next level, you have to wait for a period of time - at first it's just a matter of minutes or hours, but if you advance to the higher levels then it becomes days, weeks, and even months.
(I'm not joking about that, believe me - in the higher levels you actually have to wait months for the levels to be completed. That is how the developers make their money, by impatient people paying for upgrades; but, fair enough, the developers need some way of paying to put food on their table, I can't fault them for that).
The pictures are well-drawn; and the characters have a range of amusing sayings, so that adds some entertainment value to the game.
If you like clicker games, then you might as well give this one a try.
I can recommend Crush Crush as a clicker game, but on that basis alone.
If you're not into clicker games, then don't bother.

The Novelist is a seriously cool game. I think it’s a shining example of a step in the right direction for “walking simulators”.
In the game you observe a family via possessing lights and eavesdropping, reading personal items, and occasionally entering their memories. Each day/chapter you gather as much or as little information as you like and then at night you must make a choice of which character will get what they want. The whole spying/influencing system keeps the game undeniably linear, but being able to choose whose desires will get fulfilled gives the player just enough control to make the story mean so much more than just watching a book. There is a mode (I believe it’s called stealth mode) where the family can see you, so you truly have to be sneaky, but personally I don’t think this mode adds anything to the game. The narrative itself along with the developers method of delivery make this title an absolute pleasure to dive into.
If the whole “walking simulator” genre has left a bad taste in your mouth, give The Novelist a chance to clean your palette. Other developers should study this game and learn from it’s interactive elements.

- Graphics and Performance:
Servicable. Gone are the pizs-covered sludge of Detroit. Prague (Just so you know, it's one of the first areas you get to see in the game) is lush and with green, and blue, and yellow, and everything in between. It's like the graphics department realize that the color wheel exists. Good art design overall.
The graphics fidelity, while shows curves and shines at the best of times, doesn't justify the wallop it does to hardware, though a comfortable amount of leeway is given in the graphics tuning it provides, which is quite ample.
For massive OVERSIMPLIFICATON, (because I can't be asked to write) my system suited with a GTX 970 4GB vram and 8GB of RAM runs the game pretty well set at 'high' preset with a few handpicked settings tweaked up a level, however, performance usually dips and slogs in crowded areas with NPCs minding their own business, and there are several of those.
For more information on performance, please do yourself a favor and look up respectable sites for this shi t.
- Music:
Nothing seem to stick. The previous game got me to stop and sink in the ambience in the halls of Sarif Industries. I still get symptomal after effects from the Human Revolution soundtrack and however the soundtrack here doesn't pull out any punches, it lacks the extra oomph of its predecessor.
It stays true with the style of the previous game though. The smooth beats and grooves of electronic tunes here tickles and seduces rather than electrifies. That said, subtletly is the master here and as far as immersion goes, the music is class. Anyway, Grats to Michael McCann and the ensemble.
- Gameplay:
New and improved. Deus Ex prides itself with its collection of backdoors to different areas. Now you've got more ways to be a creepy as you snoop in every nook and crevice.
Hacking stays the same, with the same capture-the-node gameplay you came to expect from the previous game. And no, hacking doesn't look like this IRL.
Stealth is still the name of the game ,and although Run-N-Gun gameplay works, the number of bullets you can take dawns the flaws of your augmented baby skin.
Dialogue plays a big role with some conversations having a success or fail state depending on what is said together with intended consequences that affect the quests and story later on. There are major opportunities of roleplaying here though in some cases you will need to play as the interrogator/sympathizer to get the response you want. And if you don't know, all this social psych makes me all giddy inside.
All in all, more of the same. More of the things I want. Please assess your decision accordingly.
- Overall:
I quite enjoy this game so far. If you're a fan of Deus Ex HR, then I recommend the purchase wholeheartedly. Wallet caught a stray bulllet? Wait for a sale. I don't want give scores to things so, ummmmmmm...... too bad.

Somehow, after all he's been through, Van Helsing feels like he's getting too old for this ****. And not in the cool nonchalant cop kind of way, but the 'get off my lawn, you damn kids' kind of way.

I set something in motion. That's never a good thing.
— Van Helsing
Early in the game, while walking through a forest, Van Helsing and Katarina come across a gigantic crystal thingy just sitting there, doing nothing. Van Helsing is nervous. Katarina, curious. “Hit it, Van Helsing,” she says. I had the option to do as she asked, or refuse. Obligingly, curious myself, I took a shot at it. Three monsters promptly spawned and, yowling, I ran off to a safe distance from which to shoot at them. When I was done, Katarina goes, “That was exciting! Hit it again!”
Four, perhaps six times, I hit it, alternately spawning monsters and items. One of the spawns was some manner of rabid bunny. Each time, Katarina was equally excited. And I was cracking up behind the keyboard.
The third and final installment of the Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing trilogy, this hack-n-slash turned out to be a heck of a lot more fun than I had imagined. It only took ten, maybe fifteen minutes for me to get into the game – because Van Helsing offers one thing that a lot of games try at, but miss – humour.

Firstly, about the series in general:
I *love* this series.  I'm not an action RPG expert, but after having sunk over 80+ hours into Diablo 3 and expansion, 30+ hours into Torchlight/Torchlight 2, and a little bit into Grim Dawn and Path of Exile, I still find the Van Helsing series my favorite ARPG.  Yes, better than the mighty D3.  Hands down.
In terms of mechanics, the game is solid.   Easy to play, satisfying combat, and even a whole major tower defence subgame!  The developers have distilled the essense of an RPG and captured it precisely.   It's also very pretty; hand crafted dungeons are more interesting than the random generated crossword puzzles of certain other ARPGs.   Also: gamepad support for you TV players!
In terms of narrative ... love it.  The gothic steampunk world is dark and interesting (and most importantly, not a cliche).  The dialog between the characters is amusing without ever getting tiresome - and the humorous bits (and pop culture references) are genuinely funny.    Whomever did the North American localization for Neocore - you sir/m'aam did an amazing job.   There isn't too much dialog, (never too far from the action), and I was always interested in seeing what happened next.  It's also decently voice acted, too.  (Especially Katarina...actress totally nails the psychotic haughty eastern european diva)
Now, having said that, let's focus on this particular chapter, the third and final one.
Flat out ... it's a bit of a step backwards.  As much as I love the series, this one isn't quite as good as the second one (or even the first).  There's a low level cap, the skill system has been changed a bit (for the worse), there are no character imports - and the game just feels shorter than the previous games in the series.   The loot drops were much stingier, and though I didn't encounter any of the "uncompletable quest" bugs people have written about, I did suffer frequent crashes to the desktop - which was exacerbated by a painfully long load time.
Is it still a hell of a good time?  Yes.   Is it the weakest in the trilogy?  Sadly yes.
But here's the thing: if you've played the other two in the series (which you probably have), you will enjoy this.  If you haven't, then pick up the first one and check it out.    Then get the second, and then the third.
Even better, Neocore has just released word of a "final cut" edition of all 3 games that will be FREE to all owners of all 3 games.  Come on guys...that's a wackload of content there.
Ignore the haters.  BUY NOW.  And fund a second trilogy!!!!   Hey Neocore:  prequel story of Van Helsing Senior and Katarina?  Just saying...

Who's Your Daddy
First-person Multiplayer
Joe Williams
Joe Williams
is a first-person multiplayer game developed and published by Joe Williams.
Powered by the Unity engine, the house and its furniture don't look half bad. But the models of the dad and the baby are nightmare inducing: lifeless animations, creepy faces and an exorcist-like crouching movement for the dad make you wonder if it was all intentional just to make the game more fun. If that was the developer's intention, he succeeded.
Right now there are only one map and game mode. There are two players: a baby who's trying to kill himself, and his dad who must keep that from happening. As the baby, you have a moltitude of ways to suicide: drowning in the bathtub, drinking bleach to poison yourself, putting a fork in an electricity socket, cooking yourself in the oven... As the dad, you can pick up the object the kid is carrying, give him food and pills to heal him, use items to lock cabinets... There are many possibilities for both characters, and the randomly generated position of the objects makes every round fun and entertaining. However, the lack of variety starts to settle in after 30 minutes of playtime.
It all depends on the players: a good baby knows the fastest ways to die, and a good dad knows which objects to use and what to do to avoid your son's death.
The sound effects are pretty standard, but the music is really, REALLY annoying, with the same cheerful tune going on an endless loop for the entire time!!
The short lenght of rounds and different ways to die will make you play "one more round" many times. Plus, more rooms and characters will be added in the final release.
Overall, this is a fun little multiplayer game that can also be played locally. The concept is interesting and the execution is fairly good (even though a bit unpolished on the technical side). Plus, you will see a baby die. What more could you want?

Vertical Drop Heroes is a port of a web browser game, so as you might expect, the graphics aren’t the game’s selling point. Think of the game as a time killer that you can theoretically beat in about half an hour if everything goes your way, but most likely you’ll die and restart a bunch of times due to the game’s random nature. -  8/10
The game doesn’t have much of a backstory, but that doesn’t matter since you’re just trying to work your way downward through randomly generated levels gathering money and treasure keys. The gold coins you collect carry over to subsequent playthroughs, so the more times you play the game the more powerful your randomly generated character can become. You’re able to buy upgrades for things like life, damage, and treasure value.  Every time you start up the game you choose from 3 randomly generated characters with random stats / powers / perks, meaning if you get an awesome character you can make an attempt at beating the game.  If all 3 of your character options suck, just spend the game picking up as much money as you can before dying, and hopefully you will have a better character to start with next time.
As you descend each level, you’ll find various mini quests to gain money / exp as well as locked up allies that you can set free with one of your precious treasure keys. These computer controlled allies will fight alongside you until they inevitably die or until you beat the level. At the very bottom of each level is a boss with significantly higher life that you can either kill for a bunch of money, or avoid by unlocking the door to next level (using 5 of your keys). Personally I’d suggest killing all the bosses since money for upgrades is so important.
Pros:
+Despite how short the game seems, there is a lot of replay value because of the randomly generated levels and the characters you can choose. You probably won’t beat the game until you’ve amassed a large amount of gold and purchase a bunch of upgrades for your characters.
+You can play for 20 minutes at a time just gathering money, or for several hours trying to work your way through every level to face off against the final boss.
Cons:
-The random nature of the game might turn some people off. Personally I’ve never been a big fan of rogue-like games. If you’re into RPGs, it could♥♥♥♥♥♥you off if you only have crappy characters to choose from over and over. Fortunately, you can reroll for a different set of hero choices (at a small gold cost).
Overall, if you enjoy rogue-like games but don’t want to completely start over from scratch every time you die, give Vertical Drop Heroes a try. If you’re like me you will appreciate the option of grinding for gold and upgrading your hero options. I’ve never liked games where you have to start over after making a tiny mistake and dying.

If I were to compare it to other games, the Novelist would be in the same vein as Dear Esther, Stanley Parable, and Proteus.  Technically they're games, but not ones that most gamers are familiar with.
The draw of the Novelist is more in the story and presentation than in the game mechanic.  There is the stealth aspect to the game, which increases the difficulty for collecting clues that are essential for influencing the ending, but it can be turned off by those who don't want to deal with it, thus why this game is considered casual.  Toggling this option is available at anytime in the settings and having it off or on does not have any impact on the ending.  Also there are no achievements in the game so completing the game only in stealth is only a personal reward.  The only reason for playing with stealth mode is to increase the difficulty of the game for those looking for a challenge as being spotted at anytime will limit choices that alter the ending.  Unfortunately, the small, unchanging environment will probably not interest players for long as it will begin to feel reptitive after a few scenes.  I personally turned it off after a while.
In other words, play Novelist not for the game mechanic but for the story it presents.  How well rated the story is depends on how much gamers resonate with the Kaplan family.

Love action-packed adventures with an expansive statistics system? Well this is not that. This is a very different type of game. Love narrative games with an emphasis on player decisions and consequence? Great! This game is a very good example of games with a more mature, serious plot, which I've not seen very much at all.
But I do think the pricing is a bit too steep. I'd have rather payed $10 for it and have had no complaint whatsoever. It's a short game but the replay value is there.

The Novelist, though suffering from a few flaws, manages to be an emotionally involved and touching game thanks to its narrative.
There is no perfect way to resolve every scenario, as anyone who has tried to juggle the demands of a family or group of friends is aware, which in my opinion, is a strength rather than a weakness. Though the house itself can be repetitive to navigate and some of the dilemmas are pretty predictable, the strong writing (haha) and voice acting make the experience worthwhile.
A short game whether you play using the stealth mechanic or not.

This game provides an interesting story with plenty of tough choices.
What you do in the game is stated already in the description, but at the end of each day you need to decide who you want to please and who you want to disappoint.
If you play this hoping for some sort of "Haunting Simulator" type of game, this isn't it. This is a nice game with a great tale behind it, and if you appreciate that kind of game, buy this.

Narrative games are always hard to execute. They have to balance the story they want to provide, while still providing an actual gameplay. The Novelist stumbles a bit, but does provide a somewhat awkward balance between the two.
The trailer gives you an idea of the game. You're some sort of "ghost" ? that has to hide from the inhabitants of the house. You also have the ability to read their thoughts, as well as the letters and journals they leave in the house. If you manage to stay hidden, you will be able to grab theses clues and know what each character want or need (which are often at odds with one another). Then you can whisper to the main character what you think the family should do, and they will follow it, thus influencing their lives. Compromises are possible, but always, at least one of the character will get chaffed by your decision.
The game part of it come from the fact that you've got to move around in the house without being seen, and your movements will be more restricted in the later levels. There is nothing difficult about it, but at least, it doesn't feel like you're just clicking to get to the next part of a fixed story presentation, like others poorly-balanced narrative games do.
It is hard to say if The Novelist if a good game. The fact that each decision is always negative for someone is obviously very gamy. Sometimes the consequences of your decisions seem to make sense, while at others times, they have some counter-intuitive ways. The underlying mechanic seem quite obvious, but the result is a bit wonky at times.
That's why i will give this one a small recommendation. I don't think it's the best narrative game I've ever played (Gone home is far better), but it's also much better than others I've tried (Dear Esther). I think if you like narrative games, which are still in their infancy, then the Novelist is worth exploring, because it's different than both of my previous examples. You may decide it doesn't work for you, but it's worth seeing what it tries to do.

The Novelist has a very intriguing premise, interesting game design, and decent replayability. You are actually given the freedom to compromise on tough decisions that most other games lack. There's enough variability that any two people who play this game are going to get different endings AND different experiences in getting there. As an added bonus, almost every decision is difficult. Your marriage is faultering right off the bat, your son is already struggling in school, and you're going to go broke if you don't do well with your novel. Every single decision matters, and the impacts are felt in the way the characters behave the rest of the game. When you fail you will feel it, even if you you were just trying to make the best possible decision at the time.
Unfortunatly the actual game mechanics simply aren't fun. As a ghost that can jump from different light sources your movements are slow, interactivity is sparse, and the process of finding clues and memories is repetitive. The house is the only level in the game, and while there are changes to it based on past decisions oftentimes 'gameplay' winds up just being checking the same spots every day. Some rooms are so rarely utilized they just kind of sit there as window dressing. Few if any clues are genuinly hidden so there's no real sense of discovery in searching for them again. As interested as I am in trying different decisions and seeing different outcomes I really don't feel like slogging through the gameplay again to get to them.
Still, the core concept works. As repetitive as the gameplay itself may be the decision making always feels like it matters and the game fulfills its promise in making sure it DOES matter, creating an emotional and personal connection beyond what most games can achieve. I'd still recommend the game, despite my qualms.

You are an haunt in a house occupied for the summer by a dysfunctional family - a depressive, alcohol-prone father, a mother who gave up her painting career for family and a son that utterly ignores her, fixated as he it on the fatherly figure whose attention he so much craves that his happiness entirely depends on him.
What the game does brilliantly is to remind us, the players, of the tragedy of familiar life, in which the parent's goals could be fulfilled, or at least compromised, if not for the children throwing numerous wrenches in the works. The message is apparently clear: if you want to fulfill your dreams, your descendents won't be heppy, and if you make them happy, you will have failed at your path, ensuring they will fail at theirs when their time as parents come in an eternal cycle of self-denial.
Or not :) What remains is that you, the player/presence, whose actions touch so many, seen from time to time creeping right behind someone loved, whose presence is felt thoughout history and with the power to change the minds of the occupiers, you will still be alone and hiding, never really living a story of your own - not until you get out of the house.

I have previously sung the praises of the LEGO games and this goes right back to where it started. It already has the key ingredients of the success of the later games. It has the silly retelling of the story. It has the varied character abilities that allow you to replay each level and find hidden stuff. It has the mini-kits to collect, the red bricks that unlock new abilities. It has the bonus levels and the 2 player cooperative focused gameplay. All of this is great.
However it really isn’t as polished as the later games. It does not have split screen so your two characters are awkwardly, invisibly tethered together making the cooperative mode very frustrating. And conversely there are a few sections of the game which didn’t work well when playing on your own as your AI partner gets stuck or refuses to do what is necessary. Character switching is annoying as you have to be right next to the character you want to switch to and the ship controls are rubbish.
My main complaint is just how many times you have to repeat levels. You play through the level in the story and then again in free play with any characters which is fine. However the game then makes you play the level again to find a new set of canisters against the clock and then again to play all the levels in a film in one go against the clock. So if you complete each level perfectly first time you have to repeat every level 4 times but if you play without consulting a walk through you are likely going to have to play each level 7 or 8 times. Also once you have bought all the bounty hunters there unlocks a bunch of Jabba the Hut missions that, yes you guessed it, involve you playing through sections of most of the levels again. This is the first time I have failed to 100% complete a LEGO game because after spending an hour grinding my way through the entirety of Empire Strikes Back and just failing to complete it within the time limit, I just thought ♥♥♥♥ this I have better things to do.
Overall this established the massively successful formula that paid off in later games but as far as this game goes in its own right it is disappointing. I’d only really recommend this if you are a big Star Wars fan. Maybe if you have never played any other LEGO games then you would enjoy this more, then you can play other ones and see the improvement.

One word review:

Multi-word review:
It would seem the developers of this game were sniffing a certain type of paint thinner, since this game is perhaps the most inhumane and morally wrong thing to ever be conceived by any living being here or in the farthest reaches of the universe.
Why you may ask?
You either play as a baby or it's father.
As the baby, the goal is to find a means of killing yourself, that's always nice. This can be achieved through simple things like shoving a fork or a knife in the electrical outlet, drowing yourself in the bathtub, eating raw food or batteries or glass or paint or trash (crumpled up paper) or bleach or window cleaner or soap. But if you subject yourself to this long enough you can uncover more elaborate means, such as heating up the oven then hiding inside of it, covering yourself in gasoline then finding a candle, or even drowning yourself in the toilet.
As expected, the father has to prevent this from happening, by any means necessary. You have 4 in game hours to make sure your baby remains alive, which is roughly 5-7 minutes in real time.
One thing I immediately noticed is that the house you are in is quite small, even though it's two stories. The layout is very basic and easy to memorize, with the only things that change being the placement of certain objects like forks, knives, hammers, etc... Future updates may bring new maps and/or a larger house, so I may be saying this prematurely.
Minimum 2 players, easy to see why, but those who would rather play alone are SOL here
Now for the bugs:
1. At any given moment, paintings on the wall (primarilly, among other things) will fall to the floor and proceed to have a cesure, it does nothing to hinder your progress, but you can't avoid looking at it
2. As the baby, when you look at the father while he's crouching, what you see is the torso up sitting inside his legs, quite comical, personal favorite
3. There is a toaster, if you grab it's cable, it is nearly impossible to let go of it, regardless of how far away from it you are, you still appear to be holding it since if you move the camera, it moves with you
4. Not a bug but an oversight, there are places the baby can go and the father cannot, basically if the baby eats something he shouldn't, he can simply hide out in one of these places and it's an instant win. Hooray!
With all of that out of the way, I truely believe this game has scared me for life, there are things here that cannot be unseen and the whole experience is truely unique, in a not good way.

tl:dr This game is great.
A very elegantly designed....platformer?  There aren't any platforms to speak of but I can't think of another way to describe Flywrench.   You're a small white rectangle with the ability to flap yourself to ascend while turning red and tumble and bounce off walls while turning green.  You pass harmlessly through barriers of the color you currently are, whereas you die immediately if you hit a different-color wall or barrier.  The controls are extremely tight and that's good because this game quickly becomes very challenging.  Your (numerous) failures don't annoy however because upon death you respawn immediately and try again.   Also helpful is the fact that new worlds (each one introduces a new mechanic) are unlocked once a set number of stages are completed so if you find a stage particularly difficult, you can skip it and come back later without hampering progression.   It evokes both Super Meat Boy and N+ and comes highly recommended to anyone who likes difficult stage-based platform challenge games.

I picked this up on a whim since I loved Nidhogg and I'm very happy that I did. The game hits the perfect balance being satisfyingly difficult while not getting too frustrating, it just feels really good to play (I actually wandered away from writting this at least 5 times to play for a bit more).
The aesthetic of the game is really strong as well, the glitchy visuals are much more appealing than they initally appear and the various unlockable themes are welcome additions (even the one called RETINA_BURN). The music is especially noteworthy, this is probably the best game soundtrack since Hotline Miami, it might even be better.
If you have any interest in hard games or glitchy visuals and music I would highly recommend picking this up. The soundtrack alone is worth the price of the game. Between this and Nidhogg Messhof has an amazing track record, I hope this game gets as much exposure as Nidhogg because it definitely deserves it.

Flywrench is slick in every sense of the word.  Tight controls (I am playing on a gamepad) support the simple yet addictive gameplay that involves changing Mr. Wrench's color, velocity, and momentum in order to navigate tons of levels.  The game plays fast and the strong soundtrack allows you to slip into a zen state trying over and over to beat a given level.  Finally, the clean interface and readable graphics (with unlockable color schemes) produce a simple, yet impressive, presentation - with some goofy story 'scenes' occasionally butting into the game unnecessarily.
The game also has an additonal time trial mode with leaderboards and an included level editor (which doesn't seem too daunting!) that will hopefully add to the game's longevity over time.  All in all, Flywrench is a pretty sweet game.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first game in the Arkham series developed by Rocksteady.  This is my first review and I sit here wondering - where do I start?
Batman: AA is an Action/Adventure game that does an excellent job of story telling and once it has ahold of you, you'll find yourself keep coming back for more because you really want to know what happens next.  The visuals, animations, and voice acting are outstanding and does a great job of pulling you into the game.  The game takes place on Arkham Island where the Asylum is located and you'll explore all of it.
In the beginning, you transport Joker to Arkham Asylum after capturing him.  Once he is about to be imprisoned, all hell breaks loose and its up to you to kick some serious♥♥♥♥♥  This isn't the cute comic book/cartoon Batman that you may have seen in the 80's or 90's either.  This game is dark, its characters are twisted, and Rocksteady did a superb job of making them feel like "super villains."  From start to finish you will be solving puzzles, fighting inmates, taking on bosses, and using a very cool selection of Batman's gadgets that you'll unlock as you level up.
The game also has many collectibles for you to find.  There are several audio diaries that have patient interviews with famous characters such as The Joker, The Riddler, Croc, and Harly Quinn to name a few that help shed light on their histories.
If you've never played this game before, I highly recommend it.  Even if you're not a Batman fan, this game is a solid action game that keeps on giving - there's always something to do.
Overall:   9/10
