This might be as to leave the story on a cliffhanger for a sequel, but it really doesn't feel like you accomplished that much in the game. It teases you with conflict and mystery of the illuminati, but fails to display any real sense of accomplishment or resolution in the end. You basically are only going after there henchmen in the game.
The gameplay is very similar to Human Revolution with the addition of a few new skills and a abilities. The stealth and combat feels exactly the same as HR. The new additions add some more depth to the game but don't massivly change the game which is completly fine. Missons and maps feel great as well, as it allows you to complete them however you want with multiple different paths to get through. My one small criticim is that you burn through your max energy very quickly but I do not feel that its that big of a deal. Overall the gameplay is solid, and is the area I feel improves the most from HR.
Graphically the game looks really good, but I suffered from FPS drops on the higher settings. I downgraded to high settings and the game ran completly fine. That said loading screens where very long for me, and I often just started using my phone during these segements.
One of my biggest gripes with the game is the setting. While HR had this epic feel as you traveled around the globe to some really intresting places such as the chinese city with two levels (I forgot the name). Mankind Divided takes place almost entirely in Prague. The settings and places you go don't really feel that unique or inspired and just feels a bit bland. The one exception I will make is Golem City which was a really cool city that felt like it was a ramshackle city made out of shipping containers, but with that exception that majority of the areas where forgettable.
The way the game is structered is another gripe I have with the game. There are a ton of side missons now that take place in Prague. But I felt that their wasn't enough main missons to go on. This plays into my previous issue with the game, its lack of variety in its setting. You will spend a ton of time if you want to do all the side missons in Prague. Hell even some story missons take place in there. It feels like this issue is a real shame as the locations where one of the reasons I really enjoyed HR.
While this game is about Adam Jensen, it feels like the other characters in the game don't get enough time to really stand out or be memorable. The other main characters don't have the amount of interaction, or time to feel devolped. Its a small story thing that is not the biggest flaw of the game but its there.
There are Microtransactions in the game, but there really isn't a need to buy anything for the game. You don't need to spend money to complete the game or anything. Its also not really in your face and I forgot they where even a thing when I was playing.
I only incountered one bug through my playthrough when I knocked out a enemy and he clipped into a door and died.
Mankind Divided is still a good game, and I enjoyed the time I spent playing it, however I feel that its a step down in the series from Human Revolution. It's still very much the same kind of Deus Ex game, however the story and setting is a real dissapointment.

Let’s just start with the obvious: one does not have to be a comic fan to enjoy this game. And in that extremely impossible case that you somehow missed all the movies (even Nolan’s ones) here’s a quick recap. Bruce Wayne whose parents were tragically murdered is insanely rich, dresses in a suit that resembles a bat and beats the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of all kinds of bad guys while using cool gadgets. In a devilishly insane logic of superhero comic villains caught by our hero all end up in a special kind of jail which happens to be also a madhouse. It’s Arkham Asylum. Obviously, it turns out badly; asylum is overrun by criminals, and it’s up to Batman to stop them. That’s it without spoiling too many details. After all the game is set in a separate universe which tends to follow the usual canon, but also steps out of the bounds here and there. And this is a big deal for those, who can distinguish Earth-2 from say Earth-15.
The plot revolving around events of one night and set in one place results in a rather tense game. First in the series Arkham Asylum may lack the extent, size and polish of its successors, but it has that unique feeling of being trapped inside an insane maze. These corridors, buildings, underground and open air sections are so tightly stitched together, that there’s practically no room to make a breathe, unless developers intended to let you. This is non-stop rollercoaster ride accelerating to the limit and beyond it, until you finally fall in the abyss of total madness, lose all sense of time and spend sleepless night with the game. Rocksteady Studios not just break the fourth wall with this game, they destroy it with a power of nuclear explosion. Carefully crafted props, marvelously fluid animations, diverse gameplay varying from famous “flowing” combat to stealth, puzzle solving, detective mode and beyond that. And ultimately the story. I won’t spoil you the exact scenes happening in the middle of the game, but they are simply outstanding in their ability to convey a feeling of lunacy overcoming Batman in this nuthouse.
Gotham Knight’s labyrinth path expectedly twists and bends in way that returns the player to previously visited areas with a new set of toys. That differs in tone and simplicity from most of the hard-core metroidvanias. Rather than just giving tools to overcome some obstacles game gently pushes you in the right way making sure you won’t struggle with trying to figure out what to do next. It’s not a game about exploring, though there are some clever hidden optional areas containing secrets and unobvious puzzles; but that’s for those who just can’t get enough of Arkham Asylum.
When it comes to the main progression route the game won’t let off your hand. And while in general that would be a major flaw in my eyes, this time it isn’t. One can say that it’s just a matter of perspective, matter of taste; that you can’t just drop off the player in the middle of nowhere nowadays and hope, that’s he’s clever and curious enough to figure his way from the starting point towards the ending. That may be true… it actually is true, I must say, but that’s beside the point. That’s the matter of taste. Back again to perception of it. Here we have that idea of lunatic luna-park, the goal of filling player with madness. And you can’t just stop and let player wander without breaking that feeling and pace. You ever had that weird nightmare where you run in circles seeing same place again and again not being able to comprehend how many times you did it, not being able to break the cycle? Even if you haven’t, I think you can get it. And that pardons Rocksteady Studios.
This was a breakthrough for the video games back in 2009, and it still is a stellar interactive experience whether you care about Batman comics or not. And the actual secret for this success turns out to be rather simple. It doesn’t matter if player is a fan of Bruce Wayne, it matters that developer is. It’s that special attention to the tiniest of details like animation of the main character’s coat or getting original voice-artists from Batman: The Animated Series (including genius Mark Hamill, playing Joker). And this passion just won’t leave anyone indifferent. At least when it’s accompanied with such brilliant execution of gameplay mechanics. Let’s just say that a fair number of games released since then simply copied Arkham Asylum freeflow combat system. And none of them came even close.

While I have had some good times playing this game, those times are few and far between. You will either be completely dominating, or get completely dominated, there is very rarely a close fight. The best battles in this game are the close battles, but they are perhaps 1 in 100. The main issue for me was the lack of maps, you will literally get the same map sometimes 5 matches in a row and it becomes tiresome very fast.
In terms of gameplay, you will find that tanks are often doing the job of snipers, by staying on the edges of the map, hidden away as far as possible, sniping individual soldiers and vehicles. This is because tanks are extremely vulnerable to infantry and I know this from playing an infantryman the majority of the time. I literally felt like a troll, going around on my motorbike, running up to tanks and taking them out with complete ease. Tanks should be leading an attack or at least supporting breakthrough's, but you will never see this happening due to the anti tank rambo's everywhere. I never once played a tank commander because I can only begin to imagine how frustrating it is.
I'm not even going to talk about planes in this game, the AA weaponry provided is absolute garbage, and pilots will dominate AA gunners with ease. Nothing feels right in this game.
Many other reviews go into details about the problems with balancing in much more detail, so I won't bore you anymore with those specifics, but what ironically 'killed' this game for me was the latest attempt to involve the community by doing dev Q&A streams. The guys doing them have absolutely no energy or charisma about them, seem fed up with the job and need to drink alcohol to get through it. Ironically, the attempt to 'reach out' to the community and some of the terrible side-stepping of relevant questions was the tipping point for me to uninstall.
This game will tease you into believing earning lots of credits and buying better equipment will make things better, while it certainly makes things easier, the game itself is still very repetitive, especially with the lack of maps.
Overall, a briliant concept that has sadly fallen way short of its potential.

Seems like a really rushed game... short story, low level cap, (some) re-used monsters and environments, and the skill tree's have been nerfed into oblivion (to make way for their biggest selling point - new classes!).
The gear isn't much better... there is no longer any class sets, it's just a search for gear that's a slight improvement of what you already have.
So overall there's now very little depth and very little character progression.
Oh, and beware the bugs! If you play co-op certain spells and buffs may be lost or broken depending on which player zones into an area first, and fear the permanent knockdown... a fate worse than death.
BUT with all that said, considering the price (~$10USD on sale) it was still worth it for 10 hours of gameplay. Just set your expectations a little low, and don't go in expecting VH1 or VH2.

Well, I bought as a gesture of loyalty having previously enjoyed the first two Van Helsing games.
These are my first impressions after playing through the first dungeon with each of the classes. Unfortunately they are mostly negative.
- At the moment I cannot import my hero - who travelled through the first two games - even though this is a direct continuation of the plot.
- You now have a level 30 cap, having previously had a level 60 cap. Why?
- The new character 'classes' are just the old classes but spliced into their constituent parts. So no longer can you carry pistols and a sword - it has to be a pistol class, or a sword class.
- Combat is a lot less fluid. Let's take the pistol class as an example - what has happened? You have to stand still and hold down the mouse button for 3 seconds to deal maximum damage? Why?
- Sometimes your mouse and keyboard presses do not register, meaning you don't shoot or use your skills on time.
- I always start my Van Helsing games on Hard mode. The first two games were punishing (but fair), but this is ludicrous. One of the first monsters you encounter can one-shot kill you. This isn't difficult, it is bonkers.
- Katarina's AI is still wonky. In the previous games you basically had to keep her in spectral form, because she would either aggro enemies you wanted to avoid, or else ignore enemies you wanted to aggro - and would die in a heartbeat. Still happening.
- The skill trees are even more cluttered than usual with useless skills and options that are frankly unclear.
+ The music is excellent, as ever.
+ The voice acting is great, as ever.
+ The new Protector class feels like something new to the franchise and looks great.
+ Random Sean Connery gnome.
I cannot currently recommend this to anyone new to the franchise, and if you are a veteran... my advice echoes that of other reviewers: wait until Neocore have patched the thing a little more.
Gutted.
In the meantime, boot up VH1 and remember when simpler was better :)

Vertical Drop Heros is a simply indie game that started life as a Flash game on the Kongregate game portal (and possibly others). For some, this is an automatic disqualification from consideration. However the game itself is quite fun, if a bit grindy to get started with.
One of the “tricks” to the game is not buy the benefit from every point you can do so (although that is pretty much the instinct you will have because they effects are so nice): if you do, you will be short cash when the more important upgrades are discovered.
Once your heroes start the game with a few extra hit points and do a bit more damage, the earlier levels become far more fun. Still, the game itself isn’t highly polished in places and this recommendation is only a marginal one.

I try to give this game a chance a lot, but I always bounce off. It involves, platforms, hordes, loot sacrifices, boosts, enviromental hazards, RPG leveling system, randomly generated levels, and some legacy systems to have different characters show up during selection after each death. The controls are simplistic in its platforming, and combat comes to 2 or 3 buttons, basic attack can be set to automatic. It somewhat bothered me even though TBoI didn't have that many buttons either. Everything told me it should be a fun time-killer, and every time I played- I didn't feel like it was.
The thing about this game that put the nail in the coffin for me was definitely the combat; NetHack and alikes have random floors, but they are only to be conquered through usage of resources available and knowledge of RPG systems; TBoI has preset rooms, and each is a premade little challenge for the player; VDH HD has random levels, with platforms, and Hack'n'Slash formulas- including "phat loot",  chipping at enemies, and throwing everything at the boss near the end. The whole idea is chaotic, unfocused and more random than challenging. The slow progression through it is similar to my hated clicker games; and also the HnS games- unfortunately, unlike HnS genre, it does not have the semi-complex controls, focus on many skills, or timing/spacing.
This gives a feeling to this game that I always fret the most- being dull. It's not bad in a way it hurts to play it, you can't say the dev didn't try, there were probably good intentions thrown in. But when the game feels dull and makes me think of something else when playing, and still requiring my attention unlike background games- then that's the bad sign. It's not good, it's not bad, it's not even meh- it is sadly completely uninteresting.
I know however that some people do not hate clicker type of games, and like it when it requires time, and not much effort- that's cool, everyone has their opinion and right to it. The dev is probably a cool guy too.
But everyone is also me, and unfortunately I ♥♥♥♥ing hate this game, and I have a right to it. I want to love it and recommend it, but I won't recommend something I can't like.

It's ten pounds, which is a steal, and although generally less developed than Arkham City the combat will get you set for the other games and there are running plots between the two (although the main story hasn't got that much of a link). If you've already played Arkham City, lower your expectations almost across the board. If you've played Arkham Origins, raise them through the fricking roof, everything (except combat) is so, so much better, from storyboard to dialogue. Enjoy.

The cursed writer who can't write anything without getting drunk "on bourbon".
The annoying wife who want to spend more time with her husband - she is a painter, of course.
The capricious lonely child who keep asking his parents to play with him (no wonder he was bullied).
These are the three characters you have to spend the whole game with. Basically you will hear them complain all the time (the writer because he can't find ideas, the wife because her husband works too much and the child because he wants to play).
They all annoyed me after 5 minutes (which is extremely problematic when the aim of the game is about keeping a family together + when the game is mostly story driven).
But well, it can happen...maybe my problem...tastes and colours.... I still gave it a try for 40 more minutes before rage quitting.
Basically, everything is black and white. For instance, if you satisfy the child then he will be happy but the dad and his wife won't be happy - then the next day if you satisfy the wife, she will be happy but not the two others...Can't the child remember that his dad did something for him the day before and be more neutral? No! Their memory last for one day and the day (chapter) after, blank, everything starts again, they have no memories of what person X did to person Y. WHICH is extremely problematic for a game making heavy references to memories (you can read old memories of the characters but yet they can't remember what they did few hours ago?).
Of course with such system, your don't have the feeling that your choices impact the game that much. Which goes against what this game claims to be when they pretentiously advertise it as "The decisions you make will define the Kaplans’ lives, but they may also tell you something about yourself.".
Worst, you don't even care about choices you are going to make because issues the family is going through are banal to the extreme - it is more whines than real family issues.
My overall feeling is that this game is extremely pretentious - from its excessive price, fake description (your choices don't impact that much the game), and its "pseudo-intellectual" vibe.

This game is basically Sonic 1 meets something akin to Trackmania.
It's a race to get the fastest time in the levels to gain medals and progress. The game doesn't have the most mechanics, mostly consisting of the track its self, sliding and occasionally a hook shot, It starts off relatively simple and it gets much, MUCH harder as you go through the game, all while listening to a fantastic heart pumping soundtrack.
There are 10 zones in the game with 9 different themes, starting off with the easy going early worlds, and ending with face paced levels that will test you, and you will fail, many times.
As you go you will unlock more characters to play as (6 in total), you unlock them by doing their challenge at the end of each world, the later ones are instead different costumes for the characters which you can unlock and use yourself. Getting all golds in a world will also grant access to a bonus level of which you must pass by finding the most efficient way of going around the track while collecting gold medals to unlock more skins for each character. Some skins are also unlocked through achievements.
Despite all that there are some flaws.
-No re-bindable controls (at time of writing)
-Tricks that are nearly necessary in the later worlds are often taught though random loading screen tips (using the ghosts as a example can be hard to follow let alone watch without these tricks)
-The physics can feel a bit floaty at times, especially on the grappling hook
-Crashes a fair amount during multiplayer (atleast on my side)
Despite all this, the game is fantastic and is great fun to play and is constantly challenging you throughout the many worlds and I'd highly recommend it if you're into this type of game.

Disclaimer: I’ve been provided a key of this game for free.  My comments are my own.
Action Henk is a game where you race not only against the time but also your friends and, if you want, the Number 1 time holder.  Mind you, racing against No. 1 is hard and requires a lot of finding those small frames that give you an extra second.
You can race against your friends two ways: by their recorded time or online via multiplayer.  Mind you, when I tried it the game crashed but this was when it loaded twice and I'm not sure whether to chalk that up against the game.
Multiplayer is likely best played with friends or people that you can rely on being online at the same time.  The reason is that, like other indie games, there isn't a whole lot of people playing these games online(unless the statistics state otherwise.
If you are looking for something fresh in racing I'd recommend checking this out.
Here's my video supplementing the review:

Momentum, Momentum, Momentum!
Action Henk is a racing platformer developed by RageSquid studios which recently left Early Access. In Action Henk you play as Henk, obviously, an out of shape 90s action hero trying to defeat his nemesis Kentony! Run, jump, slide and wall jump your way to victory with one of the five playable characters. Action Henk's gameplay is sort of like Speedrunners meets the Trials series, I'd describe it as Trials without the bikes.
+Nice graphics
+Hilariously imagined characters
+Fun gameplay, it really has the "one more try for gold" feel to it
+Some great references throughout ranging from Thunderbirds, to MIB to the Sanic meme
+Over 70 tracks (not to mention all of the community made ones)
+Five playable characters, each with different skins to unlock
+Great soundtrack
+Lots of replayability, especially if you want to have a gold medal for each map
+A good level editor
+A fun hookshot mechanic which is introduced later in the game
+Difficulty increases at a good rate
+Great controls (I played with KB&M)
+After completing a level you can challenge your friends to try and beat your time
+Friendly devs
-At some parts in later levels it can be difficult to know what you're supposed to do unless you watch how the ghost does it first
Verdict:
9
Action Henk is an absolutely fantastic racing platformer with nice graphics, great characters, addictive gameplay and loads of levels to play. If you're a fan of Speedrunners or trials this is an absolute must buy!

Dwarf fortress inspired, but Gnomoria has definitely come into its own. This game has been a great ride, one of the first early access games I supported. Every update brought more fun and more experimentation to do, different ways for my gnomes to thrive or get brutally murdered.
I have watched my gnomes toil away so many different ways. From slaving away building a giant gnome out of a mountain range to building an upside down pyramid. I have watched golbins tear apart my guards and skeletons eviscerate my miners.
I have built a magnificent palace for them and trading posts. Barracks and factories! Farmlands and military states! There's so many ways to play this game it's crazy. Robotronic has put heart and soul into this game over the years and it shows! I am grateful that I got to experience the journey!
If you like building games, or army games, or economic games, or just like watching things die, this game is for you! Gnomoria will frustrate you and entertain you, but always leave you with a fulfilled feeling no matter the outcomes.

The game has changed very little since Feb 2015, still feels incomplete and only half finished. Since then it has mostly been bugfixes and and mod support for a game that is basically dead in the water for development. (Its still buggy and sometimes quite annoying to play.)
Positives:
A lot of the basic features are complete, you can build a decent enough base for your gnomes.
Gnomes that have fought in battles can lose limbs that impair thier abilities which helps give some of your gnomes some character which they otherwise lack completely.
So long as you only build unerground, building can be quite fun and easy to do, planning storerooms and workshops seperate to your living quarters and dining halls.
The visual style and overall presentation including the UI is nice to look at and faily easily interpreted.
Negatives:
Being that no preferances exist for food and drink, there is no incentive to vary production and create a variety of food and drink and instead produce the same stuff for the entire playthrough.
Controlling your gnome squads is difficult too, only being able to give vague suggestions of what you want them to do which can be frustrating when combat often leads to serious injury a single gnome can run into a fight before everyone else and die immidiately leading to an entire colont collapsing because you no longer have enough gnomes to fight back and the few remaining goblins take down your civilians with little resistance.
Gnomes get stuck a lot unless you remove tiles in a very specific order to prevent them removing thier only escape because they can't walk on solid blocks if they have no tiles on top. Sometimes you dig down and get them stuck or they construct something in the wrong order and get stuck on top of a wall. You have to micromanage them as best you can despite only being able to designate jobs to be done, this leads to a lot of watching them do a job then designating the next tile(s) for construction or deconstruction, the larger the project you intend to build, the more tedious the process gets.
The games hospital area just does not do its job, gnomes do a better job of patching themselves up after a battle. I have had gnomes who would otherwise have lived die in hospital of thirst despite having plenty of drink available. Plus they stay in hospital untill they are fully recovered and since there is no medicine in game this takes a very very long time, time which would be better spent doing work so we don't all starve.
Currently missing or lacking features:
No animal taming.
No personalities, life goals or religions.
No magic or enchanting.
Diplomacy overly simplistic, either friend or hostile monster kingdom with no way to change thier disposition. Friendly kindoms exists purely for trade and hostile kingdoms will only attack you. No communication and barely any interaction outside of trade or fighting.
Items, plants and animal variety feels lacking, very few rare plants and animals exist.
I've never seen a random event besides being relentlessly attacked by goblins and the Mants have never attacked because I don't make too much food.
Medical treatments besides bed rest and bandages, without any other forms of treatment the hospital is pointless. (Artificial limbs exist but they are quite late in the game and are not produced at the hospital.)
The game is fun enough to pick up on sale but not worth a full price purchase.

As the title indicates, LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga is an amalgamation of two earlier games, LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game and Lego Star Wars II: The Original Trilogy.  I'm calling this an amalgamation as opposed to a compilation due to the fact that the gameplay is presented as a single uninterrupted experience, rather than as two that are separate and distinct.  Traveler's Tales has also added some additional content that was not present in either of the earlier stand-alone games.
LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game was the very first LEGO game developed by Traveler's Tales (henceforth referred to as TT), whereas the Original Trilogy was the second title they developed under the LEGO banner.  These titles form the foundation of what are now familiar gameplay features found in nearly all subsequently developed LEGO games.  The hallmark sense of humor is here (although like all of the earlier TT LEGO games, there is no spoken dialog), as are the simple LEGO building puzzle elements.  We find a familiar hub based level structure with each level branching from that central hub, and of course the LEGO collect-a-thon aspects make their debut here including the requisite stud collection, mini-kits, red bricks, golden bricks, etc.  So while a majority of the gameplay elements will be familiar to those who have previously dabbled in LEGO games, it's interesting nonetheless see the ways in which TT was still experimenting with their formula, solidifying what would become their trademark style.  This last bit is particularly interesting in the context of The Complete Saga, because you can see Traveler's Tales incorporating lessons learned and improving their games between the separate bookends of the Prequel Levels (featured in LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game), and the original trilogy levels (as featured in The Original Trilogy).  From a historical standpoint it's striking to see how quickly Traveler's Tales was able to deftly incorporate lessons learned from the first game and use them to improve the second game.  From a gameplay standpoint though, this creates a bit of dissonance.  Stylistically, the Original Trilogy is a much more robust game.  The levels are longer and more complex, the puzzles are generally more interesting, the graphical elements are improved upon, etc.  So while the levels in Complete Saga are
seamlessly, in practice you will notice a very definitive division between the older (prequel) levels and the newer (Original Trilogy) levels.  Speaking as a bit of a Star Wars nerd I'm happy that the Original Trilogy levels are the ones with better gameplay.
As I mentioned before, the gameplay elements here will be very familiar to anyone who has played TT LEGO games before.  Given the ubiquitous nature of these games, you probably already know whether this game is for you.  If you love the LEGO formula you'll find
to love here.  If the 'break everything in sight collect-a-thon' turns you off, well … these aren't the droids you're looking for.  <groan>  As I mentioned earlier, TT was still developing their trademark style in these games, so even those who have enjoyed more recent LEGO titles might find some of the elements featured here to be a bit rudimentary.  The controls are (naturally) very familiar, but at the same time feel slightly 'looser' than later LEGO titles.  Switching between characters can be a bit tedious since TT had yet to develop the character wheel system seen in more recent titles.  This means that you need to stand directly next to the character you wish to switch to, and since you often have several characters crowding in on you this can lead to several instances of switching to the
character.  This can be slightly rage inducing when you're under attack.  Speaking of computer controlled characters, they are basically useless while not under your direct control, and even worse you may find many circumstances in which they will actively become a hindrance.  There were several circumstances in which I would need to destroy one of my computer controlled allies simply to create a clear line of fire.  Get the heck out of the way Chewie!  And while I'm on this topic, I won't lie, sometimes I would randomly just lay a beat down on Jar-Jar, because … Jar-Jar.
I need to make special mention of the collectible elements in this game, because that aspect has really been dialed to eleven.  If you're like me and you like to unlock everything these games have to offer, well … you're going to be here a while.  You'll need to play through
level no less than four times.  You'll play a level once in story mode which will unlock free play mode.  Then you'll need to play through free play mode to clean up any of the standard remaining goals in that level.  Once you've completely finished the episode you'll unlock Challenge and Super Story modes.  So you'll play each level again in Challenge mode to retrieve the blue mini-kits, and lastly you'll play through them yet
in Super Story mode which is a time-based score attack and simply adds to your completion percentage.
Once you couple this with the fact that this game features unskippable cut scenes, it can all start to become a bit … tedious.  As I mentioned, this part really only applies to completionists, so your mileage may vary significantly in this regard.  I think this is another area in which TT was still figuring out the formula, which in this case meant finding an acceptable line between "collect a bunch of unlockables" and "OMFG, will it ever end!?"
The story is … well, if you don't know it by now, you should schedule yourself for a Star Wars movie marathon, stat.  Having said that, you don't need to be a Star Wars scholar to appreciate the game for what it is.  In point of fact it can be a great introduction to the Star Wars universe for young padawan Star Wars fans looking to get a toehold on the series.  It keeps everything fairly light and deftly negotiates some of the darker aspects of the story.  It's also a great game to play co-op with young ones.  The game treats its subject matter with great reverence and humor.  As a Star Wars fan I enjoyed the game from beginning to end, and this game easily fits within the upper echelons of the greatest Start Wars games ever released.  There are six levels devoted to each movie within the Star Wars saga, and among them you will find all the standard Star Wars set pieces you might expect in a game of this nature along with some surprising gems.  The levels feature a mix of on-foot and piloted air/space craft missions.  All the missions are paced very well, and keep things moving along at a nice clip.  Furthermore the plethora of unlockable characters available keeps things fresh enough so that repeated playthroughs seldom feel stale.
Overall the games presented here are highly enjoyable and well done.  Even in their first forays into LEGO games, TT was already onto a winning formula that would continue to be refined in later games. Lego Star Wars the Complete Saga came out in 2009 on PC and combined together Lego Star Wars the Video Game (1-3 episodes) and Lego Star Wars the Original Trilogy (4-6 episodes). No, Lego Star Wars 3 on Steam is a compltely different game. Aside from combining, it also changed gameplay in vehicle chapters of 1-3 Episodes, as well as adding bonus chapters, which include original versions of those vehicle levels. And well, let's just say that Lego Star Wars was quite a sudden hit when original came out in 2005, developed by Traveller's Tales, who made few charming games in the past and now are making Legos non-stop. Also, PC version has no online multiplayer. No Lego games on PC do.
Technically it still works excellent. No glitches or crashes. Supports widescreen, as it should. It also works excellently with non-Xbox360 controllers, something that became quite rare nowadays.
So, what is Lego Star Wars? Let's just say that it's one of the most casual games in action genre. There is no such thing as "game over". You can't die, you have infinite lives. The only thing that you lose is "stud", the currency of the game. Instead the game forces on collecting, unlocking, sillyness, humor and collecting and collecting. You got over 120+ characters to unlock, for example. And in each chapter 10 minikits are hidden. And often you can't get them all in Story Mode, instead having to use Free Play where you can change character to one of the few specially selected. Even though there are a lot of useless character or the ones who do same stuff, have same powers. But hey, this is what you get when the game tries to appeal to Star Wars nerds, putting every single character from background into it, while also making them stay unique in Lego shape.
Game wants you to unlock some characters and then come back to the levels, uncovering all the secrets. There is probably too much of stuff to collect.
And I must say though that the game, due to it's relaxy nature, can get quite repetitive for more classic gamers. After all, you can't die, you immeditly respawn in same spot. Penalty on Stud isn't huge, and people who don't care about unlocking anything just will not care. As a result of this, playing through all 6 episodes will get so old, that you will want it to end ASAP by Episode 6. One of those cases where game is too long for it's own good.
Talking about story, it's probably slightly friendly to those who didn't watch Star Wars itself. Sometimes not. There is text before each chapter but the cutscenes are silent, instead being just about parody. Probably great for those who watches films first.
And I got to say that 4-6 Episodes somehow were more interesting in story part than 1-3. Didn't see movies myself. Maybe people who kick the prequels aren't so wrong.
The gameplay combines the action of fighting and puzzles in it, with some exploration for sake of gettin studs. Puzzles are quite varied. Sometimes you have to push a box. But most often it's about switching to the right character to open the door. Original trilogy got better there, making you take on a helmet to pass some doors. You don't have to get hit so the helmed will not get knocked off. Also, AI is pretty great there, as in cases where it requires 2 players, it will help you happily.
Now, there is action, fighting part. You got either got a gun or lightsaber. Gun users can shoot with attack button. Some of them can avoid incoming shots if you press attack in a moment when the enemy laser shot is nearby. In such cases character will dodge and then aim at the one who shot it. So, spamming attack can win the battles there. Gun users can also use hooks to get into some areas.
Lightsaber users can once again smash button to hit things. Hitting attack when somebody is about to hit you also makes your character block, also deflecting any laser back at attacker, so panicing by mashing attack can work there too. But they can also double jump and do area attack this way. Actually, you fight most bosses with Lightsaber character and most often the way that you can do damage on them is just spamming jump attack.
And well, such simplistic nature of fighting should compliment the game that is mostly about puzzles and exploration for sake of collecting. The thing is, there is at times way too much fighting. And it doesn't help at all that AI refuses to help you any bit, only sometimes distracting enemy attention on itself. You feel quite alone in these cases.
Actually it gets to completely frustrating moments by the end of a game. Like, after fighting a bunch of enemies, you just want to concentrate on puzzle solving to get into next area. But as you finally found that you have to move something with force, game decides that you spent your time too boring and spawns yet another bunch of Stormtroopers. By this time, you really don't want to fight them, because you know you will win by spamming attack button, you want to solve the darn puzzle already. And all of this while few AI characters stand dumbly around, doing nothing. If you try to do something with force, then suddenly every enemy will focus fire on you, so you sigh and just spend another 15 seconds on destroying them all.
There are also vehicle missions where you fly around, spamming attack, collecting purple balls in one spot and then unleashing them on purple target. Most of them are like that. You can also play original versions of vehicle chapters in bonus levels, and boy, looking at them, they were much harder than you would expect from such relaxed game.
Well, and graphics and music. Graphics are nice and fits well. It's hard to claim that Lego figures look unrealistical and lack polygons you know. Though, it feels too bright or blurry at times.
Music is mostly same as in movies. I guess. It's either something forgetable, or arrangement of either Star Wars themes or Imperial March. Which is fine for movies. Not fine for games where you need more unique and memoriable tracks for each location. But hey, at least it changes between battle and peaciful music during gameplay.
So yea. if you got two kids who love Star Wars and like collecting things, while being silly to each other, then it's perfect game right there. There is a reason why they say it's a game fo their childhood. And if you want more of traditional gaming values in it, then well, only expect to be amused.

Well, pretty much how everyone is saying; Mankind Divided has so much potential but it is wasted quite frequently on many "missions" that just have you meet with people rather than using stealth and dealing with enemies. Sure there is definitely that too, just not as much as there was in Human Revolution or Deus Ex 1 for example. The graphics are very nice and even with my GTX 1080, the game still struggled to run unless I turned off DX12 in the options before launching the game. I like that they got rid of the♥♥♥♥♥♥yellow filter that was in HR but for the most part, alot of what happens in this game is pretty forgetable in my opinion.
I did a stealth run through the game and the DLC stories, using the social enhancer praxis to work on conversations with people and get them to do what I wanted, which is done pretty well. You watch the other person's heart beating on three different personality traits (Alpha, Beta, and Omega) and then you choose whichever trait the heart beat frequented on the most. Also maxed out the cloaking skin and long-life battery so I could maneuver around the enemies with invisible powers which feels fun to me. The main story took me a little over 23 hours to do because I wanted to do every single side mission. If you want the most out of this game DO NOT SKIP THE SIDE MISSIONS! There is a lot of fun to be had in these side stories and oftentimes they are better than the main missions. The DLC was good but I don't think they should have been seperated from the main game, except for A Criminal Past. Desperate Measures is pretty short (maybe a little over an hour honestly), System Rift is a cool mission breaking in to a bank in a new area of Prague (maybe 2.5 hours here), and then A Criminal Past is probably the best one, personally put in like 4 hours for this one. This is an undercover mission disguised as a prisoner into a supermax prison. Again, as with all of Deus Ex, I think it is the best to play this the stealth way. This DLC story gets pretty crazy about halfway in when you gotta break out so expect a lot of thrills!
Overall, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a very fun trip but not worth the $60 price tag and the stories/season pass are way too expensive. I would suggest waiting for the next big Steam Sale when its $17.99 and the pass drops to like $8 (in 2017, less than a year after the game came out). Pay that and you shouldn't be too disappointed, I think.

This game is really good, one of a handful of games I've ever played that really surprised me. You can read more in-depth reviews by others, I'll just say that I Am Alive is not really like anything else you've ever played before.
It has two gameplay elements that really got me hooked - one is the climbing, which is not anything like Tomb Raider or Uncharted. It is puzzle solving and stamina management and sometimes incredibly tense. The other thing I loved is the rarity of bullets - you get maybe a handful throughout the entire game and so you are forced into situations where you might use your single bullet to kill one enemy in the hopes it scares the hell out of the other two that were with him. It might work or it might not. You never get into firefights, you get into very intense standoffs and any hesitation on your part will get you killed.
Cons? The game looks like trash, ends very suddenly and is quite liniar. It's not Fallout. But I was very impressed by the gameplay ideas the devs of I Am Alive had and it's too bad the game didn't get more critical success. I would have loved to see a sequel with a better budget.

is.. well it's not great. But it isn't the worst way to spend your time either. You play as Carlo Mestroni attempting to find his family after [the event]. It is never made entirely clear what, how, why, or indeed even when the world has become this way. It just is, so deal with it.
Early on, Carlo finds some purpose in aiding a child he mistakes as his daughter. Without going too far down the story path; She is very important to the goings on and the objectives that will befall you. I mention this only to inform that she is not a hindrance as in there is no “true” escort mission. This isn't Resident Evil 4. She is attached to you for most intents and purposes and cannot die unless you do.
The survival aspect of the game comes from needing to manage your grip meter and health. If you stay on ledges too long or over exert yourself you'll find that your overall ability to stay on non flat surfaces decreased. Throughout the environment you'll find some items that can restore your health, energy as well as replenish your overall capacity for overexertion. There is also the dust mechanic. Wherein being too low in elevation where the dust has still not settled it is impossible to recover any energy and you must get to higher ground to do so; This can lead to some tense if not annoying sequences of trying to figure out where to go whilst trying not to use all your gear and resources.
The main loop and danger of the game comes from traversal. Very tense music plays when low on energy and it can be quite nerve racking. The other side of the game is dealing with other survivors. Some hostile immediately, others just scared. The combat is not especially great. It is indeed quite functional however stilted though it may be. It consists of holding a pistol up to threaten would be assailants. And then kick them off of edges or into fires and so forth. You must keep you gun trained on all the enemies lest they take advantage of your indecision. Perhaps they may even suggest you've not got the gall. If you relax, you can trick the enemies into coming closer and surprise kill them. This is one aspect that feels great. As during their approach you must quickly ascertain which if any other members of the group have a firearm. And take them out as soon as possible after your surprise kill. It can feel very tactical and systematic especially when ammo is scarce.
The game relies on retries or continues if you will. And you can earn more through helping or aiding the non enemy combatants you'll run into. The main city you'll revisit throughout the campaign so you'll get slightly accustomed to it as well as come back for people you were not able to aid before.
As you may expect you eventually earn things that make traversing the dust less annoying. As well as other things that make running out of energy less of an issue. But they are near the end of the game and you don't really get to use them much. The game is about five-ish hours in total.

Pro: Your decisions feel like they have consequences.
Con but also a Pro: You often do not get to decide (unless death is a choice) and those consequences can make you look like a monster.
Pro: The story is compelling.
Con: The story telling is disjointed, lacking content and feels linear despite not moving the story forward one bit.
Pro: Combat is intense (because of the story content in the mechanics).
Con: The only combat scenarios not First-Person-Shooter (FPS) are Quick-Time-Events (QTE) and the game is lacking in mechanics for non-FPS resolutions to conflict.
The game music pretty much tells you if there's an enemy nearby which detracts from any need to be subtle, secret or careful.
Buy this game for the story.  The concept is good. The story is alright. The combat is rubbish. The execution needs considerable work and the graphics are not optimized. It's worth getting on sale for under $10 for the concept alone.
The climbing, the environment, the story though lacking all tied together to push me foward. It felt like Tomb Raider in a post apocalyptic dystopian wasteland amidst the crumbling remains of a once bustling city.

i will only give this a positive recommendation because its a very early beta with lots of potential. with that said, here are my pros and cons...
pros:
1. fast paced fps action. once ur ingame ur right in the front of battle
2. graphics are above average. this wont have the graphics of the latest star wars, but its still really nice to look at (other than those god awful flags in corporate park)
3. updates. the game is updated regularly and the devs r extremely active in the community and in updating the game in means to better it.
cons:
1. quickscoping is basically impossible in this game. they seem to automatically implement it, but the scope zooms in once u scope, and that forces u out of a possible quickscope. which, in turn, throws u off of ur target once ur about to fire. it wasnt like this in the web version.
2. lag. the lag is by far the worst ive ever experienced. since there are no dedicated servers u have to deal with people hosting from their isps. and even if u find a good one god forbid you kill the host more than once. if that happens dont be surprised if the server gets shut down.
3. bullet registry. in the web version when u shot at someone 9 out of 10 bullets would make contact. in this version ur lucky if 4 out of 10 hit. and in some occasions u will find urself firing endlessly at several enemies at close range. only to end up dieing just before the server kicks you. this can also be associated with the lag issues mentioned in con#2.
4. hacks. yes, even after 2 days hackers were already joining servers. the sightings of speed hackers and the rare occasion of an obvious aimbot have already been noticed. aquiris claims they r using vac anti cheat, but it seems like its not that strong against hackers if people are already taking advantage of it. this needs to be addressed asap ( right along with the lag issues)
5. lack of servers. since there are no dedicated servers you are stuck with whomever decides to host a match. that means if u log on and want to play a few games u are stuck with some serious slim pickin's. and u r seriously out of luck if the only people hosting a room are from any location that isnt remotre to urs. Im from north america. so most of the time i find that there is nothing but Asia, South America, and Europe servers... that means im logging out of the game, since chances are my ping to those servers is around 500.

This game, seemingly based somewhat on Woolf's novel 'To the Lighthouse,' was a marvelous experience. While it is heavily story based and has multiple endings, it DOES have gameplay, unlike some of the Indie walking simulators that you find. However, you'd have to be really silly to actually get punished for failing to do a good job with the gameplay, I feel. Still, it's enough to keep you actually playing the game while watching the story unravel according to your actions.
The game highlights some of the same existencial issues that 'To the Lighthouse' does: it highlights family and relationship issues in day-to-day living, and the problems balancing work with the two. It also shows that the lives of all people invovled are transient and fleeting, and all that's left of us afterwards is our art: whether it be the books we write or the paintings we craft. The shared symbol of the lighthouse and some of the shared activities of both families gives them both the same ambiance, I felt.
Regardless, definitely look into this one, as it leaves you something to learn and ponder about your own life.

The gameplay itself is very simple: you just explore a house, reading clues, looking at drawings, and listening to snippets of dialogue to figure out what each family member wants. Overall, I don't know if three hours of gameplay is worth full price, but I could recommend this on sale.

Torchlight 2 has one game-ruining flaw: resistances in TL2 are flat damage reduction.  (That is, if you have 100 fire resistance, it reduces each instance of incoming fire damage by a flat 100 points.)
If you are at all familiar with the way that RPGs, particularly RPGs with significant player power scaling, work, you will understand why this is a problem; in TL2's case, it becomes a problem by the end of one playthrough, so it's not even a case of badly chosen stat weights.  If you want an ARPG to get really deep into, pick one of the other big ones like Path of Exile or Diablo 3, which do not have this problem.
For the rest of you: Most similar games use an effective HP-based system, where a point of resistance increases your effective HP against damage of that type by a fixed percentage.  For example, if you have 100 fire resistance, you might take half damage from fire, and if you have 200 fire resistance, you might take 25% damage from fire.  Notice how the second 100 fire resistance still gives you the same amount of mitigation per point, and notice how you could scale this infinitely if you wanted (if you have 9900 fire resistance, getting another 100 will still halve your incoming fire damage; likewise you can increase enemies' fire damage and it'll all scale smoothly).
Flat damage reduction causes two undesirable side effects.  One is that each act jump is a big difficulty spike (because your flat damage reduction doesn't scale up) until you get new gear, at which point it becomes easier again.  The other, particularly later in the game, is that enemies start to sort into two categories: small enemies and big enemies.  Small enemies do zero damage, because they're intended to swarm you with small attacks which are now entirely blocked by gear.  Large enemies do big attacks that one-shot you, and no amount of gear will help you because they just hit that hard.  And so this distorts the endgame (of a single playthrough of TL2!) into basically ignoring the small enemies and desperately kiting the big ones.  If you were to continue to scale both the player and the enemies, this problem becomes steadily worse.
So yeah.  It's probably okay if you get this off a heavy Steam sale or Humble Bundle or something and just want a fun diversion for a couple hours, but this is going to be a problem for you at some point.

Okay, look.  It's not a bad game.  Ignore these reviews.  It's secretly a good game.
Yes, if you've played M&M before, you've played M&M before, and this is certainly M&M.  But this is good fun!  And you can play it co-op whenever you want.
If you have faith that you won't accidentally click "Buy 50,000,000 Logs for $100", then you'll have an unadulterated fun time, guaranteed.  You must also avoid every other useless real-money purchase this game tries to shove down your throat.  In all honesty, there are about three worthwhile real-money purchases you can make as you level up in this game.  I'm level 29 on the web browser version, have had a blast so far and I haven't paid a dime for any of these purchases.
You might consider buying inventory space.  Also, there are experience bonus shards that might be worthwhile.  But Mount speed isn't necessary since it's kind of ridiculous of a speed boost for how small the screen is.  Also, you can get every material from quests, by finding them on the map and for free about 4 times a day from your towns.  So just uhh, play the game for free, and collect materials from your towns whenever you log in (they'll stack up quickly), and you'll be good to go.  Don't spend a dime on upgrading your towns either, by the way; they are perfectly adequate without any real-money purchases whatsoever.
TL;DR: The game is fun and more than accessible without paying a dime.  Worthwhile real money purchases include exp shards, a few inventory slots and maybe some endgame materials which you won't care to worry about until maybe 100+ hours into the game.  Fun game, classic Might and Magic but online and extremely flexible co-op.  Music can get repetitive; you can turn off the music.

Action Henk charmed me from the word go grabbing me with a great art style and wonderful premise. You play as an Action Henk action figure who might be just a little bit past his prime, yeah he's put on a few pounds since his glory days but he's still every bit as great as he used to be. Right?
Let's hope so because the nefarious Dr. Kentony has just stolen Henk's prized 'Toy of the Year' trophy and Henk's gonna have to run, jump and buttslide his way across 70+ courses to get it back!
This game starts with a simple time trial gameplay mechanic and resists over complicating it with too many bells and whistles. Solid controls, well designed courses, functional multiplayer, decent humor, and a wonderful visual style all combine to make Action Henk one of my favorite releases from 2015.
If you'd like to see some gameplay and hear my extended thoughts check out the video below:

Getting back into shape has never been so fun!
Action Henk is a race against the clock platforming timed racing game. You star as Henk (not Hank) who appears to be a washed up hero of sorts within a toy-based world. Very similar to Toy Story, various action figures from what looks to be the 90’s, become animated and Henk, once a fit beefcake, is now a bit out of shape, overweight and slow. So its up to his fellow toys to get him back into shape by racing them in a series of courses.
All of the courses are based inside a kid’s bedroom. They are made primarily of wooden blocks and orange plastic smooth track, mainly for downhill sliding (think Hot Wheels). They capture the imagination very well in a detailed background, from posters, to furniture, lamps, desks, etc all of which have various easter eggs to other pop culture. Also like from our childhood and the TV show Community, the floor is lava the second you fall short of a jump or simply run off an edge.
The game plays very smoothly and the controls are tight and spot on as to what you would expect them to be. It is highly recommended to use a 360 controller, although it is playable with keyboard. The buttons are simple and straightforward, right and left to run, A to jump and left trigger to butt slide.
You begin each stage at a starting line and with a small countdown, you dash off. You use a combination of jumps and slides primarily, although later on in the levels, they incorporate wall jumping and different path options that can only be accessed through well timed jumps. Think Sonic the Hedgehog but less danger and no stomping on enemies or losing rings/coins.
The game is very fast paced and can be somewhat frustrating at times. Each stage gives you the option to earn medals for various timed finishes. For example, one stage I was stuck on the bronze medal was earned with a minimum time of 24.75 seconds, then silver at 24.50 and finally gold at 23.59. Now that separation in time looks very minimal on the surface, but it is extremely difficult to ever achieve anything better than a bronze. I had to play this particular stage at least a dozen times until I had memorized the various times when to jump and slide best to maximize Henk’s speed and momentum to get the best time. I could get 25 seconds flat almost every time, but those medals were very difficult to earn, although once I finally did, I felt very accomplished and a great sense of satisfaction.
The game also features leaderboards with friends and people worldwide, you can even race against other player’s ghosts. Add a community shareable level builder and you have yourself endless combinations of butt sliding fun.
I first encountered this game in the Indie Megabooth at PAX Prime 2014 and I met and talked with Kitty, the marketing director for developer RageSquid while demoing the game.
Aside from my own personal downfalls, Action Henk is a very well rounded game, with unlockable characters, amazingly detailed and colorful artwork, fast paced racing action, tight controls, and overall a good time.
-Matt

I actually got Ziggurat as part of the Humble Indie Bundle, so I can't say I expected too much. I went into it completely blind, not knowing what I would get, and was pleased to find a roguelike dungeon crawler, one of my favorite genres. However, my hopes were soon dispelled. After one minute of playing, two things became apparent to me: Probably no more than three people worked on this game, and they all were first year students, or hadn’t studied game design at all. Not to say that games made by only a few people are inherently bad (Cave Story is one of my all time favorites), but that the people behind Ziggurat don’t know how to make games.

Now, I said that the game felt like a first-year student’s final project, but… After researching the developers, Milkstone Studios, I was astounded to find that they have a whopping 30 games under their belt! Their first game, Little Racers (funnily another game I got with the bundle), first released in July of 2011, and their most recent, White Noise 2, came out in April of this year. 30 games over the course of a little less than 6 years means that Milkstone Studios is pushing out an average of 5 games per year! You’d think they’d have a large team to be able to crank them out that fast, but they only consist of 5 people: four artists and the CEO, who is the sole programmer AND designer! I’m surprised they manage to get their games to a playable state. Clearly, Milkstone Studios is a quantity-over-quality-developer, and it shows in Ziggurat.

For starters, the game is butt-ugly. Everything is well-modeled (though I’m not sure how much of it is pre-made assets), and I love the cartoony Hearthstone-esque visual style, but as soon as it gets put into motion, everything falls apart. It all lies in the animation. The way enemies move is stiff and unnatural, creating a kind of uncanniness that breaks the immersion.

Speaking of motion, the way the player character moves doubles that uncanniness. He’s so fast and floaty that there’s no weight to any of his movements, and it doesn't feel like I’m controlling an actual person. This, combined with the animation issue above, immediately makes the game feel cheap, like those branded yo-yos companies give away for free to promote themselves. (You know the ones:

The gameplay is… functional. There are 4 forms of attack: Wand is the starter weapon, tomes deal a lot of damage, staves are deal low damage with rapid fire, and alchemy deals splash damage. Each has it’s own mana bar, your wand recharges itself, and the other three can be refilled via drops from enemies. This system by itself alright, there’s nothing inherently wrong with it, and it adds an interesting layer of resource management to battles.

Combat itself sucks. Enemies without projectiles have only one strategy: to dash at you in swarms and overwhelm you. Dodging is one of the most frustrating and difficult things to do. Running around backwards in first person while shooting and trying not to run into walls or obstacles is almost impossible with the floaty controls, and you have to be running around for a while. Even the weakest enemies take several hits with your basic weapon, and the number of enemies in a single room gets to be ridiculous.
Enemies that prefer to shoot projectiles are another story. Most of them either fire a spread of bullets or explosives. This makes dodging feels pointless, as even when you dodge a shot you still take damage from a stray bullet or the resulting explosion. Add that onto the ridiculously high number of enemies per room, and your odds of coming away unscathed are very slim. Most encounters turn into you running in circles around a room, frantically making a futile attempt to avoid the barrage of attacks from all angles while being chased by a swarm of sentient carrots, trying your best to get in a shot of your own whenever possible.
Except it’s not possible. Not shooting bullets from guns means there attacks have travel time. Running around at a fast pace while trying to simultaneously hit a moving target is virtually impossible. You either have to get up close or slow down, both of which will get you killed. I love fast paced games, but the faster the game, the tighter the controls need to be for the player to stay in control, and Ziggurat is sorely lacking in that department.

Killing enemies will reward you with health and mana refills, but the majority of enemy drops are going to be knowledge crystals, which grant EXP. Leveling up offers you a choice between two or more cards offering various buffs. When selecting them, they seems pretty good: “Refill a small amount of mana before every battle” and “Receive more drops from enemies” sound good, but after receiving buffs, I couldn’t notice any kind of difference. Even after five or so level ups, I still felt just as powerful as I did at level one. Tangible growth is a huge part in determining a game’s fun factor, and failing to achieve it is a huge issue with the game's enjoyability. The gameplay experience of Ziggurat can be summed up to boring and frustrating.

Animation and combat are insignificant problems next to the biggest problem of all: The complete lack of design. When the only designer is also the only programmer and the head of the company, of course there are going to be problems. An example: There’s a certain room that generates onto the map rather frequently. The room itself has no enemies, and consists of a large flat area checkerboarded with fiery tiles that burst into flame on timed intervals. Navigating this room involves running in a straight line towards your destination and stopping every five seconds to wait for the tiles to turn off. It’s completely pointless and does nothing but waste your time.
Actually, that’s an analogy for the entire game. There is no reason to play Ziggurat. It’s a waste of time. If the gameplay falls flat, what else is there? There’s no story to tell or interesting concept to explore. The visual design of the dungeon is bland, the writing is non-existent, the atmosphere is forgettable, there are no characters, the level design in each room is atrocious. and I had to go back and check to make sure that the game actually had music, because I couldn’t remember if it did! The game is such a waste of time you shouldn’t still be reading this review on it. And to ask for $15 for this is basically a crime! For $15, you can get Enter the Gungeon, or The Binding of Issac Rebirth, or Crypt of the Necrodancer, or Cave Story+, or The Elder Scrolls Marrowind or Oblivion! There are so many other great games out there to spend your time and money on. Don’t waste them here.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a RPG where you play as a guy or gal that you choose at the beginning of the game who is trying to stop his or her true love marrying someone else.
This game is pretty damn good. At the beginning of the game you can choose which character to play as and who is your love interest. Every combination you make leads to a different outcome in some parts of the game: there is racism against interracial or homosexual couples,people interact differently, etc. The bad aspect is that these changes from playthrough to playthrough aren't as big as one might expect. Nonetheless, there are many choices throught the game that can lead to different paths.
The gameplay is similar to real life: you can do some small jobs to gain money, you have to eat regularly, you can pawn objects, go to the movies, play at the arcade and so on. It is a risky move and I understand why some people don't like it. However, I found it very fresh and interesting.

Overall, Always Sometimes Monsters is a solid RPG. The different choices and characters to choose from give the game high replayability, also thanks to its humor and soundtrack.

Out of all the annual series of video games, the LEGO series has been, by far, my favorite. I mean, you get to experience these movies so deeply embedded in pop culture in a new light with LEGO's quirky and charming humor. And this is the one that truly started it. That is not to say past LEGO games were bad, LEGO island being a nostalgic and fun experience for me. But it's LEGO Star Wars that truly kicked it up a few notches to what it currently is right now.
The Complete Saga has you playing through the prequels trilogy and the original trilogy. Each episodes are seperated into six missions based on the more important parts of their respective movies. But though you may think this game is just about going through levels in LEGO form, there is much to do. Each level has Red Bricks (Which are little extras that give you some new or enhanced abilities), you also get to collect 10 minikits which are hidden in the levels (sometimes completely out of your reach because your current set of characters do not possess the ability to reach it). Collecting studs allows you to buy characters and vehicles and collecting enough of them during missions gets you True Jedi status (which gives you a Gold Brick). Upon completion of the story mode, you unlock Free Play and Challenge mode. Free Play has you playing through the level with a set of randomized characters specifically for their abilites to get some of the minikits you cannot normally get during story mode, giving this game some actual replay value. Challenge has you going after 10 blue minikits within the level altough you are now on a timer and the location of these minikits has been mixed up a bit. So, basically, if you are going for 100%, you'll get to experience these levels minimum three times.
This game's soundtrack is also from the movies, which is a plus within itself. The complete Saga features also 2 player co-op (local), 6 bonus levels that were in the original installments of these two games' seperate releases (Harder versions basically). On top of that, there are 160 Gold Bricks in the game. You get 3 per level: 1 for beating the level in story mode, 1 for collecting all minikits, 1 for obtaining True Jedi status. 14 can be bought in the Mos Eisley Cantina and 6 for the aforementioned Bonus levels. All in all, you have a crap ton to do in this game.
With the plethora of content, replay value, addictive gameplay and the chance to exprience Star Wars in LEGO form, I absolutely recommend this game. Nearly 10 years later, this game is still fun and has yet to show its age.

I bought all LEGO games on impulse and this was the first one that I played and finished. I have mixed feelings about it. Pros:
- Thematic and story
- Lots of humour
- You can play with almost every Star Wars character
- LOTS of things to find in every level
- Friendly AI is impressive on some levels (pathfinding + actions)
Cons:
- Starship and flight controls and combat are really bad and stressful. Yes, the flight levels are awful. Actually I would say that vehicle controls overall are terrible in this game.
- Music and Sound can be really annoying. I know we are talking about Star Wars music, but it just doesn't stop playing anytime.
- The only challenge is to collect all coins (stud) to then buy stuff in the store, to get to 100%. I finished all levels and story mode with 27% and I don't plan on coming back to keep collecting coins just to buy some new characters.
- Enemy AI is dumb most of the time.
- Repetitive. On Episode VI I just wanted to finish it ASAP.
I don't know if this is the default recipe for LEGO games, but the next LEGO game I'll play has to be a newer one with achievements, because I want to check if the mechanics and challenges have changed - but specially the vehicle controls. So I'll decide it the other ones that I own will be worth playing.

This is game is made for speedrunners and anyone who can appreciate satire of the current state of the gaming industry with its increased DLC and freemium use.  If only one of them applies to you, you'll at least be somewhat entertained by this game.  If both, buy this game.  If neither, I'd hesitate to recommend it even on sale.
Pros: Satirical nature, meta narrative of gaming industry, great for speedrunning & achievement hunters, simple gameplay mechanics.
Cons: Short game, simple gameplay mechanics, more graphical progression could've added to the satire.

While you could argue that the main joke of the game gets old after a bit, there's still plenty of humor in the game. The jokes in the game aren't references, in fact that is something that is mocked. Much if not all of the dialogue with NPCs point out various odd things common in video games (to tell the truth that's gotten to be a cliche in itself, but a lot of the observances were new to me and funny).
There are some pretty great tunes, although one of them has a melody line that's painful to listen to. I should mention that I found the first part of the game fairly weak, however the "free DLC expansion" mission had me smiling throughout.
The game is short and the concept might get old after a while, but if you want a game that will make you chuckle you ought to check it out, especially if it's on sale when it's dirt cheap.

Ballist Overkill is a decent. Is it a revolutionary arena shooter? No. But for 6.99$ did you really expect as much? Now, I really would like to add more time to my review, but as it stands, there is one aspect that just makes playing matches too hard currently.
The make or break issue for Ballistic, at least in my case, was the networking. This is the reason I decided to go negative. Ballistic Overkill has a lot in common with Call of Duty. In that it's relatively fast paced arena shooter and the time to kill can be relatively low. You can find yourself getting one shotted at point blank with a sniper or even a shotgun. Why is that relavent you may ask?
There are no dedicated servers. You get a p2p connection with the host of the game. And there doesn't seem to be any lag compensation to make up for that fact like there is with the old Call of Duty games. What this means is in those moments where you meet someone around a corner and both of you are capable of killing each other almost instantly. The person with the better ping to the host will almost always win. You'll die putting buckshot into someone and end up not even getting a hit marker before you die. That puts a pretty large advantage on where the game host is located.
Now, I personally haven't dealt with a p2p connection based shooter in half a decade, not unless you count Black Ops 2, which used a hybrid of p2p connections and listening servers. So I have to say I'm not sure whether that was my problem or not, but generally I experienced higher pings then what I'm used to in other games, like TF2 or CS:GO. Part of my problem is I just don't have enough information. Thankfully, the developers recently gave us the ability to see what general area the host is located in. But, the issue with this is that it's still too vague. You know you're playing with someone in North America or Europe now, you just don't know what state, province, or city they are located in. Do you live Kentucky? Good for you! The host could be living in Quebec for all you know. And if you're wondering where Quebec is, it's on the edge of the East coast of Canada. This is the reason I can't tell whether the game's networking coding is the problem for my generally higher ping, or if the hosts are located in more remote areas of North America then I am used too dealing with.
In short, unless you plan to be the host every single time you're playing the game, prepare to lose some gunfights left and right, and not of your own accord either. And if you are host, you should also learn to accept your winning might be due to the crutch that is the latency advantage rather then the other guy just being a noob who likes standing there and eating your lead.

Doggone this game pisses me off, primarily because the save system is so erratic and unpredictable.  I ended up doing the same things over and over again, simply because I don't have countless hours to wander around until I can finallly find a save point.  Even then a found save point is no guarantee that, if you log off entirely, that it won't throw you back to some vague save point from the past.  Very very frustrating with no sense whatsoever.  That coupled with the mouse usage in a fight or when lifting a door - you have to tap the LMB furiously to accomplish your task and believe me you can't do it with just your index finger resting on the LMB.  NOOOOO!!!  I have to hit "E", grab the mouse with my Left hand, then using my Right index finger, pound the LMB into submission.  And half the time that doesn't work either.  Games should be FUN, not endless repetitive work, so I'm giving this game a resounding thumbs down.  It's not a pretty game, the graphics and landscape interaction are minimal, and most of the time everything is shrowded in fog.  Pointless, simply pointless.
If you insist on playing this game here's a suggestion.  Play it on EASY.  The reason to do so is simple.  On any other level the only way you get to continue after you die, and you WILL die many many times, is if you accumulate "Replays" by saving somebody.  This is the ONLY benefit of saving somebody!  On EASY you get INFINITE REPLAYS.  That is the ONLY change in the game, so why not?  You control the game; the game doesn't control you!  Otherwise the game consists of saving the same characters OVER AND OVER AGAIN to accumulate replays to move on.  FRUSTRATING IN THE EXTREME.  If your ego or pride won't let you play on EASY, even tho it makes no difference any other way, then you get exactly what you deserve.
