You know… in all honesty I’ve still got a review for the first game in the series as a draft just chilling on the site. I feel kind of bad that I never put it up… or finished it. On the other hand, it was pretty stinking awesome! Now the third installment of the game is out and it’s also blowing my mind. A built-in tank class (Protector)? Yes please!
So this takes place after the second game in which you stopped a big civil war, but the world is never truly fixed is it? No… not if we need more games in a franchise it’s not! And luckily it’s not over yet since they gave me a giant mech to play with this time. I’m a bigger fan of the thought of playing a tank (the Protector class), but not this time. I’ve figured out that class enough to know that it’s not crazy-super-tanky, it’s the regular type. It’s cool, but with my playstyle, it just wasn’t working out. Now the guy pictured above is where it’s at! He’s not a tank, but what do you need to tank when all the enemies are already exploded? Nothing really. This guy shoots out a ton of rockets and then mops up with a flamethrower! I don’t care what you think about this game, this class is fun!
The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing III (gosh that’s a keyboard full… well just call it Van Helsing III from here) controls much the same as in the (I assume since I haven’t played the second one yet) much like the earlier two titles. It uses the typical ARPG click to attack fest with hotkeys for select moves. It still works well here. There isn’t as much funky “can’t get there from here” as I experienced in the first game so the path-finding seems to be better. That did kind of drive me nuts in Van Helsing I. The only thing that bothers me is when loot drops off a cliff or behind something and I couldn’t get it. Now… I was in a giant suit of armor and I’m not that small, I get it, but why couldn’t my smarty-pants ghost buddy Katarina pick it up? She’s a ghost… it’s just physics! Or science… or ghost physcience… or whatever you want to call it where she can go nab my loot for me when it falls behind something she should be able to phase through. Luckily, this only happened twice or so in my 16-ish hours of playing.
There are, once again, skill trees to explore and different options to level up and all that jazz. There aren’t so many that it’s overwhelming, but there are plenty of options that will make you salivate since you’ll want them all if you’re anything like me. One look at the trees after about twenty minutes of play and I can usually map out where I want to go. I’m a big fan of moves that go boom and stuff, oh and feeling awesome. I love using the rocket move solely and the ability to strengthen them and add more rockets to your salvo just makes me happy. I think I would have loved a bit more destructible environments, but I don’t need that in every game… but it would have been neat.
The mini game where you play tower defense is back. While not my favorite part of the game, it is pretty cool. I do enjoy the fact that you can run around with your character and help your turrets and traps with all the nifty moves you’ve leveled up in the main game. (There’s an achievement for not helping though… jerks. Don’t they understand I’ve got rockets that need to go boom?) Plopping turrets and flame units and a few spike traps helps to kill the baddies before they reach your spherical ball of funkiness. Don’t let them touch the funk! It’s not the greatest tower defense, but it’s a neat addition to the game (again) and is a good way to break of up the “monotony” of stabbing and blowing things up by… stabbing and blowing things up… in a confined area.
There is also a way to manage the resistance (that I believe was in the second game). I’m not sure if it’s improved from the second game, but it was interesting. Having completed a few missions in it I can honestly say… I’m not sure what the point of it completely is, but it’s neat to have that part of the story be fleshed out some more. It’s kind of like it’s telling you that there is more going on in the world than just what you are doing. As if the world would stop if/when you left your base. While it may not be amazing, I think it makes the game a bit more full and better for having it in. That and the tower defense really just add to the experience.
In Van Helsing III you are starting to unravel the story behind Katarina and it’s pretty interesting. It’s not super gripping, but it’s one of those things that you’re glad you learned the back-story even if it wasn’t life-changing. The banter back and forth between Van Helsing and her is still good as good as it was in the original and will still give you a few chuckles throughout the game (maybe not when they are being all serious though… nah, there’s still humor there about ponies and such). All good things must come to an end and stuff, but I’ve enjoyed the series and I’m excited to see what else NeocoreGames has for me later on down the road.

I'm giving this a positive, mostly because I loved the first two games, and it seems such a shame that the third one felt only half-baked. The first one was a stellar entry for the genre, but the second felt a little bit of a step down, and the third which I've just finished playing was mediocre in comparison.
While the addition of the new classes was interesting, and the music was absolutely fantastic, the fact that I couldn't import my characters and items from the second was frustrating to say the least. I carried on grinding after the story ending in VH2 to get all the godlike items, and amassed a fortune, only to find VH3 WOULDN'T LET ME CARRY A SINGLE ONE OVER! ARRRRGGGGGH.
Next, what was with the loot? VH1 and VH2 let me indulge in my love of hoarding loot, with great sets or epic items being dropped. Perhaps it was just my game, but not a single set item showed up, and I had all of 2 special items. It was nice however that Katarina had her own stuff at last, rather than things I didn't want anymore.
Also, why such a low level cap?! Yes the leveling in this game has been restructured and a bit more freeing, but the level cap for my character and Katarina was just too low.
I also encountered some frustration with the final boss fight, not loading at all when trying to get in, not connecting to my co-op buddy, crashing, and then when I finally made it back in, doing some awful things with the camera so I couldn't see what I was hitting.
And what happened to the LAN? That suddenly disappeared which makes no sense at all.
Finally, this franchise has been great with all of its pop culture references, dealt out with some style and wit. Unfortunately, it felt as if the game was rushed out without putting that much of this in, so I quite missed these.
Overall, this might sound like a bad game, but honestly, it's not. It's just that in comparison to the other two, it feels more acceptable, rather than good. What I can't complain about however is the price point. It's a decent enough game for the price, £11.99. It just didn't feel like a fitting finale for what has been a great franchise overall.
I'd say buy this to support this independent developer, but for a game you can really enjoy, VH1 and VH2 are your best bets.

As much as I love these games, this was a bit of a disappointment. I'd recommend it, as the game was fun, but whether I'd recommend it at full price I don't know.
I started to get a bit worried about this game before I even started it. With VH2, there were pre-orders, you could get extras, and it felt like we could be much more involved. That wasn't the case with VH3. No pre-order, no bonuses, no benefits for those of us who owned the first two games in the series.
The Good:
The new classes are a lot of fun - I played through as the Protector and really enjoyed it. Given that these games are a bit samey, I don't think I'll play through it again as a different class.
The Bad:
I essentially see Neocore as an indie outfit, so they can be forgiven for some replication - but this is essentially exactly the same game with new maps and new classes.
The Tower Defence elements have been stripped right back. It only occurs three times and it didn't feel nearly as fun as it did previously. In the last one, one of the traps didn't actually work - you couldn't even place it. (I forget the name of it, but it's the cage that houses the werewolf-type creatures).
Buggy. Not only the trap mentioned above, but some of Katriana's skills didn't even seem to do anything.
Too easy. I played on the second-hardest setting (not sure why, usually go for the hardest settings but maybe I'm getting old!) and there was no challenge to the game. The Protector was such a powerful class that I just steamrolled everything, including the final boss, who barely took me below 100% health.
Loot. The loot was just a bit uninspired. I just kept swapping between very slightly better versions of each item. The only upgrades I ever seemed to get were from the shop. Drops were terrible. I didn't get one item better than rare, and none of the items had any interesting effects to them.
The So So:
The skill trees. I didn't like skill trees from VH2. There were too many skills, most of which were useless once you got the better versions. It didn't have the same kind of progressive feel of games like Diablo 2. In that regard, the trees in VH3 are better - but perhaps they've gone too far in the other direction. I only had four skills for the entire game. The other two were pointless. More to the point, those were the only skills available at all - there was no choice between play styles or using one skill over another.
Having read my review, I'm not sure why I'm recommending the game - but even with its flaws, it's still better than a lot of games out there. It might be samey, but at least it's samey as compared to great games.

As many have said before me, it's a great retro shooter that plays very similarly to Far Cry 3. That being said however, the vast majority of the negative reviews are all concerning Uplay, Ubisoft's attempt on Steam, basically EA's Origin for Ubisoft. Personally however, I didn't find Uplay all that bad. Sure making an account or having Uplay launch whenever you want to play can be annoying, but in my honest opinion, Ubisoft has definitely improved Uplay since I first purchased this game two years ago. Uplay just launches and then sets you straight into the game with it's in game overlay available via Shift F2 (in addition to Steam's). Sure your achievements are saved to Uplay along with the cloud storage, but Uplay also comes with some "free" addons purchaseable with credits earned by completing in game tasks.
Overall, I would say Uplay is a lot less intrusive than in the past, and would recommend this purchase (assuming you are into this type of game-see other reviews on actual gameplay) despite Uplay (which I personally  don't hate).
The game itself is pretty good. But requires to having two gaming interfaces *cough*UPlay*cough* opened?

This... is easily one of the best games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. This game is good. No, this game is downright amazing. Why is it so good? Everything about this game is why. Not a single feature was made poorly. The asylum looks amazing, it almost even has a feel to it like you are actually there. Every single little detail on every thing is very well made. And then there is the story. It's like they took a page out of the Animated Batman series and made a movie based on it, but as a game. It is really well written. And the acting, my god the acting. I can't even begin to describe it, just play it already. The gameplay is also really well made to. There are essentially three aspects to the game. The first is the combat. At first it just seems like you could just mash the attack button but as the game goes on it introduces so many features. Mainly there is a combo system where you have to only hit the button once between hits to keep it going. You want to keep it going so you can use the really good moves that you unlock. Also there are enemies that have to be hit in certain ways or you get hurt. The other aspect is stealth. It's pretty straight forward and that is what works about it. You don't have much to worry about other than staying out of line of sight while picking off the guards one by one. There are also gadgets to use that can let you do some pretty cool things. The third aspect is exploring the island. While the game is pretty much linear there is a bit of a puzzle for how to get to the next area or actual puzzle like sections and even some hidden goodies. Definitely one of the games where it is worth getting all the collectibles in.
I give the game 5 batarangs out of 5.

I'll start by saying that I don't have children and don't have contact with my family.  Not in a bad way, I'm just a deeply selfish person.  My wife and I would rather soend our money on holidays, games and cats than anything serious like bringing up a child.  What's the point of this surprisingly personal and seemingly irrelevant disclosure?  Well, despite my shortcomings as an adult human, I loved The Novelist.
The Novelist is a game that will mean something different to every person who plays it, depending on their point of view.  The way the game plays is that a small family have rented a house for the summer - the father sees it as an opportunity to work on his book, the wife sees it as a chance to rebuild their failing relationship and it is supposed to be a chance to address the problem the son has at school.  You play as a spirit that haunts the house and it is up to you to influence the father at the end of each day as to how to handle an event (or events) that will affect the family.  You do this by gathering information on each person's take on the event and coming to a conclusion as to how best to handle it.  Find every piece of information, and you will be allowed a compromise at the end of the day, meaning that one person will come away happy with the result, one placated and one potentially unhappy.
This is all simply done, and can be played as either a casual point and click style game of (admittedly limited) exploration, or as an stealth-lite game that has you trying to avoid the family seeing you, and thus becoming spooked and denying you the ability to come to a compromise with them.  Playing this way is actually quite engaging and adds a light air of tension added to by the lack of saves during the day, meaning you have to live with your decisions and mistakes.
Although I found myself drawn to the characters, it wasn't necessarily through their actual interactions.  If anything, that would be the weakest part of the game.  The characters' personalities are all explored very well through diaries and journals, but doesn't come across in the world of the game.  It can be argued that it adds to the otherworldly feel to the game, but I think a lot would be added by the characters showing more... well... character.
Anyway returning to my opening paragraph - I felt when I started the game that I would absolutely be on the father's side.  The game is called The Novelist, he is earning the money in the family and the house was rented to allow him to work on his book.  So, fine.  Cut and dried, let's get this book printed!  Well, no.  Reading the wife's personal thoughts and fears about how close to divorce they are without him realising was actually quite scary.
OK.  Let's focus on the relationship and put the book on the sidelines, the kid will be fine.  The outcome of my first decision showed that the child was disappointed and I could live with that.  What I couldn't live with, was seeing him devastated at the next outcome screen.  So, well done, game!  I felt bad and went about actually making decisions for the good of the family as a whole.
As I played, it actually took me back to a holiday where my own father had to take time to study through it, something I haven't thought about in years, and realised that the developer absolutely nailed the scenario.  I actually found myself sympathetic towards each member in the family.  I wasn't working towards some winning gamestate at the end, but toward a scenario that would make everything OK for them all.  I was drawn in completely.
I obviously had a deeply personal connection to the game, so would it stand up without that?  I don't see why not.  It is short enough that it can even make a nice talking point if you play with another person as well.
On the whole, it is easy to recommend this game - I won't deny that you need you need a degree of empathy and maturity to fully apreciate it, but that's no bad thing.

An absolute gem of a playable novel. You can tell that the creator has poured years of his love, frustration and inspiration into this work, and it pays off. The three voice actors are brilliant, and the scripts are so realistically well done. The emotional connection you inevitably - and suprisingly quickly - create with not only the main characters, but also tenants of the 'haunted' house from the long distant past, will leave you in tears or at least vocally voicing your joy or sorrow at each twist and turn of their fates that your ghostly character has helped to shape.
I've almost exclusively played this game in Story Mode so far, and I would recommend to do so for maximum replayability and exploration of the different storylines you can travel down. For a thrill and more of a 'game' feel, Stealth Mode requires your ghost self to hide among the light fixtures and investigate the Kaplan family's dilemmas without being seen.

It's quite more then a game, it's a immersive reflexive experience where you play as a 'something' (maybe a ghost) that analisis every events, thoughts and memories of each one of the three characters of a tradicional family and take the decisions for the father of the family. You can choose between take care more of your son's progress in school and life or incentivate your wife emotions, turning her hobby in a carreer or you can choose dedicate to your own book writting spending some selfish time for your personal growning. Every and each decision you whisper at the father of the family   affects the whole family during the progress of the game so then you have to be carefull in what sacrifice take in behalf of what character to accomplish the happiness of everybody.
The fact of the game presenting multiple endings (and so much) it's really impressive because it take in consideration every decision taken since the game starts and make me question: is there a bad ending or it just the way people find happiness that is different one of other?
The interesting thing you can notice is if you are not a father/mother and husband/wife you can have a notion of where you would be going if you were one and if you actually already are you will notice where you are going choosing your priorities or not instead or your family.
It's a deep, reflexive, philosophical, short, "non-replayable", conscientizing, real game that primary focus on our nowadays decisions as a family integrant.

I'm going to recommend Ziggurat, since ultimately I find it to be a decent game, but there's a few nitpicks that prevent me from showering the game with as much praise as others seem to.
First of all, once you beat the game, that's it. There's no super secret challenge or anything that would motivate you to sharpen your wand blasting skills. On the contrary, the game's design actively works against you beating the game as fast as possible, seeing that you will be severly underpowered by not exploring and that the game's ending is determined by the number of rooms you explore (the more rooms you explore, the better ending you get).
Secondly, the game feels clunky to play. It's hard for me to put my finger on what the issue is exactly, but aiming, movement, and shooting seem to be hard to control, resulting in my swerving my mouse around the target and not at it or not feeling the presence of my movement. You can manage around it, but this feeling has never quite went away.
Thirdly, fighting just doesn't have that oomph to it. I've unlocked a bunch of weapons even, but no matter what I used, I just didn't feel like I was killing all these monsters. I simply glowed them to death, and sometimes it took a while. Compounded with the clunky feel of playing, I found myself wishing all the monsters to just explode and spare me the trouble.
Finally, upgrades feel like a necessity, not a boon. You don't get cool new powerups that let you do more cool stuff. Instead, they prevent you from getting curbstomped to death by later bosses. Your weapons can become more powerful, that's true, but you'd have to count on a random prayer power-up instead of speccing into something specific as you traverse the Ziggurat. Even then, that power-up will often come with a catch.
After reading all this, you might think the game is awful and I shouldn't be recommending it. However, I can appreciate the game for what it is and enjoy the challenge it presents. It's just that there are many other well-rounded rougelikes that seem do everything better than Ziggurat that I can't help but give only a single thumbs-up instead of two.
Having said all of this, Ziggurat is a diamond in the rough and with proper polishing, the potential sequel could greatly surpass the original, since many of the building blocks have already been laid down.

In rouge-like fashion within randomly generated arenas.
When Ziggurat is rather simple in its principles there is far more complexity to it than it may seem at the first glance. You take up the mantle of aspiring sorcerer facing ultimate magic exam - the Ziggurat, a demon dimension which could deffinetly use more lore than game creators provided it with.
To complete the game you need to get the portal key and defeat the boss to progress to the next level. With either 5 or 6 level being the final depending on difficulty. Each level is generated randomly and each of its rooms has a chcance of spawning random set and number of enemies. Single run takes approximately under 1 hour although this may vary depending on your skill and how fast can you find the key and boss room.
Almost everything is random. Weapon you recieve at level beggining, shape of the rooms and level overall some room types may not appear at all. There are tougher enemies that can appear only on later levels but beside this everything is permitted. To spice things up rooms might also have modificators such as enemies being bigger, rooms spawning additional loot or everything getting pixelated. Some will aid you some will kill you.
There are numerous weapons avialable to aid you in your quest (30 with all unlocks). Only a few examples being shooting a lightning, calling a swarm of butterflies or throwing bombs around. Falling into 3 categories they all have alternative fire mode (usually being a burst of primary attacks). Weapons are balanced by mana expense which requires gems dropped by enemies to refill your reserves. When out of juice there is always the wand - basic weapon with renewing mana supply but also the weakest avialable.
Game is desinged with intention of multiplie replays and dying here is not necessarily a bad thing. Only completeing a full run or dying will provide player with unlockables for the progress they have made. There is plenty to unlock. Aside aformentioned weapons there are amulets, perks and character classes (16 total) providing quite a vareity to play with.
Classes are characters with avilable form the start perk sets. They have prefferences depending on what class that is but any character can be potentially shaped in any direction as you level up during your run. Some provide greater twist on the game than others.
Ziggurat is not the best game there is. But it is certainly very fun to play with fast-paced combat and vareity that makes it enjoyable to hone your skills with every next run.

It's not bad, though it could be much better.  It's easy to cheese the game by increasing your XP consumption to the point where you get a few levels every single room.  This increases the odds that you'll get the perk that hugely increases your max HP by cutting all your magic, the perk that gives you more perks by cutting your max HP, and the perk that doubles your wand damage by consuming a weapon.  Bonus if you can get the perk that lets you cut down on your mana usage while standing still.  You will pretty much kill everything in short time, any weapon besides the wand is absolutely useless.  Any character which focuses on the wand will probably win.  The final boss is an absolute joke if you get enough wand damage doublers.  Maybe this perk should only appear once in a playthrough.
What I'm saying here is that the game is entirely unbalanced, but that's pretty much expected from roguelites anymore; nobody plays Isaac because the shooting mechanics in that game are satisfying, they play because of the chance for a power trip.  Ziggurat follows in those footsteps: if you're expecting a challenge, you're in bad shape.  You're more of a gambler than anything else: can you get the right perks?  The start of the game can be challenging, but it's soon to devolve either into getting the right perks or having your run cut early.  There is a difficulty curve between the 5 floors you're fighting on, but assuming you get the right perks, it's pretty much negligible.
With that said, Isaac gives you a feeling of supreme power by upgrading your tears with strange benefits; some synergies are fantastic to see on-screen because they're so ridiculous.  Nothing like this exists in Ziggurat; no matter how strong or weak your weapons are, they will never seem any different.  The most difference you'll notice is firing speed which can get comically fast.  But there's no real feeling of being powerful, just a feeling of being OP.
There isn't much charcter variety.  Since it's first person that's a little expected; I think the wands are unique for each character but beyond that there's no telling who you are besides Male Voice or Female Voice, not a lot of effort was put into distinguishing each character from the next.  Mostly they're separated by the perks they get at the start of the game, which can make things a little different (particularly characters who have wand boosts or XP boosts) but aside from that it's pretty much the same thing every time.
The minions are especially boring.  You can pretty much circle around all of them and just keep shooting until they're dead.  Killing them is not very satisfying; they don't explode in blood or anything, the weapons don't make very satisfying sounds, the minions just disappear.  The level design is flat; there are no upper or lower areas in any given floor, it's all on the same level.  Rooms aren't very interesting; as far as I can tell the most variety you'll get outside of the standard minion rooms or portal-key rooms are god statues that may or may not help you, and special treasure rooms which feature some traps you'll need to get past before arriving at a treasure chest that might have things that are useful to you.  There is one secret room that you can find, and there the developers will show you some of their previous game projects.  I was annoyed by this because I wanted to play the game, but instead had to watch this mini cutscene about something I cared nothing about.  Also the secret rooms don't offer anything fantastic, it's rarely worth the time to find them.
The devs also like to advertise their other games in-game on the title screen.  Not a nice thing to do.  Maybe you should consider finishing the polish on this game rather than making more games.  Games are more than pretty graphics you know.
The bosses are very boring, much like the other minions.  Each boss is just a super-version of the regular minions.  Virtually no thought was put into them; one boss is a regular slime, but he's also wearing a crown, that way you know he's 'da b0ss'.  I'm sure the devs can be more creative than that but they chose not to be.  All bosses can be defeated in the same way every other enemy can be defeated: by circling around them and firing.  That's it.  Rarely, some enemies will be smart about how they're firing and will be able to hit you even while circling around them.  With enough damage-reduction perks (thanks to enough XP increase perks) you'll pretty much be invincible anyway so it's not like that matters.  The only boss that's remotely unique is the final boss, and he feels like a mini-boss; I think he might have some phases in his attack patterns but if he does there's no indication anything of the sort has occurred, his graphic remains constant.
I was also surprised with how short each run is; by the time I got to the final boss I was thinking there were still at least five more levels to get through before the real final boss, the boss that would actually be interesting to fight.  But no, it's 5 levels and you're out.  Hard mode is the same, except harder.  I have yet to try endless mode but I imagine the same problems will arise with getting too powerful to the point of triviality.  The reason why I loved Nuclear Throne was that it heavily relied on player skill; even the strongest weapons in that game consumed tons of ammo and usually had a high likelihood of killing you in the process.  It was the insane difficulty and heavy reliance on skill that made me love that game.  I can't say I feel the same way for Ziggurat knowing exactly how to cheese my way through it.
Also related to the boring room design is the lack of mobility options.  This game is very DOOM-like in the sense that you're usually going to be very near to the ground plane and firing on enemies from that level; you can jump around a lot if you want but it doesn't do much to avoid enemy projectiles, they tend to hit you anyway.  You cannot crouch whatsoever; maybe being able to duck under enemy projectiles would be a nice addition, and most games like this have such a functionality but no such thing exists in Ziggurat.  TF2 showed us how a first person game can be with the right tools at the player's disposal; rocket jumping is such an amazing experience once you get the hang of it and it can be used to throw yourself in all manner of places around the map.  You had double jumping, you had sticky jumping, you had options: Ziggurat seems to have skimped out on this as I've never seen any perks related to movement tech outside of increased sprint speed.  I usually don't sprint in combat because A. I don't need to I am OP, and B. I can't fire while sprinting anyway.  The most movement tech you'll use is turning away from an enemy that's a little too close and sprinting to get some distance.  What's the skill ceiling on turning around and sprinting?  It's very, very low; most you'll need to learn is when to sprint.  So much more could've been done with movement tech and yet it doesn't seem to have been on the dev's radar.  What a shame.
I don't think Ziggurat is a bad game--it seems to be free of bugs and it is also pretty good looking--I just don't think Ziggurat is a great game.  It's not a classic people will remember many years down the line.  It is a stepping stone for the devs to get on to the projects they actually wanted to make, a point on the road map.  I don't think they cared all that much about Ziggurat, or they were just too inexperienced to make anything better.  In any case I wouldn't spend 15 USD on this game.  Maybe 10 USD at most, 7.50 USD ideally.  I got my copy from a humble bundle so I pretty much got it along with some other games I wanted.  If the devs spent more time on making the gameplay more balanced and interesting, and less time on making it look decent, this game may have turned out better.

Well, I give this a thumbs up... but just barely. Have you played Diablo III? Torchlight II is the exact same freakin' game as Diablo III, with a little brighter color palette. That's about it. If you simply LOVED Diablo III and can't get enough of that kind of gameplay, then you'll most certainly love this game. They are ridiculously similar. For me, I didn't really love Diablo III, nor do I love this game. Way too much time spent in inventory management. "Is this equipment better than that one? Well, crap, I dunno, because they each have totally different effects. Better refer to the stat management system and see which stats are affected. [scroll, scroll, scroll....] But who knows if a stat change of 'x' amount is good or not? And which stats are more important, because the game system is not well defined to the user? Aw, screw it, I'll just go back to clicking around and hope for the best..."
And, to attack, you simply click on the enemy. That's it. You're just going around and clicking on things. Kinda lame. Oh, you can also click on some buttons on the keyboard occassionally to do bigger moves, but I find it awkward to look down at the keyboard in the heat of a massive battle to find the correct key to trigger the appropriate move. The quests are essentially, "Go there and click on everything." And that's about it. Kinda lame. The quest stories are a waste of time to read. I just don't care enough to read them anymore.

It's semi-enjoyable, in that you get to feel like you are cruising around, going places, doing things, when really you are just wasting time. But it's good enough for a mild thumbs up.

Always Sometimes Monsters...
If there's one constant in life: There's always sometimes monsters. It's engraved into our beings and soaked deeply into our souls; our primalistic desire to fight for love, and do anything to get it. ASM portrays this beautifully, and in many lights.
Down on your luck (and your money), you receive your final eviction notice. You're a broke author who never made it. How come?
Early on your hustle for money, you receive a wedding invitation...from your ex. What? But you haven't heard from them in a year, and now this?
So what do you do? You still love them, right? Of course! So now it's come down to this - 30 days to pick up the pieces of your life and get your♥♥♥♥♥back to them! But will you make it? Will you burn out on the way there? Will you die, lonely and destitute, as your life has become? Or will you make it, win your love back and maybe become the monster on the way?
What will you do for the chance at their heart again?
ASM is about forging your path back to the love of your life and more importantly, what you DID to get there. There are choices GALORE and many paths to follow. There's the distinct light / dark and all the in-betweens. Neat little minigames and collectibles and tons of engrossing dialogue. The music is also spot ON (big props to Laser Destroyer Team!) and definitely sets the mood for the scene at hand.
I count it as one of my absolute favorite games I've ever played, and not just because it was a great game, but because of the impact it made on me. It left me with chills and in tears and... complete fulfillment. Hell, even I as I type this, I'm shedding a few tears...
I simply can't recommend this game enough.

This game encaptures the complexity you'll find in most situations in life. This gives it a realism almost impossible to describe.

I am not a huge fan of DC (although I do have some degree of affection for the Batman franchise, however I think Catwoman's a better character than Batman). But this game? Fantastic.

The PC control scheme could be better (in all fairness my mouse may be inadequate) but that aside, the game is incredibly fun and enthralling. The plot wasn't outstanding (no shocking twists or anything) but I liked how the environments changed in response to plot events. Overall, this is one of the best games of the last generation (i.e. the 2005-2013 generation of consoles and games). Highly recommended.

I own 300+ games on Steam... own probably another couple hundred across Origin, GoG, UPlay, and elsewhere. Played everything under the sun and NEVER ONCE have I ever requested a refund on a game. Until now.
Everything about this game screams amateur and not at all ready for any kind of public access. I buy into so many Early Access games that I almost forget what EA is. This, isn't it. This is terrible.
Maps are extremely small (literally you walk out of the spawn "gate" and instantly being attacked. The maps themselves you can run across to the other side in LITERALLY 10 seconds. I kid you not, the maps are the size of my bathroom.
The animations are extremely clunky and poorly done. The player models are paper cutouts with almost no features to them and absolutely ZERO customizability.
The game has NO menu options for graphics other than "Low", "Medium", "High", and AA on/off. I wont even address motion blur because that should never be in any PC game period.
There are a whopping 6 servers, with 4 of them running the same dumb, midget sized map. Each server had a couple players on it with two nearly maxed.
Pings and latency were terrible.
Performance horrible.
Gameplay was not at all fun and I'm no beginner to twitch shooters and arena combat games.
No physics.
No BALLISTICS (you know, the name of the game).
Unpleasant on the eyes UI.
Honestly, if I were the devs of this I would be ashamed to have released it, let alone for MONEY. It should be free to play. I couldn't even recommend this game for a $1 sale. Not at the current state of the game.
I rarely downvote games and I can't even find something positive to say about this one. So, here goes my first refund... ever.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first title within Rocksteady's Arkham Trilogy (Arkham Origins not included). The title takes place in Arkham Asylum as mentioned in the title and sees The Batman taking on his arch enemy The Joker who has gained control of the Asylum.
Gameplay
- Explorable open environment set in the confines of Arkham Island.
- Simple yet intuitive combat system with additional abilities obtained through upgrades.
- "Detective Mode" ability used for solving puzzles and crime scenes within the game.
- Stealth sections within the game for quietly taking out your enemies with additional abilities also obtained through upgrades.
Visuals
- Great looking environments which helps to set the atmosphere of the game.
- Main and sub characters are highly detailed.
*Texture streaming can occur throughout the game although is rarely noticeable on a decent spec machine. Sadly a common issue present within titles built in Unreal Engine 3.
Sound
- Music and sound effects work well with the visuals and help to build up the atmosphere that is expected in the Batman universe.
- Amazing voice work including Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill who reprise their roles as Batman and the Joker from Batman: The Animated Series.
Extras
- Over 200 collectibles to be found within the story, some easier to find than others.
- Unlockable character profiles and trophies so players can learn the history of popular characters within the universe as well as view character models from the game in detail.
- Challenge maps to test the players skills in both combat and stealth.
- Additional costume for use in the challenge maps upon completion of the main story.
- 47 Steam achievments for the achievement hunters out there.
- Game of the Year edition includes four extra challenge maps to further test players skill.
Batman: Arkham Asylum is an amazing title that any Batman or even action game fans should own. Rocksteady have managed to capture the atmosphere and detail that is expected from the Batman universe and you can see the amount of detail that the team have created to give fans the Batman title they have been waiting for.
Final Score - 9/10.

The reason I marked this game as not recomended is because Steam's store page incorrectly marks this game as having full controller support.  Full controller support as described by Steam means that a game can be played from install to finish completely with a controller with out every touching a keyboard or mouse.
Batman: Arkham Asylum has a launcher that it starts every time that requires the use of a mouse to click through to start the game.  This can not be by passed from with in steam, with out altering files or making new short cuts.  On my system, the game also leaves the mouse curser on screen until you move it.
In short, this games store page in inaccruate and this title is not suited for Big Picture Mode if you use a standard wireless controller unless you make your own short cut to the game's exe or rename the game exe to the name of the launcher.
I personally don't have an opinion about the game it self that warrents a review, but Steam doesn't offer any other way to voice this issue.  I have opened a ticket with Steam support about the store listing being inacurate, but they didn't seem to be interested in correcting it.

Nerdook games aren't for everyone. And I am one of those people who finds them annoying.
Back in the day when I didn't have many games on my Steam account there was this wonderful place called the internet to search for old games, Java games or Flash games which were pretty much free and easy to pick up. When I still played Flash games I played quite some of these games made by Nerdook and they were somewhat fun to play. A lot of stuff to play for a low price of website ads.
Unfortunately the charm didn't really last after seeing the massive collection of great indie and AAA titles on Steam and finally being able to buy them. Vertical Drop Heroes HD is pretty much the same game as the Flash version with just small changes but overall features the same gameplay.
The game is roguelike 2D-verticalscrolling-"platforming"-game where your goal is to upgrade your stats, gain levels, defeat bosses and finally be powerful enough to complete the game. It certainly sounds like a neat idea and the game plays quite nicely but after a while some people will notice the reason why I can't recommend this game and some will just enjoy it hour after hour.
The keyword here is time. Overall, the game is quite easy, Money grinding is time consuming and doesn't really reward you enough to keep doing it so you'll just use all your cash on level skips instead. You either play it the long way getting all the upgrades for your run and maybe reaching the final level in a couple of hours or you take it slow and get bored with the game.
Even though the levels are randomly generated there is not much difference between the levels on each run. Same enemies and block on every certain level and the only things that do change are the bonuses and mini-quests on levels. These award you bonuses for your current run only.
This game certainly works for those who don't really like games with deep story plots or multiplayer games but still want something to play on your coffee breaks this is just the game for you. But even then this game lacks power of you wanting to complete the game for other reasons than getting the Achievements.
Might be worth picking up on Sale. But be very careful since this game maybe won't be the game you desired.

I've been playing this game for over two years. It is a settlement sim, where you create a settlement, design the layout, dig it out or build it up as you prefer, and try not to starve or get slaughtered.
Heavily reminiscent of Dwarf Fortress, but far more accessible, you don't actually control any of your gnomes. Instead, you give them jobs (which you can customize), and put orders on the map for gnomes with the appropriate jobs to do. The ability to define the jobs, combat roles, and priorities gives you a lot of control over the behavior and efficiency of your gnomes.
Like many similar games it is a balance between expanding your economy and taking care of your defenses. Gnomes that are learning to swing a sword better are not helping you shear sheep, harvest fruit, or brew wine... and if you don't have enough food and drink for you and your livestock to make it through the winter then starting over is pretty likely.
The game recently (~8 months ago) added modding support, and already several interesting additions to the game (like Glassworks) have been added. Now that the game is public, more are likely to come.
Some downsides:
I bought the game for $9, three and a half years ago, it's gotten vastly better since then. I'd happily pay $15 now, as the game is far more than twice as good as what I originally purchased.

When the legendary comic book hero Batman brings Joker back to Arkham Asylum for the 100th time, Joker promptly escapes and takes over the asylum. This is a 3rd person beat-em up, Metroid-vania-ish adventure with a lot of diversity. You'll go through sewers, brick buildings, a clock tower, libraries, ruins, caves, an outdoor courtyard and even the madness of the Caped Crusader's Mind. Since there is backtracking, the game will introduce new elements and paths to the backtracking, so it doesn't seem like a backtrack. New tricks, traps, situations, plant infestations and enemies will stand in your way. You never have a sense of being lost, but there is a lot of ground (and height) to explore.
As you work your way all over Arkham Island, you'll be taunted by the Joker who is voiced by Luke Skywalker for those that remember the old Batman: The Animated Series. Kevin Conroy reprises his role from the series as Batman, and they're both excellent.
As Batman, you've got a lot of controls here, left stick to move, right stick to control the camera, attack button, counter button, stun attack button, duck / stealth button, detective mode button, quick batterang, quick hookshot, grappling hook to climb, quick tool change, aim button, tool attack button, and finally a universal button to not only run, but holding the same button will also jump when you come to the edge, glide and its just batman auto-pilot really. You can double tap the action button to dive roll out of the way, but the times to use it are few and far between. There are more controls than buttons on the X-Box controller.
You unlock several tools / weapons for Batman to use, such as batterangs, grappling hooks, explosive gel and so on. The tools for the most part can be used on the fly against enemies by double tapping the left (batterang) or right (grappler) trigger.  You can use explosive gel to set a trap for enemies or blow up walls. Its pretty nice, but its just too slow to set up, so for the most part, you'll just be punching bad guys, dive kicking from gargoyles and grapple hooking up to safety.
Its fun to attack spam enemies and wipe out a dozen enemies. However, enemies with guns will murder you quickly, which is good, because then you need to rely and stealth and tactics instead of button mashing. The enemies will telegraph their attacks, so you can counter them or attack them before they do. Knife wielders will need to be stunned. The system feels good, but again its sometimes just mash 1 button as if Batman were dancing between a dozen partners. The final enemy in a group always has a slow motion knock out where you'll get to see ragdoll glitches and poor hit detection. Is it a game breaker no. Does it happen a lot? Yes and when it happens with every battle, it shouldn't have been accentuated.
While there is little enemy diversity, the big appeal comes from the game's characters and situations. You'll fight against some of Batman's biggest villains that are in Arkham. The situations, you'll have to use Batman's tools and some parts the game will spoon feed you what you need to do and other parts, you're free to figure it out on your own. The map will show you where you need to go, but its up to you to get there. You'll have to go through air ducts, go high, go low and every so often go through a door like a normal person. There is a lot of traversal in this game, you're able to swoop down on enemies, glide from place to place, grappling hook up to ledges, hang from ledges, shimmy around ledges. Everything that's been done in Just Cause 2, but now its slower.
As mentioned before, there is a detective mode that basically a hints mode. It will highlight air vents to crawl through, you'll be able to see through walls to enemy skeletons. You will have to use detective mode to track trails of scents and fingerprints. Detective mode will help you to find all of the Riddler trophies, which are usually in high vents. They're not hidden very well and it doesn't feel like a real reward for exploration, more like poor padding for the game.
The real problem here is the canned animations, which normally I have no problem with, but in this game, I really felt the animations. Batman grapple hooking up to a gargoyle, batman pulling a vent off an air duct, batman kicking a vent out of an air duct, Batman pulling an object with the grappling hook, Batman crawling out of a pit. You'll feel it all and some of the animations, you'll need to rapidly press the action button.
On top of all of that, you're unlocking a lot of extras as you progress through the game. Challenge rooms, character art and so on. There is a lot of extra content here.
When you die, you're taken to an animated scene of the Joker or whatever boss you die on to hear a one liner, then sent back to the last checkpoint. That just wasn't needed and wastes time like a lot of the animation. If only there was a setting to turn it off.
With all of that being said, this is still a good, fun game that compels you to play through it. The characters are bright and vibrant. It is a good story, but would it be its flaws would be accentuated more if it were not a Batman game without its cast of characters.

This is the first game in the Batman Arkham series. I never cared for action games before this game, but Batman Arkham Asylum innovates with a new, original combat system that forms the very core of the Batman Arkham experience. Batman Arkham Asylum seamlessly blends action gameplay with a well designed stealth system (and reasonable, but not perfect AI) to deliver an extremely addictive gameplay experience. All in all, it takes about 6-10 hours to complete the main story, depending on how many side activities you complete. Also, this game has lots of post game things to do ranging from collecting and solving the Riddler's riddles to challenge modes featuring both combat and stealth challenges. If you are curious about the Batman Arkham series, then I strongly recommend playing this game first. The combat and stealth mechanics improve so much throughout the series (Arkham City and Arkham Origins) that it almost becomes difficult to replay this game. Hands down, this is one of my all time favorite games.

Fun game, but definitely not as good as 1-2 IMO.
The main issue is that you have all your skills availible from the start. There's no sense of building up to something awesome at the end of the skill tree and no encouragement from the game to mix up your strategy or try new skills. The skills themselves have some variety but each class doesn't have many of them. I had the same complaint about Diablo 3, but it's worse here. Leveling up just isn't very exciting because you already have all your skills.
The itemization is a lot worse than the first two, also. Since every class has their own set of items, there are a lot fewer unique items and sets for each one (maybe more overall, but you'll only ever get items unique to your class).
Also, there's more "traditonal" horror elements like ghouls/ghosts/vampires, which I find kind of boring, instead of the mad science from the first two, but that's a matter of taste.
All those complaints aside, it's still a lot of fun and action packed... just kind of repetitive.

The Novelist is one of the greastest game storytelling games out there. You won't find another diamond like this one.
Pros:
1) The story and theme are crafted to perfection. Everything makes logical sense. The characters are simple to understand and grasp. You're intrigued at every time whether it's by curiousity, suspense, hard choices, and/or personal reactions to the result. There are backstories that don't affect the main one which increase morals taught and entertainment. I personally joyed over the latter effect obviously. To avoid spoilers, I won't go further.
2) The graphics are great and there is no lag. Even though the game itself is more important than graphics, this can be a good plus.
3) The controls feel comfortable and reasonable.
4) Anyone who aided in making this creation seemed well credited especially advisors and programs.

Cons:
1) The stealth may feel repetitious if you're not interested into the story, but I must say it's a bit fun, and it makes sense when the video game is based more on story than sneaking; otherwise, it wouldn't have been as great. A harder challenge feels worse with a terrible reward.
2) It involved a lot of reading, but I definitely enjoyed myself when the pace was mixed with stealth.
Overall, I have no regrets. If you want to hear an excellent story while pacing the reading with sneaking, buy this game. In the case that you are purely looking for a stealth game challenge, then I would reconsider. I hope the dev continues making games as great as this one, and even if he didn't, at least he created The Novelist.

When it comes to video games about superheroes Batman: Arkham Asylum ranks very highly on the list providing a unique experience unlike any that came before it, quite possibly making it the best Batman game ever created.
In Arkham Asylum you play as the Batman who is bringing the Joker back to the asylum from his last escape, however things do not feel right and as sure as bat senses tingle the Joker escapes but this time to take control of the asylum with the help of Harley Quinn and various other supervillains in a widespread plan to cause chaos, and now that the inmates run the asylum it is up to Batman to stop them.
Plotwise this game works very well, the story has dark tones to it that you come to expect from Batman these days and introduces a bevy of supervillains that Batman must take down all while exploring the more psychological side of heroes and villains and by the end of it the story will leave you satisfied despite the twist and turns that had happened along the way.
The gameplay in Arkham Asylum is masterfully done, using many elements from an amazing combat system that lets you pull off flashy moves and counters with single button presses, a stealth system that is done much better then most stealth games seem to do, allowing you to feel as if you are the Batman, hunting these criminals from the shadows ready to pounce, and also has an odd Metroidvania aspect to it where Batman will get upgraded gear along the way that lets him into more places as you explore the island, and the Riddler has hidden things in the environment for you to find such as trophies and solving riddles by finding things hidden in the background.
With how well designed this game is there are a few things I could nitpick, such as how sometimes the platforming controls get a bit wonky having you fall off if you are not careful, or how the game can at times feel a bit too easy even on the hardest difficulty, but all of my nitpicks are vastly overshadowed, the game is a tight fifteen hours or so to beat with more time needed if you want to do everything such as find all the riddles and complete the combat and predator challenges that will truly put your skills in the systems this game has to the test.
Overall Arkham Asylum is an amazing game, the graphics are top notch and the PC version shows them off even better, with a music score very reminiscent of the Christopher Nolan films, if you have any interest at all in Batman, superheros, or character stealth-action games, this game is ranked highly by me and I recommend it to just about anyone.

What can I say about this game. I mean, everybody has heard about the best superhero video-game. So I'll be quick. You play as Batman in one of the most accurate comic book hero game/movie adaptation of all time in my opinion. If you want to learn about Batman, this is the game you should come to. The Joker has come up with a plan to once and for all get rid of his archenemy- You, by conducting a grand Arkham Asylum riot. It is up to you to stop him and bring back peace to Arkham. Graphics are nice, I had a few late texture loading, but was not so bad. Now the gameplay: The whole game can be divided into three parts:  Combat, you fight as Batman against large number of enemies, the fighting system, here dubbed "Freeflow Combat" is a, in my opinion, revolutionary concept in video-games. You have punch, stun (useful against inmates with knives), evade, and counter. Freeflow means that you must hold your combo and prevent it from dropping it. That means that after third punch, Batman delivers, gymnastically and visually, unbelievable attacks, thus stacking up his "combo meter" which helps him execute instant knockout brutal attacks. You prevent your combo meter from resetting, by countering attacks, evading, even using battarangs and batclaws in combat. Main goal is to keep moving, attack and counter, in a flow combat, get it? Second part is Predator, the stealth part of the game, where the inmates are armed with guns, and you have to take them out silently, by sneaking behind them for a silent knockout, or grappling up onto a gargoyle and perform a inverted takedown (you hang them upside down). And, finally, the Free Roam part. The island consists of four big parts, with two to three buildings (you can enter them after beating the game, too) with various secrets as side content. The interview tapes which tell you the stories of famous Asylum residents, Riddler Trophies, an attempt by The Riddler to outsmart you by hiding collectibles for you to find, hiding trophies and calling you in-game to challenge you with riddles. Almost forgot, you also have challenge missions, which are predator and combat challenges with a few rules you must fulfill if you want perfect score.
And two thumbs up for Mark Hamill and Kevin Conroy for reprising their voice roles from the "Batman The Animated Series" as Batman and Joker, respectively.

There was an animated TV series in the early '90s called Batman: The Animated Series. It had a rather unique visual style that was later on dubbed as "Dark Deco" and was praised for being able to represent Gotham City as it is in the Batman comic books: a dark, Gothic-like place. Visual design was done via paintings and not really CGI and it was truly remarkable; it had a film noir-esque approach, as well. Mark Hamill (the guy who played Luke Skywalker) was the voice-actor for Joker and he did a very good job - Joker's laughter gave viewers the creeps.
So, what Rocksteady did back in 2009 was that they took a bunch of actors working on this TV show almost two decades before and they brought them on board. All the main characters are voiced by the same people and the game's visual design is reminiscent of the cartoon. The music, the voice-acting, the sound effects, everything is top-notch in this game.
Gameplay-wise Arkham Asylum is stunning: Batman can run, jump, glide, crouch and easily can get atop buildings by using his special gadget called the grapple gun. To be honest, beside the Assassins Creed franchise this is the 2nd one where your character is as fluid as it can get and controlling Batman feels just cool. In addition to this, fighting Joker's thugs seems equally easy and smooth: you go around hitting bad guys and occasionally you are prompted to counter the attack of an enemy. If you do this your so-called flow is not interrupted and you can go ahead hitting more bad guys thereby reaching a higher score which is eventually transformed into experience points. After a while you can level-up and unlock further abilities or upgrades to your gadgets.
Gadgets! Oh yes! You have the Batarang and its various versions, you have an explosive gel which can be used to destroy weaker structures / walls and you have other cool stuff, as well. You need these gadgets to get into certain places to pick up the hundreds of collectibles found throughout the island. I like that throughout the story Batman gets stronger and better gradually which also means there are more difficult enemies you encounter (whose movements are more difficult to counter or you simply need to jump in order to avoid being hit).
Detective Vision: You turn this on and you see everything in blue with certain objects highlighted in orange (objects and enemies you can interact with). It's almost like the Eagle Vision in the Assassins Creed franchise. This is a must for the predator challenges. Predator challenges take place in greater rooms indoors and you are required to take down enemies silently. If they see you they'll use their machine guns and even Batman can be riddled with bullets! You always have vantage points in these places (e.g. gargoyle statues on top of the walls) that act as safe havens - you can hide in these places and carefully plan your next move. You can attack from below: you can hide in vents or under grates and suddenly jump out of these places taking down your foes.
Challenges: Further arcade challenges await you; you can play FreeFlow combats as well as Predator challenges and earn medals. I believe the GOTY Edition even adds some extra places to test your skills so the playtime with this game is around 40-50 hours at least!
Rocksteady has done an amazing job with the Batman franchise! It should also be noted that this game is the first in a trilogy Rocksteady has been working on. While they are working on the 3rd and final installment labelled Arkham Knight a company called Splash released a prequel episode called Arkham Origins. I am currently playing this one and fully satisfied with it.
All episodes are highly recommended and they are well worth their money even if not discounted.

An overall fun game that's good to pop into if you have a few spare minutes.If you've read any of the other reviews you'll know it's a roguelight based in four randomly generated levels featuring various emenies, traps, perks and so forth. Killing enemies earns you mana for your weapons and experience to level up and get cards to upgrade your character. Dying is something that you actually need to do, as doing so unlocks more cards that get added to the pool of potential upgrades your character could get when leveling up. Once you hit certain milestones (killing certain enemies, using certain weapons etc) you unlock more characters.
The evrer present issue that you face is the one word: random. The type and number of enemies is randomised, so the amount of experience you can get from a single level is subject to this. When you level up, you choose between two randomly selected cards. When you start a level, you get a randombly chosen weapon- and it could be of a type you already have (you can only hold one of each type of weapon at a time). Your ability to be able to take on the increasing number and strength of your enemies is affected by this randomness.
With that in mind, it's still a very fun game to play. The shooting mechanincs are well put together (though I'm not a fan of the way throwing bombs are handled) and it is good at maintaining difficulty throughout.

This game definitely took care of the first person roguelike itch i've had for quite some time now. Lots of perks and plenty of guns to choose from also. However, it still does have some glaring flaws.
1. To level up, you need to pick up experience orbs, which drop from destroyed enemies and objectives.  Flying enemy drops can fall on the inaccessible parts of the level more often than not and make an already difficult game even more frustrating especially considering the fact that leveling up is crucial to games like this.
2. My first 15-20 hours of the game were INCREDIBLY repetitive. The early perks are boring, all of them similar to "increase x mana pool", "increase y mana pool" , "increase z mana pool". The cooler perks like "consume weapon to increase subsequent weapon damage" and "lose 75% of max hp but gain fast health regen" only come MUCH, MUCH LATER.This was in contrast to  games like Binding Of Isaac and Our Darker Purpose were i felt the perks, including the early ones were very fun and interesting. My first 7 runs of this game had the Boss "King Blob" ! FIRST SEVEN RUNS IN A ROW !
3. All but 1 of the bosses summon mobs. All of them. This may not be a turn off to everyone but for me personally it is. I don't mind the occasional Necromancer Boss or the Classic  Plant boss that summons tentacles to fire at you. But having every boss summons smaller mobs is a cheap way to tone up the difficulty.
4. This game is very unfair imo. Random enemies have the ability to go invisible  and it is unclear which ones actually can. Also, enemies can attack WHILE invisible! Who thought this was a good idea?In a first person game,this cannot work because you do not have eyes behind your head; you can only look at a certain part of the level at a certain time.Can be done in top-down, but not in first person. It is very common to take damage from behind and find absolutely nothing when you turn around. On hard difficulty it is insane, as you take a lot more damage from this.
5. Some enemies attack you based on where you are going to move, rather than where you actually are. This is really cool, i especially like the small blue slime that always attacks you when it takes damage  based on where you are going to move, irrespective of its attack cooldown. However, A LOT of the enemy attacks home in on you and coupled with point 4 , further adds to the unfair aspect. It may not be the case, but you WILL feel that every enemy attack is homing in nature.
However, despite these flaws i still recommend  this game simply because i had a lot of fun playing and i think someone who appreciates permadeath, procedural generation and random level up perks will very much enjoy this game!

This is the game which made me hate AAA "modern" games.
Its modern gaming in a nutshell: Huge production levels, great voice acting, good graphics, interesting (for a game) story, a powerful IP, some attention to the detail... and a hollow, boring and repetitive combat system which is continuously rewarding the player for "playing", to "unlock" new powers which makes the game even easier.
The combat system is as simple as you can get: with only two buttons (and no combos) you can beat almost every single enemy. Later in game some special bad guys are introduced which forces you to learn one new movement, but still all the combos and combinations with the gadgets are wasted, unless you get bored and use them to make Batman perform cool animations .
There are some levels in which you have to go Metal Gear and sneak behind your enemies. Those are the best moments in game, as they force you to avoid direct confrontation and button mashing, but still its way too easy to call it a challenge: Even the nice A.I. of the NPC's falls short when Batman starts to hang each one of them from different gargoyles (By the way, someone explain to me who was the smartass who placed gargoyles in an INTERIOR).
There are some smart "riddles" placed by the riddler (This is, the classic and boring "find 100 units of the prop in the map" we've all already seen and got bored of), but, being a repetitive extra task to enlarge the game's life, they all end up being the same crap over and over again: Find the special prop, pick up statues, fin the "?" painted in a wall... "yeah, I will find all of them" said everyone and did no one.
And the gadgets, allowing as they allow entry to previously blocked areas (thus being able to create a "metroidvania" gameplay style) are wasted with linear maps, being used only to find the next item the Riddler placed for you.
The story is great, and the acting is fantastic (Did I mention Mark Hammil as the Joker?), and if you like Batman and want to "watch" a really cool "movie", this is your "game". If you are looking for a good beat 'em up, a metroidvania, or just a game that don't think you are an idiot, stay away from it. This is not a game, but an interactive movie.

Pros:
- Simplistic and fun
- Players have a good amount of health and most weapons do not instant kill allowing for good tactical fights that last a good amount of time without dragging out for too long
- Nice selection of rebalanced weapons
- Great use of the unity engine, the graphics are really pleasant and clean, teammates and enemies dont blend with the environment awkwardly (I'm looking at you, Dirty Bomb.)
- Tight controls
- Shotguns that are actually useful
- Game revolves around good gunplay as opposed to spamming grenades or other similar nonesense
- Health generally doesn't regenerate meaning sustaining players will have to resupply after a while as opposed to staying in combat camping forever (there is a perk for one class that provides an exception to this)
- Very reasonable price tag
- At a stage with a minimal amount of maps and some missing features the game is still satisfying
- Developers responded to connectivity issues and fixed them immediately
- Current smaller maps encourage weapon diversity, overwhelming amounts of snipers camping is not something that occurs due to well designed close quarters maps that generally deny this behaviour
Cons:
- Perk system derives from the enjoyable simplicity and adds a few things that feel unneccesary that unbalance the experience (snipers can get a cloaking perk, a certain class can regenerate hp)
- Snipers can hip fire at close range without penalty, essentially making them function as high powered long AND close range weapons
- Gui needs work, lots of missing sounds, respawning screen (big black bar with the words loading on it) looks tacky and unpleasant
- Running animation is just the walking animation sped up, can make fights up close with someone who is sprinting look and feel very awkward
- Currently hard to find games at certain times of the day (sometimes however you can see quite a few games up)
- Usually one or two high ping players in every server due to a lack of options or unintelligent players connecting from the moon not reading the server regions
While it isn't perfect, the price point is more than fair, pick it up if you can overlook a few of its flaws in favor of a generally solid fun simplistic shooter with an arcade feel, recommended if you have a friend to play it with.

Really fun addictive gameplay. It's like Rogue Legacy, but it's actually well-designed and optimized for having fun.
For one thing, you get to keep your coins through deaths. So even if you die, you still feel like you made progress towards your next upgrade. (Unlike Rogue Legacy where all coins are taken away each death and if you don't have enough for an upgrade, you just completely wasted 20-30 minutes.)
Another positive is that there's generally a lot fewer projectiles flying all over the screen so it doesn't feel cheap like other 2D games (again like Rogue Legacy).
The various power ups also are fun, well-designed, and distinctive to make every play through surprisingly strategic. Your choice of character really changes the way you attack the game. For example, you might choose a character that has a ranged weapon, or a character with +33% damage but -33% hp, or the ability to open chests without keys (but then you forego an offensive trait). There is an extremely deep strategy in this game and you always feel like you are progressing.
Last but not least, every level has a crystal that you can activate (by spending a lot of coins) which allows you to skip to that level on the next playthrough. Something that Rogue Legacy desperately needed. If you get sick of the early levels, you can simply just skip them with a few coins (the caveat being that your character won't be as high level as if you played through those levels).
Overall, this is a fantastic 2D platforming rogue-like with fast and light-hearted, but deeply strategic gameplay. By allowing you to keep your coins through death, you're always progressing. I finished the game in about 8 hours in single-player. I didn't get a chance to play split-screen but I imagine that would be even more fun.
Highly recommended!

Arkham Asylum, being the kickstarter for the on-going Batman series, began as a close quarters arcade style fighting game. Although the story-line drags on from each supervillain to the next, I found the core gameplay to be lackluster, enforcing the beat-em-up style at almost every level without much creativity added. Being an older game, you also have to expect that not all fighting/game mechanics are spot on accurate. That 20x combo you're about to pull off might be interrupted by a pillow sucker punch by one of Joker's goonies - not fun.
The extra gamemodes such as stealth and arena are nice but don't add much extra playability to the game anyways. You already do enough of that in-game, why make a dedicated game mode for even more repetitiveness? I'd give this game a 7/10 solely because its at such a low price point right now.

Here's 5 hours of my life that I'll never get back. I managed to put off buying this game and avoiding all spoilers for about 4 years now. After finishing the game, I kinda wish I had saved my $3.75 and watched a playthrough instead.
When it comes Ubisoft games, it's either a hit and miss for me. I Am Alive, unfortunately, falls under the "miss" category. For a game that brings such an interesting atmosphere and mechanics to the table, if fails to execute on them.
The PC port is also horrendous. Good luck having a smooth playthrough playing an any OS that's beyond Windows 7. Playing on Windows 10, I encountered several crashes upon reaching a checkpoint, some of which, caused me to start the entire level over.
The story does not quite make any sense to me. The main character is somewhere on the east coast to begin the game. After some sort of apocalypse, where humanity is nearly brought to the brink of extinction; think The Walking Dead, but instead of zombies, it's dust, earthquakes, and famine; he spends the better part of a year walking across the US to find his wife and daughter back at home on the west coast. The entire time, he has a camcorder that he uses to document his adventure. During several cutscenes, you can see someone watching the videos in what appears to be current time, so all of this takes place in the past. Upon arriving back in his hometown of Haventon, he finds the city in ruin, yet he still expects his family to be sitting at home waiting for him. After surprisingly finding that they're not there, he comes across a lost girl roaming the streets. Among all the thugs roaming the streets that will shoot you on sight, he takes it upon himself to help the little girl out. Long story short, the little girl has lost her mother, whom you have to rescue, from what I take is a newly established apocalypse brothel. So while you're busy doing fetch quests for other people, you seem to have forgotten about your mission of finding your own family. After about 4-5 hours, the game kinda ends anticlimactically. You get the girl and her mother to safety. It cuts back to the camcorder again and finally zooms out, where what seems to be your wife(?) is watching it while crying, all the while all your gear and whatnot is on a table behind her, which brings me to the assumption that the main character is dead. There is no secret/alternate ending that can be unlocked, as far as I know. Lost had a better ending that this.
I Am Alive was suppose to be a franchise that would stand alongside Far Cry and Assassin's Creed. But after it horrendoues development cycle of delays and being scrapped, we're left with this. Ubisoft managed to scrap the entire full retail version, but later decided to bring it back as what is basically an XBL Arcade game. After it's all said and done, I'd recommend saving your money by not purchasing this game. If you're still truly interested in it, then watch a playthrough on YouTube.

Note: this review is written for players of the previous two installments. If you are a new player to the franchise, I would NOT start here. Play the previous two and, if you enjoy them, you might want to risk the third game just to complete the story.
I like a lot of what they did with the mechanics and streamlining. No need to collect potions or split the stack and hand some to Katarina, you both have infinite potions on (I believe) the same cooldown from the previous games. The classes are more focused to particular playstyles, so you don't waste a skill points picking up a single rank of a skill you will never use just so you can get to the stuff you want. Several of the classes possess unusual gameplay mechanics (such as the Protector's block skill) that make them unique, rather than Class A just increasing a different set of numbers than Class B. Every class has every skill available from the get go rather than having to gain 20 levels and traverse a skill tree to make your build.
On the other hand, some of it feels really shoddy. Each class has a much clearer focus than in the previous games and they could have used that to make the skills deeper and more rewarding, but instead they just tacked on two more passive upgrades per skill and called it a day. Sending your officers out on missions becomes mostly luck-based later in the game, as the mission descriptions are not as clear and your soldier effectiveness is much harder to maintain; I tried to make logical choices, but my officers failed almost every mission from midgame onwards. Tricks were removed entirely, cutting out one of several major features meant to allow customization. The level caps are insultingly low (30 levels for Van Helsing, 10 reputation ranks, and 25 levels for Katarina) and easily reached before the end of a single playthrough on Normal.
The story is rushed. They hint at some interesting lore, but ultimately the delivery falls flat. It is cool to learn about Katarina's past, but it comes so quickly over the course of a single (short) act that there is no time to really explore it or allow much interplay between Van Helsing and Katarina. The ending, especially, is anti-climactic. The big bad goes out with a whimper instead of a bang.
It's not just the story that is hurried, either. Equipment upgrades are so frequent that the few unique/set items you find are unlikely to last more than a few minutes. This also means enchanting and essences, the other major customization features in the previous two games, are a hassle at best and detrimental at worst, encouraging you to waste money on rapidly obsoleted equipment. Your chimera still has slots for summoning candles in the UI, but there are no candles in the game, and even if there were, there are no Tricks so you have no way to summon him anyway. Katarina has all of her old skills, but with only 25 levels, she can't pick up the final two points of her final tier skills because she has to be 26 and 27 for the 7th and 8th points, respectively. The game doesn't feel polished at all.
I am apparently lucky and had a bug-free playthrough. The only thing that felt like a bug was when I encountered a few monsters (including the final boss) that had immunity to every damage type. I don't know if there is a trick to fighting them or not, but Katarina can damage them for whatever reason and I played a Protector, so I tanked them and let her take care of the heavy lifting.
Overall, this is a pretty big step down from the previous two installments. I loved the previous two games, but I can't recommend this one. If you really must finish the story, go ahead and buy it. I recommend tempering your enthusiasm, though, so hopefully you won't be as disappointed as I was.
