Mankind divided is a worthy followup in the Deus Ex series and like previous titles it features a very intriguing and captivating story that will have you always excited as to what will happen next. Personally I'm a huge fan of the Deus Ex games and like to play through and enjoy each one pretty fast and then basically put them on the shelf and wait for the next game. For me, completing Mankind divided without DLCs took around 50 hours. That was 50 hours of quality entertainment and I think it was totally worth buying the game.
The gameplay in Mankind Divided is fun and pretty smooth and offers some new features since previous titles, for example key inputs to sneak around corners and sprinting to a new 'hiding place' to stay undetected. At first glance I didn't quite like it, but changed my mind about it pretty quick after playing for a while, It's a nice addition to the stealth part of the game and can sometimes come in handy, I think I thought it would get clunky in combination with moving freely, but it wasn't that bad. Mankind Divided also introduces a new and well designed way of managing augmentations and their limits that also was incorporated nicely into the story, which I liked. There are a lot of sidequests and optional content in the game to be discovered in the open world and completed.
The Graphics and overall feel in the game was also very nice. If you like the story rich, futuristic, stealthy and truthseeking  experience that the deus ex series embodies you will probably love this game, with that said, I don't think it's required to have played the prequels at all to enjoy this game to the fullest, to be honest I had kind of forgot about the specifics of the ending of the previous game when I started playing this, I think it doesn't really matter all that much.
As always you will have the choice in what kind of approach you wanna take when it comes to dealing with your enemies, whether you wanna sneak past as many as possible, use non-lethal force or go all out lethal and kick some♥♥♥♥♥ I do think I read somewhere that enemies will adapt abit to the tactics you use as the game progresses.
I would recommend this game and any of the prequels except maybe the first one or two games as these are pretty old and with todays graphics they can't really compete I think, but of course, graphics isn't important to everyone I guess.

As a fan of the first two games in this series, I am disappointed. You can't import your character as expected because of the entirely reworked skill tree and class system. The skill trees have been significantly dumbed down, many abilities are gone, auras are pointless, and each class now only has one combat style with no more switching between ranged and melee combat. Level cap reduced down to 30, Katarina's is 25. No starting on veteran mode with an imported character.
The game has its fair share of bugs too. The controller profile does not allow you to access all parts of the character creation panel, nor can it access the bonuses in the skill tree when leveling up. I've also encountered a game-breaking bug preventing progress in Valley of Frost due to my character constantly falling through the floor.
Bugs aside, this could be a decent ARPG title for ~$12, but it's not a very good Van Helsing sequel.
edit: Latest patch has addressed the falling through the map glitch. I'm not sure if the controller scheme issues have been fixed since I progressed through the game with mouse and keyboard instead. The game is less than 10 hours long. Glory points seem to be broken, so there is literally no point to importing a character at all, since those were the only things that would carry over. Multiple achievements are still broken, like reaching level 30 with a certain class, hitting an enemy over 1K damage, being hit for 1K damage, etc. There is a tower defense quest that still cannot be turned in. Even if Neocore fixes all these bugs, it still remains a really poor finale to what was once a great series.

If this had been an adventure game it would have been a lot better. As it is, the JRPG format makes the game quite tedious.
The biggest problems are the mini-games and the lack of quest markers.
The mini games just break the pacing of the story line. One example is a storyline where you have to hack the electoral system to rig an election. To me, the important thing is whether you decide to rig the election, and which candidate to favour; rather than interrupting it with Frogger-TRON.
The lack of clear quest markers is a problem because this is a top-down RPG. Think of an old style adventure game where you would scan the screen with your mouse cursor to find the interactive elements. Here, you have to walk your character around the area and try interacting with all the surfaces to find the one that triggers the next phase of the "quest". One example is when you're told to start boxing. You would think you'd go to the boxing ring, nope. How about those two guys training with the hook and jab pads, nope. The guy training at the punch bag, nope. Turns out you have to go to the guy lifting weights in the corner to start boxing. I'm not asking to be led by the nose to the next quest trigger, but some of the trigger points are counter-intuitive and/or downright obtuse. The game is about making decisions, and this element of find-the-thing/trigger just breaks the pacing of the story.
I didn't finish the game, I found the problems I've noted outweighed my curiosity at how the story would play out. The story is good, and in most places quite mature. I would like to see more from these developers, but not in the JRPG format.

For those who are looking for a shortish (~8 h) story-driven game that features a dynamic plot, Always Sometimes Monsters will be a satisfying experience.  There are dozens of permutations based on character choices that will affect not only the ending but also the plotline, which gives repeat playthroughs a purpose.  It also has a diverse cast that includes a variety of genders and sexualities.
There are a few factors that detract from the experience, however.  The game's RPGMaker appearance may bother some, though it features original sprites throughout.  The mechanics of the minigames are tedious at best and frustrating at worst.  As opposed to Cart Life, which has rote tasks that are easily and quickly done but performed ad naseum, ASM's work simulations eat up a lot of time for little payoff.  (That might be the point, but it is difficult to wade through, regardless.)  Perhaps my biggest complaint is that the content per city is uneven.  The first city has a plethora of storylines and activities, but the following cities are minimal in comparison, usually featuring the main plot and a couple of side quests.
Ultimately, the value of the game will depend on the player's ability to invest in the protagonist and the central conceit.  If you can get past the grinding for cash and the clunky minigames, there's a worthwhile story being told here...with a generous dash of fourth-wall-breaking meta-awareness, which might either be another selling point or cloying element to ignore.

Action Henk is an indie racing game with some platforming elements, Sonic the Hedgehog comes to mind. In fact, if you buy the game on early release, you will get a custom sonic costume. But we are digressing, Action Henk is an incredibly fun, fast paced racer which is, so far, everything its said to be.  More here:

"READY.................GO" and that is the saying that will be going through your head all the time as you try to best that last time on the course that is completely doing you head in (but in the best and most entertaining way).
The developer's "RAGE-SQUID" have a winner on there hand's here and even though it is in early access the game is so polished that you would be forgiven for thinking that this was an actual full blown release instead of what it is,an amazingly polished early access game (i know that early access gets a bad press but this is one game that should change a few opinions on that).
Action Henk - Early Access Launch Trailer - YouTube
The graphic's really suit this style of game and the 2 character's that are available at the moment "HENK" and "BETSY" are both well animated and you really do feel like you are playing as an action toy running round an obstacle course in some child's bedroom.
The sound's and music in game are great and even though the main tune play's a lot whilst your racing it never does what a lot of repetitive tune's do,"GET ON YOUR BLOODY NERVES" and actually you will find yourself humming along to the music as you try to best your (or a friends) time for that course.
The gameplay is very simplistic and this works in the game's favour,as making this game complicated would have taken away from all the fun you get from racing round at break neck speed's trying to better your time or get that elusive "GOLD MEDAL" (i have nearly got all the GOLD'S i can get and only 1 eludes me and trust me "OH HELL,MUMMY" that track is so hard as to be near impossible-until you work it out).
You do earn extra outfit's as you play and unlock them (and this can be done by beating other racer's or completing certain other objectives).
(OH and "HENK" does a great impersanation of a certain "MR HOFF" in one of these) but they give your character no benefit's whilst in game (other than to make you look COOL-or SAD depending on your perspective),but this may change as the game near's full release and update's are put out.
If this game carries on in the way it has so far this will be one of the best casual game's to keep your eye on and with further update's come's more character's,outfit's,track's and just all around "GAMING GOODNESS"

This is a story of a father, husband and author struggling to balance work with family life. You are a "ghost" and placed into a family house, where you must observe them to find out there problems. What makes it unique is the ability to choose your own story. As the story developed and I got to know the family, I started to find myself genuinely struggling with what decision to make for them. A sort of "slice of life" simulator, where you play a nosy ghost with the ability to bend people to your will. Sort of.
Actually, it's like The Walking Dead, except your choices have actual impact. No, but really. It's also like Dear Esther or Gone Home, but with a little bit more actual gameplay (I highly recommend the "Stealth" difficulty level), and your decisions throughout impact the entire story and the Kaplans' relationships as well as the ending. You have to balance the father's career as a writer (side note: as a writer myself, Dan hit a little too close to home), the mother's stalled career as a painter, and their son's emotional turmoil--or you can fail miserably. Doom everyone to a life of misery, focus on one family member at the expense of the others, or flail around looking for a happy medium; the choice is yours.
I'd definitely recommend picking this up on sale--$15USD is unfortunately steep for such a short game--and then setting aside an uninterrupted 2-3 hours with a cup of tea or something to play it all the way through. It's well worth your time.

I have only run this game on steam so that it would let me comment. I've accumulated a few tens of hours on it on the whatever it was platform that it used to be on. Ubisoftisomethingorother. Anyway, here's what you need to know about this game:
It CAN be a fun time waster. Run around with your army, pit them against things, cast some spells and make the people fall down and all that. The combat mechanics are unabashedly lifted from previous might and magic heroes games and I don't have a problem with that. That makes sense. That works more or less fine.
It's pretty much everything else that becomes or creates problems. Problems that they would prefer you throw real world money at to resolve. There are some very long wait timers for reinforcements in this game. On the order of days to replenish a completely decimated section of troops. Advanced troop options also cost special resources per troop, which you can only obtain a trickle of without shelling out the cash. To pervert a famous saying: all roads lead to your wallet.
Now, I didn't just give up on the game immediately when I saw these problems, I went ahead and did what I could to get as far as I could stomach into the game. Which was near level 20. 17 I think? It's been a while since I gave up on this game. But if you want to maximize what you can do in it without shelling out the money, I would suggest playing a cleric. Get healing as soon as possible. Abuse healing. Healing spells in this game will resurrect dead troops. This is how I wound up with a sizable stockpile of basic troops, as I eventually reached a critical mass in my healing capabilities to keep from losing significant numbers of troops each day that I played. But this strategy does not work forever. As mentioned earlier, advanced troops cost special resources, and the only way to get those without handing over real world money is to do little daily quests that give you just a handful of, say, crystal each day. I'm not sure what the total amount might be at the end game, but where I was it was about 6 of this crystal attached to an annoying daily quest. 6 per day is not enough. Even with resurrections and very careful healing, you're going to lose more than 6 troops of any given kind in any given day. Further, at that slow rate, it's going to take you weeks to accumulate an entire troop of any given advanced soldier. I had a unit stack maximum of something like 120 or 135 or so. Trying to fill that on 6 per day seems like too much a fool's errand, too much an investment of time and efforts, to bother with for what payoff the game provides.
The chat is not particularly good either, and it seemed very cumbersome to try and group up with any strangers as you might do in any other multiplayer game out there. So cumbersome, in fact, that I don't think I was ever actually in any combats with a player run team mate.
If you want to play it, go in expecting it to try and get at your wallet and steel yourself against the obvious tactics employed to do so. It can be fun for fooling around in, but I wouldn't make the mistake of taking the game seriously or investing in it.
Edit: To be perfectly clear- when I meant that it Can be a fun time waster, I meant for a few hours or so at best each day. And only if you already like the combat style of previous heroes of might and magic games. I've noticed in other reviews that people mention the awful build timers, and I will confirm that those take in the area of day(s) to resolve and they only get longer as you progress. Furthermore, they require basic resources like wood and gold. This wouldn't be much of a problem, but the only passive means of gaining either is a very drop in the bucket trickle. Which necessitates grinding for both, through combat, to build the buildings that you need to get the troop reinforcements that you need to do the combat that you need to get the resources that you need to build the buildings that you need to....you get the idea. At low level I could see it being a very vicious cycle if you didn't immediately pick up healing and abuse the hell out of it constantly.

I have so much I want to write about this game. I'll start with 'I love it', anyway, let's get that out of the way first.
I am Alive had a long and problematic development cycle. At one stage, Ubisoft had intended to start a franchise with this game. I can see how it could have been as successful as Assassin's Creed or Far Cry. There are similarities to The Last of Us which of course became a huge success for, developer, Naughty Dog.
The reality though, is that in the end the game was released, in a stripped down and relatively short state. It can be completed in around five hours but it does have a lot of replay value. There are achievements, which for some reason are not registered on Steam but can be found on the game's Main Menu screen.
This game is a lot of fun, the combat sytem is unique, the climbing sequences are amazing and the game world is genuinely interesting. While I am playing, I can really see the potential I am Alive had to be just as successful as any other Ubisoft game. There are gameplay elements that were innovative at the time of it's release. I'd bet money that some major game developers have been influenced by this game. I think the combat system, though, is unique even to this day and it's really cool.
However, I am Alive's tone is maybe a bit too miserable for most people, including myself. So what I did was, I turned off the depressing in game music and added a SweetFX profile for more colour. Technically, the game ran great for me on a GTX 980, running Windows 10, at a solid 60FPS. There are some low resolution textures and some dodgey lighting affects but the game looks great for the most part. The game world is dynamic and believable from the top of ruined sky scrapers, to down on the streets, below the killer dust.
I am Alive is now one of my favourite games and in a way I'm glad the game ended up as it is, It's a hidden little gem, that most people over look, which just makes me love it even more.  I highly recommend that you give it a try!!

Mankind Divided brings amazing graphics, gameplay, and aesthetics to a story that really just doesn't do the franchise any justice. New mechanics such as crafting prove to be very convenient throughout the game as well as making weapon customization much easier than in Human Revolution. The new augmentations are fun to play with and give the palette of augs carried over from Human Revolution a nice layer of new paint. Ammo types and special weapons are great for trying out different combat tactics in numerous situations present in the game especially when combining them with certain augs.
The story, sadly, is decent at best and dissapointing when compared to that of Human Revolution. Not to mention that it is quite short too.
Adam Jensen, a former SWAT officer is hired by renowned Biotech giant Sarif Industries to look after the company's security and safety of its workers. Its laboratories are attacked viciously by a group of augmented mercenaries who took Sarif's leading scientists and outright killed many other workers right on the day before their lead scientist and researcher, Megan Reed, was to reveal a groundbreaking discovery in the field of human augmentation. Said mercs also left Adam gravely wounded to the point where augumentation was his only salvation. He is augmented beyond what the normal human being would even allow themselves and even heals faster than the normal augmented human. His quest to find those mercenaries who changed his life and who took the leading scientists and researchers unfolds throughout the course of the game.
Adam is called into a mission in Dubai by Taskforce 29 to stop a smuggler from selling weapons to terrorists. The mission is foiled by an unknown group of assailants who are barely ever mentioned throughout the rest of the game. Adam arrives at a train station in Prague which is bombed shortly by an augmented terrorist. Taskforce 29 spends ♥♥♥♥all time investigating the bombings while Jensen is out there trying to figure out whos behind all the current terror attacks carried out by or against the augmented. Talos Rucker ♥♥♥♥ing dies right in front of Jensen for inexplicable reasons and then forces Jensen to spend the rest of the game finding out who killed and how did they kill Talos Rucker. Oh and terror attacks get even ♥♥♥♥ing worse and theres a huge Aug uprising in the making during all of this.
Yeah, the story is what really drags this game down.
Also, DLC was released shortly after the release of the main game so whether or not Square Enix and Eidos deliberately cut the games story short and released the actual good parts and the rest of the story as DLC hoping for quick profits is up to you.
Also did I mention this singleplayer game has microtransactions that you can only use once per playthrough? It's a minor thing really given that aquiring Praxis and money in the game wasnt made deliberately hard to promote buying from the shop but holy ♥♥♥♥ thats really pathetic from the devs.

Torchlight II is an Action RPG game that does so many things right.
Before I start, if you have played games like Diablo or Path of Exile, Torchlight II is similar to those kinds of games. If you are a fan of those, Torchlight II is a must.
Torchlight II basically casts you as the main character that must save the world from the evil alchemist and some other stuff. I actually didn't watch a single cutscene in the whole game because the gameplay was much more fun an interesting than the story. For the actual gameplay, you can choose between a couple of classes. My favorite (and the one I beat the game with) was embermage, in which I skilled eveyr single skillpoint possible into Focus. On that part, there are also 4 attribute lines you can skill as you level up (each level gives you 5 distributable skillpoints in that. Additionally, every time you level up or your fame increases (done through completing quests and killing bosses/higher tier enemies which are purple or orange barred), you can distrubute a point into your skill line for you abilities. There are a good mix of active and passive abilities for every single character. Additionally, you can dual weild or weild a two handed weapon, or even sword and shield weild. There is actually so many different ways to play the game it is ridiculous. The maps and dungeons are generally randomly generated, and the environment and enemies are all rather well crafted. Even with some random genration, there are levels with secrets also generated into them. Torchlight II is just a incredibly smooth and well designed game.
A unique thing about Torchlight II is that you are allowed a pet, which fights with you. But that isn't the coolest thing. You can actually send your pet to town to sell your items and buy stuff (e.g. potions) that you want. This feature really helped my inventory management so much, as everytime it would get close to full, I'd just dump the worthless items on my pet and send it to town to sell the items.
I just said a bunch of stuff that sounds nice for single player, but Torchlight II is most fun with friends in its coop mode. Gnomoria is a simplified dwarf fortress. For those of you who are avid fans of dwarf fortress, don't mind the ascii graphics and the keyboard hotkey menu shortcut controls, you'll probably dislike this game as simplistic. For those of you who wanted to get into dwarf fortress but didn't want to have to learn to read live matrix code and like the invention of the mouse, this game is for you.
Gnomoria puts you in charge of a small group of gnomes as you have to build them into a thriving settlement. The game difficulty can be manually set at anything from "I'm never attacked and all my resources are easily accessible" to "I hate my life, and want to discover what life would have been like in the stoneage with zombies and invading ogres."
Its system also now supports some decent modding capabilities. While it does not support an api for adding new game mechanics, large swaths of content are available for your complete control. To give an example, I recently started on a mod to redesign the entire game as a moon base simulator with either no enemies or possibly competing companies (I haven't decided which yet), and the hardest part is simply the graphics since I suck at pixelart.
However, what I have enjoyed most about this game is that I can totally play it while doing other things. As a recent college grad, I was doing a lot of note taking, and classwork. During boring parts of lectures where we reviewed things I already knew, I would set up the instructions for my gnomes and then let it run without me when something came up to work on. It would run without me just fine, and had been set up to pause whenever anything came up that really needed my immediate attention. This isn't to say that, when playing the game there's nothing to do. But the fact that I was able to get hours and hours in during class and homework made it even more fun for me because I could actually play it during busy weeks.
Some people are complaining now that the maker has declared he will be finishing it soon without completing all he said he wanted to. But pretty much everything he said he'd like to do, he has made totally available to people to mod. While this may sound like a cop out, I frankly would love to see what else the community can do with it, since the entire development team consists of one man.
I've been part of enough early access games thought to declare (in my opinion of course), that this is among the greats. While I will admit some of the features of the game are definitely not particularly strong (eg: the diplomacy system consists of inviting an ambassador and making sure he has a nice room to stay in), the base game is actually very solid and very fun. The game has felt complete to me since I bought it, everything else that's been added since then has been icing on the cake. And the addition of a decent content modding system promises lots of new content (especially when the current indev branch is released since a lot of mods-in-work are waiting on it).
The game is totally worth its current price tag of $8. I would personally buy it again for $15 myself. And while I'm normally very against people "finishing" development on a game just so they can start charging for expansion packs, I would totally be up for purchasing some dlc or expansion packs for this if he ever did that. Gnomoria is the bar by which all other village sims have been measured by me, and none have come close.

Edge is easy to learn and understand but has a good deal of complexity and attention to detail. It looks clean and sharp. One relatively minor physics detail caught my eye: when your cube is immediately between two walls, you can't climb those walls, since a cube can't roll away when it's in a cubic hole. Makes sense, and a lesser developer might have overlooked that.
The 8-bit soundtrack is fun. It's just like the rest of the game: simple on the surface but surprisingly deep and complex. It's catchy -- I caught some friends humming or whistling along as I played.
The puzzles do a good job of keeping you guessing. Just when you've got it figured out, there's a neat little twist and you have to reevaluate. Some of the puzzle themes are also pretty neat — there's a subway-themed level and a robot one. Plus, the three different categories of levels have distinct feels to them. The normal levels are basically a race to the finish where you try to die as little as possible. The extra levels provide more intellectual puzzles rather than speed or reaction based ones, with many levels featuring a face-off against the sinister dark cube.
There's a good degree of replayability for completionists: cubes collected, deaths, and speed all factor into your rating for a track, so to get the elusive S+ rating,  you'll really need to work to figure out the optimal path and timings.

Not for: People demanding polish, fov sliders, surround sound effects.

Rogue Legacy
You choose one of three heroes with different traits and abilities or reroll. With your hero you will collect gold and keys. The gold is used to buy new traits and abilities. Gold can also be used to buy starting higher starting health and damage. You will descend down each level killing enemies or not killing them and collecting passive orbs. You will find keys in each level as well. These keys unlock chests or cages to free other heroes. The heroes will attack enemies, but some do other things as well. The wizard will periodically protect you with a shield. The rogue will drop gold and if he lives long enough he will drop a gem. The black flags will turn red and summon enemies if you trigger them. Shrines also exist in the level offering the ability to replenish abilities or allow you to stealth past a section. You can also pay shrines to provide a lightining, fire, or ice attack. There is also an option to upgrade the passive orbs you can gather with gold. Keep a look out for areas that have two key locks on top that lead to a green crystal. Activating it will allow you to pay a small amount of gold to skip to that level instead of starting at level 1. Each level ends with a boss which must be killed to unlock the portal to the next level. Alternatively you can use 5 keys and skip the boss.
It's a very addicting just one more run kind of game. The cartoon graphics are fun. It's a huge leap forward from the old flash game it started as. The variety of differnt moves and passives are fun. The controls are pretty tight and don't really feel floaty like other small titles end up. It's not as difficult as Rogue Legacy so it's less likely to frustrate new comers to the genre.
The enemy AI is very stupid. I mean honestly you can beat the final boss by making him step on spikes over and over. Not all abilitis are created equal. For the most part I beat the game with confusion alone. It's very short. To be honest when I found out level 10 was the end boss I was shocked. I mean the levels aren't very long. It's probably possible to finish the game in two hours or less for someone who's already amazing at Rogue Legacy. I guess it doesn't over stay it's welcome that way, but honestly it was off putting to know I had reached the end so quickly. There is still new game plus mode granted, but still. The story... well basically it doesn't have one.
It's a good game if your just looking for a few hours of fun especially if you liked Rogue Legacy. It's easy to ignore the bad AI, short length, and no real story just because it's still fun at the end of the day.
I probably wouldn't fork over more then $3. It's just not nearly as flushed out as Rogue Legacy, but it's still a good time.

Ziggurat is a FPS game that is thankfully more rogue-lite than roguelike. The game can be completed in as little as 30-60 minutes, but it can take a few tries to beat on normal difficulty. You unlock new modes, characters, perks and other things as you re-play the game.
Pros:
- Great intro song with some epic battle music and atmospheric background music. As I'm writing this review, you can grab the OST from
- Nice variety of enemies, room types, weapons and difficulty levels to take on.
- The movement is fluid and responsive enough (though I feel like you should be able to strafe while running for even better control).
- Fun Doom-like gameplay with big rooms and a lot of space to move in.
- There is a pretty good sense of progression and the graphics are nicely stylized.
- You can save between floors by choosing to Save & Exit after entering a portal.
Cons:
- Leaderboards for Easy, Normal and Hard runs are apparently mixed together with Endless mode scores, meaning that it's useless to aim for a high score in the main mode.
- (Mainly for speedruns) The RNG to find portal key and summon a boss for each floor can be very troublesome and put you through 15+ fights with big rooms that have an objective before being able to kill the monsters. You have to be extra careful to not take any damage (while also going for the objective) and this can be hard when mobs are spawning from all directions and you don't have the right weapons to get rid of them.
- As you unlock more perks by playing through the game multiple times, you also unlock ones that are typically not very useful. This is when the RNG starts to show in runs with higher difficulty. Many times, you'll be disappointed with the perk choices and random weapons that you get when fighting the end boss. Either your DPS and mana is too low or it takes too long to get there for the 45 minute challenge.
It's not that fun to fight with Lady Audrey and the Examiner when you have low mana and low DPS because of only being able to choose between two perks for weapons that you don't even find or use (example: half of your perks are staff related when there aren't any better perks at the time of choosing, but you don't find a staff anywhere).
- Some enemies are hard to notice when they are far away and some enemies have attacks that are too quick to evade. This the reason why "getting to floor 2 without getting hit" is the second rarest achievement.
- Difficulty of aiming at imps and some other enemies while fighting a big battle and focusing on evading shots from enemies such as slimes.
- Jumping isn't smooth in rooms with platforms
- 100%ing the game can feel repetitive at the end. You might beat the game on Hard difficulty with 3 classes before dying 50 times or unlocking everything.

Well, I finally played Arkham Asylum, and I'll be damned if that isn't the great video game adaptation of the Batman cartoon from the 90s. We have the most important VAs (Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamil as The Joker), we have a gloomy to creepy atmosphere, and we have a goofy but well-written plot that is dark only for specific values of dark.
And that's where it lost me.
See, I really like Arkham Asylum: A Serious House On Serious Earth. It's a solid graphic novel with gorgeous, disturbing art and a really interesting set of villains. I love Joker's motivation, to prove to Batman that he is just as crazy as his adversaries and belongs in Arkham right beside them. I love the concept of an Arkham doctor as a malefactor who turns Two-Face into a useless wreck. The game has hints of parts of fragments of the ideas which make the graphic novel so awesome.
But it's not fair to judge the game as an adaptation of the graphic novel it's named for, no matter how much the opening credit sequence built my hopes up for a Joker who was as clever as he was wacky.
On its own terms, the game is a great adaptation of the 90s Batman cartoon. It feels like it was written by the same team. The character designs range from solid to fantastic, with Scarecrow being a particular standout. The locations are gorgeous and grimy, laid out by a madman who no doubt had Amadeus Arkham and his madness in mind. All of the signs, the lighting, the color palettes come straight out of the 90s cartoon.
In terms of gameplay, Arkham Asylum is polished and smooth. The freeflow combat system has that balance of easy to learn/hard to master. The predator missions are unique and enjoyable, compelling the player to find new and different ways to prowl and hunt. Games with an open world element depend on character mobility, and getting Batman where you want him is a satisfying affair. Remarkable, no, but satisfying.
The only fault I can make note of in terms of gameplay is the boss fights. The first true boss is satisfying and fun, but using that same mechanic in half the big fight scenes in the game? It rubbed me wrong, though that's a matter of taste. What I consider pretty much unforgivable is using a glorified mook rush as the final boss fight.
Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay in Arkham Asylum. The freeflow fighting system has more than taken off in the years since it came out, and the predator sequences are steath combat done well. It's a visually stunning game with great character design and solid, consistent writing. But at the end of the day, I feel like I missed out on something with this. I feel like I'm either too old or not in tune with the nostalgia frequency this game is broadcasting. It's a blast from someone else's childhood. I hope it's yours.

Who's Your Daddy is genre I'd like people to start using called "Creepy Simulator", on par with the games: "What's under your blanket !?" and "Shower With Your Dad".
If we're speaking specifically, it's a competitive, co-op game between a baby and father, the person controlling the baby is trying to kill himself or herself, while the father frantically runs around trying to keep the baby from death's grip.
There's not much to say about the game's story, however *I* have a number of stories from playing the game. I purchased this game to play it with my younger brother, and then laughed until I cried at all the hilarious events that took place.
To all of my friends who sent me messages saying "oh god, that game"; instead of judging me from afar, you should have joined my twitch stream and laughed along with me
.
From setting myself on fire as a baby, predicting what my brother was going to do, and hearing his frustrated screams of "don't give me those pills! Keep that apple away from me!", it really was a hilarious stream.

I'm not going to spoiler tag my whole review, but lets say this game is way more fun when you don't know very much about the mechanics of the game. Grab two copies of this game, grab a friend, skype, and enjoy.   Read on if you don't mind having basic gameplay spoiled.
I have already explained the gist of the game. If you're the father: you try to keep your child alive by moving dangerous objects away, and giving pills and fruit to your child to keep them healthy until mom gets home! As the baby your objective is to get yourself killed in one of the very many MANY ways of doing so, drowning, freezing, burning, poison, power outlets, and more that are still being added (03/07/16) as the game updates.
Some may criticize the game on it's graphics, or glitches that may happen while playing. Naturally in most games this would be a negative quality, but there's a hilarious novelty about the game, and it's not over priced for the entertainment.
There are no steam achievements at this time. This is a game which would be fun to have "dumb achievements", just so achievers can grab an easy 100%, since the game at this time is purely 1v1 co-op, an achievement for each death would be very easy to teach people the various ways you can die, or power ups you can unlock as the father.
Who's Your Daddy is priced at $4.99, now I normally grade games by 1 dollar for every hour played, but for this game I make an exception. The quality of laughter and company of my brother over ruled the standard rule.
At this time I've spent two and a half hours playing the game. I have no doubt as the game is updated we will continue to play it occasionally, so even in price and hour the game will probably make it!
There's not much else to say about the game, the developer has already made a great game, and we can all look forward to seeing what other madness will be added to the game, and hopefully the developers don't get picked up by child support services before the game comes out of Early Access.
I recommend this game for anyone to play with another friend (if you have a funny friend, it's even better), if you're generally a solo gamer this is a skip for you.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a little game about choice.
At nearly every turn the player is put in a situation in which they must make a decision, and live with the consequences. Though the game wil always guide you through the key points, how and why you get there vary with each playthrough.
The game also likes to test your morality. There are many situations in which you must decide who to screw over, or whether you're going to play dirty.
The game is fairly short, taking only a few hours to get through, but considering the sheer number of choices (and multiple endings) it has extreme replayability.
The game also has a rather unique way to pick ones charcter, and allows for you to play either sex and orientation.
While having only presently played through twice, I look forward to trying to hunt down all the hidden details and possible outcomes in hopes of getting that Happy Ending.

Always Sometimes Nonsense
This is game about making choices and seeing how the consequences shape the story. There are a few dreadful mini-games tossed in here and there but at its core this is a narrative game, a digital choose your own adventure that sells itself on the quality of the story and it's ability to be shaped the choices you make.
Unfortunately the writing is awful. The dialog is flat, the characters are a collection of unmemorable types with no depth or originality to be found. The choices offered are contrived almost always breaking down into do a bad thing for money or give up money to be a good person. The effect on the story is negligible until its time to decide which ending you get. Do to many bad things and you are judged to be selfish don't do enough and you'll be forced to play bad mini-games for money. The final act is particularly disappointing as it is largely driven by the bad choices of others forcing you into yet another contrived choice.
Tonally this game is a mess. It purports to deal with heavy social issues but the writing is too outlandish to be taken serious and the characters are too flat to make an impact. This is a deeply silly game in which you will occasionally be called a terrible slur because the creators think that this is important social commentary. It's a game that has no idea how stupid it is. The whole story is framed with a ridiculously overwrought frame narrative where the protagonist retells the games events to armed criminals in between monologues about choice that waver between ludicrous and pretentious.
This is a game that forgoes gameplay in favour of a story that is awful, choices which are contrived and shallow, and thinks it is making important statements when really it’s just using some naughty words and being stupid. It’s a complete waste of time.

"Humble thyself or ye shall be humbled." "There is none good, no, not one." During my ten hour playthrough I constantly thought of these Biblical teachings so that I would make the best possible "morally right" choices through the game. Then again, morals are only based on popular opinion, and this game really digs deep into our morals. No matter the conclusion, be it a sad, a good, or a controversial ending, the outcomes really weighed upon me, which goes to show that a game doesn't need great graphics to tell a good story. That is what I believe the developers at Vagabond Dog were trying to do: make a story to be remembered for years to come, be it sad, good, or controversial. For ten dollars, Always Sometimes Monsters will take you on a journey of love, sacrifice, hate, and greed. This game invites you to think about your own morals.

After being officially out of Early Access for one year, Heroes and Generals has gone through a lot of changes. Back when I first played, things were quite miserable: Slow leveling, spawncamping, top-notch veterans in beginner battles; it was all quite a mess. In the past 2 and a half years since I started playing this game, multiple major updates were released. Graphics were updated, vehicles were added, guns were added, and a lot of other minor changes which has made the game a bit more bearable. There are quite a few things I could brag about for this game, for example:
-
, but only some, realism.
- Quite a number of things to do, including snipe, kill tanks, planes, or trucks, push F11 and commit suicide, and make a considerable amount of people rage by using comflauge and a sniper rifle and shoot from the other side of the map.
- Doesn't require the fastest internet in the world.
- Decent graphics for a near 4 year old game.
- Free2Play!
Although I could go on and on with pros, there are quite a few cons with this game as well.
- Many, and I mean many, people will make you want to rage quit because they either spawn camp or your teammates are incompetent.
- A lot of the war battles (seem to) take place in non-US servers, meaning a bit of a problem from people in North America.
- Not the most stable physics engine in the world, which used to mean bodies would fly hundreds of feet in the sky, which has been reduced to ONLY a hundred at tops.
- Has quite the pay-to-win type of aspect to it, although things seem a little expensive in my opinion, but I'm poor, so that makes sense.
Although there are many more things I could name for either list, its time to wrap things up. If you're looking for a game which does okay at keeping things in line and adding new conetent every once in a while, then this game definitely would work for you. It's free, doesn't require you to pay-to-win, but won't steal your entire bank if you do chose to. Has planes, tanks, truck, snipers, paratroopers, and just plain infantry. Though you may not have the largest choice of those factions or vehicles, there are other games you can play for that. Overall, if you can stand playing for hours just to get another troop and to get yours to a decent level, then this game can work out for you. Just a word of advice, do watch out for bicycles, they can truly kill you if you get in their way.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is one of my favourite games ever, and Mankind Divided is such a let down.
Almost everything is worse than in Human Revolution. The characters, the story, the dialogues, the level design, the UI. Mankind Divided has much better visuals and more augmentations (but none of the new augs are really interesting to use), but generally it's a step back compared to its predecessor.
The hacking mini-game is complete trash now since they decided to "fix" it by switching the camera to isometric view and making huge icons, so you can't see the network clearly. Eidos Montreal, how could you take a perfect mini game and turned it into a thing that makes me rage quit 5 times in an evening?
On top of everything, the PC version (by Nixxes, as usual) is riddled with bugs even though I can run it on very high settings @60 fps. Using quick save often usually saves you the trouble, but sometimes the game doesn't allow you to save, so you have to pray the game doesn't crash or bug out after a long scene.
I am not even talking about glitchy achievements (as many others, I didn't get FotH even though I triggered zero alarms and didn't get "alarm tutorial"). Moreover, NPCs sometimes die after a knock out if they stuck in a wall/door/furniture, so be careful not to screw up Pacifist achievement.
I also had a huge bug when a camera detected me through a floor (I was on the first floor, the camera was on the second). Remember how I wrote that quick save usually saves you the trouble? It turns out I saved exactly at the moment that glitchy camera saw me. Half an hour down the drain since I had to revert to one of the previous saves.
Despite all of this, the game is still better than most of AAA titles nowadays. I spent the first 15 hours exploring Prague and doing side quests, and only after that I proceeded with the main story. Again, many people complain the story is half-finished. Frankly, aside from the cliffhanger in the end, it was ok and the games tells you another story about Jensen uncovering a new conspiracy. The problem is, Human Revolution still has a much better narrative.
I changed my mind whether to recomment the game a few times during the playthough, but eventually decided to recommend it. Yes, it feels rushed and needs more polish, but it's still a good immersive sim and justifies its price during a sale.
P.S. Breach mode is a complete crap. From horrible visuals to boring repetitive missions – nothing is good about it. Wish they spent more resources on singleplayer (even if Breach was developed by another team, that team could help to make singleplayer better).

As a big Deus Ex, having played all games this one is really not that good. The original Deus Ex I consider to be a one of the best games to exist and Human revolution did a solid job to reboot the franchise. However, Mankind Divided is pretty "meh" when it comes to adding anything meaningful to the Deus Ex world.
Story:
The weakest element of the game by far is the narrative. Whilst its not terrible, it really does not advance the story of Adam Jensen or Illuminati that much nor does it add much interesting lore. There are some interesting mysteries and conspiracies to discover but outside of that the story really does a poor job to continue the story from Human Revolution and not to mention that the main story is ludicrously short and can be beaten in 10 hours so yeah. It feels like they were trying to focus more on this social divide nonsense than actually trying to continuing the compelling story of HR. Probably the best part about this story is the side missions which are very well done. Each side quest is its own unique, interesting story and multiple ways to complete it. I would even say that the side quests are actually better than the main plot.
Gameplay:
The gameplay of MD is basically Human Revolution 2.0. it pretty much the exact same but allows for more approaches, play styles and lets you play the game pretty much however you want. There are a few new additions like crafting, multitools, biocells and weapon customization but its nothing to blow your load over as the original Deus Ex has all these. The guns feel like pea shooters sometimes as they sound weird and dont have much impact or do much damage but this is not the case for some of the augmentations in this game. Some augs in this game like the remote hacking and the tesla gun arm are just way too OP and make the game really easy. I get the feeling that the devs didnt play test this much as there are all sorts of balancing issues like this. In one play through i got so many crafting parts that I was able to hoard 120 multitools and had 50,000 credits at the end. If you need resources in this game, trust me you wont have to look far. Also, the hacking minigame has returned from Human Revolution annnnnnndd its the exact same just with more software things.
Environments:
The environments in this game are very well done. The main city hub of prague in 2029 is vast and packed with detail and things to do, however there is only 1 hub. In previous Deus Ex games you went al over the world and saw it from different perspectives which added variety, depth and immersion to the game. Mankind Divided just has 1 hub, although being quite complex and a joy to explore it just feels less inspired than the hubs from HR. The game tries to hard to clutter everything in my opinion as It gets too distracting sometimes. Other areas of the game like Golem city are just as detailed and immersive as Prague but they are just too damn short and theres not a whole lot you do in them aside from your main missions.
Other things to know about this game before buying are the terrible performance. If you want to run this at ultra 60fps you better have a beefy card. I have a GTX 1060 and i average 50- 60 fps with medium to high settings but this game has some insane framedrops in some places in Prague. If you have an AMD card however, youre in luck as this game is clearly optimized for that. There are also micro transactions whithin the game which is a blatant sign of Squeenix's greed. like wtf, you can literally buy praxis kits with irl money which the game gives you lots of praxis anyway. If that aint greed i dont know what is. Overall though, Mankind Divided plays it safe and leaves little to be desired with microtransactions, short and irrelivant main plot, poor performance and cut DLC content. I do not recommend this game folr these reasons and becuase of Sqaure Enix's treatment of this franchise which they are now putting on hiatus. Do not support this company.

For the price it is sold and the time you CAN spent with the game (and I have spent a lot of time) it is one of the best purchases i probably made for a game. The thing I like the most about "Edge" is that you can choose your "level of difficulty" in each stage for your own. If you decide to only go for the exit it will be pretty easy. There are a lot of checkpoints and they are mostly placed fair and reasonable. If you are playing this way "Edge" ist a normal platformer and getting to the end is not a question of knowing where to go but of your ability to move the cube the way you want. The next step would be collecting all the prisms scattered through the levels which is still easy although you have to think for some of them. The next thing to do is trying to get better times either way for the S+-rank (you need to collect all prisms for that) or competing for the leader-boards (just getting to the end the fastest way possible). At this point I would consider "Edge" as a puzzle-platformer since you need to find out what the best route is, where you should go first, looking for shortcuts and paying attention to timing for moving platforms etc. You also have to consider where you can and have to use the Edge-Time which is basically your cube clinging to a wall with just one edge. All the time spent as Edge-time will later on not be counted to your total time and therefore influence your results largely. So getting the best time possible is not only a question of sheer ability but also cleverness and like I said before is the part of the game I, personally, would consider as a puzzle.
Although the graphic is minimalistic most levels give a different feeling and are unique and interesting with many interesting themes. Beside the games main 48 levels there is a free DLC with another 44 brilliant levels and additional 17 levels can be obtained by joining the Edge group at least if you are playing on Steam. To round this experience up the game comes with a catchy soundtrack which mostly will not annoy you.

Edge would have been a fine platformer weren't it for it horrible controls. You control a cube that can move to the north east, north west, south east, south west. But you control it with up, down, right, left. It's too bad, because it makes the game frustrating instead of fun.

This is such a bizarre, bittersweet game.  The mechanics are interesting, the story engaging, the choices heartwrenching.  Highly recommend for all your emotional masochism needs.

I think there are two broad categories one needs to consider when reviewing this game: concept and mechanics.  On one hand, while there are several games in which sacrifice-based decisions have a cumulative effect on the outcome of a game, this is the only title in which the decision-making IS the game itself.  The story is at once heartwarming and heartbreaking, and its narrative bridges the chapters smoothly regardless of your decisions.  Originality in scope and a raw emotional impact that only indie devs can bring you.  On the other hand, the playability could use some serious polish.  The gameplay is quite repetitive and tedious, and I often found myself rushing through the clue-finding.  The only part of the game I truly valued was reading the results of my decisions.  Moving through the house unseen is painfully easy to the point of boredom; a more inventive, strategic means of getting around, with varying limitations and obstacles to get from one point to another in the house would help the engagement factor, and it would be wonderful to extend the map outside of the house to areas mentioned in the letters: the woods, cliffside, even small parts of town, to make the search for clues a bit more challenging.  Lastly, the voice acting was woefully lacking any degree of believability, which would have surely added to the drama and tension.  But alas, I understand the limitations of indie development, so I feel I have to grade this one on a curve.  Big big points for taking a stab at a sub-genre much less traveled, docked for mechanics and playability, and you still wind up with a game well worth playing.

The ultimate goal of any story-driven game is to provide the escapism of a movie with the benefit of immersion since you get to control the protagonist.  With the possible exception of the Spider-Man games of the PS2/Xbox generation, Batman: Arkham Asylum is the first game that made me feel in control of the all the baddassery that is Batman.  Combat follows the fine line of simple to pick up, but complex enough to make it challenging.  Occasionally, Batman’s flying through the air to tag the next mook defied physics, but the decision to keep fun and flow over reality was a better choice.
An engrossing story by comic book writer Paul Dini and superb voice acting helmed by Batman: The Animated Series stars Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill as the Dark Knight and the Joker respectively provide an experience you won’t get sick of.
If I had to complain about anything, the riddler challenges (while excellently voice acted and overall fun in concept) was tedious more often than not, though the additional backstory made it almost worth it.
Easy recommendation to make.  BUY!

Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga is the game that started it all. Sure, there were Lego games that came out before this, but Lego Star Wars sparked the idea of games based off of movies and comic books. Is it a great start to an amazing franchise? Well, let's find out. 
Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga is a combination of Lego Star Wars I and II with some bonus stuff thrown in. The game follows Episodes I-VI of Star Wars and each episode is divided into 6 levels. Each level is very unique and it never feels like you're playing the same thing over and over again, with the exception of Gunship Calvary and Hoth Battle. The game does a good job of following the movies, but can be a little confusing if you haven't seen the movies. 
Something Lego games pride themselves on is their large variety of characters, and this game's got it! You'll find numerous Jedi characters like: Luke Skywalker, Obi-wan Kenobi, Kit Fisto, Mace Windu, and many more. The Jedi characters can use the force to push droids, build stuff, and solve puzzles. They also, of course, come with lightsabers. Not feeling the light side? Well, there are Sith characters as well like: Darth Vader, Emperor Palpatine, Darth Maul, and so on. Some Sith, like Count Dooku, can use force lightning. There are also certain blocks that only Sith characters can use the force on. 
Other iconic characters include: Han Solo, Princess Leia, Boba Fett, Jar Jar, and tons more. Skills vary with the characters. Characters like Han have blasters and can grapple up to places on certain pads. Characters like Boba Fett (bounty hunter characters) have thermal detonators, which can be used to blow up certain pieces. Boba, Jango, and the astromech droids (Like R2) can also fly. Speaking of droids, astromech droids and protocol droids (Like C-3P0) have access panels that get you into different areas. There are also Imperial panels for Imperial characters and Bounty Hunter panels. Those are just a few of the characters, there are many more to explore (Including Force Ghosts and even Indiana Jones!). 
All of these characters can be purchased in the main hub, the Cantina. Characters are bought using the in-game currency, studs. Also in the main hub are different things to do and buy. In terms of buying things, you can find 'red bricks" in levels that will be unlocked in the store to buy. These can be anything from score multipliers, disarm troops, and there's even super gonk. Besides shopping, you can also do different levels that aren't the main campaign. These include bounty hunter missions, where you have to find a certain character in a map, and bonus levels unlocked by golden bricks (You get these from completing levels and getting all of the 'mini-kits'). 
There's a lot of replayablitiy with the levels as well! You can go back and collect all of the 'mini-kits' to unlock golden bricks and even complete blue mini-kit challenges. These are where you have to find all of the blue mini-kits in a given time. 
Other stuff this game offers is local multiplayer (which is a blast), a fantastic soundtrack from the movies, hours and hours of fun trying to 100% the game, and pretty good graphics, for its time. 
In all, this is probably the best Lego game ever made! It's tons of fun and I highly recommend it if you're a Star Wars fan.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a game that I just couldn't get into. Which is unusual for me since I'm a gamer with a lot of patience and wouldn't have bought this if I thought otherwise.
Sadly from the very start I felt the game suffered from bad writing and plot pacing. The writing is simplistic in nature and will probably satisfy less picky gamers, but the game sells itself as a somewhat serious take on life followed up by mature content. However it's as if the game is trying to take itself serious at times but the writing seems to take on a different form altogether.
The moral choices in the story are on the edge of black and white, and we know it's never that simple. There are also various character connections that just don't make any sense or is sufficiently explained. I can't go into detail without this turning into a spoiler review, but it feels like cheap tie-ins are made to your character in order to make you feel like your previous decisions carried weight.
There is also no real connection to the characters. At times it's as if the game wants you to feel 'connected' to a certain character in the story, a character that should mean something to you. Someone important. However, due to hardly any depth given to any character background, you're left with the mindset of just not caring. Why should I care for character A, B or C if the game doesn't bother to build up a relationship? Snippets of dialogue between characters isn't enough for a game like this and it's something that the devs/writers really missed out on.
The game makes the mistake of jumping you into the shoes of a random person and building their 'life' without actually filling in all the gaps. This leaves a gaping void that just hurts the overall game.
If the writing and general plot pacing along with improvements to the gameplay such as the rather annoying repetitive money earnings had been much better, I'd probably be playing this a lot more and pumping more time into it.
Sadly the game is a bust and I can't recommend this.

If you've played Smash, then you know the basic formula for the game. Brawlhalla changes it up a bit by replacing the item drops found in Smash with weapon drops. Each character has 2 different weapons they can use, each with their own style of play. Each character has different fighting styles, even when using the same weapon. It's fun trying out different characters to see which one suits you the best.
If there are any drawbacks it is that there are very limited play modes. I would love to see a team game, as well as possibly something involving objectives in addition to the existing FFA and 1v1 modes.
The only major frustration I've encountered is that you can form groups and clans in-game and enter matches, but since the matches are all FFA you can sometimes run into situations of clans jobbing for each other. You will enter a match and two players will be clan'd, and they will invariably gang up on people. In some cases, if a clan mmeber is knocked out of first place, the otherr member will simply suicide off them after getting hit once to bolster their score. While there are no rankings for FFA, and it doesn't occur terribly often,  it is still a major bummer and can ruin an otherwise fun and intense match.
Overall though the game is extremely fun, and you can have a great time alone or with friends without ever dropping a dime. Their All Legends pack is available for purchase if you want to unlock all heroes immediately and is very reasonably priced considering it works like Smite's and gives all current and future legends. Beyond that, all shop purchases are purely cosmetic. I definitely recommendd it to anyone who enjoys the SSB-style of gameplay.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a fantastic, narritive-driven game where it feels like your decisions actually impact the story.  However, this feels like more of an adventure game than an RPG being that there is no actual character advancement.
The mini-games are subpar (but they are only mini-games, after all) - but they are, unfortunately, occasionally required.  In fact, a particular mini-game can bog down progression temporarily until you master it (or guess your way through it).  However, the actual story narritive is great, and you'll want to talk to every person you come across to uncover both humor and drama that are thickly spackled around the story of the actual protagonist - your protagonist.
So many decisions littered so liberally throughout the game and several ways the game can end lend to a good amount of replayability - in fact, you'll probably find yourself playing the game repeatedly just to see what might happen if you choose to behave a different way, or assist different people.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a beautiful experience, though beauty does not always mean pleasant or fun or joyful. This is a great story that is a rare experience that actually had me reflecting on my real life. A crowning achievement in the "can games be art?" argument.

When I play Zigguart, I feel like I'm only getting a piece of the pie. I'd like more pie but the developers look down at me and say "you can have more pie when you finish that piece" but it's a really small piece. So I have that pie and the developers give me ANOTHER really small piece. "No, developers, I'd like MORE pie, you've got a lot there and I'm the only one eating it so just give me a bigger slice!" But they refuse and again and again I get small slices of pie. What I'm getting at is that Zigguart is an enjoyable game but by the time you really get into the meat of it you've already had your fill. Not of pie but of patience.
Zigguart is difficult and expects you to die a lot. Every time you die you unlock more items randomly(?) along with different starting characters, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. More items to change your gameplay style, more perks to do different things, and a lot of ground to cover. However what Zigguart doesn't quite understand is that from the get go, there's enough toys to play with to reliably finish the game. You could unlock additional items and perks, but then they're just added to the random pool meaning that you COULD get them next time but there's no guarentee. Even worse is when Ziggurat smiles at you and says "you can have four different types of weapons" but only gives you one or two along with your base wand for a majority of the game with the free weapon you get each floor just a variation (or the EXACT SAME WEAPON) as one of the ones you already have. I'd love to keep playing you, Ziggurat, but I really really don't feel motivated to not get the kinds of items that will drastically change my game and have you unlock more toys to - again - not give them to me at some point.
Despite this Zigguart plays well as a hectic arena-based FPS and is fun to storm through. But now after finishing the game twice on Normal (and dying two more times) I feel like I've gotten all that Zigguart has to offer. Sure there's an endless mode and a Gauntlet mode and a whole lot more items to unlock, but nothing really feels exciting about it all. I felt really drawn in on the first few playthroughs but once I beat the final boss it was like a switch. It tells me there is more to do, but I'll probably be set from what I've played already. Part of me wishes they worked with their rather grim story idea (Ziggurat is the trial by combat with which death - which is extremely likely - will result in your soul being sacrificed to the elder gods) and made it so that every win in the game had the following run be a bit longer with a different final boss and ending. While the ending as it stands is satisfying (given you go through every room in the game), it feels like a let down compared to what the setting reflects.
So is Ziggurat worth your time and money? Well, yes, despite my many complaints, Ziggurat is still fun. You might have more fun with it than I did ultimately. It is a $15 game that gives $15 worth of enjoyment for a collection of hours. But it's recommended more for those who have good FPS awareness as things get confusing and overwhelming very quickly. If you aren't a fan of FPS games, Ziggurat won't make it any better.

- Buff all of the weapons, along with the starting wand
- give more ammo drops
- slow down fast monsters and make small ones bigger.
- give wepons some more punch when you fire them. I don't want to feel like I'm shooting nerf guns.
- Make dynamic and explody death animations.
- introduce some more firearm weapons.
To balance things out you can spawn more monsters at the player or make their attacks stronger, but don't give them any more HP.
If you apply this simple fixes, the game will become ten times better. It's a solid base for a game. You just need to fine tune the combat and it will be really great. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an excellent return to the Deus Ex universe, though when compared to the previous entry in the series it has a weaker story, fewer notable characters, a larger, more sprawling hub, and (basic) crafting. Most major gameplay mechanics are copied from Human Revolution (with mild refinements); stealth gameplay is much improved and the side-quests are truly superb. Not as narratively engaging as Human Revolution, but still a good game and a worthy entry in the franchise. Go for the Digital Deluxe edition at a discount so you get all of the DLC.
Total size on my hard-drive (including Season Pass): 60GB
+ Good voice-acting. Elias Toufexis as Jensen is as good as ever. Supporting cast is great as well.
+ Impressive light rays and hair animation.
+ Excellent side-quests. While not linked with the main story, they make everything better by providing valuable context. Some unique boss battles, too.
+ Stealth encounters are better than ever. A large number of choices, paths and methods await.
+ New augmentations that allow different ways to play. But if you want to play using the same styles and methods you developed by playing Human Revolution, you can do that too.
+ Plenty of mutually exclusive choices. At least two playthroughs are needed to see everything.
+ Prague is large and complex, divided into four districts. Tons to do and explore.
+ If you love - and I mean love - stealth encounters, the arcade-y Breach mode is a nice distraction. (Breach is also
from the Steam store.)
+/- What’s the story? “Adam Jensen fights terrorism by completing quests for Interpol.” The only stake Jensen has in the fate of augmented people is that he himself is augmented. Depending on how seriously you role-play his commitment to aug-rights (versus his duty to his job), the story can feel tangential.
+/- Much of Mankind Divided feels like a copy-paste of Human Revolution (with some refinements). Prague is the main hub instead of Detroit. Inventory is the same, gun-play is much better, hacking is refined, but is otherwise the same (the addition of “fog of war” on high-level objects is a nice touch). Even the story structure (though not the story itself) is similar.
+/- Composer Michael McCann returns from Human Revolution. His ambient tracks are as engaging as ever (and in a few cases thematically linked to the ambient music in Human Revolution), but the big story moments lack a “big tune.”
+/- Resource-intensive. Mankind Divided loves cpu cores and vram. You’ll need more than 4GB of video memory to play at 1440p on ANY texture setting (even Low).
+/- Lacks boss battles (I am talking about required bosses, not the optional ones.) I’m not sure having some would necessarily have improved the game, but they did help segment the different sections of Human Revolution. Mankind Divided offers no unique encounters to punctuate major story moments.
- I never asked for crafting. There is literally zero reason for it to be in the game.
- Sequel bait ending.
- The choices you made in the main story result in different news broadcasts at the end of the game. Not much of a pay-off.
- Lack of stand-out characters. Delara Auzenne and Jim Miller are well-drawn, but the rest of the cast is incredibly weak, especially compared to the plethora of unique individuals who populated Human Revolution.
- Final boss is a joke of a fight. And you know he’s going to be the final boss from about half-way through the game.
- Steam overlay did not work (I ran the game in Exclusive Fullscreen).
- Game will occasionally lock up for a few seconds, then resume. Increases in frequency as the game advances, then disappears after the alpine level. Feels like an issue with texture stream-in optimization, but I’m just guessing.
- Looping cut-scenes are used to hide the loading screens. Annoying, given how long the load-times are. If I want to watch gifs, I’ll visit 9Gag.
- Facial animations are sub-par.
- Some textures are oddly low-res (even with textures set to High).
- Hair might look great, but skin does not. Chalky and poorly textured.
- There might be a lot of stuff to do in Prague, but the city itself is an endless sea of grey. Visually boring. A lack of obvious landmarks can make it hard to navigate. (And why is the game set in Prague, anyway?)
- How are the ending(s) of Human Revolution treated?
While not the equal of its predecessor, Mandkind Divided is worth playing for its excellent side-quests and strong stealth gameplay – and just for the pleasure of role-playing as Adam Jensen again. When I finished Human Revolution for the first time, I couldn’t wait to go back and play it again. After finishing Mankind Divided, I had more of a “That was cool. Moving on” feeling instead. It is still an enjoyable return to the Deus Ex universe, and fans of the series shouldn’t hesitate to give Mankind Divided a try.

I completed the game through my first playthrough completely satisfied with the experience.  Yet when I buckle down and try to start up a second playthrough, I find myself less than thrilled to begin again once I start going through those same motions.  I start to get reminded of some of the things I cared less about when playing through the game initially: The story isn't great, sometimes you can get the same item drops (I got some Witchfinder's leather chest piece three times in a row), the map areas are huge and filled to the brim with monsters in a way that feels less like quality and more of quantity, and the bosses aren't always particularly 'hard.'  The slow crawl through these areas reminds me of all of these and I just stop playing again.
...So would I recommend this game?  Yes, but only through a sale or if you don't particularly value 20 dollars that much.  Play it through once, enjoy it, but inevitably come to the same conclusion that I did that it isn't worth a second go.

Torchlight II is an excellent example of how to make a dungeon crawler RPG.
As a long-time player of the FATE series, I came into TL2 with expectations that were well surpassed. Similar to the FATE series in base aspects, TL2 expands on principles of unique character classes, creating a purposeful main quest and in random-generation processes. TL2 fixes the FATE grindiness factor at higher levels by providing gear that is more reasonable for your level, making fame less relevant, appropriately scaling costs and disallowing enchanters to curse your items. In addition, I would call TL2 an "old couples" game (in the good sense). Similar to the Diablo series, TL2 can be enjoyed by people of all ages and all levels of intensity from casuals to hardcore players. Difficulty settings are properly done to suit all players’ tastes and allow for maximum enjoyment to anyone who might play it while simultaneously featuring a well-scaled co-op/multiplayer experience. And with the final addition of Steam Workshop, this game has the potential to provide hours of entertainment.
A definite recommendation for players who enjoy the Diablo series, the FATE series, dungeon crawler RPGs and/or co-op games with friends.

Vertical Drop Heroes HD is a semi rouge like top to bottom platformer with some randomized level generators thrown in.
You start off each life picking a new character before being placed at the top of the level with the simply task of making down to the bottom alive and either using keys you’ve collected to open the door or killing the boss to progress to the next level. On the way down you can kill enemies to level your character up, collect coins for upgrades, and buy random upgrades and teleporters to skip earlier levels. Now you don’t have to kill anyone, in fact game rewards you for decided not to do so. As long you go through the level without killing the game is in Pacifist mode where you can collect extra XP to level you character up.
The kicker however is that when you die that character and his level progression is over with and reset. At the start of the next game you begin you pick a new character who starts at level 1. Though that makes it the basic rougelike game your powers and abilities you buy do carry over between all characters if they are able to use them.

Through my several hours in the game the more I leveled up and got further the more fun the game got. You become stronger each time and gain new powers to make the game easier. For $7 on Steam I have to recommend this, it’s a good game to play in bursts that will keep you entertained throughout it.

I'm squarely in the new-dad demographic, so this game probably has an unfair advantage. :-) That said, I think it would be enjoyable for anyone interested in a quiet, contemplative, story-driven experience that you can play through in a small number of hours.
The characters in this family are fleshed out in *much* greater detail than in most games, which makes sense. In _The Novelist_, backstory is not window-dressing to make you care slightly more about (say) running down a hallway shooting bad guys; instead, backstory *is* the game.
The tensions and tradeoffs in this little family really rang true to me, especially as someone with a career, a wife, and a child, and all of us trying to juggle and find balance, just like the game's characters. My wife watched me play through one of the chapters, and she ended up crying (but in a good way). Like me, she was a bit floored at how "real" everything felt.
My one nit is with the forced-choice mechanic employed in each chapter. At "best," you can make one of the three characters very happy, make a second character moderately happy, and leave the third character out in the cold. I understood and felt how the game was trying to really force me into the mindset of limited time+resources where I had to make hard choices for the family. But by the end this particular mechanic seemed itself seemed a bit forced and forumulaic. I would have loved for the game to mix it up a bit, be less predictable, and find some other ways to present me with hard choices where not everyone gets what they want.
Still, it was a great experience overall, and I highly recommend the game to anyone who's looking for a few hours of contemplating family, work, life, and all the cracks in between.

The Novelist is a game that explores the big question: love and family vs career. This game focuses on one particular family which you "haunt" to try and discover (and ultimately influence) their life story. Each chapter explores a new aspect to the family (a novelist, his wife and thier son) and every choice you make will affect the members of the family and not everyone is ever satisfied with your choices. Your choices will affect your overall ending.
I would highly recommend this game for an interactive story into a families life where you spend most of the game trying to decide who would be the least upset by your decisions.
