[UPDATE: After having a HC Berserker with all defensive skills, almost 4k health, and decent resistances get taken down in under a second on CASUAL NG+ by a single champion, I can now confirm that this game, specifically it's nonexistent balancing, is a steaming pile of horse $hit and is not deserving of any good rating whatsoever.]
I want to start this review by saying that it's somewhat subjective, and YMMV depending on what you're looking for in a game of this sort.
That said, I'm not recommending this game, partly because I have, fairly early on, reached a point where I don't enjoy playing the game, which is a bad indication, and also because even what I did enjoy about the game wouldn't, for me, indicate 95% overall positive reviews, so I'm "doing my part" to lower that slightly. It's a good game, but it certainly isn't great, although it could have been.
This game suffers from several of the same problems that plagued Torchlight 1, but in some cases actually worse. What I remember from playing Torchlight 1 (I 100%ed the achievements almost two years ago) is that, on my first run through the game, I got stuck partway (maybe 2/3?) because my damage simply couldn't keep up with the enemies, and I was dying more often than I should have been. This is from someone who has beaten both Diablo 1 and 2 many times (both SC and HC), and a couple other games in the same general genre. Now, that was because I had picked the Alchemist (generally agreed to be the worst character, as I found out later, though I usually prefer spellcasters in any RPG), and I had probably not distributed my points optimally—but that's also my point. I was playing on Normal, not HC, and I couldn't progress farther. That's some poor game design. I later replayed with Barbarian (the best class in T1) and then twinked my Alchemist until he could finish.
Unfortunately, I have now run into a similar problem in T2. I started out with Embermage (again, spellcasters), which, from reading some online, appears to be one of the better classes—but only if you place your skill points right. And on that front, T2 is much worse than T1, because there are simply too many options and not enough indications of where to place points, not to mention the lack of a complete respec (without using mods, I suppose). I discovered when I was close to level 40 that I really had no use for Molten Mace (I had decided to go pure Fire since I didn't know how else to pick, and I figured almost anything would be manageable on Normal), but I couldn't remove the 9 points I had already put in it. That alone may not have been what sunk me, but either way, it didn't help.
Now, I could go online, look for optimal builds, perhaps restart with a different class or something, and I may still do that at some point in the future. Right now, though, I'm pretty discouraged from playing the game, especially when I got one-shotted from over 95% health by a random enemy in Act 3, despite being overleveled! Keep in mind I'm only playing on Normal. All in all, the game is simply not well-balanced, a similar problem to what I ran into on T1. Additionally, with extra features—mostly more ways to spend gold—the game has simply become overcomplicated. I preferred the relative simplicity of T1, even with mods added.
You may disagree with a lot of this review because T2 has the kind of gameplay you're looking for, I don't know. But for someone like me, who has played quite a few RPGs, including a number of the hack-and-slash loot-a-thon variety, it really doesn't measure up, and more of it turns me away than draws me in.

Rating: 7/10
Overview: FPS Rogue Lite
The Good:
+ Fast paced first person shooter
+ Different characters each with their own pros, cons and starting equipment.
+ lots of different perks
+ good enemy variety and bosses
+ Plenty of different weapons spread between wands, spells, staves and alchemy
+ Certain rooms have random effects that will help or hurt you, i.e faster attack rate, can only shoot while jumping etc. This provides a bit more strategy and uniqueness
The Average:
+/-  Like every other first-person rogue game, you quickly experience all the level design and levels start to feel stale.  Levels are made up of rooms randomly joined together.
+/- Completing the game or dying unlocks new perks regardless of how long you play, it doesn’t feel very satisfying
+/- Leveling up increases your health, mana and allows you to choose between two random perks. These perks are not always good and leveling up doesn’t feel as satisfying as it should.
+/- more music tracks would be nice
Conclusion:
In terms of a rogue game this game offers little surprises. It has everything you want from a rogue game but still suffers from some of the same problems other games of the genre face. After a few hours of play I felt like I had seen everything the game had to offer.

Still the best Batman game in the Arkham series and probably the best Batman game ever made. The story involves Batman catching Joker easily after a recent robbery and, coincidentally, Joker's gang moved to the Asylum because of an issue at the Blackgate Prison - once inside the Asylum, the Joker escapes and taskes control of the Asylum and prepares to unearth something far worse than what you initially suspect. You play as Batman trying to unearth this plot and once again stop the Joker.
To this day, this game still has amazing visuals, Batman himself covering around half the screen, looks the part and stands strong and confident as the character should as well as the texture work on his suit are top notch - the rest of the game fairs the same, since the game has been given an outstanding amount of care and work into every area you go through. Not one area in the game feels exactly the same as another even if they look similar. Very stellar work of textures all around overall.
I don't say this is the best Batman game out there for no reason - gameplay is pretty basic "Brawler" style with very minor puzzle solving, but what makes this game different, from, say a game like Assassin's Creed - is the "Free Flow combat system" the game has. The combat is slightly similar to the first Assassin's Creed, except - the flow combat system allows Batman to basically jump from one foe to another in a very fast manner, almost rythmically, to get a combo counter to go as high as you can while still making it challenging by giving the foes still standing a fighting chance and implementing counters.
You can also explore the entirety of the Arkham Asylum as you unlock areas and you can do a variety of things while exploring, you can face groups of enemies scattered around, you can do Riddler Challenges - whom are a bunch of mini puzzles scattered around the Asylum that involves the use of Batman's Detective Mode, these range from finding a specific item found in the area or marks that require the Detective Mode to find and a "Complete the Mark" type of game that involves you scanning the area from specific places to complete a full mark, etc - Riddler trophies, and a bunch of case files to find out more background information on Batman characters and villains (as well as the history behind Arkahm Asylum) that are often very well realized and fun to hear.
The Detective Mode & Gadgets: You'll be using these a LOT on your trudge through Arkham Asylum. Ranging from the standard Batarangs and Grappling hook (used for mundane objectives such as getting to and pulling out vents from hard to reach places, etc), the Explosive Gel (Used a lot to surprise enemies, to find weak walls to find trophies and secrets and to progress in the story as well!) and a bunch more. The Detecive Mode helps you analyze weak walls to use your Explosive Gel on and other gadgets as well as analyze enemy/allies conditions and, more important later on in the game, to find out which enemies carry weapons or are special enemies.).
So in general, if you ever wanted to know and feel what a life in the day of Batman is, this is definately your game, more so than the sequels (imo). From the excellent assets and sound to follow it up with, and the pitch perfect gameplay to go along with it, this sits as one of my favourite video game experiences and currently my best experience playing as the legendary Dark Knight.

Just finished playing The Novelist, a thought–provoking adventure game about balancing the competing demands of family life. While the premise of all life–affecting decisions that affect the family being made by the titular male character is a bit offensive to modern sensibilities, given the game's setting in a era of manual typewriters and hand–written letters, it's forgivable, I suppose. The game is structured in a way that makes me suspect that there is no truly "good" ending—I think that someone (one of the game's three characters) will always be left with the short end of the stick, and while that may be a bit contrived, it achieves its intended purpose.
I would certainly recommend this game, even to so–called "non gamers"—it's more about observation, experience, and choice, then about gameplay mechanics.

Following the successes of games like Gone Home and Actual Sunlight, The Novelist is another one of those games that will make traditional gamers question whether or not it actually is a game. A huge fan of exploratory/narrative games, however, I did enjoy my 3-4 play-throughs of the game. It doesn't capture the voyeuristic feel quite as fully as Gone Home and doesn't have a story quite as deeply touching as Actual Sunlight; rather, The Novelist falls somewhere between the two as a somewhat memorable, very relatable, and surprisingly touching experience as a voyeur into regular family life. It's a decent game, and although it certainly isn't mind-blowing, it has enough to be worth a play or two.
You play as a spectre living in a house that the Kaplan family decides to move into for a summer. Essentially, you "ghost" around the house, reading minds and notes, and help the father (the Novelist) make decisions regarding his family. There really isn't much in the way of gameplay (other than a half-hearted and arguably useless stealth option), so the game could be seen as somewhat of a modern Choose-Your-Own-Adventure novel. Where the game shines is how sincerely and authentically the writing in the game reads: in fact, by the end of a playthrough, you really do care about what happens to the relationship between the mother and the father. It's because of this emotional investment that I found myself playing the game through several times, wanting to find out what would happen to the mother if I did this, or that.
Of course, while The Novelist did manage to get me emotionally invested (which, admittedly, is not a difficult task), it does fall short on a few too many things to be considered a memorable or truly laudable game. Off the top of my head, the game failed terribly at getting the audience to care about the child, the "stealth" mechanic was almost laughable and mostly obstructive, and several playthroughs of the game would reveal the endings to be somewhat shallow. Most importantly however, where the game could have been fantastic in its realism, it ended up backing itself into a corner by trying a little too hard. The problems Dan Kaplan faces that summer are very real, but by stressing that "the decisions Dan made that summer would come to define his life" (or something similar), The Novelist almost invites cynicism and throws away any chance it could have had at feeling truly authentic.
All in all, The Novelist is a decently good game for what it tries to be. Although nobody is likely to remember it a few years from now, it's a promising first foray into narrative indie game development for Kent Hudson.

Great story with lots of possible outcomes. Interesting to play a game that revolves around human being's emotional choices. Also lots of clever interaction design. The stroy is strong but is sometimes clunky, however, I did feel real emotion by the end.

While "The Novelist" isn't a big game with all the flash, spit and polish of a big time game. It has a depth that most of the big games just cannot obtain.
You play a "Ghost" who's only objective is to follow and learn about a family (Dan, Julia and Tommy) throughout their summer holiday. In doing so, you will learn about their wants and needs, through notes, diaries and by reading their minds. Then you have to make a choice about which option you wish to follow and by doing so, you impact the families life beyond the summer.
I bought and played this game for the story and in doing so I found it a worthwhile play. Definitely worthy of the two awards it almost won, but sadly didn't.
I do love how there is a comprimise option available, it allows you to give a quarter (i think) of "Dans" time to someone else without impacting the main choice (I'm glad it dosen't split it 50/50).
The ending I enjoyed, as it actually took into account the choices I had made throughout the course of the game and actually does tell you what everyone did with their lives post "Ghost" interference
The only things I had annoyances with about the game were first of all, Tommy's drawing (In his head). Even after I had spent a whole day doing what he wanted and another two days of a compromise it didn't change, he just seems to feel a little distant with Dan if you're not with him 24/7 (which may be what they learned after researching how children react to certain things, If so, I apologise to the creators).
The other annoying thing was Dans doors. In one mission I chose an option, which made Dan close his doors to work on his book. The part about this that annoyed me was that you can't walk through the doors, or jump to another light to bypass it, you're stuck waiting for him to come out and let you in. Or if you're unlucky you end up stuck in there waiting five minutes for him to open the door. Not a big one, just time consuming and slightly annoying.
To sum it up:
Pros+
+ A story that makes sense and is fun to experience
+ Character interactions that are very believable
+ Nice charming music
+ A Branching story that effects the whole game (maybe only in subtile ways)
+ Controls are simple (Only w,a,s,d for movement and space and e for interactions)
Cons-
- No action or excitement, just a nice story.
- The models aren't amazingly graphic (but really, they didn't have to be)
- What people think in their heads about a situation are silly and sometimes foolish (but isn't that something all humans share)
Total Score = 9.5/10
To conclude, I would recommend this game highly to anyone who enjoys a good story or an interactive story. My only negative that I can think of when recommending "The Novelist" is the price tag, $15 is a huge amount of money for a game that lasts no longer than possibly 2 hours. I would like to suggest that if the creators are reading these reviews, that they drop the price to maybe $10 or even $5. A little low I know and possibly stupid you may think, but sales will go down unless your prices do too, just a suggestion.
Other than that, beautiful game, beautiful story.
And FYI, yes my writing isn't the best and neither is my grammer, you don't need to tell me :P

I would imagine that Jesus had to take time for himself. And died for it.  I guess there's a quiet beauty in that.

Arkham Asylum, written by veteran Batman writer Paul Dini, is based on the long-running comic book mythos, as opposed to most other Batman games which are adaptations of the character in other media besides the source material. The Joker, Batman's arch enemy, has instigated an elaborate plot from within Arkham Asylum where many of Batman's other villains have been incarcerated. Batman investigates and comes to learn that the Joker is trying to create an army of Bane-like creatures to threaten Gotham City, and is forced to put a stop to the Joker's plans. The game's main characters are voiced by the actors from the DC Animated Universe, namely Kevin Conroy, Mark Hamill, and Arleen Sorkin reprising their roles as Batman, the Joker, and Harley Quinn, respectively. The game is played as a third-person perspective action-adventure game with a primary focus on Batman's combat abilities, his stealth and detective skills, and an arsenal of gadgets that can be used in both combat and exploration.

It's got more variety in the combat, you aren't going to have great success repeating exact same combos each attack, you have to vary it based on terrain and enemy placements (at least for Constructor class).

If you are looking for a fun cheap ARPG this is a great value.

I Am Alive was a really good Xbox arcade game, with a subpar PC port that costs way too much after 4 years.
Graphically this game is beautiful, but at the same time is almost a direct port from console with no extra effort put in to make it look better on PC, meaning it lacks the full gamut of options a game intended for PC would have. The desaturated color pallette common to movies and games that share similar themes like Fallout, The Road, Rage, Book of Eli, Mad Max and other post apocalyptic media fits the game perfectly. Unfortunately, it also garnered the game a lot of negative attention from whining casuals who only see overall trends in gaming and don't judge games based on their merits.
I Am Alive is the story of a guy who was away from home when weather disasters destroyed the world [ostensibly] and has spent every moment since trying to get back to his wife and daughter. The game combines recognizable platforming with beautiful post-civilization landscapes, but also features melee and gun combat more akin to a realistic survival game (at least until the latter part of the game where you get a lot of ammo). Ammo is scarce and healing items more scarce. Everyone you encounter is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ trying to kill you, and even some of the people you try to rescue will try to trick you into being killed like a lot of random NPCs in Witcher 3 or GTA5 will do.
The story is predictable, and I'm not sure if the title of the game is supposed to be ironic or not, but I wish that the Chinese sect of Ubisoft that developed this were working on a full fledged sequel or re-imagining. Really the negative aspects of this game are the low fidelity graphics and the awful controller support on PC - not to mention the obvious lack of Steamworks integration for things like achievements.  I really wish the controller mapping was functional, because it makes this game all but unplayable on computer.
If you can look past that or use something like Controller Companion, this game is worth the time of anyone who likes platformers or post-civilization games.

****THIS REVIEW WILL HAVE MINOR SPOILERS*****
TL;DR. Buy it, its good.
Always Sometimes Monsters is all about choice. Will you be a nice guy/gal to everyone you meet, or will you steal  and cheat your way through? A basic plot synopsis would be you are a struggling writer who is kicked out of your apartment the day before you get a wedding invitation from your ex girl/boyfriend. You make it your mission to get to the wedding and jumpstart your career, but what you do along the way, and what happens when you get there, is up to you.
It has a really cool intro in picking your character. You will talk to a bunch of people at a party, and whoever you choose to take a drink with is your character. The same idea goes for your love interest. It has a very Pokemon-esque or RPG Maker like art style, one that I quite enjoy.
But it also has some very annoying mechanics. There is no mouse based support, all actions must be done through the keyboard. There is gamepad support, but I don't have one and therefore cannot comment on it. But to me a PC game where I can't use my mouse is really frustrating. Scaling the screen is also bugged right now. I could scale my screen down to a small resolution, but if I wanted it to go back, no amount of F6 would make it so unless I restarted. There are also typos and accidents galore in the text. For example, one time it called the same person a man and a woman, in the same line of dialogue.
But this game has plenty of positives. The choices you make in this game are everywhere. You never know how important a choice is, but it is amazing how much choice you really have. It mostly does boil down to a simple Fate system similar to a Fable-like morality, but quite enjoyable none-the-less. This bonanza of choice also means a replay is almost necessary. I loved seeing the different results my second time through. On my first blind playthrough it took about 10 hours, and I have played through it twice so far, and have no plans to stop now, despite the problems. Music and the soundtrack were nothing to write home about, and there is only around 6-7 songs, little to no sound effects, and no voice acting at all.
PROS AND CONS
+ Choice. It is what this game is all about, and they did a great job with it. There is at least three endings, and almost assuredly more.
+ Characters. While what you and your love interest look like is up to you, what you decide changes how people react to you. I was a lesbian couple in the first play and lots of people were uncomfortable with it in the game. Just a nice touch.
- Mechanics. As already described, this game could absolutely use some more time in the oven and smoothing of some edges. Lots of typos, and annoying systems.
OVERALL: 8/10. For only 9 or 10 dollars, this is a great pickup. But just be aware that at least as I am writing this, there are some problems that I hope get fixed.

I will admit to having never written a review before but this game was so good that I simply couldn't not.
Always Sometimes Monsters delivers what it promises. It gives an experience where, based on race, gender and sexuality, your experiences change. However, this isn't all it provides. The story itself is gripping and amazing, with lots of different paths and lots of different consequences for your actions. I will admit that the story is somewhat stream-lined in that it's city to city to city, with fixed cities, however there is still plenty of room for diverging paths. On top of this, it provides an experience where you're often wondering whether or not you will be able to get through it; not because the game's that hard, but because the story twists in so many ways. On top of this, it also has some interesting moments when characters delve into philosophy.
There are some cons however, the first being the potential for grinding. I'll give you an example. I was in a factory, loading boxes, told I could keep going until I was finished. The counter is 2 digited, so I assumed it wouldn't be too many. I loaded 101 boxes before giving up, with no indication that there was an end or not. As well as that, the jobs can be a bit boring/monotonous, but I suppose that's part of the game so I can't judge it for that. Also, I whilst I found Easter Eggs winking at the fourth wall clever, the heavy-handedness of this at the end was not to my taste.
All in all, a fantastic game, indicated by the fact I'm going in for my second run now.
An amazing, thought-provoking game based on the consequences of choices we make everyday. Surely a memorable game.

I'll recommend it because I believe that  this game will grow on you over time, occupying a space in your heart like previous games (DX:HR needed a bit of time, this one may take several months or maybe few years for you) and the guys at Square/Eidos who did it still have a chance to apologize. But like most of the guys here I feel betrayed and won't accept any half-baked amends, so I will criticize the bad aspects this time around and put the good review on the older game.
Let's start with the good: A fantastic game, with plenty of potential, awesome graphics, top-notch voice acting, compelling script, intriguing story, smooth-buttery gameplay, AAA+ and better than Human Revolution in almost every aspect and still... is failing miserably in sales, with a horrid Mixed review status here. I can't possibly understand. I'm lying, I can, but can't believe nonetheless. They managed to throw it bad for a couple of reasons.
Everyone knows what is WRONG here:
* Worst pre-order scheme since this thing was invented.
* One-time-use Only Micro-transactions, mostly Credits and Praxis kits (last minute addition, even without it you can have plenty of EXP and praxis, sometimes too much, but you have a lot of news augs anyway). In a single-player game like this I see no sense on putting them. It doesn't brake the game either or make it an ad-ware, but it's still intrusive and a disgusting and greed business model on most.
* Abrupt ending. I was prepared to it, but couldn't believe when credits started rolling anyway. Every Deus Ex so far finished on a major note on big events that can change the whole world, but now we have some minor consequences we will possibly see in the sequel, if there's one. (I'm hoping to be wrong and gave a huge impact instead, but let's see wait the future bring us) Even if it didn't sent it away with explosions, at least should deliver a full story and not something that ends in the middle. Spoilers beware, Adam had almost no clue on whom was conspiring this time around and we finished the game with a Disc 1 Final Boss. Lame decision.
* The game is kinda short. The duration was okay, but they missed the mark in the ideal playtime department. Lacked bacon in someone's breakfast and game final time was decreased from what I expected. I played two times in a row and nearly didn't spent 60 hours. +5 for finding some extra nooks and crannies before uninstalling. I expected around the "eighties" for two full play times (Normal Game
Hard New Game+ to unlock and use all the augs). DX:HR I played and replayed, and spent a lot of extra time playing some stuff I liked again to proudly get my well spent 134 hours.
* Pieces of the actual game chopped off and sent as DLCs (one was made free later, luckily). It's not bad to have Adam's Side Stories like "A Criminal Past", but the other two I can understand within the context of the game and shouldn't be separated from it.
See: I'm okay with Breach as standalone (it should be in the first place); I'm perfectly fine with Prague being the only Hub; I actually like to have some extra story covered by novels and comics  and not in-game; I'm pretty happy with the current state of the port, the game only crashed once or twice; there is nothing else to complain almost, this game is so close to perfection. So, my conclusion is:
Basically what is wrong isn't the game
, but the way they're trying to sell it. Some commercial and business decisions that breaks with all the loyalty any fan has to the franchise. The ones who make this game, please listen: There is no way to go against the will of its players, they vote with their wallets. If you guys want success, provide just the basics: be honest and communicative with the players about the game, don't try to fool anyone around. Be fair and try to correct the mistakes made before it spreads. Wanna win some extra? Focus in bonus content that everyone loves, adds skins or cosmetic packs, or invent something else, but no more of this crap.
This time around even if they do a perfect score in the next installment, I won't be compelled to buy it at full price because the errors they did here and now. But with some decent discount, maybe I can consider buying the next one in the future. So I won't feel ripped off.
For the one who wants to play it, go ahead: Buy it (discounted, of course), play it, it is worthy of your time and money. But then face the same things that bugged me and everyone else, get angry, complain, recommend it or not and hope they fix what they did here and pray for a better game next time. So, unless something worse happens, I recommend it with all the caveats of the reviewers who already said it before me.

TL;DR: the game has its faults, but I had a lot of fun playing it.  The variety of play-style that this franchise offers keeps replayability high and that's enough for me to ignore the things I didn't like.
I think my only criticism of DE:HR was that it had too many locations and not enough depth.  In DE:MD, we generally stay in Prague so the setting is much larger and you can interact with so much more.  Over the course of the game, you visit a few other settings, but only very briefly.  There were times I felt weary of Prague, but overall the game environment was very immersive for me.
What broke the story for me was how over-powered Jensen is.  Naturally, there's a part of the game where you suffer the classic "Mega Man starts with all of his upgrades, then almost immediately loses all of them; have fun collecting all of them again" trope.  Contrived as it may be, those first neutered moments made for a much more challenging game.  After that, the upgrades pretty much put you over the top--especially if you go lethal and non-stealth.
DE:MD tries so hard to demonstrate what it might be like to live in an apartheid society.  Unfortunately, it just doesn't matter when you're a walking super-weapon.  Real descrimination leaves the victims feeling helpless; Jensen is anything but helpless.  What might have been more compelling is if Jensen were forced to tolerate discrimination against NPCs that he cares about.  In DE:HR actually wanting to save Malik when her VTOL crashed (not just for the achievement).
Similarly, DE:MD also tries to show how freedom fighters can be viewed as terrorists and how the violent actions of a few can be incorrectly applied to the whole.  As before, it was hard to empathize because much of this was explained to the player, instead of shown.
If you ignore the less-than-interesting dialog, lack of deep character development, graphical glitches, and random crashes, the game is quite fun.  I had fun.  I played it once as stealth+non-lethal and once as no-one-is-safe.
Lastly, if you work in cyber-security at all, just pretend all of the hacking and NSN non-sense is just a dream sequence... like Super Mario Brothers 2.

Fun. Fun. Fun and more fun. This game lets you use your brain and combat skills to solve puzzles and riddles while you fight your way to defeating the always entertaining Joker. Even with a very high Metascore, which I value highly, I was a little skeptical as to what this game could bring to the table. That skepticism was instantly dashed as soon as you enter your first few fights and get a hang of all the gadgets and tools at Batmans' disposal. You don't even have to like Batman at all to love this game.

*PLAY THIS BEFORE ARKHAM CITY*
I find that Batman: Arkham Asylum retains some decent elements of classic Metroidvania games: fight a few guys, explore, fight a boss, get a new gadget, then use the new gadget to explore the world and find more hidden things that were previously inaccessible.
The story is fine, but its very typical for a Batman plot. If you're okay with that, then that's cool. Just accept that you'll encounter lots of things you'd expect from anything Batman.
The combat is very floaty, and punch-punch based. After your first few fights, you'l have nearly all of it down, and that's why I recommend you play this on the hardest difficulty you can. I regretted getting halfway through the game with little challenge in the fights. This is a game that easily thrives off of a higher difficulty, and that way you'll be ready for the slew of new things you'll have to go up against in the sequel. Treat this as a prologue to combat.
If you're questioning if you should skip ahead to Arkham City, then don't. Chances are that if you're the type of person who stops to even question if they'll miss any amount of plot in a game, then you'll just want to use this as a warm up to Arkham City. Not a difficult story to grasp, but essential if you don't want to be a little confused at the beginning of the sequel.
Overall, an moderately enjoyable game with great performances from Kevin Conroy, Mark Hamill, and Arleen Sorkin(RIP original VA for Harley Quinn).

This is the second time I play through this game, and I still love it.
Who couldn't, as long as you enjoy 80s and 90s action movies. The amount of well-delivered flavour of nostalgia and especially the awesomely made music made me grin from one ear to the other. The style of the humour, served mainly by Kyle Reese / Cpl. Hicks / Michael Biehn is just icing on the cake. This is a game that doesn't take itself too serious and invites you to have fun with it, which it has in spades.
One could say, this game is better than Far Cry 3 itself, which kind of overstays its welcome, as you end up as immortal god of war about mid-game, or rather, as soon as you finish all the hunting side missions, which then trivializes the rest of the game.
Blood Dragon itself is short and sweet, performs well, has decent controls and just enough content to last you a few hours. Yes, you will probably be done with it between 3 and 6 hours, but that isn't a bad thing. It just means that all the great parts are condensed together. One could say it is the best of the Far Cry games, maybe even near perfect.
If... there weren't Uplay. Not only is this unneeded, log-in-requiring Steam-clone starting up (and usually updating something you didn't need) whenever you want to play, but because of that, you also don't get Steam achievements.

Batman Arkham Asylum is a third person action adventure where you get to play the iconic super hero.  The game was released in 2009 by warner brothers, developed by Rocksteady studios.  The game of the year edition then followed in 2010.
The game was a multi platform release and there are times it shows in the port.  Most notably the cut scenes which are rendered outside of the game engine and locked to 30 frames per second.  There are a reasonable number of graphics options.  However this can only be access in a menu outside of the main game
The story starts with Batman Capturing the Joker and driving him to Arkham Asylum.  While this may seem like the end of the game, this is far from it.  Batman suspects Joker is up to something as he caught him too easily.  His suspicions are proved correct when Joker breaks free in the Asylum, trapping Batman in there with him.  Now Batman must unravel Joker's plan and stop it from happening.
Graphically the game does look good.  there are some points where the texture quality on some surfaces could be of a higher resolution.  However in general the world of Arkham with well realised.  The animation quality is excellent and very fluid with Batman easily transitioning from running, jumping or gliding as necessary.  I preferred the in engine cut scenes better as it wasn't as noticeable and didn't break the immersion as much.
The sound design is first rate in this game.   The music is well used in this game providing the necessary backdrop. The voice acting is excellent.  The performances from Kevin Conroy as Batman, Mark Hamill's Joker are superb as are the rest of the cast on the whole.
The gameplay is very good.  The game introduces new techniques and gadgets along the way.  These vary the game play and add to the experience.  Apart from a couple of upgrades, you can unlock these with experience points earned as you progress.
Combat mainly consists of either hand to hand or stealth.  The hand to hand combat is a free flowing system of move and counter move in a way that feel fluid and becomes intuitive.  Batman's moves have punch and dynamism with other techniques added along the way.  These include using Batarangs and explosive charges to take our the enemy as well as stunning or throwing them.
The Stealth parts of the game are well realised.  This is just one of the uses of detective mode which highlights armed enemies in red and unarmed in blue.  Batman is not entirely invincible.  Against automatic weapons or mêlée weapons he is vulnerable without using the right tactics.
Detective mode is also used in a limited capacity to investigate crime scenes, solve environmental puzzles and pick up trails.  this is a nice edition to the game and a great way to lead you to the next part of the story.
The Joker is not the only villain in the mix.  Bane, Zazzs, Poison Ivy and Harley Quinn all make appearances to a greater or lesser degree.
The Riddler is there as well but never in person and doesn't feel fully realised.  Instead the Riddler challenges involve collecting items such as trophies, destroying joker teeth as well as solving riddles.  These will lead you to go back and forth to areas sometimes several times to complete them as the game progresses.
Scarecrow is well realised too with some of the more scary psychotic sections of the game; leading to 2d style platforming.  This is a great change of pace if a little disturbing at times.
The boss battles and encounters are good but a number of them use the same tactics and could have done with more variety.
Challenge.
On medium difficulty, the game doesn't provide much of a challenge in the beginning.  However the difficulty does increase at a good pace, leading to some failure states and game over moments.  Fortunately the checkpoint system is well done, leading to minimal repeat gameplay required.
Hard mode is genuinely hard; removing the attack warnings from enemies and providing more of a challenge.  However this still feels fair and very satisfying to play.
Conclusion
Batman Arkham Asylum is a great game.  apart from the riddler challenges, the game is quite linear but definitely worth playing with plenty of material to keep your interest.  This game is definitely a fine example of the genre and one that should be in your library.

Van Helsing 3 is an action RPG, similar to Diablo, Torchlight, POE, and so on.
TL;DR version: Steampunk-ish ARPG, lot of content, funny story, sightly weird sometimes. Overall at this price it is well worth it.
Detailed version
Pro:
- Nice story, great characters, the dialogues are funny and fitting, quests are interesting. You are accompanied by a female ghost, who makes witty remarks and they chat a lot and such, so it is not the silent protagonist silently killing, but something more lively.
- Kinda polished, I did not meet any freeze or bug or low FPS.
- A lot of "other" stuff to do, the game has a garrison system like in WoW where you can send your lieutenants on missions and develop them, a basic crafting system (with essences and stuff), enchanting and so on.
- A lot of ways to develop your character, passives, skills, the ghost companion's skills (and she has a lot!), unique unlockable perks, elixirs that permanently increase some stats, etc.
So-so:
- Pre-made levels take some of that roguelike feeling away. Maps aren't random (well, monster distributions and loot are random), but at least they are well done, and have hidden areas and quests.
- The character advancement is a bit weird, you can have quite some skills, but why would you spread your talent points over several skills instead of focusing just 1 or 2? So kinda the same problem that Diablo 2 had and POE has. Retalenting is cheap tho.
- I really like that the dialogues are funny, but sometimes the references and jokes are a bit too much. Like the "torturing with poem"part, I got the Galaxy reference, but that was a bit out of place.
Con:
- The skills lack impact. That is so well done in Diablo, that even basic skills have a "punch", is missing here. It is more like PoE in that regard.
- Graphics in general is so-so. It has its strong moments, but sometimes there are cheap solutions.
- Balance can be weird. You get oneshotted a few times, because your opponents skills aren't really telegraphed as clearly as in Diablo for example. Sometimes you mow down hordes, sometimes a few of the bigger ones just beat you to a pulp. I wouldn't play this game in hardcore.

DO NOT BUY
This is the worst survival game I have ever played. Where do I even start...
Bad controls. For example, you run using a left mouse button! The left mouse button! Yes, you can change key bindings but the same button is used for shooting, so you either have both running and shooting on LMB or none of them.
And this is even better: You can jump and climb only on specific spots where the developer allowed you to. Forget basic logic - you can climb this truck but not the same truck over there. You can grab this ledge but not that one. This turns the game into a guessing game. Guess where's the path the level designed made for you, because you can't go anywhere else!
The savepoint system. There is only one hard savepoint at the beginning of each chapter. So if you leave the game too soon or the game crashes (happened multiple times to me), be prepared to replay last 20-30 minutes.
There are also more soft checkpoints that you can use to spawn after death but the devs had another great idea - let's severely limit the number of respawns and if you spend them all, replay the whole chapter! Isn't it a great idea in a trial&error game where you can hardly predict or plan anything during your first playthrough? Splendid! Thankfully, the easy mode has unlimited respawns.
The savepoint system has one other major catch. It also your saves your stamina capacity, health and ammo. And this brings the last "tiny" problem with...
The stamina system. This is the thing that made me quit the game for good. I'm fine with a stamina bar that you need to recharge by resting a bit. But here, if you spend all stamina points (which is often unavoidable in this game) you maximum stamina capacity starts to decrease. And the capacity doesn't recover by itself, you need to use very rare consumables to get the full stamina back.
So it's pretty easy to end up on a savepoint with only 20 % stamina bar, no consumables, and a long climbing sequence or a dust storm ahead. At this point your're done because it's impossible to continue, you die or fall almost immediately. Restarting the checkpoint doesn't help because it doesn't restore the stamina bar. And in my case the checkpoint was also a chapter savepoint so restarting the last chapter didn't help either. My only choices were either to restart the previous chapter and replay everything again (risking the same problem in the end), or to delete this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥from my computer.
I chose the latter.

Super-hero games are usually either mediocre or just bad. Fortunately for the Batman fans, his games are the exception that proves the rule.
The game features an original story where Arkham Asylum is captured by the Joker after he lets himself capture by Batman only to infiltrate Arkham Island. With the help of Harley Quinn, Joker frees Arkham's inmates which include multiple Batman villains that proceed to take over the island. Batman's task is to figure out Joker's plans and stop him.
The graphics are nothing special, what pops out is the detailed scenery and the main characters' design. The island is a very cool place to explore, full of collectibles and references to the comic books and the Batman lore.
The combat in Batman Arkham Asylum has been an inspiration to loads of other games because it's amazing. It's extremely fluid, it's got a lot of impact behind it and it looks and feels amazing with the physics engine controlling the combat animations. It's not a very complicated combat system but it sure feels and looks great. Batman is obviously equiped with a bunch of gadgets, each with a different use, some of them being usefull for both navigating the world and varying up the combat.
This game also has a bunch of extra content. As a reward for finding certain collectibles during Story Mode, you unlock detailed character models of many different character in the game, their information and origin story and other stuff that you will love if you're a Batman fan. With the GOTY edition you get some extra game modes like Survival Mode, Time Trials and others.
For the Batman fans, this game is the best thing ever along with the following games in the series. Very well developed, some of the best super-hero videogames out there.
Score: 5/5

Except where in Gems of War you're matching colors to use special abilities, in this game you're matching them to summon your 'fairies' to push back the baddie moving from right to left across the top of the screen.

Better than Human Revolution

+ Decent visuals (I don't care for them too much, they seem very jaggy, but are impressive to
say the least)
+ Gameplay still remains phenomenal, although feels somewhat cluttered at times with the
implementation of new features.
+ A large amount of detail throughout the game.
+ Generally well designed levels, if anything more or less equal to that of Deus Ex: Human
Revolution.
+ Adam Jensen feels more mature and looks really badass. I prefered him in Human Revoltion,
but he is still a great, well designed character.
- A very shallow and uninventive story - a huge let down after the buildup of Human Revolution.
- Boring sidequests. In Human Revolution, the sidequests were often upheld by a moral narrative,
and introduced interesting characters that often gave clues as to the nature of Adam Jensens
past, building the world around you.
- Characters are not fleshed out as much, and are generally uninteresting - I had a hard time
relating to them, or having any empathy for them. A few stood out, such as Miller, but most fell
flat.
- A very short story. If you fail to find any of the sidequests help fill the gaps in the game, the
story will ultimately be the downfall of the experience. The story fails to expand upon the grand,
world-spanning story of Human Revolution, and feels less epic. There is only one real hub area
that is fleshed out, and overall the story takes place within a very small space for the most part.
- Poor PC performance / poorly optimized for some systems. This is all subjective, and results
may vary, however I have struggled to obtain solid 60 FPS on medium settings. (GTX 970, i5
4690k @ 4.0 Ghz)
The majority of the problems with Mankind Divided stem from the large focus of gameplay and sidequests to fill in the gaps where the story falls short - and even then, there are very few moments where the sidequests jump out. The story does manage to jump out towards the end, but rather feels as though it should be a part of a larger story, and not the end-all-be-all of Adam Jensen's story. This is made apparent in Square Enix's focus on releasing DLC, introducing previous characters and expanding upon the story, all to make a quick buck.
At full price, I cannot recommend the game at all, at least if you are looking for a story that expands upon the previous games and will grab your attention. If you are looking for good gameplay and shiny eye-candy, I'd recommend picking this game up on sale. However, Deus Ex: Human Revolution features a much stronger story, and more gameplay, although graphics are somewhat lacking. but will run on any modern system. At full price, I'd definitely Recommend picking up Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and on sale, it is a must buy.

Free to play from
,
can be finished in under an hour. It has five achievements, all very attainable within a single playthrough. What drew me was the Tibetan theology and philosophy. I was curious to see how that got explored through the themes of life, death, sacrifice, etc. I don't feel I came away with any deeper understanding but I'm still happy with an hour well spent on a lovely, pleasing demo.
The geometry and artistry of the architecture and environment is vastly appealing to me. The "limbo" feel of this Tibetan Bardo comes through surprisingly well in the unusually detailed, expressive and charming pixel style. There's entrancing music. It's a highly meditative soundtrack.
You get the idea of the little narrative and the game's theme through reading these wisdom totems. The phrases on some of them probably don't make much sense individually until pulled together and taken as a whole.
The platforming is 100% standard fare. I laughed once when taking a giant leap into the air and falling for ages; I somehow landed precisely where I needed to be. The map is minimalistic, which is fine. The total area is so small you'll find your way quickly enough.
I'd love to see more work from this team. The art and music are wonderful and inspired. Positive review, recommended to anyone who can spare one hour for something different.

The idea is brilliant. A hypnotic, slow paced story about conflicting interests in a troubled relation. You get to choose their priorities and witness the fallout. It's most definitely not a game for kids. Though it lacks any kind of graphic detail, there's just no way kids can relate to this game. I did however find some objectionable aspects of the game. First of all, moving around the house is very, very slow. You can jump between light fixtures to speed things up, but having the simple option to move faster would make this game 200% better. Secondly, finding the items that tell the story can be frustratingly difficult at times. Thirdly, though the script is surprisingly complex, the characters are annoyingly self centered. For instance, Linda, the wife, does not seem to be working for the sake of taking care of little Tommy. She is economically dependent on Dan, the husband. Yet she cannot let him work to bring home the dough. If she had the option to be the breadwinner, this would be fine. But she does not and her scripted selfishness is impossible to mediate.

Despite that, the story line is extremely flexible. The story is right below, in the description. The rest of the story is pretty much in your own hands. Each decision will even make the character's thoughts or insights different and has the possibility of impacting the ending.
What it does good as well as that it is impossible to balance the time and sacrifice is a need. When you make a decision, you affect others in a bad way. It actually forces you to keep questioning if whatever the character is doing is so important and whether another event is more important than the other. You will find yourself spending time on one of them and yet all at the same time, forsaking relationships.

Firstly, this is an EARLY review, written on the very first day of release.
[And then updated excessively week after, with some 70h of gameplay]
And to say this first, game is not FULLY completed - you can play story and scenarios up to level30. More features (Neverending Story, levels up to 60, probably a few completely new features). If this bothers you, wait a while, instead posting negative review.
Rather than continuing leveling from VH2 - (characters can be imported, but they don't keep levels and items, they DO keep glory points and are given Epic item at start), the game offers whooping SIX classes, some redesigned builds from earlier games, but some rather unique to the whole genre, as is strength-based-stealth class I play.
This, however, is a good thing, according to yours truly. Rather than continuing old imbalances, player is offered a 'clean' start, with a NUMBER of skills reduced, but CUSTOMIZATION possibility of each increased greatly. Some players complain about lowering number of skills - but, in my 11 years of everyday playing D2:LoD i used MAX 10 shortcut skills, and even then few were timed buffs. I found no problems with number of skills.
In my opinion, done much better than in... another aRPG game, where most of skill customization is plagued by one, dominant, choice. But, as said, this is an early review, and I'll update it soon... Anyhow, each skill is highly customizable, which would (probably) lead to many player-specific styles - you don't like how certain skill works? Customize! You like a skill above all the others? Boost it to the max! And suchfort...
Voice acting, graphics and humour - a trait really rare in the genre - is on very high level, as in previous two games. Gameplay is intensive and diverse for each class.
[UPDATE]Itemization:
Firstly, most of item slots are unique to a class. Some are not (rings, and some other), so there won't be instant-godlike characters, but rather somewhat 'boosted' ones, with shared item-slots, gold and essences, which is more fair and challenging, yet not completely overpowered.
Secondly, crafting items to be exactly to needed specification is no more. Rares can be enchanted, filled with essences and have ONE affix rerolled (as many times as gold permits, though price increases every time). This is a fine addition in my book, and fully developing character to be able to play on high difficulties and gameplay worth WON'T be a 5-6h - unless you plan to speed-run casual or normal, in case when you got what you deserved.
Casual players, playing with friends, also needn't to worry - following story, exploring maps and finding secrets and easter eggs will take over 20h of gameplay for sure. If you want to do this with different characters, more.
Sets are improved, from being useless but so hard to get in VH2. They could use more buff, as well as some Epics I found, and I believe it will be done in one of next patches. Probably more will be added, VH2 had a free patch that added 120+ Epic and Godlike items.
Multiplayer - well, I don't know about it - according to developers, a new generation of netcode is implemented, so MP problems plaguing first two games should be worked out. I can neither confirm nor deny this yet.
PvP - same applied.
Endgame:
UPDATED: As said above, finished version WILL have 60 levels and Neverending Story. Current version 1.0.2 has Story Mode (up to level30) and scenarios, which are randomly created adventures consisting of three mandatory and three bonus maps, each of which require a random victory condition (eliminate main boss, collect loot from the special chest, catch Domovoys - hilarious on later levels, and so on). When the Neverending Story, a mode that will be supposedly unfinishable, is added, scenarios will serve the purpose of training characters (Glory) and farming gold (upgrade items) and items (increased droprates) to equip character better.
I know this functions, since all my playhours were with same character :)
Every now and then, a-bit-better-rare drops, then I spend some money to improve it. Improving items is luck dependent - if it fails and gives bad affix, it can be rerolled, but there is everincresing price of that service. To put simply, there is no more one hundred click on reroll until exact affix is rolled. Perhaps if the game let me import my hundred zillion billions from VH2 :) but, fortunately, it didn't.
So, I EXPECT farm more satisfying endgame, a number of reasons led me to this. But currently, it's just as said above, farming has a good timing between better item is found and it's rather promising.
Mandatory pizza comparison:
For a value of one, perhaps two, player will get rich (and funny) storyline, where quests, even if not unique, have a genre-parody value... C'mon, everyone has killed 8 pigs, then 10 pigs, and quest can't get dumber than that. Inhere, however, even when such a quest exist, it contains a well measured quantity of biting-satire, which makes it far less boring, or even funny to do... Whatabout pizza? Well, for a price of 1-2, you'll get a game that will entertain you for at least 20 times than pizzas would, and possibly much more so.
Conclusion:
The game is of near-AAA quality, and for a price several times lower. Some things, like cultural references and jokes, are unique to the rather bleak (or at its best - gloomy and depressing) genre atmosphere.
Should you buy it? If you like aRPG in general, but value unusual storyline, humorous dialogues and  story-driven game - YES! If you expect game that works absolutely flawless (mind you, after few hours of gameplay - no bugs observed) - probably 'yes', especially if you played that other AAA aRPGs, which failed to deliver at the launch...
UPDATED: If you want completely finished, polished, bugless game - you should wait some more time, it won't take long now.
Rather WAIT, than buy it and then whine and post negative reviews advising players not to buy it... This is *mine* review, and it contains what I think is objective and how *I* feel about the game. If it misled you into buying, rate it unhelpful, that's why the option is.
But if *you* wrote own negative review after 0.2h of play, and now are going around lowering positive reviews ratings - rather mature thing to do, you should be proud - one who does that will recognize himself, though there are others, too - it kinda breaks whole point of reviews. This game is *different* in atmosphere, and close to original D2, from which all of the above derived.
EDIT: as a answer to FREDDY, in my opinion games should be played in order - if for nothing else, than for rich and high-quality storyline - from what I've heard, writer is an publisher author and it shows well - a deep and rich lore, a developing story - it looks much lighter and simpler in the VH1, but gets more grim later, with the part 1 story-revisited (to a point) from a quite different angle in VH3... If you want just one, then VH2 is more feature-rich and sports leveling up to lvl60 - and then, there is where Prisoner7 appears, whose voice-acting is nothing short of amazing!
At the end, a temporary conclusion:
If you're in situation to, support indie gaming companies who make quality games. I do it - though I was a beta-tester and therefore got the previous games for free, I still contributed financially. I'm not a rich person, but I could afford to (avoid couple of pizzas and) actually *pay* for every NeoCore game so far - developing doesn't come free and one should support what one loves, or there will be none in the future.

Hack&Slash games are one of my favorite genres. Between Diablo, Torchlight, Titan Quest and Path of Exile for example, i will always come back to Van Helsing. Why? Because it has that "je ne sais quoi" hidden flavor, that thing that makes your brain giggle, your heart pump in fear and your muscles cling to the last drop of clicking power. It has complexity, it has tons of hours of gameplay, huge storyline and references. tons of dialogues and most of all, replay-ability. And that's why i choose The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing.
Now, getting to the third part of the trilogy ... the civil war has ended around Borgovia but the sinister Prisoner 7, who betrayed Van Helsing in the end of the second game, meddled with the Ink and new monsters have risen to give our hero no time to rest. In The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing 3 you will find 6 classes which you can play with: defeat your foes as the melee-specialist Protector, be the most accurate shooter as the Bounty Hunter, master the weird science as the Phlogistoneer, engineer your tactics as the Constructor, control the magical forces as the Elementalist or become a dark, stealthy killer as the Umbralist. And bear in mind, you are still accompanied by the beautiful, humorous, lethal but loyal lady Katarina. I was glad to hear that in this last part of the trilogy we will learn the story of her past.
Set in a steampunkish-gothic environment, you will have to take your time and admire all the surroundings. Clear up the level filled with monstrosities, set back and watch how every single detail brings you closer and deeper into the grim story. There are also secrets hidden around, so watch your step and search every single corner of your road ahead.
The customization levels are vast enough so you can set your own playstyle and combat strategies. Perks, auras, skills and talent points will be a sweet experience for you ARPGs lovers and also the plethora of items you will find around. Katarina will also have all of these customizations available, so keep an eye on her level-up and the items that she can use.

In my opinion, this game missed out on so much. You're brought into a world/environment that could be rife with background and stories but somehow they manage to leave you (or me, at least) feeling both wanting to know more about it and also not caring about what is told about what happened. A lot fo the comments about whatever took place feel like a passing explanation - as if no thought has been put into it and just trying to brush it off.
The main character's story/search feels COMPLETELY dismissed for 95% of the game. I can understand being a character that wants to help people but when it comes to the point of getting home and not finding what you wanted, right there it seems to be thrown onto the backburner. The character says now and then "Oh I'm here doing this" - NO YOU'RE NOT! You get thrown on everyone else's errands. When it does loop back to the point he is going to continue onto his search, I found I just couldn't care less anymore.
When it comes to the controls, they just seem...off. I kept finding myself climbing down onto ledges without meaning to, not being able to jump down or climb up when I NEEDED to - leading to me dying. Or aiming at an enemy and suddenly it aims at the one without the gun, or on one occassion I found I died because while trying to aim at a particular enemy the auto-aim just kept looping through the FOUR that were closing in on me. And it's so very repetitive! There's so much climbing that it just ends up with no tension as your stamina decreases because you've seen/heard it a million times, and it just feels like a chore. I thought things would get more interesting when they brought in the rope-swing but found it only gets used a couple of times, and then it's so stiff and lifeless that it just sucks you out of the game further.
I've actually recorded this as a series on my YT channel and the honest reason I continued it until the end was how ridiculous it was trying to do anything. Parts were rage-inducing, but mostly it was laughable at how stupid it all seemed. I'm glad I played through it just so I know how rubbish I found it, but I would recommend others to just go onto YouTube and watch it. Or if you are going to buy it, make sure it's on one hell of a sale.

It took me 13 hours to finally beat the game on Normal, and I don't feel like I have earned it. This is coming from someone that doesn't play many shooters on PC, especially ones as fast paced as this game. I didn't win because of any amazing skill on my part, but that run through the Ziggurat just happened to work out in terms of perks, items, and rooms. This is glaring issue plagues an otherwise decently fun shooter.
The standard experience seems rather unbalanced, leaving me to believe that nearly every aspect of the game is randomly generated. I've had good runs die when two enemy types that have very difficult attacks to dodge spawn together and take me from near full health to none in seconds. This is only one of many scenarios that kill runs even with highly skilled play.
The thing I dislike the most about the game is that it's designed to get easier every time you fail a run, by unlocking new characters/perks/items. This is frustrating because you HAVE to die over and over to unlock anything good, as your win percentage with starting equipment is near zero. The game sets you up for failure from the beginning.
The final boss is wildly more difficult than any previous ones, where the fight boils down to having a large enough health pool to tank its near impossible to dodge attacks to deal enough damage to kill it. Thankfully, I had a really good staff and many perks in damage resistance and max health, so I was able to outlast its attacks.
Though it has its problems, Ziggurat has a good amount of replayability and diversity to keep me coming back for a quick run every now and again, though it usually ends in frustration. Give it a try at a steep discount or as part of a bundle if any of this appeals to you.

It's Binding of Isaac but first person 3D and you're a wizard.
The atmosphere is absolutely fantastic, captures that awesome colorful 90's dungeon feel. No brown/gray drab to be found here. It also runs incredibly smoothly. Truly unbelievable that this was made by a handful of people.
Just enough story to keep you interested without making you keep track of a thousand things. Something you can leave and come back to at your leisure.
Becomes extremely mechanically challenging without just ramping up enemy health and damage. How long has it been since that happened, huh?
Lots of very diverse characters to play as that can make one run wildly different from the next.
Lots of awesome weapons (You can have a Wizard Shotgun). I will say that a few of the spell and staff weapons are redundant, but maybe I just haven't unlocked the really cool ones (12 hours in and I've only cleared maybe 10% of content. Definitely worth the price tag).
Lots of really creative monsters with specialized attack patterns to memorize.
My only real complaint is that sprinting causes a nauseating motion blur on screen that can't be turned off (even though I explicitly tried to turn off "motion blur" - didn't work).
It's been a long time since we just had a quality gameplay experience that didn't introduce a bunch of unfun gimmicky crap in the name of "advancing the genre". That didn't have an in-game store. That didn't get preachy with real-world morality. Overall just a 9/10

Small rooms filled with enemies that turn every inch of the floor into poison. Large rooms with enemies that can read your mind and snipe you with fire bombs. Like losing the ability to choose your level ups, or damage reduction/defense increase combos that just make the game super slow. Played through on Hard first try, got about 80% of all of the collectables and secrets (there are hundreds). Very well made game, and rife with awesome Batman info/lore.
The ONLY complaint I have with this game is the combat system. The combat isn't very complicated because there are many parts where you need to neutralize enemies in stealth, as any good Batman should. The problem here is that, because the combat is stretched so thin between straight up fighting and stealth, it does neither perfectly.
STEALTH - Stealth is a very wishy-washy thing in this game, and because everything in a room is illuminated the same, you don't know if you are in hiding or if a gargoyle you've perched on is not actually putting you in the shadows. You can't fight enemies with guns straight up, so you are frequently forced into the stealth role.
HAND-TO-HAND - Much of the straight up combat in this game is luck-based. Not all of it, but enough to be minorly frustrating in Hard mode. There is a 'counter' button while you're fighting that can counter an enemy's basic attack, but the prompt to counter shows up only 50% of the time, and even at that rate, it is very unlikely that you hitting the correct button will actually counter the enemy's attack because you're already in full swing of your own attack.
And here inlies the main problem with this game - the 'difficulty'. Because of these certain flaws in the combat, the way the developers ramped up the difficulty was by not making certain enemies harder, but just simply putting more enemes in the combat with you. That isn't very good game design, in my opinion. Because not all attacks are properly counter-able, the more enemies you're fighting, the more you're at the whim of the randomness of the game and how the enemies approach you. I have often found myself having to replay some battles where I play noticeably worse, but win the overall battle becaue of the random way certain enemes approach or attack you.
Yes, this is a fantastic game, but it's minor flaws turn into glaring ones during certain parts of the game. I would still highly reccomend it, but maybe not for a scaling challenge, but more for batman and adventure / collect-em-all fans.

I LOVE(D) this game. It had great promise, a solid plan, and was the fortress builder of my dreams. Now, it goes in the same bin as Towns, another building game that will never be finished.
Upon full release,  content promised upon EA purchase, and content the game still sorely needs,  was cut out because the developer simply didn't want to work on it anymore. As a result, new features and support are expected to be added by the community. In short, this game is now MODware, and even the origianl Modders didn't stick around for long because there isn't much about the game that's modable aside from the appearence of items, resource requirements, and growth timers.
Let me be perfectly clear about this, as many continue to attack me over the issue. You WILL NOT realize how incomplete the game is until you have played for several hours, at least. Much of the incomplete content and game balancing issues rear thier ugly head only after you have played for around 4-8 game years. Those years generally take around 2+ hrs each depending on how meticulous you are with building and how grand your designs. I cannot be more honest in telling you that the game becomes an absolute bore as a result, even to the point it effects your later playthroughs, because you realize there is just so little to look foward to.
People have asked for a list of Pros and Cons so I made one.
PROS:
- Closest thing to Dwarf Fortress on the market
- A solid early game balance that's fresh every time.
- Excellent building customizeability that's sadly rare in many DF clones
- A solid (if simple) in game economy that requires all of your gnomes working together in order to progress.
- A cusomizeable military
- A gadget research path that allows the use of advanced player made mechanisms, ranged weapons, simple and complex traps systems, and automoton population replacements.
CONS:
- Closest thing to Dwarf Fortress, still far from it in terms of depth and gameplay
- Late game is incredibaly boring due to balance issues and stale enemies.
- Enemies are easy to manipulate. Even on harder difficulties it is easy to control how many and how much they attack you.
- Enemies have no ranged attacks, making gnome ranged weapons OP, especially from behind walls or on cliffs
- Enemy and gnome AI is very basic. Enemies will never try to avoid trapped entrances or find another way into your fort.
-The military customization becomes pointless in late game. Many perks and traits are just not worth taking, or are for a game with considerably more advanced enemies (heres a missing content hint). Eventually evey melee gnome will simply have plate armor. There's just no reason to do otherwise.
- Combat gnome training becomes rediculous to the point your soldiers become combat gods. Goblins, mants, and skeletons become limbed in seconds and the only way the enemies remain a threat is if you intentionally overwhelm yourself or your army decides to sleep through the attack.
- Farming options are INCREDIBLY limited. You have 3 types of livestock. 2 types of fruit trees. 2 ground fruits, Cotton, Wheat, and underground mushrooms. If you want to build underground, your stuck with just mushrooms.
- Music becomes very repetitive for this type of game. You'll eventually mute it and play something else. Unfortuneatly, goblin warnings are tied to the music, so preventing yourself from going crazy gimps you. Not that it matters after a few playthroughs.
- Building is virtually limitless but the blocks used to decorate it are incredibally limited. Again, this is more of a veteran issue and some may have no issues with it at all. Also solvable with mods.
- The gadget research is also limited. You learn everything there is to know in about 2 to 3 yrs of in game time, with just one researcher.
- Heres one many don't know about, but as a deep dweller I'll tell you. The bottom 2/3 of the map is ALWAYS the same. Every playthrough I've had has had the same layout of rock formations at level 50, the place I started building kingdoms after getting bored with how easy the surface is. THIS GAME IS NOT TRULY ROUGELIKE
TLDR: The game is missing content such as diplomacy, enemies, and building/farming options, that are required to keep one's interest beyond the first two or three playthroughs. Even after release, I just couldn't get back into the game given how dull I knew it would become. Some of the game breaking bugs have been ironed out, but I just can't play it long enough to test all of them, so I'll assume the game is considerably less buggy than it used to be. Again, the developer abandoned his project before release. This is now MODware. Whether its worth the $15 or not is up to you, but I can't in all honesty reccomend a game I know is incomplete.

Always Sometimes Monsters is an interesting game that promises to deal with the darker themes of life through the ability of choice, and its consequences and rewards. However, the game falls short.
First of all the graphics, surprisingly not a problem. I'm not a huge RPGMaker fan, but the game does what it can to make the graphics good within RPGMaker's limitations. While this may be a problem for some, it really doesn't interfere with the game.
The music for the game is very well made, but when it loops the audio can sometimes cut out for a few seconds which is a bit annoying. After listening to the same few loops it can get a bit annoying, but generally it's very good.
Now for the main part of the game, the gameplay (really the writing). A game like this isn't bought for gameplay, which just consists of running between buildings and people and talking, choosing dialogue options, finding items, etc. The writing is where this game falls short. It's promise to deal with serious topics falls short because of the game's absolutely horrible approach to dealing with serious topics. At certain times, I can't tell if it's poking fun at the topic or seriously trying to be dark. The amount of obvious tongue-in-cheek references to other video games and video game review sites also go overboard after they start to interfere with actual writing, such as the scene in the theatre, which seems to be an obvious cash-in.
From the short while I played, I really wanted to like the game, but the writing was not very good. It was goofy in too many ways, and this ruined what otherwise would have been a very good game. Maybe it'll be better if I play more, but from what I've seen I wouldn't recommend it to anyone interested in this genre of game.

At first there was Dwarf Fortress. And then there was my complete and utter lack of patience for the tedious micro-management and brutal difficulty of that particular game. (Read: I love it, but sometimes lack the attention to detail it requires.) This began my search to find a similar, but somewhat less dense version of Dwarf Fortress. I came across them in droves. Rimworld, Timber and Stone, Prison Architect, and of course Gnomoria being foremost among them. Gnomoria is a game, that while being more limited in its options and features than Dwarf Fortress, still manages to capture its charm and fun.
To say that Gnomoria is a blatant clone of Dwarf Fortress, does it little justice, though there is no denying a certain amount of inspiration must have certainly come from that title. This much is evident as you first embark to your new settlement. After naming your map (or fortress, or whatever you may want to call it), and choosing some options for difficulty, Gnomoria plants you into a procedurally generated map. You're able to determine if the map is mountainous, flat, or perhaps even a bit hilly via a few sliders if you choose to customize the advanced settings. This all ensures you'll never have the same map twice.
You'll only have a handful of gnomes at first as well as a very limited number of supplies. Now from here, it's up to you to determine the fate of your gnomish minions. While you can't directly control your gnomes, there are a number of ways to determine how they will behave. You're able to designate professions which will determine what sort of generated tasks your gnomes will be able to complete. Gnomoria even allows for you to create and name custom professions which will then carry out specific tasks. This gives you pretty solid control over how your colony prioritizes work. I've found this feature to be particularly useful in the beginning as gnomes are not apt to doing things efficiently using only the default professions. If you wish, you can create professions that will only carry out military tasks. Assign them to squads, train them, arm them. If you master these menus, which is not difficult by any stretch thanks to Gnomoria's simple but effective UI, you will be much better off for it.
Gnomoria really shines in its ability to let you sculpt the land. For anyone who has played any of a number of voxel-cube based games (Minecraft, Space Engineers, etc.,), this part will be quite familiar. However, in this instance, you will be viewing the world through an isometric perspective rather than first person. You can tunnel and dig anywhere and everwhere, but be warned, unlit tunnels sometimes spawn deadly enemies such as skeletons and even zombies. Use raw stone to craft blocks and then you can begin building a fortress. One of my favorite features here is the 'replace' tool. Using this you can easily replace any block with any other type of block. I'll often find myself following the natural geometry of the landscape to determine the layout of my settlements and simply replacing the dirt walls and floors with more permanent stone or wood. It's been quite a lot of fun being the architect of some pretty grand fortresses. Players should be careful to not get carried away with doing too much at once though as it will keep your gnomes from completing other tasks of higher priority to you.
Gnomoria has a lot of great features. You can craft arms and armor for your gnomes, or craft trinkets and statues for trade. You can farm food and brew drinks to keep your gnomes alive through the winter. Fend off goblin invasions, endure monster and animal attacks, and brave the deepest caves. There is, undeniably, a lot to do in Gnomoria. If any of that sounds fun to you, I think that you'll find this game to be worth the modest price. I've enjoyed Gnomoria, that much is true, but what's more is that I will definitely continue to enjoy it for some time.

The long wait has been worth it. If you’re a PC gamer who’s spent the last eighteen months envying the console crowd while they all got stuck into the latest, greatest GTA, then rest assured that you can now play the definitive version. Sure, the Xbox One and PS4 versions were amazing, delivering GTA 5 at higher resolutions with more detailed textures, smoother surfaces, better lighting and cool depth of field effects (see our full review below), but the PC version offers even more enhancements plus a couple of additional features that play to the PC’s strengths. In doing so, it adds a few more metres to one of gaming’s towering achievements.
Having covered the game twice already, we won’t go too far into the detail of what makes GTA 5 so good. Partly, it’s a question of experience. With four previous 3D GTAs under its belt plus Red Dead Redemption, Bully and assorted DLC packs, Rockstar has had time to refine its vision for open world gameplay and its systems, and GTA 5 has the best driving, the best shooting and some of the best mission design of the series.
It’s also a question of structure. Dividing the action amongst three protagonists with three interlocking storylines and three distinctive flavours means you nearly always have the option to flick from Michael’s ageing career criminal saga to Franklin’s ambitious hoodlum story to Trevor’s crazed, amoral brand of mayhem, where the dumb, cathartic slapstick violence we all – deep down – love GTA for finds its natural home. With repeated play, it only becomes clearer how well all three tales mesh thematically with Rockstar’s savage satirical take on the Californian dream.
