Simple Review: You're basically in a bad 1980's movie about a dystopian future, where there's lights, neon, and chrome on everything. All the cutscenes are reminiscent of an 8-bit console game in that they look like the cutscenes from the original Ninja Gaiden except with a cybernetic commando. And you'll spend a few minutes wondering to yourself about if it's harder to fake bad writing, instead of just being a bad writer in earnest. Then they drop in neon dinosaurs with laser vision and you realize that you don't really care about the answer anymore.
Longer Review: I'll get to the UPlay dynamic at the end, because at this point if you're going to get an Ubisoft game review that has become a weird requirement.
So it's in a nutshell a Far Cry game, that they went tongue and cheek with a mass of references to the 80's. Graphically it's Far Cry3, except always dusk, and with neon everywhere. It can also be completed in 18 hours. That's not a speed walkthrough, that's exploring everything and finding all the hidden bits. Also the end boss battle was kind of lackluster, in that it was nonexistent. Still I enjoyed it. It does display a framerate counter in the upper left of the screen that I couldn't get rid of, but it's not distracting enough to take you out of the immersion.
On to the UPlay bit: I work on boats. That's literally my job, I go out and sail about on large boats (or ships if you want to be weird about it) for about 50% of the year. The big thing for me in purchasing a game is knowing that it will allow me to access and use it without an incoming internet feed. Steam gives the offline option, and other than making it look like I've played certain games for 0.2 hours, but have still completed them fully there doesn't seem to be any issue there. Unexpectedly UPlay does allow you to go offline and access your games. This would be the end of it, except when I attempted to play it disabled my mouse input. Technically you can still play a FPS with no mouse, but it really won't be all that of an enjoyable experience.
Still all things considered, I enjoyed it quite a bit.

I regret writing this review, as I was really hoping the Novelist, which got a ton of main stream attention, was a worthy entry in the line of "slice of life" poetic games like Dear Esther and Gone Home.
Unfortunately, where both Dear Esther and Gone Home have something interesting to say about both games and life, The Novelist flounders and gets lost in a sea of "first world problems" that makes it hard to empathize with any of the characters.
From a gameplay perspective, the game is boring, symetical, and repetitive.  After finishing the first chapter, you'll be amazed by the potential.  By chapter three, you'll realize you're caught in a gameplay loop of boredom: Find three clues for each of the three characters until you complete each of the three chapters of each of the three episodes.  Yes, that is boring game design.
Real Life doesn't work in threes.  So, the family feels compartmentalized, fake and droning.  Unfortunately, where the game could have excelled is with allowing your choices to have meaningful effects on the gameplay paths.
Unlike The Walking Dead, this game is self-contained, so it would have been much more realistic to have a few branches based on player decisions.
Unforutnately all of the "branches" are just props placed around the house and a simple follow up letter or picture on the next day after your decision.  Ultimately, there's a recap at the end of the game which crams your decisions into three (that number again) binary "good" or "bad" results.
Ultimately, this game had a lot of potential.  The base format would be a great idea for a scenario where something interesting happens.  White Patriarch trying to decide whether he should drink whiskey or build his son's car is not interesting.   At least not in the way it's presented here.
Thumbs down, unfortunately.

I honestly really do love this game; it's poking fun at different characters, genres, and franchises (not to mention a lot of the characters themselves are actually great in their own ways.) There are two big problems I find however, though one of them seems to just be the deal w/ clicker games.
1. It gets old fast. If you don't soft-reset often and/or have a bunch of speed-boosts, it gets a bit stale...
2. The annoyingly insane requirements some of the girls have. Some of them have level requirements that are either just stupidly hard for the point in the game they're in, or are just insanely hard in general. For example, Nina's first Car-gift requirement; you might have a good deal of money at that point in the game, but not nearly enough for a car. Another stick-out example in bad placement is the later added Ayano; her starting requirements are easy, but then a few levels in you get 1000 plush toys as a requirement... (Also, the fact that her last level requirement is level 60 in 3 or 4 skills.)
And for examples of insane for the point of being insane/annoying; at least half of Eva's levels if you don't have an auto-clicker, at least half of Luna's friggin' gifts, a good chunk of Karma's (and some of Sutra's) gift-requirements.
I'm still reccommending the game though, because some of the lines are pure gold, and the references, self-jabs, and characters themselves are enjoyable and funny most of the time (and some of the girls are just really frickin' cute, tbh.)

Gah, this game needs a middle option between recommend and not.
It's not bad, it's more that its issues are exacerbated by being a roguelite.  Specifically, there's two issues that REALLY bring this game down:
1. The game is balanced around you picking up experience orbs, but doing so is often extremely dangerous, and they disappear too quickly.  This could've been mitigated by simply automatically giving you experience upon killing enemies, or at least making sure the orbs never disappear.
2. Despite this being a projectile based shooter, and not a hitscan one like Wolfenstein or Serious Sam, enemies track you FAR too well, and unless you're playing on Easy, they hit insanely hard.  Some enemies simply aim well, others actually fire homing projectiles, some can fill whole rooms with their poison/fire/etc.  It just feels unfair at times.  It's seriously easier to dodge hitscan shots from zombies in Doom than the projectile weapons here.  And then the game's final boss is just blatantly OP and unfair.
The first issue is pretty contentious by any standards (IIRC, Tower of Guns and Kingdom Hearts both have the same issue), but the second is only a problem because this is a roguelite.  Were this a game where you could save normally, you could practice and it might not feel so bad dying to a random hit from seemingly nowhere.
In spite of all this, I don't think it's a terrible game... just not one I can easily recommend.  If anything, this is probably the best FPS-roguelite, maybe even the best roguelite involving shooting period (only Binding of Isaac Rebirth, Relic Hunters Zero, and Nuclear Throne would rival it), on the market as of this post.  But the thing is, you're either playing it for the short game on Easy, which is only about 2 - 3 hours of your time, or the long game on any other difficulty, which is pure frustration.
If you're ok with such a short game at $14.99 (read, Easy difficulty) then I recommend it.
If you love roguelites in general and get pleasant tingles at the thought of a game being blatantly unfair and masochistic (read: any other difficulty besides Easy), then I recommend it.
If you get the game on a sale or Humble Bundle, then I recommend it.
If you just wanna shoot stuff and don't care about anything else, then I probably recommend it, as you could do a lot worse than this.  I mean, it doesn't have THE best shooting/combat mechanics in the world or anything, but they're pretty fun, especially by roguelite standards.
For everyone else?  I probably would not recommend it.

First of all, I didn't know of this game until I saw it on YouTube (for me, it's the best way to see the game as it is, without having to trust someone's opinion) and found it interesting enough to try. People say it could've been better (and it's not uncommon for Ubisoft to promise more and deliver less), but I only saw the final product and I base my opinion on that.
What's good
- Post-apocalyptic setting with modern day people reduced to savage state.
- The concept of making an extreme effort and losing stamina capacity after depleting the bar.
- More or less open world with lots of secrets (even a place to catch a breath over the dust-filled streets is a welcome discovery) that often require risky approach to find and reach.
- Bandits with varying attitude: some don't take you seriously and even try to attack if you hold them at gunpoint for too long without shooting, some are not too brave and submit at gunpoint or after someone else has been shot.
- Music that fits the visual style (and that creepy loop inside the boat is a full Silent Hill experience).
What's bad
- Clunky controls, with action prompt not always coming up (I had one guy standing IN the fire and still wasn't able to push him; Leonidas in me was disappointed) or the character trying to mimic the camera direction with his movements, refusing to move at all sometimes.
- Weird gamepad buttons assignment and no way to remap them.
- Camera is wayward and target switching is way too sensitive (it even allows turning backwards from the enemy, which makes no sense and only brings harm).
- Weapon slots not assigned to number keys, only to mouse wheel, which makes weapon selection hard to control mid-combat.
- The ending that feels more unfinished than simply "open".
What's broken
- Keyboard shuts down or gets stuck on one key every now and then, have to plug it out and back in 3-4 times per hour on average. The problem doesn't depend on keyboard manufacturer and is known since
2012, but has not been patched to this day. Given the Ubisoft officials' initial refusal to port the game at all (and the game is worth porting, despite its flaws) on the ground of all PC gamers being pirates, such obvious bug in PC version is appaling to say the least. Well, modern day Ubisoft can't even make a Tetris game right…
So, I give it 7.5/10. The game is overall enjoyable if you are into exploration, but it's a bit unfinished and seriously lacks quality in porting.

is a FPS Rogue-like as in there no permanent upgrades that extend beyond a single playthrough. There are cards that you unlock which you can choose from at level up and unlocking more simply alters which ones have a chance of dropping contained within each run. There are also class unlocks but these too only augment the starting health, mana pool size and basic wand attack fire rate. So far as I to what was able to glean. I only unlocked 3 plus the 2 basic of the 10+ classes but the differences were trivial betwixt them. The rest seemed to be unlocked by simply grinding more time.
The main mode has you navigate a dungeon and go into rooms with an specific objective in order to move on. Usually it's kill all the things. Occasionally it'll be destroy the obelisks and then kill all the things. There are other rooms that provide a place to offer things to the gods in exchange for upgrades. Or other rooms filled with traps and some sort of platforming navigation puzzle. The main goal being to find the portal key and summon the level guardian. Defeat them and prosper. Some rooms will have augmented rule sets: Such as certain weapons doing more damage, invisible enemies or not being able to see you health and mana bars.
Easy mode is appropriately named. Taking me only around 1 hour 20 minutes to “complete” with the main character. There is also a Gauntlet mode which entails a single room with waves of enemies sirvival mode.
Now, I realize I may be coming off a bit dismissive. The game is fun. I enjoy it. But I have to say it's a bit monotonous. The weapon types are not that diverse, you'll likely spend more time than you want waiting for your basic wand to recharge. Personally, I love rogue(ish – again like and lite) but I usually prefer slower paced ones that are a bit more mechanically involved. Being reductive, this game boils down to shooting all the things and repeating that action. That's not inherently a bad thing.. it's just not a very interesting thing.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a truly remarkable experience and one that shouldn't be missed. So what about the PC controls?
I don't know what I can say about this game that hasn't been said (probably better) by somebody else. Basically, believe the hype: it really is one of the best games ever made and shouldn't be missed by anybody who calls himself a gamer. So instead of doing a feature breakdown of the game, I thought I would discuss the PC control scheme.
Arkham Asylum is first and foremost a console game in that it's clear to me now that it was designed to be played as a console game. The good news is that Rocksteady didn't lazily port the game to the PC but actually took the time to make sure it controlled like a proper PC game via mouse and keyboard, a control scheme which actually works out pretty well. However, I do have a some criticisms:
First of all, during combat, the "counter" control is mapped to the right mouse button as a short click. The problem is that Batman's gadgets are also mapped to the right mouse button as a long click, so during combat, if you hold down the right mouse button just a little too long, Batman will equip whatever gadget is currently selected instead of countering the henchman's strike which leaves you wide open to attack. It's not game breaking, and I never lost a brawl because of it, but it happens frequently enough to be annoying, especially when going for the "Perfect Knight" bonus on a challenge map.
Another area where the PC controls fall down is during a few notable sequences where you control Batman from a fixed perspective rather than the over-the-shoulder perspective with a free camera. This means that instead of pressing W to move Batman forward and steering him with the mouse, the W, A, S, and D keys act as compass directions. This actually really screwed with my muscle memory making those few sequences more difficult and frustrating than they needed to be. The final showdown in particular had me begging for an over-the-shoulder camera to the point that I searched online to see if anybody had created a mod for one! (They hadn't).
My final comment is that some of the key combinations just never felt intuitive to me for whatever reason. Even after 20-hours of play I still found myself hitting the wrong button combinations and having trouble remembering if it was a SHIFT + right click to perform an instant takedown or a CTRL + right click, or whatever. Now maybe this is just a personal mental hang-up of mine, but I can't think of any other games off the top of my head that I've had a similar difficulty with.
So out of curiosity I bought a 360 controller to see what that experience was like, and to my surprise, it actually offers a superior control scheme to the much beloved-by-PC gamers mouse/keyboard combo. That's when it became clear to me that this is how Rocksteady intended the game to be played. I found the controls intuitive, and the game is generally easier to play with everything conveniently at your fingertips. The software is even intelligent enough to change the onscreen prompts depending on which input you're using, and I found it easier to read them because the prompts for the controller are indicated by big, colorful icons that can be discerned without having to look at them directly as opposed to the grey text you see when using mouse/keyboard. As for the fixed-perspective sequences, they work much better with an analog stick than they do with WASD. In fact I was so impressed with how well the 360 controller works with Arkham Asylum that I immediately started a new game even though I had just completed the game the night before.
In summary, I highly recommend Batman: Arkham Asylum, and while the mouse/keyboard works well enough, do yourself a favor and play it the way it was meant to be played, with a 360 controller.

The Grand Theft Auto series is like the Dan Brown of video games.  Honestly, they're way less clever than they think they are, and they have a schtick that they have been going with forever and figure that it hasn't gotten old.
People don't read Dan Brown for real-world facts or relatable characters that people like.  Similarly, people don't actually enjoy the GTA games for their hard-hitting parody of American culture as conceived by a room full of Nigels.
Don't buy it for the pathetic attempt at social commentary that comes off like someone told a 6 year old what "satire" was.  Buy it for the GAME - which is amazing.
The environments, the characters (again, avoiding the heavy-handed attempts at political or social "humor"), the actual PLOT are all fantastic.  The soundtrack is great, the amount of content is genuinely overwhelming.  The driving mechanics (at least with mouse and keyboard) are honestly some of the best I've played.  Just driving in this game is a delight.  Coming out of the hills at night to see the lights of north Vinewood spread out in front of you, blowing by traffic while "Sleepwalking" is on the radio is more compressed awesome in one moment of playing than some games can deliver through their entire game.
Long story short: the game itself is incredible.

I pretty much love this game.  The ridiculous 1980's neon future art and theming is definitely a part of that, but there's more to it then just that.  Blood Dragon takes the good parts of Far Cry 3 and leaves out a lot of the bloat, including the slow, laborious upgrade system.
Blood Dragon does take away some of the "open world" feel to the game (which is intact, but much less pronounced or "free" as in FC3), but I believe it to be a worth sacrifice for a tighter experience.  Where I feel that FC3 was probably 75% filler and only 25% "killer", Blood Dragon is probably the opposite, if not 100% killer.
That is, of course, as long as you like the sometimes-sneaky sometimes-loud first-person shooting that Far Cry 3, BD, and now FC4 all offer.
There is a caveat to all of this, however, and one that is a deal-breaker for some.  That caveat is Uplay.  Ubisoft's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t DRM/PC gaming platform that doesn't work half the time and is often a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  Honestly it didn't really interrupt my experience with Blood Dragon at all, despite being a minor annoyance to starting the game up.  If you've had bad experiences with, or refuse to use, Uplay, then obviously you're just going to have to miss out on Blood Dragon.
If you're like me and can look past Uplay, Blood Dragon offers a great FPS experience.  Don't expect a breathtaking story, but the gameplay has honestly kept me entertaining through two complete playthroughs, including restarting and completing all the fortresses at least once.

The Roguelike is one of the most obscurely defined game genres, so I'm not sure this is technically one.
It's definitely a game I enjoy a lot though.
Nerdook Productions, generally better known for their in-browser flash games has delivered a solid game somewhat comparable to
.
The player chooses one of three heroes with various traits, spells and weapons assigned randomly and sets off to conquer a dungeon that is about a dozen floors deep.
As the name implies though, each 'floor' is already quite deep, as the entire game is very much a descent through a random environment (seen from the side in colourful 2D graphics). The width of your screen is always the width of the level. You will fight your way down each floor to the bottom where a sealed portal lies. To unlock the seal you must defeat the boss or unlock it using 5 keys (which you also expend to open locked trapdoors earlier in the level and treasure chests) or, if the situation or an aspect of your character allow for it, destroy the wall surrounding the portal.
As you defeat enemies you gain experience and gold, the experience goes directly to your current character to empower him/her, the gold is primarily used between runs to get better base stats and upgrades as well as at merchants you encounter randomly on some floors that will sell you new weapons, traits and spells.
The whole thing wraps up nicely with a satisfying and challenging final boss.
One of the main things that sets this game apart from similar games (or specifically Rogue Legacy) is that not killing enemies is a viable alternative. Until you've killed your first enemy on each floor you'll be able to see and pick up pacifist sigils that are dotted around the level. Picking these up will grant experience and gold, same as killing enemies. It's not always a viable option (sometimes you'll really need to dispatch enemies in your path), but it's nice that there's an incentive to change things up every now and then and not kill everything in sight.
I've compared this game several times now to Rogue Legacy, which might not be entirely fair.
The question is, though, does this game offer anything that Rogue Legacy doesn't?
It does, and it's a game I recommend. However, if you've not yet played Rogue Legacy I couldn't recommend this
, so I would suggest playing that first.

Honestly, I really enjoyed the game. It was a fun, simplistic title where you assumed the role of a helpless suicidal baby and a rightfully overprotective father. As much as I did enjoy it though, the following cause me not to be able to recommend it yet, though I'll gladly recommend it in the future, as it becomes better:
-The join game system is clunky and non-functional at times. I spent as much as 3-5 minutes clicking constantly in hopes of being able to join a game. My suggestion for this is to make a matching system, where you'll automatically be paired up with someone, and you can immediately rejoin that queue once the round ends, you can play again with the person, or exit out to the menu. If one wanted to play with a friend, they could make a private lobby and have the friend join. This could open up doors for customizable rounds as well.
-There isn't yet enough to really do. It's fun and humorous killing yourself as a baby varying ways, and it's sometimes fun to be the overseer of the baby as the father, but on both ends of the spectrum, I found myself getting bored after a time. There was no incentive to continue, not enough to make me excited to keep playing, not enough to keep me entertained.
So, as I have said, I love this game, I find it really fun, but the novelty wears off, and then you're left to wonder "Where's My Money" instead of "Who's Your Daddy".

At first there was Dwarf Fortress. And then there was my complete and utter lack of patience for the tedious micro-management and brutal difficulty of that particular game. (Read: I love it, but sometimes lack the attention to detail it requires.) This began my search to find a similar, but somewhat less dense version of Dwarf Fortress. I came across them in droves. Rimworld, Timber and Stone, Prison Architect, and of course Gnomoria being foremost among them. Gnomoria is a game, that while being more limited in its options and features than Dwarf Fortress, still manages to capture its charm and fun.
To say that Gnomoria is a blatant clone of Dwarf Fortress, does it little justice, though there is no denying a certain amount of inspiration must have certainly come from that title. This much is evident as you first embark to your new settlement. After naming your map (or fortress, or whatever you may want to call it), and choosing some options for difficulty, Gnomoria plants you into a procedurally generated map. You're able to determine if the map is mountainous, flat, or perhaps even a bit hilly via a few sliders if you choose to customize the advanced settings. This all ensures you'll never have the same map twice.
You'll only have a handful of gnomes at first as well as a very limited number of supplies. Now from here, it's up to you to determine the fate of your gnomish minions. While you can't directly control your gnomes, there are a number of ways to determine how they will behave. You're able to designate professions which will determine what sort of generated tasks your gnomes will be able to complete. Gnomoria even allows for you to create and name custom professions which will then carry out specific tasks. This gives you pretty solid control over how your colony prioritizes work. I've found this feature to be particularly useful in the beginning as gnomes are not apt to doing things efficiently using only the default professions. If you wish, you can create professions that will only carry out military tasks. Assign them to squads, train them, arm them. If you master these menus, which is not difficult by any stretch thanks to Gnomoria's simple but effective UI, you will be much better off for it.
Gnomoria really shines in its ability to let you sculpt the land. For anyone who has played any of a number of voxel-cube based games (Minecraft, Space Engineers, etc.,), this part will be quite familiar. However, in this instance, you will be viewing the world through an isometric perspective rather than first person. You can tunnel and dig anywhere and everwhere, but be warned, unlit tunnels sometimes spawn deadly enemies such as skeletons and even zombies. Use raw stone to craft blocks and then you can begin building a fortress. One of my favorite features here is the 'replace' tool. Using this you can easily replace any block with any other type of block. I'll often find myself following the natural geometry of the landscape to determine the layout of my settlements and simply replacing the dirt walls and floors with more permanent stone or wood. It's been quite a lot of fun being the architect of some pretty grand fortresses. Players should be careful to not get carried away with doing too much at once though as it will keep your gnomes from completing other tasks of higher priority to you.
Gnomoria has a lot of great features. You can craft arms and armor for your gnomes, or craft trinkets and statues for trade. You can farm food and brew drinks to keep your gnomes alive through the winter. Fend off goblin invasions, endure monster and animal attacks, and brave the deepest caves. There is, undeniably, a lot to do in Gnomoria. If any of that sounds fun to you, I think that you'll find this game to be worth the modest price. I've enjoyed Gnomoria, that much is true, but what's more is that I will definitely continue to enjoy it for some time.

A game is not absolved of having bad design just because it critizes other games for having bad design. Just because the game presents a generic 'captured-princess' story while saying, "isn't this generic?" doesn't make it excusable. Its laziness, and makes the game appear to be as bad of a timely cash-grab as the DLC it wants to comment on.

As much as I love this game, and you can see it by the amount of hours I invested on it, and even though it has improoved largely in the last years, I can't review it positively (look at the end to see why I finally did). The last "balance" changes to some iconic weapons hurted the game, specially for SU, which was in a pretty bad spot already, but they dunked us in the mud by making other factions weapons even more OP than ever.
That, combined with the poorly development focus on what really matters  and the game needs (maps, balance, mechanics, RTS) but besides on $$ like camos, promos, etc, or even new planes (which was indeed a good addition but on a stupid prioritation level) made me loose my trust in this developers.
Tanks are jokes in this game, since any infantry can oneshot them with AT nades. Anti-personal mines spam AVIABLE FOR EVERY INFANTRY will make you look more to the floor than to the enemy itself even inside capture points and specially at chokepoints like doors or stairs. And planes are just godmode_on, because you have no real way to counter them aside for other planes.
Its so hard to see the game die the way it is right now. I wish Reto put his hands on this and save it, because it needs to be done ASAP.
To sum up, the grind is very hard at the starting levels, there will be a niche time in which you will be able to actually enjoy the game, but once you see the balance issues, your love for the game will be slowly crippled. That being said, this is probably the only decent combined warfare + RTS type of game you will find around, and its F2P.

This game is so good! I've spent a good 40 hours playing this game. But there are a few things that I wish were different:
1. Too few enemy types. This game needs much much much more enemies.
2. Enemies are too predictable. Some enemy attacks are actually more annoying than fun. Easy to fix!
3. Perks - all of the beneficial perks from the beginning become diluted when all are unlocked, and made worse when most give mediocre benefits. This is especially frustrating because getting the right perks at the right time are tantamount to a fun and successfull playthrough. I don't like perks being entirely based on luck.
4. Perks - I don't think they should be completely random. There should be some sort of probabilistic upgrade tree, perhaps.
5. The elder gods gifts and punishments shouldn't be random. There should be a way to earn the gods favor to give a higher chance of a beneficial effect. Elder god punishments can destroy a fun game. The perk to remove elder god debuffs is too important to receive early in the game, yet is far too rare to receive when all perks are unlocked.

I used to play Heretic back when it was new, and really loved that game. It was basically Doom in a dark fantasy setting with magical weapons such as gauntlets that spew green lightning at point blank range, a dragon claw shooting blue glowy blasts rapidly at a distance, a golden staff shooting either like a flamethrower, or hurling a fireball that combusts in the shape of a phoenix, and many more weapons. It was a real treat, and still holds up pretty decently as a good shooter. So Ziggurat, a first person shooter with magical weapons came along, my interest was piqued. Unfortunately, I can't say that I found myself enjoying this game like I had hoped.
Ziggurat has a story, but I knew better than to expect anything that really mattered. You get an opening video, and sometimes you'll find a scroll with two sentences in the dungeon. There aren't characters you interact with, no dialog, no events or anything...you get the reason you're there, two sentences per scroll about some lore that didn't interest me, and that's it from what I've seen.
The music and sound work well enough. I'm probably pretty spoiled by soundtracks from games like Undertale, Chrono Trigger, the Final Fantasy series, Bastion, Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines, etc. While going through the dungeon, I only recall hearing one song, but I wasn't paying all that much attention. I was rather busy trying to stay alive.
Graphically, it's nice enough, and the art style has a certain appeal to it. It got the job done and makes the game pretty recognizable compared to its counterparts; especially the little carrot monsters.
Ziggurat's gameplay is its core, with the aforementioned aspects serving as support to the game, rather than major pillars. With that in mind, its gameplay would need to stand tall as great on its own for me to recommend it, and other than looking prettier, playing Heretic again sounds like more fun to me. Although Ziggurat has randomization, that randomization means ammo is unpredictably scarce, resulting in me using the starting wand far too often, thus missing out on having fun with the other weapons, and certain runs are a cakewalk and other runs feel horribly unfair.
Movement speed/enemy attacks were some of the most off-putting things in this game for me as well. This game felt like someone liked Heretic, and wanted to get in on the rogue-lite craze by removing the well thought out level design, balance of enemy and item placement, and the relatively quick-but-strategic first person magic-spewing fights of Heretic, simply randomizing everything at the risk of throwing balance out the window and amping up the player's and enemy's movement speed so much that you wonder if the player character did ten lines of cocaine before spawning into the dungeon.
Bethesda's recent Doom game sped up the original Doom's combat a bit, and changed a few elements of it, but it retained its essence, both in and out of combat. Although Ziggurat isn't trying to be another Heretic, it's clear that it inspired it, with the Serpent Staff out of Hexen as a usable weapon (darn thing got me killed because I was trying to see if it had life drain (it doesn't seem to)), and ranged magical combat in first person as its core gameplay. I also highly question if first person was the best perspective for this game, because given how quickly the player and enemies move, and the fact that enemies spawn in behind you at times, it can become incredibly difficult to keep up with where enemies are, and where environmental hazards like acid spit sizzling on the ground is.
As for the "lite" portion of rogue-lite, rather than this being a roguelike, it's nothing that makes me want to keep playing at all. If you die, you start over, and how well you did determines how many new bonuses are added to the pool of bonuses you can choose from at level-ups. Level-ups are not persistent and are lost at death. So you start a game, level up, choose a bonus and keep it until you die. When you die, you lose all bonuses, and unlock more potential bonuses to choose from when you level up on your next life. Rinse, wash, and repeat. Also, dealing certain amounts of damage, getting certain numbers of kills, etc. also unlocks additional characters...which in a first person setting without dialog, just means different bonuses such as dealing more damage with a certain type of weapon.
Each time I died, I didn't even get upset, which is rare for me. I'm pretty easily ticked off with difficult games, but with this one, I just didn't care. The game doesn't have anything new to unlock that I care about, and thus, I have nothing compelling me to continue playing. The story is virtually non-existent, there aren't characters I interact with for me to care about, there is no thoughtful level layout/world, there isn't anything persistent that I will unlock that I want, and Heretic did ranged magic dark fantasy first person shooting better like 20 years ago.
If you want rogue-lite games that have more interesting gameplay and/or unlockables that feel like they matter much more, I would go with Rogue Legacy, Hand of Fate, FTL, and Neon Chrome (so far). Or if you just want a good first person dark fantasy magic shooter and liked the original Doom or genuinely aren't put off by very outdated graphics, give Heretic a whirl on a super deep discount sale.

Before I get into the review, I will try to spoil as little as poosible about the story. There will some MINOR SPOILERS, but I will mostly refer to the begining of the game, but ever so vague. Well, let us begin :)
Story: You are a character that has his/her life is in shambles and loses his/her boyfriend/girlfriend after the prologue of the game. Soon enough, you recieve an invitation to your ex's wedding ceremony that will occur in 30 days. It is your job to go get your ex back. Or is it?
Graphics: It's pixel art so what do you expect? Kidding aside, it suits the game quite nicely in my opinion.
Music: I love the music so much. Many songs will repeat, but you will never get tired of it, at least I didn't.
Gameplay: I did not say this before, but this game will not appeal to everyone because all you practically do is read. I see this game more as a Visual Novel rather than a game to be honest, but it is a really good one at that. There is a lot of text in the game, but with good reason. This game is all about choice. A lot of games that are out now have "choices" in them, but this has to be the best game to deliver choice thus far in my opinion (Yes I have played Mass Effect 1-3 and Witcher 1-2 and I love them both if that means anything). Every choice you make, whether it being in dialogue or in action, it carries weight. What I love even more are that these choices are very subtle. There is no moral meter, light/dark, or red/blue. All of the choices are grey and does not have a big sign showing "Make big decision here!!"
There are also various minigames to play to break the reading which are actually quite fun.
Pros:
+Story
+Music
+Gameplay
+CHOICES
Cons:
-Gameplay (I put it here twice because there is a lot of reading, but it didn't bother me)
In all, I had a great time playing the game. I believe that it was worth the $10 (got it for $9 though). The story is very engrossing and can sometimes give you the feels. In the end, we are Always Sometimes Monsters.

UPDATE 11 - 13-2015
As a resource-management / society building game, Gnomoria covers all the basics.  Basic tools, basic foods, basic livestock, basic weapons, basic combat.  It does basic very well.  What innovations it has that sets it apart and above some of the other games of its genre is how it presents itself.
As a small collective of 6 Gnomes settling the hilly (or flat) wilds of Gnomoria, you are allowed to destroy and build as you please.  The ground can be dug up and used to build homes or sifted to find rare metals to make weapons or gems to make jewelry.  Cotten can be grown in farm plots to make bandages, bags or armour or the fields can be used to grow food.  How your Gnomes live and work is up to you.
Initially, you are left to yourself, but eventually you will have to deal with Goblins, skeletons and other beasts bent on your destruction.  Build up your defensives and research new tools, like guns and steam-engines, to protect your Gnomes.
Though well-balanced and well-coded, there are some things missing.  For example:
1.) If your livestock gets hurt, you cannot heal them and if all your livestock die, you must establish a trade route with a neighboring kingdom to buy new livestock
2.)  Livestock is also the only reliable way to get meat and leather, as there is no hunting of wildlife in the game.
3.)  The only way your population can grow is through Gnomads, who will only come to your city if material worth of your city is high enough to merit a migration.
4.)  Determining what job your new Gnome is best suited to perform requires you to scroll through their entire talent list.
5.)  Distant kingdoms only exist as text on a menu screen and visiting diplomats don't do anything but wander around (and in my case, get killed by bears)
6.)  Trying to do anything more complicated than "All units kill this thing" makes the game look at you funny.
But, these are minor considering the price and the over-all feel of the game.  For $8, it is a decent but basic game.  The creator hopes to have the game released as "complete" by the end of the year and raise the price to $14.99 and in that case I would ask for, at the barest minimum, the option to bred your Gnomes to increase the population and a way to heal my livestock after a goblin raider has tried to carve its buttocks off.

As of October 6th, 2015, the creator has removed the game's development plan from the website.  He is only focusing on optimizing the game as it is right now, fixing bugs, and on improving mod-support.  He is NOT going to add any new features or content. If you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.
Enjoy! :)

You follow through set paths with many bombs, turns, and twists to take you on a possibly very non-linear experience, which is good. You collect items and get to your goal alive, it's as simple as that.
You're getting a lot for what you're paying for. A unique puzzler with bright colors and enjoyably simple patterns. The largest conflict is controlling the cube. Astonishingly similar controls of Marble Madness make it just as frustrating as before, and no doubt requires practise, but one you've got it down the controls, you've still got a decent puzzler.
Only other negative is checkpoints. Personally I'd prefer the challenge of starting over each time, but that's just me, and there might be an option for that somewhere which I haven't checked for yet.

As much as I love this game, and you can see it by the amount of hours I invested on it, and even though it has improoved largely in the last years, I can't review it positively (look at the end to see why I finally did). The last "balance" changes to some iconic weapons hurted the game, specially for SU, which was in a pretty bad spot already, but they dunked us in the mud by making other factions weapons even more OP than ever.
That, combined with the poorly development focus on what really matters  and the game needs (maps, balance, mechanics, RTS) but besides on $$ like camos, promos, etc, or even new planes (which was indeed a good addition but on a stupid prioritation level) made me loose my trust in this developers.
Tanks are jokes in this game, since any infantry can oneshot them with AT nades. Anti-personal mines spam AVIABLE FOR EVERY INFANTRY will make you look more to the floor than to the enemy itself even inside capture points and specially at chokepoints like doors or stairs. And planes are just godmode_on, because you have no real way to counter them aside for other planes.
Its so hard to see the game die the way it is right now. I wish Reto put his hands on this and save it, because it needs to be done ASAP.
To sum up, the grind is very hard at the starting levels, there will be a niche time in which you will be able to actually enjoy the game, but once you see the balance issues, your love for the game will be slowly crippled. That being said, this is probably the only decent combined warfare + RTS type of game you will find around, and its F2P.

I am not %100 sold on The Novelist, but I do think that it is a work of art that deserves an audience, and a run through of the game will only take a couple of hours.
It's an emotional experience, though I recommend you play it in Story Mode, instead of Stealth mode, which marred my first attempt at a play through.
I don't think the storytelling is anything particularly groundbreaking - structurally it feels like a choose your own adventure - but the subject matter is not one usually explored in a game, and for that I think it's worth a try.
It's called the Novelist, but it might perhaps better be called 'The Father' because the game was really more about balancing his family life with his work and passions  than actually writing a novel. If this sounds like playing your life on a computer, you may want to give this one some room until you have a little more space to breathe.
My main qualm with the game is that while the Novelist's artist wife Linda is drawn well enough (I guess)  with her own ambitions and approach to family, the game still presents a fairly patriarchal family worldview  - one that sometimes seems drawn to appeal to a fantasy of male martyrdom. Though Linda puts forward her views on family decisions, in the end it's her husband who makes all the choices about their life and their son's. So while the game can be genuinely affecting, ultimately, some of the sacrifices you make feel a little hollow. Arguably this is simply a result of the game mechanics, but my wife and I make choices about our lives together, and it's not all on my shoulders, nor hers.
That said, the dilemmas in this game are well set up, and I felt really torn between advancing Dan's career, his wife's and the wellbeing of his son.  I was glad that, in my runthrough at least, both she and Tommy led fruitful lives, even if Dan didn't get to follow his dreams.
Play it if you want an experience different from your everyday shoot 'em up.

A great balancing act between one's dreams and obligations. True to life, the conflicts that arise between a man and his family cause a sense of gravity and depth for every decision and, more importantly, omission.

Highly recommended for people who are drawn to narrative driven games like Stanley Parable, Gone Home, The Walking Dead and Dear Esther.

Story-driven "game" where alot of the enjoyment comes from how much you can relate with the 3 members of the family: father (novelist, procrastinator), mother (artist, early mid-life crisis) and son (learning issues, bullied). In each of the 12 chapters, each member has a specific need. You get to fulfill the need of one, make another compromise and disappoint the last. These choices affect how the story plays out.
The game is confined to the family's rented summer home and to advance you read through notes spread around the house, sneak up on members to explore their memories and finally make your choice. It's nothing to write home about, just a means to progress the story.
I give this game a reluctant thumbs up. It really depends on your mood and how much you can relate to a story about a young family trying to keep it together. I liked how it wasn't rosy; you had to make hard decision and almost always end up disappointing someone, but hey, that's life.

The designer for this game left his job working with huge teams to make an entire game by himself, and it shows. I'm glad I bought the game because I have hope that the money he's made with this game will lead to something worth playing in the future, but this ain't it.
The script gives the illusion of choice, but you're following a narrow path with gameplay that is little more than hide and seek. I bought the game hoping for a compelling storyline, but it rarely reached beyond evenly distributing attention into three buckets, with a unsatisfyingly easy end.
The whole game is half an hour long with no reply value. Buy the game, download it for an afternoon, then save the room on your computer content that you just donated money to a good cause.

I voted for this game to be Greenlit and was happy to see that it has mostly lived up to the potential it showed then. You play some sort of ghost or spirit that inhabits a house which a writer named Dan and his wife and son rent for the summer so that Dan can focus on working on his next book.  The game is divided into several chapters as the spirit you have to move throughout the house reading letters, reading the family members thoughts and exploring their memories to find out the desires of each family member. You do all this while trying to remain undetected (though if you want to focus on the story you can turn the requirement for stealth off).
When you've uncovered each family members desire you have to pick one and whisper it to Dan so it is acted upon. The family member who's desire you picked will be happy but the other two will not. At the end of the chapter after you've made your choice you get to see the outcomes on each character and it is quite difficult to see the negative outcomes as you do end up feeling sorry for them. It's a pity the game doesn't have more solutions that would satisfy more than one character so your decision can become an agonizing choice.
The real strength of this game is the story it weaves about the family. You get to know each character and how they feel through their memories and the letters you read and while the story this game tells about them is the typical trials and tribulations of a family, it's done so well that you do end up caring about them and that makes the choices you make that bit more agonizing.
The only downside of this game is that the exploration side where you move about the house trying to find letters and look through the families memories gets boring after a short while as it gets repetitive doing more less the same thing in every chapter.
Overall though this is a great story based games that will please people who enjoyed games like Gone Home and Dear Esther. It's a 7/10 from me.

A very enjoyable, unique, fast-paced, pseudorandomly generated wizard dungeon crawling FPS which was more than worth the $3 I got it for.
It's got heaps of fun magic weapons (wands, staves, spells, and alchemical contraptions), varied enemy design, and different playable classes and perks to change the way you play the game. In an average game, you'll be platforming through traps, fighting rooms full of enemies, picking up weapons and choosing perks to upgrade your character, and then battling a boss at the end of each level.
My only complaints were--
1: there's only a small amount of assets used to make the environments, and after the first few playthroughs, going over the same rooms again and again got dull, even if they were laid out in different ways.
2: Luck-based elements outside the player's control are capable of making a run extremely difficult to complete.
3: I would have liked to see multiplayer, though I can understand why they chose not to. Challenge mode suffices.
4: There is no tutorial (unless I missed it somehow). This isn't too bad since Ziggurat's mechanics are quickly learned, but still a minor point against it.
Overall a fun and satisfying experience, a 4/5 star game.

It was entertaining for a few hours. The combat is a fairly simple: run in circles and spam your projectile weapons. It has a few little trap rooms that can be tricky jump / timing challenges. Some hidden rooms that always give you the same thing, and tells you a little bit about the game studios past, failed attempts. It made me lol and scratch my head the first few times as I wondered why they were telling me this information, in game. The map layouts are pretty boring little square boxes in an unsymetrical grid pattern, that you enter one at a time. The doors lock, and then you proceed to run in circles and spam your "gun" basically. The room layout and type of battle can change slightly, for example you might have to destroy these floating obelisks that keep spawning creatures, or just run through the room and kill one group of spawned creatures, or have all these little evil carrot minions that are constantly spawning and chasing you around until you kill the main doods that are summoning them. But in essence, every battle is the same: run in circles spamming your weapons. Then each of the levels ends with  a boss fight, which are a bit more challenging, but the strategy is the same: run in circles spamming your weapon. I think there are 5 levels, and after you finish the 5th, it ends. It did take me a few hours of "failed" attempts before finally finishing the 5th level. After about 5 hours, assuming you complete the 5th level, you will have seen everything the game has to offer, which is why this is more of a game you want to buy on sale. I like the basic idea of this game: FPS roguelike, and in some respects they got it right, but it just feels like it could have been so much more if the game studio had spent a bit more time on it. I'll give it a thumbs up on the condition you buy it on sale, cuz it's not a $15 game in my opinion, it's a $3-$4 game, which is what I bought it for. And for a $3 game, it gets a thumbs up.

This game is genuinely funny, especially when I decided to stop being the actually good father, and just team up with the baby to wreck the house.  But, there are issues that I will list, as well as some suggestions to improve the game.
There are definitely clipping issues, especially with the walls, as I have lost several matches due to the locks or the plug covers going through a wall.  Hopefully those will be fixed relatively soon.
Lag issues.  From time to time, despite having a pretty high-end PC and 75mbps connection, I experiance catastrophic lag whenever I play in a room that I, myself, am not hosting.  I am unsure if this is a stability issue, or I have consistantly joined people with high latency.  It would be nice to see the latency of each person hosting games, in order to avoid the latter, hopefully the former is being looked in to.
Some items do NOT spawn at all at times, or sometimes spawn behind drawers, where they are unreachable.  This makes winning as the father impossible in those situations.
The one tune playing on the radio gets old, pretty quickly.  More variety in the music, possibly let people use their own music in it, would be good.
The area, while containing a diverse range of stuff to hide from baby, is kinda small.  It would be nice if we had more rooms.  Maybe allow for different areas of the house for different playthroughs,  I would LOVE to see a laundry room, since the idea of the baby being able to go into a washer or dryer (or both) is hilarious.  Maybe even add an ironing board.  Trying to keep the baby from danger in a garage, or yard would be fun, too.
Edit:  Seems most of those have been implemented.  Good joh, dev.  Only problem is that there seems to be a glitch in the garage that makes characters move sideways, almost as if I am walking against an invisible wall that is forcing me to strafe.  This is the only room that does that.
While the one on one aspect is fun,  having only one game mode does get tedious.  It would be fun to have other game modes, maybe one where dad has to compete against twins, or mom AND dad, or two dads, have to go against a faster version of the baby.  Maybe a survival mode with different rooms in the house steadily unlocking, bringing even more dangers for dad to move out of reach for baby.
Overall, I would recommend playing this game, especially with friends.  Though, I would suggest maybe waiting until it is further along in development, so more of the kinks are worked out.

The best Batman Game, and in my opinion the best use of a licensed character closely followed by this titles sequel "Arkham City". Arkham Asylum puts you in the shoes of the World’s Greatest Detective in transit to Arkham Asylum directly following catching the Joker in Gotham. In true Joker fashion though, this simple booking procedure goes wrong, and Joker takes over the Asylum. Now you as Batman has to figure out what the Clown Prince of Crime is up too. Along the way you see and battle the A-Team of batman Villains who happen to be locked up in the Asylum.
Visually Arkahm Aslyum still holds its weight and looks great. The art direction in this game does an incredible job in complementing the emotions and feelings the writers are trying to convey. From the cramped insides of the Asylum to incredible vistas from Arkham Island looking out at Gotham. I also enjoyed that despite the massive success of "Nolan’s Batman" this game is throwing you into the Batman from the Comics or Cartoon that I grew up with.
In keeping with Nostalgia, Rocksteady got the two greatest voice actors to reprise their roles as Batman and Joker.  Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill respectively. These voices are the ones that most of here when we read the comics and both Actors do a phenomenal job, coupled with great writing from Rocksteady.
For anyone is worried that because the story and visual presentation are so superb that the gameplay must be shallow, which happens often. I can ease your mind, Arkham Aslyum's gameplay is tight responsive and truly makes you feel like the Caped Crusader. Combat when out in the open completed with "free-flow" combat, which when first introduced seems like single button directional combat. But they do a great job of building on it as the game goes on adding in gadgets, parries, stuns, and diverse unit types.
Along with great combat, Arkham Island is full of Exploration and puzzles to solve. Throughout the game you will be taunted by The Riddler to solve his puzzles, which range from grabbing statues to finding hidden Easter Eggs spread out around the world with hints given in Riddle-Form, and using your Detective Mode vision to find hidden "Question Marks".  Detective mode is a vision where you can see enemies through walls in skeletal form and other important objects will be highlighted (Be warned you will spend a good amount of time in this vision a lot more than you would think)
I could go on and on but do not want to give any Spoilers because that where Arkham shines is in delivering an incredibly well-paced and well written Batman story worthy of the Title. If you  want to not only feel like Batman but be put into a great Batman Story this game is a must play

I'm willing to admit that it doesn't look like I've given the game much of a chance. It looks even worse when I sit down and say that I even waited for it to go on sale before buying it... but the truth is I just didn't find the game fun and engaging, and if that isn't present, if I'm feeling more frustrated and struggling with the game both on a gameplay-mechanics level AND on a story level.... I really questioned whether I wanted to keep going forward.
I really did like the previous installment. It had it's troubles, yes, and it seemed clunky to handle at points... but the story was engaging enough to make me want to continue DESPITE those problems. Furthermore, I genuinely felt like I was gradually unlocking Adam Jensens potential in the game as I progressed, as I became more and more adept at stealth and combat. Maybe the previous game set the bar too high, but I didn't feel like that same character in this game. I had to repeat some of the game's tutorials several times because it felt too easy to flub up and while I understand that the game was demanding a lot of care and precision, it also got in the way of feeling like I was playing a character that was well-adapated to their prostetics and augments... Instead, I felt like I was just getting used to them... again.
Ultimately, it was talking to a coworker who also games that finally got me to make the decision to stop and uninstall. I've played several sequels that have built on a game I really enjoyed, and what kept me going was the knowledge that this was going to be a new experience in a world I already enjoyed... and after a small adjustment period due to slight changes, I ate it all up. However, I don't feel that same way about this game. During the most crucial point for any newcomer, the beginning, I felt lost, I felt disconnected, I didn't feel in control of the character.
I'm sure there are others out there that can overlook all this, and I don't think they are wrong or misguided... I just am not one of those people. I don't mind challenges in the games I play, as long as they are challenges that are supposed to be part of the game itself (like making difficult strategic decisions, or deciding which character to save, etc), rather than trying to come to grips with the mechanics or story in order to feel comfortable in the game.
In the end, I just strongly advise anyone to buy the game on-sale... it softens the blow if you really don't like it.

NOTE: The text of this review is used on both my Arkham Asylum and Arkham City reviews.  The same comments apply to both.
I came to this game far too late.  I first played it on OnLive, and completed the game and all of the Riddler items, and I really enjoyed it enough to do the same with the Steam version.  If you are considering the Arkham games, I stongly recommend that you play through Arkham Asylum first and Arkham City second.  In addition to providing a continuous storyline, the expansion of the controls and items in Arkham City feels like a logical progression.  If you try to do it the other way, you will likely become frustrated by the loss of some functions.
By playing them on Steam after playing them on OnLive, I wanted to test out three things.
First, I wanted to see how the story held up for replay.  Surprisingly, both games held up very well.  I noticed that I moved through the stages more quickly the second time.  I suppose this was because I knew my way wround the island and the city well enough that my moves could be more bold and decisive.  In any case, I was pleasantly surprised to see things the second time around that I had not previously noticed.  In Arkham City, I noticed certain ironic echos between Batman and Catwoman, and I also noticed certain villains that I would later face standing in the prison line at the beginning of the game.  I wrote recently about my frustrating with games that try to explain everything, but Batman does the opposite; it lets you discover everything on your own.
The second thing I wanted to gauge was the difference in video quality.  While the local video quality was definitely better, I was pleasantly surprised to find that it wasn’t as dramatic of a difference as I expected.  The OnLive graphics were satisfactory, and sometimes the degraded quality actually made the scenes look LESS CG and more realistic.
The third thing that I wanted to test was the response time of the game.  In this area, the Steam version blew OnLive out of the water.  When I played through the game on Normal on OnLive, I occasionally struggled with some of the stages because of the lag.  I compensated for this by predicting ahead of time how I would need to make the battles flow, and was eventually able to get through them.  On the Steam version, however, no such prediction was necessary.  I played on Hard Mode, and had no trouble beating either game.  In fact, I would say that I was fighting more effectively on Hard Mode on Steam than I was on Normal mode on OnLive.  In these two games, that’s saying something.

Batman Arkham Asylum is an open world  action-adventure title that combines stealth, combat and adventure elements in  the famous Arkham Asylum itself. Since this is an open world, you can follow the story or screw around solving the Riddler's enigmas, but more on those a bit later.
The first hour or so of the game initiates one into the world of Arkham by introducing the narrative,  combat and stealth gameplay to the player so that he/she can become accustomed to the intricacies that are specific to this experience. And you will want to learn these as the game has some of the best action/stealth gameplay ever created. Combat is rhythmic, relying on precise timing in order to achieve combos which typically require stringing together strikes and counters, and with later opponents dodging and stunning will be required to even start a combo. When an enemy is on the ground you can also initiate a takedown, but this move leaves Batman vulnerable to enemy attacks.
Stealth itself is a bit more do or die than the combat, as it involves carefully scrutiny of the  surroundings and planning in order to eliminate Joker's henchmen without being turned into Swiss Cheese, as the thugs have assault firearms, and you only have batarangs, but that's actually what makes the Stealth so satisfying. Planning your attack and executing it to clear the room one henchmen at a time might seem daunting at first, but it's very satisfying to eliminate them one by one, and the inverted takedown takes the cake as one of the best ways to apply retribution on someone.
Regardless of your performance in combat or stealth , you receive XP .In both both combat and stealth  you receive even more with better performance which means  pulling off a respectable combo in combat and not being injured in stealth. This XP can be used to upgrade Batman's abilities, and even add new abilities be they stealth or combat oriented .
But there is also a unique feature comes into play: Detective mode. DM is used to find clues relating to certain objects or following a trail,but it's use isn't limited to story-related tasks,  as they are invaluable to solving Riddler's Enigmas. Among others, these involve finding secret areas and catching a shot of a particular item/ image. The most important ones are  finding the Riddler's maps though, as these point out every riddle on the map, making the entire process of solving these riddles a lot more manageable. There are also  audio recordings of sessions with the Asylum's colorful cast of inmates to find . With the exception of the Audio recordings, both types of  riddles make heavy use of the DM, to the point where you'll end up using it so often that you'll rarely get a glimpse of the environments
Which is a shame since the dark gothic look  makes Arkham feel distinct. Solid texture work, excellent animation and dark colors define the world of Arkham, although the characters kinda  look like meatheads. Granted, you get used to the look of everything not long into the game as you realize that this is a stylistic choice, and a relevant one  at that.
And when you add to that the dynamic music and performances from the voice cast of the Batman Animated Series (Mark Hamill included) you get a convincing atmosphere that makes the twisted world in front of you come to life.
And last but not least we have a intriguing story that genuinely surprises from time to time with Joker taking control of Arkham after the opening scene and letting the inmates and prisoners from BlackGate loose on the staff of Arkham and Batman. Suffice it to say, you will Batman your way through these situations, and although the story sound simple in theory, in practice you're dealing with Joker which both complicates things and keeps them interesting.
There are boss-battles, which are all unique, but that also makes their difficulty spike up and down,  kind of like a heart rate monitor. But with a bit of patience and perseverance you will be rewarded with the satisfaction of beating actual challenges.
Ultimately, you can't go wrong with Arkham Asylum, as you can find it  super cheap these days (that's if you didn't get it on sale already), and if you're looking to become Batman and Batman things up for a while (a week or so), there's no better way to do that than to play this game.

I didn't really expect Batman AA to be all that good. I picked it up on steam for $10 and was really pleasantly surprised.
Graphics-
The game runs on the Unreal 3 engine, and it actually looks quite good. The outdoor sections are a little less impressive, but the character models, lighting, and effects all look great. This game won't blow anyone away with it's mind blowing visuals, but it's very pretty. Furthermore, the art style is phenomenal. You wouldn't think being faithful to the comic books would be a good thing, but it really works here. It's a comic book world, but the artwork is dark, moody, and beautiful: it really draws you in. Little touches like the way Batman gets little rips, tears, cuts, and scratched over the course of the game just add to this.
Sound-
Voice acted by the cast from the animated series, the voice acting is generally quite good, with Mark Hamill's Joker being my personal favorite. I wasn't a fan of Harley Quinn's voice actress, but it is a matter of preference. All in all, the characters really come to life as a result of having long term actors on the series involved. The music and sound effects are all great, very moody. The audio diaries add to this, although I thought the script for some of them could have been a little better, but again it's a matter of choice. Bioshock did something similar, and I preferred it to Arkham's, but that's not to say the audio diaries here aren't fun.
Gameplay-
The game is a brawler and stealth game, mixing different elements of the two genres. I really think it's at it's best when you are given freedom to move: gargoyles and the like, with a variety of ways to take down armed enemies. Of course, there are definitely sections where you must fight mobs of guys with your fists. The fighting is easy to grasp the basics of, but hard to master, and it takes skill to really get a hold of it, which is a good thing in my book. The gadgets, upgrades, and complex under the hood sort of bits of the gameplay really add to the depth, and I'll admit I still didn't realize some of the creative ways to take guards down after I'd beaten the game- I saw them online. My biggest gripe with the gameplay was the sections where the camera was shifted. Parts of the game (first appearance is in the scarecrow section) will take the camera from behind batman and put it farther back in a fixed but tracking location. While this is meant to give you better visibility, on the PC I found that it was incredibly frustrating to deal with, because the controls in these sections are clearly designed for consoles. wasd doesn't control your avatar based on the way hes facing, but it is instead tied to the camera. The result is a clumsy control interface during these sections.
All in all though, the gameplay is really solid, and beyond the campaign there's a good amount of replay value in the form of challenges and collecting batman memorabilia.

I am usually a fan of games that are thought provoking with branching and complex storylines, as well as ethical decisions that affect the world around you. There were some points where the game was very enjoyable and others where it taught be something about my own morals (pretty straight, but willing to hose the people who try to cheat me). And I enjoyed how the creators were meta, and stuck themselves in the game. And some points were pretty hilarious, like when I broke into a doctor's mansion to recover evidence of his teddybear fetish for blackmail.
Unfortunately, there were many points in the game where I was unsure of what to do. I would spend a good half hour or more wandering around town trying to find something, ANYTHING to do to pass the evening so they game would FINALLY let me start a new day. Othertimes it was very redundant. Don't get me wrong, it was hilarious to get a job butchering pigs ALL DAY LONG... but when I've got to do that for three days in a row, it got pretty dull. I guess work is work, and that's reflective of real life. But in the end I felt it sort of forced my hand. As recommended, I named the main character after me, and the ex after my ex. But I really had no desire to travel across country to go to her wedding. I mean, inviting me to her wedding? That was a "dickish" thing to do. I'd rather work hard and get my life back on track... But butchering pigs was pretty dull, so in the end I bought a bus ticket, just so I could pull out a little more entertainment out of this game. Because there was literally NOTHING else I could do at that point.
I also wasn't a huge fan of a lot of the dialogue. There was a lot of swearing, trash talking, etc that detracted (I felt) from the game. Maybe that's just me, but it felt overused. Also some of the dialogue and cut scenes were... long and without much substance. Maybe that's another way this game tried to mirror real life. But sometimes I felt myself skipping through scenes, thinking "I really need a break, but I HAVE TO SAVE MY GAME!" 15 minutes later, I finally get a chance to save.
I really hate to say I don't recommend this game. You can tell a lot of thought and effort went into it. It's only $10, and a lot of people really enjoy it. You might really enjoy it too. Who knows? Maybe it's worth taking the chance. But for me, it wasn't worth the investment.

"Always Sometimes Monsters" was an experience, for sure. Thought-provoking, clever, humorous, and dark in all the right places. The interactive story of people at their best and worst. But I have some serious gripes. For one, there never seemed to be any consequence for starving your character. Early on I made sure my blocky textured game self was properly fed at least one brick of bacon a day. By the end of the game, however, it didn't matter. I went the last few days without so much as entering a store. No complaints of hunger, no risk of starvation... I just kept trucking.
Another complaint: pacing. Man was this game hindered by poor pacing. The game runs out of interesting tasks early on, and getting on to the next "level" require monotonous grinding under the guise of "man does real life suck or what?" And I get it. You want to buy expensive things, you've got to work for it... or be greasy enough to rob people blind. But as a game mechanic it turned the experience into a chore. But I kept on trucking, like my malnutritioned game character. I had to get to the end. Surely that would make it worth it? All of these choices - so many variables! How will my story turn out? Well, SPOILERS...
It ends the same way every time. Me in an alleyway with a gun pointed at me. Did I betray my friend? Yep. Marry my girl? Yep. Did everything end up falling apart? Yep. Okay, seems logical. If you're a♥♥♥♥♥♥ you're going to get a♥♥♥♥♥♥ending. I'll do it differently! I'll help my friend. Let my girl marry him. Maybe now I won't end up all distraught in an alley? Didn't I make friends in my travels? Friends who swore they'd help me and be there for me? Wasn't I a good person? Rescuing dogs and helping old ladies? Nope. I'm in an alley, begging for the sweet release of death. Well, that isn't very fun. Again, this feels like lazy design disguised as some seriously angsty philosophy... life sucks. It doesn't matter what you do, who you are, or who your friends are, it all ends the same way: you, in an alley, hoping some guy will execute you to make the pain go away. Really unfortunate. You can be a horrible monster or a paragon and it ends the same way. What, bad guys don't win sometimes? Good guys lose, sure, but they don't EVER prevail?
I may have to play this through a few more times, but what I'm seeing from other players is the same preachy, bummer ending. I'll rescind this review if need be; assuming there's a way to end it with me not sucking the proverbial barrel of a gun.
Edit: As of 5/24/2014 I'm seeing that there were some finale bugs that resulted in the player character  ending up in his/her homeless predicament regardless of doggy rescuing and old lady assisting. It seems the devs have corrected this. It also seems that there are a few happy endings that require a bit of finagling... choosing arbitrary reasons for the initial break-up, choosing how to make a quick buck, either planting seeds or harvesting medicinal marijuana... I don't know why. I still can't recommend it. Some people will enjoy this. It's an interesting story with some flashes of brilliance; just not enough. If you like bummerfests (as that is likely how your story will end JUST LIKE REAL LIFE MAYBE SOMETIMES ALWAYS),  and you don't mind monotonous grinding, THIS might be the game for you.

If you enjoy games like Rogue Legacy and Castlevania this is a great game. Its a mix of roguelike, platforming with some RPG elements contained in levels where you descend to the bottom of the screen. There are a few tiny glitches here and there such as automatic jumping in water randomly, enemies sometimes spawning right on top of you and a few times the game has crashed due to error in the code, but its overall very fun, great value for the money, an absolute steal when on sale and there is a lot of content and replay value to the game. Would definitely recommend this title and I certainly hope a sequel will be released from these developers!

[Summary] (Summary first for clarity and people who don't want to read a lot)
Over all a quite bad game. It would be ok as a flash game to kill an hour or two but not worth buying. The only redeeming quality is the local co-op, but the game still has fundamental issues with their design.
[Combat]
Very repetative and dull combat. Hitting someone isn't an issue of hitting them with you weapon but more of them being in front of you when you strike (as in the weapon never connects). Every battle is composed of hitting the opponent then stepping back quickly so you can go in and stab them again (with slight variation if you still have your spell left to use).
[Store system]
You can buy two things that makes you stronger. More damage and more health. You can also purchase an upgrade for the passive coins on the maps (they are worth experience and gold, they disappear when an enemy is killed).
Spread out through the map are merchants selling a single ability each. These will then be shuffled into your random spells for your new generations. Most of these purchases are regretted as there is no way to confirm if an ability is good until you purchase it and use it.
The store system is over all very underwhelming and it feels like the store system was added last minute to balance the fact that levels only get harder because the monsters have more health and hit harder.
[Level design]
Throw in random blocks in a maze where you navigate to the bottom where the boss is. Add prisoners (that help you if you let them out) and treasures. Plus a quest per level that is either find Y of X or kill Z and come back to me. The map is not designed so that you can travel upwards, to combat this there are teleporters that bring your to the beginning spread out across the map.
You start from level 1 and progress upwards.  Some levels have the ability to pay gold so that you can teleport there instantly (for a negligible price) in new generations. Monster design is pretty limited, the higher level the map is the harder the monsters hit. They look different and sometimes they might be ranged but all in all this doesn't change much.
[Stability]
Crashed only once every 30-45 minutes and never in a way that progress was lost. Starting the game is quick and easy through Steam Big Picture Mode so this was more of a nuisance than a problem.
It's really lackluster. If you like to pay for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ flashgames you can play on websites this is the perfect game for you, otherwise you should probably stay away

If you are looking for short diversion that will tug at your heartstrings, check it out.
