Heretic/Hexen meets Painkiller + random generated map!
The basic gameplay is Painkiller-style: you enter the room, the dor closes and monsters spawn, after few waves defeated the door opens again and you can move on. At the end of each level you fight the boss and after it's death the portal to the next level appears.
From Hexen/Heretic we got weapons (magic staves, books) and the whole atmosphere of magic dungeon.
But there's one big difference. Instead of many levels there are only 5, but you can replay them over and over again.
After each death you unlock new weapons, perks, that can be acquire during the game, and the new characters, each one with it's own pros and cons. The stuff you find in the levels and the levels themself are totally random, so each playthrough will be different.
Not a masterpiece but, but very fun to play:)

Ziggurat is a fps set in a fantasy dungeon with randomly generated floors - another one of those roguelites.
It's fast, it's hard, it's colorful, it's confusing - it drives me crazy sometimes.
What I like about it:
-- Responsiveness --
Its gameplay and general controls are on the spot which leaves no option for the player to blame anything on the game itself. If you lose, you didn't play well enough. Every single enemy attack is predictable, every single enemy projectile is avoidable. But the overall speed of the game is so high that you often will be overwhelmed and die in a quarter of a millisecond. That may be frustrating and sometimes you will see yourself helpless against the odds the game throws at you. But if you keep at it, you will eventually beat the game.
-- Difficulty Levels --
It is a rather rare occation that difficulty levels in games make any sense. But Ziggurat gets it right I think.
Easy: For newcomers. Most of the time you will successfully complete a run no matter what the game decides to throw at you.
Normal: 50/50. Sometimes it is manageable, other times you'll get one or two utterly insane rooms that eradicate you in a matter of seconds.
Hard: 0/100. You have to be a very lucky pro gamer with twitch reflexes and the Gods of Randomness on your side to even have a chance of success.
-- Character Classes --
After you have played a couple of runs you will automatically unlock several different classes to choose from at the beginning of a new run. These are very varied and each offer unique benefits that set them apart. For example, there is a witch names Agnes, who can freeze an enemy right after having killed another one. Or choose a templar, who is able to refill his mana reserves by consuming the souls of dead monsters. Or maybe you prefer playing a monk, who is adapt at healing himself and doesn't perish so easily. Every single character has her/his advantages and they're all fun to try.
-- Atmosphere And Design --
The game is very colorful, offers some nice texture design, lovely music tracks and an overall intriguing atmosphere. If you like fantasy stuff, this will be right up your alley.
-- Brevity And Longevity --
A typical run consists of five levels with a couple of rooms and one boss each. In case you manage to defeat the last boss, one run will usually take you about 45-60 minutes. That's a pretty good length for a gaming session imo. And in the long run (pun intended), each session will unlock new weapons, characters and power-ups, so there is always something new to see in the next session. This design choice will keep your interest in the game for a pretty long time.
What I don't like:
-- Shrines --
Often you will come across a room with three shrines in it. Each of them can potentially buff or debuff your character. If you're unlucky, these shrines terminate your current run, because they weaken your char to a degree that she/he becomes helpless. So think twice before approaching these ungodly deal breakers.
-- Secret Rooms --
On each floor there is a secret room that can be found by smashing certain walls. Generally a neat idea to include something like that. But in this case there is often some weird picture or painting about some other video games in the secret rooms. I don't get that. Maybe some easter egg, Idk. Curious stuff. Definitely breaks immersion for me.
-- Gauntlet Mode --
Basically your usual horde mode. One big room with waves and waves of enemies to defeat. Initially I found some merit in this mode as I used it to practice and get better at the game. But tbh the whole thing is pointless and superfluous.
Verdict:
Ziggurat is a fast-paced, difficult, roguelite fps set in a high-fantasy world. It offers very responsive gameplay with accurate controls, nice visual and acoustic design, as well as a kind of aura that harkens back to games like Heretic and Hexen (i.e. type "QUICKEN" or "IDKFA" during gameplay to see what I mean). If you want a breeze of a game that tells a great story and holds your hand all the time, you're wrong here. If you want a challenge and if you have a thick skin, you will love coming back to Ziggurat again and again. Overall a very good 8/10.

In my opinion, this LEGO game is one of the best ones I have ever played, and I've played almost every single LEGO game. Here's why I enjoyed it so much.
First off, replay value. I have beaten this game twice on a Nintendo Wii I had, and now once here on PC. Since there are so many levels, collectables, funny cutscenes, and it staying very true to all six Star Wars movies, it really never gets old.
Which brings me to my second point. This game lasts for quite some time, especially if you are in it to collect everything. You'll
to play through every level (36 levels) about 2 or 3 times to get everything. Sounds tedious, right? Well, no. You see, once you have done story mode, like all other LEGO games, you can go back with any other characters and power on through the level. It's very fun to go back and explore the places you can't get to in story mode.
So now the third reason why this game is so fun. Throughout the game you can collect "Power Bricks" which enable you to do things like become invincible and make the in-game currency, the studs, worth many times their original value. This makes it so you can buy vehicles, characters, and other things faster. You can also make it so your Jedi Slam does more damage, disable enemy weapons, and so much more.
And finally, the shear amount of characters is amazing. There are over 120 characters, some being different variations of the same person and lots of others. You can even be Indiana Jones! Being set in the Star Wars universe, it's only natural there would be plenty of characters to choose from, and this game doesn't disappoint.
But what are the levels like? They are all unique, providing different things to do in every level. However, a few levels are a bit repetitve and boring. One or two are extremely hard in story mode, such as one where you have to fly around and destroy enemy ships and weapons. But the rest of the levels certainly make up for them.
With this game having the replay value and normal LEGO humor, it's a fantastic game to play. I got halfway through the game about 17 hours in, so it's certainly not a short game, especially if you are a completionist like me and want to get to 100%. So if you have never played it and were wondering, I strongly recommend it! 9/10.

So yes, I'd say this is a must buy to anyone who considers themselves a Batman fan.

This game would be more fun if it didn't essentially force you to cheat in order to accomplish everything. I know there's a clean version of the game (Steam) and an adult version available on Nutaku, and if both versions offer the same drawn out game play I'd say there are games out there that are more enjoyable.
Crush Crush starts off extremely slowly with stat building and compatibility building taking a while to grind through. They combat this by getting you to soft reset the game to give time multiplier boosts (if you unlock extra time blocks you keep these while you reset- and so you can find your game speeds up, and you can allocate more blocks to learning skills/undertaking jobs so that things take quicker to learn and buy). Do NOT be afraid to take advantage of the soft reset- you'll need to use it often in order to make the speed of the game go much faster and smoother. Plus- as you progress through the game the gifts start to get a lot harder to afford- and you'll need speed boosts in order to unlock some of the gifts (via having high level jobs that give you more money- and in order to have high level jobs you'll have either needed to have played for a long time or soft-resetted the game to speed things up).
In order to pass this game you need to mess with your computers date by pushing it backwards and forwards as the game bases itself off of time played- the sooner you start making the most of this the less of a slog the game will be. Some skill levels for example will start to take a month, or even years to naturally unlock- so using your date changer becomes essential if you want to progress through the game. Another handy item to use (and the sooner you download one the quicker things will be for you) is an auto clicker (even the game recommends you use one), so that you can quickly speed through taking girls on thousands of dates, or clicking their affection up thousands of times while you go off and make yourself a cup of tea.
I guess my frustration with this game comes out of the fact that, by the time you realise how essential it is to constantly soft reset to speed the game up, or how essential it is to cheat by constantly changing the date you've already invested a fair amount of time in it. And it can feel strange to constantly reset the girl's affection only to grind it up again  in order to receive a speed boost. To me, this kind of broke the fourth wall a little, and made it more of a grind than anything. If I found enjoyment out of playing with changing my computers date settings I could do that without the use of this game.
On the bright side- a lot of peole have found different ways of progressing through the game much quicker via hacking through programs such as cheat engine - and so; this game could possibly be more fun if you're looking for something to practise your game hacking skills on. And if you want to unlock extra speed boosts straight away via buying diamonds the game will be faster to progress through (though you'll still need to soft reset and grind numerous times to increase your stats).
Overall- the game involved too much grinding for it to be as enjoyable as I'd have liked. If people are looking for a waifu simulator then I suppose it could be a good one, (though I'd think the fourth wall breaking soft reset would kind of affect that). I feel by the end of the game I spent more time on resetting dates than actually clicking through the gameplay- and to me this is a shame. I think it has a lot of potential- but somewhere along the way they set the accomplishments and dates needed to unlock stats a little too extremely for the game to be as fun.

TL;DR: Crush Crush has a charming sense of humor and reasonably engaging mechanics for an idle game. Unfortunately, its nature as an idle game works against it in the long run.
Crush Crush is a game about...well...running into girls, apologizing to them, and eventually dating them. It's a silly concept, but the game runs with the silliness. (One of the girls is a bear, for crying out loud!) Crush Crush's mechanics for doing this are simple enough. You have "time blocks," which are confusingly almost unrelated to real-world time. These time blocks can be put into various jobs to earn money and get promoted (which gets you more money), or into hobbies to increase statistics (which is needed to unlock new jobs).
To progress in your relationships with girls, you may need to have reached a certain level in a job or hobby, have a certain amount of money stored, give the girl certain gifts (which requires money), and/or go on certain dates (which requires money and a few spare time blocks); you will also need to have a certain level of "affection," which is increased by essentially all of the above plus a few other actions (like talking to the girls). This is where both the mechanics and the game itself get interesting. You'll usually have several girls unlocked but incomplete at any given time, meaning you need to figure out how to best spend your time blocks to reach the next level with the girls; it's hardly rocket science, but it's more interesting than the mechanics in most idle games.
More importantly, these activities display lines of dialogue and pictures relevant to the character, level of affection, and activity. This might sound simple, but for me it was the ultimate motivator for all the other activities. The characters are all unique, mostly charming and funny (though YMMV on which ones are or aren't); the little snippets you get after talking/dating/giving gifts to them are consistently entertaining and engaging. Discovering new dialogue is, for me, the best part of the game by far, and it's well worth playing the game just for that.
One problem with this new-dialogue-as-motivation bit is that it drastically decreases replay value. The mechanics aren't interesting enough to hold the game on their own, and it's not much fun to replay a route once you've seen all of its stuff. (Some of the dialogue/pictures/etc are entertaining enough on their own merit, but such gems are few and far between.) Unfortunately, you NEED to replay the game to finish it.
You can reset the game to increase the speed at which you earn money, increase stats, and do basically everything else. Most of the girls require at least some reset bonus (or a lot of fiddling with your system clock) to be completed in any reasonable amount of time, and a couple of the late-game ones have a reset bonus requirement (not that you would be likely to meet their other requirements without it). This is particularly infuriating as those two girls just so happen to be hinting at some kind of plot, tying together some of the weirder girls in the game (though not the bear). My reset bonus is at the point where I can complete the first several girls with nothing but a LOT of rote clicking, which is understandably dull, and it still takes ages to unlock those two. And according to the wiki, I still don't have anywhere near the Reset Bonus required to finish their routes.
I understand that this kind of mechanic is ubiquitous, perhaps required, in idle games. But I can't help but wonder; if the wit, humor, and characters put into Crush Crush had been put into some other genre, could we have gotten all of the things that are good about Crush Crush without any of the annoying stuff which makes it such a slog after a certain point?

As a fan of the franchise who has played all Deus Ex games except Invisible War, I'm not too happy with this one. I consider Deus Ex: Human Revolution to be one of my favourite games ever. So here's my breakdown of Mankind Divided.
+ If you've played Human Revolution before, you can start playing this one and you'll immediately know what you're doing.  Controls are almost exactly the same.
+ Graphics are good and detailed. The game really looks like it's from 2016 with almost no compromises.
+ The hub city and the levels are well crafted, with multiple ways to tackle each objective. This is what really drives the game for me and kept me from quitting it before finishing.
+ I like that they included a small crafting system, where you can craft some little consumable items by using so-called 'weapon parts'. These parts can also be used to upgrade weapons.
- The story of Mankind Divided sucks, it just sucks. After what happened in Human Revolution, especially after that cliffhanger ending (scene after the end credits), I was expecting something else than what we got here. Story and quests here involve a lot of busywork that is not all that interesting. The whole scope of the story is far too small and doesn't do the franchise justice. For me, hugely disappointing.
- In terms of aesthetics, Mankind Divided is a huge departure from Human Revolution (and The Fall). The gold/black colour scheme is gone as well as much of the futuristic design. That's what makes the look of Human Revolution/The Fall so absurdly cool: one look at it and you know what game it is. Both games have a very unique aesthetic with their design and colour pallet. This is completely absent in Mankind Divided: everything here looks, well 'normal'. The defining aesthetic is gone, Mankind Divided looks like any other game. Sure, there are terminals and PCs everywhere, but the rest is more reminiscent of Half-Life 2 for the most part than it is to Human Revolution. While I love HL2 and its setting, I don't want a City 17 kind of scenario in my Deus Ex game. For some reason that combination doesn't 'click' with me. In my opinion, giving up on the established design was a big mistake.
- The hacking mini game from Human Revolution is back, but in my opinion it's much worse executed and much less fun to do. There are now more hacking software thingys that you can use while hacking, which is pretty confusing. The whole hacking screen is too dark and way less clear looking than it was before. In HR, whenever I found a hackable device or door, I immediately started the mini game, because it was just fun to do. Here, it's a chore.
- The game lacks variety. In a big way. It's all about one location for most of the game. In fact, later in the game you do get to visit a research facility in the snowy mountains - awesome, I thought! But literally as soon as you get there, your next objective is to escape the whole place. What the crap!?
- Too much dialogue. Some conversations just keep going on and on an on, which annoyed the crap out of me until I started skipping dialogue lines. Some dialogues and quests are also very twisted and esoteric to a point that I felt fooled (the quest 'cult of personality' is a good example for this).
- It is nice that they included looting and have drinks and other consumables, but for my taste it is too much. Every room you enter is cluttered with items you can interact with. And that doesn't mean all is loot. No, there are boxes and other items you can pick up and throw around. I guess that is for distracting enemies or something, but I never used them for that. As far as I'm concerned, they could've toned this down a bit, especially the objects that are 'movable only' and the consumables (beer etc.).
- The game is a bit buggy at times when it wouldn't register button inputs or didn't reset the enemy status for some reason.
- Performance can be an issue. If you have a GTX graphics card, chances are you're going to have performance problems with frame drops, stuttering etc.. But even with an AMD graphics card, you might run into some issues. The game is demanding in terms of hardware.
- Microtransactions in a single player game. You can buy skill points in this game. Or in-game money. WTF!?
Overall, I can't bring myself to recommending this one. There are just too many things about it that disappoint me. Too many things that annoy me. Too many things that are less well executed than in it's predecessor.

For the people claiming the game is "rarely updated", please switch to beta updates. Gnomoria is updated

What's not to love about Gnomoria? Even in it's early access stage, this game feels very complete. Harvest resources, build your empire and vanquish your enemies. The foundation for a great game. A little imagination and you're there. You'll find yourself becoming attached to your Gnomes, caring genuinely for the welfare of those under your command. You'll start naming things, creating the story yourself, in your head. That's the beauty of sandbox games; the beauty of Gnomoria. One game, infinite possibilities, countless stories.
It does take some getting used to. Newcomers may find themselves slightly overwhelmed in the beginning, and the first winter you experience may be less than pleasant. You learn as you play, just like with any other game.
This is a game that can bring out the best in a persons imagination. Whether that means you're a brilliant general, creating new strategies to ensure the safety of your people, or a master builder drafting the blueprints to a castle.
Gnomoria is the game for you.

One of the most generous F2P MMOs on the market. Everything you see in the microtransaction shop, you can purchase just by playing the game. If you don't want to spend anything right away, you will have a harder time if you are someone that wants to rush through the game. But if you take your time, explore, do everything the game has to offer, you can unlock the entire game at no cost to you.
I currently own all the quest packs aside from 2 (Mordor expansion included in that), and I bought maybe 2 of them, only because I wanted to show support. I have also put some money into the game just for support. I have no reason at all to subscribe anymore. The whole game is open to me and it asks for nothing.
The entire epic questline is free however. You can go into areas you don't own to be able to do the epic line (same for Mordor? Not sure). But you will have to grind levels to keep up with it. I suggest actually playing the game though and doing everything it has to offer. If you don't, you will run into "pay walls". But this is a game you most definitely want to explore around in. I don't know many who actually rush through it. The game is gorgous, the story is top notch. You can tell this was a game designed by developers who have major love for the Lord of the Rings.
As for gameplay, it is your typical MMO. There is nothing really anything special about it. Most people play it to get lost in  a very large Middle Earth. The world is massive. The game does have players that claim the game is dying, and even some claiming we would never reach Mordor. We have, and the game is fine. Ever since they left Turbine, I feel the game has been in a much better place. Some server issues, but it seems better than it used to be.
All in all, if you like the typical MMO, and one where you can earn everything just be playing the game, along with a rich story and beautiful landscapes, LoTRO is the game for you.

Sure, Vertical Drop Heroes seems a bit similar to Spelunky on the surface. You are collecting tressure while dropping farther and farther into darkness. The game adds a numbe of wrinkles that differentiate it from Spelunky though. The difficulty curve is a bit less frustrating. The game has you level up while your playing and each time you level up you get more and more powerful until you are one shotting enemies... until you aren't, in which case the game gets challenging again. I find this much more pleasant than the cruelty of being killed by a neon green snake.
Using your recovered loot, you can permanetly upgrade your health and weapon damage which further changes the difficulty curve. You can also purchase portals to individual levels so that you can go straight to them. Some of the weapons you get are very fun. A spear does knockback damage, there is a buckler which will cause you block most attacks. There is a sword called a reaver that heals you as you damage others. These extra weapons add a lot of dimension to the game.
Overall, I have played this game for 4 hours, which is more than I have played any other roguelike and I forsee myself playing it for at least a few more hours. Definitely buy.

You can taste how deep this game is trying to be.
30 minutes of walking-simulator style gameplay, with mediocre but tolerable platforming, and memorable but slightly odd "pixel" art.  In quotes, because it looks like someone put Atari-era textures on a modern 3D-rendered game engine (to include remarkably fluidly-billowing banners with 5x20ish designs painted on one side, and real-time water reflections, and a protagonist who is literally a square).
There's a lot of rough edges.  The game offers to run in resolutions where the art is resized badly and the text is illegible.  The platforming feels average at best, which is unfortunate since exploration and jumping composes 100% of the gameplay.  Being underwater is slow and obnoxious, mainly because you have to wait for a timed event in order to ever get out.  The interface isn't particularly clear about what it's trying to tell you (the difference between having picked up a collectible and having found the place you need to take it involves whether the collectible is displayed with blue, white, both, or neither in your inventory, and the difference is never explained).  The writing is vague and trying slightly too hard to be open-ended and mysterious.
If you like walking simulators and stylized art, and are willing to manually suspend your disbelief, you could get half an hour out of this.  Maybe two hours, if you methodically chase down every piece of text in the game and make a go at unraveling the story.
I wish I could find something memorable about this game, aside from the beautiful sash an endgame character wears.  I suspect that the developers' projects after this one will have the potential to be much more, though.  They're almost there.

I consider myself a pretentious gamer, given that I'm a big fan of STORY when so many others seem to have abandoned it as the foremost gaming ideal. Whether it's the Sierra On-Line Quest adventures of old, the whimsical originality of LucasArts or the classic Bioware RPGs, I've always welcomed games which draw me into a mythology, a complete, hermetic tale. It never mattered what the subject was - classic fantasy, pirates, post-fallout apocalypse. Quality and consistency of dialogue and character were always the watchwords.
Yet, as pretentious as I claim to be and as much as I love the games of yesteryear, I rarely finish the story-driven games of today. I guess, over the years, I've become as impatient as all those console gamers who dominate the market. Games like Dear Esther - while I recognise their superb quality and importance in today's market - actually just bore me. As much as I want to like them, I grow dissatisfied too quickly.
The Novelist is not such a game. I was compelled from the outset to continue. I think the real world setting had a lot to do with this: the story grips you from the outset because it's completely REALISTIC. It feels like you're peeking into people's real lives. The three main characters are so wholly, so beautifully represented, that it's easy to imagine that they're your neighbours.
It's rare for a game to offer a sense that your choices really matter. This is one such game. And I know this is probably, single-handedly, the most oft-used and yet eminently inaccurate characteristic reviewers like to ascribe to RPG/adventure games. But having just completed this game, I can tell you it's completely true: I know I could go back and select different choices in order to elicit a totally different outcome.
There are so many peripheral touches that round out this experience, too. The gameplay is inspired: you can choose to dive, freestyle, right into the story without hindrance, or you can spice it up a bit with a stealth element that you just wouldn't expect in this kind of game. The sound mechanics are excellent and actually add to the gameplay, as you follow various audio cues to advance the story. The voice acting is credible and mature. And the game's author even makes the credits totally readable by paying tribute to each person's contribution to the overall game.
This is my first review on Steam, and I'm glad that The Novelist is what drove me to write it. Whether through Steam Greenlight or other avenues, we need to support developers to make more like this. They're the future of PC gaming.

Stratego is one of my old favorite childhood games.  It's easy to learn but it helped teach me how to think strategically and consider my opponent's moves in advance.  For a children's game, that's good.  It made learning chess a lot easier.
Screen resolution seems to be limited to 800x600 but it doesn't look too bad, even on a widescreen monitor.  You get a choice or different "board" designs, and three difficulties with minor differences between them.  There are default setups but you can move pieces around by swapping them to set up your board the way you like.  You can also choose whether your highest ranked piece is #1 or #9.
The unfortunate problem with this game is  the computer AI is terribly passive, even on the hardest difficulty.  It won't attack you unless it knows your piece has moved first.  To the computer, every stationary piece is a potential bomb.   The flag tends to end up in one of the two corners, surrounded by bombs.  Standard play when starting out, but when you expect the same thing over and over, charging in with a scout, a miner, and  a high ranking piece makes the game easy.
The only way this game could have be worth buying is if it included multiplayer.  Since it is not included, I can't recommend it unless you grab it super cheap or in a bundle.  Even if you're a fan of the game, you will grow tired of the computer's weak antics after a few battles.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is an incredible game. Great story, memorable characters, an absolutely hilarious villain, and awesome gameplay.
Gameplay: 10/10
Arkham Asylum is plain fun. The combat is easy to pickup and entertaining to watch. Sneak missions are amazingly fun. Nothing like going into a room with 10 armed guards and taking them out one by one, while they're wondering what the hell is going on. Seeing as this game came out a while ago and was the first Batman game of this series, I didn't expect much and was very pleasantly surprised. Each upgrade is useful and all the different gadgets are used throughout the game in different games. Unlike other games, you will constantly used each of these gadgets, not just use them once and never touch them again.
Story: 10/10
If you asked me to say what I thought about the game in one word, it would be dark. The story is pretty dark, and the world is pretty creepy at times. Every once in a while, Batman is taken to a world where he has to defeat a villain called Scarecrow, bringing back horrifying memories about the death of Bruce Wayne's parents. These parts were deep and you could really feel for Batman. I found the story itself a good length and it was a nice story itself.
World: 10/10
The world of Arkham Asylum is well-crafted. Riddler shows off his genius once again, and he mocks you each time you solve one of his cleverly hidden riddles. The AA world is riddled with Riddler's trophies, puzzles, and maps. These are just side missions, but I have to admit, the riddles give a sense of accomplishment when you figure one out. The Arkham Asylum island is not open world. It is pretty small, so after you beat the story, you can do some of the challenges, solve some puzzles, or just find some collectibles around the island that give you some insight on Batman lore, which is nice.
I really enjoyed this game, and I recommend to those who like smooth combat mechanics, a good story, and just superheroes or Batman in general.

Excellent game from top to bottom. Great story that is very intriguing. The feeling of claustrophobia that is caused by the combination of the dark, brooding environment and the fact that you're trapped in an asylum makes for an unforgettable experience. 9/10

The gameplay is split into 3 main sections. Combat, stealth and exploration. The combat mechanics in this game are a delight. Its free flowing nature allows you to build up satisfying combos that end in slow-motion bone-shattering and gratifying final blow. My only gripe is that the same mini boss is used roughly 4 or 5 times throughout the game with very little variation between each encounter.
The stealth sections of the game are forced onto the player by locking batman in a large arena with armed guards where if you are spotted the guards will likely kill you or at least take a decent portion of your health. Most of these arenas can be beaten with little challenge, and it was only the last two that caused me any distress. It's worth mentioning that that I am awful at stealth games, so more seasoned stealth fans may find it a bit of a breeze.
The exploration of the asylum is also a very enjoyable experience which is aided by batman's ever increasing slew of gadgets that he receives throughout the game. This allows for revisiting areas without feeling cheated or it being a waste of time. The new gadgets that you unlock, such as the batclaw, allow you to reach previously inaccessible locations and to find hidden secrets and collectables.
The story of the game is what you'd expect from a batman game, albeit much grittier. Though it's the character development where the writing really shines. Batman becomes more and more broken as he continues to hunt down the crazed Joker. This is shown through batman's attire becoming more and more damaged as progression is made throughout the story. As well as the intermittent scarecrow sections where batman visits his psyche through a series of hallucinations in visits to an almost psychedelic dream world. The full cast is peppered with batman characters include Harley Quinn, Bane and Poison Ivy. Fortunately Robin is nowhere to be seen.
The aesthetic fits the game perfectly and has clearly been thought through thoroughly in the games development and is used to aid the story and character development. The whole world is very dark and grey, the shadows of which batman hides in. The vibrant villains are a complete contrast to the world with the Joker showing his difference and insanity through his colourful attire, showing that he doesn't belong.

As a fan of the franchise who has played all Deus Ex games except Invisible War, I'm not too happy with this one. I consider Deus Ex: Human Revolution to be one of my favourite games ever. So here's my breakdown of Mankind Divided.
+ If you've played Human Revolution before, you can start playing this one and you'll immediately know what you're doing.  Controls are almost exactly the same.
+ Graphics are good and detailed. The game really looks like it's from 2016 with almost no compromises.
+ The hub city and the levels are well crafted, with multiple ways to tackle each objective. This is what really drives the game for me and kept me from quitting it before finishing.
+ I like that they included a small crafting system, where you can craft some little consumable items by using so-called 'weapon parts'. These parts can also be used to upgrade weapons.
- The story of Mankind Divided sucks, it just sucks. After what happened in Human Revolution, especially after that cliffhanger ending (scene after the end credits), I was expecting something else than what we got here. Story and quests here involve a lot of busywork that is not all that interesting. The whole scope of the story is far too small and doesn't do the franchise justice. For me, hugely disappointing.
- In terms of aesthetics, Mankind Divided is a huge departure from Human Revolution (and The Fall). The gold/black colour scheme is gone as well as much of the futuristic design. That's what makes the look of Human Revolution/The Fall so absurdly cool: one look at it and you know what game it is. Both games have a very unique aesthetic with their design and colour pallet. This is completely absent in Mankind Divided: everything here looks, well 'normal'. The defining aesthetic is gone, Mankind Divided looks like any other game. Sure, there are terminals and PCs everywhere, but the rest is more reminiscent of Half-Life 2 for the most part than it is to Human Revolution. While I love HL2 and its setting, I don't want a City 17 kind of scenario in my Deus Ex game. For some reason that combination doesn't 'click' with me. In my opinion, giving up on the established design was a big mistake.
- The hacking mini game from Human Revolution is back, but in my opinion it's much worse executed and much less fun to do. There are now more hacking software thingys that you can use while hacking, which is pretty confusing. The whole hacking screen is too dark and way less clear looking than it was before. In HR, whenever I found a hackable device or door, I immediately started the mini game, because it was just fun to do. Here, it's a chore.
- The game lacks variety. In a big way. It's all about one location for most of the game. In fact, later in the game you do get to visit a research facility in the snowy mountains - awesome, I thought! But literally as soon as you get there, your next objective is to escape the whole place. What the crap!?
- Too much dialogue. Some conversations just keep going on and on an on, which annoyed the crap out of me until I started skipping dialogue lines. Some dialogues and quests are also very twisted and esoteric to a point that I felt fooled (the quest 'cult of personality' is a good example for this).
- It is nice that they included looting and have drinks and other consumables, but for my taste it is too much. Every room you enter is cluttered with items you can interact with. And that doesn't mean all is loot. No, there are boxes and other items you can pick up and throw around. I guess that is for distracting enemies or something, but I never used them for that. As far as I'm concerned, they could've toned this down a bit, especially the objects that are 'movable only' and the consumables (beer etc.).
- The game is a bit buggy at times when it wouldn't register button inputs or didn't reset the enemy status for some reason.
- Performance can be an issue. If you have a GTX graphics card, chances are you're going to have performance problems with frame drops, stuttering etc.. But even with an AMD graphics card, you might run into some issues. The game is demanding in terms of hardware.
- Microtransactions in a single player game. You can buy skill points in this game. Or in-game money. WTF!?
Overall, I can't bring myself to recommending this one. There are just too many things about it that disappoint me. Too many things that annoy me. Too many things that are less well executed than in it's predecessor.

(The majority of my playtime is through the standalone LOTRO client)
I won't mince words; LOTRO is one of the best MMORPGs in the market. This isn't hyperbole and it obviously doesn't account for different tastes, but as far as traditional WoW-"clones" go, LOTRO is top-tier.
The world is massive. The visuals, though dated, have been updated (to the extend the engine allows) and the art direction of the entire game is masterful. The different areas are varied, but blend well together. The music is a masterpiece as well.
One of the strongest things about the game is its pitch-perfect utilization of the Lord of the Rings license; the liberties it takes with Tolkien's work are miniscule and don't impact the original story. Your avatar's main quest moves alongside that of the Ring-Bearer and his Fellowship and you run across many characters from the books, but your role in the story is never intrusive. There is tons of lore to pick up and in some occasions, it even helps expand upon Tolkien's work. This isn't just for the people that once saw the movies and want to play through the established events; this game makes it its task to fully immerse the player in Tolkien's Middle-Earth and succeeds at almost every step. The side-quests are fantastic and often-times even more interesting than the main quest-line. They flesh out the world and give layers to the game that most MMORPGs fail at. There are a lot of quests, but they all feel very meaty, so there is no real burn-out.
Here's the problem with LOTRO; it's very expensive. Its f2p limitations are many, but where this becomes a real problem is after level 30. The areas after lvl30 are accessible only for the purposes of doing the main quest. The other quests have to be purchased separately as "quest-packs" through the in-game store; that is, unless you sign up for "VIP", i.e. the standard subscription. All leveling content is available to subscribers at no extra charge.
Unfortunately, this doesn't include the expansions. These have to be purchased by everyone separately and they cost upwards of 150 Euros/Dollars. Turbine occasionally does sales that drop these prices considerably, but until that happens, you're sort of stuck. It's understandable the game needs to make money, but compare this to World of Warcraft, which requires a subscription, but has a very low entry-level point and only requires you to buy the latest expansion in the market to get the full content. It's just not very feasible.
Having said that, if you can wait for sales and you can afford it, I'd certainly recommend LOTRO, preferrably with subscription. It's a very absorbing game with great quest-lines, a fantastic setting and aesthetic and a very dedicated player base.

Most games with perma death tend to be quite difficult, but as long as you can circle strafe reliably, this game isn't too hard.
As you play, you unlock many different character classes that drastically change gameplay. One character starts with a huge health pool but moves much slower than the others. Another gets level experience faster but has comparatively poor starting stats.
Also this game has killer carrots that explode in your face so you know, points for that. Next to Risk of Rain this might be my favorite roguelike/roguelite/game with permadeath. Highly recommended.

I've been playing a number of casual puzzle games or, as I'd prefer, airport games, lately. And I'm pretty impressed with this one for mostly intangible reasons, but I'll do my best to explain why I think you should buy it.
Tenrow is a mobile tablet game that isn't available on any app store and can only be played with a PC. You are given a puzzle consisting of rows and columns of boxes. Some boxes have numbers and some do not. You can click the boxes to effectively turn them on and off. When activated, the numbered boxes that share a row or column with the one you activated will decrease by one. The goal is to find the right combination of active and inactive boxes to cause all of the numbers to reach zero, and then the puzzle is completed.
The reason that I call these types of games "airport games" is because they're the variety that you would pick up in a $5-10 puzzle book at the airport while you are waiting on a flight and otherwise have nothing to do. They're not the most exiting or brilliant things you've ever tried, but they're fun enough and get the job of passing the time done. Tenrow is one of those games that I would easily give a pass to for being interesting and challenging enough to keep my interest going and get through it. It also happens to be relatively easy to get a perfect game, simply by completing the puzzles.
Although my father's verdict for this game is "It's like doing your taxes", for $3 time-killer, my verdict is a strong rapid nod with squinted quizzical eyes.

I truly do like this game. The graphics for it I will call it cute, and doesn't need to be flashy to make it look great. I found the permadeath, although annoying at times, to really add to the game and to give it a lot of replayability. Also having many unlockable characters, you unlock them by completing certain challenges such as, dealing enough damage with your spells and weapons, to killing a certain number of creatures.
You don't need to be hitting headshots, actually I didn't notice a difference when hitting headshots or not, in the game to kill enemies, but some enemies can be difficult to deal with, until you get used to them. One of the things I did enjoy about Ziggurat are the different mechanics that can affect the room. Not all rooms will have them, they seem few are far apart, although not a bad thing I do feel they could of added a few more in through the game. But some of the mechanics can be decrease cost of staff by 50% everything else is 100% increase, unable to fire unless you are in the air, extra experience but no drops, and several others.
There are a few things that can be destroyed, such as barrels and certain pillars, to book stacks. Although they don't always have items that come off of them, sometimes potions or mana crystals will drop.
At level up you can pick 2 perks, which can be increased based on a perk you can get, and those can affect everything from health, to mana, to extra experience from the crystals, extra healing from potions, gain hp/mana at start of combat and many more. Perks are random at level up, which I rather enjoyed, it can add to the diffculty if you don't get certain perks that you are used to. For me my bane is when the game doesn't give me Health regen perks early on. Died several times because of it. But I do enjoy the randomness of the perks at level up.
There are also 4 weapon types, your standard wand, a spell, staff and alchemy weapon. All of them have their uses and can really change the flow of battle depending if you have them, and have the mana to use them. Only the wand (starter weapon) has unlimited ammo, but needs to recharge. The entire game is procedurally generated, but you will run into rooms that you have definately seen before. Not a bad thing, there is a good variety, and a lot of it makes sense.
Although the game is fairly short, it's main strength is replayability. When you are selecting your character it will state on the character card if you have completed the game with that character and what difficulty. Somewhat nice to see. There is a bestiary where you can go and look at the various monsters, but you need to unlock them by killing them in game. Bosses only need 1, while others need to kill multiple (dozens even) to unlock.
There are 2 playable characters to start, and I don't see much difference between them other than 1 male and 1 female. I unlocked a third character before I completed the game, but sadly only been able to beat the game with her(?) sadly. Working on the other 2. Permadeath is fun and annoying. When you die you lose all progress and perks and restart at level 1 on floor 1. When you complete a Floor you can save and quit or continue. You can also Save whenever you like. You don't need to complete every room on the floor, sometimes you can get lucky and find the summoning rune to summon the boss in the boss room and you can find them early on. But I do recommend completing the level for the experience.
The tutorial is limited to a hotkey snapshot that will show up on the left side of your screen when you start a new game (since I haven't done a save and load I can't say if it reshows when loading a previous game). Which I found to be really good in this game.
I think my only concern, which after getting used to didn't bother me much, is the ability to strafe while sprinting. But there is a perk to increase your movement speed after getting hit, and a very short invulnerability.
There is a daily challenge that you can do once per day, although I haven't it yet, when I selected it to see what it was about, you compete to get the highest score. Sounds like fun, will have to do that sometime in the very near future.
I truly do recommend this game, it runs quite smooth and I only ran into fps drops when there were a lot of enemies and lots of things happening (mostly just my hardware its not that great), but the game was still quite playable during these drops. I do recommend this game.

A good game killed by 2-3 pivotal game design mistakes:
1) You need to pick up experience, ammo and health potions. And all of it dissapears
.
This kills any type of strategy or tactics you can come up with. Want to stay at range? Not an option. Wanna kite? Can't do, you''ll have to run through your recently killed enemies in order to get anything.
There is no store or currency, your only source of everything is the loot. And you need to pick it up or it vanishes and the pick up radius is laughable.
2) All but one ranged enemies track your movement. I mean it's ok with a top-down perspective, where you can
attacks from any angle, but not in an FPS where you can see 1/3 of the screen at best (100 POV). So even if you think you're moving erratically and fast you will still get hit. And you
be surrounded by enemies because point.#1.
and by the way
2.1): Why is sprinting in the game? To make backtracking through rooms faster? Because enemies can also
. I see literally zero reason to sprint in combat. In fact in my 4 hours with the game that time I beat normal difficulty i didn't sprint once.
3) I've cursed every room with stairs I've got. Somehow it makes both aiming and dodging 3 times harder while slowing down the pace at the same time. Again, something top-down perspective doesnt have to worry about and I don't think Milkstone put too much thought into this; just decided that stairs are fun, let's add stairs. It made me think about old FPS  like Serious sam that had similar gameplay. Can't recall many Z-axis in areas designed for big fights. Maybe it was for a reason. And did I mention that EXP that enemies drop at the top of the stairs roll down so you can't pick it up, because every enemy in the room is at the bottom of that stairs? Yeah, talk about synergy of game desigh mistakes.
To clear things up - I'm not a fan of Rogue-lites but I'm ok with the genre. I'm ok with bad item RNG (and item balance by the way), unfairly tough rooms of enemies and doomed runs. I'm not ok with
having fun with the game when the run goes well.

It wasn't bad, but it wasn't great. Fairly simple. It reminded me of a good sudoku game, except the logic wasn't very tight: multiple solutions exist, so it's more like you're just taking stabs at moving numbers around rather than really using your brain and learning pattern recognition. It got boring pretty quickly, but it was a relaxing distraction for a few minutes, with accompanying and appropriate music.
The only real escalation within the game's 50 levels that makes it get more challenging was the addition of grey boxes -- they are not interactable but have counters that must still be considered similar to Sudoku or Minesweeper counters. Not much of an evolution. Don't expect the game to get much more challenging as you play.
I'm giving this a weak recommendation -- it's fun for half an hour, and you can grind it out in an hour. But considering the price, especially as part of a bundle, I can't knock it.

For me, a video game is something that I use to escape a stressful day, to get away from the high demands of life and work. With Always Sometimes Monsters I was hoping to jump into a surreal world full of death danger and decay. But it delivered an experience much like life, and rather than give it a surreal outlook it showed me how surreal it really is.
Always Sometimes Monsters sends you on the road trip from hell. Broke, depressed and just about to give up hope you must travel from place to place to reach the other end of the country to stop the love of your life from tying the knot with someone else. Whilst this sounds like a pretty easy task, it isn't. And sadly, it wasn't one I enjoyed as much as I had hoped to.
I know that this game is centred around choice, and on my first play though I came across a lot of hard decisions and I gather than everyone's experience will be different. But to be honest, I never found any of them to affect me or the characters in the game on an emotional level, up until the final hour so of the game. Everything I did just seemed to brush off, until you get a summary of everything you have done near the finale. Choice is something I long for in a game, but I feel as if Always Sometimes Monsters made these choices abrupt and I never really had much time to work up to them.
Whilst I do gather that I have gotten a different version of the story from everyone else, I never really found anything all
controversial for video game standards. I was hoping with something with a little more depth, rather than just giving me a harsh re-telling of reality. I was forced to work, make friends, loose friends just like everyday life. I found the first half of the game very tedious. Moving from place to place, scrounging for scraps, living off others and just being an all round disaster of a person is not something I long for in a video game. Choices really didn't start to get serious until the latter half of the game. My version of the ending really disappointed me. It completely destroyed the atmosphere of the game, so I will be hunting around to try and change it somehow.
Always Sometimes Monsters does have its good side, mind you. I don't know what living a broken life is like, but I really feel Vagabond Dog pulled it off. The atmosphere was amazing, I did really feel I was living a life rather than just watching someone’s life. I did really feel like if I didn't pay that rent, I would ruin my life even more, and I really did get motivated to stop the wedding. As well as feeling great, it also looked and sounded great. Lovely artwork, and a great sound track to supplement it. Great work.
All in all, whilst it had its downs, Always Sometimes Monsters is something that I think can be enjoyed by anyone, and the multiple scenarios make it something I shall visit often. I followed this game for months, watching every video, reading every story. My hopes were very high. And whilst it was something I did have a good time with it, I wanted to love it.
+ Multiple choices that will effect the outcome of certain events, highly replayable.
+ Great art direction and soundtrack.
+ Created an immersive life simulation, and the struggles that comes with it.
- Some of the game felt like a chore
- Slow paced first half. Took me a while to get into
- Some choices in my play through were brushed off too easily, i.e.
7.5/10

When I first saw this game on Steam I had no interest in it whatsoever. I just looked at it's name and dismissed it as some Rogue-lite style game, without even bothering to check up what it actually was. I'm happy that I did decide to check it out a second time.
If you enjoy a dark and depressive game with an incredible storyline then this is the game for you! It doesn't matter that it's graphics may not be impressive in any way because if you let yourself get immersed in the game then you're in for one hell of a ride. But beware, if you do give this game a chance and happen to like it then you'll have a hard time shutting it down until the story has reached it's end. I thought I had figured it out from the start, but I was thrown off by some unexpected twists in the plot, results of the choices I had made earlier in the game.
When we're on the topic of choices, this game has plenty of them! And even if it may not be something that you consider to be a huge decision then it will have an impact on the story, subtle or less so. Some of the choices are hilarious, some are disturbing and some of them will make you feel like a miserable wreck. What's not to love about that?
The game also contains some quite funny humour and interesting pop culture references.
If I had to sum up this game in a single sentence then it'd be along the lines of: The darkest and most immersive RPG that I have played up to date. I sincerely hope that this game gets the fame that it deserves because it is truly a masterpiece in my eyes.
And with that I'll end my review right here and jump straight into my second playthrough, thanks for taking the time to read it!
EDIT: Corrected some of the many typos.

Pros: Captures the look, characters and atmosphere. Open to non-fans whilst offering tons of easter eggs for devotees. Stealth is open and full of opportunities(sneak above, behind, beneath enemies. Lure away, wait for right time, or sneak up on). Combat is easy to learn but tough to master, with a rhythm to it that you have to get into and follow - making it feel "real" and hard without being frustrating or unwelcoming. Satisfying, challenging and addictive. Highly refined in all aspects. Graphics haven't aged a day.
Cons: Not quite non-linear - the only real open-world travelling is on the outside island and when you backtrack for collectibles. Some unnecessary streamlining. Short. You don't get to choose between when to use stealth and when to use combat. You barely do anything other than stealth-KO your way through a room and fight a group of enemies - puzzles, for example, are easy.

I had no idea of this game when I tried it the first time. I have never been a fan of DC either. But man, this is a great game, no matter if you like the comic or not.
Some people say, and I tend to agree partially, that this is still the best game in the batman series. The latter two games in the series are more open world, which some might prefer. But I found the story and the game play a little more contained (in a good sense) and with better pacing. It feels slightly like the open-world was added to the latter games just because that is popular, while in fact the games don't really need it. They are still great games, but it is not the open-world aspect that makes the games great.
The game is beautiful (even though it does not demand the best PC), there is so much to do, and all aspects of the game are interesting and well made. The combat is incredibly smooth and satiesfying, even though on paper it looks rather simple. You really feel strong and powerful being batman. I find it a perfect combination of stealth and fighting. But batman is also a great detective, and the gadgets are really inovative and fun to use. There are quite a few ways to "travel" around, and the games has tons of extras to find, which might make you want to come back again. There are also boss-fights, and even though I don't like boss fights normally, these are fun, and sometimes quite interesting and innovative.
The voice acting is very very good (the joker is Mark Hamill for example)
The whole lore and universe is interesting and deep. I learned a lot about the batman universe playing this game, and I really felt every antagonist had an interesting story and depth. The game is dark in the right way. It does not feel silly at all. It really feels like the game was made by people who love and respect this comic. It is a game about batman, not just a way to cash in  on a great icon. This game delivers well even if you are a fan or not.
I think it runs great with mouse and keyboard, and this time I did not try it with a controller, but I can't imagine that being a better option anyway.

I've been looking forward to this game for a while, as any game that forces the player to make difficult choices with some grounding in reality immediately piques my interest.  Ever since getting married about a year ago, I've had to "grow up" and realize that my choices are no longer my own, and that I must think of the greater interest of my wife and family in general as we both make decisions together.  Now as we get ready to give up our established jobs and prepare to move overseas for several years, where we hope to make new friends, raise any future children, and find new jobs, our choices become more and more crucial (and intimidating) than ever before.  These feelings had me anticipating The Novelist even before I played a single minute.

Some have accused me of enjoying 2Deep4U games a bit too much; while it's true that mostly indie games topped my list of games I most enjoyed last year (Swapper, Gunpoint, Brothers, Guacamelee, Rogue Legacy, Stanley Parable), I've managed to maintain a cynical stubbornness against games that I can appreciate but otherwise just do not enjoy (Proteus, Papo & Yo, Dust).  After completing The Novelist, I can unfortunately say that my verdict of the game lies squarely in the latter category.

The Novelist appoints you as a ghost in a house where you voyeuristically observe the life of the Kaplan family: Dan, Linda and their son Tommy.  The house is littered with notes, letters and drawings (Gone Home-style) which you can read to discover the daily problem du jour.  Thankfully, there is more human interaction than Gone Home, since you can also watch the family members live their lives and enter their memories to hear their thoughts.  After finding enough clues and thoughts, each member has an "item" that you can possess to convey how they would want to end their day.  If you find enough clues, you can also make a compromise possession with someone else, but at least one person will always have their daily wish unfulfilled.

From what I can tell after two playthroughs, the first choice will always carry the most weight.  The compromise choice, if selected, seems to either mildly satisfy the family member or merely hold status quo.  The member whose choice you ignore will fall into worse and worse shape.  Each playthrough can offer days in random order, but the days themselves are the same and have no variety.  I didn't like this as you never see any ramification of previous choices in future days, besides some thoughts here and there.  Everything is eerily distilled into simple black and white scenarios and outcomes.  I'll avoid any spoilers, but the daily, monthly, and eventual final decision results left a lot to be desired.  Also, the final outcomes are incredibly disjointed, with certain distinct epilogues given for each character that hold absolutely no relationship to other members' decisions and epilogues.

Actually, I think that's what annoys me the most.  For a game whose prime selling point is the idea of making hard choices and compromises for the greater good, the fact that your choices have no interrelation between members seems completely unrealistic and disappointing.  If I, as a father, take time out of my day to affirm my wife's hobbies and spend more time with my son, how does it make sense that I treat them the same horrible way depending on one of my one (father) choices, versus when I completely ignore them and put my priorities above all else?

In a game that prides itself on difficult decisions, I can give one clear recommendation on choice:
Don't play The Novelist.

Not worth the money at all. How this counts as a game is beyond me. The characters were completely unlikable and unrealistic. Why is it that everything is so cut and dry? Why can't the guy go to the beach with his family *and* write some of his book. The wife is a little whiner, as is the son. Surely moving schools would help the kid stop being bullied??

I recommend The Novelist for its take on how complicated life is. How do you balance a career and family? What if your passion gets in the way of your relationships with your spouse and child? Responsibilities conflict, and you're pulled in different directions. By this premise, I was intrigued, and I was happy to find how frustrating it was to make everybody happy. Compromising is important (as it is in life!)
However, I don't hand the game a strong recommendation. After a few chapters, the gameplay became repetitive. I wanted to see my actions more deeply affect the characters outside of short wrap-ups at the end of each chapter. In the beginning, I could see how it was realistic for these three people to mostly spend their time separately, really just giving a short "hello" as they passed by. All of the meaningful character interaction was presented in memories that you explore in the chapter.
I think The Novelist could have been better, but I enjoyed the time I spent on it. I love the idea of it, but I think it could have been implemented better. At the moment, it seems too simplistic, and that's hindering the game and the message because life is not simple. Overall, interesting game.

DLC Quest is a short parody platformer game released in 2011 on both PC and Xbox 360 service, made by Going Loud Studios. It would then get an expansion pack "Live Freemium or Die" in 2013 for both platforms. Which was free for PC, but sold on Xbox 360, probably because of Microsoft policy. Because you know, they dislike hosting free stuff on their servers, as you heard being the reason why Valve wasn't updating Team Fortress 2 for Xbox 360. Anyway, I think that this also came to Steam only in 2013 as well. Yep, expansion pack / sequel included, no worries.
And well, as you see, it's a simple platformer, that parodies everything DLC and modern. And you have to purchase DLC through in-game money in in-game shop, which after a while may start to look no different from what you do in normal games. Hm, maybe it could be more funny if they actually sold DLC as DLC for the game for extremely low-low price of one cent or such? But nah.
You know how it goes with most joke games: people say 10/10 for the premise but others start to hate them by the time they beat them. Such joke games must know boundaries and know when to end, as well as trying not to enrage people too much. Thankfully, DLC Quest knows them and ends when it should. It does seem short, but at least it kept fresh enough until the end and was enjoyable.
Not to mentioning that game is enjoyable by itself for a very short time that it playes. You just explore small map, find some curious stuff, collect money, platforming is responsible and easy. Original DLC Quest campaign doesn't allow you to die and is shortest. Live Freemium and Die adds some challenge to keep players enganged after original, mostly by adding spikes that will kill and send you back to checkpoint. But they are still pleasent and nothing compared to flood of indie "hard platformers for sake of hard".
So yea, game looks pretty enough with some 8-bit-like music that is enjoyable and doesn't try to do a horrible joke. It also makes you question many life-important things. Like, why Season Pass is called Season Pass? No, seriously. Or how much developers went insane with tiny DLCes. Even though you all probably just wait until game goes on huge sale where you buy bundle with all DLCs for dirt cheap anyway.
But yes, it doesn't overstay the welcome and has enjoyable simple platforming, so you can spend a hour or two on it. Unless you try to do two hidden hardcore speedrun achievements or try to beat scores.
Just try to get it while it's on sale. Not because game costs too much. Doesn't matter what discount. You just should be able to tell yourself that you got it during your crazy Steam sales impulses. Instead of asking yourself why you went so low into rabbit hole that you are fully purchasing joke games based on their premise and give them 10/10, while you could get some better proper game instead.
AND HEY, ZOMBIE DLC!

Vertical Drop Heroes HD is pretty neat, you have to make it from the top of a level to the bottom of a level and get out the exit, to make it to the next level ala Spelunky, with a lot more combat involved. Although a lot of it can be avoided and there are achievements for getting through levels without killing things so it's more a playstyle choice.
It is a roguelike so you get to unlock new classes and perks, you can purchase persistent upgrades with currency collected throughout each level/from killed npcs; also you can levelup your character (start each game at level 1) which increases numbers (damage, hit points).

A great little Roguelite/RPG. You choose from 1 of 3 randomly generated characters for each playthrough. The goal is simple, just go strait down and kill the boss, which unlocks the portal to the next area, rinse and repeat. But thats not all. You can unlock starting traits(perks that give various passive bonuses), and buy them too. You can spend the gold you find and/or earn to increase the starting damage and health of all you future characters. You can buy and unlock new spells that do a wide array of cool stuff. There's even a Pacifist playstyle if you want, where you simply go through the level dodging attacks and avoiding killing. So long as you don't kill anything(directly), there will be 'Pacifist Orbs' floating around which gives you a small bit of experience and gold to compensate for what you miss out on when you don't kill, which is basically experience and gold. You can upgrade the Pacifist Orbs too, so they give more experience and gold per orb. Also, just an fyi, the orbs disappear for that Level when you kill something, so be careful.
I definitely recommend this game. A Roguelite/RPG/Platformer with many things to unlock and upgrade.

4/5 stars. Vertical Drop Heroes HD is like Rogue Legacy "lite"...in a very good way.
Most of my playtime with Vertical Drop Heroes HD has been with the GOG (DRM-free + original VDH) version. So my Steam stats don't reflect my total experience with this game.
PROS:
+Pick up and play accessiblity.
+Easy to learn, difficult to master.
+Fast arcadey action.
+Stages are randomly generated, assuring replay value.
+Unlocked abilities can be used with future characters, but characters can only carry 2 unlocked abilities with them at a time. This allows for very customizable gameplay, while keeping it challenging.
+Gamepad support: Xinput (360, or Logitech F series set to "X").
+Modest hardware requirements; most PCs built in the past 8 years should run VDH-HD.
CONS:
-No Linux support at the time of this review. But, given VDH-HD uses OpenGL, Linux users may be able to run it via Wine.
-No Direct Input (Logitech and generic) controller support...yet.

Just to relive the nostalgia, I had to go back and play the original Vertical Drop Heroes on Kongregate. This truly does its predecessor justice, giving that fantastic risk-reward system and adding so much more to it. There are some aspects of the game that are easy to exploit (using Confusion on the Worm boss makes the fight ever-so easy, especially when I know recharges are around the corner), but even with that, the game provides a good challenge and requires you to put both your platforming skills and rogue-like decision making skills to the test. I especially like the addition of the pacifist system. Normally the choice of "To fight or not to fight" comes down to whether or not you can gain more than you lose, but in this case with many fights being winnable without much or any loss, a reward for avoiding the easy massacres is tempting and very worth it. The story itself is also simple but very befitting; so often do games tell of the great hero that overcame evil with the dozens of game-overs in between never even being acknowleged. Knowing that each failed attempt is simply another step in the story makes me even more anxious for the next attempt.
I look forward to seeing what comes out of Nerdook Productions next. Even if it's another remake of an old Flash game, I know it will be as good-- if not better than-- the original.

I had really high hopes for this game. Before it came out, I remember seeing all kinds of press for it, screenshots of vast urban decay, hints of in-depth exploration, all the features that make a post-apocalypse fan salivate. Yet the hype for it died completely off after release, and I actually completely forgot it existed until I saw it on a Steam sale. I finally decided to pick it up and play it. Right from the start there were multiple things that bothered me. The game doesn't seem to want to go too far in any direction no matter what the choice is, and that makes it overall very bland right from the get-go. The game is incredibly linear, guiding you in a single direction and not letting you veer off the course, yet they have tiny outlets from your linear path where you can find consumable items and whatnot. It's not rewarding to get these though. There was virtually no effort put into finding it aside from ♥♥♥♥ing off somewhere that wasn't the objective and after a short 5 second walk it's sitting on the ground for you. Why didn't they have the ability to search for supplies? checking dumpsters, containers, or piles of debris would have added so much more to this than simply walking slightly left of where you were originally going to go. The interactions with the AI are just as linear as the exploration. There are two types of people in the game, the "I'm just trying to survive, morally you shouldn't shoot me" people and the "I'm clearly up to no good, you shouldn't feel bad shooting me" people. It makes it very cut and dry to be able to decide who to kill and who not to, and don't worry, if the game decides you shouldn't kill someone it does its best to prevent that. One of the first NPCs you meet in the game is a woman protecting her storefront/residence with a gun. If you walk in front of her, she'll point the gun at you and warn you to stay back. The game clearly wants you to just leave her alone and keep walking, but the game hints from the tutorial that you should have to make the choice yourself as to what you do in that situation. Yet in this situation, you have at most 1 round for your handgun, clearly dissuading you from shooting her. You have a machete, but due to her placement you can't sneak up to her for a stealth kill like you have just been taught how to do, and if you walk at her and try to kill her with it she immediately plugs you in the head and kills you. You're supposed to think "Well duh, that's how it would be in real life" but it is disappointing that they force that kind of situation on you with the facade of choice and moral decisions being involved when in actuality the game has forced your moral compass to point to "Good". This is just one of my many complaints about the game. The camera is horrible, switching between a free camera and being locked in certain angles that gets incredibly jarring. The combat is incredibly simple and redundant, as is the urban exploration with things like traversing obstacles, climbing ledges, hanging from pipes, etc.. The stamina meter built into the climbing is nothing more than, to use a cliche term, artificial difficulty. It's meant to add a sense of urgency, stress, or fear in the game, but yet they give you the simplest exploring mechanics of all time. All of it is incredibly safe. If you mess up an input, it's not like you fall to your death, you just sit there doing nothing. You can't fall off a ledge, there is no balancing on the beams as you cross them. It's meant to give you the feeling that it's dangerous, without actually giving the player any reason to be scared. All in all, the game is a major disappointment, and I can't say I would recommend it to anyone expecting an immersive or exciting game.

I Am Alive is actually a very refreshing and entertaining game.
- Through the dusty city in fictional city Haverton in America, there was a backstory known as 'The Event', that apparently was a bunch of earthquakes, though the backstory of post-apocalyptic essentially is present. The story is a series of events that occur in Haverton, which I must admit use a variety of buildings and adventures in order to fulfill the objectives, refreshing. The overall story is powerful through emotionally engaging with characters, for example, Mei and her mother. The story does tend to rush at the end as that could have been spaced out, though I will admit the ending is very strong and I was completely shocked by the ending. Oh, its a cliffhanger too.
- The graphics are beautiful in the game. For a 2012 game, they are at a high standard for that point in time. Speaking of Ubisoft, in 2012 they had a high standard of graphics in each game they released, which was their year in relation to graphics. The atmosphere and environment and the day/night dynamic is excellent graphically, though there could be some more day/night variations.
- The gameplay is solid. I do like the motions of the character and how he engages with the environment, which I felt was again for a lack of better word, refreshing, though different to other post-apocalyptic games. These same motions however, could be expanded a lot more. For example, if your character is on the ground, your stamina will deplete due to heavy dust that will affect it and eventually your health. The character walks basically like he is having a stroll as if there was minimal dust. To combat this, more diversity in actually producing motions when in the heavy dust could add a further dynamic to the gameplay. Stamina added a new dynamic to the game, which I appreciated. I liked the fact that this element suggested planning more so you as a player wouldn't deplete your stamina as fast as if you just went out there, so it was nice. I did love the element of preserving your bullets, as they could come in at handy times. There are a limited number of bullets in the game, and you do need them, though thats why planning is essential.
Regarding crooks and other gang members, I loved that element in the game, though it did get repeatitive as it was too basic. So everytime you walked up to a crook, you would have to kill him essentially, no reasoning, nothing, just plain old re-shooting the guy, whilst good, repeatitive. The camera control is an absolute pain. For example, whilst on a cliff and you look at the scenery and attempt to plan what portions of the building you have to climb, the camera will literally screw you up by making you deplete stamina because the camera was not facing the direction your player was moving at.
- There were bugs regarding graphics and gameplay that could have been ironed out, and balancing regarding camera control would have been appreciated. It didn't overly affect the game, but it was noticeable. Not as bad as some games I'll mention. Here are my pros/cons based off this review...
Pros:
- Strong story and backstory.
- Beautiful graphics.
- Day/Night dynamic, Atmosphere, and Environment are very good.
- Solid gameplay.
- Lovely balance overall.
Cons:
- Rushed ending to story.
- Day/Night could have been used more to enhance particular missions, apparently according to the main character near the end, the entire sequence of events happened in a day...
- Vague, but gameplay could be expanded upon.
- Bugs.
Overall, I Am Alive is a good game. It has its positives and negatives, however it has a very good foundation to build upon. The gameplay was solid, though it was basic for this genre and could have been more diverse to enhance the game. The story was strong, and the graphics were great. I do recommend this game at $17.99, however it is you, the readers, choice because I played this game on easy mode (there are 3 or 4 levels of difficulty) and it took me 8 hours to complete the game. So expect at least 10+ hours if you do the side-quests as well, as in help the surviviors. I did this partially (7/20). Score: 7.5/10
EDIT: I forgot to mention, dialogue is excellent in the game. Every set of people, be it main characters or thugs had dispirate dialogue, enhancing the game. I loved that aspect. Since I forgot to mention that, I'll bump my score from 7.25-7.5/10.
EDIT 2: This game lets you run your mind run wild on what happened to Haverton, what happened at the ending. It leaves a lot of aspects open for interpretation which works for this game. I forgot to mention, this game sometimes can feel like a chore to play, but personally that is what happened to me when I raged that I kept dying in the dust :p
