This game is bit similar to Heretic/Hexen series. Part of enemies look like they were borrowed directly from them (skeleton throwing axes, wraith throwing blue magic, flying demon throwing fire, skull-lych, this is only few examples), some weapons look similar and sound alike, keybindings, mana system look like from Hexen/Hexen 2 as well.
But comparing to Hexen it don't have saves and have procedural generation of levels from pre-defined set of rooms - here it comes rogue-like part, which change gameplay pretty much comparing to Heretic/Hexen. So if you looking towards this game because you liked those games you are mistaken. There is only superficial similarity.
Pros:
+ nice graphic (even though I prefer a grimmer and darker version, that does not negate the fact that the graphics here are pretty good quality)
+ good music and sound effects
+ well-optimized smooth work
+ simple and handy map
+ relatively small price
Cons:
- it's hard to tell which atmosphere this game tried to maintain. It vary from classic fantasy atmosphere coming from stone rooms lighted by glowing candles and magic crystals with skeletons/wraiths/demons/golems as enemies to ridiculous casual game mishmash with specimens more suitable for plants vs zombies or something like that (mushrooms, carrots, featherless birds, flying one-eyed fishes, etc.).
- too challenging/random difficulty
Game can be randomly quite hard even on easy mode. There are some rooms with traps and minions (if you unlucky with level generation and shrines) which can spoil all playable character HP in 2-3 shots if you not mobile enough, while health potions are very rarely drop from defeated minions. Some health shrines may take almost all your health without giving a bonus or give a negative effect instead. You may end up with 15-25% of character HP before facing floor boss, and obviously boss can one-shot character right away.
You can't collect and keep consumables to use in harder situation, there is no such thing in Ziggurat. Nothing like basic inventory present. You can keep amulet but only one, if you find another one you can't keep both but need to choose which one you throw. Same with weapons, if you find other weapon which intended for the same weapon slot which already have weapon you can't use it for any other vacant slot (out of 4 slots, which happens quite often, so you can have only two or three weapons for most of floors).
Also you can't leave not needed health/mana drops for later pick up, they disappear from location after few seconds (that is what I dislike the most. If you earned them, why they should disappear without a trace?).
- POV very close to ground. I dunno if it problem of camera placement or scale (like developer says), but it feels like you are playing for a small animal, instead of selected humanoid character. I even double checked if he/she really not a dwarf/gnome or anything like that. No, it's not the case. It's just a design solution. If character standing near the barrel, there is a feeling that he/she have the same height.
- Random generation can work against diversity. You can face some amount of exactly the same rooms on next floor like they were on previous one. The variety of rooms in size and shape is also very small. Like you saw one floor, you saw everything, differences are small.
- Most enemies are ranged attackers, while lacking close-in attackers.
- Not many of destructible objects, you can't even break a stained glass window (like you could in Hexen)
In total, game fun enough for a start, but quickly loses its entertainment after some time. Design is pretty simple to the point of being plain and repetitive, which is not really that bad but in combination with abcence of some general goal/plot or other motivational hook (other than level final score or "go as far as possible") feels pointless.

Now having played Rainbow Six 3 it seems that Ghost Recon was meant to be a lazy spin off of that original trilogy which I will make comparisons of from the perspective of 3 assuming 1 and Rogue Spear had near exact equivalents.
First team selection and customization. There are two different types of soldiers: Standard which are the most disposable things ever and Specialists who are achieved only by completing optional secondary mission objectives. All fall in the class of Assault, Support, Sniper and Demolitions with only a pair of the last three available with Standard at a time 6 being the maximum deployment size. Equipment selection is brought to a minimal with only two pieces: primary weapon, secondary item, no armor selection and all soldiers with NVGs and Binoculars. The amount of primaries are very limited even with Specialists. Secondaries include the (suppressed) M9 pistol, grenade launcher attachments, 2 remote claymores and 6 hand grenades, 2 motion sensors (similar to heartbeat but have to be placed down), extra ammo and exclusive to Demolitions the anti-tank rocket launcher and timed explosive which both are required to complete some mission objectives.
Second team skills. Remember how each Rainbow operative had like 10 different stats despite some not being so important and each started medium to high, would increase a little if they survived a mission and if they died would be replaced only once with someone with a significantly lower amount of skill. In this game there are 4 different stats: Weapon, Stealth, Leadership and Endurance. Each of these can be filled with a maximum of 8 points each. Standards always start out with a total of 7 or 8 points with no skill ever starting with over 2 points and if they survived the mission everyone who took part gets 1 point to put on whichever skill the player wants. The problem is this does not make much diversity in selecting a team because chances are your Standard soldier will die before they make a bell curve on their skills; it is much harder for them to get wounded and it felt like you are using the Replacement Rainbow operatives even sometimes with Specialists.
Endurance which wasn't in R6 is the increased chance that if a soldier is hit they will get wounded.
Third planning and controls. Before and during a mission you are given a full layout of the map with objectives marked. So what about planning? There isn't any like in R6, instead during the mission you have to hold down the map button to select your teams waypoints, engagement options and movement options all while the game still goes on making it risky to send backup if you are engaged. The controls calling All Teams Go/Hold and switching teams/operatives was also complicated. And I guess you can also do the equivalent of Alpha, Bravo, Charlie movements by getting teams in positions, place on hold, mark waypoints moments before you will execute them then command "Advance at All Costs" but that never got to me.
If you like Rainbow Six without the long planning then perhaps this is okay. I also found it more simple using only two teams than three and you can save as much as you want during missions. But being the same price as other Rainbow Six games I would recommend those first over this.

Let me preface this review by saying that I have been a GTA fan for as long as I could remember, even before I owned a system that could play any of the games.
This game was highly anticipated by me, despite the year long waiting period between release and me getting to play this game. This review will be in two parts, firstly regarding the story and general gameplay mechanics, and the second dealing with my experience playing GTA Online.
Part I -
From what I’ve percieved, it seemed like the split-style gameplay of GTA compared to previous releases was recieved with mixed opinions. Personally, I was a fan of getting the feeling of a deeper game experience by having the story presented from three different perspectives. Transitions were much smoother than I previously anticipated before playing, and overall I do feel like the game benefitted from this.
In regards to the story, I can’t say there was too much that stood out to me, so I’d say that the story is the weakest link in this game. Characters were written extremely well, however their eventual purpose ended up being rather generic. Former criminals getting back together for one last heist, not much else you can do with that. There’s the element of choice that we saw in GTA IV making a return, which to me made the plot feel a tad bit derivative, but this is really just a minor nitpick.
Otherwise, it’s a GTA game, plain and simple, and it’s really good at being a GTA game. The world is bigger and better than ever, and there are more aircraft, boats, and cars to choose from when you want to get around.
Part II -
GTA Online, where do I begin?
Before I started playing Online, which now contributes the most to the amount of hours I have accrued, I actually had to be coaxed into starting off in it. I never really saw the appeal before I set out, but now I realize what I was missing out on. It’s all the fun of single player (post-story) with more clothing, vehicles, and more importantly, friends to hang out with. Within a week of playing online for the first time I was absolutely hooked, and despite the presence of many modders at the time I began, gameplay was largely unaffected.
Since I began playing, there have been major overhauls to the connection system, anti-cheat system, as well as the addition of several new game modes and methods of making money. This means that the experience of playing Online has only become increasingly refined, and despite most of the activities being a money grind, there’s enough variety to break the monotomy.
In conclusion, I highly recommend GTA V both for its single player and Online gameplay.

In a world made entirely of cubes (undoubtedly the inspiration for Minecraft, I'm sure), your job as a fellow cube is to make it to the end of each of 109 different levels. Each level features three different additional goals: a survival element, a collect-a-thon element, and a time trial element. The amount of nuance put into the last aspect is what makes the game perfect for speedrunners. Not only do the collectibles, in addition to being necessary for an S+ rank, increase your speed for a short amount of time, but any extra time you'd normally incur can be negated with the use of EDGE time - that is, your cube will stick to walls and edges, and any time spent hanging there does not factor in to your final level time. This adds an additional layer of strategy and timing which is sure to have you replaying the same levels again and again.
The controls are a bit clumsy at first, but you'll become acclimated soon enough (and you can change the direction of "up" in options). The graphics are not the best, but they at least accomplish what they're supposed to, and there's no ambiguity with what's traversable and what's not. The soundtrack is stellar, and makes it difficult to get very mad at the game. Overall, a rousing success, and as it's only eighty cents in the current sale - well, it's really a no-brainer.

I grew up playing this game, so I may have some bias, but this is one of my favorite games of all time. I don't think I could even describe this game in terms of other games, because it set itself apart from normal FPSs. Got 3 hitmarkers on the dude with a 9.7 K/D ratio? No, it's more like, "I just lost 2 men because our platoon was moving too loudly near a patrol."
It's perfect for all the tactic fanatics out there. You just might have more fun hatching up strategic ideas to kill all 43 enemies in the level with your 6, even if it's not necessary. I was actually genuinely surprised to find out how much detail went into the game. NPCs can't see you through bushes, they hear sounds like footsteps and shots, and they acknowledge dead bodies. In addition to that, after looking in the game's files, the game takes into account which body part you shoot (a lower arm shot has a 1/100 chance to kill compared to a headshot), different classes have different body armor ratings, and different guns shoot bullets at a higher velocity with varying damages. I actually don't know why the bullet velocities are even programmed, because I haven't been able to see far enough away for there to be bullet drop, but the point is there's so much attention to detail that almost nothing is left to random chance.

Seriously though, this is a really good game. People don't give it enough credit.
It really is a shame it isn't as well produced as it promised; the graphics suck, the main character's face gives me the creeps. The movements are awkward and the AI is really weird. Like, you're armed, and you point a gun at a guy, he'll stop and raise his hands. As soon as you put your gun down, he'll make a run for you, even if you're still looking at him. And then, you pull your gun back up and he'll stop. The concept is really really good, though, specially because you can do that even when you have no bullets at all, and they will kill you if you try to shoot when you run out of ammo.
The survival element is the best thing here. It's been yeeeears since I've played a game that really got me scared that, at some point, I wouldn't have any supplies left. The first survival games I've played were probably the only ones to give me that feeling. You can manage the health supplies if you don't risk yourself too much (you'll probably have some of them left by the end of the game if you do that), but bullets are really hard to find. The story is also quite good. It's simple (literally just a guy trying to survive and find his family), and I won't spoil anything, but it really has a good take on that "main hero" figure every game usually has. You'll (hopefully) get it at the end.
Overall, I have a feeling, and I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, that this game would end up better than The Last of Us (given it has a similar concept of survival, except that it's way easier to survive on TLoU) if it had enough budget and less production problems. Saddly, this isn't what happened and the game has its technical issues, but I'd recomend it anyway. There aren't any problems that ruined my gameplay, so I believe it'll only make things look awkward sometimes at most. Even so, it's short and it's cheap by now, so I'd say go for it.

500 hours, over 2 years playing.  I still find myself drawn to the game for it's open world chaos.  Play the missions, steal and sell cargo, fly fighters and bombers or just drive around like an idiot with your friends mowing down pedestrians and running from the cops.
The expansions continue to come, new businesses, new cars, new planes, new everything.  No paid DLC, just lots of very expensive toys that try to entice you into buying Shark Cards.  It's tough to see others on their $3Million flying bike, or driving around in a fully modified and upgraded Mobile Operation Center and not want one for yourself.  If you grind at it, you can get it without Shark Cards but RockStar gives you lots of incentive to buy them.
Hackers make the game frustrating.  They're unkillable, run faster than the fastest plane, create money from thin air and so have evry single thing in the game that can be used to murder you, they teleport, instakill, pull the entire server into one place and murder you over and over and over until you kill the game that you can't log out of.  It's the biggest downside to the game that Rockstar seems to do very little about.  The reporting process is crap (You can only report on a player that is actively in your game.  What's that, he left session after killing the entire server or you bailed out after your 5th death agaisnt an unkillalble monster?   Too bad, we don't care).
At the end of the day, I keep coming back.  Get some friends together, start a team and go make some money.  Will you play it every day for months on end?  Maybe not but you'll almost certainly get your money's worth just from the single player campaign even if you never log into Online once.

Ziggurat is a fun "procedurely-generated" roguelike FPS with weapons which remind of the Heretic / Hexen series, and cool, lighthearted enemy designs akin to something you'd see in a Pixar film.
The sound effects are well done, however I do prefer to turn off the repetitive music (and perhaps play internet radio in a separate window instead, etc..)
The gameplay itself is varied in the sense that as you explore the levels you find new weapons and upgrade your health, mana (ammo) or various other mutator effects the player selects as they level up (ie broken boxes in the environment yield health, or increased fire rate etc) however If I had one gripe it's that the environments can be very repetitive (though that is inherent to the gameplay style...)
Those expecting melee combat will be disappointed, as the game is primarily a shooter and the mage's various staves embody "shooting types" similar to that genre ie a 'machinegun' rate of fire gun, a grenade launcher / AOE, a triple shot spread etc. All weapons have an alt fire which adds some variety. The level bosses can be a bit brutal (as they should be, they're bosses...) however I think their difficulty was patched to be more forgiving..

Brawlhalla is a game about fighting your opponents and trying to knock them off the stage. Each character has a unique set of skills which allows them to have advantages. The game lacks story (aside from each character's origins), but makes up for it in gameplay. The game has several similarities to the video game series Super Smash Bros.
Gameplay: 9/10
The controls are easy to learn but hard to master, and the game also supports several different controller options. The game itself runs very smoothly and feels excellent.
Graphics: 8/10
The graphics in this game are intentionally cartoony, yet still very detailed. If you take the time to look around, you can see how much work was put into creating the environment and the characters.
Replayability: 9/10
The game has several different options to play including online, training, and many more. With all of the different characters, stages and combinations, it makes the game itself very entertaining and replayable.
Overall: 8/10
The game itself is fun, yet it feels like you're playing a lower quality version of Super Smash Bros. It's outstanding as far as a free game goes and can keep you occupied for several hours.

SINGLE PLAYER REVIEW ONLY
I have no interest in the multiplayer aspect. I don't have friends to play with (nor the time to play regularly). I tried it for a little bit, but didn't like it very much (I don't usually like multiplayer experiences like this), so my review is based off of the single player story mode only.
The story mode is great. There is a wide variety of entertaining missions and side quests are fun and worth doing. The characters, for the most part, are well made. The dialogue is often hilarious. The plot is often rediculous and over the top, much like a Tarantino movie. The motivations for the protagonists sometimes feel forced (especially with Franklin in some places), but it's a GTA game, so who cares?
Most people with negative reviews are only negative because of the multiplayer. This is one of those cases where it is a shame that the single player and multiplayer are forced to share ratings. The multiplayer may deserve a thumbs down (I wouldn't know), but the single player absolutely deserves a thumbs up. Ignore the multiplayer reviews and you won't find many negative single player reviews, with good reason. The single player experience is fully fleshed out and you don't need to do any multiplayer to feel like you're getting your money's worth.

I really can't compare this to any other game other than the recently released Gone Home, however where GH was more about discovery The Novelist allows you to shape the outcome.  The visuals and music are charming, and there is replay value as you ultimately have to decide who is going to be disappointed. The premise is that you go around the house observing the family, listening to their thoughts and examining their memories to find out what they desire. At the end of the day you will 'whisper' to the father as to what actions to take. Play cautiously and you will have the opportunity to compromise for another character but still the fact remains that you just can't please everyone.
That's the running theme. That ultimately you will have to disappoint someone. Depressing? Sure, but engaging as I found myself (a husband and father of two) able to relate to some of the plot elements if not literally than on a metaphorical level which drew me in.  You can burn through this game in 1.5 hours, but you'll be checking the box on what to do rather than getting invovled in the story or its characters.
There's room for improvement sure, but if I'm going to score this as a $15 game then I'll give it a 7/10 only because I was a bit thrown off at my first playthrough resutling in such a tragic ending I found it a bit extreme considering the life choices I made to get there.

I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this game. It's not the best art style I've ever seen but the impact your gameplay has on the characters’ lives really gets your conscious working overtime. Playing a ghost (I guess) living in a vacation house rented by a family for the summer, you spend your time learning about them. Discovering their desires and diving into their memories. Each chapter you have to make a decision about which character you want to help the most. Your decisions carry a lot of weight though because making one character happy will always make another character disappointed. I found this intense as I often wanted to make everyone happy but the game forces you to gather the information first, weigh up the information and consider the consequences carefully before actioning a decision. A great lesson to be teaching.

The Novelist is a wonderful game; it makes you think about the outcomes of every decision you make, and helps you see how your decisions affect others. It gives a variety of real-life issues and it's more often than not extremely difficult to prioritize.

I'm going to rate this positive because I cannot deny that I've had fun playing this for an accumulated online time of 37+ hours, however, there are some things you ought to consider before you invest time into it.
Starting with the negatives:
-Don't expect to ever complete this game in your lifetime. You'll grow old or die before you can get all the achievments.
-Grinding the multiplier can be very, very tedious.  You can buy time skips with real money or earn them by unlocking the girls' affection levels. Also, bare in mind, this game runs offline too.
-The music, as far as I know, is not very enjoyable. I've had it muted for 90% of the game, but it doesn't really take anything from the game itself, just a little loss on a nice bonus, especially when you're going to be spending a lot of time grinding.
Positives
+Cute art style (perhaps not for everyone, though)
+I really like a lot of characters, even though there is no real story to be told
+Dialogue can be funny
+Interface is really pretty and convenient
+Devs are cool, they update the game every now and then, adding more content and balancing the game a little.
+While grinding is tedious, finally maxing out a girl's affection level is pretty satisfying and you are rewarded with free gems that you would otherwise have to purchase with real money.
There are community guides I suggest you follow if you plan on playing this game. Check out the one that gives you advice on how to properly spend the gems you buy or earn in game, and the guide that informs you of the best and most efficient ways to progress.

I still haven't played the last part, but from what I've seen on Youtube and read on RPS, the last part is rather weak (especially I found it weird what they've done to the facial animation, since it was way better in previous parts). In any case, this game is the best in the series in my opinion. And not only because of impression back when it was released. I replayed this game after I finished the second part and it still felt awesome. Maybe because there was less needless grinding, the story was better polished, the world (or the maps, rather) was smaller but didn't feel like it's half-empty.
For me this game is very unique. The combat system is fun and challenging (if you're trying to perform well and make the best of cobmos) at the same time. Especially it's interesting that even though Batman never kills anybody, they managed to make fights feel cruel enough. The atmosphere is so deep that it reminds me of good old times. And the characters... Simply put, this game is a piece of art, a good example of how games should be made in many regards.
Don't get me wrong, I would also recommend the second part, but this game is a MUST in every gamer's collection.
One remark: the game is played better with a gamepad (I'd recommend XBOX 360 gamepad), although I played it on mouse+keyboard for the first time and it didn't feel wrong at any point.

This one gets sort of a mixed opinion from me, but I'll go ahead and throw together a (hopefully) comprehensive review.
Storyline:
Ok so obviously this is one of the main features of the game, and frankly, it's GREAT. ( SPOILER FROM HERE TO END SECTION )The story opens up with you returning Joker to Arkham Asylum and well he breaks free and takes over the asylum. OH SHNAP. From then on you, Batman, have to bring Joker back to custody while all the while dealing with assorted DC Supervillains ( e.g. Poison Ivy, Killer Croc, etc. )  , an array of henchman, huge MUTATED henchman, and walking dentures ( ya you heard right! ).
Setting:
Arkham Island = creepy. This may be a Teen action game, but the setting, in my opinion, is bordering on horror. Its just plain frightening at times. You go virtually everywere on the island, from the nastiest locales in the Medical Facility, to the lavish Halls of Arkham Mansion, this game has a gorgeous and disturbing setting.
Also, the game is 1/2 open world. At times certain areas are rendered inaccesible, but generally as the game progresses the map becomes more open world and roamable at will.
Gameplay:
Batman has an array have different abilities, and I can guarantee you you'll have fun with them. The fighting is extremely  simple yet enjoyable, and the sneaking battle tactics are incredibly satisfactory. Being able to sneak up and snuff out a henchman and then proceed to blow up his buds when they come to check it out, is great. Just plain great.
As you progress through the game you'll be given new batgear. So by the end of the game you'll have a complete arsenal of gadgets. Also included is a simple and useful tech tree where you can buy upgrades ( New battle moves, upgrades, etc ) with the XP you've gotten while fighting henchman.
Also included are some situations where you have to use "detective vision" to locate certain useful environmental situations, to track evidence to locate a person, and see enemies through walls. Yes you can do that. You'll find yourself in detective mode quite a bit; it makes the game less attractive ( kinda changes things to blue ), but its so useful during sneaky situations that its not much of a con.
At times some of the basic abilities get a little tiresome, blow up this wall, pull down this one, rip off this grate, but overall you will spend much more time fighting and having fun then mashing a button to have Batman pull down a wall.
Secrets:
Ok this is HUGE. Most games these days don't include many secrets, but Batman Arkham Asylum, DELIVERS. As you play through the storyline there are 240 different secrets, usually hidden and created by the Riddler, for you to find. You don't need to do ANY of this to complete the story, but some of the secrets will unlock special bonus content, naimly, Character bios for MANY Batman supervillains, patient interview tapes for the main antagonists, viewable 3D character and vehicle trophies, special "Spirit of Arkham" storyline, and extra challenge mode maps. Though it sounds incredibly imposing, their are maps revealing the locations of secrets that can be find, so find those and you're pretty much golden. If you have patience. I didn't *cough cough*.
Challenge Maps:
I sadly haven't really played any of these, but generally, they are special maps with special goals. E.g. kill as many baddies as possible without dying, or sneakily knock out all these guards in a set amount of time. Fun if you like bonus content. I do believe also, that the GOTY edition contains four extra challenges ( DLC otherwise I think ). Not positive about that, so please don't kill me if I'm wrong. :)
Parental Problems:
-Violence-
Gameplay wise you just knock out, by various means, bad guys, remember, Batman never kills anyone. That aside, the game is full of violence. For example, at one time you can hear the Riddler make a joke about a baby having its legs cut off, and the Joker reportedly has had his henchmen murder their siblings for no reason. Also included is Victor Zsasz, a psychotic serial killer who carves a notch in his own body every time he murders a woman. Also, some of the characters in the Batman universe, though not neccesarily elaborated on in-game, are extremely disturbing.
There is blood on the environment I believe, and some henchmen use knives, stun batons, and guns. Skulls are in certain places. Aside from huge nasty joints of meat, and references, to my knowledge there is no gore.
-Fear-
Biggest problem here. The game is freaky. There is barely any time in the game where you don't have a sense of fear. The setting, as I mentioned, is creepy in of in itself, and there a numerous parts of it that can chill you. Like for instance, when you observe a man strapped in an operating chair, dead, and with a face painted on him. There is also the repeated assault by the scarecrow on your sanity, which can be a bit "trying". To my remembrance theres only really one jump scene, but I won't give it away ;) ;).
-Sexual-
Harley Quinn and Poison Ivy are both very sensual; I wouldn't reccomend a younger, more immature player, playing this just for this reason. There are some brief suggestive references, e.g. a henchman saying that he'd let a certain lady doctor operate on him. Nothing tooooooo overt.
-Language-
Its mild. Don't remember really very much.
Main Cons:
Its a little creepy for my personal likes.
Some of the repetitive actions get tiresome.
Poison Ivy is way over the top ( and Harley Quinn somewhat ).
Harley Quinn is INCREDIBLY annoying and ugly.
Lack of ability to drive/fly any vehicles.
At times the story drags due to Joker always having another trick.
Overall:
Its a really good game if you like the genre. Lots of action, easy to pick up, and tonnnnns of secret content make it a real snag even at 20 dollars. With the campaign running at around 10 hours, its a tad long for my tastes, but maybe not for you. The Challenge maps also add a huge bit of replay content. It also includes Steam Trading card support and Achievements. I reccomend this game.

If you're like me and waited to get Batman: Arkham Asylum, I would recommend you get this game right now. The gameplay mechanics throughout do a great job of making you feel truly like Batman. You get great gadgets, you fight like a complete animal, you can fly around the more open environments like a Bat, and you are as sneaky as a ninja! The only slight issue is that the boss battles feel really lacking for the most part. There are only 3 types of bosses essentially, and they recycle the fights and tactics. But, other than that this game is phenomenal.
Last time I started playing, I listened to the audiobook as I played. The story works well with it. Good game. Glad it's not a subscription anymore.

Reviews said this game was what Survival fans have been waiting for, what the Post-Apocalyptic genre has been lacking. Well, I'm not really a Survival fan, especially when it comes to Survival Horror, but after all the latest Zombies games like Rage and Dead Island - I Am Alive is original, innovative and artistic.
Instead of killing Zombies with a somehow everlasting arsenal of weapons, from blades and clubs to grenade launchers and Molotov cocktails, this time the scenario is far more realistic. An event has occurred, a global catastrophe. The protagonist, after travelling for a full year, returns to his home to try and find his wife and daughter. His enemy? The dust in the air depleting his stamina and health, the physical obstacles (holes, collapsed structures, improvised barriers and barricades, and worst of all - most of the other survivors, stereotypically selfish, evil and deadly).
If you rush into combat in this game, you'll die. There's no "attack" option, only certain actions requiring careful planning, strategy and patience. A lot of the game is spent trying to figure out how to reach your next destination, by climbing ruins and jumping gaps. My favourite bit about the game is the attention to role-play details. Being able to threaten unarmed opponents to surrender, helping victims in need by sharing supplies for information, and how certain survivors just want to be left alone but won't attack - all create a fantastic mood and suspense of disbelief all the more easy for us deep role-play fans.
The graphics are smart, by that I mean that the use of dust in the air made it possible to have low quality details as far as the enviornment goes, but high realistic details when it comes to characters and the near surroundings. The music is also great! The actual game-play is not my cup of tea, but I've very glad to have played this game. The story, the mood, the characters, the world - all make for an extremely fun gaming experience. Survival fans? This is most definitely a must game for you lot. Not survival fans? You would still enjoy this, but I would wait a year or two so as to pay a cheaper price.

This is one of those games I enjoyed playing but I equally enjoy having completed it.
The post-apocalyptic environment is well built and you really get into the mood of the game. It's a depressing and gritty game and the designers have been spot on with creating the setting.
You spend a lot of time running around and climbing. The climbing mechanics works quite well; you climb in a manner similar to that of AC, but with the added feature that you have limited stamina that decreases while climbing. This means that you only have a limited time climbing before you have to find a secure spot to recover stamina if you don't want to risk dying mid-climb. It's a feature that I actually ended up loving as it added a (slightly) realistic pressure on an otherwise very generic climbing functionality.
The game is probably the closest you'll get to Last of Us on PC.
The graphics on the technical side is mediocre at best. It's clearly a console port and had a bit of extra work been put into the title the graphics could have been so much better.
The camera angles - my god. You are not able to zoom out when moving around and you're stuck to the neck all the time and I didn't feel any potential overview being lost. With that said; when climbing large buildings the camera zooms out (some times) to give you a better over of the surrounding routes.
The mouse controls are... wonky. Weird sensitivity and it feels sluggish.
The groups of enemies you meet are often same combinations as previous encounters, meaning that encounters, though challenging due to very limited resources, become routine.
Very linear.
Despite the concept of the game was/is great and I loved it, the technical issues and repetitions made it at the same time feel a bit... off. Had you asked me during a gaming session whether I would recommend it or not I'd probably say no. Looking back at it now I'd say yes. In the end it all depends on how accepting you are of the technical limitations of the game.

This game is nearly everything I wanted from a Post-apocalyptic game! It was still a whole lot different than I imagined, but in a good way. Unfortunately you can definitely tell that this game wanted to be more than it is, as it is missing some stuff which would have made this game even better; but I'll get back to that.
It's a good game that shows us that Zombies aren't the threat in a post-apocalyptic world (not that there are zombies in this game) but that people are threat. In this game you might hear someone crying for help, but it could just be a trap set in place so they can rob you of well you're life. So you have to beware of who you help and don't help. Also since items are very scarce, you have to ask yourself if you want to help this person giving him/her your last health pack or do you keep it for yourself. These are great questions but to my dismay the choices you make don't really impact the game.
If you for example help someone, they usually just say thank you and you get an extra retry.  In fact the only reason to help someone in this game would be to get the achievement for helping all victims in the game. If however helping someone would impact the story line; for example the person you saved ends up helping you later in the game or perhaps you helped the wrong person, and that person later then screws you over in the story. Well I think you can imagine that would have made the choices in the game so much more interesting. Now theyre just NPCS that stare at you after you help them...well umm great.
So yeah theres a lot of potential for this game to be the best post-apocalyptic game ever but it unfortunately just misses the mark. I also feel like the fighting options are quite limited but maybe im just bad at the game. Either way I still found it a really enjoyabel game to play, and I do think I will replay the game again at some point just to save all the victims in the game. However the missed potential in this game stares at me with every NPC you save (they literally just stare at you). It's just such a shame no one has tried to improve on this concept because that would make the best post-apocalyptic game ever!!!
In conclusion, you should get this game! but feel free to wait for a steam sale. As long as you play 6 euros or less, it is worth it as you will definitely get 6 hours of gameplay; even from a rushed playthrough!

This game is really, REALLY cool.  Batman is taking Joker to his usual cell in Arkham when all of a sudden, Joker springs a trap, causing Batman to be locked in the Asylum and all of the lunatics to escape!  Batman, of course, has to defeat each of the individual inmates (from Bane to Poison Ivy to Victor Zsasz and more), stop the Joker's major plot, and restore control of the Asylum, all while being taunted by the Riddler and discovering the back story of Amadeus Arkham, the founder of Arkham Asylum.
The gameplay itself is really cool...most of the action revolves around Batman's hand-to-hand combat style, which is both easy to learn (simple point and click movements deliver blows to inmates) and yet hard to master (inmates are usually armed, sometimes with pipes and bats, other times with guns that *will* kill you if you stick around too long).  You have an array of Batman's utilities to help strike back as well (classic batarangs, a batclaw, small explosives, grappler).
I found the plot to be fantastic, moving you along at a brisk pace while not hurrying you or forcing you.  The open nature of Arkham Island was really cool too.  I found myself playing this game for long stretches at a time, unable to take myself away from it; it really is a gripping game.  The graphics are pretty great too; the world is very detailed and the models of each of the individual characters are stunning.  The Riddler's challenges, while not impossible, are at least fairly difficult...unless you're paying attention to the world, you'll never find them all.  (But once you do, I advise you to listen to what happens as a result...it's really gratifying hearing that know-it-all silenced.)
My overall feeling is that you should definitely buy this game and play it.  You'll be on the edge of your seat.

This game is incredibly deep. To say that it is similar to any other game is an outright fabrication. The characters are all unique, and very relatable.
First of all, the family: It's not exactly dysfunctional, more...realistic. Hear me out: The family has very little contact with eachother. They care about eachother, they acknowledge eachother, and they do activities together, but rarely as an entire family. Like, if Linda plays with Timmy, Dan would be working. And that is a realistic thing; not all parents can give full attention to their children. They have to make sacrifices and choose between family and work sometimes, and choosing the latter is a realistic choice that they have to make, so they don't lose their job and ability to provide things to their family. And no family is totally perfect, and none of them ever make perfect choices. They can't all make eachother happy, yet they can have happy moments. That's why this family is brilliant, because they're a modern family (not that stupid show). The fact that they have emotions and outright hide them sometimes, and also show them in a subtle fashion, makes them more realistic and relatable.
The gameplay: This game does surprisingly fantastic for a point-and-click game. I'm not saying that point-and-click games are crappy, I'm just saying that not every one is able to put you in such a great sense of control that this one can. When you make the descisions, you either feel curious about your descision, or have a heavy weight of regret in your chest that you made the wrong descision, but it was somehow for the best. You never once feel confident in your descision, because you know that you have let someone down. The reason that I'm referring to it as YOUR descision, not as Dan, Linda, or Tommy's descision, is because YOU made that descision. You're the theory, and they're the action. In other words, It's never a descision until you perform it. Before that, It's just a thought. So they're the performance (action) and you're the thought (theory).
The overall story: What can be a dull story can tun inot one of the most engrossing games in the world. 'Nuff said.

Dear Esther is still the worst project I’ve ever had to endure. As an experience, I am willing to offer it some credit due to its well executed narrative, but all you do is walk around a fictitious island for no longer than an hour before the credits roll. That is not a game; that is a digital story, and those arguing the opposite possess a thwarted view of the medium that is stripping gamers like me off their money.
Why would I bring up Dear Esther in this review? Because just like it, The Novelist is a digital experience that shoe horns gaming elements in order to reach the wider audience on Steam. Art nuts will raise their fists at me preaching the advancement of the gaming culture, while I berate them for supporting such flagrant experiments with little to no gaming elements.
The Novelist is a simple project that puts you in control of a specter, floating around a house to uncover the stories of all its three occupants: A father, mother, and their son. Each of them is looking to fulfill a need, and it is up to you at the end of each chapter to choose who actually pulls it off. Should you choose an outcome that has the father focus on his novel, his wife will get lonely, and his son will get depressed because he is not spending time with him. There are compromises that you may offer characters you did not support, a pacifier to pamper their low self esteems and lack of will, by choosing to cater to them after your desired intention is completed. If you chose to support the father’s novel, for example, you will get the chance to support one of the other members: Instead of spending the day with your son, you sit with him and read, or instead of fully assisting your wife in promoting her art gallery, you help her with copy at the end of the day. These are all do-it-yourself story elements, and do not compromise a game.
Had The Novelist been on offer for a couple of dollars I would not be ranting, but when an experiment like this is sold for $15, with no mention anywhere that it is a non-game, I lose my♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you like digital experiences the likes of Dear Esther and Gone Home, then you may enjoy The Novelist for what it offers; otherwise, stay clear away and save your money for actual, deserving indie games.

I wish there were a third option between recommending and not recommending. I don't recommend Gnomoria
The pros: This is a stable game with great core mechanics. It's Dwarf Fortress with a reasonable interface, solid graphics and many of the unnecessary complications smoothed out. That's a great start.
Unfortunately, there are also a lot of cons.
As others have pointed out, there just isn't enough content. Gnomoria gets boring... fast. Most of your game is spent underground in the mines, but aside from some topography and the occasional monster there's just nothing down there. It's level after level of emptiness that you excavate because you need minerals, not because there's anything particularly interesting or dangerous that's worth finding.
The monsters represent a real threat in the early game, but once you've built up your base and gotten some good equipment they're kind of pushovers. And they're very repetitive. There are 9 types of monsters in the whole game, and even among them the only interesting one are zombies (which can turn your gnomes into zombies on death). The rest only differ in toughness.
The last update was back in February and the one before that in November.  More worryingly, though, is that the developer doesn't seem aware of what the game really needs. In the past year he's added the following: prosthetic limbs for gnomes, ceramic tiles, craftable automatons and UI/stockpile updates.
That's it.
For a game that badly needs mid- and late-game content, the developer has been more or less nibbling around the edges.
Gnomoria is a game that could be great. I keep coming back hoping I'll have more fun the nth time around. Back when it looked like it was on track this was a solid purchase. Today... follow it and look again once it's out of early access.
(I also just noticed how many hours Steam says I've played this game. That's for two reasons: the amount of time it's spent paused and forgotten, and the two weeks I once just let it run in the background to see if anything would actually happen to my gnomes. No.)

I'm really kind of tired of grim, gritty Batman. I'm not saying we need Adam West Batman or anything, but while playing through this game I also watched a bunch of the DC direct-to-video animated movies (which are mostly pretty great), and the tone of them feels much more like a superhero comic to me. Between this and the movies, I think I've had enough of the more realistic style, even though it was fun at first.
Anyway, the game itself: when it's good it's great, but it's not consistently good, unfortunately. The interactions with the main villains are handled very well, with good writing and voice acting and generally unique mechanics for their boss fights or whatever it is you have to do to deal with them. They really are the stars of the show and what make it feel the most like a Batman game. It's too bad that a lot of the time spent getting from one of them to the next is trudging through linear corridors or sewers until you get to yet another herd of generic goons who you can just button mash your way through.
It all starts to feel a bit samey after a while, except for the setpiece events with the villains that break it up. I didn't really feel like Batman or a superhero except during those moments. Honestly, aside from those moments I felt like I should've been playing DCUO instead, which except for not being as pretty, does a better job of making you feel like you're playing a superhero game and like the character you're controlling is a superhero, at least in my opinion. I personally prefer its design/presenation that feels more like the comics (at least the ones I'm familiar with), but that's a matter of taste, I guess.
I guess I'm left with a feeling of, "Eh, it was ok," after finishing it. I liked it enough while playing it to finish it, but I did have to convince myself to pick it up again a couple times, and I'm not super excited to start the sequel any time soon.
Addendum: It occurs to me that while describing my experiences playing the two games to people I know, I've used the word "Batman" more times in reference to how Just Cause 2 feels than how Arkham Asylum does. Ignoring the heavy use of guns in JC2, I've felt more like Batman dropping in unexpectedly on guards with the grappling hook or parachute as Rico than as Batman in his own game, I think largely because of the difference in mobility. Batman is relatively heavy and slow, while Rico is quicker and has a lot more freedom of movement. Outside of the recent movie trilogy, I don't think of Batman as a clunky guy who can't even jump. I've described playing Rico in JC2 as feeling like "Latino Batman swooping in from the heavens to cast judgment on his enemies" (plus a healthy dose of guns), but Batman in AA just feels like some guy punching some other guys in the face a lot of the time.

Even if you've started playing any of the previous games, give this a go! This is a great game, and holds story dear to the series. If you enjoy any batman game, give it a go. Even if you don't - go for it!

Before buying this game, I read the reviews like any normal person would. I found alot of people saying they hated the game. I did find quite a few positive reviews though and so I decided to go for it anyways. ( I think I only paid a few bucks for it during some sale )
+ What I like:
-Climbing/Stamina System
I love the climbing aspects of this game. I have to sit and carefully plan out my ascent or descent based on how much stamina I have at my disposal. Instead of blindly climbing like in Assasain's Creed, I have to think before I climb. This is the most realistic climbing I have ever seen in a game (in terms of stamina), and I love it so much.
-Fighting
The fact that you can intimidate the enemy without any bullets and shove them down a hole is an A+ in my book! Seriously though, this game seems to have a similar theme, "Think before you act". I have found myself analyzing the enemy and finding who to kill first and how to do it. The intimidation that you can produce with an unloaded gun is spectacular and I find myself using it often.
-Scenery
This game really sells the post-apocalyptic setting and between the dastardly ambushes and the unsettling music I find myslef on the edge of my seat.
+ What I dislike
Honestly there really is not that much I truely dislike about this game. The limited retry is a bit troubling, but it forces me to take my time and analyze every situation. The fighting system is a little tough to get at first but once you get the hang of it, its not too bad.
+ My Thoughts
I do indeed recommend this game. I would probably not have bought it if it had not been on sale, and I don't recommend paying $15 for it. If this game does end up going on sale then I recommend getting it, as you will most likely enjoy it as I have.
The trick to this game is to have patience and not rush into things. If you try to play this game like an FPS game, you will not enjoy it. This game is all about conserving the small pile of resources you have while trying to stay alive. It's a refreashing change from the FPS games I usually play.
Thanks for reading my review,

Solid, in a word, describes this game. Everything about it is functional. It works. It is not a truly stellar experience, but save one or two misteps, everything more or less works.
Going from a gameplay perspective, Batman Arkham Asylum is a study in simplicity. The game is built on simple but functional mechanics. A simple but functional stealth system. A simple but functional beat-em up system. What the game does though is that it uses these practical forms and builds on them over time. Mooks get new gear, each new piece representing a new tactical challenge, forcing you to use what you have in new ways. Stealth segements have less "easy" attack routes, more enemies, enemies who overwatch. The game forces you to be active and creative with what, at first, seemed like simple one trick systems, delivering a satisfying experience save for one or two major blunders.
Storywise the game is... o.k.. It's a half decent Batman comic. Not as good as some of the best Batman stories, but better than, oh, 90% of the schlock that passes for Batman stories. It ranks up there with a decent episode of the cartoons, which is unspring given that Dini wrote both and the two iconic voice actors have return to repraise their roles. That said there is no real attempt to expand or explore these characters. Joker has an evil plan, Batman figures it out, foils it, there is a confrontation, and then Batman defeats the Joker in a fist fight. Once again we have something servicable but not stellar, but unlike the gameplay the story does not build to anything much higher than where it began. There are some fascinating moments of visual storytelling, specifically the lead ins to the Scarecrow stages, but for those who want a more interesting take on the Dark Knight, it's best to stick to the Nolan movies.
All in all Arkham Asylum is a good game that, as the action builds, only gets better and better. While hampered by an only passable story and a few blunders gameplay wise (and you will know them when you see them), it is a fun ride. If you get ahold of it you have no reason not to play it.

Overview: Arkham Asylum is an action oriented beat 'em up with some minor stealth aspects.  The game takes place, you guessed it, at Arkhan Asylum and involves confrontations with some notable characters.  As Batman, it is your mission to restore order to the island and discover a sinister plot by the main villain.
Pros: The combat in this game is amazing.  Every hit on an enemy looks and feels very satisfying.  Batman can literally jump across the screen to beat any enemy in his path.  The story is well written and takes Batman through the various areas of the game.  Along the way, Batman will encounter many notable villains in the series, each with their own unique encounters.  There is plenty of lore to collect and read through if you want to know more about each character.  In addition to the main game are challenges that provide tons of re-playabilty and something for players seeking a higher difficulty.  The voice acting is also very well done.  Mark Hamill as the Joker does an amazing job.
Cons: Even though the combat is amazing, it is very unforgiving.  If you are not 100% perfect with you movement and choice of actions, your combo will be dropped.  One thing I disagree with is that to play the challenges, you have to play through the game and complete Riddler challenges to unlock them.  Why? Let the player play the game how they want.
Conclusion: Arkham Asylum has some amazing combat and does everything else really well.  You really will feel like Batman as you beat the crap out of every henchman.  It is best experienced with a controller, although it is possible to play with a keyboard and mouse.  If you like the Batman series you will love this game.
Score: 9.8 / 10

I loved DLC Quest, it was a quick and very easy game to play, and I enjoyed the comedic events that go along with it. I give this game 8/10.

This is a great game for anyone looking to enjoy a casual, laid back experience.  If you like story and decision-based games, you'll love The Novelist.  It focuses on a family and the choices they make over the course of a summer that will eventually shape their collective futures.  An interesting topic and fairly well executed.  Perhaps a bit overpriced, it took me only about 3 hours to finish one playthrough.  However, apparently the game offers a lot of replayability, as many elements are randomized and the choices you make can change as well.

I sadly was not able to enjoy this game at all, and this is coming from someone who absolutely loves these narrative non-games, such as Dear Esther, Gone Home or even more abstract ones such as Proteus.
But this... half way in, it almost felt like a chore to me. I had to force myself to finish it, and got very little out of it.
The game mechanics felt very repetitive and meaningless. Every chapter, you had to find a set of clues which all happened to be more of less in the same place, you had to look at three memories, then get the final clue and choose one of the 3 dilemmas to solve (most of which were very cliché). You didn't really get to find much insight in the characters or get attached to any. It really felt more like a game than a narrative story.
And even the main mechanic, light jumping, which you use throughout the entire game, felt very poorly constructed. Some lights were very poorly positioned, and then they started introducing annoying and useless false difficulty by turning some off...
In general, this game definitely didn't deliver in the premise, at least not the one I was expecting, of getting an emotion story and insight in a families life. It was a fun little game I guess, but most definitely not worth that price point.

The most effective look into family matters I've seen in a videogame so far. Alongside Papers Please, the best use of moral decisions and a branching narrative I have participated in. These both games allow you to use real world logic rather than in most videogames where you're trying to game the system to get the best rewards. Even though I'm not married or have a family yet, or am an author, I could still relate to all the pull-and-push of a family life and how compromises can be made but not all parties will be satisfied. How tough it is to maintain a work/life balance. I feel this game will be even more relevant further down the line in my life.
I have to applaud how solid the gameplay loop was (clues->memories->compromise), considering it could've been a much simpler tourist-y game like Gone Home. It definitely is still in familiar territory with the notes, diary entries, light stealth, and it's nice to see established gameplay mechanics can still be used for effective storytelling rather than resorting to cutscenes or QTEs. Also, you can still tell an emotional story without a grand tragedy, which I believe is the shorter path to create drama. Or maybe I have to replay to find out!
One criticism is for the stealth stuff, it never really ramped up in challenge when earlier the game mentions that lights will start being made unavailable to possess. I didn't really use the flicker distractions that much. But that didn't take away from the game's message, just solidified that it was going for a more laidback, introspective atmosphere. Either way, don't miss out on this game.

Very mature and realistic story-driven game. It is very similar to Dear Esther and others in that genre. It is not going to appeal to everyone. The game focuses on choice and consequences of the decisions you take in the game. The choices will resonate throughout the entire game, affecting the dynamics of the family.
Since you play as a ghostly entity in the house, there are 2 game modes. One which involves stealth, meaning you can not let any of the family members see you. The other focusing on story, which lets you freely wander around the house with no one being able to spot you.
The game is relatively short. However if you enjoy games similar to The Novelist then you will highly enjoy this game. You will be torn between trying to appease everyone in the family, sometimes you will be upset that even with compromises; there is someone who is going to be upset with the choices you make.

Dan needs to finish that book! Then again, Tommy has been lonely lately... On the other hand, Linda's been a bit depressed ever since the funeral. This is what runs through my mind every time I make a decision. The Novelist is a game about a family called the Kaplans, and things aren't going to well for them. Dan is a small, and failing, author. Linda's a painter, and Tommy is a child who struggles in school. The Kaplans go up to their house on the coast for the summer. This is a house that you haunt, for you are a ghost. You can influence their thoughts to help make the right decisions. Read their minds, influence their enviroment, and enter their memories. I totally reccomend the game.

This game started it all. Probably the first great Batman game of its time, combining a very intense freeflow combat system and a stealth mode that actually works well. It's a very interesting gameplay hybrid that I guarentee you will never witness in any other games (other than City and Origins, obviously). The story is very fun, especially if you know the characters well, and its simply a fun game that you can keep playing without even getting sick of it. Overall, the start of a great series that is worth checking out for anyone.

Batman Arkham Asylum, made by Rocksteady Studios and Squarenix, is a third person action-adventure game that allows you to play as Batman as he is thwarting the evil plans of Joker. Batman, like the comics, only comes equipped with his stealth, gadgets and fists. The combat system is mostly hand to hand but if an enemy ends up getting a weapon, for example a gun, the player must take out that enemy as fast as possible. The hand to hand combat system is fairly simple which involves combos, blocking and dodging. When you hit enemies you rack up a hit multiplier that allows you to do more and more complicated attacks and combos like hitting the direction keys and punching enemies across the room.

Like a lot of action adventure games, Batman has bosses that in order to beat them you must figure out the patterns of attack and what their weaknesses are without any help. This is nice to see that Batman doesn’t hand hold you throughout the entire game instructing you how to play. Even the mini bosses or larger enemies have specific weaknesses that you have to exploit in order to kill them.  On top of the very fluid combat system the game has, the upgrade system is simple enough but allows for the feel of progression in the game.  These upgrades include armor, special combos and even upgrades for some of his gadgets. Speaking of gadgets, batman has 5 primary gadgets and 3 additional variations of the batarang.  Those gadgets include the batarang, a sort of exploding gel compound to destroy walls, the batclaw to pull items from ledges down, cryptographic sequencer which allows batman to hack security fields and the line launcher that allows him to get across large ravines.

In Arkham Asylum, Batman is transporting the Joker to Arkham Asylum and when Batman is suspicious of how easily the Joker let him get captured he decides to follow him in. Eventually he finds out his hunch is right and Harley Quinn takes control of the security systems and the Joker escapes. It was all an elaborate plan to kill Batman after taking control of the Asylum. Batman finds out later that the reason that the Joker wanted to come back to the asylum was to get a chemical compound called Titan and turn all of his men into super soldiers and to destroy Gotham. All during the game Batman runs into familiar enemies including Bane, Poison Ivy, Zasaz, Killer Croc, The Riddler and even Scarecrow. Extremely nostalgic for anyone that loved to watch the TV cartoon and read the comics.

The graphics are very impressive even for a game that was made in 2009 and in a lot of ways was limited by the consoles at the time. The textures are all smooth and the details in the characters are very impressive. Along with that they kept to the design of Arkham Asylum from the comics and the cartoon pretty well and a lot of the characters also have the likeness to that of the comics. For all intensive purposes this game models after the comics and cartoon more than the more recent Nolan films.
The music is kind of non-existent but that is expected of a game about the dark knight however the voice acting is top class. The three main characters, Batman, Joker and Harley Quinn, are all voiced by the original voice actors from the tv show; Kevin Conroy as Batman, Mark Hamill as the Joker and Arleen Sorkin as Quinn. Along with that one of my favorite voice actors Steve Blum plays as Killer Croc and you can hardly tell that it is Steve voicing the character.

Overall this game is everything a fan of the Batman universe could ever want. You get to sneak around, take down bad guys, use your gadgets and even see many appearances from fan favorite villans.

This game is both a refreshing new approach to adventure gaming and a fantastic exploration of artistic expression. The story tells the tale of the Kaplan family - Dan (the novelist), his wife Linda (the artist) and their son Tommy. Interestingly enough, the player controls none of these characters but instead controls a disembodied entity (essentially a ghost for lack of a better word) whose exact origin or purpose is left intentionally ambiguous. You control said entity in the first person, exploring the Kaplan's new vacation home while simultaneously trying to avoid detection (thus spooking a given a family member). To help in this endeavor, you can possess lights and even make them flicker to attract the attention of the Kaplans, adding a stealth aspect to the game; it does, however, offer a 'story' mode where you are immune to detection as well.
It quickly becomes apparent, upon the Kaplans arrival in threir new summer home, that things are not going well for this family. Thus, for reasons unknown, it becomes your job to dig up the proper clues to help resolve various conflicts between family members. This is done through exploration, a form of mind-reading, and the ability to enter the memories of individual characters for further discovery. Stay out of sight, find all the clues, learn the secrets, and then use this knowledge to influence the situation by way of subliminal suggestion (you literally whisper suggestions into Dan's ear while he sleeps)!
All in all this is a really unique and interesting game which offers plenty of fun, as well as a really engaging story-driven narrative. Especially for that low, low indie price! If you enjoy adventure games, especially the more artistically expressive types, then definitely do yourself a favor and give it a go - if not, who knows, you may still end up enjoying it anyway!

"Survival Horror" is what these kinds of games are called, and horror is in that title.  Is it the scariest game you'll every play?!?! No, but it has it's moments and damn those moments are good.
Something I do want to mention is that this game can be disturbing.  Despite it's childish and moronic message, the "YOUR MOM HATES DEAD SPACE 2" ad campaign (despite how I try to forget it) does have a point.  If you're squimish or easily disturbed this title isn't for you.  It's been a few years since I've last played the game, and I was taken aback at how disturbing some sections were.

The struggle between augmentation and humanity reaches its peak in Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, the latest in a series of prequels to the original Deus Ex. Like its predecessors, this game is steeped in conspiracies and deep-state groups such as the Illuminati, who seek to control the entire world by using devious systems of media manipulation and corporate slavery. The game takes place after the Panchaea augmentation incident, in which augmented people around the world were driven insane by a software broadcast by Hugh Darrow. Many people are now terrified of augs and systems of discrimination and exile have been enacted with the goal of keeping natural people safe and augmented people excluded.
Though a direct sequel to Human Revolution, Mankind Divided differs greatly in its treatment of the franchise. Gone are the unnecessary boss fights, where you could only win by lethal means, and along with those the much hated pushbutton-style ending. Your decisions mid game definitely have more of an impact on the end-game this time around, giving you explicit options for at key points during the finale.
The newly added crafting and enhanced augmentation systems give Adam an incredible level of flexibility for resolving situations. Want to disable a camera quietly but can’t find the security station? Just use the remote hacking augment. Need to hack a door panel or computer while staying hidden? Craft a multitool and unlock it from out of sight. Forklift out of order? Just jam a biocell into its power outlet and up you go. You even have multiple types of non-lethal augment weapons (PEPS/TESLA) and the typhoon system can be tuned to disperse knockout gas instead of lethal shrapnel. If you prefer to run and gun there are plenty of lethal augments such as launch-able arm blades, slowing time, and a defensive system that makes you practically invulnerable at the cost of large amounts of energy. Basically, you will be spoilt for choice regardless of your play style.
Speaking of choices, the first (and only) hub-level in this game takes place in Prague, and it is absolutely massive compared to previous game hubs. You can begin exploring the entire area whenever you want or simply wait for a relevant quest to pop up and give you an excuse to visit. The other areas of the game are shorter in comparison but still will take you a few hours to clear at the very least. Be on the lookout for ventilation ducts as you wander around, because just like in Human Revolution this game is loaded with them, and some will take you to very interesting places.
I really enjoyed Mankind Divided and would rate it as the second best game in the series for story and the best for gameplay. While it is shorter than Human Revolution (mostly because the player has too many solutions making most situations very easy to resolve) I found the game to be more fun, especially for a stealth-pacifist playthrough. This game is definitely a must have if you are into cyberpunk settings and/or a fan of the Deus Ex series.

Sadly outside of The Fall, this is the weakest Deus Ex game when it comes to plot and intrigue, and the only reason The Fall is worse is because while Mankind Divided never finished it’s story, The Fall didnt even get past chapter 1. However, at the same time for sheer gameplay and ability to play how you want to, this is arguably one of the best I have played in a long time, rivalling even the original game that started the franchise.
And this really does leave me of two minds on how to score this game. Almost any other game I would put the gameplay first, but Deus Ex has always been deeply entrenched in it’s story and the conspiracy theories entwined through it, making it a much tougher call here.
If you are a fan of the franchise, you should probably pick up and play this game, because for all it’s flaws, it’s still a very good experience within the universe, and quite possibly the last we will ever get. Just don’t get to excited about the plot because it will disappoint you in every way it can. If you get into a game to play with it like a sandbox, you will probably enjoy this game a lot more then most, because even though the game doesn't use vehicles (the world locations are actually to small), it lets you loose to do what you want, and you will have a good time going about it. But if story matters to you, stay the **** away from this title. This game is going nowhere good on that front.

This game is a Dwarf Fortress clone but without the feeling you're reading the matrix. That being said it is much less complex than DF, but the learning curve is still massive. Detailed event logs and names give the game some nice immersion; I was crushed when one of my soldiers died to a lucky blow from an ogre.
Non-peaceful games can easily last 60+ hours, all of which feeling like you're rushing agaisnt the clock to arm your gnomes before the next raid. It took me (and from what I hear most people) at least a couple 5-hour games that end with a massacre to grasp the mechanics and strategies necessary to survive. The various hostiles you encounter scale nicely to your progress, making sure you never really feel like you can relax.
Updates are pretty regular (Monthly until recently, now it's unscheduled big updates). Modding community is pretty active and mod support is coming.
Cons:
- The AI is extremely frustrating until you understand how to priotize things. There is no "do this now" button.
- I've read that games that go on for 8+ years (100+ hours) can become unplayable because of low FPS.

What started out as a great game which offers hundreds of hours of gameplay has started to turn into a stagnate title with a lot of work left. The potential is all there, but development is far too slow now for me to recommend.

More than ten years after its initial release, LOTRO still keeps going with no end in sight - at least not in the near future. If you're a fan of Middle-Earth, there's still a lot to enjoy about this game, especially the landscapes and stories it presents. You should be aware of two things though:
1. You won't be able to play with a Free2Play account for long, as the restrictions are massive. But even if you're paying for VIP status, which gives you access to everything except expansion packs, it often becomes tempting to buy stuff in the store. LOTRO has amassed a lot of tedious grinding for skill points and other buffs, although it has been there since the game's original release - in one way or another. It wasn't fun ten years ago, and it still isn't now - but you can skip most of it by paying real money.
2. The game's engine had reached its limit years ago. As a result it suffers from mediocre to horrible performance in many areas from Rohan onwards, constant lag spikes and sometimes rubberbanding.. it's problematic, to say the least, and can really ruin the fun at times. These problems have absolutely nothing to do with players' hardware, and the thing is, it has been like this for more than five years now and is probably impossible to fix. It's a shame, really.
The thing that makes me still come back now and then, after all these years, are the developers. They don't always make the right decisions, never did, but to me it's clear that they still have passion. They worked hard to bring their vision of Middle-Earth alive, and with players complaining that Mordor is actually TOO dark and grim for their taste... I believe they're still on the right track.
Step into Middle Earth and fallow the Ring Bear as he destroys One Ring. Play along in the epic, meet the Fellowship of the Rings, and defeat the forces of Sauran The Dark. Welcome to Middle Earth.

TL:DR - It's fun, although once you win several times in a row, you're pitted against people who are so much better than you.
This game, without a doubt, is really fun. If you have friends, it's even better. The heroes are hard to earn, making it more satisfying as you get the next hero once you get the coin. My biggest annoyance of the game is the Balance. As of right now, I went on free-for-all, with the label "Recommended!" So, as someone who's level 15 and casually play the game, gravitate towards that gamemode. But either you win too many times or if you are level 15, you get faced against level 50's and 70's. It's not fun at that point, because they know the rotations down and will wreck you and your family in the game. My only complaint is that they should at least put a skill bracket, so if you do good, you get put with the people in your ranking. No "I'm level 15 and facing against level 50's", just if you have "5 SP, so everyone in the lobby has around 5 SP, so it's balanced. At first, it'd be a mess, but once everyone settles in, it'll be more fun and less getting destroyed because you are facing against higher leveled and experienced people.
My Second issue with the game is the "Bow User Meta," as my friends and I call it, because the bow is an extremely powerful weapon, and is arguably the best weapon. Now is it balancable? Possibly, just the side right-click is WAYY too good. My friend, who played the game for a matter of 2 seconds, got to the top of the scoreboard just from using Ember. I got 20 points against 2 of my friends and a bot with Diana. I won almost all my matches as Koji. If there's a bow user, we are actually kind of annoyed and scared, and kind of give up at that point, because it's so difficult to fight back when they can just range attack you all day and night.
Aside from those HUGE issues i have with the game, the only other one is that the cosmetics are not earnable with ingame currency, but that's just nit-picky, not really an issue. But the unlock system is sufficient and easy to navigate.
Is it worth a try? Definitely. If you decide to keep it, try the PVP as early in your level as possible. Try to get the way other people fight and see how you can adjust accordingly. I found out a little too late, right as the people turned 50. I wouldn't worry about facing 50's until either you win several games in a row or get to level 15. If you find a hero in that time and "Main" them, you will do fine. By the time i was at level 15, i had 7200 coins, just enough for the newest hero, so if you want to save for the latest hero, it takes about that amount of playing.
*EDIT: Now level 30, and it's even worse than before. Now in causal, all I'm faced against are people who seem to play the game all day and all night. I really enjoy the game, I truely do, but now it seems that I cannot land a single hit on the enemy. I know, "Do better" or "Stop sucking, then," but instead of facing off against simple bots, why do I have to face against people who bought stuff for the game, which more than likely means they bought all legends, and I'm stuck trying to earn the few I have, then get pitted against people who are leagues above me. It just turns into annoying losses over and over and starts to deteriorate my view of the game.

really stands out as one of the best superhero video games out there (another one being its sequel, Arkham City, but more about that in another review). The gameplay is rock-solid in a Metroidvania-esque fashion, the voice-over work is fantastic with many classic voices returning (like Mark Hamill as the Joker and Kevin Conroy as the Dark Knight himself), and the story is well-written and satisfying for the most part.
The whole game takes place on Arkham Island, where the Joker has gained control over the titular insane asylum. The location is really atmospheric and is a very believable setting for a Batman story, in a little contrast to the setting in Arkham City which had a little more creative freedom applied to it (again, more on that in the future).
The main story is a bit on the short side, but combined with the Riddler challenges and the combat/predator challenges, it will keep you busy for a good 20-25 hours for 100% completion. Not too shabby.
It isn't possible to review Arkham Asylum and not mention the simple, yet satisfying freeflow -combat system. It takes little skill to beat up the bad guys, but racking up massive combos takes some work and is very enjoyable. What's even more pleasing than beating them up directly is the stealth, or "predator" sections, where you use your environment to your advantage and take out your enemies without being seen.
You might enjoy this game even if you don't like Batman. Under the Batman -shell is a rock-solid game that is without question worth picking up. Who knows? Maybe you'll start to like the series after playing this?
